In addition to the American System of Manufacture, writing the history of modern design in the United States today also demands a consideration of race.
The standard of living enjoyed by the wealthy and increasingly available to the middle class in the nineteenth century through the acquisition of designed goods was generally less available, if not legally denied, to the nations Black and Indigenous populations, especially in the American South.
Institutional slavery and deeply embedded racial prejudice severely limited the circulation of such goods to the enslaved, to the poor, and to the marginalized to whom freedom of movement and opportunity for economic advancement were denied.
Yet even under the conditions of slavery, Black Americans produced compelling objects.
David Drake, an enslaved man in South Carolina, signed his large hand-thrown glazed pots with the name Dave, and also inscribed bits of text and sometimes poetry on the surface of these largely utilitarian wares, even though literacy was often forbidden in enslaved people.
The history of design under such conditions has yet to be written, and is but one instance of white privilege that has made little room for Black experience.
In the wake of Emancipation, the path toward equality was slow, and the Jim Crow laws reinforced segregation and deepened stereotypes and caricatures that persist to this day.
As noted in Chapter 7 (see here), the mass-circulation merchandise catalogs featuring an array of products published by the Sears Roebuck and Montgomery Ward companies in the later nineteenth century were essentially colorblind: unlike retail stores that refused to serve Black shoppers, catalogs allowed Black consumers access to design, contributing to the expanded market for designed goods.
Craftsmen and labor organizations, especially in Britain, often viewed mechanization as a threat to jobs and to their status and independence as artisans.
They lobbied for restricted use of machines by manufacturers, and such restrictions eventually allowed American goods to compete for the British market.
By the second half of the nineteenth century, design, eclectic historicism, and printed advertising had become regular features of manufacturing in the United States, as techniques of mechanized mass production were adapted to supply variety and choice in stimulating consumer demand for goods and furnishings.
With improved transportation, patents to protect invention, and reduced tariffs, products such as soap, biscuits, condiments, and breakfast cereal (for example Quaker Oats) became national brands with recognizable logos and packaging.
Changing styles were often viewed as a barometer of improvement and ingenuity while at the same time product standardization communicated reliability and consistency  just as new frontier settlements, reaping machines, and railways were transforming nature by making it more productive and civilized, manufacturers were transforming raw materials into finished consumer goods, augmenting their usefulness, availability, and consumer appeal. # Chapter 4 # Design, Society, and Standards

## Early
Design Reform Cities were the focus of an expanding industrial and commercial economy throughout the nineteenth century.
The scope of industrial development was increasingly global, culminating at mid-century with the first of numerous Worlds Fairs (Londons 1851 official name was the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, see here) that brought together the goods, raw materials, and markets of Europe, North America, Asia, Africa, and South America, promoting a Eurocentric world view identifying Western technology with material and cultural progress.
The growth of urban populations throughout the nations of Europe presented challenges to governments in terms of housing, sanitation, unemployment, safety, and conflicts between classes and levels of economic opportunity.
The years 1830 and 1848 saw outbreaks of social unrest in Europe with working-class rebellion and the threat of socialist revolution leading to armed conflict and its suppression through stronger central authority.
A portion of the emerging class of industrialists, merchants, and professionals during the first half of the nineteenth century took an interest in the living and labor conditions of factory workers and artisans whose numbers swelled in the cities of Europe and whose labor was essential to owners profits.
Along with industrial wealth came a desire, even a sense of moral obligation, to address economic inequality and the ills of rapid urbanization, even if the motivation toward reform was often tied to maintaining a hierarchical social order within a more commercial, complex, and diverse society.
Reform efforts included an active role for the arts in promoting progressive social values (for instance, the establishment of government-sponsored museums of art such as the National Gallery, London, in 1824), as well as a focus upon the role of design in manufacturing as a means of increasing the appeal, enjoyment, and civilizing value of useful goods.
While some reformers presented moral arguments supporting the Gothic style as the model of beauty and nostalgia for a shared faith and unified, harmonious society, others took more modest initiatives to cultivate a broader shared taste in the public at large through education and the founding of collections whose displays would develop discriminating judgment.
Design reform aimed to establish standards for taste in the public interest that combined aesthetics, politics, and ethics, part of a broad response to the changing social dynamics that accompanied industrial and commercial expansion toward the middle of the nineteenth century.
Self-interest merged with groupinterest, as reformers argued that manufactures were a source of wealth, prestige, and economic and social progress in a competitive, international free-market economy.
While reformers often employed polemical rhetoric for effect, their efforts seldom achieved the results they intended, took account of the increasingly heterogeneous market for manufactured products, or fully understood the commercial forces (generally criticized as the effects of fashion) that operated across the broad spectrum of desire for such goods.
For this reason, until the 1860s design reform was mostly limited to the luxury market and to those manufacturers that catered to that clientele, whether private or public.
From the 1860s until the end of the nineteenth century, design reform initiatives expanded to include consumer guides, published as books or as installments in periodicals, often directed toward women, who bore the responsibility for creating a proper home and family environment.
Both before and after 1860, reform efforts further invested the applied arts with cultural meanings, attributing to them the ability to shape values and behavior, establishing a basis for shared standards and a canon of modern design that continues to influence our understanding of its history today.

## Industry
and Its Discontents Not all observers welcomed the expansion of production and the emergence of a consumer society with the same enthusiasm as economist Adam Smith.
In the early nineteenth century, Britain experienced a staggering growth of industrial manufacturing, particularly in the production of textiles in steam-powered mills, in cast iron, and in the construction of railroad engines, rolling stock, and track, accompanied by an increasing pressure to mine coal as a source of fuel.
The large-scale production of commodities accelerated the dynamic relationship between production and consumption created by rationalized labor, the introduction of mechanization, and marketing to an elastic market for manufactured goods.
Free trade, competition, and overproduction combined to make large-scale manufacturing a volatile and uncertain business, often with decidedly negative consequences for workers.
Even as emerging urban industrial areas in Britain such as Manchester, Birmingham, and Liverpool gained a legislative voice in Parliament, and as the industrialists who were chosen to represent their interests lobbied for free trade and the further expansion of markets for their products, there was ample cause for concern about the negative human consequences during these early stages of industrialization.
The demand for labor in factory towns resulted in problems of crowding, inadequate sanitation, disease, and increasing alcoholism.
Workers remained socially and politically marginalized, with little if any electoral power and with few choices but to suffer low wages, poverty, dangerous working conditions, and long hours, the last enabled through the new technology of gas lighting that extended evening working hours.
Working-class discontent led to uprisings and revolts between 1810 and 1830, followed by the beginnings of workers organizations (trade unions) and the practice of organizing strikes to protest against low wages.
The circumstances of factory life also led to some legislative reforms such as child labor laws and the first experiments in socialism in Great Britain and the United States by manufacturer-turned-reformer Robert Owen (17711858).
In Owens New Harmony community in Indiana, workers lives were organized along a collective and egalitarian rather than an individual and hierarchical basis with communal responsibility for education and child-rearing.
Poverty and working-class exploitation were themes for a number of writers, including Scottish-born Thomas Carlyle (17951881), who lamented the extreme contrast between the prosperity of the upper and middle classes and the poverty of the working class, pleading for reform: The condition of England ... is justly regarded as one of the most ominous, and withal one of the strangest, ever seen in this world.
England is full of wealth, of multifarious produce, supply for human want in every kind; yet England is dying of inanition.
With unabated bounty the land of England blooms and grows; waving with yellow harvests; thick-studded with workshops, industrial implements, with fifteen millions of workers, understood to be the strongest, the cunningest and the willingest our earth ever had; these men are here; the work they have done, the fruit they have realised is here, abundant, exuberant on every hand of us: and behold, some baleful fiat as of Enchantment has gone forth saying, touch it not, ye workers, ye master-workers, ye master-idlers; none of you can touch it, no man of you shall be the better for it; this is enchanted fruit! On the poor workers such fiat fall first, in its rudest shape; but on the rich master-idlers nor any richest or highest man escape, but all are like to be brought low with it, and made poor enough, in the money sense or in a far fataler one.
In response to the demands of an expanding working class in Britain, and fearing that unrest might lead to revolution, Parliament undertook efforts to implement standardized codes for the due process of law, access to broad-based educational opportunities, the founding of public museums and parks, restrictions to employers exploitation of child labor, and reformation of the nations prison system.
Just as attempts were made to regulate working conditions, so too governments undertook legislation to standardize and regulate aspects of industrial production, seen, for instance, in the adoption of standardized widths for the laying of railroad track in England.
With many privately owned and competing companies, such shared standards designated a role for central government, regulating untrammeled industrial expansion by ensuring compatibility in connecting one railroad line to another.
Such efforts remind us that the history of design extends beyond private middle- and upper-class consumption of household goods and furnishings associated with individual creators; it also involves decisions in the broader public interest undertaken by political process and consensus, whether for safety or compatibility, whether railroad track or (in the early twentieth century) battery sizes, or receptacles for electrical current and elsewhere in the utility industries.
Whether stirred by the fiery rhetoric of Carlyle or by other progressive calls for social justice, many reformers, whether artists, architects, industrialists, or politicians, were motivated by a sense of social responsibility and a desire to address social inequality and improve the lives of working people.
As noted above, such efforts may be viewed as a genuine concern for improving the quality of life and serving the public interest, or as measures to exert social control, promoting values imposed from above in order to ensure compliance and prevent disruptive protest or revolution.
Understanding the context of early design reform involves reconciling these conflicting views and motivations, and recognizing that reform embodied complex attitudes aimed at balancing the desire for shared values with a recognition and appreciation for the democratic, spontaneous impulses of an emerging popular culture and managing the speed and direction of change.
In Britain, design reform was directed toward establishing common ground through taste.
In most cases, the study of the past was the best guide to designs present and future, but this approach, usually referred to as historicism in art, did not mean slavish imitation of particular examples, but rather a starting point that might inform the manufacture of products using new materials and production methods.
In short, history and modernity were compatible rather than antithetical.
Architect and writer Matthew Digby Wyatt (18201877), welcomed technology in the form of new materials and processes to which guidelines might be applied, especially in relation to metals and casting; others, such as A.
W.
N.
Pugin (18121852), called attention to the moral and ethical implications of style, ignoring the varied preferences of consumers.
Still others, such as Parliament member Sir Henry Cole (18081882), lobbied for schools of design, the creation of a museum devoted to the decorative arts, and public exhibitions to display national and international contemporary design to inform manufacturers and educate consumers.
In all cases, however, reformers believed in the existence of universal fixed standards for design, in the erosion of those standards due to a combination of industrialization and commercialism, and the need to establish and implement them in the best economic, social, and moral interests of an ever-expanding consuming public.
Thus design reform was in this basic sense political, and many reformers understood that in order to be effective it was necessary to be persuasive.
They used the latest technology in the printing industry to publish illustrations of designs that demonstrated their standards in books and journals in order to familiarize an expanding middle-class readership with the practice of good design, and staged exhibitions that promoted their point of view.

## Reform
and the Gothic Revival One of the strongest advocates for standards or principles of design was A.
W.
N.
(Augustus Welby Northmore) Pugin.
Pugin, an architect, designer, and author who collaborated with Sir Charles Barry on the design and interior decoration for Londons Houses of Parliament (1837 ff.), contrasted the eclectic tastes in contemporary English architecture and design with the stylistic unity of its medieval and specifically Gothic past.
For Pugin the consistency of the latter expressed moral truths as well as aesthetic harmony.
Pugins conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1835 and his enthusiasm for the beauty and truth of the Gothic style led him to a passionate investigation of and appreciation for the style.
He criticized the indiscriminate and superficial application of any type of carved, printed, and painted decoration to a wide variety of furnishings and utilitarian goods, which he felt was motivated by commercial greed and self-interest.
The equation of decoration with excess was not entirely new, but the focus upon the Gothic style as the purest expression of the appropriate relationship between construction and decoration, and the urgent pleas for reform in Pugins writings, are characteristic of a polemic tone and an ethical undercurrent in the nineteenth-century design reform movement.
Pugins principles of design stemmed from his understanding of Gothic architecture (recall that architecture was also the basis for Percier and Fontaine in recommending ancient Greece and Rome as models for interior design, see here).
He believed that painting and sculpture (whether decorative or figural) were essentially embellishments of architecture and as such should be subordinated to, rather than independent from, the structure they decorate.
Pugin argued that this rational, subordinating principle of organization is best exemplified in the Gothic style.
Looking at the early-thirteenthcentury north transept portal of Chartres Cathedral, for example (fig.
4.1), one can observe that the jamb statues maintain their character as columns supporting a porch, other carved figures do not project beyond their containing niches, and virtually all individual elements are part of a larger unit that is in turn related to the tripartite division of the doorway.
As suggested by art historian Margaret Belcher, within such a framework a unity is imposed upon all of the arts that might also serve metaphorically for an ideal society in which all individuals are unified by a single faith and live in harmony  individual difference yields to an ideal unity.
In addition, Pugin advised respect for the characteristics of materials and argued, for instance, that carved materials, such as wood, should not look as if they are molded (nor should gutta percha masquerade as carved wood), and that while it is natural for artists and artisans to transform the materials they work with, stone should always retain in some measure its essential stony character, and should not pretend to be something else.
Such truth to material remained a tenet of design reform well into the twentieth century, whether exploring the malleability of reinforced concrete or the tensile strength of steel to create the curtain walls of steel-and-glass office towers.
Disrespect for the true nature of materials not only violated the example of Gothic architecture and design but was also dishonest.
The arbitrary use of pointed arches and quatrefoils for the base of a lamp or the back of a chaise was for Pugin a superficial appropriation of details, which revealed a lack of understanding of both the stylistic and symbolic unity of the Gothic style.
Other grievances against contemporary design included the use of scenic or illusionistic patterns for wallpapers or carpets since the modeling of forms might be inconsistent with the effects of natural light, and such views interfered with the structural function of walls and floors.
He registered some of his objections in a satirical drawing of monstrosities where the Gothic style is used to construct a collection of elaborately decorated doorstops, lamps, and other objects that misappropriate the styles principles.
His disdain for the modeled forms and detail in examples such as the Gothic wallpaper design illustrated in figure 3.12 was registered in the following comments: What are commonly termed Gothic pattern papers for hanging on walls, where a wretched caricature of a pointed building is repeated from skirting to cornice, door over pinnacle and pinnacle over door. His remarks are condescending in both social and aesthetic terms, as when he comments that a particular misguided style of decoration was a great favourite with hotel and tavern keepers. North transept portal, Chartres Cathedral, France, c.
1210–1220.
In 1841, Pugin enumerated his principles derived from the Gothic style in True Principles of Pointed or Christian Architecture, illustrated with engravings based on the authors drawings.
In this book he noted that there should be no features about a building which are not necessary for convenience, construction, or propriety, and all ornament should consist of enrichment of the essential construction of the building. He also published books of illustrations intended as models for the design of furniture, metalwork, ceramic plates and tiles, and ecclesiastical garments.
A number of firms manufactured his designs, the moral as well as aesthetic dimension of which can be seen in a plate manufactured by Minton in 1849 whose border is inscribed with the admonishment Waste Not Want Not in bold Gothic letters.
Elaborated in many forms by other contemporary designers and authors, Pugins true principles became the basis for many nineteenth-century approaches to design standards that advocate the harmony between utility and beauty. Art criticism for Pugin was inseparable from social criticism, and a disregard for design principles as he defined them was also a deviation both from beauty and moral principles.
Eclecticism and lack of discrimination were signs of disorder and decay, while disregarding the proper use of materials was deceitful as well as ignorant of enduring standards.
On the positive side, the understanding and practice of fixed principles were socially as well as aesthetically desirable, contributing to the well-being of society, instilling common values during a time of uncertainty and change brought about by industrialization and rising materialism.
Wedded to a discriminating historicism and looking to the past as a guide to the future, the moral dimension of Pugins views lent urgency to his writings.
His views were based on a firm belief in the ability of the arts to shape behavior, and were shared by a number of artists, tastemakers, manufacturers, and politicians during the Victorian age.
Many of Pugins designs for patterns and interior furnishings were inspired by fourteenth- and fifteenth-century examples he studied and recorded in England and on visits to France.
Motifs such as the quatrefoil or fleur-de-lys are common, as are other plant or lobed forms that share the same characteristics  repetition or symmetry as a basis for composition, crisp contours, and flat shapes.
This approach can be seen in the bright Fleur-de-Lys and Pomegranate wallpaper pattern used for conference and committee rooms at the Palace of Westminster in London (fig.
4.2).

## 4.2 A. W. N. Pugin, Fleur-de-Lys and Pomegranate pattern, block-printed and glazed curtain
, 88 $^ 2 / _ { 3 } \times$ 59 in (225.2 × 150 cm), 1851.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
A good number of Pugins designs for furniture and interiors were commissioned by or intended for august religious or other ceremonial settings and circumstances, in particular the chambers of the Houses of Parliament along with less imposing parish churches.
The House of Lords adhered to Pugins True Principles, but its deeply coffered ceilings, carved wall paneling, gilt screens, and carved stone figures were more appropriate to the public display of power than to domestic comfort or the habits of daily living.
Pugin holds a well-deserved place in the Western canon of modern design, but his direct legacy is perhaps best seen in the widespread construction of Gothic Revival churches in Britain and North America in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
A more modest example of his design is a cast-iron umbrella stand manufactured by the firm of John Hardman in London from around 1850 (fig.
4.3).
Here Pugin applied his principles to a contemporary household object made using a modern manufacturing process; a twisted vertical stem serves as an axis for eight circles above to hold umbrellas and a related octagonal tray below to catch dripping water.
The base is supported by four feet attached to curved straps that also are repeated above on a smaller scale to hold in place the eight circles.
There is little if any molded decoration to interfere with the design, and the visual organization is both practical and unified.

## Henry
Cole and the “Cole Group” Beginning in the 1830s the British government, fearing foreign competition for its manufactured goods, took an interest in design, primarily sponsoring schools devoted to the education of artists to produce designs specifically for manufactured goods.
A lengthy government report of 18356, prepared by Parliaments Select Committee on Arts and Manufactures under the auspices of the Board of Trade, noted a decline in demand for British goods abroad and an increase in foreign imports at home (a negative trade balance, in contemporary economic terms).
Drawing was an essential component of this education, based upon the belief that the noble and didactic aims of the fine arts would also elevate the general standards of public taste in manufactured goods.
The Select Committee also advocated specific recommendations for such standards, based, not surprisingly, upon a balance between utility and beauty, and the use of decorative patterns derived from the study of botanical forms and select examples from the past as well as from other cultures including India and West Asia.
Among the most prominent advocates for design education was Sir Henry Cole (18081882), a civil servant who believed that an alliance between fine art and manufactures would promote public taste as well as restore Britains competitive edge in the expanding global market for manufactured goods.
Coles attitudes were strongly influenced by the House Report of 18356.
Under the pseudonym Felix Summerly, Cole edited a series of illustrated travel books and storybooks intended for children (known as the Home Treasury) that were intended to improve the quality of childrens literature available in the market.
Throughout his long career in public service, he argued that public museums should serve the interests of the working class and be the antidote to brutality and vice, providing models for responsible behavior and social harmony.
Turning to design, the harmony of utility and beauty in the decorative arts also served as a metaphor for the socially cohesive virtues of moderation and restraint, and government-sponsored design education provided practical training for artisans as a necessary component in the expanding production of a wide range of domestic products.
As a model business venture, Cole furnished designs (both his own and those of his artist friends) for tea sets and other manufactured goods, founding Summerly Art Manufactures in 1847 as a model for manufacturers.
Richard Redgrave (18041888) was a painter of frequently moralizing subjects who contributed to a number of Coles initiatives, providing illustrations for the Home Treasury and designs for Summerly Art Manufactures.
Redgraves glass Well-Spring carafe of 1847 (fig.
4.4) is an example of early design reform efforts.
The painted decoration of reeds, appropriate as a subject to the vases function as a water container, derives from the direct study from nature, but the drawing results in a simplified, linear style that grows organically from a more abstract, regular crisscross pattern of roots at the base.
Glass allows for the tentative exploration of three-dimensional space, since it is naturally transparent and thus permits such effects while remaining true to its material.
Summerlys products did not always adhere to such concerns: Redgraves Well-Spring design was later produced by the Minton Company in porcelain, where at least some of its subtle spatial effect is lost when applied to a more opaque surface.

J.
F.
Christy, Stangate Glass Workshop, Lambeth, London, 1847.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Neither Pugin nor Cole condemned the use of unskilled and increasingly divided labor or the use of new technologies to increase the efficiency of production.
Rather, they were interested in articulating, practicing, and disseminating common standards of taste in design.
If machines or specialization (sometimes taking the form of piecework, that is, the hiring out or subcontracting of particular parts of a product that are later assembled and sold) could increase efficiency and lower cost, it was only natural that manufacturers employ such means to their advantage.
While concerned with the welfare of working people, the reform efforts of Cole and his group applied more to finished products than to the labor practices by which they were manufactured.
Unlike Pugins insistence upon the morality and unity of the Gothic style, however, Cole and his group advocated a broader range of styles in their approach to reform, and direct studies from nature formed part of their program to educate designers for industry.
Cole recognized that his ideas would never gain acceptance without lobbying for education and attempting to shape public opinion.
He helped to sponsor a periodical entitled The Art Journal (184951) that published illustrations for designers and manufacturers to follow, and also played a role in determining the curricula of Britains government-run schools of design, focusing upon drawing as a mainstay of training rather than the development of workshop skills.
Following the Crystal Palace exhibition of 1851 (see below), Cole realized his longstanding ambition to establish the South Kensington (later Victoria and Albert) Museum as a collection devoted to the decorative arts and the improvement of public taste (his portrait, in mosaic, is still found in a stairwell in the older part of the building located on Exhibition Road).
In the 1860s the South Kensington Museum installed gas lighting to permit working people to view the collections until ten oclock in the evening three nights a week.

## The
Great Exhibition of 1851 The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations held in London at Hyde Park in 1851 was a watershed for design at mid-century; this first of many Worlds Fairs emphatically confirmed the reality of a heterogeneous middle-class consumer culture in Britain, Europe, their imperial territories, and North America, that linked commodities with technological progress, abundance, social transformation, competition, and the forging of national identities.
Never before had the decorative and industrial arts been the focus of such widespread international attention, crossing class boundaries and stirring the popular imagination.
Supported by royal consort Prince Albert (1819 1861) and organized by Henry Cole and his group of reformers, the Industry of All Nations or Great Exhibition of 1851 expanded upon earlier national exhibitions of industry in France (see here) and was the model for numerous international exhibitions in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries in Europe, Australia, and the United States.
The exhibition was originally conceived as a national fair, but in the process of planning became international, drawing 14,000 producers, half of whom were from outside Britain.
It was housed in a temporary structure (fig.
4.5) designed by architect Joseph Paxton (18031865), attracting great interest by its frank use of cast and wrought iron, breathtaking expanses of glass, and the complete absence of traditional building materials such as stone and load-bearing walls.
Relying upon uniform prefabricated parts, the Exhibition Hall was built in the short span of eight months, a necessity resulting from a lack of agreement among organizers in earlier planning efforts.
Although Paxtons choice of materials and method of construction had previously been used in utilitarian structures such as railroad stations and greenhouses, the Crystal Palace, as it was dubbed at the time, with its colorful painted ribs of the arches of the nave, high vaults, rhythmic arcades, and cast structural elements, aspired to rival if not to surpass the great architectural landmarks of the past, sounding a note of modernity, progress, and confidence in the aesthetic possibilities of industrialized technology.
Joseph Paxton, Crystal Palace, north water tower and transept, London, built 1851, photographed by Francis Frith.
Although the goods on display were not for sale, the display of myriad products in close proximity to the spectator linked the exhibited objects to the promise of abundance, unlimited availability of goods for the middle class, and the fulfillment of dreams and desires in the near future.
Historian Thomas Richards placed the exhibition in the context of nineteenth-century theatrical spectacle, suggesting the transformation of goods as they entered a vast space of association. Such magical, quasi-religious reactions to the Crystal Palace and its exhibition were not uncommon.
Queen Victoria herself remarked that when standing inside the structure she was filled with devotion.
By the early 1860s, enterprising investors and merchants had translated the magical associations of such vast spaces into a new kind of shopping experience with the first department store, the Bon Marché in Paris in 1869, followed shortly after in the United States with Wanamakers in Philadelphia, Macys in New York, and then in Britain with Londons Selfridges.
These large, multi-storied businesses co-existed with boutiques and other smaller, specialized retail establishments.
Department stores introduced uniform pricing (rather than bargaining with merchants), seasonal sales, and a large and diverse inventory of ready-made goods and fabrics.
The combination of optimism and the embrace of materialism as the measure of economic and social progress seen in the broad public reaction to the Crystal Palace is mirrored in the confident social aspirations of characters in contemporary fiction on both sides of the English Channel.
In Honoré de Balzacs (17991850) novel César Birotteau (1837), the protagonist comes to Paris as a poor provincial with no formal education or connections, rising through hard work and prudent investment to become a respected and successful Parisian perfume merchant.
Upon being awarded the prestigious medal of the Legion of Honor for his support of the monarchy, César undertakes the expansion and decoration of his Paris apartment with the help of an aspiring architect in order to host a ball celebrating his financial success and social achievement.
While subsequent investments and speculations bring disaster to César and demonstrate the unpredictability of both fortune and friendships based upon it, the novel portrays self-improvement and social advancement as realistic middle-class aspirations in this nineteenth-century novel.
The spirit of progress, expansion, and nationalism associated with manufactured goods at the first Worlds Fairs defines the iconography of the Albert Memorial in Kensington Gardens (fig.
4.6), built between 1864 and 1876 and dedicated to the Prince Consort, who died in 1861 and who had strongly supported the Crystal Palace exhibition.
The seated Albert, holding a copy of the exhibition catalog (rather than a traditional symbol of authority), peers out over the four corners of the earth, each represented by a beast and symbolized by an allegorical figural group referring to the continents of Asia, Africa, Europe, and America.
Corresponding to the four continents are four categories of productive human endeavor: manufactures, agriculture, engineering, and commerce.
The manufactures group includes the bearded Herculeslike figure of a blacksmith representing labor and a seated figure holding a plate and urn as examples of human-made products.
A standing female figure holds an hourglass and beside her sits a beehive, both referring to time-saving production efficiency.
The symbolism of this orderly vision of the world seems clear: Britain stands at the intersection of heaven (note the cross at the top of the baldachin) and earth: natures riches under Gods watch are increased by the creativity and ingenuity of the human race, an orderly vision of prosperity and peace.
It is not surprising that the markedly Anglocentric vision of the Albert Memorial coincides with aggressive imperial expansion that provided raw materials to an expanding industrial empire under British and other European nations control.
Popular reaction to the Great Exhibition may also be gauged from the proliferation of printed materials in the form of illustrated catalogs, books of illustrations featuring masterpieces from the exhibition or views of its varied displays, and smaller-scale ephemera in the form of sheet music, souvenir plates, even Christmas cards celebrating the event and printed using the recently developed process of chromolithography.
While the Great Exhibition celebrated productivity and progress in manufacturing, the reform-minded organizers themselves were disappointed with the results, for there was little evidence that public taste had been improved or that standards of design had been widely adopted by British manufacturers.
The cover of Coles Art Journal devoted to the exhibition illustrates the didactic aspirations of the organizers (fig.
4.7).
An allegorical figure of Peace holding a dove stands in front of a globe flanked by two kneeling figures  a designer and a craftsman.
To her right, a well-groomed gentleman, clearly designated as the designer, holds a drawing of a chalice and is surrounded by books and a painters palette.
These attributes  in combination with his groomed, stylish hair and long-sleeved tunic, both of which are impediments to physical labor  associate the designer with the fine arts, their inclusion in the liberal arts, and their place in design education at the London School of Design.
In contrast, the craftsman kneeling opposite him, and whose hand he clasps, has cropped hair and wears a workers smock with rolled-up sleeves, and is surrounded by the tools of his trade, including an anvil and some finished products.
This somewhat simplistic characterization of the relationship between design and production suggests that the healthy (if subservient) collaboration between craftsman and artist produces useful goods that contribute to prosperity and peace.
LOSDON: PUBLISHED POR THE PROPRIRTORS, IY GEORGE VIRTUE Catalog of the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, front cover, published in The Art Journal, London, 1851.
Ralph Wornum, Keeper of the Queens Collection of Pictures, won a prize for an essay devoted to the goods on display at the exhibition, published in the Crystal Palace Illustrated Catalogue (the same book that Prince Albert holds on his lap in the Albert Memorial).
Wornum embraced the tenets of design reform, namely the harmony of utility and beauty, and criticized the use of naturalistic flowers and plants for the decoration of carpets and other floor coverings as a violation of fitness to purpose.
He also disapproved of the whims of fashion and argued that principles of good taste provided a reliable and permanent foundation for excellence in design.
Wornum described an immense Renaissance Revival sideboard exhibited by the French firm of Fourdinois (fig.
4.8) as if it was a work of sculpture, commenting upon its appropriate use of imagery (the subjects include allegories of the continents of Europe, Africa, Asia, and America, foods associated with them, and four hunting hounds, all relating to a dining room setting) as well as its expert carving and the ability of modern work to rival the masterpieces of earlier periods.
Such an iconographic analysis might well have appeared too elevated for the general public to grasp or even care about.
Moreover, it ignored the motivations of many middle-class consumers, who looked to commodities not for instruction or narrative meaning, but rather as symbols of status and luxury.
At the same time, Wornum lamented the preponderance of deluxe furniture at the expense of less costly and more practical examples of good taste directed toward shaping the needs and improving the taste, and lives, of average middle-class consumers.
Critics often focused their attention upon the more ornate objects of carving in wood, cut glass, silver, and other materials on display.
Size and decorative richness naturally drew attention in the vast interior space of the Crystal Palace, and ornament was often seen as evidence of art that added value to objects of use.
In addition, ornate work often won medals and prizes that contributed to manufacturers reputations.
Henri-Auguste Fourdinois, sideboard, manufactured in Paris.
Wood engraving from Dickinsons’ comprehensive pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851.
Many if not most of the critics of the Great Exhibition were architects and fine artists.
For instance, German architect and theorist Gottfried Semper (18031879), who lived for a time in London and taught at the government-sponsored School of Design there, was dismayed by the uneven quality of goods on display at the Great Exhibition, comparing it to the biblical Tower of Babel (Genesis 11: 19).
Richard Redgrave arrived at much the same conclusion, writing that the absence of any fixed principle in ornamental design is most apparent in the Exhibition. Semper, however, was optimistic that the study of the exhibitions best objects might form the basis of standards that considered the rational use of new materials and techniques along with function and the appropriate use of decoration; the public reaction to Coles Marlborough House exhibition (see below) suggested otherwise.
Owen Jones (18091874), an architect and designer who also was an organizer of the exhibition, was responsible for the color scheme of the buildings interior, and an advocate of design reform.
Following the opening of the Great Exhibition, he wrote that the majority of goods on display demonstrated novelty without beauty, beauty without intelligence, and all work without faith. One can understand his disappointment, for Jones had published examples of decorative patterns based upon drawings from the fourteenth-century Nasrid Alhambra palace in Granada, Spain.
The plates of Joness Alhambra volume were intended not only as illustrations of a famed site, but also as didactic models for designers and manufacturers.
In spite of his reaction to the Great Exhibition, Jones continued his reform efforts, both as a designer and as the author of The Grammar of Ornament (1856), the most extensive dictionary of design standards at that time.
The Grammar of Ornament contained 100 color plates (using the chromolithographic process, see page 69) of patterns based upon historic Western and non-Western examples, in media ranging from carpets to ceramic tiles, from relief sculptures to illuminated manuscripts, selected to illustrate universal principles of design.
Jones advocated a broad historicism based upon principles (32 in all) printed at the end of the volume.
The principles are reminiscent of those established by Pugin from the study of Gothic architecture, but extend to a wider variety of examples both geographically and chronologically.
Joness principles include: Construction should be decorated.
Decoration should never be purposely constructed; Flowers or other natural objects should not be used as ornaments, but conventional representations founded upon them sufficiently suggestive to convey the intended image to the mind, without destroying the unity of the object they are employed to decorate.
Universally obeyed in the best periods of Art, equally violated when Art declines. The Grammar of Ornament went through numerous printings in the late nineteenth century, and its approach to ornament and color was adopted for the decoration of numerous buildings and interiors during this period.
In addition to advocating the use of models from other periods and cultures, as in one of three plates devoted to Moorish decoration (fig.
4.9), Jones included the possibility of constructing original patterns based upon the study of nature tempered by the rules he enumerated and as taught in the British Schools of Design (see also the Global Inspiration II, here).
British designer Christopher Dresser (18341904) contributed original plates to the Grammar featuring ornamental shapes based upon leaf and floral motifs in a style that simplified organic forms into flattened linear contours (see fig.
6.1 and Chapter 6, here).
Dresser was a student at the London School of Design and was hired by manufacturers to create original designs for workshop production.
During his career, along with other contemporary artist- and architect-designers, Dresser attempted to expand the reform standards by embracing greater originality and freedom in pattern design, and greater invention in borrowing from the design of other cultures, including Japan, that attracted his interest during the 1860s and prompted his visit there in 1876 as a representative of the South Kensington (renamed Victoria and Albert) Museum.
Owen Jones, Arabian, no.
4, plate 34, color lithograph, 13 ${ ^ 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 8 ~ { ^ 7 } / _ { 8 }$ in (33.7 × 22.5 cm), from The Grammar of Ornament, London, 1856.
Private collection.
Public reaction to early design reform often varied with the views of experts such as Wornum, Semper, or Jones.
For his efforts to establish standards for taste through exhibitions, publications, and education, Sir Henry Cole was much in the public eye, and was frequently a target for ridicule.
In the novel Hard Times, published in serial form in 1854, Charles Dickens (18121870) poked fun at government efforts to dictate taste.
A commissioner (a thinly veiled portrait of Cole) visits a government-run school and asks the students whether they would use a carpet bearing representations of flowers.
A young girl, sent to the school by a well-meaning benefactor, replies that indeed she would, because she is very fond of flowers.
But the commissioner sternly asks whether in that case she would put tables and chairs upon them and have people walking over them with heavy boots. It wouldnt hurt them, sir  they wouldnt crush and wither if you please, sir.
They would be the pictures of what was very pretty and pleasant, I would fancy. But the commissioner replies, Ay, ay, ay.
But you mustn’t fancy [italics added].
While the motives behind reform were perhaps well-intentioned in a paternalistic sense, Dickens is here defending the democratic freedom of choice as inherently more fundamental than parameters of good taste, whether or not they result in excess or sentimentality.
Effectively, Dickens used the example of a child to connect the absence of good taste with innocence rather than vulgarity or dishonesty.
In 1852 Cole established a Museum of Manufactures (precursor to the Victoria and Albert Museum, officially opened in South Kensington in 1857) at Marlborough House in London.
There he put on view a comparison between objects that conformed to reform principles with a selection of those that violated those principles, dubbed the Chamber of Horrors. The latter ranged from illusionistic patterns on wallpapers (see, for instance, fig.
3.13) to objects whose excessive ornamentation interfered with their practicality; whether out of curiosity or delight, the majority of visitors spent their time viewing the examples of false rather than true principles.
Although elevating the taste of the public remained part of the political mission of design reformers, the polemical tone and moralizing arguments of Pugin are less pronounced in Joness Grammar.
Later, reform efforts generally assumed the friendlier tone of advice books by tastemakers such as Charles Eastlake (18361906).
Eastlakes Hints on Household Taste in Furniture, Upholstery, and Other Details was published in 1868 and was popular in both the United Kingdom and the United States.
Directed toward a mostly female readership who were expected to be responsible for creating a restful home environment, Eastlake wrote: We require no small amount of art and instruction and experience to see why direct imitation of natural objects is wrong in ornamental design.
The quasi-fidelity with which the forms of a rose, or a bunch of ribbons, or a ruined castle, can be produced on carpets, crockery and wallpapers will always possess a certain kind of charm for the uneducated eye, just as the mimicry of natural sounds in music, from the rolling of thunder to the crackling of poultry, will always delight the vulgar ear.
Both are ingenious and amusing but neither lie within the legitimate province of art.
A comparison between one of Eastlakes wallpaper designs (fig.
4.10), manufactured by Jeffery & Company and appearing in Hints, and the printed or woven designs at the Great Exhibition (fig.
4.11) conforms to design reform principles.
Eastlake criticized the lack of discrimination in matters of design, but his prose focuses less upon the moral dimensions of design than upon the cultivation of taste as a vehicle for selfimprovement as well as the reinforcement of middle-class cultural attitudes that identified the home as the sphere for womens activities.
Such attitudes pertain to womens role as consumers, but also, as seen in Chapter 6, as practitioners (see here).
Charles Eastlake, example of wallpaper design from Hints on Household Taste, London, 1868.
