## Images
for All The expansion of design in manufactured goods and the creation of a consumer economy was accompanied and stimulated by advances in print technology, particularly in the reproduction of images for illustrations in books, magazines, and newspapers as well as advertising.
A competitive free press, coupled with printing technologies and the gradual elimination of taxes on paper and printed materials, provide the technical and political context for the success of illustrated weekly journals aimed at an emerging mass market, including working people, that reached a circulation in Britain of over 200,000 copies by the middle of the nineteenth century.
One of the earliest examples of this type of affordable illustrated journal is The Penny Magazine (beginning in 1832), published by Charles Knight (17911873), who began his career as a craftsman and printer.
Knight is known for developing an economical method for producing color images from multiple engraved woodblocks.
The Penny Magazine contained wood-engraved reproductions of works of art intended to provide examples of personal and social virtue.
Knights venture was endorsed by the Society for the Distribution of Useful Knowledge, which supported the role of the arts as a civilizing force in Victorian society.
The Penny Magazine was joined by other weekly journals, often called miscellanies, that included illustrations of examples of the decorative arts.
While a paintings narrative might provide edifying models of behavior, the useful arts also could convey, through form and decoration, an appropriate balance between utility and beauty that elevated ordinary goods into artistic ones.
In addition to Knights civilizing content, miscellanies also featured illustrations accompanying popular serialized and sensationalized fiction dealing with crime, intrigue, sex, and the occult.
Thus illustrations and text that encouraged self-improvement, restraint, temperance, and social harmony coexisted with the broader commercial appeal of aberrant behavior, escapism, and political radicalism  a rich and diverse combination of conformity and non-conformity better known as popular culture.
Aside from lithography, printers developed other methods such as wood engraving to satisfy a growing demand for illustrations for reproduction in books, magazines, advertisements, and newspapers during the first half of the nineteenth century.
Owing to the efforts of printer Thomas Bewick of Newcastle-upon-Tyne in northern England (17531828), the technique of producing woodblocks by cutting with engraving tools against rather than with the wood grain resulted in greater precision and a more subtle tonal range in the rendering of texture and three-dimensional form.
Prior to the invention of the half-tone photomechanical process, wood engravers worked directly from blocks traced from photographs and drawings.
Fine detail was also achieved beginning in the 1820s using a process that created steel-engraved plates, replacing previously used copper plates.
The surface of steel plates was more durable than copper  greater numbers of prints could be run on a steel plate with minimal loss of quality.
Steel plates also offered more precision when printing large quantities of thin lines to suggest minute gradations of tone in relief.
The method, developed in the United States by Jacob Perkins (17661849), was particularly effective for secure forms of printing such as postage stamps and paper currency, where complexity increased the difficulty of counterfeiting.
English printers such as Charles Whittingham, Joseph Cundall, and Henry Shaw were knowledgeable in all phases of print technology, and combined a respect for craft with the benefits of new techniques of mechanical reproduction.
Whittingham collaborated with publisher Thomas Pickering at the Chiswick Press in that London suburb to publish a number of titles, and was respected for maintaining the highest standards of typography, illustration, layout, and binding (though generally on cardboard rather than more expensive leather).
Whittingham and other book printers rejected modern typefaces with their stronger contrast of thick and thin strokes (more common in the nineteenth century for larger display types; see fig.
3.11) and revived more traditional faces derived from William Caslon.
Many printers took an avid interest in the expanding market for childrens illustrated books, printed from wood engravings in both black-andwhite as well as color.
The firm of Robson, Levey & Franklyn published James Burns Nursery Rhymes, Tales and Jingles in 1844, using Caslon types, rustic frames sometimes hung with vines, and wood-engraved illustrations (fig.
4.12).
The asymmetrical yet balanced relationship between framed text and illustration provided both consistency and variety from poem to poem, suggesting a desire to create designs with a clear hierarchy of information that could be easily grasped by young readers.
Other contemporary publishers were more lavish in the use and variety of decoration and typefaces.
This is most evident in the title pages of contemporary fiction that often appeared in serialized form.
George Routledge (18121888) of London published a series of novels known as the Railway Library, presumably meant to be read while traveling and a forerunner of portable paperback fiction (and todays smart phones, tablets, Kindles, and other digital readers) that, along with the days headlines, continues to occupy commuters on suburban trains and airlines.
The cost of most illustrated books was generally beyond the means of working people.
But the appeal of stories told with pictures, before the widespread emergence of photomechanical reproduction and the advent of film (and later of television) was strong, satisfied through less expensive illustrated broadsides and weekly journals such as The Penny Magazine.
4.12 James Burns, drawings printed from woodblocks, 6 × 8 in (15.2 × 20.8 cm), Nursery Rhymes, Tales and Jingles, 1844.
Images in popular weekly journals and broadsheets were printed in black-and-white.
But concurrently with these strictly tonal processes, a significant development in color printing, known as chromolithography, was also emerging.
Patented in the 1830s by Godefroy Engelmann (17881839) in France, the new technology quickly spread to Britain, Germany, and the United States.
Chromolithography produced images in color using a series of stones with flat, polished surfaces, each inked with a different color and printed in succession using exact registration of the paper.
The process, as perfected in England by William Savage (17701843), was used initially for the accurate color reproduction of paintings for expensive, high-quality prints and illustrated books beginning in the 1840s.
A number of early books with illustrations produced by chromolithography were facsimile editions of manuscripts such as the ninth-century Hiberno-Saxon Gospel book known as the Book of Kells.
Others were private devotional books meant to rival their exquisite medieval forebears, such as H.
Noel Humphreys chromolithographed plates for The Miracles of Our Lord, published in 1848 (fig.
4.13).
In the late nineteenth century, the chromolithographic process was adopted for the color printing of popular greeting cards and souvenirs.
The application of chromolithography to trade, business cards, and advertising (often a giveaway inside a product box) would soon follow, attaining immense popularity in the United States (see here).

## 4.13 H. Noel Humphreys, chromolithograph in about 12 colors, 6 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> ×
4 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (16.5 × 11.4 cm), from The Miracles of Our Lord, London, 1848.
Private collection.
In France, popular nineteenth-century color woodcut and chromolithographic images were known as images d’Épinal, named for the city in northeastern France where they were printed.
Subjects ranged from portraits of heroes and political leaders to saints, representations of virtues and vices, illustrations of contemporary events such as natural disasters along with advertisements, board games, aids to learning the alphabet for children, and playing cards.
They demonstrate the increasing role images were playing in the dissemination of information for political, religious, and entertainment purposes.
Popular prints varied in technique and quality, though a tendency toward simplified and easily recognized flat areas of color, undifferentiated by modeling, is frequently the case.
Figure 4.14 is an example of a colored lithograph illustrating a disastrous flood of the Loire River dating to 1866.
Here the palette is limited to primaries and the secondary color green, against a pale tan and gray ground.
The scene depicts the rescue of a farm family from the roof of their half-submerged cottage by three figures in a boat.
The figures gestures are theatrical and the pyramidal composition dramatic rather than journalistic.
Such conventions rely heavily upon academic convention combined with modern techniques of reproduction to re-create current events in a sensational manner, in the midst of an event rather than after the fact.
Image d’Épinal, 11 $^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 1 6 ^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (28 × 41.1 cm), depicting the rescue of a farm family from a flood of the Loire River, 1866.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.

## Popular
Graphics in the United States Illustrated weekly magazines were also popular in the United States, beginning in the 1850s with the publication of Frank Leslie’s Weekly and Harper’s Weekly in New York.
Harper’s Weekly reported on contemporary domestic and international events and used wood engraving to reproduce drawings by a number of artists who served as reporters, recording events based upon first-hand (eyewitness) experience.
Artist Winslow Homer (18361910), for instance, supported himself early in his career by documenting battles of the American Civil War for Harper’s Weekly.
Later his paintings and those of other fine artists were reproduced as wood engravings, often covering an entire page or even a double-page spread in the weekly magazine.
Another illustrator for Harper’s was Thomas Nast (18401902), a gifted draftsman whose family had moved to New York from Germany in 1846.
As a young man, Nast traveled at the magazines expense to Europe to cover a prizefight in Britain, as well as reporting on Giuseppe Garibaldi (18071882), who led military campaigns in the movement to create the nation of modern Italy in 18601861; Nast was also sent to report first-hand on events during the American Civil War.
Both during and after the Civil War, Nast increasingly sought to shape public opinion through illustrations aimed at a broad readership.
In addition to documenting actual events, he illustrated generalized themes relating to the Civil War that had tremendous popular appeal.
One of numerous examples, Christmas Furlough (fig.
4.15) appeared in late 1863 during the second full year of the Civil War.
The design consists of several separately titled and framed vignettes set against a background suggestive of a winter landscape.
The focus is upon a returning Union officer visiting his wife and family, with all of the common, safe, and reassuring associations of a homecoming.
Nast reinforced his sentimental message through composition and the use of light.
Our attention is drawn immediately to the pyramidal unit formed by the embracing couple in the center scene.
In a smaller vignette to the left, a warm glow of light from the window envelops sleeping children, enhancing the homespun ambience, while a stream of heavenly light bathes the small Nativity scene below.
One might also note that to the left of the main scene, the officers sleeping children receive a visit from Santa Claus, an image Nast helped to popularize, giving visual form to the subject of Clement Moores 1823 poem A Visit from St.
Nick. Nasts enduring version of Santa Claus combines Moores description of a jolly, bearded (though diminutive), and mischievous St.
Nick with the artists own memories of folk traditions in his native Germany that included a figure known as Pelznickel or furry Nicholas. Thomas Nast, Christmas Furlough, wood-engraved illustration from Harper’s Weekly, double-page spread, 16 × 22 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (40.6 × 57.2 cm), December 26, 1863.
Private collection.
Carefully staged and employing figural arrangements dependent upon the Western academic tradition of religious and historical painting, Nasts approach to drawing often emphasized bold tonal contrast and the careful orchestration of descriptive detail.
His original drawings were translated into the medium of the engraved woodblock by other artisans.
Nast also popularized enduring caricatures of human and animal figures such as Uncle Sam, Columbia, the Republican Partys Elephant, and the Democratic Partys Donkey as shorthand metaphors for familiar entities or concepts.
Such symbols persist today, though in the United States Democratic Donkey and Republican Elephant are more regularly identified by color, Blue (Democratic) and Red (Republican).
Nast also drew political cartoons that made use of exaggeration or caricature.
While he certainly had precursors who used caricature as a tool of political change (George IV, patron of the Royal Pavilion at Brighton, was a frequent target of satire; see here), and may have borrowed from them, the combination of clearly recognizable images of contemporary political figures and an inexpensive vehicle for distribution gave new power to the role of images in mobilizing public opinion.
Public officials feared Nasts pen and were well aware of his ability to influence opinion against their untrammeled greed and corruption.
The most celebrated of his campaigns, between 1869 and 1871, was directed against William Boss Tweed, a New York State senator and Sachem (leader) of New York Citys Democratic Party with its headquarters in Tammany Hall.
With both Harper’s Weekly and the New York Times supporting the reform of city government, Tweed and his so-called Ring fared poorly in the November 1871 elections, and were later indicted on charges of fraud, bribery, and corruption; in time the reign of the Ring came to an end.
Weekly journals such as Harper’s, and editors such as Fletcher Harper, demonstrated the power of the emerging profession of illustration, both in bringing matters of public concern to a politically engaged readership, and in turning awareness, or even outrage, into direct action.
Nasts image of Tweed in an 1871 illustration entitled The Tammany Tiger Loose—What Are You Going to Do About It? provides a particularly powerful example of the artists activism (fig.
4.16).
The issue in which this double-page cartoon appeared on newsstands was delivered to subscribers before the election on November 7, when several members of New Yorks Democratic Party were defeated, a victory for the Republican party that Nast and his editors at Harper’s Weekly supported.

## 4.16 Thomas Nast, The Tammany Tiger Loose—What Are You Going to Do About It?, wood-engrave
d illustration from Harper’s Weekly, double-page spread, 16 × 22 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (40.6 × 57.2 cm), November 11, 1871.
National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC.
The scene depicts a group of contemporary politicians, but is set in a Roman amphitheater, staged to call to mind the unevenly matched contests in Roman imperial times that pitted animals against enemies of the state in a very public display of state power.
A fierce tiger with gaping mouth and four sharp teeth dominates the composition at its center, turning its body, rendered in a three-quarter view, to stare the viewer directly in the eye.
The tiger is the most detailed rendering in the scene, creating a sense of clear hierarchy for the viewer not only in terms of its size and center placement but also in the sheer amount of visual information this part of the illustration contains.
It wears a collar inscribed with the word Americus, a reference to the name of the neighborhood volunteer Fire Company and Social Club of which William Tweed was a founding member and where he earned his early reputation as an affable and community-minded New York citizen.
The tiger stands astride a supine female figure wearing a tunic fastened at the right shoulder.
She is faceless, but a crown lying nearby identifies her as the Republic. Faintly etched stars suggest she once held the American flag, now in tatters, the attribute of Columbia, a popular literary and pictorial personification in the nineteenth century and also depicted by Nast and other artists of the time as a symbol of the United States and its citizens, the female counterpart to the more familiar Uncle Sam. In the lower right corner the blade of a broken sword is named Power, and to the left of the Tigers massive head is a broken sphere labeled Ballot, a reference to elections and abuses of the voting process.
Two other bodies, one lying face up, the other face down, also appear to the tigers left.
One is a male figure, who once wore a helmet and carried a caduceus signifying trade (the word is written on the nearby helmet), symbolized by Roman god Mercury, while the other figure, a female, also lies next to a broken sword and scales, both attributes of the personification of Justice.
Above and to the left of the tiger is the imperial box, where the corpulent figure of William Boss Tweed sits, wearing a cape, pendant, and belt from which hangs three straps, in the manner of sculptures of Roman emperors in military dress.
He holds a staff labeled Iron Rod, and is surrounded by a group of soldiers and attendants, many of whom would have been identifiable to readers.
The various symbols not only portray the Rings accretion of political power, but also serve as a visual summation of Tweeds political career, including his association with the familiar civic-minded fire companies and social organizations in New York, branded by their emblems, buildings, engines, and liveries.
The illustration is carefully constructed: viewers attention is drawn to the tiger at the center, then diagonally below to the sword and figure of the Republic and diagonally again, upward to the imperial box, followed by the vast throng and accompanying dead victims in the arena.
The three focal points of the composition (tiger, victim, emperor) may be circumscribed within the triangle that unites them, creating a clear sense of unity, order, and hierarchy: William Tweed and the Spoils standard sit at the apex of the triangle, normally the culmination of a complex scenes visual drama, but here the attention is diverted to the Tammany Tiger and its victim, occupying stage center and attracting visual interest by the tigers size, detail, and degree of contrast, and standing also at the juncture of two crossing diagonals, first from lower right to upper left and second from upper right to lower left.
The three victims on the floor of the arena are also linked: a line from the broken sword near Columbias body and ballot box leads to the foot of Justice and then from her body to that of Mercury, forming a zig-zag pattern leading the eye in a step-wise movement to explore the receding space to the right of the tiger.
The captions for Nasts illustrations appear below the wood-engraved images.
The use of upper-case letters (THE TAMMANY TIGER LOOSE) is of the same size and transitional Scotch Roman font often used for body type in Harper’s Weekly.
In all cases, texts are subordinate to the illustrations and yet essential to supply information and clarify meaning, reinforcing the editorial moral high ground.
Tweed himself expressed worry about the treatment he was receiving from Nasts illustrations in Harper’s Weekly: on one occasion Nast was offered a lengthy trip to Italy as a bribe if he stopped his visual attacks.
We shall never know, of course, to what degree Nasts cartoons, culminating in THE TAMMANY TIGER LOOSE, played in the outcome of election and Tweeds subsequent arrest and prison sentence.
But the cartoon reveals not only Nasts sources and his ability to communicate effectively with his readers, but also the means by which progressive reform may become activism and stimulate direct political action, in this case by casting the viewer as the tigers next victim, and the ballot as the best defense against the abuse of power.
The pictorial devices and references Nast employed were frequently depicted in paintings of the period and thus were part of a common Western visual language that stretched across boundaries of education and class.
The development of any mass media depends not only upon technology that is able to reach a large audience but also upon the ability to communicate popularly, that is, to a socially diverse cultural formation.
The emerging art of illustration in wood engraving and chromolithography accomplished this during the later nineteenth century, reflecting and shaping common experiences and attitudes through a range of imagery that readily communicated with an expanding reading and viewing public.
The art of illustration lived on well into the twentieth century, reemerging during the 1960s, when familiar images from the American past were appropriated by graphic designers and invested with subversive meanings (see here and fig.
13.39).
The efforts of chromolithographic printers in the United States were even more enterprising and widespread than their European counterparts.
Louis Prang (1824 1909) was a German-born printer who emigrated to Boston before 1850 and, using the painstaking methods of other experimenters in the field such as William Savage in Britain, produced a wide range of chromolithographic reproductions of paintings that were distributed in albums or individually.
Marketed as chromos, such prints satisfied a demand for framed wall art for middle-class homes, displayed as signs of status and social progress.
Prang extended his market by printing small popular color images for a variety of new purposes, including trade cards, advertising cards, and decalcomania that people cut out and pasted on pieces of paper to exchange notes and greetings, or collected in scrap books as a personal gallery of familiar images.
Beginning in the 1850s, color images on decals and cards were reproduced on large sheets that were cut and sold separately in packaged sets.
Manufactured by Prang and other commercial printers, their initial success soon led to their application on product labels, eventually leading to the proliferation of brands and images that would become part of everyday shopping experiences in the late nineteenth century.
Examples range from bizarre anthropomorphic carrots, corncobs, and peapods recalling the type of playful invention sometimes seen in medieval decorated initials, to innocent images of toddlers and mischievous pets (most often cats) linked to a variety of domestic products.
Such advertising techniques, which became more common in the 1920s, are seen in an advertising card for Mrs.
Winslows Soothing Syrup, depicting a mother and child whose happiness is connected with alleviating toddler teething pain (fig.
4.17; the preparation contained codeine and alcohol, and was denounced by the American Medical Association in 1911).
Chromolithography was also used extensively on a large scale for advertising posters in the later nineteenth century (see here).

## 4.17 Trade card for Mrs. Winslow’s Soothing Syrup, chromolithograph, 2 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2
</sub> × 3 in (6.4 × 7.6 cm), c.
1885.
National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland.

## A Balance
Sheet of Reform Early design reformers sought to identify and promote standards for the application of art to manufactured commodities, based upon the study of nature, examples from history, and the art of other cultures.
Their efforts were in part political, in that the reformers attempted to claim as universal a rather narrow set of criteria and felt a responsibility to educate, and hence convince manufacturers and a growing consumer public to accept their views.
The effort was epistemological as well, grounded in a belief that laws underlie all spheres of human endeavor, from mathematics and the physical sciences to architecture, extending as well to the application of ornament to a wide variety of furniture and household goods.
Such views ignored the reality of free trade, technological change, innovation, and a free enterprise economy, in which the harmony of utility and beauty was only one among many motivations for consumers to purchase clothing and manufactured commodities.
Indeed, the tastes of new classes of consumers might be dictated by a different set of criteria, in particular their relation to individual identity and social aspirations.
The reform agenda also did not sufficiently recognize the sheer excitement and flow of imagination stemming from experiments with new processes and materials, and the promise they held for personal expression in the form of material possessions.
It has been argued that those who lamented the spectacle of eclecticism, decorative variety, and ostentation among the middle class were seeking to perpetuate not only traditional tastes but also a conservative social system based upon the well-meaning but exclusive preferences of a small, dominant elite.
While design reform and the harmony between utility and beauty formed a cornerstone of the narrative of a canonical modern movement in design as described by art historians such as Nikolaus Pevsner, a more recent appreciation for eclecticism, popular culture, and the broader cultural values and commercial underpinnings of retail shopping and global markets as revealed in Worlds Fairs, suggests that recognizing and embracing competing points of view is necessary for a cultural appreciation of design history and of modern society in the nineteenth century and beyond.
And while issues of taste are essential to such a design historical narrative, reforming taste played less of a role under certain conditions, for instance in the design of industrial equipment such as the first Singer sewing machines of the early 1850s, or the Model T Ford in the early twentieth century (see here).
The search for standards or common ground seems in many ways a natural response during any period of rapid change and the consequent erosion of traditional values and authority amid rapid industrial and commercial expansion, and this certainly applies to the history of modern design.
Whether they are standards for decoration, utility, performance, or environmental or social responsibility, the desire for common ground continues as part of the political, social, aesthetic, and technical dimensions of design.

## Conclusion
So if one seeks to understand it [society], one must realize that it embodies at one and the same time everything that it has been, is, and will be in future; it is an accumulation over the long term of permanent features and successive inflections.
So wrote French historian Fernand Braudel (19021985) in his three-volume study that examines the social and economic order in Europe roughly from the fifteenth to the eighteenth centuries.
Braudels words and his reference to permanent features of society sound a note of continuity that might be applied as well to the history of modern design: both what it had been and much of what it was to become are embedded in the complex interplay between changes in the technology of production and the social dynamics of consumption in the eighteenth and early to mid-nineteenth centuries.
Beyond Braudel, we might add that a history of modern design should consider a world view beyond the Eurocentric formulation found in the Albert Memorial, one that allows as much as possible an appreciation of the interconnectedness of the design enterprise and that permits diverse cultures to speak for themselves rather than through a Western lens.
Perhaps a central issue to emerge during the first half of the nineteenth century in the industrializing West is the apparent conflict between technology, commercialization, and democratization on the one hand, all of which signify change and a state of flux, and the search for standards on the other, the desire to regulate change through the application of principles that might stand beyond the whims of fashion, the quest for profits, and the speed of innovation in industry.
It is in this context that early design reform may be analyzed.
Although decoration may have been the battleground for the proponents of design reform, such debates were part of a broad effort on the part of a group of designers, theorists, and politicians, to educate (or perhaps better, to indoctrinate) an expanding public and merchant class whose own interests might prove threatening to traditional authority.
We might also keep in mind that in addition to traditional class barriers, prejudice and racial theory limited the benefits of design from reaching minorities, whether Aborigines in Australia, the arctic Sámi people, the Black population and Indigenous Americans in the United States, or the nomadic Roma of Eastern # Global Inspiration II Muslim West Asia and North Africa This second installment of Global Inspiration looks at the decorative arts of the Arab-Islamic world as produced, displayed, and consumed during the mid-nineteenth century.
Several of the regions most notable design achievements are its use of color, ornament, and calligraphy: the vivid colors and rich geometric, abstract, and/or calligraphic (and usually aniconistic) arabesque, paisley, girih or strapwork, and graphic ornamentation of Islamic buildings, ceramics, textiles, carpets, miniature paintings, and furniture.
Europeans had their own tradition of decorative calligraphy, but by the mid-1800s it was nowhere near as vibrant as it was in script- (rather than print-) dominated Muslim West Asia and North Africa.
Moreover, Europe  except for formerly Muslim regions of Spain  did not have anything comparable to the colorfulness and ornamental complexity of, for example, Isfahans Blue Mosque.
And by the mid-nineteenth century, European males had undergone the great masculine renunciation, meaning they wore black suits instead of colorful clothes, so places where men still wore colorful clothes seemed exotic and pre-modern to them.
Among the 100 chromolithographed plates illustrating examples of decorative patterns from different time periods and cultures in Owen Joness 1856 The Grammar of Ornament (see here), more than twenty were labeled Persian, Moresque Turkish, or Arabian (see fig.
4.9).
Joness color scheme for the interior of the Crystal Palace, incorporating curtains, railings, colonettes, and other iron structural elements of the architecture, featured a combination of hues (red, blue, and yellow) that drew upon his familiarity with Islamic architecture and decoration found at the Alhambra palace in Granada (the last Islamic stronghold in Spain until 1492) and elsewhere in the Arab-Islamic world.
Visiting the Crystal Palace, English author Charlotte Brontë (1816 1855) remarked that she imagined herself a Great princess of the Arabian Nights, a reference to the exotic tales of adventure and erotica that had been translated into French and English in the eighteenth century.
GI2.1 Arab Hall of Lord Leighton’s house, mosaic, 1877–1879.
Leighton House, London.
There has never been a time when Western Europe was not in some kind of contact with people from this part of the world.
Even before Islam and the Crusades, there was plenty of interchange both militarily and commercially.
The Latin alphabet derives from the Egyptian Semitic acrophonic abjad by way of the Phoenician abjad and Greek alphabet.
Alexander the Great and the Roman Empire both conquered this region.
Almost all the Silk Roads ran through this area.
The people of this region were responsible for a lot of the technology transfer of things like paper and printing from China westward to Europe.
Mathematics, too, and HinduArabic numerals.
In terms of design, Umayyad Spain was significant as the point of entry for West Asian ideas and technologies and styles to enter Europe (for example, the Alhambra, and the paper mill at Xátiva, Spain, which was the very first one in Europe).
Furthermore, the block-printing of amulets that happened in Egypt in the 1000s1100s also made its way northward to Spain.
After that, the Crusaders brought back silk textiles with (often, but not always, Kufic) Arabic script on them and used them as shrouds for saints or as liturgical vestments (or for other Christian purposes) in Europe, despite the Arabic script often praising Allah or Muhammad (for instance, the Shroud of St.
Josse).
As early as the early 1300s, Italian paintings of the Virgin Mary by artists such as Duccio and Giotto featured pseudo-Kufic ornament and Mongolian Phags-pa script in the embroidered borders of their robes.
The decorative arts of the Arab-Islamic world were widespread and highly developed, characterized generally by intricate geometric and floral patterns in a variety of media ranging from calligraphy interspersed on elaborately decorated pages of books (for example, the Koran) to woven textiles, carpets, ceramics, metalwork, glass, ivory, and wood carving.
These goods reached both Western Europe and East Asia via trade and exchange; examples include the Turkish carpets and precious blue-and-white Persian vases depicted in scenes of the Annunciation and other religious and secular subjects in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century paintings during the Renaissance in Italy and Northern Europe.
Bottle (ashkdan), Iran, 19th century, mold-blown glass, height 6 in (15 cm).
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
In the nineteenth century, exchange between the Arab-Islamic world and Western Europe expanded greatly, with Western producers and merchants negotiating trade agreements with their Arab-Islamic counterparts for raw materials, minerals, and the import and export of manufactured products.
Turkey, with Istanbul the capital of a weakened Ottoman Empire, as well as the semi-autonomous states of Tunisia, Persia, and Egypt, invested in modernizing reforms (known as Tanzimat) that included education, infrastructure, industrial technology, aspects of dress, and urbanization that created closer (and often dependent) political and economic relations with the West, while at the same time preserving distinctive features of their Arab-Islamic heritage, including religion, traditional aspects of dress, diet, and the vestiges of a nomadic heritage.
However, it must be remembered that in the nineteenth century, the level and type of interest was different because European countries colonized many of the majority-Muslim countries in the Mediterranean basin, plus India, and what is now Pakistan, Myanmar, and Bangladesh, as well as large parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
They controlled these regions militarily, politically, and commercially, so had a very different kind of interest in them than they had ever had before.
This becomes apparent in the visual arts in important new ways.
First, the French painters (for example, Delacroix and Gérome) who visited Tunisia, Algeria, Egypt, and Morocco returned home and made paintings in especially intense colors.
Second, the European (particularly the British) fascination with Islamic pattern design began.
Owen Jones lavished much praise on the decorative patterns of what he calls the Mohammedan countries and India, too.
What caught the eye of design reformers in England, especially, was the conventionalized, often aniconistic patterns from these regions of the world.
They fitted with the theories nineteenth-century Europeans were promoting about the superiority of conventionalized medieval flat patterns to hyperrealistic modern ones, and their praise of imperfect skilled handicraft over alienating machine manufacture.
Owen Joness plate, titled Arabian, no.
4 (see fig.
4.9), illustrates patterned decoration and Arabic calligraphy (Kufic) taken from a Koran (probably from the fourteenth century) that exemplify both the regions rich geometric and floral elements, and compositional strategies that rely upon repetition, symmetry, color harmonies, and strong figureground contrast.
The border of the partial page to the left of the illustration is decorated with alternating schematized lozenges and flowers in green, reddish-orange, and pink, against a deep blue background, while the border in the starshaped design above consists of vines with green leaves and white flowers with small red buds that are interrupted by red circles divided into six pie-shaped triangular parts or petals.
The central section of these page designs features complex, radiating geometric star-like shapes that are varied and truly kaleidoscopic in their effect.
Jones admired the combination of invention and discipline in such designs and designers respect for twodimensional space that accorded with his universal principles of design (see here).
He was also selective, ignoring examples that included representations of the human figure (proscribed for religious imagery), though hunting and garden scenes with schematic figures on horseback, musicians, and courtesans integrated amid a rich web of vines, trees, and flowers are not uncommon in Arab-Islamic objects intended for secular use.
Aside from serving as a vehicle for categorizing examples by style and broad statements like the one quoted in Chapter 4 (for example, that universal standards of design are obeyed in the best periods of Art, culture played little if any role in Joness The Grammar of Ornament.
The Arab-Islamic world was a source for the discovery and validation of universal principles of design across time and space  Jones and his likeminded British design reform colleagues believed that the rules that governed ornament were constant, could be taught, and would inspire products of consummate quality, competitiveness in world markets, and improved taste for an expanding consuming public, respecting the integrity of two-dimensional surfaces and conventional representation of flowers and other natural objects enshrined in The Grammar.
Western merchants and collectors acquired and even commissioned examples of the Arab-Islamic decorative arts.
English painter Frederic Leightons Kensington home and studio included an Arab Hall (187779, see fig.
GI2.1).
The tiled walls of this room feature large, rectangular seventeenth-century blue-and-white earthenware tiles, possibly of Syrian origin, with repeated grape cluster and leaf motifs within connected lozengeshaped frames.
Leighton (18301896) collected examples of Persian tiles and vases (the latter located in niches in the illustration), augmented by purchases he made from diplomats and other friends who spent time in the region.
While Leightons wealthy father disapproved of his sons purchases, the younger Leighton defended his collection as a wise investment.
English ceramic artist William de Morgan (18391917) provided advice as well as ceramic tiles to match those Leighton had acquired.
De Morgans own ceramic vessels and plates relied heavily upon interpretations of high-quality Turkish and Persian glazed pottery from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (see here and fig.
6.7).
American artist and designer Louis Comfort Tiffanys series of slender glass flasks was inspired by nineteenth-century Persian mold-blown glass bottles known as ashkdans (fig.
GI2.2), with gently curved swan-like necks and swirling ribbed surfaces.
Art historian and curator Aimée E.
Froom notes that ashkdans are believed to have been used (perhaps symbolically) to collect the tears of wives while their husbands were away.
Wooden door, from the official descriptive and illustrated catalog of the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, part 5: Foreign States, division II, and index (London: Spicer Brothers, 1851).
The Arab-Islamic decorative vocabulary found in Joness illustrations for The Grammar persisted into the nineteenth century, as seen in a page from the catalog of the Crystal Palace exhibition that illustrates a contemporary example of a carved wooden door from the fairs Tunisian Court (fig.
GI2.3).
Here, too, are the radiating geometric star-shaped patterns found in the Arabian plates of The Grammar of Ornament.
While traditional patterns and artisanal production techniques continued in the Arab-Islamic world, and certainly appealed to Jones as he assembled examples for The Grammar of Ornament, the practices of West Asian and North African artisans in the nineteenth century were not static and artists did not simply reproduce time-honored traditions.
The decorative arts in these regions developed internally, attesting to their vitality in response to competition and increased contact with the arts of Western Europe.
For instance, fig.
GI2.4 illustrates one of a series of thirty-six tiles that decorated the interior of a room in the nineteenth-century mansion of a Persian aristocrat in Iran during the Qajar dynasty (17891925).
One can see why such examples of a living Persian art did not pass muster for Owen Jones.
While the frame and even the leaf and vine background decoration of the tile preserve color choices and motifs found in traditional Islamic decoration, and even the presence of stags and hounds is common in courtly imagery, the treatment of the subject is decidedly pictorial, with a ground line, illusionistic space, and tonal gradations to suggest volume and weight, though the dogs nipping at the stag at the bottom of the tile seem to inhabit a separate scene with its own horizon!
Qajar dado tile, Iran, Qajar period, 19th century, stone paste; polychrome painted under transparent glaze, 27 <sup>1</sup>/ × 19 <sup>3</sup>/ × 2 in (69.2 × 50.2 × 5.1 cm).
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
At the Crystal Palace exhibition in London in 1851, the display from Tunisia contained close to 300 samples of raw materials (including a Bedouin tent made of animal hides, and minerals to convey the abundant natural resources in the region), as well as almost 200 examples of carpets, woven silks, wood carvings (fig.
GI2.3), and precious metalwork displayed in cases or under glass: a total of around 500 objects and samples.
The chromolithograph in fig.
GI2.5 depicts a partial view of the Tunisian Court.
The official exhibition catalog notes that the Tunisian court resembled a bazaar: while no items were offered for sale, they included price tags, and the text accompanying the illustration describes the seated figure (identified by name) as squatting (though he looks to be seated on a ledge or counter) wearing a picturesque costume, speaking loudly in Arabic, and gesturing energetic[ally], projecting the ambience of an Arab market where bargaining with merchants is part of the experience of shopping (for tourists as well as locals), indeed, an element of Arab-Islamic cultural identity (and difference) that is also depicted in paintings and illustrations of the period.
At the far end of the display in the illustration and above the two figures to the left foreground, one sees hanging textiles or rugs.
The nearby Persian Court (located across the aisle from the central Crystal Fountain) featured woven rugs, many of them ordered by English merchants who, in turn, commissioned local artisans and often determined the styles and textures that might appeal to the European market.
While furnishings and textiles from West Asia and North Africa were prized for their quality, craftsmanship, and authenticity, it is likely that the raw silk used in workshops to weave hangings or articles of clothing was imported rather than produced locally.
Expanded production, free trade, and the hope of reaching new markets broke down barriers between nations and conditioned to some extent the practices of design and production; while nationalism and national identity played a major role in a competitive international market, the world of commerce, and by extension the world of design, was increasingly interdependent, much as it is today.
“Tunis No.
2,” plate from Dickinson’s Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851, London, Dickinson Brothers, 1851.
Advocates of design reform admired the quality of the manufactured goods from Tunisia and other West Asian states at the Crystal Palace: among the first items purchased for the South Kensington Museum (founded after the conclusion of the exhibition and renamed the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1899) were 17 Tunisian textiles.
The illustrated catalog of the exhibition, published by The Art Journal, remarked that a Tunisian basket in silver filigree belongs to those delicate and beautiful works which must be seen to be fully appreciated, ... and exhibits all the patient manipulation and elaborate ornament which we associate more with eastern climes than with our own northern latitude.

## Orientalism
In light of the fairs overarching and Eurocentric theme of technology as the engine of progress, some observers remarked that artisans from Tunisia and other parts of the Arab-Islamic world were slow to adopt modern manufacturing techniques for their products, resulting in high prices, a wealthy, exclusive clientele, and declining wages for workers in order to remain competitive with the products of more industrialized nations.
Tunisian ruler Ahmad Bey (reigned 183755) welcomed the invitation to participate in the exhibition and was eager to encourage trade and adopt elements of Western-style modernization, but displays such as the large tent made of animal pelts suggested to critics a culture that was primitive in comparison with a European standard of living thought to be modern and superior.
Nonetheless, design reformers like Jones admired the handmade objects such as carpets from Persia, Tunisia, and India, seeing them as a lesson for manufacturers.
The combination of praise and criticism, envy and condescension, is characteristic of European attitudes toward cultural difference in the middle and later nineteenth century.
Though Europeans greatly admired the works made by people from these regions, they at the same time scorned the people who made the work as backward and barbaric, in need of civilizing and modernizing. Even as Europeans said they were trying to civilize and modernize (i.e., assimilate) the people of this region, they were simultaneously co-opting their traditional aesthetics into their own (European) design playbook (quite literally, in the case of Owen Joness Grammar of Ornament).
Nineteenthcentury design reformers, especially, thought adopting aniconistic Islamic ornamental design/flat patterns would improve or reinvigorate Western flat pattern design that had become over-civilized, enfeebled, and degenerate. Womens clothes became brighter in the late 1800s after the invention of mauve and aniline dyes, and European patterns got more abstract, at least at the high end of the market where the reformers had some sway, culminating in the later Japanese-inspired patterns of the Arts and Crafts movement.
The wealth, luxury, and sensuality associated with courtly life in West Asia and North Africa produced a school of Orientalist painting in France and England.
English artist John Frederick Lewiss painting titled The Harem dating to c.
1851 (fig.
GI2.6) is among the more chaste examples of the genre, which continued well into the twentieth century.
A group of women lounge causally, attended by dark-skinned servants.
The women are dressed in an array of loose-fitting (and in one case low-cut) garments (contrasting with the tightly corseted dresses worn in England at the time); in the interior, carved wooden screens and poly-lobed horseshoe-arched windows gently filter light falling into the room from the right.
The setting is that of a harem, reinforcing stereotypes of polygamous, lustful sultans and promiscuous concubines found in the tales of the Arabian Nights.
Lewis (18041876) lived in Egypt for a period of ten years but most likely was never permitted to view a harems private quarters.
He painted this and other harem scenes in his London studio from his imagination after his return, using props he acquired during his travels in the Mediterranean, Egypt, and Turkey to impart a sense of verisimilitude.
John Frederic Lewis, The Harem, c.
1851, oil on panel, 35 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 44 ¾ in (91.1 × 114 cm), Birmingham City Museum & Art Galleries.
Many scholars note the unequal power relationship between Western European nations and West Asia and North Africa, pointing to trade agreements favorable to the West, along with increasing imperial expansion and colonization, beginning with the French occupation of Algeria in the 1830s, followed by Tunisia becoming a French protectorate in the early 1880s, and British control of Egypt.
Increasingly this controlling viewpoint or gaze found expression at Worlds Fairs, with observers praising the products of West Asia and North Africa as precious but also technologically backward, indicative of a less highly developed stage of civilization than the more rational and disciplined Western nations.
Displays tended to support a Western bias that combined a romantic attraction to an authentic, pre-industrial culture with a sense of technological and moral superiority.
Countries such as Tunisia sought to project an identity that communicated compatibility between Arab-Islamic tradition and modernizing reforms based upon European models for education, urban infrastructure (with rulers often hiring Western architects to design buildings and residences), and dress (the short conical felt fez hat was part of the Tanzimat reforms mentioned above, here), but the reception of such efforts by European visitors was not always positive.
Although on the one hand admired as models of skill and respect for universal principles of decoration, on the other hand, the work of these craftsmen was also prone to demeaning cultural stereotypes, the result of a controlling, Eurocentric gaze that reduced cultural difference to a set of hierarchical ethnic tropes that included a pre-modern nomadic way of life, duplicity in commercial practice, a penchant for violence, tyranny, the subordination of women, and an unbridled appetite for sex.
Such attitudes became more prevalent as the Worlds Fairs began to include separate national pavilions in the later nineteenth century (rather than courts within a single, large structure), seen, for instance, in the Tunisian pavilion at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, illustrated in a weekly periodical that featured a staged Turkish Café with slouching musicians and an exotic dancer.
At the 1867 Exposition Universelle in Paris, a life-size diorama depicted in gruesome detail a pair of lions attacking a Bedouin riding a camel, another example of Orientalism.
The diorama was purchased by the American Museum of Natural History in New York, displayed again in Philadelphia in 1876 for the Centennial Worlds Fair, and now resides in a large glass case in the entry foyer to the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
III Arts, Crafts, and Machines: Reconciling Progress and Fears of Industrialization (1866–1914) n the second half of the nineteenth century in Britain and extending to Europe and North America, the efforts of the early design reform movement dovetailed with other reform initiatives that contributed to elevating the cultural significance of the applied arts.
Beginning in the later 1850s, the writings and activities of John Ruskin and William Morris in England placed the design and manufacture of the applied arts within a revitalized ethical framework based upon an almost religious conviction that united craft and art with social, and often radical political, change directed against industrial capitalism.
Ruskin and Morris criticized the dehumanizing consequences of mechanization and the increasing division of labor in factories, and their efforts inspired others who established workshops, crafts organizations, and crafts communities on both sides of the Atlantic dedicated to the individual human and social benefits of handicraft as a replacement for, or antidote to, the often alienating effects of an urban, industrialized world.
While never unified and often quite varied, the results of Ruskin’s and Morris’s activities are generally referred to as the Arts and Crafts movement.
The immediate context for the elevation of craft in aesthetic and social terms was a widening gap between fine and applied art in the West, but a broader cultural perspective included the threat to human rights, sovereignty, and self-determination posed by industrial expansion and imperialism.
Only slightly later, and again in North America, Britain, and throughout Europe, a number of architects and fine artists began to direct their creative activities to interior design and home furnishings.
These designers called attention to the aesthetic and expressive character of the home and its decoration as a “total work of art,” emphasizing originality and the unity and integration of all the visual arts.
At the same time, a number of younger designers sought to reconcile individual expression with issues of manufacturability and competition, forming organizations and publishing journals that highlighted the value of practicality and the shaping of public taste.
Their initiatives reached a broader public through participation in the increasing number of well-attended national and international exhibitions both in Europe and in the United States.
The continued expansion of commerce and industrial manufacturing hastened the search for new markets and the need for increasing supplies of raw materials.
The vast natural resources of the African continent were a target for exploitation through Western colonization in the name of progress, and this is the focus of Part III of the Global Inspiration (see here): Britain, France, and Belgium each competed for control of African territory, accompanied by the often brutal subjugation of Indigenous populations used as enslaved laborers in the mining and rubber industries.
The colonization of the Congo by King Leopold II of Belgium beginning in 1885 left its mark on Belgian decorative arts and utilitarian objects through the use of imported ivory and rubber, and imagery that suggested power, violence, and domination.
African societies had a well-developed and varied materia culture that included locally produced dyed and woven fabrics for dress, scarification, and ritual, as well as utilitarian objects with distinctive forms and decoration.
A small number of European companies designed and manufactured textiles for the African market that are still being produced today (see here and here).
In the United States, printed advertising and illustrated mail-order catalogs beginning in the 1880s spurred demand for and access to manufactured goods and furnishings, accompanied by new methods of rationalized and mechanized production as well as branding and national distribution.
The success of the department store beginning in the 1860s also stimulated the marketing of manufactured goods to an expanding consumer-oriented middle class.
Such democratizing tendencies produced a wide variety of historicizing styles such as the Renaissance and Rococo Revivals as well as more original or “modern” approaches to design recommended by tastemakers such as Charles Eastlake in his Hints on Household Taste, first published in 1868 and directed toward cultivating a discriminating judgment among a female readership (see here).
Finally, with Germany and the Austro-Hungarian Empire playing important roles, designers, design organizations, schools, and exhibition organizers sought to address and reconcile what were seen as conflicting attitudes toward technology, standardization, ornament, national identity, and the scientific management of production on the one hand and individual identity and self-expression on the other.
This was aimed at maximizing production efficiency and reforming the tastes of middle-class consumers by establishing and reinforcing more standardized and socially responsible forms for modern manufactured goods.
Amid various debates and activities on an increasingly global scale, the aesthetic, technical, commercial, and social meanings of the applied arts enlarged the scope of design enterprise activity in the years leading up to World War I.

## Chapter
5 The Joy of Work Ruskin, Morris, and the Arts and Crafts Movement in Britain English writer and art critic John Ruskin (18191900) played an important role in shaping attitudes toward the decorative arts in the second half of the nineteenth century.
Like his fellow Englishman A.
W.
N.
Pugin, Ruskin admired the crafts of the Middle Ages and saw the decorative arts as a vehicle for enlightenment, both for the artisans who made goods and furnishings and for the public who might own and appreciate them.
The values he attached to the Gothic style, however, concerned the nature of work, an elevated view of labor, which he felt was fundamentally undermined by mechanization, the division of labor, and a capitalist system that increasingly alienated workers from the products of their efforts in the name of progress. For Ruskin, the specialization inherent in the division of labor, and commercial pressures that stimulated cheaper, faster production, deprived workers of the satisfaction of making products from start to finish as he believed they were made in the guilds during the Middle Ages: We have much studied and much perfected, of late, the great civilized invention of the division of labour; only we give it a false name.
It is not, truly speaking, the labour that is divided; but the men: divided into mere segments of men  broken into small fragments and crumbs of life; so that all the little piece of intelligence that is left in a man is not enough to make a pin, or a nail, but exhausts itself in making the point of a pin or the head of a nail.
Ruskins views on art and design drew in part upon his own travels and careful observations and drawings of architecture and decoration; the sensitivity he developed to the working methods of craftsmen formed the basis for conclusions about the nature of craft and inspired sweeping, if unrealistic, solutions to the social ills of an industrial society.
In looking at carved architectural ornament from the Gothic period, Ruskin admired the dialogue between artisan and materials, the imperfections, the differences between one carved capital and another, the struggle to overcome the resistance of stone or wood with the tools at hand in the realization of an idea.
The methods of the craftsman were, for Ruskin, the basis for satisfying work and an equality among the arts in which craftsman and artist alike shared in the redeeming act of human labor.
Ruskin deplored the machine, because machines made work easy or just plain dull, and because they resulted in uniform products lacking the individuality of their handmade counterparts: All the stamped metals, and artificial stones, and imitation woods and bronzes, over the invention of which we hear daily exultation  all the short, and cheap, and easy ways of doing that whose difficulty is its honour  are just so many new obstacles in our already encumbered road.
They will not make one of us happier or wiser  they will extend neither the pride of judgement nor the privilege of enjoyment.
They will only make us shallower in our understandings, colder in our hearts, and feebler in our wits.
It probably comes as no surprise that Ruskin was no admirer of Joseph Paxtons Crystal Palace, for no cast-iron structure, regardless of its grand proportions or economy of construction, could aspire to being art in the sense of having been the product of the direct manipulation of materials that Ruskin understood to be the essence of all artistic endeavor.
Ruskin questioned the equation between technology and progress as the defining characteristic of modern civilization, raising awareness of loss as well as gain, much as critics today debate the role played by robots and artificial intelligence and the ways they impact contemporary life.
In addition to his analysis of the cultural meaning of art and architecture, Ruskin articulated his views with a renewed sense of urgency regarding social reform.
The only child of a wealthy wine merchant and the beneficiary of a comfortable inheritance, Ruskin was nevertheless sensitive to the levels of poverty, unemployment, and poor working conditions in Britain.
He felt a sense of social conscience and responsibility not uncommon among wealthy families of his day, which found outlets in political activism, philanthropy, and other private initiatives aimed at the well-being of the poor and working classes.
Rather than applauding the economic expansion and increased productivity of his own time, he blamed industrialization and materialism for exacerbating income inequality and misery, and saw the restoration of meaningful work as a means to alleviate them.
Indeed, his exaltation of labor may be seen as a compensation for his own loss of faith, for if religion provided little comfort to humanity in a materialistic modern world, then it might be replaced by some substitute spirituality.
For Ruskin, that substitute was the happiness provided by work, and thus the products of work acquired a spiritual dimension.
It follows that if labor was its own reward, then the technological and material progress of the nineteenth century represented for Ruskin only a kind of empty materialism that ignored the spiritual values that should inform an ideal society: The foundations of society were never yet shaken as they are at this day.
It is not that men are ill-fed, but that they have no pleasure in the work by which they make their bread, and therefore look to wealth as the only means of pleasure. [Italics authors own] Earlier in his career, Ruskin had championed the cause of the British landscape painter J.
M.
W.
Turner (17751851) in his book Modern Painters, vol.
1 (he appears in the 2014 biopic Mr.
Turner with Ruskin played by Joshua McGuire), but Ruskin grew to question whether the uplifting qualities embodied in Turners works would enrich the lives of working people.
Ruskin then focused his attention on the decorative arts because their cost as well as their utility might have a greater impact upon the workers who made and might enjoy them.
Work was a common element in the lives of both the middle and working classes, a basis for social equality linked to mutual respect among people.
Unlike Pugin or Owen Jones, it was joy rather than taste that governed Ruskins attitudes: The right question to ask, respecting all ornament, is simply this: Was it done with enjoyment  was the carver happy while he was about it?
It may be the hardest work possible, and the harder because so much pleasure was taken in it; but it must have been happy too, or it will not be living.
In other words, Ruskin advocated no particular style or set of rules for designers to follow other than that the work be a unique creation reflecting a craftsmans skill, pride, and effort.
His views share with designers of the Aesthetic Movement an interest in individuality (see Chapter 6), but Ruskins overriding emphasis was upon the moral and spiritual benefits of handwork, that is, as much upon the doing as upon the finished product.
While Ruskin remained primarily a writer and theorist commenting on the relationship between art and society, William Morris (18341896) was more interested in integrating theory with real-world practice.
Like Ruskin, Morris came from a wealthy middle-class background and benefited from an annual income from his familys investment in the lucrative copper-mining industry, yet he also possessed a strong sense of social conscience and responsibility characteristic of the Victorian age.
As a student at Oxford preparing for a career in the clergy, he was deeply moved by Ruskins ideas concerning the relation between the arts and social reform, and also shared friendship and ideals with a group of young Romantic artists and poets who called themselves the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (PRB).
The group criticized modern materialism and industrialization and was committed to creating a closer relation between art and craft in reaction against the established policies of the Royal Academy in Britain and the elevated status it accorded the fine arts.
It was Morriss kinship with the PRB that led him to abandon his training for the ministry and pursue a career as an artist-craftsman, with art equated to any form of making. One can detect the echo of Ruskin in Morriss own writings, which had a lasting effect upon designers in the later nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and which find echoes in phrases such as learning by doing that stress direct skill-based education: Yet I cannot in my own mind quite sever them [the arts of architecture, painting, and sculpture] from those so-called Decorative Arts ... it is only in latter times, and under the most intricate conditions of life, that they have fallen apart from one another; I hold that, when they are so parted, it is ill for the Arts altogether; the lesser ones become trivial, mechanical, unintelligent, incapable of resisting the changes pressed upon them by fashion or dishonesty; while the greater, however they may be practiced for a while by men of great minds and wonder-working hands, unhelped by the lesser, unhelped by each other, are sure to lose their dignity as popular arts, and become nothing but dull adjuncts to unmeaning pomp, or ingenious toys for a few rich and idle men.
In addition, Morris was a poet, novelist, publisher, social activist, translator, preservationist, and public speaker, whose myriad interests and activities proved influential in Britain, Germany, Belgium, France, and the United States (in fact, Morriss writings were influential even for those, such as Frank Lloyd Wright, who freely interpreted his views).
The spiritualization of craft, its connection with social justice, and skepticism toward the widely held view that equated industrialization with progress characterize Morriss values and became the basis for a number of organizations and related initiatives that are known generally as the Arts and Crafts movement.
Morriss design activities began with the interior decoration of his home, Red House, in Kent, beginning in 1858, and designed by his friend Philip Webb (18311915).
The house eschewed the tendency toward historicizing period styles as well as expensive (or expensive-looking) materials in favor of straightforward brick and painted wood, modest Gothic pointed arches, and a less formal, asymmetrical plan.
Rather than purchase furnishings from a catalog or commission them from a showroom or workshop, Morris and his friends took on the task themselves.
At the outset, Morriss wife, Jane (18391914), took an interest in embroidery, while Webb, painter Edward Burne-Jones (18331898), and poet and artist Dante Gabriel Rossetti (18281882, a member of the PRB) designed furniture and stained-glass windows.
The ideal of a more direct and self-sufficient lifestyle appealed to Morris, who later wrote, If I were asked to say what is at once the most important production of Art and the thing most to be longed for I should answer, A beautiful House. In 1861 he formed Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., opening a showroom in London, for the design and manufacture of a wide variety of furnishings, including furniture, wallpapers, textiles, stained glass, carpets, woven tapestries, and ceramics.
In 1875 Morris reorganized the venture as Morris & Co.
The company, or Firm, as it was known, put Morriss ideas into wider practice and might be considered the beginning of the Arts and Crafts movement.
An example of the Firms furniture is the Sussex line of chairs with handwoven rush seats using turned spindles for legs and backs. Sussex chairs were designed by Webb and Rossetti, but were based upon country examples found in southeast England (fig.
5.1).
Such furnishings established a link with pre-industrial craft traditions only minimally affected by contemporary commercial practice or by the use of more modern machine tools and materials.
Not all furniture manufactured by the Firm was economical or even restrained in decoration  indeed individuality, the love of nature, and the joy of work all contributed to the Arts and Crafts movement, and found expression in ornament.
Armchair from the Sussex range, possibly designed by Philip Webb, ebonized beech with rush seat, 33 $^ 3 / _ { 4 } \times 2 0 \ ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times$ 17 in (86.6 × 52.4 × 43 cm), c.
1860, manufactured by Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
As a craftsman himself, Morris first relied upon his training as a painter in the design of stained-glass windows and the painted decoration of wooden furniture; from the 1870s onward he primarily designed patterns that were applied to the manufacture of ceramic tiles, embroideries, wood-blocks for wallpaper or fabric printing, and carpets.
In many cases Morris relied upon local craftsmen to execute his designs, but he also practiced techniques himself, installing equipment at home, first in London then in the western suburb of Hammersmith after 1878.
He also leased facilities for weaving at Merton Abbey, Surrey, where he experimented in the development of vegetable dyes for fabrics rather than commercially available aniline dyes, patented in 1856 and produced as a by-product of coal tar.
For ceramics he seems to have entrusted production to artistcraftsman William de Morgan (18391917; see here and fig.
6.7), an independent potter who had worked previously for the Firm, and who also produced his own designs, including tiles for the home of Lord Frederic Leighton (see fig.
GI2.1).
Whether directly or indirectly involved in actual production, Morris advocated close collaboration between designer and craftsman and refused to use machines even for the printing of blocked wallpapers or fabrics: It is not desirable to divide the labour between the artist and what is technically called the designer, and I think it desirable on the whole that the artist and designer should practically be one. Here Morris describes a fluid working method that differs from the collaborative but hierarchical relationship between artist and craftsman, where the craftsman carries out the creative design of the artist.
Morriss own pattern designs seem to follow the general tendency of earlier design reform principles that viewed decoration in the context of architecture, that is, as planar, if often rich, patterns that embellished construction; it was the unity and implied collaboration in his understanding of architecture that guided his approach.
He also believed in the importance of individual expression, and advocated original designs in addition to those inspired by the decorative patterns in medieval illuminated manuscripts that he admired and collected.
We might think of Morriss patterns as a dialogue, often tense, between a love of the richness and diversity of nature found in plants and flowers and the discipline needed to transform that appreciation into patterns suitable for the embellishment of flat surfaces.
An example is his Pimpernel wallpaper of 1876 (fig.
5.2).
Against a dark green background, lighter green flowers are symmetrically arranged and repeated, but varied in their positions; each is framed by interlocking spiral vine tendrils in brown loosely entwined by thin green leaves.
A secondary motif consists of smaller and flatter green leaves with round blue morning glories placed at regular intervals along the stems.
The naturalism is at its height in the windswept flowers and their undulating contours, slightly reduced for the thin leaf forms and becoming more schematic for the blue flowers, tendrils, and smaller oval leaves.
The sense of natures luxuriant variety and vitality, and the care with which the designer preserves this freshness within the constraints of pattern for a two-dimensional surface, is remarkable in much of Morriss best work.
