The firm of Morris & Co. was commercially successful during the 1860s and $1 8 7 0 \mathrm { s } ,$ profiting from bespoke commissions to design and execute stained-glass windows and other furnishings for churches, as well as private orders from wealthy clients for comprehensive furnishings in domestic interiors.
These patrons could afford the labor costs of Morriss production methods and shared his vision for a just society based upon independent, satisfying work.
In 1866 Morris & Co. designed and produced the Green Dining Room at the South Kensington (now Victoria and Albert) Museum in London, commissioned as a lunchroom for visitors, restored in the 1990s, and still in operation today (fig.
5.3).
The interior is coordinated through a wall-treatment of painted vinescroll patterns in molded and painted stucco relief, rug, stained glass, lighting, ceramic panels, painted panels with repeated figural and plant motifs, and painted furniture, all intended to convey the love of nature transformed through the artists imagination and skill.
The Green Room, which opened to the working classes on Sundays when they were admitted free of charge to the South Kensington Museum, enabled Morris to unite his ideal of art as mans pleasure in labor with his hope of making art the basis for a satisfying life and an egalitarian society.
5.3 Morris & Co., the Green Dining Room, Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1866.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
In addition to operating facilities at his residence and leasing separate facilities for production in and around London, Morris & Co. maintained a storefront showroom on Oxford Street, London, where other fashionable retail establishments were located, and the Firm exhibited work at Worlds Fairs, for instance in London in 1862 and at the Centennial Exhibition held in Philadelphia in 1876.

## Morris,
Activism, and Socialism Despite the success of the Firm, and projects such as the Green Room that were open to the public, Morris became increasingly disillusioned by the inability of his design activities to effect broad social change and to reach his intended working-class audience.
Labor and material costs precluded all but the wealthy from commissioning or purchasing the Firms products, and his views on labor and society were mostly embraced by a well-to-do clientele motivated by conscience to contribute to the wellbeing of the working class.
In the 1880s he became actively involved with the socialist movement in Britain as a means of creating social equality and reducing the pressures for production and consumption that fueled the capitalist economic system and an aggressive foreign policy: What I mean by Socialism is a condition of society in which there should be neither rich nor poor, neither master nor masters man, neither idle nor overworked, neither brain-sick brain workers nor heart-sick hand workers ... in which all men would be living in equality of condition, and would manage their affairs unwastefully and with the full consciousness that harm to one would mean harm to all  the realization at last of the meaning of the word COMMONWEALTH.
Another recurrent theme in his writings, echoing Ruskin, is the excessive self-interest that was created by competition: Manufacturers are so set on carrying out competition to its utmost, competition of cheapness, not of excellence, that they meet the bargain-hunters half way, and cheerfully furnish them with many wares at the cheap rate.
Morris was active in organized socialist activities in London, and his views, delivered in public speeches and in the journal he founded entitled The Commonweal, echo themes of alienated labor, the concentration of wealth and growth of capital in partnership with industry in quest of profit, and the fetishism of commodities found in the writings of Karl Marx (18181883) and Friedrich Engels (18201895).
Morriss politics were radical; he sensed that it was not enough merely to make and enjoy handmade objects as a craftsman and socially conscious businessman, and that real change would only come with more direct political activism to foment working-class revolution.
But while Morriss ideology was opposed to industrial capitalism in terms of the economic inequality it brought, he could not account for or effectively fight the increasing attraction of consumption (and shopping) across all classes of modern society.
Ironically, the success of Morris & Co. depended almost entirely upon an exclusive market, thus in a sense it was supported by the same capitalist system he hoped to eliminate.
Eventually Morris acknowledged a role for mechanization in the production of goods and furnishings, particularly if it reduced drudgery.
But his acceptance of the machine was narrowly circumscribed and he felt that mechanization should never deprive a craftsman of the opportunity to find pleasure in work.
Nevertheless his views appear to have become, not without some irony, the basis for the later equation of machine-made goods with simple designs and smooth surfaces: The more mechanical the process, the less direct should be the imitation of natural forms. Such an approach, an extension of the design reform dictum of truth to materials, was espoused by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright (18691959), whose own attitudes toward the machine are considered below (see here; 142).

## Morris
as Publisher William Morriss last design venture was the founding of the Kelmscott Press in 1890, which brought together his attitudes toward art and design with his activities as poet and author.
The press printed an illustrated edition of his own poem Story of the Glittering Plain as well as a short volume containing Ruskins Nature of Gothic chapter from The Stones of Venice, which eloquently praised the dignity of work.
In Morriss introduction to the Nature of Gothic, he wrote: For the lesson which Ruskin here teaches us is that art is the expression of mans pleasure in labour; that it is possible for man to rejoice in his work, for, strange as it may seem to us to-day, there have been times when he did rejoice in it; and lastly, that unless mans work once again becomes a pleasure to him, the token of which change will be that beauty is once again a natural and necessary accompaniment of productive labour, all but the worthless must toil in pain, and therefore live in pain.
So that the result of the thousands of years of mans effort on the earth must be general unhappiness and universal degradation; unhappiness and degradation, the conscious burden of which will grow in proportion to the growth of mans intelligence, knowledge, and power over material nature.
Morriss close friend Edward Burne-Jones designed woodcut illustrations for another Kelmscott Press publication, The Kelmscott Chaucer (fig.
5.4), while Morris himself designed border patterns for pages with illustrations, as well as the Latin typeface and block initials of various sizes.
The Kelmscott Chaucer used a calligraphic typeface with characteristics of Gothic (Blackletter) letter forms that Morris drew, and which he called Troy, one of three faces he designed for the press.
His Roman font, known as Golden, was influenced by fifteenth-century printers working in Venice such as Jacobus Rubeus and Nicholas Jenson, who were responsible for some of the very first Roman (as opposed to Blackletter) types beginning around 1470.
Morriss Golden avoided the mechanical precision of modern fonts (see figs.
1.13 and 1.14) in favor of heavier forms with modulated transition from thick to thin strokes and the low x-height characteristic of fifteenth-century Venetian models.
Morriss interest in these Venetian types, sometimes known as humanistic, in turn stimulated a revival of letterpress printing known as the Private Press Movement.
The richly decorated pages of The Kelmscott Chaucer fulfilled Morriss objective to make the book itself an object of beauty, even if some historians find many of its more elaborate pages less well suited to reading, perhaps a result of the distraction from elements other than type.
The Kelmscott Press was located at the artists home in Hammersmith on the bank of the Thames river.
The venture emerged at a time when photomechanical reproduction was transforming the character of illustration, and when steam presses were finally being introduced into the bookpublishing industry.
Inspired by the example of the nearby Chiswick Press (see here) and the independent efforts of printers and other craftsmen to maintain the craft traditions of the printed book, Morris succeeded in revitalizing fine printing, even if the cost of such efforts limited their readership, generally attracting only a well-to-do clientele and published in short print runs.
William Morris (wood-engraved illustrations after designs by Edward Burne-Jones), folio from The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, 16 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 11 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (42.5 × 29.2 cm), printed at the Kelmscott Press, London, 1896.
Cheltenham Art Gallery and Museums.
Morriss Kelmscott Press was one among several private publishing ventures initiated in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.
Illustrated books, art journals, and a burgeoning illustrated childrens literature constituted the means by which the Arts and Crafts movement reached different audiences.
Publishing is a collaborative enterprise, and a number of printers, founders, binders, and illustrators participated in Morriss Kelmscott Press venture.
Emery Walker (1851 1933), for instance, worked as a printer at the Chiswick Press not far from where Morris lived.
Prior to the establishment of the Kelmscott Press, Walker had contributed to The Hobby Horse journal, published by the Century Guild (see here).
After Morriss death in 1896, Walker and lawyer-turned-bookbinder T.
J.
Cobden-Sanderson (18401922) founded their own publishing company known as the Doves Press, also in Hammersmith (in fact, directly across the alley from Kelmscott on the Thames riverside).
Their efforts combined concerns for the quality of paper and ink, the aesthetics of calligraphy, legibility in type and the spacing of lines and letters, ample white space, harmonious relationships among borders, initials, and illustration, and the overall unity of the page or open double page.
Walker designed a Roman font for the press (called Doves), while the calligrapher and teacher Edward Johnston (18721944) designed initials, often printed in red, to enliven the page layouts, as seen in a page from the Doves Bible, printed between 1903 and 1905 (fig.
5.5).
The Doves Press embodies the idea of the book as a work of craft and beauty that achieves a unified interrelationship of its parts.
Its margins are ample, the initials and title lettering fluid and elegant (recalling a restrained form of the hand-painted initials in early printed books), and the typeface equally refined.
It has a taller x-height for lower-case letters and an ample use of white space not found in the darker and shorter forms of Morriss Golden font, but resulting in a purity and restraint in comparison to the busier pages of The Kelmscott Chaucer.
A rift between the two partners of the Doves Press resulted in its closure in 1916.
It must have been quite a disagreement: one day Cobden-Sanderson threw the Doves types (and matrices, presumably) off Hammersmith Bridge into the Thames so that Walker would never be able to use them.

## 5.5 First page of the Doves Bible, 13 <sup>5</sup>/ × 9 <sup>1</sup>/ in (33.8 × 23.5 cm),
Doves Press, Hammersmith, London, 1903–1905.
Library of Congress, Washington, DC.
Toward the end of his career, Morriss vision for a better society took the form of utopian writings, often published first in serial form in the socialist journal Commonweal.
The romance News from Nowhere (1890) takes place in England in the twenty-second century, but its setting is reminiscent of the riverside village community of Hammersmith where Morris lived and worked.
The books frontispiece illustrates the pathway leading to the eighteenth-century farmhouse known as Kelmscott Manor that Morris purchased and renovated in West Oxfordshire, near to where he is buried: ... all work is now pleasurable; either because of the hope of gain in honour and wealth with which the work is done, which causes pleasurable excitement, even when the actual work is not pleasant; or because it has grown into a pleasurable habit, as in the case with what you may call mechanical work; and lastly (and most of our work is of this kind) because there is conscious sensuous pleasure in the work itself; it is done, that is, by artists ...

## The
Influence of William Morris in Britain William Morriss ideas and example found fertile ground in Britain, continental Europe, and the United States, but his views, touching on the connection among social relations, politics, and design, underwent considerable transformation and wide interpretation.
Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo (18511942) was a friend of both Morris and Ruskin, and traveled with the latter to Italy in 1874.
He also shared with Morris an interest in the preservation of historic buildings.
Mackmurdo designed the woodcut title page of a book that he published privately in 1883 entitled Wren’s City Churches (fig.
5.6), containing illustrations of churches designed by English architect Sir Christopher Wren (16321723).
An architect by training, Mackmurdo advocated the abolition of the distinction between fine and applied art.
He was a founding member of a group of artists who formed the Century Guild, dedicated to the following goals: to render all branches of art the sphere no longer of the tradesman but of the artist, to restore building, decoration, glass painting, potter, wood-carving and metal to their rightful place beside painting and sculpture.
Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo, title page of his Wren’s City Churches, woodcut on paper, 11 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>17</sub> × 8 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (29.2 × 22.25 cm), printed by G.
Allen, Orpington, Kent, 1883.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

## 5.6 5.7 Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo, chair, mahogany with leather upholstery, 38 <sup>1</sup>
/<sub>4</sub> × 19 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 18 $\bar { 1 } ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (97.2 × 49.5 × 47.6 cm), manufactured by the Century Guild, 1883.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
The flamelike shapes for the title page from Wren’s City Churches, framed by two tall birds, are based upon plant forms but clearly are exaggerated and abstracted to create a heightened sense of rhythmic movement, strengthened by the strong contrast between figure and ground.
Banners displaying the title (as well as the letterforms themselves) have the same sense of elastic movement as the floral decoration, and stand out against the larger expanse of white ground.
Mackmurdo used the same design for the back of a chair manufactured by the Century Guild in the same year (fig.
5.7).
The abstract, subjective treatment of natural forms seen in Mackmurdos cover illustration may be compared to contemporary Post-Impressionist painting in France and elsewhere in Europe, seen for instance in Dutch artist Vincent van Goghs still life Irises from 1890 (fig.
5.8), with its twisted leaves, sense of growth and movement, and emphasis upon the flatness of the picture plane.
In 1887 an Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society was founded to organize annual shows of craft objects.
The versatile designer William Lethaby (18571931) established a school in London based upon a close relationship between designer and maker and the practical value underlying and uniting all art: a work of art is first of all a well-made thing.
It may be a well-made statue or a wellmade chair, or a well-made book....
Most simply and generally art may be thought of as the well-doing of what needs doing; every work of art shows that it was made by a human being for a human being.
Other craft associations, both in Britain and the United States (see here), followed in the wake of Morriss efforts to elevate the aesthetic appreciation and egalitarian social values of craft production.
Charles Robert Ashbee (18631942) was another versatile designer and educator who founded a community of workers with the goal of living and working together in utopian harmony.
After graduating from Cambridge University in 1886 Ashbee moved to Toynbee Hall, a residence for university graduates in a workingclass section of London established to rebuild relationships between social classes and improve the lives of workers.
In 1888 Ashbee helped to found the Guild and School of Handicraft, based in Londons East End (this section of the city was associated with high-volume piecework that supplied the furniture industry and that was criticized by social reformers), employing as many as 50 workers.
Ashbees interest in the preservation of craft traditions stemmed from his experience with materials and process as an artist and a belief that the applied arts provided the means for original, satisfying work: the education of the hand and eye are only fully achieved in the education of the individuality of the workman. Ashbees designs respect and explore the nature of handcrafted materials; his work possesses a striking originality in both its slender, attenuated shapes and its respect for the integration of ornament with construction as seen, for instance, in a music cabinet dating to c.
1895 (fig.
5.9).
The cabinets rectangular form and joinery are simple and straightforward, as are the majority of its materials: oak rather than imported or exotic woods, and patinated wrought-iron pullers and hinges (though these are fastened to red leather backings often imported from Africa) and hammered-copper rectangular panels.
The metal decoration reveals the irregular marks of the hammer, while the abstract vine- and leaf-shaped relief forms just as easily resemble the legs of an imaginary spider.
Charles Robert Ashbee, music cabinet, oak, stained green with well-patinated wrought-iron mounts backed by red Morocco leather, c.
1895, 66 $^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 2 7 \times 1 9 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in $( 1 6 8 .
9 \times 6 8 .
6 \times 4 9 .
5$ cm).
The Huntington Library, Art Collections, and Botanical Gardens, San Marino, California.
As early as 1902, Ashbee relocated his guild to the Cotswolds region in rural Gloucestershire (the same general area as Morriss Kelmscott Manor), a move suggesting that the ideals of the Arts and Crafts movement were more compatible amid village rather than urban conditions; instead of posing a threat to the combined forces of capitalism, competition, and industrialization, the ideal of the craft guild became an escape from or antidote to modern alienation, directly for its practitioners and vicariously through those who shared their beliefs as patrons and clients.
After meeting architect Frank Lloyd Wright on a trip to the United States in 1901 and following the economic failure of the Guild and School of Handicraft in 1908, Ashbee came to accept the role of machinery and to admire Wrights efforts to reconcile an elevated view of craft with machine production and social responsibility (see here).
Alongside the Arts and Crafts communities was the Garden City Movement, initiated in England by the American-born reformer Ebenezer Howard (18501928).
Howard sought to remedy the alienation and poor working-class living conditions that accompanied industrial development, envisioning communities of single-family dwellings connected by rail to larger industrial cities.
Here residents could cultivate gardens and preserve the satisfaction of self-sufficient living, independence, and the joy of work that they believed existed in pre-industrial societies.
The Garden City model provided for trees, neighborhood parks, and residential zoning that separated the office, retail shop, or factory from peaceful domestic life.
In separating work from family, however, Howards model also limited the activities of middle-class women to the private sphere, where their primary role was to create a comforting home environment.
Letchworth in Hertfordshire north of London was the first garden city, begun in 1903; its designers were the architects Barry Parker (18671947) and Raymond Unwin (18531941).
Both were sympathetic to Arts and Crafts ideals, and in 1901 had published The Art of Building a Home, a series of lectures illustrated with wood engravings of interiors and plans for homes they had designed.
A photograph of the living room of the Letchworth home known as Crabby Corner (19041905) shows a plain brick wall surrounding a fireplace with a hammered-copper hood, built-in benches and cabinets, and a woven rush-seated chair (at the right below the window) that closely resembles the ladderback chairs produced by Shaker communities and discussed below (see here).
The built-in (fitted) furniture maximizes living space for the type of modest, smaller, middle-class home preferred by the architects (fig.
5.10).
In their lectures, the architects praised the openness of Japanese interiors as they are depicted in colored woodblock prints, and stressed the ideals of honest living based upon need and convenience rather than luxury and display: Let us have in our houses, rooms where there shall be space to carry on the business of life freely and with pleasure, with furniture made for use; rooms ... plain, simple, and ungarnished if necessary, but honest.
Let us have such ornament as we do have really beautiful and wrought by hand, carving, wrought metal, embroidery, painting, something which it has given pleasure to the producer to create, and which shows this in every line  the only possible work of art.
Letchworth interiors promote the pleasures of a wholesome family life, removed from the fast pace, distractions, materialism, and pretensions of urban life.
Not all women found their domestic role satisfying, however, and other housing experiments, especially in the United States, focused upon a shared model of household chores that permitted women to work outside the home (see here).
Barry Parker and Raymond Unwin, view of the interior of Crabby Corner, sepia tint photograph, c.
1904–1905.
Garden City Collection.
Ambrose Heal (18721959) was a London-based furniture-maker whose use of oak and plain, restrained designs was sympathetic to the vision of Garden City planners and architects.
Heals furniture used basic joinery (carpentry) techniques, but his attitude toward technology and the use of machines was pragmatic rather than antagonistic.
He advocated an accommodation to factory (rather than workshop) production, emphasizing product rather than process; as a result, the manufacturer remained responsible for improving the lives of workers not by maintaining craft skills and a closer relationship between designing and making, but by providing affordable goods that defined and contributed to a modest but comfortable lifestyle.
Heals approach to furniture in England has parallels in the United States (see here).
It also relates to models for design education, at the time known generally as Industrial Art. Industrial arts education was a compromise, an attempt to preserve elements of the doctrine of meaningful and satisfying work while acknowledging the advantages of time-saving technology, rationalized production, and the promise they might hold for higher standards of living and the quality of life for middle- and working-class families.
The shift from craft to industrial production was neither sudden nor total in the manufacture of consumer products, nor were the individual autonomy and creative freedom that united the fine and applied arts entirely sacrificed as new production technologies took root.
Leaders of the various permutations of the Arts and Crafts movement devised strategies to empower and protect the value of meaningful work, while business leaders promoted the Industrial Arts in relation to civic responsibility and pride, providing outlets for the development of skills and promoting social activities outside the workplace, such as museums and libraries.
While industrial workers were no longer artists in the way Ruskin and Morris may have envisioned, neither were they entirely deprived of agency in a modern culture of design.

## The
Arts and Crafts Movement in the United States A number of social critics, writers, and artists were sympathetic to John Ruskins critique of industrialization and its negative effect upon the arts in the United States during the second half of the nineteenth century.
In addition to the circulation of Arts and Crafts ideas in print, a display from Morris & Co. was on view at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
The influence of the Arts and Crafts movement may be seen in the establishment of craft societies and craft education in cities such as Boston, Syracuse, Cincinnati, and Chicago.
Reaching a peak in the decades between 1890 and 1910, craft workshops, artisan communities, and journals addressed the challenges and threats posed by mass production, mechanization, and advertising.
Gustav Stickley (18581942) is perhaps the best known of many American Arts and Crafts furniture manufacturers in the early twentieth century, in part because furniture bearing the Stickley name continues to be produced, and also because it has been featured in popular films such as A River Runs Through It (1992, directed by Robert Redford).
Stickley learned furniture-making while serving as an apprentice at an uncles chair factory in Massachusetts.
He became familiar with Arts and Crafts ideology through the writings of William Morris and the published designs of British architect M.
H.
Baillie Scott (18651945) that appeared in decorative arts journals on both sides of the Atlantic.
In 1898 Stickley visited Britain, and in 1900 he founded the Craftsman Workshops near Syracuse, New York, with himself as master craftsman.
He published The Craftsman journal beginning in 1901 to market his furniture along with essays that reinforced values of honest construction and the personal satisfaction of handicraft.
Stickley hoped his designs would appeal strongly to the directness and common sense of the American people with furniture that was solid, used local woods such as oak and basic (joinery) techniques, avoiding carved decoration and time-consuming marquetry as unnecessary and impractical for modern living.
The Craftsman included plans for building your own house, essays introducing readers to the writings of Ruskin and Morris, and designs for furniture, textiles, and other crafts to encourage readers to engage directly in handicraft, hoping to extend the principles established by Morris, in both the artistic and the socialistic sense, equating beauty with simplicity, individuality, and dignity of effect. Other journals, such as California-based The Bungalow illustrated interiors that embodied the Arts and Crafts ideology.
In the cover illustrated in figure 5.11, a family sits on matching built-in oak settees flanking a tiled floor and fireplace decorated with a mosaic landscape set into the wooden frame above on the wall.
The woman occupies herself with embroidery, while the man, in business attire, relaxes with an issue of the journal; the home has become a place of rest and refuge for the family, restoring privacy, autonomy, and self-sufficiency in an increasingly interdependent and fragmented modern world  in short, as noted by historian Jackson Lears, the Arts and Crafts movement in the United States was therapeutic, protecting men and women against the often alienating experience of modernity and compensating for its anxieties and uncertainties.

## 5.11 Cover illustration, The Bungalow, Los Angeles, California, October 1909. Library of C
ongress, Washington, DC.
Although he admired and promoted the virtues of hand craftsmanship, Stickley, like Ambrose Heal in England (see here), accepted the realities of the marketplace.
In the Craftsman Workshops, machine tools were used to save production time in a competitive mid- and high-end market.
Sometimes referred to as a new industrialist, Stickley accommodated his production methods to the pressures of efficiency and the machine; to compensate he included vocational education for workers, maintaining an affiliation with social reform ideology.
His small work cabinet from 1901 (fig.
5.12) is devoid of carved ornament: the plain surfaces and rectilinear shapes of the joinery, exposed mortise-and-tenon joints, and small pyramidal door handles exemplify the virtues of simple, honest craftsmanship, while the severity of the form is relieved by hammered-copper hinges and irregularities of the cabinets sanded edges and surfaces.
Stickley furniture shows great respect for the skill and intelligence of the craftsman in the selection and treatment of natural materials, and reveals care in the preparation of surfaces, as well as in the construction of joints and other fittings.
The slats that appear in many examples of Craftsman furniture reduce the block-like heaviness of the design and serve as a modest decorative feature integrated with construction techniques.
Other furniture designed for Gustav Stickley has been attributed to the Rochester-born architect Harvey Ellis (18521904) and features taller proportions, thinner forms, and delicate inlay decoration in lighter woods reminiscent of Charles Rennie Mackintosh and the Wiener Werkstätte (see here and fig.
6.40).
While some of Stickleys production methods deviated from the ideals of Ruskin and Morris, the style of his furniture embodied the virtues of clean, comfortable, natural, and modest living, giving expression to the longing for independence, honesty, and appreciation for the dignity of labor in a world increasingly dominated by large, impersonal companies and nationally advertised brands rather than local products.

## 5.12 Gustav Stickley, work cabinet, oak and copper, 36 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 21 × 15
in (91.9 × 53.3 × 38.1 cm), 1901.
American Decorative Art 1900 Foundation.
Stickleys commercial success encouraged him to move into new and larger headquarters in New York City in 1913.
By that time he had numerous showrooms and distributors throughout the country, and participated in furniture exhibitions as a means of marketing his name and products.
Despite expanding into the production of leathercraft and textiles, however, less expensive imitations and the waning of taste for the particular Craftsman style (his only product line) led Stickley to declare bankruptcy in 1915, and The Craftsman ceased publication the following year.
From 1908 to 1911 he designed and oversaw the construction of Craftsman Farms in Morris Plains, New Jersey, as a home and gathering place for his family and workers, along with workers cottages and a planned school.
Now restored and furnished with original Stickley and other American Arts & Crafts goods, the building and grounds provide the domestic and broader social context for his companys efforts.
Other self-contained craft communities exemplified the Arts and Crafts movement in the United States.
Among the most successful was the Roycrofters, founded by Elbert Hubbard (18561915) in 1893 and located in a suburb of Buffalo, New York.
The Roycroft workshops concentrated primarily upon the printing press, publishing editions of the founders periodical The Philistine and a series of small paperbound books entitled Little Journeys, as well as metalcraft, leather-making, and furniture resembling the Craftsman style.
Some of the designers employed by Hubbard also worked independently for other manufacturers, but the Roycroft community was based upon Hubbards somewhat paternalistic concern with the physical, intellectual, and spiritual well-being of the workers.
Like Stickley, he had visited Britain and was familiar with the writings of Ruskin and Morris as well as with Morriss Kelmscott Press.
Early books of the Roycroft community were written by Hubbard but also contained verse by American poets such as Ralph Waldo Emerson (18031882) and Edgar Allan Poe (1809 1849).
Among the most popular series from the Roycroft press was the Little Journeys, a series of short biographies of famous writers, teachers, and businessmen (the first volume was a biography of William Morris) in a small format.
Hubbard used a heavy serifed typeface named Bookman, though with a taller x-height and shorter ascenders and descenders than Morriss Venetian-inspired Golden type (see here), and he included decorated title pages as well as hand-coloring for wood-engraved decorated borders and illustrations (fig.
5.13).
The Little Journeys and other Roycroft publications attempted to reconcile the individuality and craftsmanship of the private press movement initiated by Morris with an effort to create a democratic design, if not for the masses, then at least for a broader middle class.
As part of his commercial enterprise, Hubbard built a hotel on the premises of the Roycroft village as a retreat for businessmen seeking the therapeutic benefits of the rustic life.
Hubbard, formerly a successful salesman for the Larkin Soap Company in Buffalo, was a zealous and tenacious reformer.
He was able to lower costs by printing books in a small format, but his success also depended upon a tight control of wages and autocratic authority to dictate how welfare was to be defined and administered on behalf of his worker community.
Not all of his workers reacted well to Hubbards control of the communal enterprise: some of his most original and gifted designer-craftsmen, including the printer Dard Hunter (18831966), left the community intermittently to work independently.

## The
Roycroft Shop GREETING HE ROYCROFTERS are a community of workers who make beautiful Books and Things-making them as good as they can.
The paper on which Roycroft books are printed is the best procurable, and some of the initials are illumined.
As a gift you probably cannot present anything at equal cost that would be more acceptable than a handillumined Roycroft book.
Our work is the product of Hand & Brain in partnership.
In things made by hand there are no duplicates; and further, there is a quality of sentiment attached to articles thus produced that never clings to fabrics made in vast quantities by steam, If you desire we will gladly send you" on suspicion" several volumes to choose from-a postal card from you will do it.
We pay express both ways.
THE ROYCROFTERS East Aurora 5.13 Elbert Hubbard, The Roycroft Books.
A Catalog and Some Comment Concerning the Shop at East Aurora, New York, and Its Workers, The Roycrofters, $7 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 5 ~ { 1 } ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (19 × 14.6 cm), 1902.
Hagarty Library Archive, Drexel University, Philadelphia.
The motto for the Roycrofters was head, heart, and hand, and in addition to the practice of design and craftmanship in the workshops, the community lived together, participating in a Roycroft band and baseball team.
Many products of its copper workshop were designed by Karl Kipp (18821954), a former banker who worked in the metal shop at the community from 1908 to 1911 and again beginning in 1915 following Hubbards (and his wifes) death in the sinking of the steamship Lusitania off the coast of Ireland en route to Liverpool.
His work includes a small tabletop jardinière dating to c.
19121915 with hammered-copper surfaces and modest but hand-cut geometric decoration (fig.
5.14).
It is interesting to note that Hubbard, and to a lesser extent Stickley, promoted the Arts and Crafts ideal of satisfying and rewarding work (direct or vicarious) yet borrowed from the practices of industrialized labor (and managerial control in the case of Hubbard), and benefited from advertising and branding in a rapidly expanding competitive consumer economy, where distinctions between product and process became blurred.
Other craft communities, such as Rose Valley near Philadelphia, founded by architect Will Price (18611916), maintained the Ruskinian ideal in a purer form.
Price coined the phrase the art that is life to characterize his experiment, hoping to unite artist and artisan in utopian harmony.
But few could afford the cost of Rose Valley products, and the community ceased craft production in 1906, only five years after it had begun.
5.14 Karl Kipp, jardinière, copper and German silver, $5 ~ ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 } \times 6 ~ ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 }$ in (15 × 17.5 cm), Roycrofters, East Aurora, New York, c.
1912–1915.
American Decorative Art 1900 Foundation Artist colonies, such as Byrdcliffe near Woodstock in New Yorks Catskill Mountains, were also a product of emerging interest in both art and a return to nature, often founded by wealthy patrons committed to encouraging artistic endeavor in all media including metalwork, furniture-making, bookbinding, painting, pottery, and fabric printing.
Byrdcliffes founders were Ralph Whitehead (d.
1929) and his wife Jane (18611955).
Whitehead was educated at Oxford and admired the communityminded ethics of the English Arts and Crafts movement.
Although never achieving its aim of being self-supporting through the sale of its products, Byrdcliffe sustained the efforts of a number of original artists working in the decorative arts, among them painter Zulma Steele (18811979), who designed pottery as well as carved and painted panels for simply constructed furniture.
More eccentric but indicative of a degree of independence and inventiveness directed toward the decorative arts during this period is the work of Charles Rohlfs (1853 1936), who established a furniture workshop in Buffalo, New York, that was most active between 1898 and 1906.
Rohlfs trained as a designer of patterns for the decoration of cast-iron stoves, but was inspired to pursue a more independent artistic path first as an actor and then more successfully through the design and production of oak furniture.
While the simple construction of many of his pieces recalls the straightforward construction techniques of Gustav Stickleys Craftsman style, his carved patterns display a highly original and creative imagination, at the expense of considerations of cost or social benefit.
Such imagination takes the form of asymmetrical spiral patterns inspired by Hiberno-Saxon and other medieval decorative patterns as well as more unusual sources of inspiration.
According to art historian Joe Cunningham, the open carving on the back of the oak desk chair of 18981899 (fig.
5.15) strongly resembles the structure of the oak molecule as seen through a microscope.
While Rohlfss work shares common elements with Arts and Crafts attitudes, he did not espouse the social mission that inspired other designers associated with the movement: his workshop maintained a separation between designing and making, with a clearly implied hierarchy favoring the creativity of the former.
Charles Rohlfs, desk chair, oak 53 <sup>15</sup>/ × 15 <sup>15</sup>/ × 16 <sup>7</sup>/ in (137 × 40.4 × 42.9 cm), Buffalo, New York, c.
1898–1899.
American Decorative Art 1900 Foundation.
Brothers Charles Sumner Greene (18681957) and Henry Mather Greene (1870 1954), architects who also designed interior furnishings for a number of exclusive Eastern and Midwestern clients who enjoyed spending winters in the comfortable climate of southern California, combined an interest in natural materials and direct contact with nature with exquisite craftsmanship, often carried out by Swedish-born craftsmen John and Peter Hall, who gave form to the Greene brothers subtle custom designs with skill and sensitivity.
The houses of the firm Greene and Greene show the integration of all aspects of interior design: elements inspired by Japanese architecture and furniture, an interest in natural materials, soft edges, and repeated Asian motifs such as the abstracted cloud lift, as seen in the horizontal window moldings behind the built-in sideboard designed for the dining room of the Gamble House in Pasadena, echoed elsewhere in accents throughout the furniture and other carved details of the ensemble (fig.
5.16).
Greene and Greene employed inlay decoration and relief carving that added refinement to the Craftsman style, along with the combination of colored woods such as mahogany, walnut, or teak, and more sophisticated methods of construction than oak joinery.
The result is an awareness of nature carefully cultivated and transformed by imagination and skill.
While homes such as the Blacker House or nearby Gamble House were commissioned for wealthy clients, the wood shingles, exaggerated overhanging eaves, and low profiles of these homes became the basis for more modest bungalow houses that extended the idea of a contemporary architectural style more broadly, in Charles Sumner Greenes words, to make common things beautiful (see fig.
5.11).
The European Middle Ages were the inspiration for the elevation and spiritualization of craft in aesthetic and moral terms for both Ruskin and Morris.
The emulators of the Greene brothers bungalow houses in southern California employ a look often referred to as Mission Style. The original meaning of this term is disputed: for some scholars it refers to the missionary zeal of the Arts and Crafts movement and its efforts to integrate art and life in harmony with nature; for others it pays a debt to the utilitarian furniture of the Spanish missions established in California, which were viewed as part of a romantic past in the late nineteenth century (see here).
Charles Sumner and Henry Mather Greene, Gamble House, dining room with window showing cloud lift motif, Pasadena, California, 1908–1910.
Certainly parallel but not always included in the literature on the Arts and Crafts movement in the United States are the craft activities of the Shakers, a sect that emigrated to America from Britain in the late eighteenth century, settling in selfsufficient communities with the aim of uniting life and work, guided by beliefs in simplicity and humility.
Shaker furniture, like the ladderback chair, utilizes local materials and certainly is an outgrowth of ethical conviction (for a related example, see the chair beneath the window in fig.
5.10).
Shaker communities designed and produced handcrafted baskets, linen weavings, and wooden kitchen implements for utilitarian domestic use and eventually for sale to the general public.
Yet the Shaker concept of meaningful or dignified work lacks something of the element of individuality that united artist and craftsman.
As a result, Shaker designs, while fashionable among Arts and Crafts consumers (and remaining popular with the buying public today), are anonymous, less subject to the innovation and change inherent in more individualistic conceptions of design activity.
The contemporary market for Shaker furnishings raises interesting questions about personal identity and lifestyle choices today, affirming the desire for modest forms of domestic living associated with Shaker branding of ladderback chairs, woven rush seats, and other products of anonymous, ageless craft. ladderback chairs, woven rush seats, and other products of anonymous, ageless craft.
Henry Chapman Mercer (18561930) founded the Moravian Pottery and Tile Works, located in Doylestown in southeastern Pennsylvania, around the turn of the century to produce molded ceramic tiles and mosaics for use primarily as architectural and mural decoration.
Independently wealthy and well respected as an anthropologist and archeologist, Mercer lamented the decline and disappearance of local, pre-industrial crafts in Pennsylvania.
To preserve this endangered legacy, he began collecting tools and artifacts from the area and eventually built a museum (more like a warehouse today) to house the objects.
He built his private residence and the museum using reinforced concrete with himself as amateur architect and hiring local laborers to help with construction.
At the same time he founded a tile workshop and produced tiles using plaster molds with designs based upon historic models primarily from the Middle Ages but also from a variety of other sources.
Mercer experimented with a process of two-coat glazing that varied the finish of each tile, and though hand-operated machines were used for shaping the slabs and pressing the tiles, each had an individual character from glazing and the many stages of the process that involved handwork.
Although Mercer may not have been directly acquainted with the British Arts and Crafts movement, his lifes work and writings are entirely sympathetic to the movements ideals.
Perhaps the consummate do-it-yourselfer, Mercer stated that the value of the products of the Moravian Pottery and Tile Works lay beyond the beauty of the colors and designs and had more to do with the dignity and usefulness of work.
Perhaps the most ambitious commission of the Moravian Pottery and Tile Works was for the floors of the State Capitol Building in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, completed between 1902 and 1907.
Even if they were only moderately successful or long-lived, Arts and Crafts workshops, communities, and publications in the United States offered solutions to the dehumanizing aspects of urbanization and industrialization, to the threat that modernity posed to individuality, self-sufficiency, and the meaning and value of work.
Ceramic ware was also an outlet for the Arts and Crafts ideal of achieving a closer relationship with nature through an appreciation of natural materials and the process of handmaking.
As with furniture, the design and manufacture of ceramics ranged from the highly eccentric and individual work of George Ohr (18571918) of Biloxi, Mississippi, to the more production-oriented output of the Marblehead Pottery Company of Marblehead, Massachusetts.
Ohrs pink vase (fig.
5.17) dating to around 1900 shows the irregular surface decoration associated with his hand-thrown and delicate, shell-like bodies.
The Marblehead Pottery began in 1904 to provide therapy for patients recovering from tuberculosis.
The pottery shifted to a professionally run business when the patients were unable to meet production schedules.
The simple, even heavy form, grainy surface, and matte green glaze of the Panther vase illustrated in figure 5.18 suggest the natural qualities associated with the Arts and Crafts movement.
There is also a strong individual element: at the top of the vase the green glaze becomes a series of bands alternating with gold rectangles.
This creates a border in which a frieze of repeated panthers carved in low relief strides stealthily as if through shrubbery, with one rear leg behind and the other in front of the green vertical bands.

## Printing
in the United States For his Kelmscott Press (see here), William Morris drew typefaces based upon earlier approaches to type design that he admired for their even stroke weight and the retention of calligraphic tendencies.
His efforts, in effect, gave new life to old faces, reviving interest in the Blackletter forms of the Middle Ages and suggesting variations to the thickness of letterform strokes based upon Roman old-style faces of the later fifteenth century.
In the United States, two typographer-book designers based their work upon the example of the Kelmscott fonts, and variations upon it that became widely used in more commercial printing.
Frederic Goudy (18651947) and Bruce Rogers (18701956) admired the beauty of Kelmscott books, which they encountered as young men, and embarked upon lifelong careers in type founding and book design.
Their interests included type and page design, and their careers testify to a respect for craftsmanship practiced in the broadest sense of the word as celebrated by Morris.
The model set by Goudy and Rogers extended to others including William Dwiggins (18801956) and Morris Fuller Benton (18721948), both of whom developed influential typefaces used in modern book printing.
Dwiggins is sometimes credited with coining the term graphic designer to describe the varied professional activities that stemmed from craft origins in the printing industry but expanded to include typography, advertising, and page design.
Each of these designers studied historical typefaces and created their own types suitable for text and titles.
In addition to old-style (humanistic) faces by Caslon, Rogers produced a version of the Bodoni font for modern typesetting.
Benton was employed as a punch-cutter for the American Type Founders Company (ATF), where he cut the type for Goudy fonts as well as developing his own typefaces.
As noted by typographic historian Alexander Lawson, small variations in these historically inspired typefaces led to their wider use: by adjusting the height of ascenders and descenders, old-style typefaces could be more economically set without decreasing legibility.
Will Bradley, whose advertising posters and illustrations are described below (see here), was also employed at ATF, which published The American Chap-Book.
Along with other publications such as Inland Printer, The American Chap-Book introduced examples of printing that emphasized new typefaces, lettering, and inks used for chromolithography.
Technology contributed to the development of the printing industry in the later nineteenth century, mainly through labor-saving machines that increased speed and productivity.
Among the most significant changes was the introduction of automatic mechanical typesetting.
As in the first half of the century, it was the newspaper industry, with its high-volume circulation and daily editions, that stimulated invention, leading to a system known as Linotype at the New York Herald in 1886, and quickly spreading through Europe and the United States.
Ottmar Mergenthaler (18541899), who immigrated to the United States from Germany, invented the Linotype machine, which released negative impressions of letterforms through the operation of a keyboard, then cast each line of type from molten metal for the letterpress, eliminating the need for hand-setting type.
As a result of this invention, the price of newspapers decreased and the number of pages grew, further increasing circulation and space for advertisements.
The Monotype machine, developed by Tolbert Lanston (18441913) in the 1880s and 1890s, offered an alternative to the Linotype.
It produced multiple impressions of letters from a single matrix containing the entire alphabet, operated by a perforated tape that positioned the matrix to make molds for casting (the perforated tape resembled the cards used for Jacquard looms; see here).
While developed for the newspaper industry, typesetting machinery such as the Monotype was also adopted for book printing.
In both cases typographers wrestled with the challenges of maintaining consistency and legibility while adopting new and increasingly complex mechanized technologies.
Achieving that balance led to interest in the humanist roman letterforms of the later fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
This development was, in some sense, a reconciliation between respect for the highest achievements of craft traditions dating to the development of movable type and the inevitable push toward mechanization as the printing industry and the reading public expanded.
Another invention during this period was the pantograph (delineating machine), developed by Linn Boyd Benton (18441932), who worked at ATF.
The pantograph was a mechanical device that facilitated the drawing of variations of a single typeface to be produced as punches from a single exemplar, both expanding the range of a font (using extended and narrowed letterforms) as well as its point size with greater precision and speed.
Another technical development in printing was the mechanical reproduction of images using photographs.
Translating a photographic plate into a mechanically produced image required the use of a screen to reproduce the tonal complexity of the image in a simpler form.
Known as half-tone, the process made photography the basic tool of reporting and recording events for newspapers and magazines, and at the same time threatened the jobs of those craftsmen who had met the expanding demand for images using the technique of wood engraving (fig.
5.19).
The simplified shadows of the half-tone method of reproduction was adopted by graphic designers in the illustration of products in a larger format, for instance in the posters of Lucian Bernhard in Germany (see fig.
7.6).
Enlarged photographic reproduction using half-tone printing process.
Photographic reproduction was also used in the field of illustration.
While journalism shifted to photography as an eyewitness to faithfully record events, illustration still thrived in the realm of fiction, political and social commentary in the mass media, advertising, and in childrens books, carrying on a tradition of narrative art outside of easel painting, where this tradition was challenged by avant-garde ideas advocating the autonomy of art.
Scribner’s Monthly, Harper’s Magazine, Century, and other publications were among the journals that provided a sphere of activity for illustrators.
Howard Pyle (18531911) was one of several artists who worked at Harper Brothers under art editor Howard Parsons, providing illustrations to stories that were published serially.
Early illustrations were wood engravings.
Pyle brought to life stories of danger and adventure, taking readers to distant lands and places peopled by heroes and villains.
Pyle lent immediacy to his scenes, often juxtaposing near and distant space and using strong contrast to heighten dramatic effect.
An example is a tonal reproduction from Pyles Book of Pirates, originally published in Harper’s Magazine (August 1887), illustrating a shipwrecked sailor on a beach against a backdrop of empty sea and sky (fig.
5.20).
The appeal of Pyles illustrations was to escape and fantasy.
The gap they filled in the lives of their vast readership was soon shared with a new medium in the early twentieth century: the moving picture, which introduced a set of real-life heroes and heroines in the form of celebrity actors whose portraits adorned the covers of fan magazines and whose offscreen lives, expected to match their on-screen personas, filled the pages of newspapers.
A new demand for narrative also arose during the same time through advertising, although not all illustrators were comfortable with the use of illustration techniques to sell products.
To some degree a middle ground was achieved in the late nineteenthcentury advertising poster, which managed to appeal to audiences on different levels, that is, promoting the individual expression of the artist, fostering a healthy relationship between art and business to bring high culture to the masses, and generating appeal by linking products and services to a carefree or hedonistic lifestyle (see here onward).

## 5.20 Howard Pyle, On the Tortugas, wood engraving from original illustration for “Buccanee
rs and Marooners of the Spanish Main,” Harper’s Magazine, August 1887.

## Chicago
and Frank Lloyd Wright In 1896 and again in 1901 the British Arts and Crafts designer and advocate Charles Ashbee (see here), founder of the Guild and School of Handicraft, visited the United States, traveling extensively and reporting on the contemporary design activities that he observed.
Ashbee, who was a firm believer in hand craftsmanship, the well-being of workers, and a close relationship between designer and artisan, was impressed by a young American architect named Frank Lloyd Wright (18691959).
Wright was one of a group of Midwestern architects and designers who created a Prairie School based in Chicago, Illinois.
Many of Wrights early houses share features with the Arts and Crafts movement in the United States in their effort to harmonize with their surroundings through low-hipped roofs and horizontal extension, overhanging eaves, a restrained use of ornament, and an avoidance of overt historicism.
Significantly, however, Wrights approach to the decorative arts departed from an important tenet of Arts and Crafts ideology, particularly in regard to the role of the machine, and by extension the relationship between designing and making.
In a wellknown lecture delivered in Chicago in 1901 at Hull House, a home founded in the city in 1889 by Jane Addams (18601935) and Ellen Gates Starr (18591940) to improve the lives of working-class women by providing a variety of social and educational services, Wright told his audience that the dream for a democratic architecture could only be achieved by embracing the machine, which saved time and reduced drudgery.
He stated that the machines ability to produce simple products of high quality and noble beauty had been obscured only by the greed of manufacturers and the ignorance of the public: William Morris pleaded well for simplicity as the basis of all the art.
Let us understand the significance to art of that word  SIMPLICITY  for it is vital to the art of the machine! It is not clear what Morris himself may have meant by simplicity, whether a less complicated lifestyle or aesthetically simple forms of furniture and furnishings.
In regard to the machine, perhaps Wright was recalling the British designers comment, quoted earlier, that the more mechanical the process, the less direct should be the imitation of natural forms. In any case, as mentioned above, Charles Ashbee modified his own views to acknowledge a role for the machine along the lines envisioned by Wright, admiring the American architects courage in confronting the challenge of industrialization rather than ignoring its possible social benefits in improving the lives of a broader public.
Wrights linking of machine technology, aesthetic purity, and a democratic art provided an ethical dimension to modern design that emerged in the interwar period in Europe, although under different historical conditions and often along utopian lines.
Wrights views and designs also ran parallel with initiatives in Germany to shape middleclass taste in relation to industrial manufacturing that also took place in the early twentieth century (see Chapter 7).
For these designers, decoration was viewed as being dishonest and vulgar if produced mechanically (a variation on the dictum truth to materials), and exclusive or elitist if made by hand: the modern designer should strive rather to create new and original forms designed for factory production to meet the needs and accompany the practical lifestyle of an expanding middle-class audience.
Wrights approach to design using restraint in decoration might also be examined in connection with critiques of consumption by contemporary economists such as Thorsten Veblen (18571929), who criticized the purchasing habits of middle-class Americans as a form of conspicuous consumption, linking buying not with comfort but rather with the acquisition of social position that substituted the status acquired through buying with real status, formerly the result of honor and respect earned on the basis of actions and accomplishments.
For Veblen, fashion and consumption were menacing threats to the existing social order; for Wright, they were threats to the creation of a true and natural modern taste, appropriate to its time and taking full advantage of new production technologies.
Also contemporary with Wrights approach was the theory of Viennese architect Adolf Loos (18701933), who also criticized the role of decoration in design.
Loos visited the United States in the 1890s and was familiar with the work and theories of the Prairie School.
He equated decoration with cultural decline, arguing that modern urban life demanded a sophisticated but unpretentious style of living, in dress (where he favored the uniformly tailored black business suit worn by English gentlemen) as well as in architecture, where he advocated the use of modern materials such as reinforced concrete, flat roofs, and smooth walls using richly grained woods or marble but without carved, molded, or printed decoration.
He expounded his views in a provocative essay titled Ornament and Crime dating to 19081910 and reprinted in later publications.
Wright published some of his early designs for domestic architecture in illustrated mass-circulation magazines such as Edward W.
Boks (18631930) Ladies’ Home Journal with the title A small house with lots of room in it and a suggested cost of less than \$6,000.
But despite the simple elegance of Wrights designs in comparison with the more traditional preference for carved or molded ornament and adaptations of period styles ranging from Gothic to Baroque, Wrights homes were almost invariably custombuilt for affluent clients, and his domestic furniture was neither mass-produced nor achieved broad appeal for consumers, who preferred more traditional expressions of comfort and beauty linked to richness of effect.
Even the design published by Wright in the Ladies’ Home Journal may be misleading for a modern reader, since a \$6,000 home in 1901 would correspond more to the median than to low-end price of houses today.
Another expression of Wrights preference for simple (but not necessarily inexpensive) forms was the design of colored leaded glass windows, as in the set of bay windows for the dining space of the Susan Dana House in Springfield, Illinois (completed 1904; fig.
5.21).
The windows are abstract geometric generalizations of foliate forms.
The composition of these and other windows in Wrights Prairie houses suggests they might be assembled from a small number of prefabricated units or shapes (like childrens blocks), but their manufacture was still time-consuming, intricate, and ultimately craft-based.
In other words, Wright seems to have created the converse of Morriss recommendation that machines should not imitate hand-work  the windows are handmade yet suggest how machines should make things.
Despite the arguments presented in his writings and speeches that the Machine is the great forerunner of democracy, Wright was hardly advocating democracy in the sense of freedom of choice for consumers.
Instead he equated an aesthetic preference based upon simplicity with a self-evident but entirely theoretical technical determinism, then assumed that the result shaped and elevated the taste of his intended middle-class audience, that is, an original modern design that the public should want.
The concept of design unity not only applied to the open rather than enclosed interior spaces, but also stimulated Wright to design ceramics, metalwork, windows, and lamps, all of which contributed to the warmth and aesthetic harmony of the home, and also to the interrelationship between architecture and furnishings.
Frank Lloyd Wright, dining room furniture, Susan Dana House, Springfield, Illinois, completed 1904.
As noted above, Wrights career in Chicago should not be considered in a vacuum, for the city was a major metropolitan center, and his ideas took shape in an active artistic environment.
After a disastrous fire of 1871, architects and artists were attracted to Chicago during an intense period of rebuilding and modernization that included the hosting of the Worlds Columbian Exposition of 1893, and the construction of an elevated mass transit system.
A premium on office space in the citys center led to the design of several tall buildings, constructed from steel and utilizing motorized elevators.
One of the most prominent architects during this period of artistic activity was Louis Sullivan (18561924).
Sullivan was acquainted with the writings of Ruskin and with the Arts and Crafts movement.
Despite his well-known and often-quoted dictum form follows function, Sullivan believed decoration to be an essential component of architecture.
This view was based upon an appreciation for nature and the spiritual energy embodied in natural forms as they were integrated into and contributed to the value of the built environment.
He designed intricate, original patterns for architectural and interior decoration, used as framed panels (whether stencil-printed, molded in terracotta, or cast in iron) to balance and enliven the repetitive grid-like structure of tall buildings such as the Wainwright Building in St.
Louis, Missouri, dating to 1890 1891.
His wallpaper pattern for the interior of the Chicago Stock Exchange (fig.
5.23) from 1894 also featured complex interlace patterns, strongly linear and abstract, complementing the crisp contours of columns and other structural elements of the design.
Similar curvilinear patterns appear in the windows, carpets, and other domestic furnishings designed by George Grant Elmslie (18711952) and George Washington Maher (18641926) for homes in the Midwest around the turn of the century.
Elmslie, born in Scotland, worked for Sullivan and for Frank Lloyd Wright.
Mahers Thistle textile, for the Patten home in Evanston, Illinois (1901; fig.
5.22), is one of the more exuberant examples of his work, while window designs remained more restrained and geometric.

## 5.22 George Washington Maher, Thistle textile, silk velvet with appliqué of silk damask, 8
0 $^ { 3 } / _ { 8 } \times 4 6 ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 }$ in (204.1 × 119 cm), 1901.
Art Institute of Chicago.
William Morriss approach to socialism was avowedly anti-industrial, but efforts to connect design with social justice and equality resonated in a variety of ways and extended beyond nostalgic anachronism.
Such efforts remain a powerful historical thread in the twenty-first century, tempering the uncritical embrace of industrial technologies with concerns for labor welfare, social justice, and, more recently, environmental responsibility.
We might say that ethical consumption in our own time is another legacy of the Arts and Crafts movement, encouraging consumers to think about where and how the things we buy are made and disposed of, and the well-being of those in the wider global community who make them.
The contradictions and compromises seen in the various applications of Morriss example, whether in Britain, Europe, or the United States, attest to designers reaction to his work and writings in the face of industrialization, balancing benefits with risks and threats: in short, managing change.
That this resonance extended to an appreciation for Japanese design (see here) or to Spanish Colonial-inspired California missions attests to an increasing degree of global awareness as well as the persistence, vitality, flexibility, and broad scope of craft throughout the history of modern design.
5.23 Louis Sullivan (and Dankmar Adler), trading room of the Chicago Stock Exchange, 1894, reconstructed 1977.
