## Chapter
6 The Equality of the Arts

## Beyond
Design Reform While design reform promoters stressed a discerning historicism and a careful selection of decorative art examples from other cultures as models of universal standards for ornament applied to objects of use, they also encouraged the direct study of nature as a source of inspiration for designers.
At the London School of Design, artist Richard Redgrave (see fig.
4.4) taught a course in Artistic Botany that encouraged students to carefully study the forms of nature in order to understand their underlying structure.
And in his 1856 The Grammar of Ornament, Owen Jones (who also was an instructor at the school; see here) included ten illustrations of ornamental motifs drawn from the direct study of nature, where renderings of various flowers and leaves transform the varied and organic qualities of their models into carefully repeated or symmetrically arranged flat structures and patterns (fig.
6.1).
In the preface to this section of The Grammar, Jones reminded his readers: The more closely nature is copied, the farther we are removed from producing a work of art....
His (the Creators) works are offered for our enjoyment, so are they offered for our study.
They are there to awaken a natural instinct implanted in us,  a desire to emulate in the works of our hands, the order, the symmetry, the grace, the fitness, which the Creator has sown broadcast over the earth.
Figure 6.1 was drawn by a student at the school named Christopher Dresser (1834 1904), who promoted himself first as an ornamentalist, providing patterns to manufacturers for wallpapers and decoration applied to other useful domestic goods.
He considered design an intellectual and professional endeavor essential to elevating the quality and increasing the appeal of a wide variety of products, and worked with manufacturers to realize his designs in the most cost efficient way possible. Knowledge is Power was the motto and logo for his business practice: knowledge was the engine of invention and progress, something to be shared rather than kept private or secret.

## 6.1 Christopher Dresser, Leaves and Flowers from Nature, no. 8, color lithograph, 13 <sup>
1</sup>/ × 8 <sup>7</sup>/ in (33.7 × 22.5 cm), from The Grammar of Ornament by Owen Jones, 1856.
Private collection.
Rather than concern himself with historicism or the appropriateness of representational decorative forms in relation to use, Dresser concentrated upon transforming naturalistic motifs into original expressive pattern and on the integration of decoration with methods of production.
A serving plate of 1872, manufactured by the Watcombe Pottery Company and attributed to Dresser (fig.
6.2), illustrates his approach.
Its composition is a lively yet balanced play of regular triangular and circular shapes, composed to harmonize with the form of the plate and abstracted from a variety of plant forms.
The Watcombe plate follows Joness prescription to use schematic or conventionalized natural forms to decorate flat surfaces.
It also emphasizes the designers creativity in transforming nature into original decoration.
Thus manufactures held the promise of the democratization and accessibility of art. Christopher Dresser, earthenware plate with partial glazing, diameter 13 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (34.3 cm), manufactured by Watcombe Pottery Company, Torquay, England, 1872.
Dresser also designed metalwork, including tea sets, toast racks, and other serving dishes and utensils.
The striking series of electroplated silver tea sets designed for the Dixon Company of Sheffield beginning in 1879 (fig.
6.3) emphasizes the beauty of the materials smooth, mirror-like surface, and features identical parts for feet and brackets for handles.
Dresser was inspired by examples of metalwork he had seen during a trip to Japan in 1866 to 1867, and critics at the time praised his designs for their originality in comparison with more contemporary work featuring naturalistic relief decoration produced by casting and traditional craft techniques (see the Elkington examples, fig.
3.1).
The lack of decoration and elementary geometry of Dressers work for the Dixon Company anticipates the early twentieth-century concern with stable product types designed for mass production, but the great variation of shapes, materials, decoration, and surfaces in Dressers designs in silver seem as concerned with originality as with standardization.
A number of historians commonly refer to Dresser as the first industrial designer, but his works were not produced on an industrial scale and their market was generally exclusive.
Moreover one must be careful using the word simple to describe such work: metalworkers complained that Dressers plain-surface teapot designs were more difficult and time-consuming to manufacture, that adding decoration around rivets, for instance, actually saved rather than added time to production by hiding imperfections in those areas of the surface that would otherwise have taken time to correct.
In other words, just because something looks simple does not mean that it is simple or inexpensive to produce.
A more successful example of integrating original design with production efficiency is Dressers earthenware vase for the Ault Pottery Company in Swadlincote, England, dating to 1892 (fig.
6.4).
Dresser designed the asymmetrical spiraling vase to be serially produced from a mold rather than shaped or turned by hand.
Christopher Dresser, silver-plate designs from the costing book of James Dixon and Sons Limited, Sheffield, England, c.
1879.
Christopher Dresser, vase, earthenware, height 12 <sup>1</sup>/ in (31.1 cm), Ault Pottery, Swadlincote, England, 1892.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
The originality of Dressers designs and patterns also characterizes the work of artists and architects for whom the equality of the arts emerged as a provocative theme pointing to new directions and potential for the history of modern design.
The term Aesthetic Movement is often used to refer to these activities, which were labeled as such during the 1870s and 1880s and even satirized in the British periodical Punch and in forms of popular entertainment such as Gilbert and Sullivans 1881 operetta Patience.
The movement succeeded in shaping the attitudes of artists, manufacturers, and wealthy consumers toward the decorative arts and in elevating their status.
The Aesthetic Movement may be seen as an outgrowth of early design reform while at the same time moving from a preoccupation with standards and paternalism toward a reconsideration of the sources of inspiration, materials, processes, and in particular the importance of individual subjective expression.
Designers associated with the movement adopted a freer approach to the use of historical styles, and exhibited greater freedom in their exploration of materials and decoration.
They advocated for the essential equality and unity of fine and applied art, in particular as realized in the coordinated interior, in which every element contributed equally to the unified expressive or emotional effect of the whole.
Interiors became total works of art, imaginative spaces in which the barriers between art and life ceased to exist.
While important aesthetic designers of the period might specialize in a medium such as glass, ceramics, or furniture, many designers and high-end manufacturers sought responsibility and control for all aspects of interior planning and decoration in order to achieve a coordinated and unified result that included fabrics, lighting, wall treatments, furniture, and furnishings.
The centers of Aesthetic Movement activities were the growing modern cities of Britain, Eastern and Western Europe, Scandinavia, and North America, and colonial territories such as Australia.
These urban centers were also the locations of the numerous Worlds Fairs that took place at the time, including London (1862), Vienna (1873), Paris (1867, 1878, 1889, and 1900), Brussels (1897), Turin (1902), and the United States (Philadelphia in 1876, Chicago in 1893).
Aesthetic design was also illustrated in journals and commissioned for boutiques specializing in contemporary crafts and interior design as well as for restaurants, tearooms, department stores and other public spaces.
Inspiration for Aesthetic Movement designers was far-ranging geographically and chronologically, drawing upon past Indigenous, as well as recent, national histories, and the decorative arts of non-Western cultures.
But Orientalist bias (see here) often remained, casting non-Western cultures as the primitive other, exotic but inferior technologically (for example the vast machine halls constructed at fairgrounds), and displayed as such in ethnographic exhibits at Worlds Fairs.

## Aesthetic
Adventures Painter James Abbott McNeill Whistler (18341903), an American-born artist who studied in Paris and resided in London beginning in 1859, is regarded as one of the leading figures of the Aesthetic Movement in Britain.
Whistlers involvement with interior design exemplified the equality and integration of the arts and is seen in the painted decoration and easel painting he contributed to the design of the Peacock Room (fig.
6.5) in the London home of Liverpool industrialist F.
R.
Leyland (1832 1892) in 1876 (now in the Freer Gallery in Washington, DC).
The room was designed by architect Thomas Jeckyll (18271881) to display Leylands collection of blue-andwhite Chinese porcelain (see here).
Its shelves, hanging globe lanterns, ceiling coffers (with peacock feathers painted on leather), and rectangular-backed chairs share a common vocabulary consisting primarily of rectangles and hexagons and a color scheme of a dark blue-green contrasting with gold accents.
Leyland also purchased and displayed a painting by Whistler hung above the fireplace.
Entitled Princess in the Land of Porcelain, the canvas depicted a young female figure wearing a Japanese kimono standing on a blue-and-white carpet in front of a painted screen.
The artist also painted the Spanish leather applied to the walls, adding delicate undulating, asymmetrical clouds in gold against the deep blue-green of the paneled walls and cabinets, an effect resembling Asian lacquerware (see fig.
GI1.6).
Without Leylands permission the artist painted peacocks (also in gold) on the door screens on one side of the room.
Whistler demanded remuneration for the additional work, and Leylands refusal to pay led to a bitter legal dispute between the two men.
In time Leyland agreed to pay one-half of Whistlers fee, but insulted the artist further by paying him with a check written for pounds, the currency of trade, rather than guineas, the currency generally exchanged for the work of artists and professionals.
James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Harmony in Blue and Gold: The Peacock Room for the Frederic Leyland House, oil paint and metal leaf on canvas, leather, and wood, 1876; with painting of Princess in the Land of Porcelain.
Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC.
Irish-born writer and critic Oscar Wilde (18541900), a vocal proponent of the decorative arts, articulated the attitudes that informed the creation of such exotic and personal interior spaces as the Peacock Room.
In a passage from his essay The Artist as Critic (1891), Wilde praised the expressive value of abstract form in the applied arts and acknowledged their elevated status: The art that is frankly decorative is the art to live with.
It is, of all visible arts, the one art that creates in us both mood and temperament.
Mere colour, unspoiled by meaning, and unallied with definite form, can speak to the soul in a thousand different ways.
The harmony that resides in the delicate proportions of lines and masses becomes mirrored in the mind ...
The marvels of design stir the imagination ...
By its deliberate rejection of Nature as the ideal of beauty, as well as of the imitative method of the ordinary painter, decorative art not merely prepares the soul for the reception of true imaginative work, but develops in it that sense of form which is the basis of creative no less than of critical achievement.
Dressers comments on the design for a pattern from his 1862 book The Art of Decorative Design, although written in more analytical prose, share the same spirit as Wildes essay: both statements claim that design ennobles the ordinary, but through expressive rather than representational form: I have sought to embody chiefly the idea of power, energy, force, or vigour; and in order to do this I have employed such lines as we see in the bursting buds of spring, when the energy of growth is at its maximum ...
I have also availed myself of those forms to be seen in certain bones of birds which are associated with the organs of flight, and which give us an impression of great strength.

## Japan
and Japonisme The Peacock Room and other interiors of the period demonstrate an affinity for the decorative arts of Japan shared by many Aesthetic Movement artists.
Dresser traveled to Japan (his visit was partially underwritten by Charles Tiffany in New York, who asked the designer to return with examples of Japanese metalwork) and lectured widely on the art of that country, praising both the quality and character of Japanese craft as well as noting the ritual purposes different types of household objects served for individuals and families.
After the re-opening of trade with Japan in 1854, artistic and commercial exchange was stimulated by objects brought to Britain by its first official representative, Sir Rutherford Alcock (18091897), displayed at a Japanese Court for the London International Exhibition of 1862, and by the acquisition of a collection of Japanese objects by the South Kensington Museum in the early 1870s.
In 1875, collector and merchant Arthur Lazenby Liberty (18431917) opened his London shop featuring Japanese craft, while popular interest in Japan emerged with the success of the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta The Mikado (1885).
Such activities influenced attitudes toward design and the decorative arts in Europe and in the United States.
Japan offered collectors and European artists and designers a highly developed tradition that valued the decorative arts, their role in domestic life, and the creativity of the artisan.
In his book The Traditional Arts and Crafts of Japan (1882), Dresser wrote extensively on the practice of Japanese craft, admiring the strength of Japanese craft traditions.
The combination of skill with intelligence Dresser noted reinforced his interest in promoting the professional and creative status of designers: I cannot help thinking that the Japanese are right in regarding the man who can make a beautiful pot, a lovely cabinet, a charming fabric, or a perfect netsuki as a being superior to the mere buyer and seller of goods; for while the one denotes his best energies to mere money-making, the other ennobles matter by the impress of his mind, love, intelligence, and skill.
It was, at least in part, the high regard for Japanese decorative arts that allowed artists and artisans greater freedom in drawing, permitting them, in the words of art historian Ernst Gombrich, to break the rules, for instance in the uneven spacing of motifs applied to surface decoration or in the irregular forms and textures of ceramic vessels.
But the Japanese connection was not a one-way street: just as Dresser was visiting Japan to profit from first-hand knowledge and experience of Japanese decorative arts, so were Japanese artists and government officials traveling to Europe to purchase industrial equipment to modernize the production of silk and ceramics for the export market, and acquire technology and foreign investment in the development of transportation and infrastructure in Japan.
These changes were parallel with the installation of the new centralized government beginning in 1868 (Meiji) and the need to replace traditional forms of regional patronage in the arts with commerce in domestic and international markets.
Worlds Fairs were one means the Japanese government used to display the nations silk, ceramics, and metalwork, along with establishing technical schools for the training of designers along European models.
The appearance of Western merchants and other businessmen and travelers occurred in Japan with the end of a long period of isolationism, providing an opportunity for Japan to communicate on equal terms with the Western world by demonstrating the international appeal of their higher-end material products in porcelain and metalwork, profits from the sale of which might be invested in modern industrial equipment.
Their success may be demonstrated by recalling that Dressers Japanese excursion was sponsored by Charles Tiffany, whose New York jewelry company modeled some of its work on examples of Japanese precious metalwork.
Thus the phenomenon known as Japonisme, referring to the popularity of Japanese products in Europe and North America, was the result not only of its reception in the context of the Aesthetic Movement that championed the equality of the arts, but also of the efforts of the Japanese government to stimulate economic growth through foreign trade and technology transfer, and creating a modern, competitive, and independent national image.
Japan figured prominently in the history of the Aesthetic Movement in Europe and the United States as a source of inspiration for designers and artists as well as providing an example of sophistication and for the elevated place of the decorative arts in visual culture.
Japan also offers an exception to the theme of Orientalism that applies so often to Western views of non-Western cultures.
Protective of its sovereignty and independence, the nation was receptive to industrialization and adapted industrial technologies and business practices to its own economy under the Meiji government and presented a progressive rather than primitive identity at its pavilion (called the Hôôden) for the 1893 Worlds Columbian Exposition in Chicago, combining traditional crafts and interior decoration with a series of paintings that catered to contemporary Western practices.
Other Aesthetic Movement designers in England, including Charles Eastlake and Bruce Talbert (18381881), looked to their nations past, turning to the Gothic style as advocated by Pugin or to the solid forms of the seventeenth century in what is known as the Queen Anne revival, approaches that respected the harmony of utility and beauty advocated by the early design reformers.
Eastlakes designs achieved popularity through their publication in his Hints on Household Taste (1868, see here), but while Eastlakes standards in design were linked to reform and education, his concerns were more aesthetic than ethical, and lacked the overt political or moral overtones of Cole or Pugin.
Eastlake acted as an advisor in matters of taste and his advice was not free from cultural assumptions about the role of design in society.
He directed his comments to female readers whom he presumed took responsibility for creating the ideal domestic environment, one that combined an appreciation for beauty with practical considerations such as a recommendation to avoid furniture with extensive carved decoration so as to reduce dust, require less time for cleaning, and promote healthier living.
In this latter sense his and other tastemakers advice books share a concern for efficient and healthy living with American writer Catherine Beecher (18001878), whose relationship to modern design is also considered below (see here).
Art Furniture (1882) was the title of a book published by English furniture-maker William Watt (18341885) that featured the work of Aesthetic Movement designer E.W.
Godwin (18331886).
Watt displayed his companys furniture at the 1878 Worlds Fair in Paris; figure 6.6 illustrates an interior with several prominent art furniture cabinets along with ceramics, window dressing, stenciled decoration on the upper walls, all coordinated stylistically and employing floral motifs whether carved, printed, woven, or painted.
The cabinets in the illustration are rectilinear in overall construction but allow ample opportunity for decoration in the panels, using complex techniques of marquetry rather than carving.
The illustration also implies a gendered reading: the man (presumably the husband) sits comfortably in an armchair reading a newspaper near the fireplace while the woman, standing to the right, carries a large bowl, perhaps to be placed in an empty center area of the nearby sideboard.
Responsibility for creating and maintaining a comfortable, healthy, and aesthetically pleasing home added a creative dimension to household management, but nevertheless maintained the gendered division between domestic and political, the private and public spheres of activity.
Out of such practices emerged the field of domestic science (or home economics) in the early twentieth century, providing professional opportunities for women outside the home.
William Watt, Art Furniture, plate no.
7, 1878, from designs by E.
W.
Godwin and others, B.T.
Batsford, London.
Recognizing increasingly commercial circumstances and opportunities in their profession, artists were eager to enter the market for decorative arts as designers and broaden the sphere of their activities.
As figure 6.6 implies, aesthetic furniture was directed toward a wealthy clientele.
Manufacturers of these products, such as Watt, Gillows, Holland and Sons, or Collinson & Lock in England, or Herter Brothers in New York, were willing to produce items from artists designs for display at international exhibitions in major European cities as well as in the United States, and art furniture was marketed as well through entrepreneurs and collectors such as Liberty in London, and later Siegfried Bing (18381905) and Julius Meier-Graefe (18671935) in Paris (see here, fig.
6.47).
Where they exist, the business records of these firms show they provided comprehensive services for commissioned interior design rather than retail sales of stock items, relied upon a long list of raw materials suppliers, and employed dozens of skilled workers in a variety of media to fulfill contracts.
Another form of Aesthetic Movement marketing was the studio.
Artists such as Whistler were known for the design of the interiors in their own homes and studios, at least in part to attract the attention of potential clients.
Another well-known fine artist with an interest in the decorative arts was Lord Frederic Leighton (18301896), a painter who served as President of the Royal Academy of Art and was made a peer in 1896.
Leightons house in Kensington was built from 1878 to 1880 and contains a two-story Arab Hall (see fig.
GI2.1, here) combining seventeenth-century Persian tiles with contemporary examples of tiles designed by London-based artists Walter Crane (18451915) and William de Morgan (18391917).
Both contributed to the flowering of the decorative arts in the later nineteenth century: Crane as a designer and illustrator, and de Morgan as a craftsman devoted to ceramics.
The dish in figure 6.7 by de Morgan is a free interpretation of a maritime subject frequently found in seventeenthcentury Turkish (Iznik) pottery.
A vessel in full sail floats against a blue background with birds and a flag atop the ship mast, with a lively border of flowers in a darker blue against an oyster- or shell-like burgundy ground.
Like their Turkish counterparts, the forms seem to expand, even burst against the framed areas that contain them.
William de Morgan, plate, glazed earthenware with enamel overlay, 1882–1888.
Birmingham City Art Museum.
Leighton was also responsible for a large mural painting in one of the hallways of the South Kensington Museum (renamed the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1899), an endeavor that realized Sir Henry Coles dream for a major building to house collections primarily devoted to the decorative arts and welcomed visitors from all social classes.
The mural is titled The Industrial Arts as Applied to Peace (a small sketch of the composition hangs in Leighton House).
The mural recalls one of the themes of early design reform, but Leightons narrative is decidedly more aesthetic, showing a group of Athenian maidens trying on clothing and jewelry while muscular workmen hoist ceramic containers and rolled-up woven carpets that have recently arrived by boat.
The benefits of peace in this mural appear to be equated with trade along with goods that occupy the leisure time of women in adorning themselves with exquisitely crafted objects (fig.
6.8).
Thus the meaning of the applied arts is portrayed primarily in relation to an almost dreamlike cultivation of private aesthetic experience and personal transformation via the consumption of luxury goods (one might compare this vision with more political associations of the industrial arts in the tapestry depicting Louis XIV inspecting the Gobelins Manufactory, fig.
1.1).
Lord Frederic Leighton, The Industrial Arts as Applied to Peace, cartoon for mural, 77 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 177 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (196.8 × 450.8 cm), 1872–1883.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Clearly there were shared, overlapping elements between the Arts and Crafts and Aesthetic movements; neither movement was unified, and some designers, such as de Morgan, Edward Burne-Jones (see chapter 5), and Walter Crane, seemed to move comfortably between the two.
Proponents of both movements believed that the decorative arts were important as vehicles of aesthetic experience and as the products of meaningful labor.
But there were differences in terms of emphasis.
For Morris, artists with a social conscience could best direct their efforts by being craftsmen, where their products would best address the needs of a troubled society.
For the Aesthetic designer, the decorative arts were the vehicle for subjective experience and expression.
One might say that the Arts and Crafts movement was directed toward process and reducing the alienation between an artisan and the products of his or her labor caused by technology and competition in a capitalist system.
In theory at least, manufacturers and buyers would support such an aim as an expression of social conscience and skepticism toward the facile equation of industrialization with progress.
Efforts ranged from advocating for working-class revolution to creating alternative craft communities or making accommodations to the machine compensated by communal activity for workers outside the workplace.
Artists of the Aesthetic Movement identified with and gave visible form to subjective experience through the decorative art object or product, often in relation to an aesthetic view of life most often realized in the interior, where all elements of design were united by abstract, expressive qualities of color, shape, line, and texture.

## Books,
Illustration, and Type Aesthetic, expressive interests in printing emerged further in Britain with the monthly journal The Studio in 1893.
In addition to examples of contemporary furniture and furnishings, The Studio included illustrations by artists with a highly subjective approach to representing nature and the human figure, parallel to contemporary Symbolist attitudes discussed above (see here).
The first issue of The Studio featured illustrations from Oscar Wildes poem based upon the New Testament story of Salomé, published originally in French and designed by the young English artist Aubrey Beardsley (1872 1898).
Beardsleys The Climax (fig.
6.9) represents Salomés embrace of the severed head of John the Baptist.
The scene is divided into two zones, with Salomé floating in the upper half, the faint contour of her body barely visible against the white ground, while her black hair focuses viewer attention on her face as she stares at the head of the Baptist that she holds.
Areas of strong contrast attract attention as well, whether the pools of blood in the lower half of the composition (and strange plants that issue from them) or the circular wave patterns in the upper-left corner, a motif that was employed by Whistler in his decoration of the cabinets in the Peacock Room (see fig.
6.5).
The drawing, in addition to its overtones of lust and violence, provided Beardsley with considerable freedom for decorative invention.
Aubrey Beardsley, design for The Climax, from Oscar Wilde’s Salomé, print, 9 × 5 in (22.9 × 12.7 cm), 1893.
Private collection.
Another prominent figure in the publication of books involving artists connected with aesthetic ideas was Charles Ricketts (18661931).
Ricketts carefully considered the unity of page design involving typography, illustration, and decoration.
He published a collaboration between Wilde and Beardsley, an illustrated poem entitled The Sphinx.
Much lighter in overall tone than the books of Morriss Kelmscott Press, the pages of The Sphinx use blocks of text, decorated initials, and framed illustration to suggest the relationship among individual elements unified by shared qualities of weight and density.
Ricketts worked with different printers to publish books under the name of the Vale Press.
Other titles include a large but thin volume of De Cupidinis et Psychis Amoribus Fabula Anilis, an erotic Latin poem translated by Charles Holme (editor of The Studio) with woodcut illustrations, dating to 1901.
Here the textured paper and ragged edges, Venetian-style humanistic typography, and varied width of columns to accommodate intimate scenes of lovers (fig.
6.10) are characteristic of private enjoyment meant for discriminating taste and requiring the skills of a designer sensitive to the page or doublepage spread as a unified graphic composition of type and image.

An aesthetic approach to printing is also found in illustrated books for other markets, including children.
Interest in childrens literature was strong among early design reformers such as Henry Cole, who saw these books as a means to cultivate taste and instill the values of work and moderation (see here and here).
In the later nineteenth century, attitudes about childrens books changed to include a more innocent, playful, in short, a more childlike, less didactic point of view.
In attempting to adopt the viewpoint of a child, illustrators entered into an imaginative state of mind that was akin to other work in the fine and decorative arts at this time.
The embossed gold seal found on many well-known childrens books today is named for a pioneer in childrens illustration, English illustrator Randolph Caldecott (1846 1886).
Caldecott was a self-taught artist who became a professional illustrator only after moving to London from Manchester in the early 1870s.
He served as a freelance illustrator for popular weekly news journals in London, and several of his illustrations were reproduced in Harper’s New Monthly Magazine published in New York.
Among his bestknown works is a series of books published by George Routledge from color wood engravings by Edmund Evans (18261905).
The collaboration of illustrator and engraver is significant, for Evanss skills as an engraver preserved the simple, abbreviated quality of Caldecotts drawings, set off against broad unmodulated areas of lightly tinted color: Evanss efforts were creative rather than mechanical and contributed to Caldecotts success.
Eliminating more conventional detail and cross-hatching used in the wood-engraving process, picture books such as Hey Diddle Diddle (1882; fig.
6.11) achieved wide popularity in both Britain and France.
Caldecott also earned respect among noted designers such as Walter Crane and artists Van Gogh and Gauguin, both of whom owned copies of Caldecotts relatively inexpensive picture books.
The recognition, in artistic as well as popular circles, of Caldecotts illustrations, along with the emergence of exhibitions and galleries devoted to print media, demonstrates the inter-relationship among the arts that animated both artists and the public during the later nineteenth century, and that contributed to respect for the emerging field of graphic design.
6.11 Randolph Caldecott, illustration from Hey Diddle Diddle, wood engraving, 7 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 8 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (18.8 × 22.4 cm), published by George Routledge & Sons, London, 1882.
Contemporary with Caldecotts picture books were those of another British artist, Kate Greenaway (18461901).
Greenaways father was a freelance wood engraver who had worked with Edmund Evans for the publisher of the satirical illustrated journal Punch, and Evans was also responsible for the engraving and color printing of Greenaways drawings.
Greenaway received training at the government-sponsored design schools established around the middle of the century that prepared designers for industry, and Ruskin praised her work for its idyllic recreation of natural beauty in a preindustrial era.
Her simplified drawing and frequent use of blank space reveal an affinity to the graphic tendencies of Aesthetic design, and as a woman her creative energies found an outlet in the applied arts rather than in the male-dominated fine arts at this time.
Greenaways first popular success was an illustrated book published by George Routledge in 1879 entitled Under the Window.
A frontispiece for Marigold Garden; Pictures and Rhymes (first published 1885; fig.
6.12) features high-waisted dresses that recall the simpler fashions of the late eighteenth and earlier nineteenth centuries and a type of idealized childs face (it has been suggested that the artist derived the type from her collection of dolls).
Greenaway also used bands of flowers to frame the illustration and serve as a motif to suggest a landscape setting.
In this case a garden twists around the playful composition of figures in various poses dancing in a circle.
This component in her illustrations grew out of her own sketches from nature as well as the conventionalized approach to drawing she learned at the schools of design and adapted to the genre of childrens illustration.
Critics have also suggested that the strong contours and areas of flat color found in Greenaways as well as Caldecotts childrens illustrations were derived from similar effects in Japanese woodblock prints that contributed so much to the contemporary Aesthetic Movement in Europe as well as in the United States.

7 \times 1 7 .
3$ cm), published by Frederick Warne & Co., London and New York, c.
1900 (first published 1885).
Print technology played an instrumental role in the success of childrens illustration.
The illustrations of Greenaway, Caldecott, and Walter Crane were reproduced from these artists original drawings rendered on wood for engraving, and, in the case of Greenaway, translated later onto stone for chromolithographic reproduction as greeting cards for a mass audience.
Black-and-white illustrations for more timely publications such as newspapers and weekly magazines used specialized labor to quickly translate drawings into wood, and by the 1880s photomechanical methods of reproducing images were beginning to compete with and eventually eclipse both relief and chromolithographic techniques for the reproduction of images.
At first, photographs of original drawings were printed on wood for hand-engraving, eliminating either the artists or engravers role at this stage of production.
A more significant development was the use of acid to engrave a wood or metal block printed with a photographic image, eliminating the need for any handwork at all except in the finishing stages.
Direct methods of printing involving artists and craftsmen persisted, however, in the genre of book illustration, and flourished in poster design, and in more editorial forms of imagery for political cartoons and caricatures in newspapers and magazines.

## The
Aesthetic Movement in the United States In the United States, numerous displays of Aesthetic design as well as a Japanese Pavilion were included at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia.
Five years later, Oscar Wilde made a lecture tour of major American cities where he promoted new attitudes toward the decorative arts.
Institutions such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art began to add examples of contemporary furniture and other decorative objects for the home to their collections in an effort to inform and elevate public taste, and schools of design and societies promoting the study and practice of the decorative arts thrived in a number of American cities.
In the last quarter of the nineteenth century, American artists turned to the design and manufacture of stained glass and metalwork, achieving considerable success at home and exposure abroad through displays and prizes at Worlds Fairs.
In the field of stained glass especially, American painters John La Farge (18351910) and Louis Comfort Tiffany (18481933) received numerous commissions for their work  mostly from private clients but also from public institutions.
Both men studied painting in Paris before turning to the decorative arts (La Farge practiced law before becoming an artist).
The elevated status of the decorative arts as well as commissions for all aspects of interior design influenced Tiffany, who wrote, I believe there is more in it [i.e. the decorative arts] than in painting pictures. After establishing his own company for interior decoration in 1879, Tiffany became artistic director of the company founded by his father, Charles Tiffany, which manufactured jewelry and virtu in silver and other precious metals.
Both Tiffany and La Farge experimented with new materials and techniques to achieve subtle coloristic and textural effects in their works: Tiffany introducing Favrile glass in 1892 for bowls and vases, and La Farge developing opalescent glass for windows.
The varied colors and surfaces of La Farges opalescent glass enriched the iridescence of his windows, producing a luminous effect that resembled the thick impasto of oil paint (fig.
6.13).
Tiffanys windows achieve the same richness, but the designer also reached beyond unique commissions to produce vases and other household objects aimed at a wider market, including desktop utensils and table and standing lamps with cast bronze bases.
In an electric lamp (fig.
6.14) manufactured between 1904 and 1915, the rust and yellow colors of stalks and leaves dominate a few remaining touches of pale green, suggesting an autumnal mood.
This mood is echoed not only in the drooping curves of the stalks but also in the fallen leaves and petals casually strewn on the base.
The subtle coloristic effects, close relationship between form, techniques of construction, and decoration, lack of reference to revival styles, as well as the mood and expressive unity of the whole, mark the high level of attention devoted to the decorative arts in the United States during this time and express the aspirations of the movement to achieve equality among the arts.
Tiffany designed early versions of his lamps for oil, with the fuel stored in the base and a shade to provide ventilation for an open flame.
Electric wiring for home lighting gained ground against gas and oil slowly, beginning in the 1880s; in 1907 8 percent of homes in the United States were wired for electricity, rising to 13 percent in 1912.
Electricity for home lighting (and later for a wider range of appliances) created opportunities for designers and manufacturers, including modern aesthetic possibilities for Tiffany studio artists, and the company was awarded a grand prize for its lamps at an international exhibition of decorative arts in Turin in 1902 in competition with entries of electric table lamps and chandeliers from Britain, Belgium, and France.
Consumers appreciated the advantages of safe and odorless energy; incandescent bulbs were brighter than gas or oil flames, and Tiffanys colored glass shades produced subtle effects more comfortable to the eyes of people accustomed to softer light, creating introspective aesthetic interest for artists and consumers alike.
John La Farge, Peonies Blown in the Wind, leaded opalescent glass, 75 × 45 in (190.5 × 113.7 cm), from the Marquand House, Newport, Rhode Island, c.
1880.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

## 6.13 Louis Comfort Tiffany, Waterlily table lamp, bronze and leaded Favrile glass, 26 ${ ^
1 } / _ { 2 } \times { 1 8 } { ^ 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (67 × 47 cm), manufactured by Tiffany Studios, 1904–1915.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
In addition to inventive experiments with techniques and materials, Tiffany was inspired by a variety of non-Western traditions.
For example, he may have been influenced by glass flasks from Persia, in terms of their translucence and their irregular and asymmetrical shapes (see fig.
GI2.2).
For his home near Oyster Bay, Long Island, known as Laurelton Hall (19021904 and after), Tiffany created an aesthetic interior in which it was difficult to discern the difference between art and nature: the dining room carpet, like the dome chandelier above the simple table and chairs, set an understated tone in blue and cream, while the transom of the picture window at the far end of the room was decorated with hanging wisteria in stained glass, looking out onto a terrace with hanging potted plants.
Visitors remarked the panels looked lifelike in relation to the real garden beyond the room (fig.
6.15).
Louis Comfort Tiffany, Wisteria panel, dining room, Laurelton Hall, leaded Favrile glass, 36 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 47 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 1 in (92.2 × 120.2 × 2.5 cm), manufactured by Tiffany Studios, New York, 1910–1920.
The Charles Hosmer Morse Museum of American Art, Winter Park, Florida.
One outcome of efforts to elevate the status of the decorative arts in the later nineteenth century was to associate manufactured products with the names of individual designers, much as we associate works of fine art with individual artists.
Such identification (or branding), however, ignores or undervalues the collaborative nature of the design enterprise.
We freely label as Tiffany the work produced at his studio in Corona, Queens, New York, and yet the products of that workshop involved a large workforce of skilled artisans who were essential to Tiffanys success, many of whom were women.
Clara Driscoll (18611944) not only oversaw a group of women who selected and assembled glass shades for electric lamps (the Glass and Cutting Department), but also designed several patterns for the lamps, including shades featuring dragonflies, peonies, and daffodils (narcissus).
In 1895 the Chicago Public Library commissioned the Tiffany Glass Company to design two large glass domes for its new building on Michigan Avenue.
One dome covered the large reading room near the front of the building, while a second, smaller dome served as a memorial to soldiers who had died in the Civil War.
The glass dome of the larger reading room rises on pendentives from white marble piers covered with inlaid mosaic tiles.
The color scheme of green, gray, and white is cool, and the overall impression is bright and radiant.
The memorial dome is more meditative: somber in color, utilizing mostly orange and brown tones, with foliate motifs filling the leaded glass panels as well as nine sections of frosted glass blocks set into the floor and emitting soft light from below (fig.
6.16).
In both rooms Tiffany utilized color and light to create a mood appropriate to the function of a designed space, calling to mind Oscar Wildes statement, quoted above (see here), that mere colour, unspoiled by meaning, and unallied with definite form, can speak to the soul in a thousand different ways.
The harmony that resides in the delicate proportions of lines and masses becomes mirrored in the mind ...
The marvels of design stir the imagination. 6.16 Louis Comfort Tiffany, War Memorial Room, interior with leaded glass dome and blocks of frosted glass flooring, 1896.
Chicago Cultural Center (formerly Chicago Public Library).
The influence of the Aesthetic Movement may also be seen in the highly individual approach to architecture by Philadelphia architect Frank Furness (18391912), who contributed furniture designs to a number of interiors for the buildings he designed.
His furniture displays a logical relationship between construction and ornament, and also an original and eclectic combination of Gothic and Islamic features that may derive from familiarity with the plates of Owens The Grammar of Ornament as well as Dressers The Art of Decorative Design.
Art furniture is also often associated with the Herter Brothers (Gustave and Christian), German immigrants who established a successful business in New York City that provided comprehensive interior design services in period and original styles featuring the highest levels of skilled craftsmanship and expensive materials for the apartments and mansions of wealthy industrialists such as Jay Gould and William Vanderbilt.
Herter Brothers regularly exhibited at Worlds Fairs, first with elaborate examples of carving in the Renaissance Revival style, often executed by German and Italian carvers who had emigrated to New York, and then shifting to refined marquetry characteristic of the Aesthetic Movement.
An example of the latter is the wardrobe (fig.
6.17) dating to 18751883.
It is rectangular in form (following Eastlakes recommendation to avoid extravagant contour or unnecessary curves), but displays delicate marquetry of simplified sprigs and blossoms in cherry wood against a black ground that appear to float randomly (though the composition follows a complex pattern).
Both the wardrobes form and decoration strongly resemble seventeenthcentury Japanese lacquer furniture.
The bedrooms, sitting rooms, and dining rooms that featured such costly and coordinated ensembles of furniture were the subject of magazine articles with photographs during the 1870s and 1880s, in particular a collection entitled Artistic Houses, published in 1883, that served to demonstrate American awareness of and identification with current European design trends, stimulated by the displays at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876.
Wardrobe, cherry, 78 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 49 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 26 in (199.4 × 125.7 × 66 cm), Herter Brothers, 1875–1883.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
The Tiffany Glass Company and other firms occasionally received important public commissions, but the focus of the Aesthetic Movement, both in Europe and in the United States, was the cultivation of the domestic interior as a setting for individual and family life.
Rather than the pre-modern concept of household in which generations of parents and children lived or even worked under the same roof, the family home in the later nineteenth century cultivated a new ideal of comfort, intimacy, social status, and individual identity, providing refuge from the anonymity and uniformity of the workplace and opportunities for private, personal experience.
Within this private sphere, women were encouraged to participate in an expanded range of crafts traditionally practiced in and associated with the home, including embroidery, woodcarving, and the decoration of pottery.
Local decorative arts societies and schools organized exhibitions and offered classes aimed primarily at middle-class women, who might engage in pursuits that were becoming more appreciated as art, while at the same time maintaining their status and respectability in society and not threatening traditionally male-dominated professions.
Household furnishings opened up a sphere of creative activity to women.
Candace Wheeler (18271923), for instance, founded the Society of Decorative Arts of New York in 1877, the aim of which was to promote art forms traditionally viewed as hobbies, such as embroidery and other forms of needlework, as creative and economically viable activities for women.
Her designs frequently show asymmetrical compositions inspired by the decorative arts of Japan, and in addition to working in partnership with Tiffany in the early 1880s, she produced designs independently for manufacturers of machine-woven fabrics and wallpapers.
Designs such as the Waterlily textile panel printed on silk in figure 6.18, produced by the successful Cheney Brothers Silk Manufacturing Company (with factories in New Hampshire and Connecticut), use patterns based upon the structure of flowers and vines but freely treated to convey movement and an almost pulsating growth, and reminiscent not only of Japanese decoration but also of Tiffanys experiments in glass or even William Morriss own wallpaper patterns (see fig.
5.2).

Despite an elevated status ascribed to the decorative arts as individual expression, womens creative activities continued to be associated with traditional domestic roles.
Moreover, the women who painted pottery were rarely involved in its production or in the areas of sales or marketing.
Such a separation of gender roles can be seen at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, where womens decorative arts were displayed in a separate pavilion; in 1893, Candace Wheeler was invited to participate in the 1893 Worlds (Columbian) Exposition in Chicago, as designer of the displays for the fairs Womens Building.
Ceramics was among the more prominent media for womens involvement in the Aesthetic Movement in the United States.
In Cincinnati, Maria Longworth (1849 1932) became aware of the Aesthetic Movement through the efforts of British designers who were commissioned to decorate a number of homes for wealthy local families in the area.
The list included her fathers estate, called Rookwood, as well as the home she lived in with her first husband, George Nichols.
Longworth studied ceramics at the University of Cincinnatis School of Design and helped to organize the Cincinnati Pottery Club.
With the backing of her father, she founded Rookwood Pottery in 1880.
Examples of Rookwood ceramics received medals at the 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris and a number of them (fig.
6.19) show the assimilation of Japanese-inspired techniques in the use of irregular forms and asymmetrical arrangements of decorative motifs; indeed, the presence of Japanese ceramic artist Kataro Shirayamadani (1865 1948) at Rookwood beginning in 1887 had an impact on the companys production.
Rookwood Pottery and the work of other local ceramicists, such as Longworths rival Mary Louise McLaughlin (18471939), made Cincinnati a hub for aesthetic ceramics, fostered through the publication of books and the training offered at the University of Cincinnati and private schools.
Harriet Elizabeth Wilcox, vase with sprays of freesia, earthenware with painted slip, height 22 <sup>1</sup>/ in (56.6 cm), manufactured by Rookwood Pottery, Cincinnati, Ohio, 1900.
Adelaide Alsop Robineau (18651929) also explored new directions in ceramics around the turn of the century.
Robineau traveled freely throughout her career, working in Minnesota, St.
Louis, Missouri, and later in Syracuse, New York, and became aware of aesthetic tendencies in the decorative arts through international exhibitions, particularly the Worlds Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.
Her Viking Ship vase from 1905 (fig.
6.20) combines carved relief decoration with smoother wheel-thrown shapes and fascination with the irregularities of surface and overlapping glazes to suggest a wind-tossed sailboat in a turbulent, vast, and forbidding sea.
Robineaus work explored the expressive possibilities of her medium in original directions more commonly associated with the arts of sculpture and painting.
It is difficult to pinpoint the inspiration for the subject matter of the Viking Ship vase; early in her career she and her husband lived in Minnesota, where a large number of Norwegian families immigrated in the later nineteenth century.
Norse mythology contributed to the construction of Norwegian identity as displayed at international exhibitions, and a replica of a Viking ship (the Gokstad ship) was on view on Lake Michigan for the 1893 Columbian Worlds Fair in Chicago, traveling from there along the Mississippi River to New Orleans, attracting a good deal of media attention.

## 6.20 Adelaide Alsop Robineau, Viking Ship vase, porcelain, $7 \ ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 2
\ ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 }$ in (18.4 × 7 cm), 1905.
Everson Museum of Art, Syracuse, New York.
Despite traditional gender-based limitations, womens achievements in the decorative arts were considerable and their participation more common than in the fine arts.
Notwithstanding the emphasis upon the equality of the arts in the Aesthetic Movement, women still moved less easily into the fine arts, and even painters such as Mary Cassatt (18441926), who studied in Philadelphia before settling in Paris in 1874, tended to be confined both in their choice of subject matter and of medium.
Cassatt, for instance, worked extensively in pastel, which was thought (by men) to be a less demanding and more appropriate medium for women artists than oil paint.
Some women rebelled against the restrictions implied by their traditionally domestic role.
Gaining momentum in the early twentieth century, a group of early material feminists looked to apply modern production technology toward liberating women from the drudgery of household work.
While books such as Catherine Beechers 1869 The American Woman’s Home advocated a scientific approach to household management  in short a domestic economy or science that would enable women to organize household work more efficiently and provide opportunities for more creative and intellectual pursuits  they did not question the underlying assumption that a womans place was in the single-family home.
Other feminist writers and activists felt that a socialized approach to household management, where facilities for laundry, cooking, and childcare were maintained communally rather than within the nuclear family unit, promised greater freedom for women and could marshal technologys time-saving benefits more efficiently.
Some feminists saw potential in machinery for institutional dishwashing and laundry services that might be constructed in separate facilities rather than in the home, while others felt that communal facilities for childcare would facilitate womens entry into the workforce.
Some of these ideas reached fruition in settlement houses and apartments that redefined a more communal approach to modern living in response to industrialization and urbanization in the later nineteenth century.
Such facilities, often open, spacious, and with a factory-like functionality, were meant to replace private kitchens in houses with efficiently designed areas where working women would be able to pick up prepared meals for their families.
Such experiments reveal alternatives to the traditional nuclear family and the private home that are part of the context for both the Arts and Crafts and the Aesthetic movements.
In focusing upon the decorative arts, both movements recognized and even encouraged the creative participation of women, yet at the same time often reinforced the identification of woman within the domestic sphere.
On the other hand, material feminists sought a more radical gender equality based not upon the elevation of craft to fine art but rather upon a shared, communal approach to modern living that questioned the primacy of home and family.
In the period between the twentieth centurys two world wars, designs for social housing with communal services also emerged as radical alternatives to the family unit along socialist lines (see here and fig.
9.39).

## Dress
Attitudes toward women in the later nineteenth century may also be gleaned through the study of dress and fashion.
Another indication of the wider diffusion of ideas about the equality of the arts and the new, elevated status of the decorative arts is the emergence of the high-fashion or haute-couture industry in Paris in the second half of the nineteenth century.
The profession of fashion designer is almost synonymous with Charles Frederick Worth (18251895), who worked in London in the textile trade before moving to Paris with his wife and securing commissions for garments from the Spanishborn Empress Eugénie (18261920) as well as other wealthy clients beginning in the 1850s.
Worth created the ideal image for aristocratic women in the later nineteenth century  in an age when some fashionable ladies rarely, if ever, wore the same garment twice, and when weekend parties might require several changes of clothing in a single day.
Worths wider success in Parisian society would hardly have been possible without industrial technology, in particular the sewing machine, which saved considerable time in constructing elaborate garments through the work of the many seamstresses he employed.
Worth also introduced more comfortable surroundings for shopping, invented fall and spring lines to stimulate consumer interest, and designed his clothing in closer relation to the human body, reducing if not eliminating some of the confining undergarments that characterized earlier formal dress.
Certainly Worths success grew from an emerging aesthetic interest in and appreciation for the varied textural and coloristic effects of fabrics, as seen for instance in the portraits of French artist Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres (17801867), whose painstaking technique captured the nuances of light falling on the folds of the dress of Madame Moitessier in a portrait from 1856 (fig.
6.21), and whose skin has the appearance of unblemished porcelain.
Curiously, as interest in womens fashion grew in the mid-nineteenth century, fashions for men became both more practical and more standardized in the general adoption of trouser suits and a preference for black.
While men and women competed for individual distinction in dress through the early nineteenth century, the increasing emphasis upon womens fashion in the later part of the century provides telling evidence of gender discrimination: womens preoccupation with fashion signaled they had no need to work; indeed to do so would be to bring into question their husbands ability to support them.
Furthermore, married women were not encouraged to work, and the elaboration and complexity of much womens fashion reinforced inactivity.
6.21 Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, Madame Moitessier, oil on canvas, 47 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 36 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> in (120 × 92.1 cm), 1856.
The National Gallery, London.
Worths place in the emerging high-fashion industry stems from his sovereignty as an artist-designer, creating an individual look for each patron, reflecting the patrons good taste and the designers creativity and originality.
Worth experimented with varieties of fabric for nuances of color, texture, and light, not unlike the interest of designers such as Tiffany or La Farge in the subtleties of reflection for colored leaded glass (see here).
Such effects can be seen in the portrait of one of Worths clients by the German portrait painter Franz Xavier Winterhalter (18051873), displaying the stiff folds and sparkling accents of gold thread in a garment made of silk tulle (fig.
6.22).
Not surprisingly, the best-known photographic portrait of Worth depicts the designer wearing a banded velvet beret, reminiscent of Rembrandt self-portraits in the collection of the Louvre in Paris.

## 6.22 Franz Xavier Winterhalter, portrait of Princess Tatyana Alexandrovna Yusupova wearing
a spangled tulle dress by Charles Worth, oil on canvas, 57 $^ 7 / _ { 8 } \times 4 0 ~ ^ { 1 5 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (147 × 104 cm), 1858.
The Hermitage Museum, St.
Petersburg.

## The
Aesthetic Movement and Shopping While the products of the Aesthetic Movement were often made to order or sold in small shops and boutiques for an exclusive clientele, the newly established department stores benefitted from the movement in creating a unified approach to interior design as a worthwhile investment in marketing to attract the attention of a wider range of consumers.
The emergence of the department store in the 1860s revolutionized the experience of shopping for the middle class in Europe and in the United States.
These large stores, with a variety of goods sold under the same roof, provided a permanent setting for the spectacle of consumption as experienced in the displays at international exhibitions.
Department stores such as the Bon Marché in Paris and John Wanamaker in Philadelphia endeavored to turn shopping into a pleasurable and transformative experience that encouraged shoppers to identify consumption with the fulfillment of an idealized dream of comfort, luxury, self-improvement, and self-realization.
Aesthetic design, in elevating goods above utility and function, played an integral role in this commercial expansion.
Department stores housed displays for furniture, fabrics and other home furnishings, as well as foods, all ordered in large quantities and sold at fixed prices (rather than by bartering between customer and vendor) with specials and seasonal sales to entice buyers, along with snack bars and even reading rooms.
Their success depended upon quantity production of basic types of goods differentiated by a variety of styles of decoration, whether dresses with applied trims of different patterns of lace, or cabinets ordered from manufacturers with decoration in a variety of historical period styles that had begun to emerge around the middle of the century.
As an example, see figure 6.23: two plates from a book of furniture designs published in England by furniture manufacturer Henry Whitaker in 1847.
The illustrations reveal the strong similarity among the sideboards, differentiated only by carved decoration in the Elizabethan and Italian styles.
While perhaps a far cry from the bespoke furniture that aspired to be art by Herter Brothers and other high-end manufacturers, such furniture rose above utility to some higher level of meaning, signifying material progress and discriminating taste for the new middle-class retail market, evidence of art applied to industry, higher levels of increasing production, employment, and channels of distribution.
Henry Whitaker, two illustrations of sideboards in Elizabethan and Italian styles, from the furniture catalog Practica Cabinet Maker’s Treasure, London, 1847.
Advice books such as Eastlakes Hints on Household Taste and others demonstrate the close relationship between women, shopping, and individual identity.
Rather than emphasizing the making of objects, in terms of labor, commerce, or design, the focus of this expansion of shopping rested upon associations between buyers and objects, as projections or extensions of their individuality.
By the end of the century, shoppers visiting department stores such as Harrods in Knightsbridge, London (only a short walk from the Victoria and Albert Museum), were treated to colorfully designed and brightly lit interiors with walls and ceilings covered with enamel-like patterned glazed tiles: an example is Harrods Meat Hall, dating to 1902 (fig.
6.24).
In addition to commercial activity, department stores offered free concerts and recitals that provided elevated forms of public entertainment  another demonstration of the link between design and generalized individual and social progress in an emerging consumer society.
An example is the Wanamaker Organ, displayed at the 1904 Worlds Fair in St.
Louis and installed in the city of Philadelphias Wanamaker department store in 1911 for business-hour as well as weekend afternoon family concerts.
Meat Hall with tiled walls, Harrods department store, London, 1902.
Although the image of Art Nouveau brings to mind the swirling linear style associated with posters, furniture, and applied decoration in the 1890s in France, the term is perhaps best understood in the broader context of later nineteenth-century ideas about aesthetic design and the unity of the arts as they took root on French soil.
As numerous Realist and Impressionist paintings of the period reveal, the 1860s and 1870s in Paris witnessed far-reaching changes in the experience of urban life, beginning with the construction of grand boulevards, bridges, monuments, piazzas, and public gardens under Napoleon III (r.
18521870) and civic planner Eugène-Georges Haussmann (18091891), and continuing with the building of the Paris Opéra and the emergence of venues for other middle-class forms of entertainment.
There was significant commercial expansion of the city as well, for instance in the opening of the Bon Marché in 1869 and other department stores that soon followed.
Middle-class leisure was viewed as a spectator sport, and writers coined the term flâneur to describe that type of gentleman who delighted in strolling the avenues, window shopping or meeting friends at a café.
Painter Édouard Manet captured casual slices of this new life of strolling and coffee breaks in his Corner in a Café Concert (18789, fig.
6.26), with a barmaid serving mugs of beer to a crowd of mixed social class customers and a dancer (or singer) performing on stage in the background.
International exhibitions of art and industry, the earlier ones modeled on the Crystal Palace, were also part of Parisian public life during the second half of the nineteenth century, being staged first in 1855, again in 1867, and repeated in 1878, 1889, and 1900.
6.26 Edouard Manet, Corner in a Café Concert, oil on canvas, 39 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 30 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (100 × 77.5 cm), 1878–1879.
The National Gallery, London.
The department stores need for larger quantities of furniture placed inordinate pressures upon the system of workshop production, forcing artisans to increase production while receiving the same or even lower wages, leading to standardization, a decline in quality, and deterioration in working conditions.
In part as a response to these circumstances, a private organization of manufacturers and skilled artisans known as the Central Union of Fine Art as Applied to Industry was created as early as 1864 to promote high standards in design based upon the harmony of beauty and utility, standards inherited from the design reform movement in Britain (see here onward).
The Central Union sponsored exhibitions and even created a library where artisans and manufacturers might consult drawings as models for production.
The silver and gilt beer service (fig.
6.25) by Fannière Frères dating to 1865 embodies the aims of the Central Union at this time.
Rather than references to historical styles, the ensemble depicts the planks of wooden kegs, bound with twisted rope and strewn with vegetation, exemplifying the fitness of decoration to purpose.
Certainly the members of the Central Union took an interest in elevating the quality of the applied arts in France and in educating consumers and manufacturers, but increasingly the efforts of this organization stressed the renewal of the luxury crafts and the reputation they enjoyed during the eighteenth century, with specialized labor and the use of machine tools to maintain high levels of skill and refinement.
After 1889 the organization dropped the word industrial from its title, and concentrated instead upon promoting the strength of the nations artisanal heritage.
Reformers generally viewed industrial production with uniformity, poor quality, and unfavorable competition with other nations, and also as a betrayal of a significant national cultural legacy.
Contemporary critics debated these issues, often commenting on the displays at international exhibitions.
Some critics praised the high levels of technical skill and art as applied to manufacture, while others were critical of the absence of more practical and affordable products and furnishings.

## 6.25 Fannière Frères, beer service, silver with gilt, pitcher 9 × 5 in (23 × 12.5 cm), 186
5.
Musée d’Orsay, Paris.
In addition to reviving appreciation for the high quality of eighteenth-century production, advocates for design reform in France also encouraged the combination of high levels of skill together with originality.
German-born merchant Siegfried Bing contributed to the activities of the Central Union.
Bing collected and sold examples of Japanese decorative arts in Paris, published a journal devoted to his vision of Japanese art and culture (Japon Artistique), and helped to mount exhibitions of Japanese crafts that he admired for their refinement and the craftsmens feeling for nature and for the nature of materials.
Bing encouraged contemporary French designers to create new and original work, and visited the United States in 1893 where he saw and praised the work of Louis Comfort Tiffany in stained glass (see here).
In 1895 Bing transformed his gallery of Japanese arts into coordinated ensembles of furniture and furnishings displayed in showrooms bearing the name La Maison de lArt Nouveau featuring Japanese crafts as well as contemporary interiors designed by Tiffany and Belgian artist and designer Henry van de Velde (18631957; see fig.
6.47).
Despite the eclectic and international character of La Maison de lArt Nouveau, Bing felt that the work was unified by shared levels of refinement and quality, demonstrating the kind of modern renewal of the decorative arts that would inspire artists and artisans and appeal to a discriminating taste.
Some critics, however, complained that La Maison de lArt Nouveau showrooms lacked a more obvious stylistic coherence; as a result, Bing realized the importance of appealing to a French audience with a more consistent and recognizably French style that revitalized the legacy of French preeminence in the decorative arts.
In this climate of strong national feeling and international competition, a number of French designers emerged whose work demonstrated respect for and continuity with the high levels of craftsmanship in eighteenth-century luxury goods and furnishings, yet without directly imitating their forms.
This pride in the national past merged with more modern concepts of artistic freedom and originality seen, for instance, in the works of French Symbolist artists, who saw the arts as the vehicle for subjective expression moving beyond the more optical style of Impressionism in the 1870s and the early interest of those painters in the leisure pastimes of the middle class.
Such qualities may be seen in the glass objects designed and crafted by Émile Gallé (18461904), who trained and worked as a glassmaker in the city of Nancy in northeast France.
Gallé experimented with color, light, and texture in the medium of glass, exploring effects beyond the traditional associations with the material.
Many of his works are highly individual, more like relief sculptures in glass than utilitarian objects.
In his vase of 1900 (fig.
6.27), flowers in shades of purple emerge in relief against a light-brown background.
Gallé often used an array of colors to accentuate the effects of changing light while mottled textures hinted at reflections.
Gallés heightened sensitivity to nature and obsessive manipulation of materials to obtain the most delicate effects of light are contemporary with the series of studies of the same subject by Claude Monet (18401926) as well as similar explorations of translucence and iridescence in glass by Tiffany and La Farge (or in silk by Candace Wheeler).
Although less abstract, the feelings for growth and transformation in Gallés works anticipate the automatic techniques of Surrealist artists in the 1920s, and in fact both movements were influenced by a fascination with dreams and the unconscious.
Gallés work shares with Symbolism an interest in private, psychological experience, and the primacy of feeling and mood over purely optical experience.
Gallé was inspired by the Symbolist poets Charles Baudelaire (1821 1867) and Paul Verlaine (18441896), and phrases from their verse are sometimes etched directly in the glass surfaces of his vases.
Such works achieve one of the aims of the later Central Union: to revitalize the arts by obliterating any boundary between them and restore the shared esteem in which French luxury products in several media were held in an increasingly competitive international market. Émile Gallé, Waterlilies, vase, multi-layered glass with filigree, glass inlay and carved details, 1900.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Like Tiffany, Gallé not only produced unique objects but also was interested in the unified interior as a total work of art.
He designed furniture for workshop production featuring carved forms but relying primarily upon elaborate marquetry for intricate linear and spatial effects.
By employing more modern production techniques and woodworking machines, Louis Majorelle (18591926), who also worked in Nancy, designed furniture in the Art Nouveau style appearing not only in private homes but also in public spaces (the Parisian restaurant Bouillon Julien is now restored to Majorelles 1906 design).
His writing desk (fig.
6.28, also titled Lady Waterlily) with matching side chair includes gilt mounts that recall more directly the cast fittings of eighteenth-century Rococo furniture, but here treated in an original manner that transforms flowers, leaves, and vines into abstract linear patterns.
Related desks by Majorelle include attached electric light fixtures with frosted glass shades in the shape of exotic orchids.
Throughout the design of the desk, Majorelle conceives of decoration as something both expressive and integrated with rather than added on to construction, seen to great advantage in the back of the chair, everywhere investing a sense of living, breathing form to inert materials.
Louis Majorelle, Waterlily lady’s writing desk (detail), mahogany with marquetry and carved gilt bronze fittings and pullers, c.
1903.
Royal Museum of Art, Brussels.
The boundary between sculpture and furniture is virtually eliminated in the highly original works of Rupert Carabin (18621932), who worked in Paris beginning in the later 1870s.
Carabins one-of-a-kind pieces often sacrifice utility to a highly original artistic vision that undermines traditional assumptions about furniture.
A carved chair (fig.
6.29) dating to 1898 not only tests the limits of comfort, but also surrounds the sitter with the unsettling feeling of a primeval forest inhabited by menacing snakes and dryads.
Rupert Carabin, armchair, walnut, $4 3 ~ ^ { 1 1 } / \ i \times 2 4 ~ ^ { 3 } / \ i \ i$ in (111 × 63 cm), 1898.
Private collection.
In addition to glass and furniture, French decorative artists took a lively interest in ceramics.
Asymmetrical forms, irregular surface textures, and the subtle overlaying of glazes suggest experiment and intuition in the manipulation of the medium, again parallel to the contemporary interest in expressive brushwork and surface among the Symbolist painters.
Pierre-Adrien Dalpayrat (18441910) experimented with uneven or unfinished textures and irregular shapes, revealing a strong sense of process and the intuitive manipulation of materials by the artist, as in the gourd-shaped stoneware vase illustrated in figure 6.30.
While this type of work does not have a stylistic similarity with the linear rhythms more commonly associated with French Art Nouveau as a style, it nevertheless shares with other examples of the period the vision of craft as a vehicle for psychological expression through the exploration of original aesthetic effects.
It is interesting to note that this emphasis upon the expressive possibilities of texture and overlays of glaze is parallel to the increasing autonomy of the artwork noted by artists such as Maurice Denis (18701943), who stated that a picture, before being a battle horse, a nude, an anecdote or whatnot, is essentially a flat surface covered with colors assembled in a certain order.

## 6.30 Pierre-Adrien Dalpayrat, gourd stoneware vase, 14 ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 6 { }
^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (36.8 × 16.5 cm), 1893–1900.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
In 1901, a group of like-minded artists established the Société des Artistes Décorateurs (S.A.D.) to protect the status of the applied arts against any encroachments by industry and to reinforce the unity and equality of the arts.
During this period the decorative arts acquired associations with originality and expression, while the fine arts were recognized for their autonomy from the imitation of nature and an appreciation for their truth to materials or medium.
Artists freely crossed the increasingly permeable border between fine art and applied design, among them Odilon Redon (18401916), Pierre Bonnard (18671947), Maurice Denis, and Édouard Vuillard (18681940).
Auguste Renoir (18411919) penned essays and letters expressing his strong belief in the unity of the arts.
He trained as a porcelain painter before pursuing a career as an easel painter, and lamented the hierarchy between fine and applied art.
These artists pursued associations of the word decorative that suggested personal and expressive possibilities in a variety of media beyond easel painting: working, for instance, in lithography, wallpaper design, and painted screens, though often as private commissions rather than more broadly commercial manufacture.
Among their efforts might be included those of Lucien Pissarro (18631944), the son of Impressionist painter Camille Pissarro (18301903), who pursued a career in book publishing, but left France for London where an active private press movement held the promise of greater opportunity.

## Art
Nouveau in Print and in Public As mentioned above, strengthening the connection between art and industry served many interests, including extending individual artistic activity beyond the fine arts, elevating public taste, stimulating production, creating national identity, and investing useful goods with the promise and satisfaction of aesthetic pleasure.
In the increasingly commercial conditions of metropolitan centers such as Paris, the new aesthetic sensibility seen in the decorative arts formed part of a more generalized modernity that extended beyond private ownership and collecting to a broader and more heterogeneous public.
At the Exposition Universelle held in Paris in 1900, lArt Nouveau dominated the architectural constructions for the fair, and French pavilions featured coordinated ensembles of decorative art in the new style.
French architect and designer Hector Guimard (18671942) was particularly conspicuous in expanding elements of lArt Nouveau formal vocabulary on an urban scale using modern industrial technology.
Guimard adapted the elastic plantlike tendrils associated with many products of aesthetic craft to the railings and entrances of the newly constructed Paris underground transportation system known as the Métro, a few of which are still in use (fig.
6.31).
Cast iron was used for this vast project, integrating aesthetic invention with modern industrial production.
Guimard also used cast iron for window grilles and designs for a series of original numbers to mark the entrances to houses and buildings.
In these ways the arts served a socially progressive role, beautifying and creating a visual identity for the city, attracting tourism, stimulating commerce, and suggesting synergy rather than an antithesis between art and industry.
Hector Guimard, Métro station entrance, Paris, cast iron, c.
1900.
