Elements of Art Nouveau were also popularized via print media, chiefly in the design and printing of publicity posters, made possible through chromolithography along with more lenient laws that relaxed the regulation of public space enacted in France in 1881.
Posters were a prominent, colorful means of promoting products, retail businesses, nightclubs, and cafés, and were a ubiquitous presence in the city, enlivening walls, buildings, and kiosks along the citys grand and pedestrian-friendly boulevards.
Among the most significant patrons for poster advertisement during this time were the providers of popular entertainment, and the lithographic printers themselves, who produced posters in smaller format for sale to collectors as well as in larger dimensions for viewing on the street.
The dance halls, circuses, and cabarets located in Parisian districts such as Montmartre served as a magnet for middle-class urban leisure, activities that allowed for freer, less structured, uninhibited public forms of self-expression.
Whether directly as participants or vicariously as spectators, this public found an outlet for playfulness, fantasy, and sensual pleasure in a vibrant Parisian nightlife  in short, posters sold fun.
Jules Chéret (18361932) was an early master of poster design, beginning his career as an apprentice to a printer and spending time in England mastering the technique of chromolithography, which had been successfully developed in the printing of color images primarily for illustrated books (see here and fig.
4.13).
Chéret often approached the composition of the poster as an integration of lettering and image to create a unified design on a monumental scale, even when the actual size of the poster was not particularly large.
In the poster advertising a group of acrobatic dancers known as Les Girard from 1879 (fig.
6.32), for example, areas of bold text at the top and bottom of the tall rectangular format announce the venue and particular act or time of the performance.
The placement of the letters deviates from a horizontal base line, and instead connects and interacts with the three silhouetted dancers in the center, almost like an apparatus to demonstrate the flexibility of their elongated limbs.
The sense of movement is strengthened by pinwheel-like shapes of arms, legs, and coat tails, and by the virtual elimination of detail and background.
Chéret explored the medium of chromolithography in order to attract attention from a distance, working directly on the stone in an abbreviated, seemingly spontaneous manner.

## 6.32 Jules Cheret, Les Girard, poster for the Folies-Bergère, color lithograph, 21 <sup>1<
/sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 17 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (54 × 44.5 cm), 1879.
Musée de la Publicité, Paris.
An expressive treatment of line, as well as simplified compositional elements derived from Japanese woodblock prints, also appear in the lithographic posters of painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (18641901), which often advertised the performances of popular Montmartre entertainers such as Loïe Fuller and Louise Weber (known as La Goulue).
The latter is featured in a poster of 1891 for the Moulin Rouge (fig.
6.33), printed in a large edition of 3,000 for display throughout Paris.
In this poster the illustration is simplified by strong contours for the foreground figures of La Goulue and her partner Valentine le Désossé, while the silhouetted forms of the crowd and the typography maintain the planarity of the surface and unify the elements of the composition into a compact whole.
Toulouse-Lautrec also worked directly on the lithographic stone, using strong contours as well as a technique known as crachis to splatter rather than to brush ink on broad areas of the stone.
The result is a vitality that matches the mood of gaiety and hedonistic abandon that generates appeal for an evening of casual socializing and entertainment.
The chromolithographic poster led a double life: as advertisement and as artwork.
Designers signed their work and printers issued them in separate, reduced sizes for collectors.
They provided commercial printers with an added value as promotions for a new, reproducible form of modern art, made popular entertainment appealing through associations with a carefree lifestyle, and at the same time enabled the expressive ideas of the Aesthetic Movement to extend beyond a narrow, exclusive circle of initiated viewers.
They also demonstrated the power of reductive images to attract attention and for the public to identify performers such as La Goulue, Aristide Bruant, or Loïe Fuller, in effect branding them with characteristic gestures, attributes, or signs.
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, La Goulue (Louise Weber) at the Moulin Rouge, poster, color lithograph, 48 × 33 in (122 × 83.8 cm), 1891.
Turning to the Chicago-born performance artist Loïe Fuller (18621928), both Chéret and painter Manuel Orazi (18601934) designed advertising posters featuring this popular entertainer (fig.
6.34).
Orazi hints at eroticism in the dancers performance by outlining Fullers partially nude body beneath a sheer garment.
Orazis poster also has a stronger sense of abstract and suggestive forms: hair, flowers, drapery become swirling and cascading shapes making it difficult to distinguish representation from more purely expressive, abstract decoration, along with bursting circular shapes that become more abstract as they descend and morph from the bouquet at the upper left.
Fullers dance was also the subject of a series of 15 ceramic figurines designed by Agathon Léonard (18411923) for the Sèvres manufactory in 1898 and displayed at the 1900 International Exhibition in Paris.
In addition, Fullers performance was captured on moving film in the early years of this new mediums development.
On film there appears to be little if any suggestion of nudity.
Rather we see the dancers white scarf and circular arm movements combine to somehow transform her body into the form of a flower in bloom as if by magic.
The theme of metamorphosis, seen in the transformation of letterforms into representation or hair into flames or pure decoration in the chromolithographic art poster, is not uncommon in Art Nouveau.
Historians have noted a relationship between artists aesthetic fascination with the theme of transformation in nature and Darwins theory of natural selection (first published in 1859), which revealed nature in a constant condition of flux rather than permanence, while at the same time guided by a process of selection toward perfection.
The dancers appeal certainly incorporated an abstract aesthetic dimension, but also extended to other audiences, who were excited by novelty, fantasy, sensuality, and the surprise of the unexpected.
Manuel Orazi, poster for Löie Fuller, color lithograph, 78 <sup>1</sup>/ 1D4 × 25 <sup>1</sup>/ in (198.7 × 64.1 cm), 1900.
Eugène-Samuel Grasset (18411917) was an illustrator and advertising artist who developed a style for graphic images sometimes referred to as cloisonné.
He employed strong black lines and figureground contrast to reinforce the planarity of the surface, while the linear treatment of drapery folds or strands of wavy hair create secondary patterns resembling the cells of leaded glass, enamel, or jewelry  media in which Grasset also worked.
In an advertisement for Encre L.
Marquet (Marquet Ink, The Best of All Inks), the diagonal lettering runs parallel to wavy cloudlike shapes that balance the opposing diagonal direction of a woman who sits thoughtfully, pen in hand (fig.
6.35).
Grassets figures are less spontaneous and abbreviated than those of Chéret or Toulouse-Lautrec.
Nevertheless, female images dominate the art of the poster; they represent the good life when linked to the purchase of products and entertainment, and they offer new models for defining women in more active roles outside the home, as in American artist Will Bradleys advertising poster for Victor Bicycles (fig.
6.36).
Eugène-Samuel Grasset, advertisement for Marquet Ink, color lithograph, 47 <sup>15</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 31 <sup>13</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (121.8 × 80.8 cm), 1892.
Will Bradley, poster for Victor Bicycles, color lithograph, 25 $^ { 1 3 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 3 9 ^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (64.4 × 99.7 cm), 1896.
Alphonse Mucha (18601939) came to Paris from his home in Moravia (Czech Republic, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire) after studying painting in Vienna and Munich.
His posters advertising the performances of actress Sarah Bernhardt (18441923) are among his best-known works.
In the large 1895 Gismonda poster (fig.
6.37), the actress holds a palm sprig that relates to the plays final act in which her character participates in an Easter Day procession.
Her garlanded hair is echoed in the shawl and tunic, both inscribed with floral patterns.
Unlike other poster artists who sacrificed detail to emphasize bold shapes, Mucha delights in inventive decoration.
Yet the semicircular arch above the actresss head, as well as a banner below the ground line, contain the text and help to focus rather than distract the viewers attention.
Despite foreshortening and shadow, the simplified modeling and empty area behind the actresss figure emphasize an heroic monumentality and suggest the dreamlike space of the stage.
Later posters are freer in the use of abstraction to allude to metamorphosis, especially in the abstract shapes that suggest hair or lush plant forms.
Alphonse Mucha, Sarah Bernhardt in Gismonda, poster, color lithograph, 84 <sup>3</sup>/ × 30 in (215.3 × 76.2 cm), 1895.
In the United States, Harper’s Magazine published cover illustrations by Grasset as well as by American designers such as Edward Penfield (18661925), while some of the boldest approaches to the medium appear in the oeuvre of Will Bradley (18681962).
Bradleys early illustrations, influenced by Aubrey Beardsley (see here), had appeared in the British journal The Studio, and examples of his work were exhibited at the opening of La Maison de lArt Nouveau in 1895.
In the United States Bradley was active in many areas of an expanding print industry.
He published illustrated books for his own private and short-lived Wayside Press in Springfield, Massachusetts, and also contributed to a magazine called The American Chap-Book, published by the American Type Founders Company (see here) as well as the trade journal Inland Printer.
In an 1896 advertising poster for Victor Bicycles (fig.
6.36), Bradley used four colors to create a bold, reductive image.
Repetition in the black silhouettes of the riders and in the elongated floral decoration are both products of simplification, while the use of black ties the border with its lettering to the image.
Bradleys posters and illustration create effective figure ground reversal  for instance, in the negative shapes between the arm and torso of the foreground female rider to the left of the composition.
The design incorporates a carefully considered hierarchy of information: the red lettering against the black border attracts the viewers eye, first with the larger letters at the top left and then with the company name diagonally at the lower right, while the black silhouettes of the riders serve to connect top to bottom.
The placement of white flowers reinforces left to right eye movement that focuses attention on the company name and the head of the larger female figure.
The public and commercial face of Art Nouveau extends to the design of interiors and displays related to fantasy and enhancing the experience of shopping.
Jeweler Georges Fouquet (18621957) collaborated with Mucha on several brooches, and Mucha designed Fouquets boutique on the rue Royale in Paris in 1900 (fig.
6.38), completed in time for the Paris Worlds Fair of the same year.
Patterned tile floors and friezes, plantlike pilasters and other architectural details, relief sculptures of peacocks, and wall-mounted curving glass cases in the shape of bubbles unify wall, ceiling, and floor into a total work of art.
Mirrors serve to make the space appear larger, indulging the fantasy of the spectator in an imaginative setting for effectively merchandising the exotic creations offered for sale.

## 6.38 Alphonse Mucha, interior for boutique, Paris, for Georges Fouquet, jeweler, 1900. Pho
tograph: Musée Carnavalet, Paris.
Mucha achieved success as a poster artist, although his posters include more detail than those of contemporaries such as Jules Chéret.
To be persuasive, advertising posters had to arrest the attention of the pedestrian viewer, that is, to stand out from a distance with audacious color and broad execution according to the English critic Charles Hiatt, and to project a mood of gaiety, in other words, to sell, often depicting young, idealized, and alluring female figures.
Could such objectives have conflicted with rather than stimulated artistic freedom?
Mucha left France to return to his native Moravia in 1910.
At the conclusion of World War I, his homeland became part of the newly independent nation of Czechoslovakia.
Deeply patriotic, Mucha spent the remainder of his career engaged in a series of 26 mural-size paintings narrating the history of his country (The Slav Epic), striving to create a serious national art freed from the commercial constraints of the advertising poster.

## Glasgow:
Charles Rennie Mackintosh In Glasgow, Scottish architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh (18681928), his wife Margaret MacDonald (18641933), and a small group of fellow students and colleagues navigated the territory between the aesthetic and broader public context for the decorative arts before World War I.
Situated on the River Clyde, Glasgow became an important seaport and international trading hub during the nineteenth century.
The construction and outfitting of ocean liners and railway locomotives bolstered the local economy and led to the widespread use of standardized industrial methods of production for furniture and interior decoration.
The Singer sewing machine company operated a factory in Glasgow, and the city prospered amid economic growth, new wealth, and a modern, progressive image.
In his own architecture and interiors, Mackintosh strived to create a distinctive and original approach to design, combining straightforward construction clearly stated through vertical and horizontal structural elements, integrated with restrained decorative elements that either played upon this geometry (as in the Library of the Glasgow School of Art, 19071909) or incorporated a free interpretation of the tense linear rhythms of Hiberno-Saxon decoration.
In many of his projects Mackintosh collaborated with his wife, Margaret MacDonald.
The picture frame illustrated in figure 6.39, designed by Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh and her sister Frances (18731921), is made from hammered aluminum on wood.
Experimenting with a new metal that was becoming more affordable as a result of cheaper industrial methods of extraction, the frame features highly personal and abstract interpretations of floral and vegetal forms.
Moreover, aluminum was a local resource, since Scotland was a center for aluminum production in Britain beginning in the later 1890s.
Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh and Frances MacDonald, picture frame, aluminum and oak, 27 ${ ^ 3 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 1 2 { ^ 3 } / _ { 4 }$ in (69.2 × 32.4 cm), 1897.
Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh.
The same vocabulary of an attenuated rectilinear framework forming borders for more organic floral and human forms can be seen in the murals MacDonald designed for Miss Kate Cranstons Buchanan Street Tearooms in 18961897 (fig.
6.40).
The tearoom afforded several opportunities for Mackintosh and MacDonald to create unified, original interiors between 1895 and 1903, and was a unique expression of Glasgows original and modern identity.
Frequently owned and managed by women, Glasgows tearooms introduced the kind of coordinated aesthetic interior found in privately commissioned homes into a public commercial setting.
Mackintosh designed several tearooms for Miss Cranston from 1896 to 1902, where middle-class clientele might enjoy the aesthetic ambience produced by the unity and equality of all the arts.
Mackintoshs design activity extended to flatware, dishes, glassware, and tablecloths, as well as furniture, windows, and lighting.
He believed that an individual approach to design could be reconciled with efficient industrial production, and that the decorative arts were integral to a satisfying modern lifestyle and not just for the discerning few.
His interiors and coordinated design ensembles offered an alternative to historical revival styles and demonstrated that aesthetic experience need not be sacrificed to the demands for standardization in industrial production.
Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh, interior, Buchanan Street Tearooms, Glasgow, 1896– 1897.

## Austria
Mackintoshs interior designs were illustrated in journals, displayed at an international exhibition in Turin in 1902, and stimulated the efforts of a group of artists and architects in Vienna known as the Secession.
These artists, like the Pre-Raphaelites in Britain and Les Vingt in Belgium (see here), reacted to the rigidity and elitism of academic practice in the fine arts and sought both freedom of expression as well as embracing the decorative arts.
The attitudes of the Secession group appear in the motto inscribed on their exhibition hall, designed by Joseph Olbrich in Vienna in 1898 (fig.
6.41): Die Zeit ihre Kunst, Die Kunst ihre Freiheit (To every time its art, to every art its freedom).
Vienna proved fertile ground for elevated attitudes toward the decorative arts, where new ideas resonated with connoisseurs and were directed as well toward a broader, open-minded public.
Joseph Olbrich, façade of the Secession building, Vienna, 1898.
Josef Hoffmann (18701956), an architect and leading member of the Secession, and versatile artist-designer Koloman (Kolo) Moser (18681918) created an organization that linked designers, craftsmen, and manufacturers in a shared enterprise to improve the quality and elevate the status of the decorative arts in Austria.
The organization, known as the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshops), was founded in 1903 with the financial backing of industrialist Fritz Wärndorfer (18681939).
Hoffmann was inspired by the example of Ashbees Guild of Handicraft (see here) as well as by Mackintosh (whose work was featured in a Secession exhibition in 1900), and wrote to the architect for advice.
In his response, Mackintosh encouraged his Viennese colleagues, sounding a note of optimistic liberal idealism in his plea for the role of the artist in improving the quality of everyday life through design: If one wants to achieve an artistic success with your programme ... every object which you pass from your hand must carry an outspoken mark of individuality, beauty and most exact execution.
From the outset your aim must be that every object which you produce is made for a certain purpose and place.
Later ... you can emerge boldly into the full light of the world, attack the factory-trade on its own ground, and the greatest work that can be achieved in this century, you can achieve it: namely the production of objects of use in magnificent form and at such a price that they lie within the buying range of the poorest.
First those who [look down at applied art] must be overcome and taught that the modern movement is not a silly hobby-horse of a few who wish to achieve fame comfortably through eccentricity, but that the modern movement is something living, something good, the only possible art  for all and for the highest phase of our time.
Products of the Werkstätte include a range of domestic items from clothing to glass and tableware, to wallpaper and individualized calling cards (presented to domestic servants when paying a social visit), all of which were generally produced on commission from wealthy private clients.
Each product bore the stamp of the artist, the manufacturer, and the workshops distinctive interlocked W monogram, as an expression of individual responsibility and the spirit of collaboration between designer and manufacturer.
Designers varied in their approaches, but all were committed to originality rather than historicism.
Hoffmanns designs parallel those of Mackintosh in incorporating repeated geometric decorative patterns as a distinctive but restrained approach to decoration on otherwise simple, even plain, objects, as seen, for instance, in the chairs manufactured for the exclusive Purkersdorf Sanitarium in 1905 that feature a series of small circular perforations cut in their backs (fig.
6.42).
The absence of carved or molded decoration, as well as the light, open interior of the dining room, help to create not only an aesthetically unified interior but also a modern, hygienic one, in sympathy with the views of design reform writers who viewed carved decoration as unhealthy because it attracted dust (see fig.
6.48) and required more cleaning.
Other examples of Werkstätte objects include wine glasses manufactured in 1907 by the Meyr Neffe company in Bohemia (now the Czech Republic) but sold in Austria by a Viennese retailer.
The longstemmed glasses, based upon traditional techniques practiced in the region but treated here with great subtlety and sophistication, were designed by Otto Prutscher (1880 1949), and are made of clear mold-blown glass overlaid with colored glass and then carefully cut to make the stem appear like links of a fragile, translucent chain (fig.
6.43).
6.42 Josef Hoffmann, dining room of Purkersdorf Sanitarium, 1905.
6.43 Otto Prutscher, wine glass, wheel-cut glass, height 8 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> in (21 cm), Meyr Neffe Glassworks, Vienna, 1907.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Mosers designs were no less original or ingenious.
While his early work in graphic design was inspired by French Art Nouveau, Moser turned to severe rectilinear shapes and forms after 1900 in graphic design, exhibition design, architectural decoration, and furniture.
His striking poster for a Secession art exhibition from 1902 (fig.
6.44) features three severely abstract bust-length female figures whose circular coiffures intersect with a large central circle.
The almost illegible mono-weight letterforms (note the similarity between the odd upper-case R and A), without spacing between words, suggest that clarity of information was not the primary purpose of Mosers visual communication.
The grid-like design unifies the composition and subjects the three female heads to geometric simplification, their wing-like black hair silhouetted against blue circles that intersect with a white circle and lozenge shapes filled with small triangles placed on their upper torsos.
Moser appears to ignore the compositional reduction and ease of recognition characteristic of successful advertising posters designed to attract attention from a distance, yet at the same time the Thirteenth Secession Exhibition poster might have effectively announced its subject to a reasonably well-informed Viennese citizen of the time: the three women echo the three arts carved in relief above the doorway to the Secession Building (see fig.
6.41), the circles above their heads alluding to the gilt dome atop the building, and the checkerboard designs at the end of lines of text finding their counterpart in the decorative patterns on the same edifice.
Mosers use of abbreviated signs looks forward to the design of corporate identities; it is worth remembering that the design also appeared in a smaller format in the Secession journal titled Ver Sacrum, where readers could examine it at closer range.
Koloman Moser, poster for 13th Exhibition of the Vienna Secession, color lithograph, 69 × 23 in (175.3 × 58.4 cm), 1902.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
Among the works associated with the Wiener Werkstätte is the decoration of a home in Brussels for wealthy Belgian banker Adolphe Stoclet, built between 1904/5 and 1911 by Josef Hoffmann, with interior design and furnishings executed almost exclusively by designers and artisans associated with the workshops.
No expense was spared for the materials, design, and construction of the home, including different varieties of rare marble and an elaborate series of mural mosaic decorations for the dining room designed by Viennese Secession painter Gustav Klimt (18621918; fig.
6.46).
Here Klimt explored his personal vision of the intensity of human love connected with natures fertility and abundance in a unit formed by an embracing couple and female figure on either side of a flowering tree composed of spiraling branches, all treated as flat, simplified shapes.
These themes have a particular resonance in fin-desiècle Vienna, where the topic of modern societys alienation from nature and suppression of sexual instinct was brought to light by Sigmund Freud (18561939), through whom terms such as repression and drive have become part of our everyday vocabulary and culture.
The Vienna Secession and Wiener Werkstätte were elements of the citys café society or culture, where a rising and diverse middle class met and mixed with the traditional aristocratic elite to produce a vibrant artistic and intellectual milieu outside of the official and more restrictive enclaves of court, salon, or university: more casual, more public, more inclusive, in a word, more modern. For Australian poet and writer Clive James (19392019), the informality of the café and the discourse that resulted from its unofficial status and diverse make-up were keys to the creativity that energized the city.
James praised Viennas cultural legacy and lamented its passing after World War I.
Josef Hoffmann, Palais Stoclet dining room, with murals designed by Gustav Klimt, Brussels, 1905–1911.

## Belgium
Adolphe Stoclets choice of the Wiener Werkstätte for the design of his Brussels home was not surprising, for the wealthy Belgian banker spent much time abroad.
Yet Belgian artists, in a region experiencing tremendous economic growth through trade and colonial expansion, also embraced modern attitudes toward design and the equality of the arts.
One of the countrys most articulate spokesmen and practitioners for the unity and revitalization of the visual arts was Henry van de Velde.
As a painter, Van de Velde was affiliated with the progressive Belgian Modernist movement known as Les Vingt.
In the early 1890s he began to adapt a Symbolist style featuring abstract shapes and linear rhythms derived from organic forms to the design of furniture, books, and metalcraft.
In almost all of his works the decorative elements, characterized by taut curvilinear contours invested with whip-like energy, are integrated with rather than added to structural elements such as the legs of a chair or the branches of a candelabrum (fig.
6.45).
6.45 Henry van de Velde, candelabrum, electroplated bronze, 23 ${ ^ 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times$ 20 in (58.5 × 50.8 cm), 1902.
Trondheim, Nordenfjeldske Kunstindustrimuseum (Museum Of Applied Arts).
Van de Velde attempted to fuse aesthetic expression with efficient production, as if the designer was thinking like a craftsman, or the craftsman as a designer.
While deeply concerned with the negative social consequences of industrialization and influenced by the ideals of the English Arts and Crafts movement, Van de Velde found that his aesthetic interests often outweighed his commitment to design as a vehicle for social reform and equality.
Invited by Siegfried Bing to install a showroom at La Maison de lArt Nouveau in Paris in 1895, Van de Velde designed a coordinated interior for a study in which murals, fabrics, furniture, and a stained-glass, skylit ceiling create a unified aesthetic effect in which all elements contribute to the overall effect (fig.
6.47).
For Van de Velde, individual expression was compatible both with industry and with business practice, at least in theory.
He exhibited widely, contributed to publications on modern decorative arts, and was equally interested in the reform and elevation of craft education with stronger ties to the fine arts.
In this latter role he was appointed in 1904 as director of a school of craft (Kunstgewerbeschule) in Weimar, Germany, a post he held until the outbreak of World War I.
In 1919, following the war and under Germanys Weimar Republic government, the school was consolidated with Weimars Academy of Fine Art to become the first home of the Bauhaus (see here onward).
Henry van de Velde, home office interior from Bing’s Maison de l’Art Nouveau showroom, Paris, 1895.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Scholars often use the term whiplash when describing the spring-like energy that Van de Velde and other Belgian Art Nouveau artists employed in their work through shapes and contours.
Art historian Debora Silverman (see here) has noted an iconographic connection between the distinctive whiplash motif found in Belgian Art Nouveau and the nations brutal treatment of African workers under Belgian rule in the Free State of Congo in the 1890s, a reference to the human costs of colonial policy under King Leopold II (18351909).
Belgian Art Nouveau was on display in the Congo Pavilion at the 1897 International Exhibition held in Brussels and Tervuren, while in other projects Leopold preferred other visual means to communicate Belgian wealth and power, for instance, in the great dome and relief decoration of the 1905 Antwerp Central Railway Station designed by Louis Delacenserie (18381909).
The human consequences of industrial development that fueled the Arts and Crafts and related movements in Europe and the United States also emerge in literature and in the early work of Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh (18531890) and contemporary Belgian artists who were sympathetic in their depictions of the difficult lives of miners in the region known as the Borinage.
Polish-British author Joseph Conrad (18571924) chronicled the brutality in the Free State of Congo in his novella Heart of Darkness (1899) based upon his experience working on a steamer on the Congo River.
Another designer associated with Belgian Art Nouveau was Gustave Serrurier-Bovy (18581910).
Serrurier-Bovy designed original furniture featuring expensive woods, carving, and inventive approaches to materials.
Beginning just after 1900, he also designed a line of more practical and inexpensive furniture under the name Silex (fig.
6.48) that offered a more utilitarian alternative to the aesthetic Van de Velde interior illustrated in figure 6.47.
The design for a Silex dining room was illustrated in a contemporary decorative arts magazine published in Paris in 1904, and features simple construction techniques using inexpensive light woods perforated by a pattern of abstract squares for decoration, relieved by the orange walls and stenciled floral border on the dining rooms upper walls.
While individual and original expression remained important elements of design thinking in Belgium, the promise of integrating art into everyday life also remained a goal, realized in advertising art, in commercial interiors, and in the restrained unified domestic interior.
As art historian Amy Ogata explained, this aim resonated both with conservative attitudes aimed at shaping middle-class values, and with socialist interests in reducing class difference.
Gustave Serrurier-Bovy, scheme for an interior with Silex furniture, from L’Art Décoratif, Paris, 1904.
Van de Velde as well as other Belgian artists experimented with imaginative letterforms and transformations of representation and decoration in the design of advertising posters.
An example is the poster advertisement designed by Fernand Toussaint (18731955) for a brand of Belgian coffee (fig.
6.49).
In this poster the hot steam from a cup of coffee held by a young, well-dressed female figure materializes in swirling rhythms that form the undulating letterforms of the words Café Jacqmotte. On the bottom right is a circular monogram for the coffee containing elastic forms for the letters C and J making use of figureground reversal.
Such manipulation and combination of letters into a single unit appears in artists signatures as well as in monograms for organizations and companies such as the interlocked Ws of the Wiener Werkstätte or the well-known, though anonymous General Electric trademark, contained within a circle and dating to c.
1890.

## 6.49 Fernand Toussaint, poster for Café Jacqmotte, color lithograph, 43 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>
8</sub> × 31 in (110 × 78.7 cm), 1896.
Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe, Hamburg.

## The
Netherlands Like Belgium, the Netherlands benefitted economically from the shipping trade and from colonial holdings in the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia) that supplied raw materials, food, and spices to the global market.
Manufacturers exploited craft techniques and distinctive patterns and colors from Indonesia, in particular the waxresist process known as Batik used to print dress fabrics.
Dutch merchants brought luxury goods to the West while Dutch artists supplied designs to the Vlisco company, founded in 1846 (and still in business today), for roller-printed dress fabrics and marketed to the local population of West Africa (see Global Inspiration III, here).
The Dutch version of Art Nouveau is known as Nieuwe Kunst (new art).
The movement was varied and extended to ceramics, architecture, textiles, and print.
It also included aesthetic and material exploration, inspiration from Dutch colonial expansion, the construction of national identity, and the role modern design might play in addressing social inequality.
In ceramics, J.
Jurriaan Kok (18611919) was art director of the Rozenburg Factory in The Hague where he developed a thin eggshell porcelain and experimented with a variety of unconventional forms for vases, as seen in figure 6.50.
The decorative patterns on this vase were designed and painted by Samuel Schellink (18761958) and J.
M. van Rossum, and consist of brilliant colors disposed with clusters of flowers and leaves, contrasting with large areas of white ground adapted to the swelling and contracting forms of the thin, slightly asymmetrical vessel.
T.
A.
C.
Colenbrander (18411930), whose career continued well into the interwar period, designed similar vases, and tea and coffee services.
The large areas of white ground, with restrained repeated patterns, are also a feature of production-oriented ceramic tiles often seen on the walls of domestic kitchens and entranceways.
Vase, porcelain with enamel decoration, $8 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 2 ~ ^ { 1 5 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (20.5 × 7.5 cm), c.
1910, designed by J.
Juriaan Kok; decorated by Samuel Schellink.
Made by Haagsche Plateelfabriek Rozenburg, The Hague, Netherlands, 1883–1917.
Philadelphia Dutch design circa 1900 also includes the work of architect Hendrik Berlage (18561934), whose projects, including the prominent Beurs van Berlage commodities exchange building on the Damrak in Amsterdam (18961903), seem in some ways the antithesis of the highly refined and often exuberant individual work of Kok and other Dutch artists highlighted above (fig.
6.51).
Javanese-born Dutch artist Jan Toorop (18581928) designed three murals for the Beurs van Berlage entrance hall (now a bistro), representing the themes of labor and social consciousness in the past, present, and future.
This and Berlages other architectural projects embraced the integration and unity of the arts and placed value on the dignity of work in kinship with Arts and Crafts ideals, yet solidly within an admittedly capitalist society.
German-born engineer and writer Charles Steinmetz (18651923) believed that industrial capitalism represented a stage in a historical development toward a more equal distribution of wealth based upon corporate responsibility and political necessity under the guidance of enlightened corporate leaders.

## 6.51 Hendrik Berlage, interior entrance (now coffee shop and bar) of the Beurs (Bourse), A
msterdam, 1896–1903.

## Munich
The southern German city of Munich had a history of public support for the arts in the nineteenth century.
In addition to museums built in the first half of the century, the city sponsored construction of a large exhibition hall in 1854 inspired by Londons 1851 Crystal Palace.
A number of Munich-based artists felt constrained by traditional distinctions between the fine and applied arts in terms of education and the organization of exhibitions.
Contemporary with debates in Britain, Vienna, Brussels, and elsewhere in Europe, artists took a keen interest in design, and through their efforts an international art exhibition of 1897 in Munich included two rooms devoted to the decorative arts.
In 1896 the journal Jugend (youth) was launched in Munich to promote contemporary arts and entertainment, its circulation reaching 200,000 copies per week around the year 1900, acknowledging the prominent role of the visual arts, including the decorative arts, in contemporary life.
The journals title was the basis for the word Jugendstil (youth style), a label for modern ideas in art and design in Germany.
A second Munich-based journal, Simplicissimus, also appeared in the same year.
A key figure in the practice and promotion of new attitudes toward the equality of the arts was Otto Eckmann (18651902), who, like Van de Velde in Belgium, abandoned painting to pursue a career in design.
Eckmann designed woodcut illustrations for the periodicals Jugend and the Berlin-based Pan that depicted plants and flowers with strong outlines and gently undulating flattened shapes emphasizing strong figureground distinction that demonstrated familiarity with Japanese woodblock prints.
Decorative forms derived from this approach were developed in distinctive furniture designs, tapestry, and other media, including lettering and even typography.
Painter and illustrator Ludwig von Zumbusch (18611927) dramatically transformed the abstract linear qualities that characterize Eckmanns oeuvre in an 1897 cover for Jugend (fig.
6.52) The chromolithograph illustrates two exuberant female dancers with wavelike hair floating against a simplified seaside landscape and framed by two attenuated elm trees into whose foliage the word Jugend is cut using original freely drawn letterforms emphasizing elastic circular and spiral shapes.
The floating letterforms of the title are an expressive part of the page design, and the integration of the lettering with the image, both in expression and in their flatness, demonstrate an approach to type and image that emerges in the chromolithographic posters and cover art of the period.
6.52 Ludwig von Zumbusch, cover for Jugend, vol.
40, color lithograph, 11 <sup>2</sup>/ × 8 <sup>4</sup>/ in (29 × 22.5 cm), 1897.
Private collection.
Another figure who played an active role in the arts in Munich at the time was Richard Riemerschmid (18681957).
Riemerschmid was particularly versatile; he participated as a designer in the newly formed craft organization in Munich known as the Vereinigte Werkstätten für Kunst im Handwerk (United Workshops for Art in Handicraft) and later worked in Dresden, producing original designs for furniture, ceramics, and metalwork.
His designs successfully combined expressive curvilinear decoration with constructive elements for a variety of furnishings, as seen in a brass candlestick of 1898, whose asymmetrical vinelike arms function as handle and support (fig.
6.53).
At the time, and perhaps surprisingly to twenty-first-century eyes, critics remarked that such work was austere in comparison with more historicizing examples of luxury metalwork.
Likewise, a curved knife handle for a set of silver cutlery is not only a graceful decorative accent but also efficient to use, even allowing an opening for the users little finger (fig.
6.54).
In 1907, Riemerschmid became involved with the Deutscher Werkbund, an organization that debated the relationship between art and industry in the German national interest (see here).
6.53 Richard Riemerschmid, candlestick, brass, 7 <sup>7</sup>/ × 10 <sup>5</sup>/ × 3 <sup>1</sup>/ in (20 × 27 × 7.8 cm), 1898.
Private collection.
Richard Riemerschmid, cutlery, silver, knife length 9 <sup>3</sup>/ in (23.7 cm), manufactured by Werkstätten für Kunst im Handwerk, Munich, 1899–1900.
Jugendstil in Munich certainly constituted a collaborative renewal of art and handicraft, based in part upon the ability of artists to integrate a modern, original aesthetic character to the objects of everyday use.
Through the formation of workshops, the publication of journals that included design as a relevant contemporary subject, and the establishment of schools to educate designers and craftsmen, Jugendstil artists were interested in creating a peoples art, even if the market for their products tended to remain exclusive.
Indeed, the integration of art and everyday life remained a persistent, if elusive goal.
The social benefit of Jugendstil was at times a target of satire, even within the movement itself, as evidenced by a short verse appearing in Simplicissimus: The world will not be cured with blazing fire or knives, But painlessly improved  by being stylized.

## Scandinavia,
Eastern Europe, and National Romanticism Aesthetic ideas nurtured new directions in the decorative arts in the nations of Eastern Europe and Scandinavia beginning in the 1890s, when designers and manufacturers drew upon a selection of native folk traditions to create distinctive, if artificially constructed national styles, displayed at Worlds Fairs and marketed at home and abroad.
The search for national identity was indeed a creative rather than historical exercise, and was both highly selective and eclectic, supported through government agencies and associations of designers and manufacturers.
Through travel and training outside of their respective homelands, the circulation of journals, and attendance or participation at international exhibitions, countries such as Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Hungary, and Bohemia, each demonstrated the increasingly international scope of design movements that championed the unity, equality, and cultural contributions of the visual arts.
In Finland, architect Eliel Saarinen (18731950) used native building materials such as granite to construct a national artistic identity distinct from Russia (of which Finland was then a semi-autonomous province) or Germany, based upon a Romantic vision of Finnish history and mythology.
Cultural identity and nationalism were thus linked to political independence, international recognition, and a revitalization of the Finnish economy through manufacturing and international trade.
Saarinens Koti chair of 1897, designed for an exhibition, emphasizes simple, solid craftsmanship, with forms and simply carved decoration that recall forms of Indigenous architecture (fig.
6.55).
Such designs may be seen as a visual counterpart to widespread interest in oral folk traditions of Karelia (a region of Finland), whose poems and songs were collected and first published in the second half of the nineteenth century.
Historians often refer to the concern with a primitive, authentic past as National Romanticism.
Eliel Saarinen, Koti chair, oak and reupholstered seat, $5 2 \times 3 3 \times 3 1$ in $( 1 3 2 \times 6 8 \times 6 3$ cm), designed 1897.
Museum of Art and Design, Helsinki.
Finnish artist Akseli Gallén-Kallela (18651931) studied painting in Paris and contributed a series of murals to the Finnish Pavilion at the 1900 Worlds Fair in Paris, but also was interested in reviving traditions of Indigenous handicraft, seen, for instance, in a wool rug titled The Flame (fig.
6.56).
The rug is woven using a native technique known as ryijy, and the abstract flame motif appears in contemporary Finnish stoneware as well as in other textile and wallpaper patterns.
Finnish artists looked to the past to create a national style in the arts, but their efforts were less a recreation or revival of the past than a modern, hybrid phenomenon, renewing craft traditions and mining Indigenous decorative motifs while responding to competitive economic conditions and a desire to construct a coherent nationalist sentiment and identity.
Thus these emerging national styles were at once nostalgic, selective, and progressive; Finland was successful in lobbying exhibition organizers for its own pavilion, separate from that of Russia, at the 1900 Worlds Fair in Paris.
The pavilion was designed primarily by Saarinen, with mural paintings by Gallén-Kallela, and also featured carved display cases with examples of Finnish handicraft.
As art historian Bart Pushaw has written, such (architectural) eclecticism was actually representative of the way in which pavilion officials distilled a diverse culture into a single representation, inevitably simplifying, essentializing, and exoticizing an unknown people to gain international acclaim and respect. Indeed, the construction of Finnish identity at the turn of the century excluded both the culture of the long-standing Russian population of Finland as well as the marginalized nomadic Sámi people who had a rich but under-represented role in Finnish history.
Conscious of an increasingly international context and market for modern design after the end of World War I, Saarinen participated in design competitions abroad, and eventually emigrated with his wife Loja (18791968, a textile designer) to the United States in the early 1920s, becoming director of the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan (see here and fig.
10.1).
Akseli Gallén-Kallela, The Flame, ryijy rug, wool, $1 2 0 \times 6 7 ~ ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 }$ in (304.8 × 172 cm), 1899 (woven 1884).
Gallén-Kallela Museum, Espoo, Finland.
Original and aesthetic approaches to the decorative arts are also found in Denmark  for instance, in the studio established by Georg Jensen (18661935) in Copenhagen in 1904.
Jensens silver coffee and tea service (fig.
6.57) dates to 1905.
The lid of each bowl and pitcher is decorated with a swirling stem resembling the petals of a closed flower, imparting an organic quality to the ensemble through the curving ivory handles and swelling forms of the spouts.
Delicate floral motifs are also seen in the ceramics of the Bing & Grøndahl Porcelain Manufactory, and were among those goods featured at international exhibitions in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Thorvald Bindesbøll (18461908) was a Danish artist whose ceramics and silver were exhibited at the 1900 Paris Worlds Fair.
Though trained as an architect, Bindesbøll turned his attention increasingly to the decorative arts.
His dish, dating to 1886, features large asymmetrical S shapes in light blue against a reddish background that creates a strong tension between positive and negative space (fig.
6.58).
The dishs surface texture is rough and rustic, and scholars often point to the similarity between the abstract shapes of his designs and the swirling patterns and figureground reversal in examples of Japanese porcelain and metalwork that may be seen today in the Danish Design Museum (founded 1890).
But the colors, texture, and simplicity of the designs are highly original.
Like the contemporary Victoria and Albert Museum in London or the Museum für angewandte Kunst (MAK; Museum of Applied Art) in Vienna, the mission of these government-sponsored public collections was to encourage the creative efforts of designers and manufacturers in the decorative arts and stimulate the interest of an expanded commercial market at home and abroad.
Georg Jensen, coffee and tea service, chased silver, ivory, height 2–9 in (6.3–23 cm), 1905.
Private collection

## 6.58 Thorvald Bindesbøll, dish, glazed earthenware, size, 1886, Design Museum, Copenhagen.
Until 1918 the present-day Czech Republic was part of the Habsburg Empire with its capital in Vienna.
The region, comprising Bohemia to the west (including Prague) and Moravia to the east, developed original approaches to the decorative arts in the later nineteenth century, building upon distinctive local craft traditions in media such as glass, exhibited at Worlds Fairs and benefitting from and contributing to international design trends in Vienna and elsewhere, forging a modern identity and marketing strategy that mingled local and contemporary elements.
Glass manufactories in Bohemia, such as Loetz in the town of Klastersky Mlyn or Meyrs Neffe in the south, experimented with new techniques in that medium (see fig.
6.43).
Pragues Municipal House (1911) features architectural ornament strongly recalling the elongated tendrils and other curvilinear motifs of the Viennese Secession and Jugendstil, while also proudly displaying embroidered curtains with a vocabulary of abstract spiral, lozenge, and simplified symmetrical floral motifs derived from the Indigenous crafts of the region (fig.
6.59).
As noted above (see here), Moravian-born artist Alphonse Mucha was a successful graphic designer in Paris but later returned to Prague, where he worked on a large series of murals celebrating the history and folklore of his native country.

## 6.59 Curtain (detail), c. 1910. Municipal House, Prague. One of the more original Czech ar
tists involved in the design of manufactured products was Jan Kotĕra (18711923).
He designed buildings and interiors as well as a wide range of furnishings for several manufacturers, studied in Vienna under architect Otto Wagner, and held professorships in the School of Applied Art and Fine Art in Prague.
Kotĕras textiles often incorporate decorative motifs freely adapted from Czech folk traditions, but a number of his designs exhibit strikingly simple geometric forms in a style later labeled Czech Cubism that emerged during the second decade of the twentieth century.
An example is a grand crystal punch bowl and glasses exhibited in 1904 at the Worlds Fair in St.
Louis (fig.
6.60).
The bowls thick glass and simple columnar and prismatic forms eschew more conventional techniques for cut crystal, while its regular series of carefully channeled surfaces produces unexpectedly brilliant effects and reflections.
The plain, smooth surfaces are also mirrored in Kotĕras architectural projects that abandoned linear decoration in favor of basic rectilinear forms and are also seen in the decorative arts after World War I (see fig.
8.9).
6.60 Jan Kotĕra, crystal glass punch bowl, diameter 12 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in(30.8 cm), manufactured by Harrachow Glasworks, Prague, 1904.
UPM, Prague.
The city of Budapest in Hungary had become one of Europes larger urban centers by 1900, with a population of more than a million residents.
Like Bohemia and Moravia, Hungary was part of the Habsburg Empire, but artists from the region prized their distinctive heritage and were inspired both by vernacular craft traditions and contemporary aesthetic ideas in constructing a national Hungarian identity.
The unique character of Hungarian design around the turn of the century is seen in the production of the Zsolnay Pottery in the city of Pécs, in the southern part of the country.
Much of the glazed stoneware produced there, beginning in 1862, incorporated decorative motifs based upon Indigenous Magyar folk traditions, whose flat, brightly patterned work was collected and published by ethnologists and used as the basis for architectural decoration in buildings designed by architect Ödön Lechner (18451914).
Examples of this work include the plate (fig.
6.61) designed by Jósef Rippl-Rónai (18611927), a painter who devoted attention to the decorative arts, including pottery, weaving, and book illustration.
The Zsolnay factory, employing as many as 1,000 workers at the turn of the century, also produced pottery with stronger ties to contemporary design, focusing upon elongated and asymmetrical organic forms and a wide variety of coloristic and textural variations (fig.
6.62).
For businesses such as the Zsolnay Pottery, modern design was an essential component in fueling wider demand for an international market.
József Rippl-Rónai, decorated plate, Zsolnay earthenware pottery, diameter 9 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (24.1 cm), 1889.
Zsolnay Museum, Pécs.
Vase, Zsolnay, earthenware, 9 ½ × 4 <sup>9</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 4 ½ in (24.2 × 11.7 × 12.4 cm), 1898.
Zsolnay Museum, Pécs.
The preceding pages provide only a glimpse of the contribution of vernacular traditions to modern design during a period of rising nationalism and expanding trade and commerce.
Folk traditions helped to create national identity, fuel patriotism, and promote economic and political independence.
Ironically, the interest in ethnography and nostalgia for pre-industrial societies emerged in an increasingly competitive commercial and international modern economy with the participation of cosmopolitan artist-designers engaged with the manufacturing industries whose travels and education often took them abroad and fostered awareness of similar efforts elsewhere.
In forging national identities, designers and manufacturers drew freely, and selectively, upon both past and present, as Thorvald Bindesbølls Japanese-inspired ceramic dish demonstrates, with a mixture of invention and nostalgia, and the distinction between the national and international was not always clear.
Whether the Western Middle Ages or the folk traditions of Scandinavia and Eastern Europe, the authenticity associated with preindustrial societies exerted an attraction for artists and designers linked to the Arts and Crafts and Aesthetic movements in an age of national independence movements and international competition.
Nordic as well as Eastern European nations within the Austro-Hungarian Empire competed successfully for international recognition in design at Worlds Fairs and in the eyes of critics, while, as noted in Part II of the Global Inspiration (see here), their Arab counterparts, as well as other Indigenous peoples remained victims of cultural bias directed toward non-white populations.

## Italy
and Spain Following unification in 1861, Italian artists, craftsmen, and manufacturers consciously promoted the equality of the arts and the creation of a modern and original approach to design in the later nineteenth century, all on view at the Worlds Fairs of the time.
The city of Turin, in northern Italy, was the new nations first capital and a center for design activity, hosting an important international exhibition in 1902 that included recent displays and interiors from Scotland, Vienna, and Paris.
As in other countries, the economic benefit of competing in the international market for manufactured products was an incentive for design both creatively and economically, stimulating new directions in a country where the classical and Renaissance past continued to figure strongly in national heritage.
Despite instances of tentative or even derivative approaches to more abstract and expressive elements in late nineteenth-century design, the creative use and combination of materials and virtuoso craftsmanship are characteristic of Italian design at the turn of the nineteenth century, for instance in the elaborate chimneypiece, made of walnut, brass, and ceramic tile, manufactured by Vittorio Valabrega (18611952) for the 1900 Paris Worlds Fair (fig.
6.63).
On the panel directly above the tile border framing the fireplace is a particularly striking carved motif suggesting licks of flame.
Despite these aesthetic characteristics, the overall symmetry and kneeling female figures framing the central area demonstrate that this work did not represent a complete break with the past, as it connects with the tradition of sculptural carving in the Renaissance Revival style practiced by Italian artists such as Luigi Frullini (18391896) and exhibited at earlier Worlds Fairs.
6.63 Vittorio Valabrega Company, chimneypiece, walnut, glazed ceramic, brass, and glass, 119 $^ { 1 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 7 5 \times 1 5 ^ { 1 3 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (304 × 190.5 × 40 cm).
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Miami Beach.
There are also examples of highly original, idiosyncratic approaches to the decorative arts in Italy, best seen in the furniture of Carlo Bugatti (18561940).
Bugatti, father of the automobile maker Ettore Bugatti (18811947), was trained as a painter but began creating his own furniture in the later 1880s.
An ensemble, known as the Snail Room, was featured at the International Exposition held in Turin in 1902 (fig.
6.64).
Its furniture, including chairs, tables, and a massive, twisting bench, was constructed of wood carved into elastic-seeming curved and stretched shapes, covered in vellum (sheepskin) with rivets and inlays of hammered copper.
Despite the eclectic sources of inspiration for the decorative vocabulary employed in his furniture, Bugattis designs are hardly historicist.
Rather they exhibit a freedom from precedent and an inventiveness seen throughout this chapter in later nineteenth-and early twentieth-century design.
6.64 Carlo Bugatti, Snail Room, 1902.
Photograph from the International Exposition of Modern Decorative Arts, Turin.
Another city that experienced a revitalization in art and design in the later nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was Barcelona in the region of Catalonia in northeastern Spain.
Barcelona hosted an international exhibition in 1888, and a group of the citys wealthy industrialists and professionals were avid art patrons and collectors, commissioning apartments and villas, and helping to underwrite the expense of public buildings and theaters as showcases of a vibrant urban culture.
Designer Gaspar Homar (18701955) was trained as a furniture-maker, but the range of his work extended to integrated interior ensembles with a unified aesthetic effect.
His SofaDisplay case from 1903 uses elaborate marquetry with the central panel (designed by Josep Pey, 1875 1956) depicting a group of dancing nymphs (fig.
6.65).
Peys inlaid panel depicts a popular dance in the region known as La Sardana, yet another combination of national and international tendencies in fin-de-siècle design.
Homar also produced designs for wallpapers and fabrics that feature floral motifs as well as more abstract linear patterns.
It is interesting to note how frequently the theme of popular dance appears in the posters and decorative patterns of design during this period, whether for Loïe Fuller, La Goulue, or La Sardana.

## 6.65 Gaspar Homar, Sofa–Display case with La Sardana marquetry panel, various woods with m
etal and bevel-edged glass appliqué, 95 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 104 $^ { 3 } / _ { 8 } \times 2 7 ~ ^ { 5 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (240 × 256 × 70 cm), Barcelona, 1903.
The Catalan architect Antonio Gaudí (18521926) also worked in all aspects of interior design and the design of outdoor public spaces, including parks and religious buildings, as well as apartments.
His oeuvre is characterized by ceaseless invention and the exploration of modern materials in pursuit of a highly individual and unified expression.
Frequently the organic treatment of materials takes on an anthropomorphic character.
Early furniture with Islamic-inspired decorative patterns gave way after 1900 to more abstract designs in which decorative and structural forms are integrated.
Examples include a group of strongly sculptural metal fittings from the Casa Milà in Barcelona, dating to around 1910; these are frequently asymmetrical and have twisting forms suggestive of natural rock formations or even the strange inhabitants of Gaudís vivid imagination (fig.
6.66).

Fundació Caixa Catalunya, Barcelona.
Barcelonas early twentieth-century modernity is also seen in the rich and integrated interior decoration of Lluís Domènech I Montaners (18501923) Palace of Catalan Music (fig.
6.67).
Traditional regional craft materials such as ceramic tiles exhibit expressive freedom through novel colors and shapes, and natural light emanates from the blue windows at the sides of the auditorium as well as from a massive bell-shaped inverted dome, surrounded by busts of singing female choristers.
Columns supporting the roof are reminiscent of Gothic fan vaults, a feature of later medieval religious as well as secular architecture in the city, here reinterpreted to resemble webbed plants with flowers that spill out into sculpted bosses carved in relief on the ceilings horizontal beams.
Montaners concert hall has a rich, celebratory quality, with designers being given great freedom in creating a mood of excitement and celebration to accompany theatrical performance.
Lluís Domènech I Montaner, Auditorium, Palace of Catalan Music, Barcelona, 1905–1908.
It is remarkable that the majority of the cities featured in this section remain centers of economic activity and design in their respective nations, dependent in part upon tourism, preserving the reputation they earned in the later nineteenth century, the era of Worlds Fairs, expanded means of rail and sea travel, and print communication, all of which nurtured their artistic vitality and allowed them to weather two world wars, fascism, a cold war, ethnic strife, terrorism, and most recently a global pandemic beginning in 2020.

## A Critical
Look at Aesthetic Movements As art historian Gabriel Weisberg noted in his review of the 2008 exhibition Barcelona 1900, there was a dark side to Barcelonas growth at the turn of the century: the city and other modern European and North American centers may have rivaled Paris in the outward signs of technological progress, upward social mobility, construction, infrastructure (such as public transportation, parks, indoor plumbing, electrification, and public art in the form of posters), and the emergence of liberal democratic values, but urbanization and industrialization also exacerbated an unequal distribution of wealth and social tensions that occasionally led to outbursts of terrorism, armed police reprisals, and calls for social justice and solidarity among the disenfranchised.
From a global perspective, the aesthetic movements examined in this chapter are also contemporary with nationalism, Western imperial conquest, and colonization, the extension of orientalizing attitudes that cast non-Western and non-white populations as less developed culturally than their Western counterparts.
The ethnographic displays of Indigenous populations on the Midway Plaisance at the 1893 Worlds Columbian Exposition in Chicago provide ample evidence of such racial and cultural bias, challenged at the time in the work of anthropologist Franz Boas (18581942).
Examples from these movements also mirror their complexity and varied expressions in modern design of the era, producing at the same time in the Netherlands, for instance, Berlages Beurs building (fig 6.51) and the rich decoration of Koks porcelain vase (fig.
6.50).
The dynamic forces of technology and capital that created wealth and nurtured opportunity also fed disaffection and seething tensions that could erupt in violence, anarchy, and reactive repression in the name of law and order.
One is unlikely to gain a sense of social and political tension from advertising posters or home furnishings that are aligned with freedom of expression, promises of the good life, the economic benefits of colonial expansion, and the embrace of progressive ideals, but Toulouse-Lautrecs 1893 chromolithographic poster advertising the conservative newspaper Le Matin presents an unusually grim illustration of a public execution depicting a chained and possibly defiant prisoner approaching the guillotine, silhouetted against an anonymous row of soldiers mounted on horseback (fig.
6.68).
Here Toulouse-Lautrec contrasts the intimidating face of authority with the helplessness of the victim (what has he done to deserve the death penalty or, has he been unjustly convicted?) without taking sides.
Design occurs in a political, social, and economic context, the product of beliefs and values about individuals and their relationship to the society in which they live and the wider world they inhabit.
Dominant views coexist and vie for power with marginal views.
Conflicting, resistant viewpoints do not always find expression in design, especially if one relies upon advertising, exhibition displays for evidence.
Alternative, varied efforts to redirect the design enterprise toward the working classes and idealistic utopian hopes for a new, universal world order emerged in the wake of World War I and the Russian Revolution and are considered in Part IV.
