## Chapter
7 Industrial Cultures Design, Big Business, and the Workplace Frank Lloyd Wrights reformed approach to the machine production of furniture did not attract widespread interest among commercial manufacturers for the domestic market, where a variety of revival styles appealing to heterogeneous tastes dominated the industry and could be ordered from illustrated mail-order catalogs or purchased in department stores.
In an era that witnessed the rise of national product brands in the food industry and beyond, however, the workplace offered the architect an opportunity to develop a new paradigm for design, distinct from the more individual aesthetic associations of the private home.
In 1906 Wright designed the Buffalo, New York, headquarters of the Larkin Soap Company, a large and successful national, industrialscale manufacturer.
There Wright addressed the design of the modern corporate office, organizing the functions of the emerging white-collar professions who functioned as part of a complex business model that manufactured, marketed, and distributed a nationally branded product.
In some ways the Larkin Building (fig.
7.1) is the antithesis of Wrights Prairie Style houses, contrasting the horizontality and open flow of space in the former with the verticality and spatial insulation of the latter, with direct light entering only from the ends of the central rectangular workroom and from high above the floor level.
In this workroom, the clerks and secretaries anonymity is stated through the repetitive, axial arrangement of desks (and uniform dress) in a vast space that dwarfs the individual and eliminates privacy.
The standardization is a visual counterpart to the efficiency and specialization required for the bureaucratized functions of large-scale business, requiring workers to become conditioned to increasingly routinized and repetitive tasks.
In exchange or as compensation for conformity to these modern working conditions, Wright offered the security of community, of feeling part of a larger whole, as well as hope for advancement and the rewards for the sacrifice of individuality and selfdetermination to the demands of corporate management: at the top of the workroom an inscribed motto, taken from the seventh chapter of Matthews Gospel in the Christian New Testament, reads: Ask and it shall be given you; Seek and Ye Shall Find; Knock and it shall be opened unto you. Perhaps we will never know if such words and communal spaces provided reassurance and incentive for the clerks and secretaries who toiled in the Larkin Buildings workroom, but Wrights design articulates a managerial point of view regarding the nature of labor and its wider business context of standardization and conformity in the early twentieth century.

## Germany
In Germany similar attitudes, fueled in part by large manufacturing and utility companies, took root in the early twentieth century, producing reform initiatives advocating modern design standards based upon practicality rather than luxury and individual expression, and finding support in applied arts schools in Düsseldorf, Breslau, Weimar, and Berlin.
German companies and workshops uniting designers with craftsmen also participated in international exhibitions in Paris (1900) and St.
Louis (1904), and mounted an exhibition in Munich (1908) that received a positive critical response.
In 1907 a group of artists and manufacturers formed an organization to promote the German applied arts, known as the Deutscher Werkbund (German Work Federation or German League of Work).
A significant figure in the Werkbund was Hermann Muthesius (18611927), who visited Britain from 1896 to 1899 to study English architecture (published as Das Englische Haus), and subsequently became the Minister of Trade for the Prussian government.
Like other advocates of design reform, Muthesius believed in the harmony of utility and beauty, but felt that individuality should be subservient to more practical, durable, and rational forms for manufactured products.
Through modularity, interchangeability, specialized and mechanized production, Muthesius and his supporters argued that the benefits of efficiency in design and production outweighed individual expressive, artistic concerns.
The benefits of his approach included not only the capital cost savings of standardization to manufacturers, but also the reform of consumer taste, advocating a more modest, comfortable ideal for modern living, stressing moderation rather than luxury and individual identity.
Such attitudes may be seen in Muthesiuss criticism of contemporary Scottish design as being impractical in its degree of refinement and out of touch with the habits of modern middle-class living: Once the interior attains the status of a work of art, that is, when it is intended to embody aesthetic values, the artistic effect must obviously be heightened to the utmost.
The Mackintosh group does this and no-one will reproach them on this particular point.
Whether such enhancement is appropriate to our everyday rooms is another question.
Mackintoshs rooms are refined to a degree which the lives of even the artistically educated are still a long way from matching.
The delicacy and austerity of their artistic atmosphere would tolerate no admixture of the ordinariness which fills our lives.
Even a book in an unsuitable binding would disturb the atmosphere simply by lying on the table, indeed even the man or woman of today  especially the man in his unadorned working attire  treads like a stranger in this fairy-tale world.
There is for the time being no possibility of our aesthetic cultivation playing so large a part in our lives that rooms like this could be general.
But they are milestones placed by a genius far ahead of us to mark the way to excellence for mankind in the future.
The willingness of a number of artists and architects to work within the shared design ethos outlined by Muthesius and like-minded designers and businessmen is an important characteristic of German design in the decade leading up to the outbreak of World War I, stemming at least in part from a desire to construct a national identity in the wake of German unification (1871) and a willingness to compromise expressive freedom in order to achieve common ground through design.
Although criticized by the Belgian architect-designer Henry van de Velde for the constraint on artistic freedom and individuality it implied, and opposed by a number of smaller manufacturers for being undemocratic and giving undo weight to larger manufacturing companies, Muthesius had many adherents, especially among Germanys industrialists and a number of leading artist-designers.
Among these, Munich-based Richard Riemerschmid (see here) abandoned the abstract rhythmic curves of the Jugendstil for restrained designs in furniture and other household consumer goods.
His set of cutlery manufactured for Karl Weisshaupt in 1912 (fig.
7.2) features straight, mildly elongated handles and plain surfaces, contrasting with the engraved decoration and more delicate, asymmetrically curved handles of the Jugendstil (see fig.
6.54).

## 7.2 Richard Riemerschmid, cutlery, manufactured by Bruckmann, Heilbron, for Karl Weisshaup
t, silver, length $5 \%$ to $6 \%$ in (14.4 to 17.2 cm), Munich, 1912.
Peter Behrens (18681940) was another designer associated with the Werkbund and early twentieth-century design reform in Germany.
Like Riemerschmid, Behrens abandoned the expressive rhythms of the Jugendstil for more sober forms, seen for instance in his turbine factory for the German General Electric Company (Allgemeine Elektrizitäts-Gesellschaft or AEG) of 1908 to 1909.
From 1907 Behrens worked as a consultant for the AEG to develop the companys promotional materials and to work with product engineers to design industrial equipment and electric appliances for domestic use in order to increase demand for electricity.
Incorporating standardized forms and parts to reduce labor and equipment costs, Behrens also introduced variety into AEGs line of electric tea kettles through variations in material, finish, and handles to provide for consumer choice.
He also preserved associations with handicraft in the use of a molded exterior that resembled a hand-hammered surface (fig.
7.3).
Aside from these concessions to broader consumer taste, the visual unity among AEG electric products realized Muthesiuss ideal of a coherent style for industrially manufactured goods.
The result was an Industry Culture that reimagined the relationship between fine and applied art (the harmony between utility and beauty), advocating reform based upon an equation between efficient production and simple, unified forms with little or no decoration.
Although never a national policy in Germany, this practical or objective approach to industrial design and production represented the outlook of large businesses and corporations who benefitted not only from production economies resulting from standardization, but also from products that achieved recognition in the marketplace by possessing a common visual vocabulary, along with a trademark that provided brand identity and recognition.
Like most reform efforts, Industry Culture rested upon an architectural paradigm that rendered ornament unnecessary, an ethical belief that valued plain forms as an expression of self-restraint and moderation, and a disdain for the excesses of fashion in a competitive, free-market system.
Modernist movements, treated below in Part IV, developed this approach with greater urgency after World War I, often on a universal and utopian rather than national scale (see here).
Peter Behrens, electric tea kettle, brass, chromium-plated metal, bakelite, and cane, $8 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 6 ~ ^ { 3 } / _ { 8 }$ in $( 2 1 \times 1 6 .
5 \ : \mathrm { c m } ) ,$ manufactured by Allgemeine Elektrizitäts-Gesellschaft (AEG), Berlin, c.
1908–1912.
Behrenss work for the AEG included the design of a typeface (using Roman rather than the more common Blackletter forms used in German printing), trademark, and layout for all company products and printed materials.
These characteristics in turn became a recognizable marketing strategy communicating consistency and building consumer trust for the company; that is, an appeal to a sense of permanence and stability in contrast with the confusion and uncertainty of varied styles and fashions.
Behrenss hexagonal trademark designed for AEG suggests (the logo appears in fig.
7.4), in its analogy to a beehive, the subordination of individual elements to a larger unified corporate organization.
The mark may also refer to the chemical compound benzene, represented visually as a ring or hexagon by the German chemist Friedrich Kekulé, and the applications and benefits of science to industry.
Behrens was a well-known architect whose work for AEG helped to create as well as to promote the companys contemporary image and contribute to the recognition and positive associations of their products.
The Behrens trademark appears in a 1912 illustration for a corporate prospectus that limits communication to a straightforward drawing of the AEG filament lightbulb above the bold Roman typeface designed by Behrens for all the companys materials (fig.
7.4).
It is interesting to compare the straightforward character of this illustration to a catalog illustration for the same corporation designed in 1900 by Munich Jugendstil artist Otto Eckmann (fig.
7.5).
In the earlier poster, a fluid elasticity characterizes idiosyncratic lettering that merges paired letters and combines lower- and upper-case forms, while its rectangular frame abstractly communicates visually the energy of an electrical current passing through bell-shaped transformers at top and bottom.
The expressive line and letterforms communicate a graphic equivalent for electric current (as steam functions in an advertisement for coffee, or smoke for cigarettes and cigarette papers; see fig.
6.49), while Behrenss promotion concentrates upon an identity between AEGs trademark and one of its most recognizable products, without reference to an expressive transformation of electric force.
Art historian Frederic Schwartz has referred to this approach as semantic restraint, a term that could be applied to graphic design in Switzerland after World War II (see here).
Advocates of this approach to design reform often used the term Typisierung, substituting the typical for the unique, and abiding, responsible standards of efficiency and practicality for consumer as well as designer preferences.
Peter Behrens, prospectus for AEG Lighting, color lithograph and letterpress printing, 4 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 6 in (11.2 × 16.5 cm), 1912.

## 7.5 Otto Eckmann, cover for AEG catalog, Paris World Exhibition, color lithograph, 1900. B
ehrenss graphic design for AEG shares a directness of approach with the advertising posters of self-taught Viennese artist Lucian Bernhard (18831972), who was working in Munich in the first decade of the twentieth century and had joined the Deutscher Werkbund.
Bernhard produced advertising posters reduced to the bold company name juxtaposed with the straightforward presentation of its product, in contrast to posters that involved the use of young women, or children, who address the viewer.
An example is the 1908 poster for Adler Typewriters (fig.
7.6).
Critics have suggested that the simplified treatment of shadow is the result of the influence of photography, where the half-tone method of commercial reproduction (see here) reduced the tonal range of the original image, creating a more abstract effect, especially on a larger scale.
Although the typewriter appears in three-quarter view, the simplified tone and justification of the image with the border at the left virtually negate spatial recession.
In Bernhards posters rarely are the products themselves distinctive: whether matches, shoes, or cigarettes, these national brands are represented as generic rather than by unique goods, with the letters of the company name itself providing recognition as a sign that generates association and trust, in place of product differentiation or more persuasive advertising techniques employing narrative illustration associating products with lifestyle, or slogans.
Closer to our own time, clothing labels often serve the same function.
For instance, casual clothing such as jeans or khakis is often differentiated as much by labels as by distinctive styles (think Dockers or GAP).
Lucian Bernhard, poster for Adler Typewriters, color lithograph, 27 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>5</sub> × 37 in (69 × 94 cm), Berlin, 1908.

## The
American System of Manufacture and Fordism Standardization and the emergence of nationally branded (rather than local) products and services also stimulated new perspectives on industrial production in the United States in the early twentieth century.
For some industries, the American System of manufacture continued to wrest control of production from independent workshops and workers in favor of factory owners and floor managers who determined production schedules for goods that could be met only by increasing the division of labor as well as the use of labor-saving, electric-powered machinery and interchangeable parts that required routine assembly rather than skilled labor.
To assist companies in reducing labor costs, Philadelphia-born Frederick W.
Taylor (18561915) conducted experiments in the 1880s to increase worker productivity.
Using a stop-watch Taylor measured the amount of time taken by workers to perform routine tasks.
In one experiment he demonstrated that a man shoveling coal would work at optimum efficiency with individual loads of 22 pounds, and even made drawings for the design of a shovel to best hold the load.
Once determined, Taylors recommendations were enforced in the workplace by managers and became the measure for labor productivity and rewards (wages), demanding higher levels of compliance and conformity on the factory floor.
Taylors analyses are described under the heading scientific management. His findings reinforced Adam Smiths description of a pin factory (see here), but further analyzed in relation to the number of movements necessary to perform a given task in order to save more time and increase productivity.
Taylors system required a degree of conformity that might have made John Ruskin shudder, but the sacrifice was part of the bargain (see Frank Lloyd Wrights Larkin Building, here).
As described by author Robert Kanigel: There it was, the Faustian bargain in embryonic form: You do it my way, by my standards, at the speed I mandate, and in so doing achieve a level of output I ordain, and Ill pay you handsomely for it, beyond anything you might have imagined.
All you have to do is take orders, give up your way of doing the job for mine.
Taylors approach to production on a large industrial scale accompanied the emergence and growth of giant corporations, and also may be seen in relation to government- and manufacturing-imposed standardization.
Examples of regulation include the United States government uniform standards for the sizes of plumbing and electrical fittings, or standard sizes in the construction industry for wooden beams or windows in order to ensure compatibility among manufacturers without the confusion that might be caused by unfettered competition.
Standards also applied to public utilities, for instance, in the telephone industry.
The Bell Telephone Corporation exercised a monopoly on the manufacture of handsets, which as a result were only available in a limited number of models.
Industrialist Henry Ford expanded upon Taylors scientific management.
According to historian Peter Ling, rather than analyzing existing tasks, Ford and his managers saved time and increased productivity by rethinking the location of parts and the sequence of operations in manufacturing, eventually developing the moving assembly line with the help of electrically operated conveyer belts.
Through the assembly line, and Fords decision to manufacture only a single model of automobile, labor was defined primarily as a factor of time rather than skill or thought, maximized by demanding production schedules dictated by floor managers and humorously satirized by Charlie Chaplin in a memorable sequence from his 1936 film Modern Times.
Fords assembly line required an open and easily expandable interior factory space to accommodate increased production.
Through steel-frame construction, inexpensive building materials, and the use of a modular principle to facilitate expansion, Fords architect Albert Kahn (1869 1942) created large, open, well-lit factory spaces to serve the flexible needs of the moving assembly line, first at the Highland Park plant in 1908 (fig.
7.7) and then at the larger River Rouge facility beginning in 1920.
End of the line, Ford Motor Plant, Highland Park, Michigan, c.
1913.
From the collections of Henry Ford Museum and Greenfield Village, Michigan.
Fords production methods transformed the automobile from a luxury item requiring fine, specialized craftsmanship for details of construction, assembly, and finish into a middle-class form of personal transportation through complete uniformity, standardization, and interchangeable parts for ease of repair and replacement.
Between 1907 and 1916 the price of Fords Model T (Tin Lizzie) actually decreased as demand increased.
The car, available only in black, remained virtually unchanged and unchallenged in the market until the mid-1920s.
The ability of the industry to produce an automobile within the means of many through the application of technology was almost universally admired and contributed to making mechanized mass production part of the ideology of economic progress in the United States and abroad in the period between the two world wars.
Until the later 1920s, Ford did not invest heavily in advertising, as the appeal of affordable personal transportation offered by his Model T required little additional promotion or techniques of persuasion.
Factory owners addressed the human costs of this system of factory production in a variety of ways, including Fords own Five-dollar Day in 1914 that compensated for the loss of worker independence with higher wages and the promise of putting aside a portion of wages each week toward the purchase of an automobile of their own, and through company efforts to build identity and reinforce compliance among workers through public and corporate relations (see here).
Eventually labor unions helped to confront these issues with threats of strikes as leverage for higher compensation and other benefits.
Indeed, Fords mechanized mass production demanded conformity, repetition, and strict obedience to managerial control in the workplace, and such practices differed profoundly from the ideals of joyful and meaningful work that animated Arts and Crafts reform and various aesthetic movements in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
As discussed above, the crafts workshop founded by Elbert Hubbards Roycroft community (see here) was an attempt to humanize the workplace by creating a sense of cooperation among employees while incorporating more modern methods of production, provision for housing, and low wages for commercial viability.
Ironically, Hubbard admired the success of Ford and other industrialists, whose biographies he published under the heading Little Journeys to the Homes of Great Businessmen.
These and other pamphlets were printed in great quantities for corporations who hoped to inspire loyalty among their work force.
Such efforts suggest a desire to reconcile Arts and Crafts ideology with competitive market conditions profoundly affected by mass production; to its credit, the Roycroft community remained in business throughout most of the Great Depression, only declaring bankruptcy in 1938.
It is also interesting to note that both Stickley and Hubbard opposed the modern labor reform movement: deeply influenced by William Morriss attitudes toward craft, they felt that the concept of organized labor excluded a satisfying role for the individual beyond wage compensation.
Fordism did not include a place for design in the general way that we have used the term in relation to craft and manufacture during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, or even the German Industry Culture model that included an aesthetic component based upon the theory of Typisierung: decision-making was directed almost exclusively toward achieving maximum efficiency for production and minimum cost for labor.
Only the pressures of competition made design, in the sense of adding value to the utility of a product, an element in the companys approach.
In 1927 Ford introduced its Model A in response to competition that made design as well as advertising components of corporate business practice.
After all, the Model T retained the basic form inherited from the horse-drawn carriage, and there was little aesthetic concern for decorative detail, harmonious proportions, or a sense of a unified or simplified external form, as seen, for instance, in Behrenss domestic products for the AEG.
But then again, Behrens was a designer, and the reform of taste was part of the strategy of Germanys Industry Culture, including product forms that communicated modern middle-class values of moderation and efficiency.
Here design appeared to be the appropriate (rather than inevitable) outcome of technical considerations leading to limited standardized types that communicated production efficiency and a shared modern, restrained taste.
Following World War I, the moving assembly line, machine production of interchangeable parts, and standardization were adopted by American industries, most notably in the uniform mass production of household appliances such as refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, and washing machines.
As in Germany, many appliances were powered by electricity and were marketed by power companies hoping to increase domestic consumption of electric energy.
Scientific Management also extended beyond the assembly line: American author Christine Frederick (18831970) studied food preparation along the lines of Taylors time-and-motion studies, applying its principles to the overall coordination of kitchen tasks, contributing to the reduction of drudgery and an increase in leisure and opportunities for other productive pursuits for women.
Fredericks Scientific Management in the Home (1912) included diagrams demonstrating the most practical spatial arrangements among various tasks in the kitchen in order to save time, and her efforts became the basis for domestic kitchen design for governmentsponsored public housing in Frankfurt, Germany, in the 1920s (see here).
Frederick also emphasized the personal satisfaction of making rational choices for where to store utensils or determine the height of cabinets and sinks, whether for comfort, safety, or improved efficiency.
The use of white enamel paint for washing machines and refrigerators connoted personal hygiene, making the ideal kitchen or laundry a combination of well-managed factory and laboratory (figs.
7.8 and 7.9).
Advertisements emphasized the practical advantages of electrical appliances, such as toasters, wafflemakers, and irons, requiring less care (just plug it in) and less frequent shopping.
Aside from the white enamel finishes, manufacturers devoted little attention to aesthetics, an exception being electric coffee percolators that would have been brought to the dining room table to harmonize with tableware and dishes.
In the 1920s, Swiss-born architect Le Corbusier included compact travel cases among the objets types he recommended for household furniture and furnishings (see page181).
Advertisement for electric appliances manufactured by Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company, Good Housekeeping, December 1923.
Modern kitchen and storage space, article from Good Housekeeping, November 1923.

## Developments
in Merchandising, Printing, and Advertising Together with the Ford Model T and the application of scientific management to the home in an effort to improve efficiency and reduce toil, the American System of manufacture was also applied by manufacturers to a variety of household products with applied decoration that created variety and differentiation geared toward diverse consumer tastes.
Here, as historian Regina Blasyczyk explains, production economies and the division of labor led to flexibility in manufacturing that enabled standardization to co-exist rather than to replace variety and consumer choice.
Store owners and managers played an important role here, not as reformers as in Germany or as tastemakers, but as observers who monitored rather than attempted to control or influence consumer preferences, participating in a feedback loop that responded to and stimulated varied and changing styles.
Notwithstanding the success of scientific management for the kitchen and its promotion in magazines such as Good Housekeeping and Ladies Home Journal, the reality of the factory and office as primary locations of managed and increasingly routine work helped to create a stronger need to disassociate living space from workplace; if the factory turned men into machines and the kitchen into a scientifically managed space, for many consumers other domestic spaces functioned as a refuge and antidote to the anonymity and uniformity associated with the managed workplace.
Communication through print catalogs and mass-circulation magazines extended these attitudes to small towns and rural areas as well.
The distinction between home and work has been cited as the primary reason why manufacturers at first found it difficult to successfully market sewing machines for domestic use.
Standardized models manufactured by Singer in the mid-nineteenth century were too reminiscent of the factory to appeal to consumers (the earliest models could be mounted on their wooden packing crates), and only by acquiring domestic associations through painted detailing in gold, a more tapered appearance, and a more traditionally carved table (fig.
7.10) did they successfully enter the home as a piece of artistic furniture rather than as an industrial tool. Rather than competing for work in the public world, women were encouraged to cultivate a comfortable and worry-free (as well as efficient) environment for their families  both were components of design, adding value and appeal to products.
This role might allow for their direct participation in production via handicraft, but as primary consumers of household goods and furnishings they were increasingly targeted by advertisers.

## 7.10 Singer sewing machine, 1866. National Museum of American History, the Smithsonian Ins
titution, Washington, DC.
In addition to distinguishing home from office or factory through design, manufacturers were able to increase sales by creating variations of products targeting particular markets.
Their efforts are evident in the mail-order catalogs published by national distributors such as Montgomery Ward (1872) and Sears, Roebuck and Company (1891), in monthly periodicals whose circulation increased dramatically through illustrated advertisements that covered the costs of production and reduced the price to readers.
Household products were also available in national retail chain stores such as F.
W.
Woolworths (1878).
Leafing through the pages of mail-order catalogs, one confronts images of a seemingly limitless array of domestic products with minor variations meant to appeal to the desires of different groups of consumers.
What these various outlets or intermediaries have in common, however, is their ability to negotiate social relations and individual identity through consumption (fig.
7.11).
While urban consumers found such variety in large department stores such as Macys or Wanamakers, mail-order catalogs catered mainly to rural populations and small towns whose range of options for consumer goods was previously limited to the local general store. While racial segregation and discrimination in the United States discouraged or prevented African Americans from retail shopping in department stores or local stores, mail-order catalogs were inclusive, encouraging a freer exchange of goods, and were untapped markets for the catalog companies that accompanied the migration of African Americans to the more industrial cities of Midwest and Northeast America in search of economic opportunity (see here).
After the end of World War II, a more widespread acknowledgment of the African American market led, slowly, to the use of Black people in product advertising by the early 1960s.
The relationship among different approaches to modern production technologies, Catalog page, clock department, Montgomery Ward, 1896. branding strategies, and advertising may be seen in the piano industry.
At the Great Exhibition, piano manufacturers used design to connect their products with art and the associations between music and refined culture.
Despite increasingly standardized soundboards and even sizes, cases were differentiated to reflect individual preferences and varying consumer aspirations.
Yet the Steinway & Sons Company of New York (founded 1853) abandoned this strategy and adopted an approach where piano cases were more typical yet branded both by trademark as well as advertising that used the personal endorsements of professional musicians and concert halls to help market their high-end products.

## Conclusion
The numerous individual, workshop, corporate, and national design strategies and initiatives described in chapters 5, 6, and 7 demonstrate particular responses to technological change during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
These range from the protests and anti-industrial initiatives of John Ruskin and William Morris to the aggressive pursuit of rapid uniform production by Henry Ford.
Between these two extremes lie the approaches of aesthetic design and reform (whether art furniture, Jugendstil, or Art Nouveau), Werkstätten, Werkbund, and other associations, and large commercial ventures such as department stores, retail chain stores, and mail-order catalogs that sought to balance the uniformity and rationalization demanded by an emerging system of industrial production with the individuality of the designer and managing motivations of a growing consumer culture.
Each phenomenon constitutes a particular reaction to industrialization and mechanization, whether as a threat or a promise, the dream of providing the many with what was once the privilege of the few, of elevating aesthetic awareness of household objects and interiors, of improving the standard of living and quality of life through design allied with technology, of introducing art into everyday life, of defining the products and behaviors of an industry culture.
At the same time, technology threatened the very nature of craft production, depriving workers of independence and increasing the disparity among social classes in competitive economic conditions.
Various efforts toward creating an alliance of art and industry addressed these complex issues, including the well-being of workers outside of the workplace, and the role of designers, manufacturers, and consumers, all of whom were stakeholders in the design enterprise.
In France, as Debora Silverman and other historians have remarked, the political milieu in which design initiatives developed at this time was a conservative (top-down) one in which the cultivation of a refined Art Nouveau style was expected to create economic opportunity as well as to reduce middleclass fears of unrest among an industrial working class.
The multi-faceted design enterprise greatly expanded during this period; artist-designers, craftsman-artists, tastemakers, the early professional industrial designers such as Christopher Dresser, manufacturers and retailers such as Woolworth, all believed in the economic, social, and political significance of the decorative arts; all debated the uses and applications of technology, the role of labor, the relationship between fine and applied art, and even more importantly the meanings and definitions of progress.
The emergence of new nations (Italy in 1861; Germany in 1870) and efforts toward national independence in Eastern Europe and Scandinavia also contributed to an appreciation of the economic and political benefits of a unified design identity.
The social, economic, and political meanings brought to bear upon design activities in the period from the mid-nineteenth century until the beginning of World War I make this period one of great vitality, originality, and tension, in which there emerges a critical dialogue between art, craft, industry, social and international relations and reform, and an ever-expanding culture of commodity consumption.
With expanding trade and travel, artists and designers during this time drew inspiration from myriad sources historically and culturally.
Their interaction with other cultures, whether in Africa or Asia, was sparked by curiosity, by travel, and by exposure through books, collections, and displays on view in museums and at exhibitions.
Western attitudes toward non-Western cultures were complex: on the one hand, appreciating the authenticity of pre-industrial cultures, but, on the other hand, generally revealing bias that cast differences in skin color, religion, and lifestyles as primitive, that is, backward technologically, and at a less well-developed stage of civilization.
This cultural bias was contemporary with imperial and colonial aggression, sanctioned to promote progress globally.
Part III of the Global Inspiration looks at examples of the decorative arts of Central and West Africa in relation to cultural as well as commercial interactions.
Exported African textiles were commodified, disrupting traditional, local patterns of production and consumption, surviving, yet subject to a changing relationship with the modern world.
At the same time, Western colonialism fostered varieties of racial and cultural attitudes that combined commercial opportunity with nostalgic longing for the primitive (as displayed, for instance, in ethnographic villages at Worlds Fairs) and revealing prejudices that persist in our own time. # Global Inspiration III Central and Western Africa The third installment of Global Inspiration looks at the decorative arts of Central and Western Africa (the north of Africa was treated in Global Inspiration II).
Centuries before Europeans began sailing around the western coast of Africa to trade, they were already in contact with African raw materials and goods and design.
There would have been no ivories and very little gold in medieval Europe were it not for the extensive medieval overland trade with West Africa (modern-day Senegal, Niger, and Nigeria) via the kingdom of Mali.
People in Ilé-Ifè· were skilled metalworkers, glassworkers, and sculptors, producing highly realistic portraits and glass beads, at a moment when very few Europeans could make anything comparable.
Contact between Central Africa and Western Europe began with the arrival of Portuguese traders, merchants, and Catholic missionaries toward the end of the fifteenth century.
Scholars describe the early trading interactions between cultures as respectful, and wealthy Europeans (armchair travelers or their agents) collected examples of the continents material culture for their Kunstkammer (cabinets of curiosity) to satisfy their interest and display their worldliness.
Many African leaders and the inhabitants of the areas they controlled converted to Christianity while maintaining traditional tribal allegiances and craft practices.
Gifts by African leaders played a role in this interaction, demonstrating pride in highly developed local traditions of ivory carving, jewelry, and textile manufacture, while merchants exchanged cloth, metals, and arms for African goods and agreements that provided access to raw materials.
Prominent among the material products of Africa reaching Europe were woven and printed textiles worn for dress and as caps; these often employed a central schematized knot or diamond motif that formed the basis of staggered or repeated motifs on square shapes that were sometimes sown together.
A Congolese fiber-woven example from the late nineteenth or early twentieth century is illustrated in figure GI3.1; in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, woven textiles were often made into cushions with tassels to accompany the interior furnishings of European collectors.
Pile cloth, fiber, Dengese culture, Democratic Republic of Congo, 19th or 20th century.
But European attitudes toward cultural difference shifted from curiosity to exploitation with an active trade in enslaved African people that brought Africans (estimated at 20 million during a 400-year period) to Latin America and the Caribbean to provide labor for sugar and coffee plantations and mining (silver, copper, iron, and other metals) from the later sixteenth century, with human beings (rather than luxury goods) as the objects of exchange.
Artistic evidence of the slave trade survives in nineteenth-century carved ivory tusks with spiraling bands of relief depicting various aspects of subservience in the slave trade, produced for export to Europe and displayed at the Kongo: Majesty and Power exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, in 2015.
Despite the abolition of the transatlantic trade of enslaved African people by the USA and several European states in the early nineteenth century, illegal activity continued until the 1870s.
Meanwhile trading in raw materials and manufactured goods continued to accelerate with improved transportation via railways and steamships.
Imperialism and exploitation figured prominently in African history during this time, affecting trade (and by extension, design).
Over the course of the nineteenth century virtually all of Central Africa was subject to European control as colonies with a minority European ruling class as settlers.
In most places imperialism continued until well after World War II, and, in South Africa, the system of racial segregation and inequality known as Apartheid, established in 1948, lasted until 1994.
Agreements among France, Belgium, and Portugal, enacted between 1884 and 1885 (the Berlin Conference), divided Central African territories into the arbitrary states of Angola (Portugal), Moyen Congo (France), and the Congo Free State (King Leopold II of Belgium).
Local craft traditions survived while European merchants collected samples of textiles for manufacturers to produce more inexpensively to compete with African exports.

Increased contact with Europe produced changes in local African craft traditions.
In South Africa local weavers (men and women) incorporated glass beads into their woven fabrics, received in trade with merchants from Italy and Bohemia.
Entrepreneurial traders increased, for example, Englishman Charles Beving (18581913) collected examples of printed and woven textiles from Africa as well as Indonesia as an agent for Manchester-based (UK) industrial manufacturers (he also co-owned a printing company).
His extensive collection, now in the British Museum, London, offers evidence of an active global trade in manufactured goods.
Figure GI3.2 is an example from Bevings collection, a textile from Ghana with a multicolored and tightly woven geometric design, not unlike the patterns reproduced by Owen Jones in his Grammar of Ornament.
Manchester manufacturers used wax-resist (Batik) roller printing rather than weaving when adapting African textile designs for British manufacture, often without regard for the subtleties of composition and color found in their models (fig.
GI3.3).
GI3.3 Printed cloth, Manchester, c.
1900–1913.
Sample of machine plain-woven cotton cloth decorated using the Batik technique.
The cloth is decorated with a repeating pattern, which consists of a grid which is subsequently divided into triangles and decorated.
The pattern is constructed in yellow, red, and indigo.
The cloth is unhemmed.
British Museum, London.
A further example of European manufacturers fascination with African textiles, in this case still active, is Dutch company Vlisco, founded in 1846 in the city of Helmond.
Vlisco first adapted the patterns and techniques of Indonesian (Javanese) Batik printing (using a wax resist) to roller-printing technology.
When Indonesian craftsmen and women improved the efficiency of their own printing techniques to compete with Vliscos products, the company turned to West Africa (Ghana, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso) as a new market.
There company designers incorporated decorative motifs used by local West African artisans to provide familiarity for their products.
An example is the printed textile illustrated in figure GI3.4, dating to 1904 and distinguished by a pattern of repeated eyes and wavy lines, alternating with bands of closely spaced crossing lines.
Possibly derived from representations of the Egyptian god Horus (a falcon), interpretations of the motifs meaning range from protection and good health to desire in the Ivory Coast, where the textile is worn by women to show interest in a male mate, known as the Lustful Eye. Today Vlisco continues to design and manufacture its dress fabrics for the West African market.
GI3.4 Printed textile, Vlisco, Helmond, North Brabant, Netherlands, resist-dyed and printed cotton plain weave, 144 × 47 ½ in (365.8 × 120.7 cm), 1904.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Imperialism and colonialism rested upon the belief in racial hierarchy that justified the mining of natural resources as cultural progress and a Western, white, and Eurocentric bias that equated civilization with technological development as a universal and inevitable goal.
As a result, in some sense to be different was to be inferior, even as the term primitive or savage also connoted a closeness to nature and instinct admired, even envied, in the West for being authentic and in some sense desirable when embodied in craft objects.
As noted above, objects of African craft were exported in large quantities to Europe, and geometric textile patterns and other decorative motifs were appropriated by European industrial manufacturers for their own markets as well as directed to the African market.
As historian Debora Silverman states, Belgian artist and designer Henry van de Veldes belief in the equality of the arts were in part informed by his interest in the African practice of scarification, in particular ways in which patterns carved into the skin of Congolese natives were naturally adapted to bone structure in the way ornament might be integrated with the construction of a chair or the trunk and branches of a candelabra (see fig.
6.45).

## Appropriation
and Cultural Interaction The Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Design defines the term appropriation as the deliberate act of using preexisting sources such as objects, images, or any cultural element to recontextualize them with little or no modification into commercial products or new artistic creations. This definition is useful, but does not quite fit the examples illustrated here, since original African designs were certainly modified or transformed either through different production processes or to market such products to different audiences.
But the important part of the definition is the word re-contextualization, because it affects meaning both for the borrower and for the receiver.
The appeal of Vlisco dress fabrics reproduced with Javanese printing techniques and motifs to West Africans, or of African geometric patterns to British consumers, makes light of cultural difference in the interests of commerce as the generator of value.
Does appropriation of this kind constitute exploitation?
One might argue that African and Indonesian artists were not asked for permission to appropriate their creative effort or given credit or remuneration for their designs when reproduced, and that appropriation and broader availability weakened the political functions and social meanings that African textiles had for their local communities as signs of authority, social distinction, or ritual function.
In these cases the engine of appropriation is free trade and competition, which generally (whether East or West) erodes traditional social structures through the less restricted circulation of goods, even at the expense of workers independence and livelihoods, often forcing them to compete amid changing circumstances, altering the conditions in which production, and business, are conducted.
A more disturbing instance of the unequal power relationship between Europe and Africa under colonialism emerges in the research of historian Debora Silverman, who examined Belgian Art Nouveau as the visual expression of colonial repression and violence in the Congo Free State in the 1890s (Belgian Congo after 1908; Democratic Republic of Congo since 1960).
The Congo was a source of natural rubber, a plentiful and lucrative export used for a wide variety of products including hoses and bicycle tires (bicycle riding had become a popular form of transportation and leisure in the 1890s with the introduction of pneumatic tires around 1890).
Abundant rubber was extracted from the forests of the Congo by brutally enforced labor to meet harsh production quotas in lieu of unfair tax burdens imposed upon the native population.
What we now call Belgian Art Nouveau was in some instances known at the time as Congo Style. Belgian artists incorporated abstract interpretations of rubber-tree stalks in the furniture, furnishings, and architectural decoration of the Congo Pavilion at the International Exhibition held in Brussels and Tervuren in 1897, and the taut, so-called whiplash linear decoration seen in Henry van de Veldes 1902 candelabra (see above, fig.
6.45) is not only an expressive aesthetic abstraction or exaggeration of a vegetal or floral form, but also a reference to the public floggings that were used to punish and control Congolese rubber workers, the price of progress and the attending wealth it brought to Belgian industrialists.
Ivory from elephant tusks was another Central African natural resource, and was regularly employed in sculpture and the decorative arts.
A reference to its elephantine source appears in the large central and side panels of a stained-glass window designed by architect Octave van Rysselberghe (18551929) and Van de Velde for the home of Paul Otlet in Ixelles, southeast of Brussels in 1898 (fig.
GI3.5).
In the panel, one can detect the symmetrical frontal outline of an elephant skull along with its curved tusks in the center and half-heart-shaped ears that extend outward in the side panels.
As revealed by Silverman, Belgian Art Nouveau offers explicit evidence of appropriation-as-exploitation, embodied in imagery and tense, dynamic energy, acknowledging power and the violence that lay at the heart of Western imperialism and the objectification of populations in the rush for resources and wealth.
As noted above, writers such as Joseph Conrad exposed the brutality of Belgian colonial rule in his serialized novella Heart of Darkness (1899); subsequent worldwide media attention targeted the inhuman conditions of rubber extraction.
GI3.5 Octave van Rysselberghe and Henry van de Velde, windows for the Otlet House, Ixelles, Belgium, stained glass, 1902.
IV After World War I: Art, Industry, Commerce, and Utopias (1918–1944) W <sup>orld</sup> <sup>War</sup> <sup>I</sup> <sup>mobilized</sup> <sup>artists</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>illustrators</sup> <sup>on</sup> <sup>both</sup> <sup>sides</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>conflict</sup> <sup>to</sup>build broad public support through the mass media of posters and build broad public support through the mass media of posters and billboards.
Governments sponsored such patriotic efforts as part of their campaigns to enlist recruits, sell war bonds, and create a sense of shared national responsibility, unity, and purpose.
Using mass media to shape public opinion is a theme inherited from nineteenth-century reform (see Chapter 4) and was renewed during World War I with increasing emphasis upon the power and impact of visual images and short accompanying catchphrases.
There is a remarkable similarity among such war posters regardless of which side of the conflict they promoted, for they rely upon a combination of romantic idealism and monumentality inherited from the Renaissance that identifies war with heroism, as seen in Jules Abel Faivre’s (1867–1945) 1916 poster image of a young soldier with arm raised high in a plea to buy war bonds (below, top).
The direct appeal of gesture and imperative tone of both frontal image and bold slogan in Alfred Leete’s (1882–1933) Your Country Needs You poster of 1914 in Britain (below, middle) made for powerful rhetoric.
Such images combined the contrast and simplicity found in German posters by artists such as Lucian Bernhard (see fig.
7.6) with a sense of confrontation with the reader derived from the stock techniques of advertising copywriters exhorting potential customers with slogans to buy particular products.
War posters blurred boundaries between art, advertising, and patriotism, contributing to the enormous role that the advertising industry, political propaganda, and illustration assumed during the 1920s and 1930s.
In Germany poster artists sometimes explored more reductive and sophisticated techniques for engaging the viewer, approaches that laid the foundation for modern graphic design.
Hans Rudi Erdt’s 1917 U-Boats Launch poster (below, bottom), announcing a recent film glorifying Germany’s submarine fleet and officers, not only simplifies the representational elements of the composition, but also exploits abrupt scale contrasts with the diminutive sinking warship at the top, as well as integrating lettering and image, with the letter “U” becoming an exploded view of the hull of the submerged submarine.
Such sophisticated integration of word and image coexisted with more traditional forms of visual persuasion during the war.

## Dimensions
of Interwar Design Part IV encompasses the years 1918 to 1944, and includes three touchstones of modern design history: the long-awaited Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes in Paris (1925) from which the label “Art Deco” derives; the foundation of the German school for design education known as the Bauhaus (1919–1933), whose curriculum, publications, and exhibitions shifted from a craft- to a factory-based model amid similar and related contemporary initiatives taking place in France, Soviet Russia, the Netherlands, Eastern Europe, and Austria, motivated at times by a desire to address working-class needs and living conditions; and the 1939 World’s Fair in Flushing Meadows, New York, displaying an array of retail products and imagined futuristic projects, the fruits of an emerging industrial design profession in the United States in the 1930s, navigating the competing and often conflicting aesthetic, commercial, social, and political dimensions of design during this period.
Design functioned prominently in the major historical events of the era: the suffering and lingering trauma of World War I; economic recovery in the 1920s; a crippling economic depression accompanied by social unrest in the 1930s; the rise of repressive authoritarian regimes in Europe; collectivization in the Soviet Union; and large-scale social welfare and infrastructure projects in the United States.
With the advent of radio communication and faster means of transportation by rail, steamship, and auto, the design enterprise during this period was more global than ever, but the design history story has for the most part remained stubbornly Eurocentric, with non-Western nations generally relegated to the margins of the historical narrative.
And as broad and encompassing as the three touchstones may appear, they do not include an even wider range of design activity during this period, in particular those areas that lie outside the collections of art and design museums and are more likely to be found in trade journals and mass advertising that reached a broader consumer market.
Moreover, there is a tendency to view these three landmarks as distinct as well as monolithic, pitting, for instance, the luxury of Art Deco against the reductive approach to design at the Dessau Bauhaus or the “consumer engineering” of American industrial design.
As the following pages demonstrate, there was considerable overlap and crossover among these approaches to modern design during the interwar period, corresponding to complex attitudes toward technology, work, leisure, and lifestyle.
We might begin thinking about the expanded role of design during this period as varied responses to the experience of World War I (1914–18) and its aftermath.
The origins of the style known as Art Moderne or Art Deco may be traced to the years just before the war.
But the persistence of French organizers to host an international exhibition devoted to modern decorative and industrial arts in 1925, originally planned to take place in 1915, suggests that the active promotion of French pre-eminence in the design and manufacture of luxury goods to accompany a “modern” lifestyle that embraced travel, tourism, entertainment, and hygiene was motivated by a combination of renewed nationalism and economic reconstruction in the wake of the Great War that extended to many of the countries that participated in the exhibition.
The majority of Art Deco designers who took part in the exhibition saw themselves as artist-craftsmen, proud of the equality they had earned and shared with fine artists and cognizant of an exclusive and discriminating international market for their goods.
Marketing, advertising, and promotion through posters, merchandising, and lifestyle magazines such as Vogue expanded the audience and commercial exposure of Art Deco.
The Bauhaus presents a complex and shifting institutional history.
Its first director, architect Walter Gropius (1883–1969), was a World War I veteran.
The school’s first home was the city of Weimar, capital of the republican government that replaced the imperial state following Germany’s defeat.
The Bauhaus manifesto (see here) proclaimed a utopian faith in the creativity and unity of the arts culminating in the art of building, the exaltation of craft, and an ideal integration of art into life.
In the early 1920s the Bauhaus mission shifted its focus, championing industrial materials and production, eliminating overt signs of handwork, and adopting the mantra “Art and Technology: A New Unity.” The shift was apparent in the appointment of new faculty, in the construction of an austere factory-like building for the school’s new home in Dessau in 1926, and in the design of prototypes for furnishings that eliminated ornament in favor of spare forms emphasizing an underlying, elementary geometric abstraction with universal aesthetic and social pretensions.
The shift at the Bauhaus was contemporary with (and to an extent influenced by) international efforts of artist-designers in Soviet Russia and in other countries who, under banners such as Constructivism (Russia), l’Esprit Nouveau (France, see here and fig.
9.5), and De Stijl (the Netherlands), embraced prefabricated building techniques and materials, and espoused a reductive visual vocabulary for design as a basis for an egalitarian society.
Such radical and utopian views, often referred to by the label “Modernism” (with a capital “M”), were meant to replace outmoded individualistic and nationalistic values that were viewed as contributing to competition, international tensions, and eventually conflict and world war.
The experimental use of modern industrial materials for furnishings, elimination of carved or molded ornament, and use of sans serif typography as well as photomechanical processes for printing are often associated with these movements, but such technologies and practices were not limited to them nor to their particular aesthetic, social, and political ideologies.
Clean lines, smooth surfaces, undecorated forms, experimental typography, and asymmetrical page layouts in printing emerged in the 1930s in commercial as well as radical experimental contexts.
Depending upon the specific historical circumstances, “Modernism” could signify a variety of attitudes toward modern life, from austerity in response to economic hardship, to practical, socially responsible middle-class modern living, to utopian projects for radical collective or communal living, to an embodiment of the spiritualized experience of non-objectivity, or to a more transparent, “natural” lifestyle freed from convention and conformity to tradition.
It is no wonder that in assembling material for its 2006 exhibition devoted to Modernism, the Victoria and Albert Museum catalog could only conclude that Modernism was a “loose collection of ideas” rather than a consistent approach to design.
The United States emerged after World War I as an international leader in the mechanized mass production of automobiles and related products of industrial manufacturing such as kitchen appliances, owing to the unparalleled success of Henry Ford’s moving assembly line in the production of the standardized, unchanging Model T (see here).
But in the wake of the nation’s participation in the war, America’s foreign policy turned inward and isolationist, and included withdrawal from the fledgling League of Nations founded in 1920 and worries at home over liberal immigration policies.
After the mid-1920s, the market for furnishings and industrial products began to decline and needed to be sustained through aggressive advertising as well as through design innovation.
The emergence of Art Deco in the United States was stimulated by the emigration of European designers after World War I in search of creative and economic opportunity and the receptivity of manufacturers and retailers in providing consumers with modern luxury goods and furnishings.
Business magazines such as Fortune touted the application of modern art to industrial and workshop production achieved through the efforts of artists, collectors, museums, manufacturers, and retail merchandisers.
One outcome was a modern design style sometimes known as “Skyscraper,” inspired by the tall buildings that were beginning to dominate the skylines of North American cities, the excitement of city nightlife, the rhythms and improvisational spontaneity of jazz music, interpreted visually using Cubist fragmentation, and marketed through the popular cinema, museum exhibitions, department stores, and illustrated magazines.
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York, founded in 1929, exhibited and promoted a more austere approach to architecture and design, showing architectural models by Le Corbusier, Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe (the last director of the Bauhaus), and other European and US architects, proclaiming an “International Style” based upon the use of modern industrial materials (steel, reinforced concrete, large expanses of glass [curtain walls], and the idea of the elimination of ornament), which a curator noted “would seem to mar rather than adorn the clean perfection [italics added] of surface and proportion.” The appearance of the professional industrial designer in the United States, beginning in the later 1920s and 1930s, was primarily a product of industrial manufacturers’ desire to stimulate consumer interest for their products and appliances through an appeal to novelty and fantasy in an increasingly competitive economic climate.
Desire for household appliances was often advertised in the language of paternalistic reform: that is, as a contribution to social progress, hygiene, and the application of domestic science and technology to everyday life, clearly expressed in the modern style known as Streamlining.
The planners of the 1939 World’s Fair in New York saw design as encouraging employment, economic growth, and improved living standards for the middle class on a vast scale with large corporations and government as sponsors of ambitious urban and suburban planning, including an interstate highway system.
Organizers and manufacturers hoped that a streamlined vision of the future would reduce social ills amid the hardships of the Depression, and would act as a bulwark against populism and the attraction of fascist dictatorships in Europe as well as socialism and the threat it posed to capitalist free enterprise.
The Fair’s vision of the “World of Tomorrow” combined exhibits to attract the attention of consumers such as electric dishwashers and the first television sets, with sci-fi novelties such as robots, the General Motors Company’s Futurama, and the space-age Trylon and Perisphere that housed a future miniature “Democracity.” The Americas, the subject of Global Inspiration IV, exhibit the complexities that a global perspective brings to bear on the history of modern design, from early colonial ties to Spain as displayed at World’s Fairs, to the search for (or construction of) an Indigenous national identity in Mexico in the wake of independence and its marketing in the United States through tourism and the film industry; to an engagement with international Modernism that includes the education of Latin American designers in Europe and the emigration of Europeans to the Americas.
Once again, a full picture and appreciation of the history of modern design has much to gain by expanding our vision beyond a Eurocentric geography and cultural perspective.

## Chapter
8 Paris and Art Moderne (Art Deco) Before and After World War I By 1905 Siegfried Bings La Maison de lArt Nouveau showrooms had closed, following the recent fate of a similar contemporary design workshop venture in Paris under the direction of the German connoisseur Julius Meier-Graefe known as La Maison Moderne.
Scholars have argued that competition from antique dealers and manufacturers offering period furnishings for the luxury market may have eroded the market for Art Nouveau, and it is also possible that department stores selling less expensive imitations and reproductions of the style may have reduced its appeal to the high-end market for modern decorative arts.
Competition also came from Germany: French writers at the time praised examples of German design at exhibitions for their modern practicality and restrained decoration as debated by the Werkbund (see Chapter 7, here).
Emerging attitudes toward modern living valued efficiency, seen in the success of scientific management in business and industry, in the writings on domestic science by Christine Frederick, and in the recommendations of taste-makers such as Elsie de Wolfe (1865 1950), who advocated the cultivation of uncluttered interiors, light, and good ventilation in her 1913 book The House in Good Taste.
Even as designers explored more practical attitudes toward modern living in a variety of goods and interior ensembles, the values that nurtured Bings and Meier-Graefes showrooms persisted, particularly as they encouraged innovation in materials, original decoration, and a belief in the unity and equality of the arts.
In France these values persisted under the auspices of the Société des Artistes Décorateurs (S.A.D.) and the annual Salon dAutomne where fine and decorative arts were exhibited together.
In addition, periodicals devoted to design (Art et Décoration, for example) promoted the work of modern designers for a luxury market.
French designers continued to embrace the reputation for individuality and originality they had fought for as well as continuity with a distinguished national heritage of craft excellence prior to and after the French Revolution.
Designers explored a wide variety of new sources of inspiration, including contemporary painting and sculpture, original adaptations of restrained late eighteenthcentury Neoclassical furniture and fashion, along with sensational entertainments in Paris such the Ballets Russes and the jazz and dance clubs that emerged after World War I, associated with a spirited and youthful modernity.
As most students of early twentieth-century painting are aware, bold, non-naturalistic Léon Bakst, costume design (Odalisque) for Schéhérazade, 1910. color and a higher degree of abstraction distinguished the work of a group of artists at the 1905 Salon dAutomne who acquired the nickname Fauves (Wild Beasts), coined by critic Louis Vauxcelles.
A similar boldness and intensity of expression characterized productions of the Ballets Russes in Paris, particularly the striking costumes and colorful stage sets designed between 1909 and 1913 by Russian artists Alexandre Benois (18701960) and Léon Bakst (18661924) for productions of Cléopatre and Schéhérazade, the latter based upon the tales of the Arabian Nights, including an orgy that takes place between the concubines of a sultans harem and a group of Black enslaved people.
These productions featured an element of eroticism and primitivism associated with Western views of West Asian and North African cultures (on Orientalism, see here) expressed in costume design and provocative movement.
Such a shared milieu involving the fine arts, entertainment, and fashion may be seen in a comparison between costume design by Léon Bakst for Schéhérazade (1910), and the sheer, loose-fitting harem pants designed in 1911 by French couturier Paul Poiret (18791944), both aimed at an elite audience (figs.
8.1 and 8.2).
A similar exoticism and sensuality is found in a series of paintings and sketches of nudes by Henri Matisse (18691954) based upon the artists visits to Morocco in 1911 to 1912.
The Ballets Russes remained a source of inspiration for fine and decorative artists throughout the 1910s and 1920s, serving as the subject for the Firebird electric table lamp designed by René Lalique in 1926 (fig.
8.13).
Georges Lepape, Mme.
Poiret wearing “harem” pants designed by Paul Poiret, gouache, 1911.

## Some
Varied References for Art Moderne While reminiscent of the refined craftsmanship and restrained carved decoration of French later eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Neoclassical furniture, there is much originality in the luxury French furniture that emerged beginning in the second decade of the twentieth century, often labeled Moderne. Taut curves and tight spirals, Art Moderne furniture exhibits bold color contrasts created by mother-of-pearl, featuring silver or ivory inlays against mirror-like reflective black lacquer backgrounds; more subtle and varied surfaces produced by the application of lacquer finishes; prancing stags, and luxurious vegetation that evokes a bold sense of natures energy and abundance, only slightly held in check by symmetry and careful consideration given to integrating decorative elements and construction.
Maurice Dufrènes (18761955) upholstered mahogany armchair (fig.
8.3), based upon an eighteenth-century type known as a bergère (see here) and exhibited at the 1913 Salon dAutomne, exemplifies the new direction pursued by French artist-designers in the years just before the outbreak of World War I.
Dufrène began his career as a painter, worked as a furniture designer and manager at Julius Meier-Graefes La Maison Moderne showrooms, helped to found the Société des Artistes Décorateurs in 1901, and managed the retail design studio known as Maîtrise for the Parisian department store Galeries Lafayette beginning in 1922 that marketed artistic designs for the retail trade.
Dufrènes furniture reveals continuity with highly skilled workshop production, and from the second decade of the twentieth century embraced a robust yet controlled modern sensibility.
In the armchair, for instance, the broad contours of both the back and seat are comfortably balanced and embellished by the carved spiral scroll at the termination of the armrests and the seams of the silk upholstery to create a design remarkable for its harmony and unity of structure and decoration.
The broad, sweeping curves of Dufrènes designs recall the ripe fullness of nature found in the still lives and interiors of Henri Matisse, and also bring to mind Matisses analogy between painting and furniture in his 1908 essay Notes of a Painter. In this essay, the artist compared the tranquil mood he hoped that his canvases would provide his bourgeois urban audience with the comfort of a good armchair: What I dream of is an art of balance, of purity and tranquility, devoid of troubling subject matter, an art which could be, for every mental worker, for the businessman as well as for the man of letters, for example, a soothing balm, a mental calmative, something akin to a good armchair which eases his physical fatigue.
Maurice Dufrène, chair, mahogany and upholstery, 30 × 23 in (76.2 × 48.4 cm), shown at the Salon d’Automne, Paris, 1913.
The suggestion that paintings and furniture bring relief from the pressures of whitecollar work and the routines of daily life (Matisses remarks stem from a similar statement made by French writer Charles Baudelaire; 18211867) reinforces a shared milieu for modern artists and high-end artist-designed furnishings in common pursuit of original creative expression that contributes to the joy and sense of well-being found in everyday acts of modern living for a discriminating audience with sufficient leisure and imagination (and financial resources) to find aesthetic pleasure in everyday experience.
Like several of his contemporaries with careers in design, Frenchman Jacques-Émile Ruhlmann (18791933) studied to be a painter but turned to the decorative arts around 1910.
Many of his designs are free interpretations of French Neoclassical or Empire furniture, augmenting the French patrimony of virtuoso marquetry using expensive and rare materials and involving the most exacting standards of craftsmanship.
As seen in a desk from c.
1919 (fig.
8.4), his furniture is replete with invention, employing veneers of exotic woods such as amboyna imported from Laos and macassar ebony from Indonesia (both were French colonial territories at the time), with ringed drawer pullers of ivory attached by green silk thread accenting a grayish-green sharkskin writing surface (Ruhlmann used other materials such as crocodile skin for cabinet doors in place of glass or fabric).
The desk is supported by gently curving thin legs that project outward from the desktop and are delicately tapered (known as fuseau).
Ruhlmann was a member of S.A.D.; in his view, luxury and artistic freedom were the bedrock of modern French design.
In an interview from 1920 he stated: Only the very rich can pay for what is new and they alone can make it fashionable.
Fashions do not start among the common people.
Along with satisfying a desire for change, fashions real purpose is to display wealth. As seen below, not all interwar designers agreed with him.
Jacques-Émile Ruhlmann, desk and tabouret, designed for David-Weill residence, Paris, beech, amboyna veneer, shagreen, and ivory; desk: $3 7 \times 4 7 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 2 9 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (94 × 121 × 75 cm); tabouret: 27 $^ 1 / _ { 2 } \times 1 6 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 2 8 ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 }$ in (69.9 × 41.9 × 71.8 cm), c.
1919.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
References to the decorative arts in the early Cubist paintings of Georges Braque (18821963) and Pablo Picasso (18811973) consist primarily of the incorporation of pieces of cheap printed wallpaper and the borrowing of wall painters techniques for imitating wood grain.
Such borrowings constitute encroachments from the industrial products of ordinary domestic life upon the territory of high Art, in terms of their lower middle-class associations and the implied blurring between mechanical reproduction and the individual, original, and exclusive work of fine artists.
But while Cubist paintings appear to challenge the exclusivity associated with fine art, early twentieth-century critics did not generally acknowledge this provocative crossing of boundaries.
More often they found parallels for the geometric shapes and abstract, compositional strategies of Cubist artists in contemporary luxury craft such as those ensembles displayed at the 1912 Maison Cubiste that reinforced the elevated aesthetic views of S.A.D.
And while Picasso and Braque explored their hermetic approach to Cubism in 1911 and 1912, a more accessible and sociable adaptation of the style may be found in the work of French artists Albert Gleizes (18811953) and Jean Metzinger (18831956), sometimes labeled Salon Cubism. Pierre Chareau, pochoir print, study with desk, sofa, and lamp, from Les Arts De La Maison, 1924.
One can detect a debt to Cubism in the furniture and furnishings designed by Frenchman Pierre Chareau (18831950) who marketed his custom designs through a boutique he owned and operated in Paris beginning in 1924.
Figure 8.5 is a colored pochoir print (a technique of reproducing color images using stencils) of a home office.
The beveled contours of the desk and angles of back and armrests of the desk chair suggest Cubist abstraction, and both pieces are devoid of carved decoration or marquetry.
Also Cubist-inspired is Chareaus standing lamp with intersecting, faceted pieces of smooth, translucent alabaster attached to a metal armature, adapted as well to desk lamps, chandeliers, and sconces.
Chareaus boutique catered to an elite audience and used expensive materials, including imported woods as well as labor-intensive craftsmanship, with wrought iron produced by master craftsman Louis Dalbet, who collaborated with Chareau on many of his commissions.
At the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, 1925 (International Exposition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts), a tall painted mural by Robert Delaunay (18851941), featuring a Cubist rendering of the Eiffel Tower, was included in one of the interiors for the exhibitions model French embassy, but a more persistent link between the fragmented and dynamic style seen in this and related paintings by Delaunay and the decorative arts was made by Delaunays Ukrainian-born wife, Sonia Terk Delaunay (18851979).
Sonia Delaunay used overlapping or interlocking abstract geometric shapes and prismatic color for the design of interiors, fabrics, clothing, and other furnishings.
The Delaunays used the term simultaneity to describe the dynamism and transcendence of solid form that characterized the aesthetic experience of modernity, and in 1925 a Boutique Simultanée was included as one of the Gallery of Boutiques featured at the Paris Exhibition.
The following year, the Delaunays collaborated on the costumes and set designs for a new production of Cléopatre performed by the Ballets Russes in Paris.
A cover illustration by Georges Lepape in British Vogue from January 1925 featured a model wearing a dress designed by Sonia Delaunay beside a roadster also decorated with painted simultaneous patterns (fig.
8.6).
The fragmentation also associated with Cubism may be seen in a silvered bronze and enamel clock designed and crafted by Jean Goulden (18781946) dating to 1928 (fig.
8.7).
Goulden was a physician who learned the art of enamel (glass paste) while serving in the French army in Greece during World War I, where he encountered Byzantine enamels at the monastery of Mount Athos.
The simple circles and diamond shapes on the clock dial as well as the plain rectangular hands appear to tumble and splinter onto the asymmetrical base, without recourse to traditional classical allegory (see fig.
1.11) Gouldens timepiece nevertheless alludes to the often hurried, frantic experience of modern time.
Jean Goulden, clock, silvered bronze with enamel, 14 $^ 1 / _ { 4 } \times 1 0 ^ { 2 } / _ { 5 } \times 4 ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 }$ in (36.2 × 25.7 × 12.4 cm), 1928.
Collection Stephen E.
Kelly.
Fascination with Cubism and its relationship to modern living and the decorative arts ran deep and extended beyond France.
As early as 1911 architects and artist-designers in Prague and elsewhere in the modern-day Czech Republic (then still part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire) created designs for furniture, ceramics, and metalwork that substituted beveled and intersecting planes for more traditional forms in the construction of cabinets, chairs, and a variety of ceramic vessels and tableware.
Some of this work was manufactured by the cooperative workshop Artĕl based upon the model of the Vienna Workshops.
Restrained in comparison with the flowing rhythms and forms found in Art Nouveau or the Jugendstil, the work produced by Artĕl and other manufacturers provided an opportunity for artists and architects to directly engage with the design of domestic interior furnishings.
Vlastislav Hofmans (18841964) stoneware vase dating to 1919 and sold through Artĕl is an example of this Cubistinspired work: the angular form of the vase is hand-painted with black zigzag accents, highlighting the vases diagonal thrust, and the triangular opening at the top (fig.
8.8).
In general Czech Cubist furniture and ceramic forms were symmetrical, and designers integrated modern and original decoration with, rather than added to, constructive forms.

## M A
similar but even more pared-down abstract aesthetic characterizes the work in silver designed by Jean Puiforcat (18971945), who came from a family of silversmiths in Paris.
His father had directed the family business toward the luxury market.
