Throughout a career that began following his return from service in World War I, Puiforcat maintained interests in both stone sculpture and silver.
A perfect sphere supported by an attached armature/handle, Puiforcats teapot from c.
1928 (fig.
8.9) shares the smooth surfaces and reductive three-dimensional form found in the work of contemporary Romanian-born sculptor Constantin Brancusi (18761957).
The perfection of Puiforcats surfaces suggests machine-like precision, but required painstaking craftsmanship; it would be a mistake to equate uncritically aesthetic simplicity with ease of production, utility, or cost savings; something that is simple to look at is not necessarily easy to make or conducive to machine production.
Curiously, one may trace the connection between the reduction or elimination of decoration and machine production to William Morriss dictum: The more mechanical the process, the less direct should be the imitation of natural forms, or Frank Lloyd Wrights equation of machine-making with simplicity (see here; 142), as if the latter were the natural or inevitable outcome of the former.
Jean Puiforcat, tea set, silver, c.
1928; teapot: silver, walnut, 5 × 6 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 4 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (12.7 × 17.2 × 11.5 cm).
Cooper Hewitt Museum, New York.
A simplified abstraction also informs the advertising posters of Russian-born artist Cassandre (born Adolphe Jean-Marie Mouron; 19011968) from the 1920s through the mid-1930s, seen, for instance, in a travel poster for the luxury steamship L’Atlantique in 1931 (fig.
8.10), in which the monumental shape of the hull is inscribed within a rectangle, again emphasizing its abstract character, further exaggerated in contrast to the small tugboat at the lower left that eased such ships in and out of harbor.
To further suggest the association between the geometric purity of the forms and modern industrial technology, Cassandre used a pneumatic airbrush to apply color to the lithographic stone, introducing an element of subtle and precise tonal control beyond the capability of more direct means of drawing or painting with brushes.
A.
M.
Cassandre, poster for L’Atlantique, 24 <sup>3</sup>/ × 39 in (62 × 99 cm), 1931.
Cassandre likened his task as a poster artist to that of a telegrapher who was the instantaneous conduit of condensed information to be seen rather than read.
Cassandres designs were highly selective in spite of the matter-of-fact tone of his selfassessment: he drew upon abstract elements in contemporary fine art such as Cubist painting and abstract sculpture as well as popular forms of visual communication including film sequencing and branding.
He also incorporated sophisticated verbal as well as visual puns that helped to integrate text and image.
His mural-sized 1932 poster featuring Monsieur Dubo for Dubonnet wine (part of a series of posters he designed for the company) features a seated figure in a bowler hat in three stages of pouring, sipping, and pouring a second glass of the beverage (fig.
8.11).
In each iteration the letters of the brand are completed as Monsieur Dubos form fills out.
The successive words beneath the first two images play on the French word for good (bon) that was already in use by the company (Good Dubonnet), ending with the brand name itself.
The deft combination of repetition and variation to attract and maintain viewer attention is remarkable.
There are subtle variations in pose, as well as in color.
Cassandres little man (aka Monsieur Dubo) is composed entirely of straight and precisely drawn semicircular curved lines, whose regular contours are repeated from part to part in each of the three variations, creating a strong sense of visual unity within each poster and as a sequence that is read left to right.
The little mans torso and legs remain in the same position while the upper body, head, and right arm reveal slight variations in the sequence.
Straight lines are generally parallel or drawn at a 90-degree angle.
Other angles create parallel lines, such as the pouring bottle in the third of the three images, which matches the angle of Dubos head and his bent left leg.
The angle of the head is at 90 degrees in the first image in the series, turning more acutely in the middle drinking image.
In each of the three posters the viewers eye follows a diagonal path downward from upper right to lower left and then continues across horizontally with the letters of the word Dubonnet, suggested in the numerous horizontal contours and shapes of the little man, table, and chair.
Circular and semi-circular shapes are found in Dubos tightly fitting bowler hat, with echoes in the shapes of the wine glass, elbow, eye, eyeball, sleeve buttons, and the fingernails of the left hand.
They also are found in the counters of the geometric sans serif, upper-case letters and the shapes U, B, O, and D. Unlike poster advertisements for alcoholic beverages in the later nineteenth century, or even ads for wine or beer on television today, Monsieur Dubo drinks alone rather than in the represented or implied company of others.
Typical and yet at the same time remarkable, even personal when triggered by one of its attending objects, the café celebrates an aspect of our experience of modern time, offering a respite (whether private or social) from the demands and obligations of work (when time is not our own) and the hurried pace of the day, a small indulgence that reminds us of our autonomy, lending significance to unimportant moments rather than dramatic or climactic ones.
Cassandres work helped to define the profession of graphic design in the interwar years, eschewing more conventional narrative advertising illustration in favor of bolder, reductive ways to identify products and create an immediate and memorable visual impact.
In 1936 the Museum of Modern Art in New York devoted an exhibition to Cassandres posters; he was the first graphic designer to be so honored; an earlier exhibition at MoMA devoted to design (1934) was entitled Machine Art (see here).
A similar sophistication, integrating fragmentary or pictographic images with blocks of text to create visual variety and interest, is found in books and high-end journals in Paris in the interwar period, as practiced by publisher Alfred Tolmer (18761957).
In 1930, Tolmer issued a book entitled Mise en Page that helped to define new techniques that explored creative approaches to visual communication in the publishing industry.
Writers such as Blaise Cendrars celebrated Cassandres achievement and viewed his posters as a modern form of public art contributing to the stimulating spectacle of the street. A.
M.
Cassandre, Dubo-Dubon-Dubonnet, 1932, chromolithograph, 17 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 45 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (44.5 × 115.6 cm)

## Glass
and Lacquer Art Moderne was, of course, not limited to wood furniture and techniques that built upon the tradition of the great eighteenth-century French ébénistes.
New materials and techniques, whether industrial or imported from colonial territories, particularly challenged early twentieth-century designers in a variety of media.
An examination of glass design in the period around 1910 reveals a lively interest in a variety of techniques to permit individual and original expression in the medium.
Perhaps as a result of Gallés success and reputation (see here), early twentieth-century glass does not always make a distinct break with Art Nouveau.
The enameling technique known as pâte de verre, produced by refiring colored ground glass in molds, resulted in translucent surfaces of varied color whose rich effects were reminiscent of the earlier movement, even if the technique, to be successful, required thick walls and more patient attention to the cooling process.
Other French designers directed their efforts to clear glass, often with thick walls pressed into molds to accentuate relief, or sometimes trapping air bubbles in a technique known as verre soufflé or bubble glass. Maurice Marinot (18821960) abandoned an early career as a painter to work in glass.
After experimenting with the process of pâte de verre, Marinot explored effects using transparent as well as colored glass.
Results were thick-walled and sculptural, incorporating bubbles and streaks produced in the process of making rather than as applied decoration, and seen in a jar dating to 1924 (fig.
8.12).
Maurice Marinot, jar with cover, glass with enclosed bubbles; jar: $7 ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 4 ^ { 3 } / _ { 8 }$ in (17.9 × 11.1 cm); cover: $4 \% \times 4 \%$ in (11 × 11.3 cm), 1924.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
René Lalique (18601945) operated his own glassmaking facility near Paris for the manufacture of limited editions of his designs, many of which are manufactured today in boutiques that bear the founders name.
Lalique trained as a jeweler, and earlier in his career created some of the most celebrated examples of Art Nouveau jewelry using precious metals, stones, and enamel.
Before the end of the first decade of the new century he began working with glass as an inexpensive industrial material rather than using precious gems, purchasing a lightbulb factory in 1911 to work directly with the medium.
Lalique explored glass primarily as a transparent rather than translucent medium, etching with acid to achieve contrast in texture.
Critics admired Laliques work for its purity and perfection, seen in the Firebird lamp (fig.
8.13), which took its name from the title character (half-woman/half-bird) of a well-known production (with music by Russian composer Igor Stravinsky; 18821971) at the Ballets Russes, staged first in 1910 and performed again in 1926.
In this work, ordinary glass becomes almost magically invisible, revealing an etched floating female figure whose feathered wings and plantlike tail echo the contour of a fan-shaped shade poised on a darker cubic base.
The reputation Lalique established before World War I continued after the Armistice in 1918.
As early as 1907 he was asked by perfumer François Coty (18761934) to design labels for perfume bottles.
The partnership grew to include the design of the glass bottles themselves, strengthening a link between art glass and the marketing of fragrances in the wake of the expansion of this industry with the introduction of synthetic perfumes in the early twentieth century.
Many Lalique perfume containers included glass stoppers that were an integral part of the design, and generated appeal through associations with exotic plants whose extracts were the ingredients used for the scents themselves.
The French national perfume industry hired Lalique to design their display using etched-glass walls and ceiling at the 1925 Exhibition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, another instance of designers increasing role in merchandising, whether in display or packaging (see below on Morris Lapidus, here).
René Lalique, Oiseau de Feu (Firebird) glass lamp with bronze base, height 16 $^ 7 / _ { 8 }$ in (43 cm), c.
1925.
Private collection.
Other early twentieth-century designers were also attracted to the idea of creatively transforming inexpensive industrial materials into highly original designs.
For instance, Swiss-born Jean Dunand (18771942) came to Paris originally to study sculpture.
His teacher, Jean Dampt (18541946), advocated egalitarian views toward the arts, and with his mentors encouragement Dunand pursued and achieved critical success in the field of dinanderie, referring to small vases and utensils manufactured from nonprecious metals such as copper and brass, applying patina for textures and colored surfaces as well as the repoussé technique to introduce relief patterns based upon geometric and schematic floral forms.
Occasionally the organic shapes of Dunands early dinanderie vases recall the irregularity of Art Nouveau pottery or glass, but often his works exhibit a preference for more regular contours and classically inspired forms (such as the Greek amphora), as well as spiral decorative motifs.
Other forms, in the 1920s, recall bulbous gourds used as bowls and containers in French colonial Africa decorated with abstract geometric patterns.
Such works were shown at exhibitions sponsored by the Société des Artistes Décorateurs and were reproduced in the publication Art et Décoration.
In 1912 Dunand studied the technique of applying lacquer to a variety of hammered copper dinanderie under the guidance of a well-known Japanese craftsman named Seizo Sugawara (d.
1940) who was working in Paris at the invitation of French jeweler Lucien Gaillard (18611942).
Lacquer is a colored or transparent substance made from the sap of trees grown primarily in East Asia.
A long process of refinement and purification is required to produce lacquer, and its application to surfaces of wood or metal objects is equally painstaking.
Although lacquer was used primarily as a protective coating to preserve and protect materials (with Dunands assistance the French air force used lacquer to coat the surface of plywood propellers for airplanes during World War I in order to prevent the dangerous deterioration of the material in wet or humid weather), Dunand became interested in lacquers potential for design, which he developed more fully after the war.
His exacting methods produced layered surfaces of great subtlety and brilliance on a variety of wooden screens, metal bowls, and furniture.
An idea of the variety of surface effects in lacquer is seen in a composite photograph in figure 8.14.
The following description of the lacquering process for a wooden screen demonstrates Dunands obsessive dedication to craft: As many as forty coats of lacquer had to be applied and, as the lacquer in drying tended to contract and could thus twist the wooden panel of a screen out of shape, another coat had to be applied on the reverse side to counteract the tension: both coats drying simultaneously ensured that the base remained true.
The drying process presented complications, taking any time between three and four days, and paradoxically could only be satisfactorily accomplished in a room kept perpetually damp by means of streams of water flowing down the walls.
Further complications were added in that the drying process could only take place in a darkened room and for some mysterious reason was affected by the moons influence, the best result occurring when the moon was full.
After each coat a process of careful rubbing down and smoothing to a perfect surface had to be performed before another coat of lacquer could be applied.
8.14 Jean Dunand, samples of decorative lacquers.
Other examples of lacquer include the large black cabinet incised with thin strips of silver to create the reductive form of a hedgehog, a collaboration between Dunand, Polish-born painter Jean Lambert-Rucki (18881967), and metalsmith Jean Goulden; this monumental cabinet, more than eight feet in length, was exhibited in 1925 in the interior of the Grand Salon of the Hôtel dun Collectionneur for the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes (figs.
8.15 and 8.16; and see here).
Jean Dunand and Jean Lambert-Rucki, cabinet, black lacquer with incised strips of silver, 77 × 98 × 29 in (195.5 × 248.9 × 73.6 cm), from Grand Salon, Hôtel d’un Collectionneur, Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, Paris, 1925.
Jacques-Émile Ruhlmann, Grand Salon, Hôtel d’un Collectionneur, Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, Paris, 1925, with black lacquer cabinet from the workshop of Jean Dunand on the left and Jean Dupas’ painting Les Perruches (The Songbirds or The Parakeets) on the right.
While many of the designers associated with the Art Moderne style were active in the years 1905 to 1915, others emerged more fully only after World War I.
Metalsmith Edgar Brandt (18801960), who worked with wrought iron and experimented with combinations of forged metals and alloys, was an artist-craftsman who explored new technologies, such as autogenous welding, allowing him to combine different metals to create furniture, lighting, plaques, doors, and screens.
Examples include the plaques and screens Brandt created for special commissions, such as the Cigognes d’Alsace (fig.
8.17), a large grille in patinated wrought iron and tin.
This design of 1922 was repeated, supported by a plywood surface, in a 1928 commission for the interior wall panels of elevators in Selfridges department store in London (removed in 1971 to comply with new fire regulations and relocated to the Museum of London with an additional example in the Victoria and Albert Museum).
These large relief panels rival the effects of an illusionistic ceiling from a Baroque church or palace, with circling birds floating against an asymmetrically placed octagonal opening from which schematically rendered rays emanate outward.
Brandt embellished the composition with spiral cloud forms in relief, repeated in smaller and more shallow variations.
The Cigognes is a showpiece that tests the limits of a medium often associated with a vocabulary of stock motifs, textures, and patterns; in this example the inherent tensile strength of the wrought iron is maintained in the rodlike projections from the octagon containing the storks, while the Edgar Brandt, table clock, 1925. varied textures of the clouds and the illusionism of the radiating composition itself suggest a softness or malleability that transcends the materials usual associations through the artists imagination and skill.
A table clock (fig.
8.18) from 1925 exhibits the same degree of virtuosity on a smaller scale, with the clock dial surrounded by tightly bunched clusters of buds; below a sleeping nude is gently awakened by chirping birds.
Edgar Brandt, detail of Les Cigognes d’Alsace, grille, patinated wrought iron and tin, 8 ft 2 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in × 6 ft 7 in × 3 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in $( 2 6 0 \times$ 200 × 9 cm), exhibited at the Salon des Artistes Françaises, 1922.

## Traveling
in Style: Tourism, Luxury, and Promotion Venues for such dazzling technical displays include the interior design of luxury oceangoing steamships during the 1930s.
Promotional materials for the companies who financed and built them, including advertising posters (see fig.
8.10), incorporated the ships tapered bows and slim oval smokestacks, touted the powerful coal-fueled steam engines and capable engineering that permitted transatlantic trips between Europe and New York in a little over four days, but also advertised orchestras, dancing, sports, and luxury accommodations, service (the Normandie had over 1,300 crew members) and furnishings geared to first-class passengers who made up the majority of travelers.
A wellknown example of interior decoration from the Grand Salon of the French luxury liner SS Normandie, also evoking a Baroque theme, is The Chariot of Aurora lacquer and metal leaf on plaster relief, designed by the painter Jean Dupas (18821964) and executed by Jean Dunand in 1935 (fig.
8.19).
The Chariot of Aurora (26 feet long) is one of four panels depicting mythological gods and goddesses associated with travel and navigation.
Sunrays radiate across clouds and schematic wavelike imbrications from a flaming disk.
Aurora (the dawn) rises in a chariot accompanied by nude figures and representations of winds, rain, spring flowers, and the autumn harvest.
Such luxury interior design contrasted with the hardship facing the working class during the economic depression that followed the New York stockmarket crash late in 1929 and whose repercussions were felt worldwide.
On the popular level, the cinema provided escape and distraction in vicarious form to the middle class, while manufacturers looked to celebrities to market cosmetics that promised buyers the smooth, unblemished skin they envied in their Hollywood screen idols.
An example from a 1930 advertisement in American Vogue (fig.
8.20), features the Paris-based Houbigant companys perfume and face powder in cardboard packaging decorated with simplified star and floral shapes often found in Art Moderne wallpapers and textiles.
Jean Dunand, Aurora panel from interior of the Normandie, 1935.
Perfume advertisement from American Vogue, November 10, 1930, here, Houbigant company.
Fashion designers were patrons of the Art Moderne movement in French decorative arts, and included Jeanne Lanvin (18671946) as well as fellow couturier Paul Poiret (18791944).
Poiret was a patron of the Salon dAutomne of 1911 and the Maison Cubiste exhibition of 1912, and employed the Fauve painter Raoul Dufy (1877 1953) to design patterns woven or printed by textile manufacturers for curtains, upholstery, and dress fabrics.
Dufys designs often include figures set amid foliage or stage-like props and were widely imitated.
The painter-designers lively and freely sketched figures, landscapes, and buildings lend themselves to repetition and reinforce surface pattern.
An example, from 1929, is a block-printed wallpaper depicting paired ice skaters (fig.
8.21).
The emphasis upon carefree leisure pastimes has much in common with the themes of eighteenth-century tapestry and porcelain described in Part I (see fig.
1.5).
Photographs of Dufys wallpaper patterns were reproduced in a contemporary issue of the fashion magazine Vogue in a section devoted to the arts.
In a later monumental mural painting, the artist decorated an enormous hall for the 1937 Worlds Fair in Paris with hundreds of figures and motifs illustrating the history of electricity.
Dufy emphasized the discovery and benefits of electricity in human terms, depicting scientists who contributed to its development (Benjamin Franklin is among them), along with turbines and leisure, for instance, outdoor lighting for an evening concert with orchestra, chorus, and dancers (on view today at the Musée de la Ville de Paris).
Raoul Dufy, wallpaper design, woodblock print, 1929.
Private collection.
As mentioned above, Poirets own fashions made use of bold and even discordant color combinations of sets and costumes of the Ballets Russes, and staging of ballets based upon Schéhérezade and other themes taken from the lore of West Asia and North Africa.
He created the idea of harem pants for women (see fig.
8.2), and his fashion designs permitted more freedom of movement and a closer relationship between garment and body that was considered quite provocative, and boldly modern for its time.
Poirets own celebrity contributed to his success, and his considerable selfpromotional efforts stand within a late nineteenth-century tradition of artists studios that were specifically designed as meeting places for potential clients (see here).
Poirets reputation was damaged at the outbreak of World War I, when the popularity of his designs in Germany led to false accusations by some critics that he was an enemy sympathizer.
With his reputation restored in the 1920s, Poiret experimented with fabrics and forms that permitted freer movement and benefitted from links between fashion and fine art that he also nurtured through associations with fine artists such as Dufy, and that helped to maintain the aura of exclusivity surrounding original works of art while cultivating the public exposure that brought greater opportunities for wider sales, markets, and serial production.
An example of his work from the period is an evening dress from c.
1926, woven with silk, plastic, and glass that shimmers, especially in movement.
The silhouette is columnar rather than tightly fitted.
Poiret used the services of specialized craft firms for embroidery, pleating, and lacing, essential if underappreciated elements in the interwar fashion industry upon which the fashion designers success depended.
After World War I, economic reconstruction and a renewed sense of patriotism in France helped to expand the commercial scope of Art Moderne.
One element of this expansion was the growth of retail outlets for the marketing of modern design and decoration.
In 1919 furniture and interior designers Louis Süe (18751968) and André Mare (18871932) founded the Compagnie des Arts Français to provide a showroom for their own products and those of their collaborators, and in the same year Ruhlmann established a storefront business as an addition to the private commissions that were the basis of his earlier work.
During the same period, metal craftsman René Joubert founded a company to market the works of modern designers, called Décoration Intérieure Moderne (D.I.M.), and the prominent French department stores also inaugurated special showrooms for the display of modern furnishings: Bon Marché opened Pomone in 1923 under the direction of furniture designer Paul Follot (1877 1941), and in 1921 Galleries Lafayette opened La Maîtrise directed by Maurice Dufrène (fig.
8.3).
Many of these retail ventures supported an active engagement of art with serial production to maintain and strengthen the French reputation for original modern design and compete with traditional period styles.
It is no surprise, then, that the four major Parisian department stores erected pavilions for the 1925 Paris Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes.

## The
Paris Exposition of 1925 As early as 1911, the French government began to plan for yet another large international exhibition of the decorative and industrial arts to take place in Paris, but the effort was delayed due to disagreements over the criteria for exhibitors and finally to the outbreak of World War I.
Planning resumed after the war, resulting in the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes of 1925.
Due to lingering wartime hostilities, Germany was not invited to exhibit, and the United States declined to participate, citing an inability to comply with the criteria established by the organizers that stipulated all designs be modern and not based upon historical period styles (see here onward).
Despite efforts on the part of the organizing body to encourage arrangements of furnishings that suggested real living and working spaces and that embodied new modes of life, most of the exhibits featured custom interiors aimed at an exclusive market, unique works and ensembles created by individual artist-designers.
Participating nations, such as the Soviet Union, sponsored pavilions, while other sponsors included the Société des Artistes Décorateurs, national associations of manufacturers from the perfume, tourism, graphic arts, and other industries that mounted displays, a Gallery of Boutiques (see here), and pavilions erected by the four major Parisian department stores.
Several S.A.D. members also contributed ensembles individually, and after much discussion the organizers asked the group to design a lavish model French embassy with reception areas and living rooms assigned to different members.
Ruhlmanns Hôtel dun Collectionneur was a separate structure consisting of furnished rooms designed both for living and lavish entertaining.
The Hôtels Grand Salon (see fig.
8.16) was oval shaped with ceilings over 20 feet (6 meters) high and a crystal chandelier resembling a cascading fountain created with strings of glass beads strewn over tiers of concentric metal circles.
The monumental black lacquer cabinet mentioned above, produced in the workshop of Jean Dunand, was placed opposite the fireplace.
The centerpiece of the room was a grand piano in macassar ebony with an accentuated S-curve; the pianos tapered legs (fuseaux) were inlaid in ivory and flared outward like the hooves of a fawn where they met the floor.
Above the marble fireplace hung a large painting by Jean Dupas entitled Les Perruches (The Songbirds or The Parakeets, see fig.
8.16), depicting a group of draped and nude women with elaborate coiffures, some clothed or partially clothed in heavy satin or silk brocaded fabrics, and set in a landscape of lush fruit, foliage, flowers, and plump birds.
Photographs of the painting in situ reveal harmonies in color between the skin tones of the nudes and the light background of the fabric wall covering as well as the grained marble of the fireplace.
Dupas image of abundance, leisure, and sensual pleasure, both in nature and through the products of a resurgent textile and fashion industry, is a fitting component of Ruhlmanns Grand Salon.
The ensemble reinforced the continued strength of craft traditions supported by modern workshop production, and the close relationship between fine and applied arts.
The new modes of life sought and promoted by the expositions organizers might refer to grand settings for luxury living such as Ruhlmanns Grand Salon in the home of a collector under the auspices of the S.A.D., featuring exotic materials and the highest levels of craftsmanship and original design.
Modern living could also refer to the restrained formal elegance of Pierre Chareaus study-library for a French embassy in rare hardwoods, which incorporated moving panels that could modulate the amount of light from above and conceal shelves.
This space seems deliberately designed for conditions in a tropical climate in a French colony.
The exhilarating pace of modern urban life is also suggested in Sonia Delaunays clothing and textile designs, or her husband Robert Delaunays Eiffel Tower compositions (see here).
Elsa Schiaparelli, fashion sketch of wraparound dress for summer 1930.
The Fashion Institute of Technology, New York.
Art Moderne designers also responded to a contemporary interest in athletics and exercise that found expression in freer, active sportswear, seen in Elsa Schiaparellis sketch for a dress dating to 1930 (fig.
8.22), or even earlier designs for tennis sweaters and outfits.
Francis Jourdains (18761958) Physical Culture Room and the adjoining Lounge designed by Chareau, part of S.A.D.s French Embassy (fig.
8.23), employed smooth wood paneling attached to walls and ceiling to resemble riveted metal sheeting.
A daybed in Chareaus Lounge was suspended from thin steel bars attached to the ceiling (rather than supported by legs from below); the bedspread, square clock, rectangular sliding screens, and regular, plaid patterns for curtains and fabrics contributed to articulate an open and sparsely furnished space in which to exercise and relax.
The Physical Culture Room is a private and exclusive space, with exercise understood here as a modern, active, and fashionable pursuit for those with ample leisure.
8.23 Francis Jourdain and Pierre Chareau, Physical Culture Room and Lounge, French Embassy, Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, Paris, 1925.
At a more social level, physical fitness was connected with travel and tourism, as seen in the colorful advertising posters of Roger Broders (18831953), for instance in figure 8.24, for the Mediterranean port of Monte Carlo, featuring thin, casually dressed men and women relaxing in the foreground of a vacation resort with a view of tennis courts in the distance.
Other posters by Broders present winter sports such as skiing in the Alps.
Rail travel and cruises to more exotic locations, including to French colonial Africa, provided a basis for the use of imported materials such as crocodile skin applied to the design and manufacture of products for modern living, whether Louis Vuitton luggage, on view at the 1931 Exposition Coloniale Internationale held in Paris, or African geometric patterns for the furniture upholstery of a modern Parisian apartment.
Curator Ghislaine Wood described European colonialism as exploitation in the name of progress. Roger Broders, Monte Carlo, poster, 1930.

## Chapter
9 “Modernism”: Design, Utopia, and Technology Economic recovery and progress after World War I provide the background against which Art Moderne (Art Deco) flourished in the 1920s, demonstrating confidence in the beneficial relationship between art, industry, and business, culminating in the Paris 1925 exhibition described in Chapter 8.
Yet the period just before World War I and lasting into the 1930s also witnessed tremendous political ferment and dramatic upheaval, during which the relationship between design, technology, and progress was redirected, often toward broader, utopian ends.
In addition to the destruction wrought by a four-year international conflict in which close to 40 million military and civilian lives were lost, the period witnessed the 1917 Revolution and ensuing Civil War in Russia, political revolution in Hungary (1919), widespread political upheaval and revolution in Mexico (191020), the end of the Qing dynasty in China (1911), and the post-World War I partitioning of the vast Ottoman Empire.
Art historians often use the term Modernism (with a capital M) to refer to the loose collection of movements, manifestos, journals, and projects (planned and less frequently realized) that arose in response to the tensions of the era.
The champions of Modernism argued that the future they envisioned demanded a rejection of, rather than continuity with, the past whether in aesthetic, social, or political terms.
As a result of architectural exhibitions in Stuttgart (1927) and New York (1932), Modernism became recognized as an international style, based upon principles believed by their designers and advocates to be universal (see here), independent from the national contexts in which they emerged as well as from subjective expression and the commercial practices of fashion.
While we may refer to Modernism as a movement in design, it was not unified.
There were differences and contradictions among various Modernist individuals and groups as well as areas where distinctions between Art Deco and Modernism became quite fuzzy, for instance, both embraced physical fitness, exercise, and hygiene, and associated casual clothing, and had an aesthetic preference for elemental geometry linked at times to machine-like precision.
But polemical rhetoric was often a Modernist strategy, imparting a sense of urgency, opposition, and missionary zeal to efforts that aimed to reinvent society and redefine human values and behavior, constructing images of the new man and new woman and their place in the future mechanized world.
The seeds of Modernism were sown in revolutionary talk and nourished by manifestos and exhibitions that demonstrated impatience with the status quo, but again, the politics of Modernism were quite varied, veering at times to the left, center, and right.
Imagining and designing utopia was one thing, but realizing the future was another, and might require a concentration of power in revolutionary or elected governments in the 1920s, faith in autocratic dictators and the power of propaganda in the 1930s, or compromise aiming to achieve more modest goals within existing capitalist economic structures.

## Futurism
In the years both preceding and immediately following World War I, a number of artistdesigners in Italy turned their attention to machines, factories, and cities rather than to nature as sources of inspiration for their work.
They developed a new visual language that embodied the dynamism of air, railroad, and automobile transportation, and heroized the factory and industrial workers who operated machines, provided the physical labor that built the infrastructure of the modern industrial city, and devoted their leisure time to dance halls and weekend sports.
There are numerous references in the poetry of Italian poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti (18761944) to the particular beauty and excitement of machinery as symbols of speed, freedom, and the harbingers of revolutionary change, suggested in a passage from his Manifesto of Futurism, published in the French newspaper Le Figaro on February 20, 1909: We declare that the splendor of the world has been enriched by a new beauty  the beauty of speed.
A racing car with its bonnet draped with exhaust-pipes like firebreathing serpents  a roaring racing car, rattling along like a machine gun, is more beautiful than the winged victory of Samothrace.
We will sing of the stirring of great crowds  workers, pleasure-seekers, rioters  and the confused sea of color and sounds as revolution sweeps through a modern metropolis.
We will sing the midnight fervor of arsenals and shipyards blazing with electric moons; insatiable stations swallowing the smoking of the smoke; bridges flashing like knives in the sun, giant gymnasts that leap over rivers; adventurous steamers that scent the horizon; deep chested locomotives that paw the ground with their wheels, like stallions harnessed with steel tubing; the easy flight of aero-planes, their propellers beating the wind like banners, with a sound like the applause of a mighty crowd.
Futurist artists derived their strategies for visualizing the excitement of speed and change from the fragmentation and spatial dislocations of Cubism (see here and fig.
8.7) as well as the experiments of Jules Marey (18301904) and others with time-lapse or chronophotography, a technique that showed movement as a sequence of overlapping and abstracted linear patterns.
In the medium of painting, efforts resulted in the frenetic rhythms in works by artists such as Gino Severini (18831966) and Giacomo Balla (18711958), and were the inspiration for American artist Earl Horters (1880 1940) painting Rhapsody in Blue (1927), reproduced as an advertisement for Steinway pianos (see fig.
10.15).
Crossing the boundary from fine to applied art was a natural extension of Futurism.
Marinetti was a tireless activist in promoting the Futurist cause, using the popular press as a vehicle for communicating his ideas in print, and addressing the reader with an aggressive, imperative tone borrowed from the persuasive techniques found in contemporary print advertising.
Bright electric street lamps, the internal combustion engine, and the wonders of early air travel suggested a spirit of liberation that removed barriers to the possible, whether the conquest of darkness or of space.
Such developments in turn called forth new techniques of expression in art that dematerialized form and demanded freedom from convention and tradition, pitting the liberated future against a stagnant, moribund past, the latter impeding the progress of the former.
Marinetti hoped to move beyond the salon, the gallery, the museum, and the refuge of the bourgeois domestic interior, identifying with and appealing to an audience of industrial workers and youth in factories, on streets and athletic fields who exulted in the vitality of the city and reveled in its intoxicating state of flux.
He praised Italys large industrial manufacturers as paving the way to the future, including the Pirelli tire company, Olivetti typewriters, and the Agnelli family, one of the founders of the Fiat motor company.
One might say that the industrial proletariat were both the inspiration and the imagined market for the Futurists  a youthful public who might mobilize to tear down and supersede all that was traditional and static, both in art and in the status quo that maintained existing political and social institutions and resisted radical change.
Marinettis tone was revolutionary, utopian, and apocalyptic: building the future and tearing down the past went together.
While rooted in poetry and finding an outlet in the fine arts, his vision for Futurism extended to visual communication and other areas of design in the political sphere during World War I and in its turbulent aftermath in Italy.
Marinettis medium for spreading the gospel of Futurism to the masses was the written word, not as phonetic symbol but as expressive visual image.
In his poetry he built upon the lead of Symbolist poet Stéphane Mallarmé (18421898) in arranging type on the page to visually convey the meaning of words or sensation of sounds.
Different sizes of type within the same line, and different fonts within the same word, liberated the printed page from its usual directional order and traditional standard spacing.
An example is the poem At Night in Her Bed from a published collection entitled Les mots en liberté futuristes (Futurist Words in Liberty) dating to 1919 (fig.
9.1), describing a letter from an artillery soldier to his girlfriend, who lies supine at the bottom right of the page.
Sounds of gunfire disrupt the handwritten words into fragments, to which are haphazardly added abstract shapes and words such as explosion and simultaneity. The readers attention shifts from place to place without clear or prescribed organization aside from a tendency for the eye to wander downward.
While earlier examples of Marinettis Futurist poetry operate within the regularizing framework of parallel vertical and horizontal spacing of letterpress typography, At Night in Her Bed appears to have been composed somewhat like a collage, with portions of cut-out text pasted on the page along with other cut-out shapes and handwritten words.
The collage was then photographed and exposed as a negative on to a metal plate for offset printing.
This technology permitted far greater freedom for typographic experimentation, and was employed by graphic designers increasingly in the later 1920s (see page208 onward), often with a freer but still hierarchical order of information.
Just as Western painters in the early twentieth century were challenging the window as a paradigm for the art of painting, experimental poets were challenging the grid of the type form and printed page as a paradigm for the written word: in Marinettis printed poetry, words and letters are not just the equivalent of spoken words but operate visually as images and symbols; they are meant to be seen rather than read. Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, “At Night in Her Bed,” fold-out poem, 15 × 10 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (38.1 × 25.9 cm), from Les mots en liberté futuristes, Milan, 1919.
From 1912, Futurist painter Giacomo Balla took an active interest in fashion (mainly mens) and published treatises on the subject beginning in 1914.
Asymmetrical, geometric, conical, spiral, and elliptical patterns printed on or applied to clothing mirrored the fast-paced rhythms of urban life as seen in a vest with appliqué patterns designed by Balla and made in 1915, or a drawing of the so-called anti-neutral suit of 1914, designed by Balla for Futurist poet Francesco Cangiullo (18841977) to wear and to attract attention at demonstrations supporting Italys entry into World War I (fig.
9.2; at first aligned with the Central Powers but remaining neutral at the outbreak of war in August 1914, Italy joined the war on the side of Britain, France, and Russia in 1915, hoping to gain territory then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire).
According to Balla, modern clothing should avoid faded and murky colors and symmetry, strive to liberate emotion and action by being aggressive, agile, and dynamic, and should permit free movement.
Balla and other Futurists appreciated the fashion worlds seasonal changes that provided continuous opportunities for creativity for designers and excitement for consumers.
The Futurists attraction to consumer goods differed from views on fashion by other Modernists who argued for permanent, universal standards for designed products based upon function that might mold a more collective future society.
In other media, Futurist artists Tullio dAlbisola (born Mozotti, 18911971) and Giacomo Balla each designed earthenware vessels and plates decorated with speeding motorcyclists or colorful asymmetrical shapes in the 1920s, manufactured in clay-rich areas of Italy traditionally known for ceramic manufacturing.
Giacomo Balla, illustration of the “anti-neutral suit,” Futurist Manifesto, published in Volantino della Direzione del Monumenti Futuristi, 1914, Milan.
The Futurists formed their own political party in 1918 to promote the role of modern art and design in Italy, and Marinetti and other Futurists supported the government of Italian fascist military dictator Benito Mussolini (18831945) who seized power in late October, 1922, and ruled Italy for the next twenty years.
Nationalism, militarism, machismo, and faith in modern industrial technology as an instrument of change drew the two movements together, along with impatience toward slower, more democratic efforts to bring about economic, technological, and social progress in Italy.
Futurist artist Fortunato Depero (18921960) installed a room of his work (Salone Depero) at an exhibition in Monza in 1923 and again at the 1925 Paris International Exposition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts (though not in the Italian Pavilion), and promoted his services as a graphic designer through the publishing company Dinamo Azari in Milan in the 1920s.
He was unsuccessful in securing work from Pirelli, but designed advertising for the Italian distiller Campari, manufacturer of a refreshing rose-colored aperitif, along with the single-shot, carbonated version of Campari whose conical bottle echoes the shapes Depero used in his advertisements.
For Campari, Depero created a series of high-contrast, black-and-white newspaper advertisements without copy or product representation that made use of simplified angular shapes for letterforms, the cone-shaped drinking glass, and a mechanical, toylike addressing figure (fig.
9.3).
The product name in this example is composed of letters in descending size, resembling a megaphone and visually corresponding to the reverberating blare of a shouting vendor.
Deperos playfulness and visual puns were part of a strategy that was only marginally political, suggesting that the visual arts could contribute to instilling Futurist attitudes and behaviors in viewers and consumers.
He was the co-author, with Balla, of a treatise entitled Futurist Reconstruction of the Universe (1915) arguing that Futurist toys would foster imagination and spontaneity, and included the following advice for adults: The Futurist toy will be very useful to adults too, keeping them young, agile, jubilant, spontaneous, ready for anything, untiring, instinctive and intuitive. While perhaps not the direct call to political activism envisioned by Marinetti, the Futurists expressive manipulation of letterforms and the nervous energy generated by sharp contrasts and the rhythmic repetitions of geometric shapes found an outlet in advertising in the later 1920s, communicating the liberating spirit of a Futurist sensibility to a popular audience.
Indeed, while the free association of word and image in Marinettis explosive poetry may have signaled a new and more revolutionary modern sensibility, its application to commercial visual communication usually involved a stronger degree of simplification and order.
Design also played a prominent but not official role in propaganda for the fascist regime in Italy, primarily through exhibitions and the staging of public demonstrations of fascist power and solidarity.
Futurism appeared in but did not dominate propaganda under Mussolinis fascist regime.
Mussolini also invoked monumental classicism and the glory of the Roman empire in architectural projects to appeal to rural and conservative constituencies, along with the more dynamic and abstract visual language found in Ballas anti-neutral suit, Deperos graphic design, or the series of painted and photomontage murals by Giuseppe Terragni (19041943) for the exhibition celebrating the tenth anniversary of the fascist revolution (Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista) in Rome in 1932 (fig.
9.4).

## 9.4 Postcard Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista – Sala dei Fasci all’Estero (Exhibition of
the Fascist Revolution – Hall of the Fasci Abroad), c.
1932, Istituto Italiano d’Arti Grafiche, Bergamo, 3 <sup>1</sup>/ × 5 <sup>1</sup>/ in (9 × 14 cm).
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Miami Beach.

## France:
L’Esprit Nouveau and Purism While the Société des Artistes Décorateurs (S.A.D.), the couture fashion industry, and other luxury boutiques and pavilions dominated Frances contributions to the 1925 International Exposition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts in Paris (see here), a more practically oriented, functional approach to design and modern living also emerged, whether in Elsa Schiaparellis casual summer and sporting outfits (see fig.
8.22) or Pierre Chareaus and Francis Jourdains spartan (if still exclusive) Physical Culture Room for S.A.D.s model French Embassy (see fig.
8.23).
Le Corbusier, Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau, Paris, 1925.
Equally austere but more ambitious than these examples was a model unit for lowcost housing titled the Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau, designed by Swiss-born architect Le Corbusier (18871965).
This structure was the most radical French expression of new attitudes toward design and the application of construction technology to modern living to emerge after World War I, combining a commitment to the use of standardized, prefabricated modern building materials and construction with a rejection of almost all decoration as a vestige of outmoded craft methods of production (fig.
9.5).
Housing shortages after World War I, sympathy for returning war veterans (and the millions whose lives were sacrificed along with civilian casualties), and concerns over social justice all provided an impetus for designers to imagine and pursue a broader, inclusive vision for design in shaping the nations future with renewed urgency.
The furnishings of the Pavillon included bentwood chairs and modular built-in storage units as well as tables supported by thin, straight, dowel-like legs that merged living, dining, and study areas into a single continuous space.
Modularity was a key concept for Le Corbusier, permitting flexible units of space that could be repeated to construct living spaces on an industrial scale for affordable public housing; the concept also played a role in the architects Unité dHabitation project in Marseilles after World War II (see here and fig.
11.34).
While visionary in terms of its proposed mass scale, much of the apartments furniture was available commercially through office-supply catalogs (rather than for homeowners; but for the exhibition, the pieces were custom-built to better conform to the units compact proportions and the size of the doors), and the Thonet bentwood chairs were more commonly found in cafés, theatres, and restaurants than in domestic living- or dining-room spaces.
Le Corbusier preferred the term equipment rather than furniture, with chairs defined as machines for sitting. After 1925, Le Corbusier teamed with interior designer Charlotte Perriand (19031999) to design original furniture using tubular steel; examples include the swivel or rotating chair, based upon square and circular shapes and emphasizing lightness and transparency (fig.
9.6).
Charlotte Perriand, Le Corbusier, and Pierre Jeanneret, Swivel chair, chrome-plated tubular steel and leather, manufactured by Thonet Frères, Paris, France, 29 ¾ × 22 × 21 ¼ in (75.4 × 55.9 × 54 cm), 1928.
Museum of Modern Art New York.
Le Corbusier thought of furniture and furnishings as type-objects, that is, basic, anonymous forms that developed naturally from a process of gradual refinement based upon utility and economy  the beauty of such objects was not the result of added or integrated decoration but rather from an appreciation of their purity and permanence.
His affinity for the typical shares much with the notion of Typisierung embraced by members of the German Werkbund (see here) whose exhibitions Le Corbusier praised.
The architect used the term mechanical selection to describe his approach, asserting design as an inevitable process leading to final forms, conducive to mass production for a variety of man-made products.
Described as a machine for living in, and compared to similar descriptions of automobiles as machines for transportation and airplanes as machines for flying, Le Corbusiers Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau was an appropriate model for modern living, based upon the simple fulfillment of universal functional requirements rather than luxury and individual expression in the traditional home or apartment.
Satisfying those requirements depended more upon the skills and working methods of the engineer and the practical sensibility of the modern architect than upon the methods of fine artists  a rebuke to the values of the Société des Artistes Décorateurs.
As with earlier design reform initiatives, architecture provided a framework for Le Corbusiers functional standards: structural steel and expanses of glass had rendered load-bearing walls unnecessary, and reinforced concrete was a more efficient and industrial building material than traditional stone or brick.
As an example of product design as the inevitable outcome of technical progress, he offered the industrially manufactured wine bottle, a type object that fulfilled its function without need of decorative embellishment, operating efficiently and independently from fashion or fine art.
Le Corbusier linked his approach to design with the modern accomplishments of engineers in the construction of ocean liners, airplanes, roadsters, and other products of modern technology, recommending prefabricated mechanized mass production as the solution to meet urgent housing needs in the aftermath of World War I.
His polemical tone emerged in his 1923 book Vers une architecture (Towards a New Architecture), which concludes with the rhetorical question Architecture or Revolution? His hope, it appears, was that government investment and support from industrial manufacturers would combine to fund and implement his proposal for lowcost housing on a mass scale in order to stave off social unrest and political instability in France.
Some manufacturers and large building-supply companies helped to underwrite the cost of Le Corbusiers pavilion and recognized economic advantages to standardization, but the architects vision for modern design conflicted with the traditional practice of most manufacturers, retailers, and consumers in a competitive commercial market.
For Le Corbusier, designers should search for underlying, elementary forms based upon the type-object principle, not subject to the whims of fashion, the traditional role of decoration, or the elitism of artist-designers.
Along these lines, he and Jourdain had reprinted Adolf Looss 1908 Ornament and Crime essay in a 1920 issue of their L’esprit nouveau journal (see here).
The Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau and the pavilion of the Soviet Union at the 1925 Paris International Exhibition provide a sense of competing design visions for shaping the experience of modern living that would intersect throughout the interwar period.
The definition of progress varied, as did the relationship between design and technology.
Technology might serve as the vehicle for the mechanized mass production of standardized goods to satisfy the perceived living requirements of the many, or equally as a tool for aesthetic experiment and invention, or metaphorically for the liberation of the individual from traditional values and lifestyles.
Each interpretation might be considered modern, and all were part, at times, of a polarized design discourse during the interwar period.
The projects and ideas generated by Le Corbusier gained adherents during the midand later 1920s.
Le Corbusier and Amédée Ozenfant (18861966) coined the term Purism to refer to the simplified abstract paintings they produced, beginning c.
1918, and Le Corbusier published essays about art, architecture, and design in the journal L’esprit nouveau, co-edited with Ozenfant and poet Paul Dermée (18861951).
In their writings, the authors explored pairs of polar concepts such as intuition and logic, the eye and the mind, the individual and the universal to argue for the existence of permanent standards for beauty in all forms of art, defined as harmony, proportion, and clarity, and independent of fashion.
They claimed that manufactured goods, including architectural construction, were governed by principles of logic and economy, determined as it were by the law of mechanical selection analogous to the process of natural selection proposed in Darwins theory of evolution, and resulting in an elemental aesthetic purity and functional efficiency, along with equal attention given to space as well as mass, solid as well as void: From all this [previous discussion and observations] comes a fundamental conclusion: that respect for the laws of physics and of economy has in every age created highly selected objects; that these artificial objects obey the same laws as the products of natural selection and that, consequently, there thus reigns a total harmony, bringing together the only two things that interest the human being: himself and what he makes.
Despite polemical rhetoric and the presentation of selective evidence, the principle of mechanical selection was largely symbolic: aside from ship cabins, railway compartments, and the standardized office furniture ordered (and modified) by Le Corbusier to furnish the Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau, neither Le Corbusiers logic nor claims of universality had much appeal beyond private, custom commissions for wealthy clients who shared the aesthetic rather than radical social and political aspirations of LEsprit Nouveau.

## The
U.
A.
M.
In the years following the Paris exhibition a group of designers including Le Corbusier, Jourdain, Chareau, and even Puiforcat (whose use of precious materials precluded his designs from reaching all but the very wealthy) questioned S.A.Ds focus upon luxury and the organizations perceived failure to consider the broader social benefits of industrial materials and standardized mass production, in short entering the debate over the relationship between art and industry.
Polarized attitudes and claims were more theoretical than actual in many ways, since the aims of department stores and other retail distributors of Art Moderne were certainly to promote goods beyond an exclusive market, and the work of designers such as Puiforcat and Chareau was often produced on commission for wealthy clients.
Nevertheless, in 1929 a group of dissenters split with S.A.D. and formed their own design organization known as the Union des Artistes Modernes (U.A.M.), displaying their efforts at several exhibitions during the 1930s.
The work of U.A.M members centered around factory assembly, industrial materials, the use of interchangeable parts, and eliminating overt signs of specialized skilled craftsmanship associated with decoration.
The group does not seem to have articulated a particular social or political agenda, nor collaborated with manufacturers or governments on projects for low-cost social housing.
The tall dressing cabinet, dating between 1926 and 1929, and designed by Irish-born designer and U.A.M. member Eileen Gray (1878 1976) for her villa at Roquebrune on the Mediterranean coast, illustrates one example.
Constructed of aluminum, cork, glass, and cellulose (fig.
9.7), the cabinet also functioned, in place of walls, to divide the homes master bedroom from the bathroom for privacy, and to complement other fitted shelving and tables that created more open interior space.
Stationary rather than portable, Grays cabinet resembles the compact steamer trunks admired by Le Corbusier for their efficient use of space.
In addition, Gray eliminated attached pullers in favor of carved-out circular apertures to open the cork drawers.
Eileen Gray, cabinet, cork, plywood, cellulose, aluminum, glass, blue paint, 63 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> × 23 ½ × 65 in (161 × 60 × 165 cm),1926–1929.
Les Art Décoratifs, Paris. dating between 1927 and 1928, is constructed of tubular steel connected at the seat and the back by rubber strips with hooked ends resembling todays bungee cords, resulting in a lighter weight and an open, almost transparent appearance (fig.
9.8).
In eschewing traditional decoration and upholstery, and embracing industrial materials, such furniture evoked parallels with building principles in which steel construction eliminated the need for load-bearing walls, defining architecture, in Le Corbusiers words, as the interplay of solid and void.
Herbst named his chair Chaise Sandows for the German-born and internationally known body-builder Eugen Sandow (1867 1925), who promoted physical fitness and marketed a line of elastic exercise equipment to build strength and physical conditioning.
Yet while the experimental use of industrial materials in furniture was bold and inventive, featured in exhibitions at the time, and was also endorsed by the French steel industry as being in the national economic interest, Herbsts designs for assembled furniture were expensive to produce and proved marginal in the retail trade, failing to achieve large-scale production or to connect with consumers.
English writer George Orwell had little sympathy for tubular-metal seating (or for collectivization and totalitarian regimes), referring condescendingly to them as gaspipe chairs in his 1937 book of social criticism titled The Road to Wigan Pier.
René Herbst, chair (Chaise Sandows), tubular teel and rubber straps, 32 × 18 ¼ × 17 ¼ in (81.5 × 46.5 × 44.5 cm), 1927– 1928.
Vitra Design Museum, Germany.
Jean Prouvé (19011984) was also a member of U.A.M.
Trained as a blacksmith, he owned and operated a factory for metalwork production beginning in 1927, and directed his business toward institutional commissions for schools, hospitals, and offices.
Prouvés direct knowledge of the structural properties of metal led him to experiment with sheet rather than tubular metal, which he thought was structurally weaker and required reinforcement for stability and durability.
Prouvés standard chair of 1934 to 1935 (fig.
9.9) combined tubular with solid-sheet metal and molded plywood and was featured in his companys 1936 catalog.
Prouvés furniture was heavier and less aesthetically pure or reductive than Herbsts Chaise Sandows, but he shared Herbsts belief that the future of modern design lay in industrial materials and assembly rather than traditional craft, motivated strongly by a belief in the democratic promise of industrial technology on an institutional scale.
During World War II, Prouvé designed and manufactured prefabricated army barracks, and after the war he successfully manufactured sturdy furniture for schools, libraries, and other public buildings.
Prouvés furniture sacrificed aesthetic purity to durability and demonstrates the wide range of U.A.M. members approaches to design.
Jean Prouvé, standard chair, steel and plywood, 16 ¼ × 19 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 32 in (42 × 48.8 × 81.3 cm), 1934–1935 (chair no.
4).
Vitra Design Museum, Germany.
The gap between the U.A.M. and the outlook of manufacturers and clients in the 1920s is seen in seating used in sidewalk cafés or other outdoor settings.
Such massproduced seating was certainly utilitarian but generally lacked the theoretical baggage, elementary geometric aesthetic preferences, or refinement of U.A.M designers.
More an equivalent in furniture to the Model T Ford, the anonymously designed French terrace chair (fig.
9.10), is constructed of a roughly welded, two-piece, varnished-steel frame, where the uneven surfaces created by the welds are not disguised in any way.
The seat is made of thin embossed plywood (imitating leather tooling) riveted to the frame, and the splayed, grooved chair legs permit convenient stacking.
The inexpensive chair was manufactured in Lyon from around 1926.
Unlikely to be listed among Le Corbusiers objets types to exemplify his theory of mechanical selection, or found in many museums today (readers can find one in the collection of the Wolfsonian Museum in Miami Beach, Florida), it nonetheless belongs to a more inclusive history of modern industrial design.

## 9.10 Anonymous, French terrace chair, varnished steel and wood veneer, 32 ½ × 18 × 18 ½ in
(83 × 45.7 × 47.5 cm), 1926.
Vitra Design Museum, Germany.

## De
Stijl De Stijl (The Style) was the title of a journal published in the Netherlands, founded in 1917 by painter-designer Theo van Doesburg (18831931).
Contributors included Dutch painters Piet Mondrian (18721944) and Vilmos Huszar (18841960), Belgian sculptor George Vantongerloo (18861965), Dutch furniture-maker and later architect Gerrit Rietveld (18881964), and architects Robert van t Hoff (1887 1979), J.
J.
P.
Oud (18901963), and Jan Wils (18911972).
Although De Stijl designs were not exhibited in the Dutch pavilion at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, designs by Van Doesburg, Rietveld, and other artists associated with De Stijl were shown in 1923 at the Galerie de lEffort Moderne owned by art collector and dealer Léonce Rosenberg (18791947), where they were seen by Le Corbusier.
Furthermore, Mondrian lived and worked in Paris both before and after World War I, and Van Doesburg spent time in Weimar, interacting there with faculty and students at the Bauhaus in the early 1920s (see here onward).
The term movement can only be used loosely in connection with De Stijl: no group exhibitions of De Stijl were ever held, and maintaining shared ideals and a spirit of collaboration among its participants proved challenging, especially in light of Van Doesburgs strong personality.
Indeed, for one reason or another many contributors to early issues of De Stijl severed their relationship with the journal over differences with Van Doesburg during the course of its eleven-year history.
Then again it could be argued that neither the U.A.M. or the Bauhaus maintained consistent, unified approaches to design.
The manifesto published in an early issue of De Stijl cites individualism and nationalism as the causes of the conflicts that led Europe to World War I, and proposed a new balance between the individual and a new, universal world view, with modern art in the vanguard: There is an old and a new consciousness of time.
The old is connected with the individual.
The new is connected with the universal.
The struggle of the individual against the universal is revealing itself in the world war as well as in the art of the present day.
The war is destroying the old world with its contents: individual domination in every state.
The new art has brought forward what the new consciousness of time contains: a balance between the universal and the individual.
Despite the radical rhetoric of the De Stijl manifesto, the work of the journals contributors recalls the work of Dutch architect Henrik Berlage (see here), who had used the phrase unity in diversity to advocate a balance between unique and standardized elements in modern architecture and design.
Another Dutch architect, J.
L.
Mathieu Lauweriks (18641932), promoted designs based upon carefully constructed geometric compositions governed by mathematical relationships of parallel and perpendicular planes.
As noted by Philip Meggs, Lauwerikss influence as a member of the faculty at the Düsseldorf School of Arts and Crafts may be seen in the consistent and standardized layouts for promotional material developed in Germany by Peter Behrens for the AEG (see fig.
7.4).
Berlage, in turn, praised the designs of Frank Lloyd Wright (see here).
The American architects use of flat roofs, wide overhanging eaves, open living spaces, and the interpenetration of interior and exterior space were circulated through print publication and were admired in the Netherlands and by De Stijl contributors.
Dutch designers incorporated elements of this approach in many of their own architectural projects.
They extended the principle analogously to the equality between figure and ground in painting and between solid and void in sculpture and architecture; that is, in each of these media they noted the active role of negative space as an aesthetic principle, with built-in furniture replacing standing cabinets, furniture that reduced mass, and sliding partitions that created more flexible living spaces in open interiors.
Blurring the boundaries between fine and applied arts by suggesting their unity through underlying formal principles was a fundamental tenet of De Stijl, demonstrating the ultimate integration of painting, sculpture, typography, furniture, interior ensembles, and architecture.
For Van Doesburg, furniture was sculpture for the interior, and architecture a sort of walk-in painting, which placed the viewer within painting instead of in front of it and thereby enable[d] him to participate in it, that is, to integrate aesthetic experience into the acts of everyday living.
Mondrian expressed such ideas in utopian language, writing that architecture and the applied arts would more fully realize what painting had achieved in its own but more limited way, that is, the attainment and enjoyment of harmony and balance, based upon the rejection of representation and naturalism, and achieving an equilibrium among elementary rectangular shapes of primary color created by the intersection of black strips of uniform width.
Mondrians numerous essays on this topic employ dualities similar to the writings of Ozenfant and Le Corbusier on Purism (see here), though without explicit reference to engineering or mechanical selection.
Paired terms such as individual/universal, conscious/unconscious, subjective/objective, and mutable/immutable argue for equilibration between opposites, realized through the interplay of positive and negative space and the asymmetrical balance of rectilinear elements in walls, floors, furniture, and windows.
Mondrian referred to his new conception of art as Neoplasticism or the New Plastic, and anticipated, through metaphor, its application to the built environment in essays published in De Stijl and elsewhere: The new spirit must be manifested in all the arts without exception ...
As soon as one art becomes plastic expression of the abstract, the others can no longer remain plastic expressions of the natural.
The two do not go together: from this comes their mutual hostility down to the present.
The New Plastic abolishes this antagonism: it creates the unity of all the arts...
Our age has reached the climax of individualism: the mature individual can now increasingly find equilibrium with the universal.
When our mentality actually attains this equilibrium, it will also be clearly expressed in every aspect of outward life, just as it is expressed abstractly in the new plastic.
Mondrian also insisted that there should be no distinction between art and life, that the work of art should not be separate from living, an idea articulated in an essay of 1923.
Before proceeding to develop the theme that both the machine and the urban environment are demonstrations of progress from the natural to the abstract, he writes: Indeed, the evolution of art consists in its achievement of a pure expression of harmony: art appears only outwardly, as an expression that (in time) reduces individual feeling.
Thus art is both the expression and (involuntarily) the means of material evolution: the achievement of equilibrium between nature and non-nature  between what is in us and what is around us.
Art will remain both expression and means of expression until (relative) equilibrium is reached.
Then its task will be fulfilled and harmony will be realized in our outward surroundings and in our outward life.
The De Stijl principle of balance between universal and individual and the identification of the universal with an elemental geometric vocabulary of forms found expression in a variety of media.
Gerrit Rietvelds armchair of 1918 (fig.
9.11), painted in primary colors in 1923, was assembled from varied lengths of standard milled stock to which a rectangular plywood back and seat were attached.
In Rietvelds chair, joints extend beyond the point where right angles meet, accentuating the incorporation of negative space and a relationship to non-objective sculpture.
The aesthetic dimension of Rietvelds chair is inherent in its design and construction rather than resulting from additive or even integrated decoration: aside from the color scheme, there is no further reduction possible  to do so it would cease to be a chair!
9.11 Gerrit Rietveld, red/blue armchair, 33 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 26 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 26 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (86 × 68 × 68 cm), 1918 (painted 1923).
Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.
In 1920, Mondrian and Van Doesburg worked together to revise the cover for De Stijl that further provides a concrete illustration of Neo-Plastic ideas.
In this simple cover, using a sans serif typeface (fig.
9.12), typographic elements are arranged as horizontal rectangular fields in a balanced, asymmetrical composition.
The size of the sans serif letters and orientation of words determine a hierarchy of information, and even the overlapping of the letters spelling De Stijl with the bold letters N B (Nieuwe Beelding/New Plastic) suggests the visual equivalency of the two elements; moreover the vertical rather than usual horizontal orientation of words at the far right reinforces their relationship to the large NB/DE STIJL shape in the upper right, and color also reinforces the hierarchy of information.
Printers rules, part of the typesetters toolbox and used for spacing, are here raised and printed, playing a part in creating information hierarchy; they also result in active diagonal eye movement rather than the conventional left-right and top-down reading of the traditional printed page.
This approach is a mainstay of Jan Tschicholds New Typography in Germany in the 1920s (see here onward) as well as in Swiss graphic design after World War II (see here onward).
9.12 Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg, cover for De Stijl, volume 4, 8 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 10 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (20.5 × 26 cm), January 1921.
Courtesy of the University of Iowa.
Other graphic design initiatives in the Netherlands paralleled the work that appeared in De Stijl.
Peter Alma (18861969) was an Indonesian-born Dutch graphic designer who trained with Viennese sociologist Otto Neurath (see here) at his Museum of Society and Economy before traveling to the Soviet Union and returning to the Netherlands in the early 1930s.
Alma was not connected with De Stijl, but abstract reduction formed an essential part of his graphic design practice, directed toward communicating statistical information visually with pictograms.
Reduction was accompanied by variations to reveal distinctions among groups, maintaining clarity while acknowledging complexity and the dangers of overgeneralization.
An example of his work can be seen in figure 9.13, illustrating increases in population in comparison with the expansion of rural, urban, and coastal areas of the Netherlands.
Sympathetic to communist ideology in championing the rights of the proletariat, Alma used abstraction to demonstrate growth in industrial production and advocate for its broad social benefits. ÉÉN GROEP MENSCHEN = 100.000 INWONERS ÉÉN RECHTHOEK = 500 ha Peter Alma, chart illustrating increases in Dutch population between 1898 and 1938.
Perhaps the best-known De Stijl project is the Schröder House in Utrecht, built in 1924 to 1925 for a widow (Mrs.
Truus Schröder-Schräder) and her three children, and designed by Gerritt Rietveld (figs.
9.14 and 9.15).
Schröder-Schräder contributed many suggestions that Rietveld incorporated into the design, including the use of folding and sliding partitions that moved on tracks cut into the floor.
Rietvelds open design was meant to encourage shared family time after Schröder-Schräders husband died and to limit the isolation of family members as they dealt with loss.
With its geometric areas of floors, furniture, and window moldings painted in bright blue, red, and yellow, projecting balconies with tubular-steel railings, a flat roof, expanses of square and rectangular glass and corner windows to suggest continuity between the built and natural environment, rectangular slab construction (actually brick-faced with cement rather than standardized prefabricated units of reinforced concrete), the Schröder House fulfilled many of the principles embraced in De Stijl, in particular the attempt to create a living work of non-objective art.
According to art historian Paul Overy, Schröder-Schräder was concerned that the furniture be simply constructed (like the Red-Blue chair, assembled rather than requiring specialized craft skills) and that the décor specifically avoid associations with luxury.
And while the proposed use of reinforced concrete suggested economical industrial building materials and modular prefabrication, the house was in a sense customized to meet specific individual family needs, and, through color and its vocabulary of rectilinear elements, promote aesthetic experience rather than serve as a model for low-cost public housing.
Beginning in 1931 Rietveld built a series of privately funded housing units only a short distance from the Schröder House.
Known as Erasmuslaan, these connected units did not employ color, used steel, concrete, and glass, and were designed with a large open interior living space sparsely furnished with lightweight tubular-steel chairs and tables designed by Rietveld along with fitted shelving (fig.
9.16), and are still occupied today.
9.14 Gerrit Rietveld, Schröder House, Utrecht, 1924–1925.
Gerrit Rietveld, first-floor interior of Schröder House, Utrecht, 1924–1925, restored 1985–1987, photographed 1987.
Gerrit Rietveld, interior, Housing Block Erasmuslaan 9, Utrecht, The Netherlands, 1931.
Despite shared principles, individualistic preferences and differences among De Stijl contributors persisted.
Some De Stijl designers and movements stressed more standardized functional priorities (seen in the work of J.
J.
P.
Oud, here) in the design of low-cost housing on a large scale based upon the reduction of mass and a preference for efficient production of typical furnishings, but these considerations did not emerge as overriding laws or principles in De Stijl projects of the early 1920s.
As Rietveld noted in commenting upon his furniture: Function was for me a thing by itself which I never overlooked, it is true, but it did not come into play until the construction and spatial exercises in De Stijl had been completed.

## Modernism
and Communism: Constructivism Between March and June 1925, Russian artist and designer Aleksandr Rodchenko (18911956) was in Paris installing a furnished Soviet Workers Club and assisting with other Russian exhibits for the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes (fig.
9.17).
These included the Soviet Pavilion designed by architect Konstantin Melnikov (18901974), which projected a distinct modern identity for the new Russian communist state in contrast to the majority of displays on view (see here onward).
The Workers Club was a rectangular reading room containing two long, plain wooden tables with hinged leaves that tilted to hold newspapers and journals, and a series of chairs with curved, open backs assembled from eight standardized components painted in gray and white to match other furnishings in the room and lacking carved, painted, or inlaid decoration.
Rodchenko also designed and built a pair of armchairs, each with a shelf to the side that could be attached to form a chess table when the chairs were placed facing one another.
