The room included a moveable platform with an elevated speakers rostrum, folding table for displaying pamphlets and books, and a folding screen for mounting posters or projecting films.
The Workers Club was a shared communal rather than private space, whose design aimed to define the leisure time of industrial workers, eschewing the overt signs of personal comfort, luxury, and skilled craftsmanship.
Working-class leisure consisted of reading materials, posters, film, and a speakers rostrum that promoted communist working-class values following the Russian Revolution.
The austerity of the Workers Club was relieved by a lively and bright color scheme of white, red, and gray that helped to create an inviting modern interior space.
Aleksandr Rodchenko, Soviet Workers Club, 1925, reconstructed at Tate Modern, London, as part of the Defining Constructivism exhibition, 2009.
The Workers Club was a mature product of Constructivism, one of several evolving movements initiated by artists who wished to participate directly in the reshaping a new Soviet society following the revolutions of February and October 1917, and the Bolshevik victory in the civil wars that ended in 1920.
In 1918 the new communist Russian government established a ministry of culture known as the Peoples Commissariat of Enlightenment (Narkompros) under the direction of Anatoly Lunacharsky (18751933), a Communist Party official as well as playwright who was tolerant of experimental artistic ideas in the belief that they could contribute to the molding of public opinion for the new Bolshevik government.
Narkompros and its various institutes and schools replaced Russias more academic, exclusive, and conservative pre-revolutionary predecessors, permitting the participation of progressive artists (including women and Jews) to put into practice utopian projects that linked nonobjective abstract art with working-class revolution and the promise of a new enlightened society that would replace the vast autocratic Tsarist Empire.
Many revolutionary artists shared the goal of liberating the masses from the tyranny of the past, and for a time they affirmed together the hope that art and design would radically reshape the values and conditions of modern life.
Founded upon Marxist ideology, revolution was viewed as the inevitable outcome of the working-class struggle against capitalist greed, inequality, and oppression.
Achieving social justice might require sacrifice, and all efforts were directed toward imagining a future society in which shared collective goals replaced individual aspirations for personal wealth and luxury.
Despite years of civil war and a devastating famine that claimed millions of lives between 1917 and 1921, by 1924 the new Soviet Union had reoccupied territories lost during World War I, was recognized as a sovereign state internationally, supported nascent communist parties abroad as part of an international communist workers movement, and embraced the use of propaganda to promote its goals, create an identity, and inspire support among the working classes in other nations through publications and participation in international exhibitions.
As with the other Modernist movements included in this chapter, abstraction played a significant symbolic role in the early formation of Constructivism, as the rejection of representation signified a radical break with the past, a clean slate upon which to construct a new, utopian future.
Abstractions most articulate spokesman in Russia both before and after the revolution was Kasimir Malevich (18781935), who used the term Suprematism to refer to his non-objective style of painting.
Malevich defined Suprematism as the expression of feeling in art, and noted the formal similarity between the simple geometric squares and rectangles of his canvases and the forms of modern technology and industry in their transcendence of organic naturalism.
Malevichs paintings manipulated abstract geometric elements to suggest states of mind, seen in titles for his works such as Suprematist Composition Expressing the Feeling of Movement and Restraint or Suprematist Composition Expressing Magnetic Attraction.
He encouraged the integration of art into life, and through his association with the art organization renamed UNOVIS (Affirmers of the New Art) in 1920 and a Peoples Art School (1919) located in Vitebsk helped to coordinate efforts to use Suprematist compositions for signs and banners on tram cars and for the embellishment of temporary architectural constructions such as theater stages and speaker platforms, often referred to as agitprop. An example is Nikolai Suetins (18971954) design for a tram car in Vitebsk, consisting of the slogan Long Live the Revolution accompanied by a bold red circle (based upon Suetins sketches) and a darker wedge shape to attract attention (fig.
9.18).
The expanded agenda for art within UNOVIS most likely prompted members such as Vasily Kandinsky (18661944), who had pioneered an expressive abstract nonobjective style in Germany before World War I and returned to Russia after the revolution, to adopt a more precise geometric vocabulary in his paintings, and to approach abstraction analytically as well as intuitively, experimenting with the psychological effects of shapes and colors.
According to art historian Christina Lodder, Kandinsky even conducted a survey of his colleagues to study their psychological responses to colors and other formal elements of design.
Nikolai Suetin, design for a tram car, photograph, Vitebsk, 1918.
Malevich used the term collective creative art to promote Suprematism as an agent of change, and encouraged UNOVIS artists to exhibit works anonymously.
The idea that a poster, banner, costume, or set design could function as both propaganda and as nonobjective abstract art suggests Suprematisms underlying aesthetic basis: the experience of non-objectivity might be found on the street as well as in the gallery or the home.
In a similar vein Vladimir Tatlin (18851953) used ordinary industrial and mass-produced materials to create abstract collages, where works of art become objects and are grouped together with tools and other commodities as equal elements of the everyday proletariat environment.
Strongly influenced by examples of Cubist collage that he had seen in Paris as early as 1913, Tatlins work after the Russian Revolution combined ordinary materials such as wood, metal, and stucco in abstract relief compositions.
Although hardly functional, such experiments, sometimes referred to by their creators as laboratory work, were intended to provide a basis for future utilitarian products that reinforced an abstract aesthetic sensibility.
The collage technique emphasized the imagination of the constructor rather than sophisticated artistic skills and suggested that the making of art could not only be appreciated widely but also made by everyone, that is, a liberating, democratic art.
In the decorative arts, the former Russian State Porcelain Manufactory came under the control of the new Soviet government after the revolution, and a new group of revolutionary artists joined the designers and artisans at the manufactory.
In addition to continuing to produce more traditional work, the manufactory introduced Suprematist designs by Malevich, Kandinsky, and Suetin as propaganda.
Sergei Chekhonins plate from 1918 (fig.
9.19) offers a compromise, with the Soviet Unions hammer and sickle symbolizing agriculture and industry, along with a semicircular cog amid a floral background, suggesting an integration of Russias traditional agrarian economy and vast peasant population and the increasing role of industry and its urban workforce who constituted the future focus of optimistic post-revolutionary economic planning.
The survival of Suprematist porcelain in museum collections today is due in part to its export and display at exhibitions abroad.

## 9.19 Sergei Chekhonin, plate, blue emblem with flowers, diameter: 9 <sup>2</sup>/<sub>3</s
ub> in (24.5 cm), 1918.
Private collection, London.
Malevichs efforts were closely associated with an organization known as INKHUK (the Institute of Artistic Culture) in Moscow beginning in 1920, and with an exhibition that took place there in 1921 known as the Third Obmokhu, named for the Society of Young Artists.
From these organizations a Working Group of Constructivist Artists was formed.
Constructivists viewed their efforts as being more in line with Marxist ideology that embraced a materialist view of culture (as opposed to a spiritual or aesthetic view) as most appropriate and urgent to address the collective needs of a new working-class society.
The emphasis upon production among the artists at INKHUK created a tension with those who felt that imposing practical restrictions in design represented too narrow an approach compared with earlier interpretations of Constructivism that focused upon the integration of art and life.
As a result of this growing conflict concerning the role of artists in the new communist state, some artists left Russia for the West, including Kandinsky (who joined the faculty of the Bauhaus, see here onward) and sculptor Naum Gabo (18901977), who also moved to Germany in 1922.
INKHUK members became actively involved in the Higher State Technical Workshops, established by the Communist Party in 1920 to further integrate fine artists with production.
By this time Rodchenko had come to question the compatibility of painting and sculpture with the evolving practical direction of Constructivism.
He promoted the training of artist-constructors, a new kind of versatile and non-specialist creator who might integrate a new vocabulary of simple geometric shapes with prototypes for the efficient manufacture of clothing, furniture, lighting, architecture, and other basic goods and furnishings for the working class.
Rodchenkos wife Varvara Stepanova (18941958) designed lightweight two-piece athletic outfits, advocating sport as a healthy, active communal leisure activity for working-class men and women (fig.
9.20).
The loose-fitting garments allow for freedom of movement with colorful geometric designs in both the top and the shorts angling inward at the waist.
It is to this phase of Constructivism that Rodchenkos Soviet Workers Club at the 1925 Paris exposition belongs (fig.
9.17), designing and furnishing spaces to house appropriate leisure activity for the new men and women of the collective, egalitarian future.
The designers role was envisioned as more akin to the methods of a draftsman than those of the fine artist.
The furnishings were designed to employ modern industrially manufactured materials and a minimum number of standardized parts.
Evgenia Sokolova (Zhemchuzhnaya) wearing an athletic outfit designed by Varvara Stepanova, photograph, 1923.
Photograph by Alexander Mikhailovich Rodchenko.
Despite being designed with mechanized mass production in mind, the furnishings for the Workers Club were one-of-a-kind products, and few if any prototypes were produced by industrial manufacturers, whose activities were hampered by a depressed economy and the lack of necessary investment and support to produce the new designs.
It is unlikely that workers were consulted in Rodchenkos design process that focused upon an imagined, utopian future.
To judge from the indifferent reaction to Rodchenkos project within Vkutemas and later attempts to replace traditional representational textile designs with decorative patterns based upon themes of industrialization and collectivization (fig.
9.25), the public (and eventually the Communist Partys) reception of Constructivist design was equivocal.
In addition a number of younger artists and former Constructivists during the early 1920s had turned (or re-turned) to realism.
These artists embraced easel painting and an idealized naturalistic style as appropriate to an art of mass persuasion to build support for official policy along more traditional lines, employing techniques consistent with narrative illustration and advertising; in short, propaganda.
By the mid-1920s, tolerance for the utopian pretensions of abstract art and Constructivism during the early years of Narkompros had diminished.
Increasingly Soviet artists were encouraged to comply with a state policy demanding an idealized naturalism (or socialist realism) depicting working class, athletic, or military activities designed to provide hopeful images of heroic individual and collective achievement to gain the support of the Russian masses.
In this less tolerant environment, artists such as Rodchenko and El Lissitzky (the latter working primarily in Germany) continued to produce graphic designs using photography that still permitted a measure of experimentation while satisfying state oversight and the conformity it required.
El Lissitzky (born Lazar Markovich Lissitzky; 18901941) studied architecture in Germany and later worked with Malevich (as well as Marc Chagall) at the Peoples Art School in Vitebsk, marshaling abstraction as an effective means to communicate confidence in Soviet strength and industrial progress, primarily through publishing and exhibition design.
He directed a short-lived program in architecture at UNOVIS, and later created his imaginative series of PROUNS (acronym signifying for the new art), a group of paintings and lithographs composed of abstract geometric shapes with an ambiguous suggestion of perspective and three-dimensional projection to suggest future applications to the built environment.
El Lissitzky referred to PROUNS as stations of interchange between architecture and painting, affirming the utilitarian possibilities of geometric abstraction.
His identification of artists with engineers and workers was almost a commonplace among Constructivists both in Russia and elsewhere in Europe.
Some of El Lissitzkys best-known contributions to Constructivism were in graphic design, showcasing the ability of print to communicate ideas visually and dynamically connect text with symbols and photographic images.
His work includes a book of poetry by the revolutionary poet Vladimir Mayakovsky (18931930) entitled Dyla Golossa (For the Voice or To Be Read Out Loud), designed for public performance and audience participation.
El Lissitzky, cover for Vesch/Objet/Gegenstand, 12 ${ ^ 5 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 9 { ^ 5 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (31.3 × 23.5 cm), Berlin, 1922.
In 1922 El Lissitzky began to publish an international journal of the new art entitled Vesch/Objet/Gegenstand.
Translated simply as Object in English, the journal featured articles and photographs of works of fine art, decorative art, and industrial products, including projects by De Stijl artists as well as by Le Corbusier (work by El Lissitzky was featured in a 1922 issue of De Stijl as well).
The use of half-tone photographic reproductions rather than etchings or engraving conveys Lissitzkys interest in promoting photomechanical process rather than craft-based techniques as a form of mass communication.
The cover of one of the journals issues from 1922 (fig.
9.21) reinforces abstract relationships between bold sans serif typography, asymmetrical compositions of related geometric shapes, and industrial forms, in this case a locomotive with a cowcatcher diagonally connecting to the Russian word Vesch. The vertically and diagonally oriented letters, horizontal and vertical printers rules used as separation, and use of different letter sizes recall the typographical experimentation of the Futurist poet Marinetti (see fig.
9.1).
But whereas Marinetti used such elements to make the page into a kind of poetic image to communicate a frenzied sensibility characteristic of the dislocations and simultaneity of modern life, Lissitzky and other Russian Constructivists tempered such explosive dynamism with discipline in order to communicate clearly, quickly, and dramatically.
This required attention to page layout, in which text, symbol, and image worked together to actively engage and direct the viewers attention.
For the international 1928 Pressa (Press) exhibition in Cologne, El Lissitzky designed the USSRs display: it featured a photomontage and accompanying fold-out booklet documenting the latest innovations in the speed, volume, and distribution of printing juxtaposed with images of groups of industrial workers, the Red Army, and party leaders, often photographed from below as if on pedestals or above as part of public demonstrations of military might and solidarity.
Some photographs were mounted on constructed kiosks resembling working press machinery (fig.
9.22).
El Lissitzky, USSR display at “Pressa” exhibition, Cologne, 1928.
Another Constructivist, Gustav Klutsis (18951938) used photomontage as a form of modern assembly in a series of propaganda posters that promoted Communist Party programs under Soviet leader Joseph Stalin (18781953), who succeeded Lenin on his death in 1924.
Klutsiss posters often employed official and often-reproduced photographs of modern machinery with dramatic changes in scale to stimulate eye movement as well as to communicate increase in production, as in a poster for the development of transport from 1929 (fig.
9.23).
Klutsis juxtaposes a diminutive figure of a camel in front of a modern locomotive to contrast past with present, with smaller locomotives suggesting stages in the progress of transportation as a growth chart.
The red star and use of red behind the other engines refer to Russia, while the diagonal letter points to the future to reinforce the visual hierarchy in a dynamic asymmetrical arrangement.
Constructivists saw photography as inherently modern because it was both reproducible and mechanical rather than being tied to illustration and fine art.
Nevertheless, Klutsiss use of photomontage communicated both the general meaning of dynamic progress in transportation as well as providing evidence that reinforced faith in official party slogans, in this instance Transportation is One of the Most Important Tasks in the Fulfillment of the Five-Year Plan. On one level there is a connection to be made both with advertising slogans in the United States during the 1920s and 1930s as well as advertisements juxtaposition of before and after results to proclaim the efficacy and promote the desirability of products.
On the other hand, one might compare Constructivist posters with Lester Bealls poster for the Rural Electrification Administration in 1937 in the United States (see fig.
10.43), where the latters emphasis seems to be less upon the productive power of the machine than upon the benefits of electricity to the single home in the form of electric light or the washing machine.
Indeed, Klutsiss posters glorifying industrialization have more in common with Charles Sheelers Stamping Press photograph for the Ford Corporation plant at River Rouge from 1927 (see fig.
10.19): in both cases, abrupt changes in scale communicate the power of machinery in the hands of the state or the corporation.

## 9.23 Gustav Klutsis, Development of Transport, Five-Year Plan, poster, intaglio, 27 <sup>7
</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 19 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (73.3 × 50.5 cm), 1929.
In the Soviet Union, selling the benefits of state ownership of property and the means of production was a major initiative that required the efforts of graphic designers to promote collective solidarity rather than individual agency.
Photography and film used images to create a sense of community among the Soviet Unions vast and ethnically diverse territories.
Images of the Red Army on parade, of locomotives and groups of workers in factories, fields, and participation in collective leisure were repeated in journals, newspapers, and in exhibitions, contributing to a sense of shared identity and experience that might require the sacrifice of individual or a particular ethnic character.
Examples include Arkady Shaikhets 1928 photograph titled Assembling the Globe at the Moscow Telegraph Central Station, coinciding with the initiation of Stalins first Five Year Plan (fig.
9.24).
The two figures, easily identified as workers by their coarse clothing and short-billed caps, stand physically and metaphorically at the center of the universe they are building through their physical labor, while modern radio communication spreads communist revolution around the globe.
Another example is Rodchenkos cover for the journal Novyi Lef (For the New Left) from 1927, in which the profile head of a smiling worker extends to the left and right limits of the unframed page, and the square title at the upper right corner touches the figures hat, creating a strong figureground tension (fig.
9.25).
Through juxtaposition, overlap, and contrasts in scale, photographs also acquire a sense of drama on their own or in relation to the text and the bold contrasts of the composition.
Arkady Shaikhet, Assembling the Globe at the Moscow Telegraph Central Station, photograph, 1928.
Aleksandr Rodchenko, cover for Novyi Lef, no.
6, 9 × 6 in (22.5 × 15 cm), Hoslow, 1927.
Stalins tight control of propaganda in the Soviet Union beginning in the later 1920s made it difficult for Constructivists to pursue their experimental approach to graphic design.
While slogans proclaiming faith in the industrialized future remained, idealized illustrations of workers and peasants co-existed with photography and the dynamic asymmetrical compositions that closely related text and image more interactively.
The more illustrational approach is usually referred to as socialist realism and represents a form of communication designed to reach the Russian masses, but was decidedly not the kind of modern abstract visual language that inspired the Constructivists, whose efforts were marginalized.
In some cases artists were seen as threats to the state: for unknown reasons, Gustav Klutsis was arrested in 1938 and executed three weeks later.
Among the examples of a lingering Constructivist sensibility is the sketch for a rollerprinted textile illustrated in figure 9.26.
One of several patterns designed in the later 1920s and early 1930s by a number of different artists working for the state-controlled industry, this example from 1930 by Sergei Burylin (18761942) has as its subject Coal Recycling. It uses flat two-dimensional pictographic symbols for mountains of coal, scaffolds, conveyor belts, and workers.
The subject, with its patterned repetition and emphasis upon work, demonstrates the desire to use textiles as a means to reinforce the belief in collective industrial labor.
Yet such designs, despite the ideological aspirations to create a proletarian art and the inclusion of figuration, were unpopular among consumers, who were more familiar with pre-revolutionary floral and scenic Western designs (compare Raoul Dufys wallpaper design, fig.
8.21, or Sergei Chekhonins plate, fig.
9.19).
There was little room for resolving the conflict between Constructivist motivations and popular taste in the area of textile design.
Constructivists complained that the return of traditional representations constituted an acquiescence to popular forces at odds with the new art and its ability to forge a new consciousness.

## 9.26 Sergei Burylin, sketch for “Coal Recycling” textile pattern, gouache, ink, and whitin
g, 5 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 5 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (14 × 14.6 cm), late 1920s or early 1930s.
Ivanovo State Museum of History and the Revolution.
The overthrow of the Tsarist Empire and success of the Bolshevik Revolution provided the political context for artists to design and implement utopian projects with state support.
A lasting legacy of Constructivism was in graphic and exhibition design: photomechanical reproduction, photomontage, dynamic asymmetrical compositions, striking photography made possible by portable cameras, the integration of type and image, all were marshaled as propaganda to communicate a collective consciousness for a new social order, inspired by faith in Marxist revolutionary ideology, mechanized mass production, and the state-controlled economic planning that would realize its promise.
The graphic design strategies developed by Rodchenko, El Lissitzky, Klutsis, and others contributed to Jan Tschicholds New Typography, where they served a far wider variety of purposes that included business communication and advertising.

## The
Bauhaus The Soviet Workers Club at the 1925 Paris exposition was but one indication of the international reach of Constructivist activities: El Lissitzkys essays on modern design were published in issues of De Stijl, and the short-lived journal Vesch/Objet/Gegenstand contained texts by Van Doesburg, Mondrian, Le Corbusier, and other designers advocating the use of reinforced concrete, tubular metal, and standardized mechanized industrial production.
These ideas also found expression in a school of design established in Weimar, Germany, known as the Bauhaus.
The Bauhaus (from the German verb bauen; to build) opened in 1919 from the consolidation of Weimars Academy of Fine Arts and the citys Arts and Craft School (Kunstgewerbeschule), both of which had closed during World War I.
The schools first director was Walter Gropius (18831969), an architect who had worked in the office of Peter Behrens prior to the war.
Gropiuss architectural commissions included the well-known Fagus shoe-last factory at Alfeld an der Leine near Hildesheim, designed in 1911 in collaboration with Adolf Meyer (18811929), and often viewed as an early example of modern steel-frame construction, exhibiting large expanses of plate-glass, curtain walls, and an absence of traditional moldings and decoration.
Gropius was also active in the Deutscher Werkbund and had designed railroad cars with efficiently equipped standardized compartments and fitted furniture.
Within the Werkbund, however, he supported artistic freedom and individuality rather than Typisierung and the industrial logic advocated by Hermann Muthesius (see here).
Composed during the liberal Weimar Republic that governed Germany after World War I from 1918 until Adolf Hitlers appointment as German Chancellor in 1933, the idealistic text of the Bauhaus manifesto (1919) shows little interest in specific standards for design or a particular application of industrial technology, and is concerned instead with championing the collaboration of artist and craftsman, pointing to the medieval building as a collaborative model to overcome the opposition between fine and applied art and to create a living art integrated into rather than separated from life: Architects, painters, sculptors, we must all return to crafts!
For there is no such thing as professional art. There is no essential difference between the artist and the craftsman.
The artist is an exalted craftsman.
By the grace of Heaven and in rare moments of inspiration which transcend the will, art may unconsciously blossom from the labor of his hand, but a foundation of handicraft is essential for every artist.
It is there that the primary source of creativity lies.
Let us therefore create a new guild of craftsmen without the class-distinctions that raise an arrogant barrier between craftsman and artist!
Let us together desire, conceive and create the new building of the future, which will combine everything  architecture and sculpture and painting  all in a single form which will one day rise towards the heavens from the hands of a million workers as the crystalline symbol of a new and coming faith.
The model of the medieval guild, and with it the idealistic legacy of William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement, emerges in this strongly utopian passage in which the products and activities of design will transform both the material and more broadly human conditions of society.
The guild model also emerges in Gropiuss practice of calling the Bauhaus faculty masters rather than professors, and in the manifestos cover illustration for the school, featuring a woodcut by early faculty appointment Lyonel Feininger (18711956), depicting a church bathed in the light of three stars, symbolizing perhaps the collaboration and essential unity of painting, sculpture, and architecture in the Gothic cathedral.
Such ideas formed the founding basis of the philosophy of education at the Bauhaus, even though architecture was initially not among the fields of study offered at the school in its early Weimar years.
Although Gropius inherited a small number of faculty from the Weimar Academy of Fine Arts, many of them were hostile to the revamped curriculum for the Bauhaus and lobbied successfully to maintain their independence from the new school.
As a result the director was able to appoint several new masters for the school.
The new faculty were almost exclusively fine artists, who embraced abstraction and freedom of expression as the basis for art, but who at the same time were committed to a less elitist role for artists that encouraged the integration of art and life.
The shared goal among the faculty and director seems to have been a healthy collaboration between artist and craftsman in educating new designers to reinvigorate the production of useful goods culminating in the construction and interior design of buildings, informed and conditioned by the discipline and unity implied in the architectural enterprise, and contributing to German economic recovery and cultural renewal.
Faculty appointments in 1919 included Johannes Itten (18881967), Gerhard Marcks (18891981), and Feininger, as well as painters Paul Klee (18791940) in 1921 and Kandinsky (see here) in 1922.
Kandinsky had worked as an artist and teacher in Russia after the 1917 revolution, but departed for Germany late in 1921.
Klee was born in Switzerland but studied painting in Munich, and it is difficult to believe that he was unaware of the artistic milieu of that city in the heyday of the Munich Secession and Jugendstil (see here).
His views on the social role of the decorative arts in promoting a broad-based audience for aesthetic ideas emerges in a letter he wrote to a fellow artist in 1919, revealing the charged political climate of the time: Of course, exaggerated, individualist art is not suitable for the general public  it is a capitalist luxury.
But I think we are more than just curiosities for wealthy snobs.
And all that in us which is in some way or the other is striving for eternity would be more likely to be encouraged in a communist community ... this new art would grasp craftsmanship and bring forth a great new flowering.
For there would no longer be academies, but only art schools for craftsmen.
A key element in the curriculum of the Bauhaus was a required common first semester of study (Vorkurs) before students selected one or more areas of specialization in the Bauhaus workshops (ceramics, glass painting, mural painting, furniture, metalwork, textiles).
Munich-trained painter and printmaker Georg Muche (18951987) assisted with the Vorkurs, and other mandatory but non-specialized courses in form and theory were taught by Klee and Kandinsky.
The purpose of the Vorkurs under the direction of Swiss-born artist and educator Johannes Itten was to encourage students direct contact with materials and textures, drawing techniques, and forms so that their innate creative energy might be best directed toward study in a specialized workshop.
Surviving examples of student work demonstrate contrasts of textures among different materials in an abstract composition, drawings from life that exaggerate a sense of rhythm in nature, and underlying formal relationships among geometric shapes in the analysis of works of art.
While male students might choose freely among areas of specialization following the Vorkurs, women were almost always directed toward the weaving workshop, viewed by the faculty as appropriate for female students (only with difficulty did Marianne Brandt obtain permission to pursue her apprenticeship in the metal workshop).
In fact, so strict was the gender bias that a separate Vorkurs was taught to the women students at the Bauhaus.
One of the important elements of the Bauhaus Vorkurs was its role as a foundation for all of the workshops.
Implied is the notion of an underlying basis connecting all of the arts that might be applied to a variety of forms in architecture, ceramics, metalwork, furniture, or printing: principles that had their basis in elementary, abstract geometric forms and that culminated in the built environment.
This intellectual or even spiritual part of the Bauhaus curriculum was balanced by later specialization in the workshops, but even then a Form master (fine artist) collaborated with a technical master to provide continued guidance to students.
Bauhaus graduate Grete Marks (18991990) owned and operated a ceramic workshop in Marwitz, Germany (near Berlin, but now Marwice in western Poland), with her husband and brother-in-law (both were killed in an automobile accident in 1928), named the Häel Workshops for Artistic Ceramics from 1923 until she left Germany for Jerusalem in 1933 (after Hitler was named Chancellor), moving to Britain in 1936 where she continued to design and manufacture modern ceramics.
Until the later 1920s the workshop was a successful commercial enterprise, employing as many as 120 workers.
The Haël Workshops produced earthenware tableware in bright colors, most often without glazed, hand-painted, or printed decoration (decoration, when present, was abstract and resembled the geometric designs found in Kandinskys paintings and lithographs of the same time), derived from elemental geometric forms (often placed asymmetrically), handles, and spouts, as seen in figure 9.27.
Grete Marks, tea service, Haël Werkstätten Factory (Marwitz, 1923–1933), c.
1930.
Scholars have been careful to point out that the early Vorkurs did not seek only to familiarize students with the underlying elements of all the arts, but also to draw connections between artistic activity and the discovery of unconscious reality.
Itten practiced a form of mysticism known as Mazdaznan, conducted breathing exercises, and imposed a vegetarian diet for the schools kitchen.
Not all students (or faculty) adhered to the Mazdaznanian (as well as racist) elements of Ittens teaching that appear to have ended with his dismissal in 1923.
Despite the fact that a non-specialized preliminary course had been introduced in some form earlier by Peter Behrens in the Düsseldorf Kunstgewerbeschule and also formed part of the curriculum in design education in Soviet Russia at INKHUK, the preliminary or foundation course tends to be associated with the Bauhaus.
This is perhaps a result of the emigration of Bauhaus faculty and their students to the United States and Britain in the 1930s, where the concept became institutionalized as a cornerstone of design education after World War II.
Design education was envisioned as a problem-solving activity, unified by faith in the underlying basis of all artistic activity, balancing creativity and experimentation with technical and aesthetic decisions based upon a consideration of materials and production.
The foundation model for art and design education persists to this day in the United States and worldwide, though it has been increasingly challenged by designers and educators who believe its basis in craft as well as the notion of designers being able to do it all are both anachronistic and ill-suited to address urgent needs for action in the face of social and environmental threats that pose impediments to progress in the twenty-first century.
Results from the Bauhaus in the early Weimar years may be summarized in the construction and interior design and decoration for the Sommerfeld House in Berlin, a residence (now destroyed) commissioned privately from Gropius but constructed with the collaboration of the Bauhaus workshops (fig.
9.28).
The client was shipping industrialist Adolf Sommerfeld, who provided a large quantity of teak wood normally used in boat building; the project demonstrates the early Bauhaus emphasis upon craft techniques and the integration of construction and original abstract decoration.
The horizontal emphasis of the elevation and the strongly projecting eaves of the roof of the Sommerfeld House recall the Prairie houses of Frank Lloyd Wright (see here).
The doorway and staircase of the entrance area are decorated with wooden relief panels that develop the angular construction of the teak paneling, exploring relations of geometric forms in two and three dimensions, as well as a variety of textures created by sanding and chiseling.
These motifs, in either regular patterns or asymmetrically balanced compositions, are repeated in a series of leaded glass windows behind the staircase as well as in embroidered appliqué curtains, all produced in the Bauhaus workshops.
Like Wrights Prairie houses, the Sommerfeld House remains strongly based on handicraft despite employing abstract geometric shapes rather than organic forms in decoration.
Decoration at the Sommerfeld House remains subordinate to, rather than integrated with, construction, as in the more collaborative approach envisioned by Van Doesburg and realized in 1924 to 1925 in projects such as the Schröder House in Utrecht (see figs.
9.14 and 9.15).
There Rietveld applied color to sliding panels, furniture, and walls to create a greater degree of unity between decorative and structural elements, realizing the living work of art central to the aims of De Stijl in the early 1920s.
9.28 Joost Schmidt with students, wood carving for the staircase of Sommerfeld House, Berlin (now destroyed), photograph from 1921–1922.
Despite the collaborative effort on the Sommerfeld House and some limited commercial success in the weaving and ceramics workshops, the Bauhaus struggled for adequate funding from the Weimar government and battled local resistance directed at its unorthodox approach to applied arts education.
In addition, the school was criticized by designers more aligned with Constructivism who felt the schools methods and products were allied too closely to craft production, rather than to mechanized industrial production in the service of more efficient, socially responsible modern living.
Detractors claimed that the Bauhaus produced the kind of individual and indulgent design that was at variance with the inclusive aims expressed in the 1919 manifesto.
One of the most vehement attacks appeared in De Stijl.
The journals editor, Theo van Doesburg, moved to Weimar in 1921 and attended an International Congress of Constructivism held there in 1922.
Although Van Doesburg never officially taught at the Bauhaus, he was acquainted with Gropius who seems at one time to have considered the Dutch artist for a teaching position.
Gropius was sensitive to criticisms of the schools shortcomings.
He had already been in contact with Dutch architect J.
J.
P.
Oud (associated at one time with De Stijl and employed by the housing authority of Rotterdam) and was interested in new developments in Dutch architecture related to standardization and newer prefabricated materials for government-sponsored, low-cost public housing.
In response to financial, political, and ideological pressures, Gropius began to shift the focus of the Bauhaus mission and curriculum.
One of the most important changes that took place was Gropiuss decision in 1923 to force the resignation of Itten and to hire Hungarian painter and Constructivist László Moholy-Nagy (18951946) as his replacement.
The two men had met in Berlin, where Moholy-Nagy was living, having left Hungary following the nations short-lived 1919 communist revolution.
Moholy-Nagy took responsibility for the Vorkurs and for a more industrial focus that began to inform Bauhaus education and activities.
He brought with him a strong commitment to mechanized mass production and new material technology in design, reducing the importance of craft specialization and traditional workshop training.
To emphasize the point, in what has become part of the canonical literature of Modernism, Moholy-Nagy designed a series of abstract geometric paintings and communicated instructions by telephone to assistants to have them produced.
His efforts parallel Rodchenkos call for a new conception of the designer as the artist-constructor rather than artist-craftsman, and Moholys series of paintings share a vocabulary of intersecting planes floating in a projected space similar to El Lissitzkys series of PROUNS (see here).
The new approach de-emphasized unconscious and spiritual associations with the creative process.
In their place, Moholy-Nagy identified the artist with the engineer, creating designs for factory production, promoting aesthetic unity and control through the use of modules and the grid.
Moholy-Nagy placed photography on an equal footing with the fine arts and experimented with kinetic sculpture.
He praised the machine as a liberating force both in creative and in social terms: Constructivism is not confined to the picture frame and the pedestal.
It expands into industrial designs, into house, objects, forms.
It is the socialism of vision  the common property of all men. Moholy-Nagy disdained specialization in favor of versatility: in his view, students familiarity with underlying elemental form, mechanical processes, and industrial materials would enable them to direct their energies creatively to a variety of fields rather than be limited only to the Joost Schmidt, poster for Bauhaus exhibition, lithograph, 28 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 19 in (60.5 × 48 cm), Weimar, 1923.
When the Bauhaus mounted an exhibition of its work in 1923, Gropius proclaimed the new orientation in a speech entitled Art and Technology: A New Unity. The poster (fig.
9.29) for the exhibition was designed by former Bauhaus student Joost Schmidt (18931948) and is composed of tilted rectangular and circular shapes, creating an X-like axis or grid.
The grid imparts hierarchical and ordered relationships to the placement of the text for the words State Bauhaus, Exhibition as well as location and date.
The poster also contains the new logo for the Bauhaus designed by Oskar Schlemmer (18881943), a simplified pictogram of a profile head drawn with a ruler and built upon rectangular and circular shapes.
The use of ruler and compass to imply technical drawing and virtual absence of representation, along with the economy of means, were striking at the time and had a strong impact upon a number of younger designers such as Jan Tschichold, who visited the Weimar exhibition and incorporated elements of Bauhaus printing into his New Typography (see here).
The 1923 exhibition was a collaborative enterprise  the construction and decoration of the Haus-am-Horn (fig.
9.30), a model for an efficient, single-family housing unit designed by Georg Muche and Adolf Meyer; Muche formerly had served as an assistant to Itten in the Vorkurs and continued to be master of Form in the Bauhaus weaving workshop.
The centrally planned Haus-am-Horn is designed with a large clerestory-lit living room surrounded on all sides by smaller, modular rectangular rooms, each designed to efficiently meet a particular need for domestic living.
It was constructed of prefabricated building materials (concrete) and, like Le Corbusiers 1925 Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau (see here and fig.
9.5), was offered as a prototype for public housing that could be built cheaply and quickly.
Georg Muche and Adolf Meyer with Bauhaus workshops, Haus-am-Horn, living room, 1923.
Faculty and students in the Bauhaus workshops were responsible for the design and manufacture of furnishings for the Haus-am-Horn.
Photographs of the living room show furniture simply assembled from standardized lengths of wood, with chairs conforming to the grid-like intersection of horizontal and vertical shapes, using overlapping joints; all are devoid of carved decoration or paint.
Lighting was designed by Moholy-Nagy and employed slender tubular-metal forms (also conforming to a grid) emphasizing lightness, geometry, and standardized components.
Textiles and carpets provided color and abstract patterned decoration, and spaces were devoid of carved or molded architectural detail.
Features of the Haus-am-Horn kitchen were employed in the rational kitchen designs of the later 1920s and 1930s, associated with low-cost public housing in the city of Frankfurt (fig.
9.38).
These also stemmed from studies by Christine Frederick that introduced a more scientific approach to design arising from the analysis of domestic work and reduction of time in food preparation (see here).
Renewing the Bauhaus commitment to educating a new type of designer for industry, Gropius hired a number of the schools own recent graduates as masters, replacing the former system of Form master and Craft master in several workshops.
Fine artists such as Klee and Kandinsky continued to offer courses in form and theory, but their role in the workshops was reduced as the relationship between designers, materials, and production was re-examined in light of mechanized technology and familiarity with commercial industrial production.
The new direction, however, failed to please the regional government that sponsored the school.
In 1925 the Weimar Bauhaus was closed and relocated to the industrial city of Dessau.
With renewed local support, Gropius designed new facilities for the Bauhaus, renamed as the Bauhaus Hochschule für Gestaltung or Institute for Design. At Dessau new facilities included modern printing presses and Jacquard looms for the weaving workshops.
Gropiuss studio building for the Bauhaus resembled a factory more than a traditional art school, with exposed steel construction and broad, uninterrupted expanses of plate glass.
The relocation provided the possibility for some faculty to acquire direct industrial experience, and faculty and students began to create prototypes for industrial production.
Another change was the creation of a Bauhaus department of architecture.
Marcel Breuer, tubular metal chair, chrome-plated steel and wood, and cane, $3 2 \times 1 8 ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 2 2 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in $( 8 1 .

2$ cm), manufactured by Gebrüder Thonet, 1928.
Design historian John Heskett has emphasized that the effect of the Bauhaus upon industrial manufacturing in Germany was limited, notwithstanding the success of Grete Markss Häel Workshops in Marwitz.
Nevertheless some ties were forged, and Bauhaus designs were manufactured commercially, such as Marcel Breuers tubular-metal and wood chair with cane seating (fig.
9.31), manufactured by Thonet beginning in 1928, desk lamps and other electric lighting for the firms of Körtung and Mathieson, and Schwintzer & Gräff, wallpapers manufactured by Gebrüder Rasch & Co., and a full range of commercial printing services at the Dessau printing facility.
Breuers grid-like design for his tubular-metal side chair was based upon a novel cantilevered principle of support requiring two rather than the traditional four legs for support, a result of substituting applications of new materials and assembly of traditional craft-based techniques of furniture-making.
Dutch Constructivist designer Mart Stam (18991986) also developed a similar cantilevered tubular-metal chair as early as 1925, but that design was not manufactured in large quantities (a lawsuit ensued, and Thonet was forced to delete Breuers name from its catalog).
The steel industry in Europe supported the use of metal primarily for office furniture and hundreds of tubular-steel chair designs were developed during the later 1920s.
In addition to exhibitions, furniture companies such as Standard-Möbel in Berlin, Wohnbedarf in Zurich, and Büro in Czechoslovakia manufactured Modernist designs using tubular steel for chairs, desks, and tables, but directed toward the office and institutions such as hospitals and schools rather than the domestic housing market.
Marianne Brandt (18931983) designed lighting for Körtung and Mathieson, and Wilhelm Wagenfeld (19001990; see here and fig.
9.34) worked privately in Germany as an industrial designer during the 1930s after the close of the Bauhaus in 1933.
Gunta Stölzl (18971983), who was a Bauhaus student in Weimar, directed the weaving workshop, and was sent to the city of Krefeld to study industrial fiber and dyeing technology.
Stölzl maintained a middle ground between early Weimar and Dessau, never abandoning handweaving and craft as a source of direct contact with materials, process (warp and weft) and individual expression, while encouraging experimentation with newer industrial materials such as cellophane.
She also focused attention upon other ideas, such as reversible fabrics and the relationship between fabric wall coverings, acoustics, and lighting effects that considered new aspects of user experience.
Following the shift in focus in 1923, Bauhaus master Georg Muche began to question the possibility of balancing aesthetic expression with the realities of industrial-scale production and commercial business practice, stating that fine art and design had been on the same path but that now they should pursue separate development. # abcdefqhi iklmnopqr s tuvwxyz a d'd 9.32 Herbert Bayer, universal alphabet, 1926.
The printing workshop at the Bauhaus, with the support of Moholy-Nagy and under the direction of former student Herbert Bayer (19001985), introduced Constructivist approaches to visual communication including photomechanical reproduction, photomontage, and non-traditional layout for letterpress printing.
The workshop published a series of Bauhausbücher, exhibition displays and advertising posters, stationery, business forms, and a Bauhaus journal.
In Dessau, Bayer created a series of universal sans serif typefaces based upon modular geometric shapes and a limited number of Latin letterforms that decreased or even eliminated the vestiges of hand-lettering and traces of Germanic blackletter forms (fig.
9.32).
He also eliminated capital letters, used in German for all nouns as well as at the beginning of sentences and proper names, creating regularized heights, a bowl rather than traditional lower-case a, and in some cases a combination of lower- and upper-case forms, as in the letter k. Bayer considered new possibilities for arranging text on the page outside of conventional centered layouts and hierarchies of information.
The printing workshop introduced page layouts in which typography, photography, white space, and heavy rules were all considered equal and complementary design elements, serving to attract and direct the viewers attention and impart a new sense of active viewing with an asymmetrical order to the arrangement of information.
An example is Moholy-Nagys title page for the prospectus of the Weimar Bauhaus from 1923 (fig.
9.33), printed in red and black.
Here, uniform sans serif typography is used in a variety of sizes to direct viewer attention and an asymmetrical balance of horizontal and vertical elements based upon an implied geometric grid.
Decorative borders based upon plant or geometric patterns are purged, leaving large areas of white space that become equal partners in the overall page layout, activated by rectangular shapes, even extending to the stem of large B to the left of the page.
These plain black bars of different thicknesses, or rules, are part of the printers type case used for spacing, but are printed here as part of typographic design: the vertical bar of the large B relates to the odd, vertically placed WEIMAR nearby.
Moholy-Nagys layouts promote a more broadly visual, modern form of reading.
While experimental in the use of novel letterforms and word orientation, they also display a strong sense of discipline and clarity, certainly in contrast to Marinettis Futurist poetry, which also explored more expressive and visual approaches to the printed word (see fig.
9.1).

## 9.33 László Moholy-Nagy, title page of the Weimar Bauhaus prospectus, 10 × 10 in (25 × 25
cm), 1923.
In 1928 Gropius resigned as director of the Bauhaus, naming the Swiss-born Hannes Meyer (18891954), who served as professor of architecture, as his successor.
Meyer was an unpopular choice at the outset.
His approach to design was more narrowly circumscribed than his predecessor, proposing that design was a product of function × economy. He placed design solely in the service of universal working-class needs based upon the use of economic materials and efficiency in standardized production, to be brought to fruition through participation of the workshops in real projects for low-cost public housing and home furnishings.
Meyer tended to view design at the Bauhaus as a largely deterministic process, resulting more or less automatically from considerations of climate, hygiene, economics, and engineering.
His approach marginalized the value of fine art in the design process, forcing the resignation of several members of the faculty.
Ironically, under Meyers directorship, the Bauhaus became more commercially successful and financially independent through commissions and sales of its prototypes to manufacturers, including wallpapers, textiles, advertising, and lighting.
Bauhaus designs produced under his directorship (regardless of his political ideology) found a niche in a capitalist consumer economy in Germany, were reproduced in fashion magazines and were manufactured at the Bauhaus workshops or companies who purchased rights to produce and market them.
Although equally committed to technology and the social mission of the Bauhaus, Moholy-Nagy resigned quickly after Meyers appointment as director.
Moholy-Nagy held that modern design required an accommodation to standards and uniformity to maintain a sense of social responsibility, but that versatility and more open-ended exploration of new technology and materials preserved a necessary sense of intuition and creative expression in the design process.
In Moholy-Nagys view, versatility and experiment helped to relieve the fear of mindless conformity to dehumanizing factory work and narrow specialization.
Until the end of his career, he maintained the value of a creative role for design and design education rather than how that value might be compromised too heavily by more pragmatic economic or social considerations, whether consumerist or collective.
The differences between Meyer and Moholy demonstrate that Modernism was far from a unified movement, but was rather a loose collection of ideas with differences, contradictions, and strongly held, often polemic, opinions among its theorists and practitioners.
Was the Modern designer an engineer?
A worker?
Or an artist?
Today perhaps we need not choose among such options.
Yet the stakeholders in these debates were often unbending, as the stakes were felt to be high: shaping a future with little or no reference to the past, proposing solutions to urgent social problems on a vast scale in a climate of political unrest that often seemed to demand positions of firm authority rather than democratic compromise and reform.
Despite inconsistencies and ambiguities, the term Modernism remains part of the literature and history of design, tied to many of the most canonical names, institutions, and iconic products of the first half of the twentieth century.
But even in the politically volatile interwar period, there was a gap between intention and public reception of Modernist movements and their designs, and the meaning of undecorated products and furnishings, and the efficient use of space was in constant flux.
Perhaps the most enduring aspect of interwar Modernism was not the trajectory of its various groups and organizations, but rather its flexibility, an ability to be adopted, and adapted, to a variety of individual, social, and political agendas.
In time Meyers position became untenable.
Gropius had always attempted to avoid political confrontation with government officials in the interests of the schools survival, but Meyers leftist political views (despite his accommodations of commercial considerations) were radical; under his directorship, political theory was taught as a classroom subject and a communist student group was formed.
Nationalist sentiments in Germany raised government suspicions toward Bauhaus politics.
Meyer resigned in 1930, relocating to Soviet Russia, where he hoped his design activities and principles would find more ready acceptance.
His place was taken by the well-established German architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe (18861969), who moved the school from Dessau to facilities in Berlin.
In 1933, the National Socialist (Nazi) Party came to power in Germany and the Weimar Republic ended.
This governments strong anti-communist position continued to cast suspicion upon the international sympathies of the Bauhaus despite Miess efforts to solicit architectural commissions from the Nazi government.
The schools association with left-wing radical politics was linked to the influence of foreigners and Jews, bringing about its demise, 14 years after its opening in 1919, coinciding with the rise and fall of the Weimar Republic.
The importance of the Bauhaus is not the result of its success in developing prototypes for industrial production, which was limited, but rather of the compelling nature of its ambitious ideal of collaboration between art, craft, and industry in the education of designers.
This contribution is perhaps best exemplified in the career of Moholy-Nagy, who is remembered less for particular masterpieces of art or commercially successful industrial products than for his embodiment of the new and versatile artist-worker-engineer, engaged in the creative process of design to address a broad range of human and social needs.
Also the emigration of Bauhaus faculty to other colleges and universities outside of Germany, the respect for many of its faculty and students among institutions such as New Yorks fledgling Museum of Modern Art, and its celebration in countless exhibitions and anniversaries (most recently the centenary of its founding) have all added to the continuing power of a Bauhaus image that may vary somewhat from the institutions actual history and underwent considerable change in the 14 years of its existence.
Nevertheless, and in the face of calls for the revision of its craft-based curriculum, the Bauhaus continues to exert an influence upon postsecondary education in the visual arts and design, where many of its features, including some sort of common core, still form the basis of art and design curricula.
Despite a recognition that the school perhaps never realized the utopian vision of its directors and spokespersons, the Bauhaus provided an environment in which artists were encouraged to design for industrial production and to shape and enhance the experience of modern living; the boldness of that effort has remained a significant legacy.

## Beyond
the Bauhaus A small number of Bauhaus faculty remained in Germany after the schools closing in 1933 and designed products as consultants to industrial manufacturers.
Mies van der Rohe stayed until 1938, though his projects found little if any traction in the conservative political climate under the Nazis.
As mentioned above, German industrial designer Wilhelm Wagenfeld, who had studied and taught at the Bauhaus, designed a line of Kubus glassware as art director of the Lausitzer Glasverein in 1938 (fig.
9.34).
These inexpensive containers for kitchen use were made of a newly developed heatresistant pressed glass, and had interchangeable lids, slightly pinched corners for pouring the contents more evenly, and dimensions that permitted stacking for spacesaving kitchen countertop storage.
Wagenfeld was successful throughout the 1930s as a designer, and his own leftist political leanings do not appear to have raised Nazi suspicions.
The absence of molded relief decoration surely owes a debt to the Modernist aesthetic, along with similarities in efforts promoting standardization and efficiency in the design of offices and kitchens that took place in Frankfurt and elsewhere in Germany during the later 1920s.
Wilhelm Wagenfeld, Kubus-Geschirr (cube-shaped dishware/storage containers), 3 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 7 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 7 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (7.9 × 18.1 × 18.1 cm), manufactured by Lausitzer Glasverein, Weiswasser, Germany, c.
1938 Another instance of Modernist design in Germany under the Nazis was the Peoples Car, or Volkswagen, developed by Ferdinand Porsche (18751951) and manufactured beginning in 1937 (fig.
9.35) through a government-sponsored program called KdF (Kraft durch Freude, Strength through Joy).
The Volkswagen featured a unified sloping body based upon wind-tunnel testing to reduce resistance, and an air-cooled rear engine to simplify mechanics and operation.
The design provided economical fuel consumption along with adequate passenger and storage space.
The Third Reich also sponsored a program that encouraged workers to save five marks weekly toward the purchase of their own Volkswagen.
The beginning of World War II halted production of the Volkswagen in 1939 as factories re-tooled production to military machinery, and it was not massproduced until after the end of the war.
Nicknamed the Beetle, the Volkswagen remained in production with few changes well into the 1970s, and enjoyed renewed popularity in the United States during the 1960s in part as a reaction against the luxury styling and mass-marketing strategies of large American automobile manufacturers (see fig.
14.19).
Despite closing the Bauhaus in 1933, the Third Reich benefitted from the efforts of former students and faculty who remained in Germany and from aspects of its approach to industrial design.
Like the Volkswagen, the Peoples Radio was a government-sponsored initiative that served the needs of the working class with a basic, affordable, standardized manufactured product using modern materials that provided mass access to the Führers broadcasts and limited access to other programming  a combination of entertainment, propaganda, and censorship.
The Nazis used the term Gleichschaltung (enforced conformity) to monitor cultural expressions that were sympathetic to the Reich and to censor or monitor those that posed a perceived threat to their policies.
Their approach to modern design was selective and could, as with the Volkswagen or Peoples Radio, support elements of a German national identity.
Ferdinand Porsche, Volkswagen, Wolfsburg, Germany, c.
1937.
Trude Petri (19061998) studied ceramics in Hamburg (not at the Bauhaus) and designed the Urbino line of porcelain dinnerware for the Staatliche Porzellan- Manufaktur in Berlin, manufactured from 1930 to 1934 (fig.
9.36).
The milk-white color, glasslike surfaces, and pure, circular forms of plates and serving platters, feet, and handles all suggest the abstract beauty of elemental purist geometric form.
The gently tapering forms for tureens and lids introduce both an organic element and a sense of precision and elegance also found in the contemporary tubular-metal furniture of the schools last director, Mies van der Rohe (fig.
9.37), or the silver tableware of French designer Jean Puiforcat (see fig.
8.9).
Both of these examples were produced in limited quantities by prestigious manufacturers for wealthy consumers by star designers, anticipating the international market for Modernist products and furniture after World War II related to formalist abstraction yet ideologically removed from the social mission we associate with Moholy-Nagy or Hannes Meyer.
Trude Petri, Urbino dinnerware, porcelain, manufactured by Staatliche Porzellan-Manufaktur, Berlin, 1930–1934.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, MR armchair, chrome-plated tubular steel and painted cane, 31 × 20 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 32 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (79 × 52 × 82.5 cm), manufactured by Berliner Metallgewerbe, Berlin, 1927.

## Design,
Socialism, and the New Frankfurt Initiatives in Germany to develop standards in the design of the workplace and in the home applied Frederick W.
Taylors theory of scientific management, maximizing productivity in factory work through the study of movement in the performance of a variety of tasks (see here).
Books such as American author Christine Fredericks Scientific Management in the Home (1915) proposed that the placement of sinks, cabinets, serving tables, ovens, refrigerators, and work surfaces should derive from a systematic study of food preparation, food service, and storage, defining a new dimension to research-based design that might be coupled with industrial production (see here).
Fredericks research runs parallel to the success of Henry Ford and was adopted in Germany and elsewhere.
Housing shortages after World War I and a sluggish economy suggested to local officials in some areas that new construction should maximize efficiency and fulfill affordable minimum requirements for working-class families, and that manufacturers should adopt standards based upon such requirements.
In an era when fewer families could afford servants, a rational approach to housework reduced its menial connotations and added an element of science and cultural progress to tasks and responsibilities usually assumed by women.
Indeed, home economics was once a required subject for young women in high schools across the United States.
In addition to efficiency, the designs for kitchens and office furnishings considered the effect of glare and brightness in lighting as well as posture in the design of furniture, maintaining some commitment to design standards based upon considerations of human factors.
One of the goals of such research was to make objective criteria the basis for a science or engineering rather than an art of design, circumscribing the role of subjective expression.
Adopting such practical considerations for design often required the backing of local governments, as in the city of Frankfurt in the late 1920s, when Ernst May (1886 1970) held the position of City Architect for the Social Democratic Party that was in power under the Weimar Republic at the time.
May designated inexpensive land on the outskirts of the city for the construction of housing estates to address urgent needs for affordable housing built on a large industrial scale, using prefabrication, flat roofs, zigzag elevations, and purpose-built beds and cabinets, seen, for instance, at Bruchfeldstrasse, built in 1925.
Eventually more than 15,000 housing units were built under Mays tenure.
One influential result of housing in the city was the Frankfurt kitchen (fig.
9.38) designed under the direction of Grete Schütte-Lihotzky (1898 2000).
The kitchen (a mere 6.2 × 11.2 ft.) featured moveable track lighting and continuous work surfaces with built-in storage cabinets and sliding doors.
The contracts for low-cost, Existenzminimum housing (minimum existence: a term used to emphasize new standards in housing design and a vast improvement over older, more cramped dwellings) enabled designs for furniture and fittings to be mass-produced inexpensively in large quantities according to standard measurements.
Smooth surfaces and the absence of decoration were recommended for ease of cleaning and hygiene, along with gas rather than wood for fuel and radiant heat to vastly reduce preparation time for cooking as well as cleaning, while government sponsorship of the project assured industrial manufacturers of a viable market for the products without the need for variations to attract the consumer.
As noted by John Heskett, the unique social, political, and economic circumstances in Frankfurt between 1925 and 1930 provided the basis for a rational and standardized approach to domestic design beyond office furniture or prototypes such as those commissioned by Le Corbusier for his Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau.
A public relations program accompanied the introduction of the Frankfurt kitchen, including a promotional film.

## 9.38 Grete Schütte-Lihotzky, the Frankfurt kitchen, 1924. Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nur
emberg.
Efficient housing and a demonstration of the possibilities of the new architecture (neues Bauen) were the focus of a Werkbund-sponsored exhibition held in 1927 at Weissenhof near Stuttgart, titled The Dwelling, and directed by Mies van der Rohe, who invited architects to participate, including the Dutch architect J.
J.
P.
Oud, at one time a contributor to the De Stijl journal.
In terms of projects on a civic scale, Oud followed a course that increasingly moved away from the collaboration envisioned by Van Doesburg and the spiritual, anti-materialistic views of Mondrian.
Already in 1921, Oud, who served as municipal-housing architect for the city of Rotterdam, had rejected color designs supplied by Van Doesburg for the housing blocks Oud had designed at Spangen (Rotterdam).
His approach to low-cost public housing leaned toward uniformity and an increasing emphasis upon efficiency and cost, focusing upon collective need similar to the views of Hannes Meyer at the Bauhaus (see here), precluding the incorporation of the more aesthetic and balanced De Stijl vision to create a living work of art. J.
J.
P.
Oud, housing, Weissenhof Seilung, 1927.
Photograph: Nederlands Documentatiecentrum voor de Bouwkunst, Amsterdam.
Ouds group of housing units constructed at Weissenhof (sponsored by the Deutscher Werkbund) relied upon standardized dimensions for rectangular windows and doors set into flat expanses of plain white walls, but without color or threedimensional effects characteristic of the Schröder House.
Ouds Weissenhof project incorporated Modernist aesthetic elements such as asymmetry and the elementary rectilinear geometry of the elevation.
It offered an economical and modern solution to urban housing using prefabricated materials and industrial methods of construction (fig.
9.39) directed toward meeting housing shortages and defining essential or minimum living needs.
Such an approach gained adherents in the later 1920s and 1930s as deteriorating economic conditions in industrialized nations seemed to support more sober, functional, and responsible solutions to housing and other architectural projects, and an avoidance of overt signs of luxury in the form of decoration.
The polemical nature of the debate concerning the relationship between aesthetics and social progress is captured in a poster for the Weissenhof exhibition by graphic designer Willi Baumeister (18891955) (fig.
9.40).
A broad red X slashes across a photograph of a middle-class living room at the upper right with ornately framed pictures, twisted columns, and upholstered Louis XV period furniture.
The words how to live? written in cursive appear at the bottom of the photograph.
Below to the left are bold sans serif capital letters, also in red, announcing the exhibition, and clearly critical of decoration, historicism, and luxury as elements in a vision of modern living.
Weissenhof continues to function as low-income housing in Stuttgart and is frequently cited among the early examples of a broader International Style emerging in the later 1920s (see here).
Willi Baumeister, Die Wohnung (The Dwelling), exhibition poster, lithograph, 45 × 32 <sup>1</sup>/ in (114.3 × 81.6 cm), Weissenhof, Stuttgart, 1927.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
The oeuvre of Viennese architect and designer Josef Frank (18851967) exemplifies the diversity of Modernist practices in the interwar period.
Although he participated in the design of low-cost social housing in Vienna in the 1920s, Frank rejected a single, allembracing approach to design.
His flexible method included dozens of textile patterns for curtains and upholstery that were contemporary interpretations of plant designs inspired by nature rather than by the machine or reductive geometric abstraction, such as Seaweed (fig.
9.41), designed between 1925 and 1930.
Meandering patterns of lines and leaf clusters suggest the movement of water and the beauty of organic forms.
Such patterns relieve the austerity (and perhaps sterility) found in many Modernist architectural projects and proposals.
Franks remarks on interior design in the later 1920s appear to recognize the varied considerations that contribute to comfort: The goal ... in designing an interior is not to make it as luxurious as possible or as simple as possible, but rather to make it as comfortable as possible....
The most comfortable interiors have always been those that the occupant himself has put together over the course of time which betray no sense of intention or plan.
In a manner not unlike that of Matisse, who compared his paintings to comfortable armchairs (see here), Frank also wrote: The modern person who is increasingly more exhausted by his job requires a domicile cozier and more comfortable than those of the past.
He has to obtain relaxation in more concentrated ways in a much shorter time.
Therefore the domicile has to be the absolute opposite of the workplace.
This applies not only to the...sitting and resting areas but to every visible object...; ornament and variety create peace and eliminate the pathos of the purely functional.
The emphasis upon the occupant or user rather than an overriding doctrine of aesthetic purity or perceived homogeneous working-class needs is prescient in considering individual psychological rather than universal criteria in the design process.
Historians have suggested that Franks Swedish wife, Anna, may have influenced his less doctrinaire approach to modern design, since Swedish as well as other Scandinavian designers in the interwar period tempered the more radical and polemical expressions of Modernism with traditional craft-based practices and decoration (see here).
Josef Frank, Seaweed textile pattern, block-printed chintz cotton, repeat: 14 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 10 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (36.2 × 27.3 cm), 1925–1930.

## The
Printing Industry and the “New Typography” Sans serif typography and a new aesthetic approach toward printing reached beyond the limited circulation of books and journals such as De Stijl, the Bauhausbücher, and the shortlived Vesch/Objet/Gegenstand during the later 1920s and 1930s.
Much as European steel companies invested in the manufacture of tubular-metal furniture, large industrial type foundries in Europe and the United States expanded their range of new typefaces in the interwar period to promote their products to the commercial printing industry.
Lifestyle magazines, such as Vogue (first published in 1892), incorporated photography and asymmetrical layouts to present contemporary fashion and leisure pastimes for the modern, active woman, independent of radical social or political agendas, and industrial manufacturers adopted photomontage, striking layouts, and new approaches to information design to promote their products.
The absence of serifs and other calligraphic features of typography, as well as the integration of type and image, and the reductive language of pictograms, all had a symbolic meaning for the movements associated with Modernism in the interwar period.
For instance, the sans serif typefaces designed at the Bauhaus by Bayer (see fig.
9.32) embodied the principle of generating a variety of letterforms from a limited number of related modular units as a metaphor for standardized mechanized production, even at times at the expense of legibility.
The major foundries had introduced versions of sans serif faces primarily for newspaper headlines and advertising around the turn of the century, contemporary with the Werkbund in Germany and the introduction of efficiency standards in other industries, for instance, in the sizes of pipefittings or electrical wiring, adapters, and sockets.
In printing, this effort also produced national standards for envelope and paper sizes, invoices, and other common business needs, including the dimensions of office filing cabinets.
In Germany these reforms took place under the auspices of the national Institute for Standards, known as the DIN (Deutsches Institut für Normung), founded in Berlin in 1917.
Terminology in the field of typography is at times confusing, as the sans serif faces were known in Europe as Grotesk and in the United States as Gothic. Franklin Gothic (fig.
9.42) was designed for the American Type Founders Company (ATF) and cut by Morris Benton between 1903 and 1905.
Although it lacks serifs, Franklin Gothic retains Latin letterforms for the characters a and g, and rounded letterforms narrow as they approach vertical stems rather than being of a uniform width (or weight) throughout.
In Germany, the Berthold Foundry of Berlin introduced the closely related Akzidenz Grotesk font at about the same time.
Both fonts were used primarily for titling, newspaper headlines, and advertisements rather than for body text. # ABCDEFGHIJKLMN OPQRSTUVWXYZ? abcdefghijklm nopqrstuvwxyz!
