Developing sans serif fonts for more widespread use required control of letterforms, spacing, and weight.
The commercial foundries addressed concerns of legibility and precision to meet the varied printing needs of the market.
Foundries developed large, extended families of fonts in a variety of weights as well as in expanded and condensed forms.
Such efforts maintained continuity with traditions of expert craftsmanship established in the eighteenth century, and were often the result of a number of individuals working under contract for large companies whose resources enabled them to undertake large-scale efforts.
It is not surprising that ATF, which introduced Franklin Gothic around the turn of the century, was itself a product of the merger and consolidation of a number of smaller foundries joining forces in response to competitive market conditions.
A page from the 1923 ATF Catalogue demonstrates the quality and variety of letterpress printing produced by large foundries during this time, in this example the Caslon family of letterforms based upon the well-known English eighteenth-century printer (fig.
9.43).
Business circumstances and new technologies for cutting and casting type promoted the development of new types and their large, growing families. Collaboration involved artist-calligraphers such as Rudolf Koch in Germany and amateur experts such as Stanley Morison in England (see here), who supervised the design of new typefaces as well as the revival or reinterpretation of older types utilizing new cutting and casting methods.
In 1927 Munich-based typographer and teacher Paul Renner (18781956) introduced the influential sans serif typeface Futura, including bold, light, condensed, and expanded variations demanded by the commercial printing industry (fig.
9.44).
The font was produced by the Bauer Foundry in Frankfurt.
Futura is known as a modular sans serif because several of its letterforms share the same element, for instance, the circular lower-case o is used for the letters a, b, d, e, p, and q; and geometric because all strokes are of a single width (also known as monoweight).
The modular principle is certainly inherent in earlier experimental typefaces but was applied with greater attention to legibility and the effects produced by modern automatic typesetting equipment.
Futuras modernity derives, of course, from its name, from the precision of its modular, geometric rather than calligraphic letterforms, approximating symbolic associations with interchangeability and mechanized production.
Other foundries responded with their own versions of modular sans serifs typefaces in Germany; for instance, Rudolf Kochs Kabel (Cable) for the Klingspor Foundry in 1927 (fig.
9.45).
One difference between the Futura and Kabel typefaces was Kochs preservation of features of the Latin alphabet, for instance, the a as well as the slanted crossbar of the e, a characteristic found in the earliest Venetian fonts of the later fifteenth century.
Despite the identification between sans serif and Modernism in typography, this type of letterform has a history going back to early nineteenth-century display faces, renewed with expanded technology and the explosion of mass-circulation printed materials in newspapers, magazines, and catalogs requiring headlines in the early twentieth century.
While Koch agreed to introduce a Modern sans serif with Kabel, he is best known as a master calligrapher, knowledgeable in a variety of printing types as well as their historical traditions.

## Jan
Tschichold and the “New Typography” One of the strongest advocates for Constructivist principles in commercial printing during the later 1920s and early 1930s was Jan Tschichold (19021974).
Tschichold was trained in calligraphy in Leipzig, using his skills to design display lettering in newspaper advertising, and brand names for products and services.
As a young man he visited the Bauhaus exhibition in Weimar in 1923 (see fig.
9.29).
Tschichold was enthusiastic about the printing on view there, and saw sans serif typography and asymmetrical page design as exciting and effective means toward modern and direct communication of information to readers for a variety of printing applications, including advertising.
He embraced a new approach and discipline for the composition of text and image without traditional decorative borders and flourishes.
The trademarks he developed from the later 1920s onward, often commissioned by publishing companies, appear somewhat conservative by present-day standards, but reveal an ability to combine letterforms and abbreviated, recognizable images into unified pictographic symbols, as seen in an example for the Bücherkreis (Book Circle) of Berlin (fig.
9.46).
Jan Tschichold, trademark for Der Bücherkreis, Berlin, line drawing after Tschichold by John Langdon, 1931.
Tschichold directed most of his attention to the varied tasks of commercial printing, ranging from posters to stationery, catalogs, and books.
In a manifesto published in 1925 and again in book form in 1927 as The New Typography, Tschichold questioned traditional approaches to printing and advocated principles of clear and direct communication favoring the use of sans serif typography, half-tone reproduction of photographs rather than hand-drawn illustration, and asymmetrical layout.
In The New Typography, Tschichold explained the Modern context for a disciplined approach that defined the emerging profession of graphic design: Every part of a text relates to every other part by a definite, logical relationship of emphasis and value, predetermined by content.
It is up to the typographer to express this relationship clearly and visibly, through type sizes and weight, arrangement of lines, use of color, photography...
He also explained the rationale for asymmetry in light of stimulating eye movement for the modern viewer who is often too busy for leisurely reading and demands a more active engagement with printed material for effective communication: Reading presupposes eye movement.
The New Typography so designs text matter that the eye is led from one word and one group of words to the next.
So a logical organization of the text is needed, through the use of different type-sizes, placing in relation to space, color, etc.
For posters, rectangular elements relating to the frame dominate, while the use of diagonal type and shapes, or other deviations from the strict discipline of the sans serif letters, create tension and arouse interest (fig.
9.47).
This example is one of several film posters produced not by the distributor but by the movie theater to provide a distinctive visual identity.
Like his Constructivist contemporaries, Tschichold attached importance to white space, making it an integral compositional element.
Jan Tschichold, film poster, Casanova, for Phoebus-Palast movie theater, letterpress, $4 7 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 3 3 ^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 } \mathsf { i n } ( 1 1 9 .

Tschicholds New Typography and related articles published in trade journals provided practical information for printers to adapt asymmetrical layout and an ordering of elements based upon content within the structure of a geometric grid to the needs of title pages, stationery, announcements, invitations, and other prosaic printing tasks, known as jobbing. The grid, still based upon the process of letterpress printing, ensured precise relationships between parallel and perpendicular elements on the page.
Elements of this approach became the basis for consistent identities developed for corporations working on an international scale and for Swiss graphic design after World War II.
The New Typography imposed a certain degree of conformity upon the designer, but still required careful adjustment rather than the rote application of a formula.
As a result, Tschicholds designs, much like Mondrians abstract paintings, have an inherent sense of rightness in their abstract balance and in the feeling for the relationship among the various elements of the page in relation to a desired hierarchy of information.
The guidelines for the New Typography could be listed as rules or even described as laws, but they could not be programmed; in addition to the logical and effective communication of information, the abstract aesthetic pleasure of a New Typography poster also offered an independent, aesthetic level of appreciation to the viewer.
Tschichold actively promoted the use of half-tone photographs for modern printing.
He wrote that photography was the most obvious means of visual representation in our time, and embraced the interrelationship between the graded tonalities of photographs and blocks of text that offered unity and maintained the attention of the viewer.
The reproduction of photographs opened up new possibilities for the printing industry and provided the basis for much experimentation.
Like El Lissitzky and Moholy-Nagy, Tschichold was fascinated with the process of photography and its application to printing, and illustrated examples of photograms in The New Typography, where objects were exposed directly on light-sensitive plates in the darkroom.
This technique, as well as photomontage, where photographic images were juxtaposed and related to lettering, opened up a variety of possibilities ranging from advertisements to covers for politically charged underground publications.
There was a strong affinity between the New Typography and industrial manufacturers: German photographer and designer Max Burchartz (18871961) used photomontage to create a trade prospectus for the Bochumer Company, a manufacturer of industrial parts for machines and railway switching equipment (fig.
9.48).
For Burchartz, the power of the photograph was its unmediated, truthful representation of the visible world in comparison with the more interpretive techniques of drawing and illustration.
In addition to providing the viewer with a general idea of the companys products, the Constructivist-inspired composition is asymmetrical and uses diagonal shapes to create a sense of drama and dynamism characteristic of modern transportation.
The prospectus cover is at least partially promotional, whereas the content of the companys catalog was more strongly informational.
Burchartz used photography and layout effectively to familiarize readers with products along with printed descriptive information and consistency from product to product and page to page, using printers rules for spacing and visual continuity.
The relationship between information and promotion was at times fluid; Tschichold believed that the New Typography had a role to play in all types of printed materials, including advertising and promotion, in which more visual approaches to communication functioned with immediacy and effectiveness.
Max Burchartz and Johannes Canis, trade prospectus for Bochumer Verein für Bergbau und Gussstahlfabrikation (Bochum Association for Mining and Cast Iron Manufacture), 11 ${ ^ 3 } / _ { 4 } \times 8 ~ { ^ 1 } / _ { 4 }$ in $( 3 0 \times 2 1$ cm), Bochum, Germany, 1925.
Private collection.
German Dada artist and communist activist John Heartfield (18911968) also used photography effectively in graphic design as an instrument of political commentary and agitation.
Unlike the work of the Constructivists in Russia who were part of a system of state-sponsored propaganda, Heartfields oeuvre in Germany during the 1930s was an underground effort meant to attract working-class attention and undermine Nazi authority after the fall of the Weimar Republic.
Many of his works appeared on the covers of the communist journal AIZ (Workers’ Illustrated Newspaper).
Heartfields posters and covers were often cut-and-pasted together, then re-photographed for printing.
The power of the composed images derives from the contradiction between an image with familiar associations and an unfamiliar, even opposite meaning.
The contrast is heightened through the objective and impersonal qualities of photography.
With increasing technical proficiency, the designers manipulations of the medium became less readily apparent, and the power of manipulation more provocative.
This technique was common in Dada collage, but often more complex, open-ended, at times humorous and playful in its interpretation.
There is little humor (except perhaps black humor) in Heartfields designs: his image for an issue of AIZ in 1932 (fig.
9.49) is entitled the meaning of Geneva. The image juxtaposes the League of Nations Building (forerunner to the United Nations) with the Swiss flag turning into the Nazi swastika, a sword, and a dead dove.
The end of peace seems to be the clear conclusion for the viewer to draw; in 1932 a demonstration in Geneva against the Nazi Party had resulted in the death of several activists, and in 1933 Germany withdrew from the League, as part of an effort to rearm despite restrictions imposed by the Versailles Treaty at the end of World War I.
John Heartfield, Der Sinn von Genf, cover for AIZ (Arbeiter Illustrierte Zeitung: das Illustrierte Volksblatt), 15 × 11 in (38 × Whether for advertising or in the context of shaping public opinion politically, artists, as well as governments and businessmen, recognized that photography was a mass medium with great powers of persuasion.
After departing the Bauhaus in 1928, Herbert Bayer worked for an advertising agency in Berlin and was art director for the German fashion magazine die neue linie (the new line; his typography for the magazine used all lower-case sans serif lettering).
Covers for die neue linie employed high-quality four-color printing technology.
Bayer took advantage of the resources of this high-end commercial publication to utilize the techniques of montage and photomontage extensively, exploring expressive possibilities with the more varied technical means at his disposal.
Results were often startling and provocative juxtapositions of scale that triggered viewers associations with tourism or contemporary events.
Aside from the monoweight sans serif used for the title, text was rarely used on cover art.
A cover from 1930 is a study in reduction and contrast (fig.
9.50).
Bayer constructs an image of Mediterranean travel, suggested by a bright blue ground, and a simplified, slightly oblique view of a sunlit Doric temple seen from below.
A fashionably dressed woman with a modern kneelength skirt stands on the stereobate.
Projecting from the entablature is the large head of a second female figure wearing a fashionable cloche hat.
Her heavy eyelids suggest a comparison with the so-called Severe style of Greek sculpture (and its psychological detachment) in the early fifth century BCE, reinforcing the connection between idealized past and present.
Herbert Bayer, cover for die neue linie, 14 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 10 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (36.5 × 26.7 cm), Leipzig, 1930.
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Herbert Bayer Archive.
New Typography practitioners found numerous commercial outlets for their modern approach in advertising and other forms of graphic communication.
Magazine art direction, as practiced by Bayer and elsewhere in Europe and the United States during the later 1920s, was one outlet, in which photography and double-page spreads were creatively explored.
Even the Nazi Party in Germany marshaled techniques of photomontage to mobilize support and foster loyalty to the party and to their leader, Adolf Hitler.
A poster from 1936 (fig.
9.51), by an artist known only as Leonid, superimposes the image of the plain, standardized Peoples Radio against a birds-eye view of a vast crowd that bleeds to the edge of the frame.
The radio was first manufactured in 1933 to promote access to Hitlers pubic addresses.
The juxtaposition combined with the bold text signify radio as a form of virtual reality, a substitute for actually being at a rally, reinforcing solidarity and communal listening, evidence for the reassuring myth of a vast nation unified behind a single voice.
In place of modern sans serif lettering, the traditional, nationalistic German Blackletter type reads All of Germany listens to the Führer with the Peoples Receiver.
Leonid, Ganz Deutschland hört den Führer mit dem Volksempfänger (All of Germany listens to the Führer with the People’s Receiver), lithograph, 47 × 33 <sup>1</sup>/ in (119.4 × 84.8 cm), printed by Preussischer Druckerei und Verlgs AG, Berlin, 1936.
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Miami Beach.
As in much contemporary poster art from the Soviet Union in the later 1920s and 1930s, the Nazi government favored idealized monumental images of healthy youthful workers and athletes as a form of patriotic nation building.
Both illustration and photography promoted a sense of duty and sacrifice at times on the part of all citizens toward the good of all, as seen, for instance, in an anonymous poster of 1937 (fig.
9.52).
In this example, images of young workers against a background of factories are carefully placed below two clean-shaven soldiers with swastika armbands on their sleeves, creating a stable pyramidal composition illustrating the phrase Students to Work! There also seems to be an identity between technical work, including construction and industrial production, and the German army.
This theme is echoed in patriotic posters in Allied countries in both of the twentieth centurys world wars (see fig.
10.49).

## 9.52 Anonymous, Studenten an’s Werk! (Students to Work!), poster, color lithograph, 46 <su
p>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 32 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (117.8 × 83.2 cm), published by Deutschen GmbH, Berlin, 1937.
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Miami Beach.
Notwithstanding instances of their appropriation of New Typography techniques, the Nazi Party in Germany was suspicious of the activities of the Bauhaus and other independent artists and designers sympathetic to Constructivism.
Tschichold, as well as Paul Renner, fell victim to these suspicions, and after being arrested in 1933 Tschichold fled to Switzerland, where he continued to work as a freelance designer.
Other graphic designers were not so lucky: Dutch graphic designer H.
N.
Werkman (18821945), who had produced experimental typography in the Netherlands in the 1920s and 1930s, began publishing illustrated stories critical of the Nazis, who had invaded and occupied the country beginning in May 1940.
He was arrested and executed by firing squad in 1945.
At certain times, and in particular under authoritarian and repressive regimes, printing, as well as graphic design, have been dangerous professions.
In time, Tschichold came to regret the polemical tone of his own early writings, recognizing that no single typeface or approach to layout can meet the varied demands for legibility and promotion required of every printing need or for every audience.
In short, there were authoritarian, dogmatic implications of the New Typography; Tschichold instead avoided ideology in favor of a more flexible dialogue among designer, text, publisher, and audience.
As a tool of communication, he believed that creative modern graphic design should not be determined by dogmatic principles nor imposed upon every task.
His initial enthusiasm for a new form of visual communication was tempered by his professional experience during and after World War II, an acknowledgment of and respect for difference and for history.
Outside of Germany, Switzerland, and the Soviet Union, several designers took an interest in the New Typography.
Henryk Berlewi (18941967) established the advertising firm Reklama Mechano in Warsaw, Poland.
His sans serif typography, asymmetrical layout, ample white space, and abstract geometric shapes for advertisement are certainly in sympathy with the guidelines of the New Typography, while a statement from 1924 appears both as a rejection of individualism and an embrace of the dynamism of a modern lifestyle accessible to all: Art must break with the practices of the perfumed, perverse, hypersensitive, hysterical, romantic, individualistic, boudoir-type art of yesterday.
It must create a new language of forms, available to all and in harmony with the rhythm of life. Both tendencies appear in advertisements encouraging companies to use radio as a form of advertising.
In figure 9.53, the printers rules and diagonal type of different weights suggest not only the electronic communication of information but also the antennae of a modern radio tower.

## 9.53 Henryk Berlewi, advertisement for radio station advertising, c. 1924, illustrated in
Jacques Damase’s Révolution typographique depuis Stéphane Mallarmé, Geneva, 1966.

## Britain
and Modern Design In Britain, a number of artists with varied backgrounds took an interest in modern visual communication.
Edward Johnston (18721944), a master typographer and teacher who designed decorative initials for the Doves Press established by Emery Walker and T.
J.
Cobden-Sanderson in Hammersmith (see here and fig.
5.5), created a sans serif typeface for the London Underground in 1916 that remains in use to this day (fig.
9.54).
The illustration also includes the London Underground logo, a pictogram of a locomotive wheel reduced to a circle with horizontal bar that was used throughout the system to identify stations on walls, benches, and printed schedules.
The commission for this sans serif typeface for the expanding transportation network came from Frank Pick (18781941), who at that time was Manager for Underground Electric Railways.
Pick also commissioned posters from a number of younger artists to upgrade the appearance of Underground stations and advertise travel and promote the use of public transportation.

## JOHNSTON
This broadsheet is set in Johnston type.
Edward Johnston (1872-1944) was one of the followers of William Morris (1834-1896) who took a leading part in reviving an interest in good lettering after the decadence of the late-Victorian fashions.
In 1916 Johnston was commissioned by Frank Pick (1878-1941) to design a special fount for the exclusive use of London's Underground and its associated companies.
The resulting Johnston sans-serif type was the forerunner of many sans-serif founts both in England and abroad, including that of Eric Gill (1882-1940) who was Johnston's friend and pupil in-this specialised field of design.
Johnston is the standard type used for all official signs and notices throughout the London Transport system, and it is also used, where appropriate, for much of London Transport's general typographical publicity.

tudents was Eric Gill (18821940), a sculptor who developed a family of typefaces known as Gill Sans (fig.
9.55) for the British Monotype Corporation in 1928.
The London and North Eastern Railway used Gill Sans for all of their printed materials.
Whether proprietary or not, designers and foundries were happy to oblige corporate customers who wanted to unify print and signage through a unique typeface that formed part of a branding strategy.
Historians generally find the British sans serif typefaces less mechanical and geometric than their continental counterparts, though they certainly rely more upon compass and straight edge than calligraphic faces based more directly upon the Latin alphabet. # ABCDEFGHIJKLMN OPQRSTUVWXYZ? abcdefghijklm nopqrstuvwxyz!
1234567890 9.55 Eric Gill, Gill Sans typeface, 1928, line drawing by John Langdon.
Both Johnston and Gill, like Tschichold, wrote frequently on typography for trade journals, contributing practical, aesthetic, historical, and social commentary on the subject.
Many were published in the journals The Fleuron and Signature.
Both men explored the advantages of sans serif typography and were eager to expand its application, particularly in the transportation industry, where clear signage and immediate recognition of information often at a distance were primary considerations.
At the same time, they continued to produce typefaces of great sophistication and subtlety based upon Latin letterforms and the detailed study of historic types for British Monotype and private presses.
Eric Gills Perpetua, for instance, released in 1929 and seen on the cover of a book of Gills essays (fig.
9.57), has long ascenders and descenders in the lower case, as well as a gradual narrowing of the strokes of letters such as d or p toward their stems.
Our example also includes Gills woodcut illustration, whose graphic character is typical of private press publications of the period using traditional letterpress printing. # ART NONSENSE AND OTHER ESSAYS BY ERIC GILL LONDON CASSELL & CO., LTD. & FRANCIS WALTERSON 1929 9.57 Eric Gill, Perpetua typeface, 1929. # ABCDEFGHIJKLMN OPQRSTUVWXYZ? abcdefghijklm nopqrstuvwxyz!
1234567890 Stanley Morison, Times New Roman typeface, 1932, line drawing by John Langdon.
Stanley Morison (18891967) of British Monotype supervised the design of several typefaces derived from historical precedent but adapted to the requirements of modern, high-volume printing technology.
His best-known face was developed in collaboration with advertising artist Victor Lardent (19051968) for the London Times, known as Times New Roman (TNR; fig.
9.56).
First printed in 1932, Times New Roman has been widely praised for its legibility combined with economical considerations such as shortened ascenders and descenders that reduce the space between lines in the text.
Gill, Johnston, and Morison each invented or supervised the development of fonts adapted to new production technologies, often focusing upon body text rather than titling or display.
They explored the use of sans serif typography and were open-minded to its advantages, but their own training and experience prevented them from adopting it exclusively.
Tschichold reached the same conclusion, probably for the same reason: in book design, serif typefaces and symmetrical layouts remained a direct and effective means of communication.
Some of those principles may be seen in the work of Edward Young (19132003), who designed book covers for the series of paperback books published by Penguin.
These books, issued first in 1935 and slightly modified by Tschichold in 1949 when he began working for Penguin, were certainly modern in the sense of being small, inexpensive, portable, and thus geared to a more active lifestyle, as well as simply and economically designed.
The paper covers used horizontal bands of bright color at top and bottom (color-coded for the type of literature), with the title set in sans serif against a white background.
The design, along with the Penguin logo, identified the book as part of a series, with the parent company (The Bodley Head) set vertically to each side of the bold black title, printed in Gill Sans Bold (fig.
9.58).
Edward Young, book cover for Penguin paperback, 7 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 4 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (18 × 10.8 cm), London, 1936.
In many ways, book and type designers in England in the interwar period continued the tradition of great typographers from the eighteenth century described above and revived by William Morris in the late nineteenth century.
Certainly many aspects of the industry had changed.
Commercial printing had expanded, the half-tone screen permitted the mechanical reproduction of photographs, and typographers had to take into consideration the way in which mechanical typesetting affected the look of a printed page.
The design of new type required a combination of invention, a respect for tradition, knowledge of industrial process, and a feeling for the purposes of and audiences for printed communication.
The collaboration and dialogue within these large typefounding companies, which included the viewpoints of consultants such as Morison, designers, and printers, remain a vital part of the history of graphic design, as printed materials served increasingly varied roles in the modern world and vied with newer massmedia technology such as radio.
One expression of that dialogue is a brief but famous essay published in 1930 by Beatrice Warde (19001969), who worked at the Monotype Corporation.
In The Crystal Goblet, Warde uses the metaphor of a wine glass to describe the ideal typeface: like a crystal goblet, it should reveal rather than obscure its content, and otherwise be invisible. Warde could not have been referring to advertising type or to the ways in which graphic designers were experimenting with the interaction of type and image.
Her subject was body text for book printing and private reading, and in that venerable but limited context, the metaphor resonated with her professional readership, as well as being compatible with a Modernist aesthetic preference for the reduction of mass and decorative excess seen in examples of tubularsteel furniture or interior design.
Penguins inexpensive and portable paperbacks were geared to the modern lifestyles of commuters traveling by or waiting for trains, and a more compact and casual form for storing those books was manufactured by the Isokon Company in England (founded in 1931) through their Donkey bookcase (fig.
9.59), designed by Vienna-trained architect and émigré Egon Riss (19011964) and manufactured beginning in 1939.
Certainly non-traditional in form and making use of curved panels of thin molded plywood (imported from Estonia), the bookcase was also small and portable, and the dimensions of its asymmetrical shelves were designed to hold Penguin paperbacks stacked either upright or on their sides.
The U-shaped form in the center was meant for a folded newspaper, while the ends playfully resembled the ears of a reductive donkey.
The Isokon company was founded by Jack Pritchard (18991992), who hired architect Wells Coates (18951958) to design the Lawn Road Flats apartment complex in Hampstead, north London, in 1934, aimed at young professionals rather than workingclass occupants.
Egon Riss, bookcase (“Penguin Donkey”), plywood, 16 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 23 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 17 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (41.9 × 59.1 × 43.8 cm), manufactured by Isokon Furniture, London, 1939.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
As Vice-President of the London Passenger Transport Board (established in 1933 through the merger of remaining independent service companies), Frank Pick again had the opportunity to apply skills of visual communication to issues of communication and identity in the public transportation industry.
Pick created a comprehensive and cohesive visual identity for the London Underground transportation system.
For the public, the unified identity system created the impression of order, reliability, compatibility, and control among the various lines and interchanges that comprise the Underground transit system.
Colorful travel posters on station walls reminded travelers to consider exploring the attractions of urban and suburban London.
An example is American-born McKnight Kauffers (18901954) Winter Sales poster illustrated in figure 9.60.
A group of women is swept into the vortex of a pattern of swirling lines and cool colors suggesting the unpleasant experience of shopping on a wet wintry day, and reminding us to avoid such discomfort by traveling under ground.
The simplified forms and lack of consistent viewpoint contrast with more conventional illustrative techniques used in other contemporary travel and advertising posters.
For the employees, visual identity created the sense of a single entity, while the newly formed London Transport Board (LTB) was previously composed of competing private companies.
Other series of posters reassured passengers of the safety of the system.

## McKnight
Kauffer, Winter Sales poster, 1922.
For a new map of the LTBs routes, Pick turned to an industrial draftsman named Henry Beck to reduce the confusion and uncertainty of navigating the vast interconnected routes of the system.
The map (fig.
9.61) is a model of reduction to efficiently communicate information, based upon a geometric grid, and limiting the direction of routes to angles of 90 and 45 degrees.
In this way the parallel lines not only make the system itself appear carefully planned, but also make it easier for the traveler to locate stations and connections between routes when changes are necessary.
The design assists commuters and visitors by breaking down barriers that inhibit the use of a service that might otherwise appear confusing, using color coding to identify the interconnected routes as if part of a well-planned system.
As noted by Adrian Forty, the simplicity of the London Underground map was not in every respect a virtue.
The map had no uniform sense of scale to gauge distances between stops or walking distances between stations when line changes were necessary.
One result was that suburban locations often seemed far closer to the center of the city than they were.
Such distortions might indeed make what looked like a simple trip from Piccadilly to Hampstead or Walthamstow into more of an adventure than a tourist had bargained for.
Yet aside from the deception (and perhaps the weather), the trip still remains worth the while.
Picks strategies for London Transport engage several related approaches to design: posters advertised appealing leisure activities or destinations related to Underground travel and were also works of art displayed in the midst of the everyday activities of commuters and other travelers; the signage used a combination of consistent lettering and distinctive symbols for easy recognition and familiarity, becoming mainstays of corporate identity; and the Underground map used a grid to make the complex appear simple and inviting, reducing the fear of getting lost or confused as well as removing an impediment to intercity and suburban travel.
While we may rightly refer to the London Underground map as an example of information design and public service, it is difficult not to see the revised map as a form of promotion that made concessions to accuracy in order to reduce resistance.
H.
C.
Beck, map of the London Underground, chromolithograph, 6 ${ \cdot } ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 9$ in (15.7 × 22.6 cm), 1933.
London Transport Museum.
Geometric abstraction is also found elsewhere in the transportation industry, for instance as the basis for transportation symbols or pictograms designed in the early 1970s for airports (see fig.
13.37).
Austrian sociologist Otto Neurath (18821945) initiated the Isotype Movement in Vienna (International System Of TYpographic Picture Education) before moving to the Netherlands in 1934 (see here).
Neurath worked with Marie Reidemeister Neurath (18981986; they married in 1941) and artist Gerd Arntz (19001988) to create a series of pictorial symbols to communicate statistics in a concise and direct manner intended to encourage the sharing of information on social and economic issues with the general public, on view in Neuraths Museum of Society and Economy founded in 1925 (Gesellschafts- und Wirtschaftsmuseum).
Isotype charts tracked statistics on income growth and distribution, population, and industrial production to inform the public and provide a basis for distinguishing between fact and political propaganda.
Isotypes reliance on reductive symbols eschewing perspective and depending upon consistency is parallel to the Modernist belief in underlying forms as the basis for a new and inherently democratic visual language.
Like the London Underground map, the Isotype Movement was a product of its time rather than neutral or objective.
The choice of subjects and conventions of representation, whether subtle or blatant, were often selected to promote a particular point of view: Marie Neurath commented that when she designed charts in the Soviet Union the goal was to represent statistics to demonstrate progress, what graphic designer and historian Ellen Lupton has called a motivated context. Neurath left Vienna for the Netherlands in 1934 and then London; their example was followed by their student Rudolf Modley in the United States during World War II and Peter Alma in the Netherlands (fig 9.13 and here).

## Scandinavia
and Modern Design In the interwar period, designers in Scandinavian nations developed original approaches to addressing social, commercial, and aesthetic issues raised by modern industrial technology in an increasingly international context, steering a middle ground between standardization and efficiency on the one hand, and psychological considerations of modern living and the persistence and revitalization of regional craft workshops and national traditions on the other.
This approach continued to attract attention and praise internationally after World War II (see here onward), and helps to demonstrate both the widespread acknowledgment of Modernist ideas and their flexible adaptation.
The trajectory of Nordic design in the interwar period might begin in Sweden when large glass manufactories such as Orrefors hired artists like Edward Hald (18831980) and Simon Gate (18831945) to design modern art glass for a mostly luxury international market.
Hald had studied painting with Henri Matisse and examples of his work in etched crystal glass, as well as those of Gate, were displayed at the 1925 Paris Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes.
Halds designs shared characteristics with contemporary work being produced by Lalique in Paris and later by Steuben in the United States (see here) and are seen in a festive 1920s blown glass vase depicting Girls Playing Ball (fig.
9.62) with accompanying underplate.
Edward Hald, “Girls Playing Ball” vase, blown glass, engraved with underplate, 11 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 9 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (29.5 × 23.5 cm), Orrefors Glassworks, 1920.
At the same time, a Swedish organization known as the Svenska Slöjdföreningen, under the direction of art historian and critic Gregor Paulsson (18991977), encouraged manufacturers to adopt standards based upon practicality, and strongly influenced by the German Werkbund (see here).
Swedish exhibitions at the time focused upon reform rather than revolution, directed toward people of small financial means and incorporating variations upon traditional decorative motifs such as the Lily Blue (Liljblå) pitcher and serving plate, part of a ceramic service designed by Wilhelm Kåge in 1917 (fig.
9.63).
But by the mid-1930s, a Scandinavian approach to modern design was becoming identifed, which embraced modern industrial materials and manufacturing methods while preserving elements of national identity and traditional craft.
Wilhelm Kåge, “Lily Blue” (Liljblå) tableware, manufactured by Gustavsberg, 1917.
This Scandinavian approach to Modernism found expression in furniture designed by Swedish architect Gunnar Asplund (18851940), but is perhaps better associated with the molded plywood and laminated birch chair designs of Finnish architect Alvar Aalto (18981976).
Aaltos furniture was featured in an international exhibition in Paris in 1937, at a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1938, and at the 1939 New York Worlds Fair, for which he designed the Finnish pavilion.
His armchairs (fig.
9.64), still manufactured by Artek, the company he established in Helsinki in 1935, were inspired by the light tubular-metal furniture designed by Marcel Breuer at the Bauhaus (see fig.
9.31).
While committed to the use of modern industrial processes of manufacture, Aalto preferred plywood to tubular metal, and experimented with laminated birch (although bentwood chairs made of beech were also manufactured in Germany and Czechoslovakia by Thonet).
Birch was an abundant natural resource in Finland, traditionally used for lightweight laminated wooden skis, that Aalto adapted to the structural requirements of a variety of chair designs (including those based upon the cantilever principle).
The armchair was first designed for the Paimio Tuberculosis Sanitarium in Finland, built between 1929 and 1932, where hygiene was a consideration and molded plywood required less maintenance than upholstery.
Moreover, the quantity of furnishings needed for the commission allowed Aalto to give serious consideration to efficient quantity production; in particular, the use of laminated rather than carved woods permitted uniformity and ease of assembly.
Thus while making use of industrial materials and committed to their advantages in terms of serial production and the economical use of materials, Aaltos molded designs incorporated organic forms and preserved the natural grain and finish of wood surfaces.
As a result his experimentation in molded industrial furniture appears softer than the more gridlike and often austere contemporary furniture in metal or wood constructed from standardized components (see figs.
9.31 and 9.37).
Whether for individual residences or public buildings and institutions, Aaltos furniture reduces mass and is designed to maximize open space and flexible, informal arrangements of furnishings.
In place of geometric purity and to a certain extent the cool formality of contemporary European Modernist designers of the later 1920s and 1930s, his designs maintain a connection with nature, and his furnishings offer a closer analogy with the freer and more irregular abstract forms of Automatic Surrealism.
Alvar Aalto, Paimio armchair, laminated birch and plywood, manufactured by Huonekalu-ja Rakennustyötendas, Turku, Finland, $2 6 \times 2 3 ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 } \times 3 4 ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 }$ in (66 × 60.3 × 88.6 cm), 1931.
Aalto explored such connections further in the design of glassware that also suggests analogies with the suggestive forms of Automatic Surrealism, particularly the sculptures of Belgian-born sculptor Jean Arp or the meandering shapes found in the paintings of Catalan artist Joan Miró.
This can be seen in Aaltos Savoy vase of 1936 (fig.
9.65), with its amoebalike forms and activation of negative space.
In all design media he collaborated with his wife Aino (born Mendelin, 18941949).
Aaltos approach emerges in the following excerpt from a speech he delivered to the Swedish Arts and Crafts Society in 1935.
The expansion of the rational basis for industrial design to include psychological and varied aesthetic considerations distinguishes Aaltos understanding of modern design from contemporary approaches to prefabrication and standardization, in which industrial design was often viewed as a vehicle for solving social problems on a mass scale, tied to an ideology of universal collective need rather than individual expression: We can say that one of the ways to arrive at a more and more humanely built environment is to expand the concept rational.
We should rationally analyze more of the requirements connected with the object than we have to date....
A series of requirements that can be made of almost every object and that up to now has been given scant consideration surely belongs in the sphere of another science-psychology.
As soon as we include psychological requirements, or, let us say, when we can do so, then we will have already expanded the rational method to an extent that, to a greater degree than previously, has the potential of excluding inhuman results.
Also absent from Aaltos comments and design practice are the utopian proclamations, the rejection of the past, the revolutionary zeal, heralding of the new man and new woman, and the polemical tone that characterizes the more politically charged rhetoric of other interwar Modernist movements.
While embracing the advantages of industrial technology, perhaps nothing better illustrates the difference between reform and revolution than the careers of the couple in their approach toward change and modernity.
9.65 Alvar Aalto, Savoy vase, mold-blown glass, height 5 <sup>1</sup>/ in (14 cm), manufactured by Karhula-Ittala, Finland.
Alvar Aalto Museum, Finland.
In Sweden, the use of laminated woods and organic forms was pioneered in the 1930s by Bruno Mathsson (19071988), who manufactured original furniture designs in a family workshop.
His 1934 armchair (fig.
9.66) consists of a broad curving seat with webbing rather than upholstery, the sculptural contour of which conforms to Mathssons studies and measurements for ideal sitting positions for the human body for a variety of tasks, including simply lounging. The legs of the chair repeat and balance the gently curving shape of the combined seat and back, while the arms provide additional structural support for the back.
9.66 Bruno Mathsson, armchair, beech and birch plywood, hemp upholstery, 32 <sup>3</sup>/ × 19 <sup>1</sup>/ × 29 <sup>1</sup>/ in $( 8 3 \times 4 9 \times 7 4$ cm), manufactured by Karl Mathsson, Vämamo, Sweden, 1934.
Danish designers also contributed to the development of Scandinavian modern design both before and after World War I.
Silversmith Georg Jensen (18661935) established an international reputation for original high-quality handcrafted designs for cutlery and tableware, and was represented at the Paris International Exhibition of 1925 and earlier in St.
Louis in 1904 (see here and fig.
6.57).
At the same time, however, some Danish designers took an interest in standardization stemming from the Werkbund, including furniture maker Kaare Klint (18881954).
In addition to reducing or even eliminating carved ornament while retaining the beauty of natural wood surfaces, Klint based his designs upon studies undertaken in the Furniture Department of the Royal Danish Academy of Arts, which he helped to found and where he served as an instructor.
The dimensions of Klints sideboard (fig.
9.67) were based upon standard sizes for dishes, cups, saucers, and other dining-room utensils, and its sliding doors required less handwork in the fitting of hinges or need for pullers.
Klints furniture was handcrafted and employed a variety of woods selected for the appeal of grain and color.
The simple geometric forms and absence of decoration in Klints furniture bear some similarity to the elemental geometry of European Modernist designers, though a resemblance to examples of Chinese wooden cabinets has also been noted by historians as a precedent.
But Klints motivation for a new and modern design was not primarily social or even industrial: his furniture was time-consuming to produce and expensive to purchase, restrained aesthetically but hardly austere.
He believed that through the study of everyday household tasks like sitting or preparing a table for dining, designers could determine lasting solutions to address and shape the daily rituals of modern living.
He offered a response to modern concerns that combined a variety of perspectives at the time  a problem-solving activity that did not preclude craftsmanship, poetry, and the application of elements of scientific management.
Kaare Klint, mahogany sideboard, $3 7 \mathrm { ~ } ^ { 9 } / _ { 1 6 } \times$ 59 $1 ^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 2 4$ <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (95.4 × 152 × 62 cm), manufactured by Rudolf Rasmussens Snedkerier, Denmark, 1930.

## Taking
Stock: Was Interwar Modernism Universal?
Chapter 9 introduces many canonical examples of modern design in the twentieth century.
Throughout the chapter the words international and universal appear, for instance, in the name of Herbert Bayers universal typeface (see fig.
9.32) or the title of the Museum of Modern Arts 1932 exhibition of architectural models whose curators identified and promoted an international style (see here).
But just what did these designers and critics mean by these terms?
Were they thinking or projecting globally?
Given the selection of examples from the MoMA exhibition and Bayers Latin letterforms, one might be wary of employing either international or universal to their efforts.
Despite universal pretensions and an avowed rejection of the past and nationalism, the expressions of the international style were not only varied (see above on Scandinavia) but also deeply Eurocentric, stemming from a faith in a particular and selective adaptation of industrial technology, minimizing difference and offering a solution to resolve Western polemics, whether between fine and applied art, art and engineering, or individual and society.
Such distinctions do not always apply in non-Western cultures, and they tend to ignore, for instance, Chinese furniture as a source of inspiration for the furniture of Danish designer Kaare Klint.

## Chapter
10 Design, Industry, and Advertising in the United States In the United States, craft-based industries tended to remain conservative in terms of design until the mid-1920s, unaffected by the self-consciously modern aesthetic approaches of Art Deco designers in France and elsewhere in Europe.
Following World War I, the United States pursued a policy of isolationism, limiting earlier waves of immigrants amid fears of social unrest and communist agitation in the immediate wake of the Russian Revolution.
On the recommendation of then Secretary of Commerce Herbert Hoover, the United States declined to participate in the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes in Paris because, in Hoovers opinion, manufacturers were unable to comply with the conditions that specified displays of objects that were modern and original.
The United States did, however, dispatch a large delegation to the exhibition, headed by the President of the American Association of Museums, Charles Richards, whose charge included organizing a traveling exhibition of works selected from the Paris exhibition.
The traveling exhibition, and others sponsored by institutions such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art, stimulated public and commercial interest in newer designs, aimed mostly at a sophisticated audience.
By the later 1920s, ensembles of interior furnishings by Jean Dunand and other French designers of modern luxury goods could be seen in the windows of New York department stores such as Lord and Taylor and Macys.
American retailers and advertising executives began to recognize and publicize the commercial benefit of contemporary artistic designs in a wide range of consumer goods.
Museums promoted modern styles along broadly educational lines, emphasizing the integration of art into the lives of the middle class and the ability of the decorative arts to raise the level of public taste and contribute to cultural uplift.
This general receptivity to modern design in the United States was accompanied by a wave of émigré designers from Europe including Peter Muller-Munk (19041967; Germany), Raymond Loewy (18931986; France), Ilonka Kárász (18961981; Hungary), and Alexey Brodovitch (18981971; Russia, by way of Paris) who began successful careers as consultants in a wide range of media from the mid-1920s.
In addition, magazines such as Vogue and Vanity Fair used photography and illustration to promote an idealized image of modern life associated with fashion, sport, travel, entertainment, and other active leisure activities.
Eliel Saarinen, side chairs, fir with black and ocher paint, red horse-hair upholstery, $3 7 ~ ^ { 5 } / _ { 8 } \times 1 7 \times 1 9 \mathrm { ~ i n ~ } ( 9 5 .

5$ cm), upholstery fabric by Loja Saarinen, 1929–1930.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art was one of eight venues for the traveling exhibition from Paris, and the museum continued to sponsor annual exhibitions devoted to modern decorative and industrial arts throughout the 1920s.
In such exhibitions a variety of new forms and new materials emerged.
These included the wooden (fir) chairs with flared backs accentuated by black painted vertical strips designed by émigré Finnish architect Eliel Saarinen (18731950; fig.
10.1), as well as the etched crystal glass bowls designed by Massachusetts-born sculptor Sidney Waugh (19041963) for the Steuben Glass company (fig.
10.2), the art-glass branch of the Corning Glass Company in Corning, New York.
10.2 Sidney Waugh, Gazelle bowl, cut glass with engraving, $7 ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 6 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (18.4 × 16.5 cm), manufactured by Steuben Glass, New York, 1935.
Toledo Museum of Art, Ohio.
Saarinen was named director of an artists community founded in 1923 by newspaper publisher George Booth in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, which became the Cranbrook Academy of Art and focused upon graduate-level fine and applied arts education.
Saarinens wife, Loja (18791968), was trained as an artist in Finland and initiated a handweaving workshop at Cranbrook.
Other American manufacturing companies produced artists designs for rugs and embroideries.
California-born Marguerite Zorach (18871968) studied painting in Paris but returned to the United States with her husband, sculptor William Zorach (18891966), where they were part of an artist community in Massachusetts.
Marguerite produced handhooked rugs featuring Fauve-inspired imagery and patterns.
She also experimented with the Indonesian technique of fabric dyeing known as batik.
Figure 10.6 is a Marguerite Zorach rug woven from wool and jute for the Crawford Shops in New York, dating to 1936.
Entitled Jungle, the rug makes use of muted red-orange, gray, and brown hues arranged in a densely packed composition that achieves remarkable unity through consistent tone and abstract organic shapes based upon birds and wild animals merged with landscape forms.
Marguerite Zorach, Jungle, handhooked rug, wool, jute, 42 × 60 in (106.7 × 152 cm), 1936.

10.4 Paul Frankl, Skyscraper bookcase, birch, lacquer, $8 4 \times 3 9 \times 1 4$ in $( 2 1 3 \times 9 9 \times 3 7$ cm), 1926.
Private collection.
Following the 1925 Paris exposition, several American manufacturers hired nativeborn as well as European émigré artists to design furniture and a variety of home furnishings in a contemporary style.
Such work often integrated a new angular vocabulary of expressive decoration that echoed the great set-back profiles and sculpted relief decoration of skyscrapers built between 1925 and 1930 in the United States.
Indeed, the term Skyscraper Style is sometimes used to refer to the expressive architecture and furnishings of the era, whether William van Alens Chrysler Building of 1927 or German-born Paul Frankls series of Skyscraper bookcases (fig.
10.4) from 1926.
Architects such as Raymond Hood (18811934), who designed the McGraw-Hill Building in Manhattan, and Ely-Jacques Kahn (18841972) played a leading role in creating furniture and interiors showcasing industrial materials such as aluminum and angular geometric decoration.
An example is Donald Deskeys (18941989) chrome-plated metal and glass table lamp of 1927 (fig.
10.5), manufactured by a company he managed with a partner and illustrated in House & Garden magazine in 1929.
Hoods Business Executives Office for The Architect and the Industrial Arts exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art early in 1929 (fig.
10.3) features furniture whose aluminum structural elements relate to the aluminum mullions in the large glass picture window at the rear.
Carpet and sofa use rectangular patterns, while the desk, curtains, and sofa frame angular and tapered forms.
Despite the smooth, industrial aluminum surfaces, some of the elements in Hoods model office owe a debt to French Art Deco, for instance the sunrays that frame the sides of the upholstered sofa on the far wall, a motif seen earlier in Edgar Brandts 1923 Cigognes d’Alsace panel (see fig.
8.17).

American artist Ruth Reeves (18921966), who had studied painting with Fernand Léger in Paris, designed textiles that featured the new vocabulary of skyscraper and abstract Cubist-inspired forms.
Her Electric design (fig.
10.7), manufactured by the Sloane Carpet Company in 1930, uses zig-zag overlapping shapes to convey the speed and man-made power of electricity, while Kneeland Green (18921956) used stenciled letterforms to create dense abstract patterns such as Cheerio in 1927 for printed fabrics and wall coverings (fig.
10.8).
Such excitement for the accelerated pace of modern life in the metropolis is seen as well in the paintings of American artists such as Joseph Stella (18771946) and John Marin (18701953).
Textile designers also explored new processes and materials.
British-born Henriette Reiss (18891992) produced textiles using the technique of screen printing, as seen in her abstract Rhythm Series pattern of 1928 (fig.
10.9).
Reisss designs were applied directly or transferred to thin, porous screens of tightly woven silk.
After the non-image areas of the design were blocked out, fabric was placed beneath the screens, through which ink was pressed using a squeegee.
The ink passes through the design and is resisted elsewhere, and the screen may be reused for printing in more than one color.
The works of these artists demonstrate a reverence for the exhilarating and liberating character of the modern metropolis.
The aural equivalent of this sensibility is found in the African American jazz music that emerged in urban centers along the Mississippi River such as Kansas City, in Chicago, and also in the Harlem section of Manhattan.
The return of soldiers who served in World War I accelerated the pace of migration of African Americans from the rural South to cities of the industrial North, Midwest, and further west in search of higher pay, business opportunity, safety, and freedom from institutionalized segregation and violence, chronicled in a remarkable series of 60 panels by New York-based painter Jacob Lawrence titled The Great Migration in 1940 to 1941, several of which were reproduced in color in the business journal Fortune.
The African American migration and the culture it forged was itself spurred by technology: the railways brought migrants north (African Americans working as porters on passenger trains were the first to unionize and affiliate with the American Federation of Labor, in 1925), while commercial radio and the recording industry brought jazz music to the attention of white as well as Black listeners.
It would be difficult to accurately describe interwar design and culture in the United States without acknowledging its increasing diversity and vibrancy through the contributions of immigrants and migrants, despite their virtual absence in mass advertising and product promotion in this period.

Modern design in the United States during the later 1920s was strongly promoted through museum exhibitions and upscale department stores, and in architecture through the design and interiors of skyscrapers.
For the most part, the examples cited appealed to an up-scale market.
Certainly modern design reached a broader and more diverse public through illustrations and advertisements in mass-circulation magazines and in public entertainment through fashion and the constructed interior sets of the popular cinema.
In the later 1920s, decorative motifs derived from Cubism and Futurism began to appear in less expensive products as well.
Until the stock market crash in late 1929, industrial production was fueling an economic boom and lowerincome householders were able to aspire to the lifestyle of their wealthier countrymen and -women through the purchase of inexpensively manufactured personal items and domestic products.
Examples include Pittsburgh-born Reuben Haleys (18721933) Ruba Rombic line of faceted frosted-glass vases, designed for the Consolidated Lamp and Glass Company in the Pennsylvania town of Coraopolis, near Pittsburgh (fig.
10.10), and manufactured from 1928 until 1930.

5$ cm), manufactured by Consolidated Lamp and Glass Company, Pittsburgh, c.

Toledo Museum of Art, Ohio.
In ceramics, clean, modern shapes, original patterns, and bold colors are seen in the work of brothers Victor (19062008) and Donald (19112001) Schreckengost.
Victors activities were not limited to ceramics, but both brothers worked as consultant designers for small and large ceramic manufactories in Ohio during the 1930s, producing a variety of original designs.
An example is Donald Schreckengosts Tricorne tableware manufactured by the Salem China Company in 1933 (fig.
10.11).
Large manufactories such as Salem supplied tableware to middle- and working-class buyers distributed by Woolworths and other low-end retail chain stores as well as grocery stores.
While large-production potteries introduced contemporary designs such as Tricorne with thin walls, smooth finishes, bright colors, and novel shapes with sharply angled handles, traditional decorative patterns applied as printed decals rather than handpainted continued to dominate the eclectic consumer-driven mass market.
Even novelty tended to be less of a striking break with the past, as with the popular and widely imitated Yellowstone dinnerware introduced by the Homer Laughlin China Company of Ohio and West Virginia in the early 1920s (fig.
10.12).
As noted by historian Regina Blaszczyk, department-store and chain-store buyers as well as store managers exercised an enormous influence upon design, observing shoppers habits and selecting designs and shapes that appealed to the desire for attractive design that suited informal dining and a generally conservative taste.
Today this function is performed, and enhanced, by CCTV cameras in stores that track and record consumer behavior, which is used by marketers to influence design decisions.

## 10.12 Yellowstone dinnerware, manufactured by Homer Laughlin China Company, Ohio and West
Virginia, from Ladies’ Home Journal, October 1929.
Whether contemporary or traditional, consumers embraced design in the United States in the 1920s as proof of material and social progress, and the connection between design, progress, and modern life was strongly reinforced through advertising.
In his 1922 novel of middle-class American life, Babbitt, Sinclair Lewis described the billboards with crimson goddesses nine feet tall advertising cinema films, pipe tobacco, and talcum powder. Chum Frink, one of George Babbitts friends in the fictional city of Zenith, is a poet-turned-advertising copywriter.
Just as the poetry of advertising slogans left an uplifting impression in the readers mind, so design gave products like Georges new electric alarm clock an aura that made him happy simply to own it. It is possible that our own innate desire to create categories and distinguish between modern and traditional is belied by the realities of the marketplace: Babbitts electric alarm clock has a lighted phosphorescent dial but sounds like church bells, and Schreckengosts Tricorne design presents a novel shape for dinnerware yet is named for the eighteenthcentury three-cornered hats associated with the United States revolutionary past and the patriotic nostalgia it brings to mind.
It is contemporary with the popularity among consumers and collectors of Colonial Revival furniture, found in the construction of Colonial Williamsburg, Virginia, in the later 1920s and entrepreneurial promoters such as Wallace Nutting (18611941).

## Industrial
Design and Fordism Design change was slower to reach the large-scale mechanized industries that manufactured automobiles and electric or gas appliances for the home than the tableware and other domestic goods mentioned above.
Mechanized mass production extended to the manufacture of household appliances in the 1920s, and was admired almost without reservation by capitalist as well as socialist governments in Europe and the Soviet Union.
Standardized production vehicles such as the Model T Ford and electric appliances demonstrated the social benefits offered by machine production and assembly, extending the comforts and conveniences of modern living, formerly reserved for the wealthy, to the mass market through technology with less concern for individual consumer choice.
Such products exemplified the democratization of culture and widespread improvement in the general standard of living.
The Ford Company opened an automobile factory in Germany in 1924, and by 1929 the United States was responsible for more than 80 percent of automobile production worldwide.
American industrialization was seen as the basis for prosperity and economic growth.
Praise of business, the machine, and the assembly line had overtly religious overtones: skyscrapers were dubbed cathedrals of commerce, and Calvin Coolidge commented: The factory is a temple  the worker worships there. In the Soviet Union, Communist Party observers also praised the assembly line but criticized private ownership of the means of production, the exploitation of workers, and the uneven distribution of wealth under capitalism.
As argued above (see here), in the Soviet Union industrialization was linked with collectivization, requiring sacrifice of individual ownership in exchange for higher levels of production and equal distribution of its benefits for all by the state, to be realized through ambitious five-year plans.
The revolutionary success of the Ford Motor Company took place within a decade, and by 1927, when its production halted, more than 15 million Model T Fords had rolled off the assembly line, virtually identical in their black lacquer finish and traditional carriage-based body form.
Sometimes dubbed Fordism, this approach to industrial production was summarized by Henry Ford himself, with echoes of Adam Smiths encomium to the division of labor in a pin manufactory (see here): The way to make automobiles is to make one automobile like another automobile, to make them all alike, to make them come from the factory all alike, just like one pin is like another when it comes from a pin factory. The Model T suppressed elements of individual choice, artistic invention, and product differentiation associated with art and design  all effort concentrated upon the reduction of cost and the acceleration of routine and worker productivity in the plant under the strict supervision of management under pressure to meet ambitious production quotas.
Capital investment in equipment and the rationalization of labor mitigated against product differentiation; and, as pointed out by several observers, this combination of factors produced lower costs.
In 1916 the Model T sold for \$360, less than one-half its cost in 1910, and well below the cost of other domestic automobile manufacturers; in 1919 the cost for each model was \$265!
Without real competition in the marketplace, Fordism succeeded in delivering on the promise for personal transportation to an expanding middle- and working-class market.
And productivity was hardly limited to the automobiles themselves: service stations, paved roads, real-estate prices in vacation areas, and mechanics for service and repair represent only a handful of ancillary industries and services that blossomed as the direct result of the Model Ts success.
Unlike the German Werkbund, there was no movement or organization in the United States to forge an Industry Culture that considered a unified or national approach to the aesthetics of the products of mechanized mass production.
To help offset the pressures of the assembly line and the unrest caused by accelerated production schedules and the repetitive routine of the assembly line, Ford introduced a profit-sharing plan labeled the five-dollar day for workers in 1914.
In time, and through credit-purchase, factory workers were able to own their own Model T, turning workers into mass consumers.
Further concessions in the form of reduced working hours and benefits to labor occurred as the result of union organizing in the interwar years.
After World War II, paid vacations and a government-sponsored interstate highway system contributed to the emergence of a robust tourist industry.
As more Americans became owners of second cars and as the automobile became integrated into the leisure as well as work activities of the public, comfort, luxury, and styling increasingly influenced consumers decision to purchase new vehicles.
General Motors, formed in 1918 through the consolidation of a number of individual manufacturers under the leadership of its new president, Alfred P.
Sloan (18751966), responded to these consumer trends by establishing stronger ties to its retail dealers.
In time Sloans strategy was adopted by Ford, who could not fail to notice that market saturation and competition had slowed the pace of Model T purchases and that usedcar sales were beginning to outstrip demand for new cars (after all, older Fords were virtually identical to the most recent models).
General Motors began to distinguish their vehicles first through the introduction of variety in color, made possible by new enamel paints that dried almost as quickly as the standard black lacquer.
The company also introduced a series of minor styling changes and options for buyers to customize their purchases.
These are first seen in the 1923 Chevrolet Superior (fig.
10.13), the contours of which appear more unified and compact than those of Fords Model T.
General Motors also invested more heavily in advertising as a means to stimulate sales, a strategy with important ramifications that are more thoroughly discussed below.
In short, the automobile became not simply a means of transportation but, like fashion and other consumer goods for the home or for clothing, a reflection of personal taste, individual identity, and a means to measure self-improvement.
Chevrolet Superior, 1923.
General Motors Corporation, Flint, Michigan.

## Advertising,
Art, and the Selling of Modern Design in the United States The history of modern design in the United States in the interwar period cannot be written without stressing the importance of advertising in the formation of a culture of consumption. The overwhelming achievements of materials technology and mechanized mass-production technologies could not be sustained without exciting desire and channeling it through the sale of products.
Advertising functioned to erode traditional resistance to spending based upon the virtue of self-denial grounded in religious faith and social obligation.
Loosening the social constraints on leisure and consumption is among the themes of English author Elizabeth van Arnims 1922 novel The Enchanted April, in which a young married woman persuades an acquaintance to join her in renting an Italian villa (without their husbands) to escape dreary winter weather at home for the freedom to enjoy the pleasures of a fragrant springtime by the Mediterranean, enticed by a newspaper advertisement that began To those who appreciate wisteria and sunshine. Before the advent of television, the tools of advertising included commercial radio as well as print communication and its effective, provocative use of text, illustration, photography, layout, and typography.
Museum initiatives supporting modern decorative arts and a closer connection between fine and applied art dovetailed with the strategies of advertising agencies to build and strengthen the link between products and the hedonistic lifestyle of confident and energetic participants in the ever-changing modern scene.
In the 1920s, advertisements were decidedly upscale, promising charisma and success in exchange for the purchase of a wide variety of products ranging from toothpaste to toasters.
An example is a 1923 advertisement from American Vogue for a Dodge Brothers automobile (fig.
10.14).
The copy mentions the speed of the vehicle as well as the enthusiastic response of hunters, golfers, and polo players for the car, which acquired its very own aggressive personality to match that of the prospective owner: Wielders of the polo mallet, hunters of the moose, hard hitters from the tee  are enthusiastic about this car.
For them its virility and boundless eagerness to go have irresistible appeal. Advertisement for Dodge Brothers Senior Line, Vogue, 1923.
Advertisers defined an emerging good life, grounded in physical activity and experienced by an elite group of people engaged in active and social leisure pursuits with whom an increasingly diverse audience could identify through the products they purchased, the books and magazines they read, and the films they watched.
The triumphs and conflicts of this group formed the subjects of popular fiction in masscirculation magazines such as True Story and Ladies’ Home Journal, and included color illustrations to augment the frequently serialized stories.
Companies and the advertising agencies they hired to promote their products turned to artists and illustrators to provide suitable, usually idealized addressing figures for products in magazines and even on large billboards that lined the boulevards and highways of a more mobile American society.
Fueled by the success of persuasive posters in government-sponsored public relations campaigns to enlist recruits or sell war bonds during World War I, advertising agencies saw illustration as a vehicle to shape the consumer values shared by an expanding and increasingly heterogeneous mass market, although racism continued to limit opportunities for economic and social advancement for Black Americans.
Some companies promoted the use of fine art in advertising, part of an initiative to familiarize a broader audience with modern art and link companies with cultural uplift and education.
These ads often had little to do with products but rather established a paternalistic role for companies in support of values of quality, integrity, and culture.
An example is a 1927 advertisement by Philadelphia artist and illustrator Earl Horter (18811940), whose Futurist-inspired painting Rhapsody in Blue (the title of a 1924 piano and orchestra composition by George Gershwin) was reproduced in an advertisement for the renowned piano manufacturer Steinway (fig.
10.15).
Advertising executive Elmo Calkins (18681968) supported such an approach, and employed artists such as Horter to demonstrate that advertising art was in the public interest and enhanced the reputation of businesses.
Earl Horter, advertisement for Steinway piano with reproduction of Rhapsody in Blue, watercolor and graphite on board, 21 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 27 in (54.5 × 68.6 cm), 1927.
Private collection.
Many advertising executives, however, believed there was a difference between publicity and advertising.
They felt that the purpose of advertisements was to sell products, and that references to individual artists or to works of art focused attention upon the ad as an object, an end in itself, rather than as the vehicle for persuading a reader to purchase a product.
Art directors and consultants from the advertising industry recognized the importance of images in selling products, but also felt it was necessary, more often than not, to present familiar and recognizable images that could be easily grasped by a diverse public.
Companies turned to illustrators to accomplish this task, creating the idealized types with whom buyers readily identified and connected with products.
The blurring between illustration and advertising was felt as a constraint by Joseph Leyendecker, poster advertisement for Arrow Shirt and Collar Company, 1920s. some artists.
On one hand advertising provided a steady and lucrative income for their work, while on the other it could lead to stale repetition of formulaic representations at the expense of the individual expression that often formed the basis of their training at art academies.
In general the advertising profession equated effective techniques of persuasion with naturalism rather than with more modern abstract styles.
In the later 1920s and 1930s, art directors began to experiment with photography, typography, and layout in new ways that offered an alternative to illustration, particularly in fashion magazines, to excite viewer interest (see figs.
10.41 and 10.42).
Those experiments were often pioneered by émigré designers such as Alexey Brodovitch or M.
F.
Agha, who assumed the role of art director and contributed to establishing the professional practice of graphic design.
In the early part of the century, Charles Dana Gibsons (18671954) Gibson Girl provided an ideal for the modern active woman on numerous magazine covers.
As early as 1907, Joseph Leyendecker (18741951) created the Arrow Collar Man in a series of popular ads that drastically reduced the amount of text often found in magazine advertisements (fig.
10.16).
Leyendeckers chiseled, confident ideal may have been removed from the lives of white-collar working men, but any threat to the readers selfesteem created by the image offered at the same time its solution.
Buying an Arrow shirt collar reduced the fear of not conforming to the modern culture of business.
It is interesting to note that filmmaker and actor Charles Chaplins (18891977) recognizable silent film anti-hero represents an alternative to popular advertisements of the period; often victim rather than hero, Chaplin, along with comic actor and film director Buster Keaton (18951966), revealed some of the challenges and uncertainties of modern working-class life.
Another popular advertising image or ideal was McClelland Barclays Fisher Body Girl, appearing in advertisements for this manufacturer and supplier of automobile chassis to General Motors brands Chevrolet, Cadillac, Buick, Oldsmobile, and Pontiac (fig.
10.17).
This slender, well-dressed figure was usually found in the company of men in connection with cars, as well as on the covers of the Saturday Evening Post engaged in a variety of leisure pastimes.
McClelland Barclay, Fisher Body advertisement, American Magazine, 1928.
In 1927 General Motors (GM) hired Harley Earl (18931969) to head an Art and Color Section within all brand divisions of the giant corporation, based upon Earls success in redesigning the 1927 Cadillac Lasalle (fig.
10.18), a less expensive variation of the companys traditional luxury sedan.
Earl came to GM as a designer of custom automobiles, in which lower profiles and a more unified approach to body design, found in expensive European automobiles such as the Hispano-Suiza, were substituted for the traditional high chassis and collection of unrelated elements such as bumpers, wheel covers, and headlights of more standardized American cars.
One of Earls contributions as a designer for the automobile industry was to introduce new features that rarely required significant engineering changes or substantial capital investment in new machinery.
Providing choice and variety in the automobile market without significantly raising production costs constituted an industrial design strategy that was in line with a consumer-oriented business and manufacturing practice.
The competitive, freeenterprise economic climate of the later 1920s made manufacturers recognize that Fordist uniformity and standardization in industrially manufactured goods were not sufficient to continue to guarantee profits: the need for change was a necessity for generating continued growth.
Significantly, the Art and Color Section of General Motors was renamed the Styling Division in 1937: the new name appears to reflect the corporations acknowledgment of its strategy for frequent model changes, as well as its understanding that design functioned to generate desire, and in effect was a branch of advertising.
Later dubbed planned obsolescence (see here320), the strategy encompassed the annual or seasonal introduction of new colors, patterns, or forms that made existing industrial products appear outmoded and encouraged consumers to purchase the latest, most modern item.
It helped to reduce the risks of introducing substantively new products.
Obsolescence was part of a new business model that used design as an investment to help stimulate consumer sales.
