Although some writers criticized this approach as a form of consumer manipulation and acquiescence to market pressure (it certainly deviated from Le Corbusiers search for permanent objets types), planned obsolescence operated on what Roland Marchand has called the new consumer ethic, a recognition that consumption fueled production, putting people back to work and bolstering buyer confidence.
Many industrial manufacturers began to think of this approach to design as an integral part of their business, and turned to advertisers, retailers, and designers to suggest new or modified products.
Indeed, the incorporation of design into the business strategy sometimes spurred technical innovation: as explained by cultural historian Jeffrey Meikle, Harley Earls lower and more integrated, sculptural designs for automobile models of the later 1930s used newer and less time-intensive stamping processes that produced broader, curved, allsteel bodies, taking advantage of the availability of longer lengths of steel, something engineers may not have otherwise been motivated to consider.
10.18 Cadillac Lasalle Model 303, designed by Harley Earl, 1927.
In 1927 Henry Ford yielded to pressure to modify his stance on uniformity and standardization, introducing a new Model A together with a massive advertising campaign (virtually the first in the companys history) and the completion of a vast new production plant at the River Rouge near Dearborn, Michigan.
The Ford Motor Corporation commissioned the painter and commercial photographer Charles Sheeler (18831965) to produce a series of photographs of the Ford Motors River Rouge facility that coincided with the introduction of the Model A, intended to communicate the inspiring grandeur and efficiency of the machine-dominated environment (fig.
10.19).
Historians have noted that in these photographs, as well as in a series of paintings by Sheeler of the Rouge plant reproduced in the new business journal Fortune (first published in 1930), the human presence is often entirely absent or overwhelmed by the machinery the worker operates (for comparison, Diego Riveras 1933 series of frescoes in the garden court of the Detroit Institute of Arts titled Detroit Industry celebrates the power of industry but with workers and managers playing a more active role).
This in turn reflects the view that the progress guaranteed by mechanization, for better or worse, diminishes the agency or requires the submission of the individual worker to carefully monitored routine tasks controlled by managers and owners, a telling indication of an inherent tension between man and machine as well as between labor and management in the capitalist factory system.
Indeed, the success of Fords moving assembly line was due to the replacement of skilled by unskilled labor, with increasing emphasis upon the performance of single tasks in required sequences measured against the clock and under the watchful eye of factory foremen.
But while the focus of Sheelers River Rouge photographs from the later 1920s was upon the power and productivity of machines, the commercial strategies of large manufacturing corporations, including Ford, were moving toward the consumer and the need to stimulate desire through promotion, advertising, marketing, and merchandising, all of which defined and expanded opportunities for designers.
As noted above, the alienating effects of the assembly line and the general mechanization of the workplace were balanced by consumption in which workers now participated and the myths of personal and social progress that the purchase of commodities promised.
The power of Sheelers River Rouge photographs lies in their combination of documentary truth with the reinforcement corporate authority.
10.19 Charles Sheeler, Stamping Press, photograph of Ford Plant at River Rouge, Michigan, 1927.
Library of Congress.
While General Motors and Ford used in-house styling departments and advertising to direct their design activities, some companies looked to independent or consultant designers to modify and market their products.
The phenomenon of the consultant industrial designer is significant in the history of American manufacturing in the 1930s.
It indicates that aside from in-house styling departments created by the automobile industry in the later 1920s, industrial manufacturing corporations had to look outside of their own personnel to introduce eye-catching design or respond creatively to surveys of consumer preferences.
In the business language of the time, companies thought in terms of product engineering, focusing upon what Jeffrey Meikle describes as the functional arrangement of a products mechanical parts instead of those features of a product that might generate consumer appeal.
The stock market crash of October 1929, precipitated by inflated stock prices and widespread speculation on company growth and rising real-estate values, marked the beginning of an economic depression with high unemployment (reaching nearly 25 percent in 1933), falling domestic production, and an erosion of consumer confidence and spending.
During this period the United States government took a stronger role in providing welfare and funding large-scale infrastructure projects as well as public art and the Social Security Act.
To encourage people to spend rather than save, more manufacturers turned to designers in an effort to bolster sales of their products.
In the 1920s, advertising executive Elmo Calkins argued in business journals that design added appeal and value to products  during the 1930s this strategy was not only adopted but also refined to produce consumer engineering that sought to guarantee desire, and in which designers played a significant part.
The emergence of a business model for stimulating consumption helped to define and promote industrial design during the 1930s in the United States.
Kem Weber (born Karl Emmanuel Martin in Germany; 18891963) traveled to California in 1914 to assist with the German Pavilion for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915 (celebrating the opening of the Panama Canal and its promise for increased trade for Californias port cities) and remained in the United States following the outbreak of World War I.
He opened an industrial design office in Los Angeles in the early 1930s, having worked in the later 1920s as a draftsman for the Barker Brothers Department Store in Los Angeles.
As a consultant for industry, Weber designed an electric clock with continuous numerical readout (rather than traditional dial) housed in a copper and aluminum case (fig.
10.20), manufactured by the Lawson Time Inc. of Alhambra, California, in 1934.
The rectangular form of the clock is swept back at the left edge in a curve rather than at a 90-degree angle to produce a smooth, streamlined look suggestive of flowing movement rather than the angles and abrupt staccato rhythms of Cubist or set-back Skyscraperinspired forms of the 1920s.
Historians have noted the use of such forms in the buildings and project designs of German architect Erich Mendelsohn (18871953), whose work, such as the 1928 Schocken Department Store in Stuttgart, was also admired by Frank Lloyd Wright and exhibited at the Museum of Modern Art in 1932.
Such forms may also be seen in the lower stories of the 1932 Philadelphia Saving Fund Society Building designed by the firm of Howe and Lescaze.
The electric numerical readout offered a sense of precision to the owner, and the flow of Webers case suggested smooth, continuous mechanical movement like that of the assembly line.
10.20 Kem Weber, Zephyr electric clock, brass, bakelite, $3 { ^ 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 8 \times 3 { ^ 1 } / _ { 8 }$ in (8.3 × 20.3 × 8 cm), manufactured by Lawson Time Inc., Pasadena, California, 1934.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
A number of consultant industrial designers were artists who had worked directly in advertising or were successful in fields such as stage and set design for the theater.
Often recommended to manufacturers by advertising agencies, industrial designers absorbed an eclectic array of sources for inspiration in their work, defining a middle ground between advertisings concerns for visual appeal and broadly humanistic concerns with efficiency and progress through improved performance and the introduction of art into everyday life.
Industrial design consultancies often employed large staffs, and in addition to redesigning products were responsible for package design, labels, advertising, and merchandising.
Although the success of the profession in the 1930s was often based upon the value and marketability of individual names such as Raymond Loewy, whose portrait appeared on the cover of a 1949 issue of Time magazine, industrial design office practice generally involved collaboration and compromise among many individuals working together as a team according to a division of labor and a dialogue between competing viewpoints and objectives.
The team-based approach of industrial design offices approximated the existing conditions and complexities of the manufacturing industry more than the ambience of the artists studio or the idealism of the academy, where isolation often produced compelling ideologies but few massproduced goods or realized grandiose schemes for future planned societies.
Designers such as Loewy and Norman Bel Geddes (18931958) used their celebrity to publicize the emerging profession and its value to consumers and manufacturers alike through books and magazine articles; articles and advertisements in journals such as Fortune mediated the advantages of design to the business community and a wider readership.
Advertisement for gas range, Geo.
D.
Roper Corporation, Rockford, Illinois, from Good Housekeeping, August 1923.
Studies of the projects of American industrial designers in the 1930s reveal the dynamic interrelationships between aesthetic, commercial, user-centered, and manufacturing considerations.
For example, Bel Geddes was hired by the Standard Gas Equipment Corporation in 1933 to redesign its kitchen ranges in the hope of stimulating consumer demand.
Market research revealed that ease of cleaning was the primary consideration of housewives when purchasing a new range.
Bel Geddess response was to use large rectangular panels of enamel-coated sheet metal (including a panel to fit over the burners) rather than cast iron to create a more enclosed and unified, essentially round-edged boxlike form, eliminating open areas that collected dust as well as the clutter of decorative handles and other hardware (fig.
10.21).
Bel Geddes hung the panels from a sturdy tubular-metal frame, as if constructed as a model of gridlike Corbusian architecture.
The new model presented a more integrated, unified housing or envelope, while advertisements identified smooth polished surfaces and unobtrusive form with improved hygiene as well as reduced housework.
Many of these characteristics are also found in a 1933 stove manufactured under the brand name Magic Chef for the American Stove Company of St.
Louis, Missouri, where the thin, tubular-steel frame is left partially exposed (fig.
10.22).
Anonymous, gas range, “Magic Chef,” enameled steel, chromium-plated steel, cast iron, stainless steel, plastic, 60 × 45 × 27 in (152.4 × 114.3 × 68 cm), American Stove Company, St.
Louis, Missouri, c.
1935.
The Wolfsonian Florida International University, Miami Beach.
This approach, balancing unified housing with mechanical or structural change for improved performance, appears to have been the ideal toward which many consultant industrial designers directed their efforts, that is, to a point somewhere beyond mere superficial styling or cosmetic change but squarely within a free-market competitive economic model.
It also created a connection and balance between design and engineering (rather than advertising), between the creativity of the designer and the objectivity and problem-solving associations of an applied scientist.
Another oft-cited example is Loewys design for British manufacturer Sigmund Gestetners duplicating machine of 1929.
Gestetner came to Loewy in New York for assistance in improving the appearance of his machine.
Loewy provided a unified housing that concealed many of the machines working parts.
Whether by intention or happy accident, the new shell reduced cost by making the nickel-plating of exposed mechanical parts unnecessary and improved performance by reducing the amount of space between parts where dust tended to accumulate and lead to malfunctions.
Walter Dorwin Teague (18831960) worked as a staff artist for an advertising agency in New York before designing products for industrial production.
Many of his designs aimed to reduce complexity as well as improve the quality of life through an awareness of taste and discrimination.
He redesigned several cameras for the Kodak Company, including its line of Brownie models, introducing smooth plastic housing with vertical ribs to each model, as well as the small 35-millimeter Bantam Special or bullet model of 1936 (fig.
10.23).
Teague enclosed the lens in a unified shell with rounded sides and thin, horizontal metal ribs, explaining that the ribs functioned to reduce the cracking of the casings black lacquer finish  as much a solution to a technical problem as of modern styling, achieving a balance between novelty and improvement.
10.23 Walter Dorwin Teague, Bantam Special camera, painted brass, $3 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 4 \times 1 ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 } ( 9 \times 1 0 \times 4 .
4$ cm), Eastman Kodak Company, Rochester, New York, 1936.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
In some designs, small improvements were made annually after a major innovation was introduced.
For instance, Loewys 1935 Coldspot refrigerator for Sears Corporation (fig.
10.24), as well as an earlier 1933 refrigerator designed for General Electric by Henry Dreyfuss, integrated the condenser element into the appliance housing.
This created a unified shell, distinct from earlier models in which the condenser appeared on top of the refrigerator (fig.
10.25).
As Jeffrey Meikle has explained, Loewy added refinements each year to the Sears Coldspot, virtually eliminating protrusions and accentuating vertical elements through the introduction of ribs both above and below the large refrigerator door.
Such changes conformed to the strategy of obsolescence (see here), making each years model new, and identifying the new with the improved.
The Coldspot broke records for sales, even though the US economy was steadily approaching pre-Depression manufacturing levels by 1937.
The title of Loewys autobiography, Never Leave Well Enough Alone, offers examples of his approach to design, acknowledging its connection with the need for change to maintain levels of production and consumption in a competitive economy.
The new sensitivity to consumer psychology emerges in Loewys acronym MAYA, standing for most advanced yet acceptable. Raymond Loewy, Coldspot Super Six refrigerator, porcelain on steel and aluminum, 58 $^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 3 0 \times 2 6$ in $( 1 4 7 .
8 \times 7 6 \times$ 66 cm), Sears, Roebuck and Company, Chicago, 1935.
10.24 Advertisement for electric refrigerator, General Electric Company, Cleveland, Ohio, from Good Housekeeping, July 1927.
Henry Dreyfuss (19041972) shared with his fellow industrial designers of the period a belief that successful and more or less final solutions to design problems for many products were possible.
He defined a products survival form as being simple and having a satisfying aesthetic that fulfilled its practical, production, and commercial requirements.
This theory, less doctrinaire than Le Corbusiers objets types, allowed for changes while retaining a memorable feature or form that created product identity and promoted familiarity and appeal.
The Type 300 combined handset for the Bell Telephone Corporation, designed in 1937, is one of Dreyfusss best-known pre-World War II projects (fig.
10.26).
The combined handset replaced earlier upright models with separate speakers and microphones in the later 1920s.
Not subject to competitive market pressures, the design could be developed on the basis of ease of use, stability, ease of cleaning, and durability.
When he learned that he would be unable to consult with engineers when preparing a new telephone design for AT&T, Dreyfuss initially withdrew from the competition.
After the company rejected proposals from other designers, Dreyfuss was offered the commission for the new phone.
The Type 300 was more unified than its predecessors, and indeed appears to adopt some of the basic (survival) features from a combined handset phone designed by artist Jean Heiberg (18841976) for the L.
M.
Ericsson Company of Stockholm, Sweden, in 1930.
After World War II, Dreyfuss made several improvements to his design, switching from a metal to a lighter-weight plastic housing, and placing the numbers outside rather than inside the dialing mechanism for legibility and reduced wear.
Perhaps the most important improvement to the post-war phone was its receiver, whose lightness and flattened handle enabled the user to cradle it between ear and shoulder, freeing the hands to multi-task while talking on the phone.
Henry Dreyfuss, Type 300, handset, black phenolic resin, Bell Telephone Corporation, 1937.

## The
United States and International Modernism During the 1930s, the Museum of Modern Art in New York (MoMA, founded in 1929) embraced and promoted a more European-based model of industrial design that selectively incorporated elements of Constructivism, the Dessau Bauhaus, and the theories of Le Corbusier.
The museum preferred a more restrained functional architecture, referred to as the International Style and featured in a well-publicized show in 1932 titled Modern Architecture: International Exhibition, rejecting decoration and embracing well-lit open interior spaces, fitted furniture and the elimination of mass through thinner, lighter-weight materials.
MoMA favored visual similarities over differences and even contradictions in local contexts, lumping together the aesthetically pure and exclusive private homes designed by Le Corbusier and Mies van der Rohe with the efficient public housing projects of Oud in the Netherlands and Ernst May in Frankfurt as exhibiting a common vocabulary of formal elements deriving from modern building materials and new construction technologies.
What was important was the rejection of revival styles and the substitution of superficial modernistic (Art Deco) decoration and sentimental attachment to the past with the clean lines, smooth surfaces, modular units, and elemental geometry.
In 1934, MoMA housed an exhibition entitled Machine Art, curated by architect Philip Johnson (fig.
10.27), and published a catalog with an introductory essay by museum director Alfred H.
Barr, Jr.
The exhibition featured more than 400 objects, drawn from the scientific laboratory, institutional kitchens, machines, and machine parts, along with tubular furniture and bathroom fixtures for office or home.
The catalog essays acknowledged the contributions of the Dessau Bauhaus and of modern abstract artists such as Constantin Brancusi.
Many objects were lent by industrial manufacturers such as Alcoa (Aluminum Company of America), who also served as one of several sponsors. Machine Art advocated an approach to design for modern living that renounced handicraft in favor of machine production and emphasized the elemental, enduring beauty of the geometric forms of machines and the goods they produced.
At times elemental geometry was not intentional, as in a bearing spring, while at other times it was a matter of selection and a modern aesthetic sensibility.
The exhibition organizers argued for a universal machine aesthetic, promoting geometry, utility, new materials, and the rejection of decoration and signs of hand-crafting.
In the museums view, ornament was a vestige of craft and of privilege, unnecessary to the practical needs of the modern family; not being necessary, decoration was therefore extravagant, even irresponsible in the context of widespread unemployment and hardship during the Depression.
Barr wrote that in order to end the divorce between industry and culture, we must assimilate the machine aesthetically as well as economically. It is worthwhile remembering that Machine Art revived, or updated, a strain of modern design history that includes William Morriss recommendation that machines not try to imitate handwork, and Frank Lloyd Wrights equation of machines with simplicity.
10.27 “Machine Art” exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1934.
In promoting the relationship between geometric purity and the methods of industrial production, Machine Art presented a reductive and somewhat limited interpretation of modern design and the role of the designer or artist-engineer. Divorced from function by being placed on pedestals and hung on walls with dramatic lighting, objects in the exhibition such as trays or pitchers were accompanied by price lists and could be appreciated for their abstract, geometric purity as machine-age works of art as well as commodities to be purchased for the home; in other words, an exercise in design reform and the elevation of public taste  of selling the advantages of modern design with the museums authoritative stamp.
In furniture the curators relied almost exclusively upon European designers using tubular steel, ignoring creations of American designers no less innovative in their use of modern industrial materials.
Among those ignored was Warren McArthur (18851961), an engineer who created chairs and tables constructed of lightweight tubular aluminum, ingeniously joined by a system of patented internal cables that produced clean joints (fig 10.28).
McArthur received a patent for his invention and also designed numerous versions of aluminum seating for aircraft for the US Army during World War II.
Gradually an expanded International Style of modern industrial furniture and furnishings, exhibited at MoMA and at other museums around the country as good design, gained broader acceptance after World War II, incorporating standards reminiscent of reform in their balance among individual expression, restraint, comfort, and practical advantage.
The context and genesis of this approach to industrial design is a focus of Part V.
Warren McArthur, chair, aluminum and leather, c.
1932.
More traditional craft-based manufacturers in the furniture and ceramics industries hired contract or in-house designers to develop modern products for industrial manufacture during the 1930s based upon smooth forms, new materials, and restrained decoration.
Gilbert Rohde (18941944) designed modern displays and furnished rooms for the 1933 Worlds Fair in Chicago, but is perhaps best known as design consultant for the Herman Miller Furniture Company of Zeeland, Michigan, from 1932 until his premature death in 1944.
Miller furniture was sold primarily through department stores such as Macys in New York and John Wanamaker in Philadelphia, and on a contract basis to architects in the design of office and other institutional interiors.
During the years he spent at Miller, Rohde developed a series of furniture designs based upon sectional or modular rectangular units for seating, storage, and shelving (fig.
10.29).
D.
J.
DePree, President of Herman Miller and who hired Rohde, promoted the relationship between modern design and socially responsible values of modesty and efficiency, especially relevant to the business community (and its reputation) in the economic climate of the Depression.
Diagram for modular desk units based upon designs of Gilbert Rohde, Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, c.
1935.
One popular domestic application for practical modern design was in production ceramics, seen in the line of table service known as Fiestaware, designed in 1936 by British-born ceramicist Frederick Hurten Rhead (18801942) for the Homer Laughlin China Company in West Virginia, where he worked as artistic director during that time.
Fiestaware (fig.
10.30) eschewed traditional connections with patterned decoration, historical styles, sculptural contours, and relief decoration in favor of plain circular shapes with slightly raised concentric ribbing.
Fiestawares uniformity invoked the standardization of industrial manufacturing, but such uniformity was balanced by a wide variety of brightly colored and highly durable glazes developed by Rhead.
Certainly the name Fiestaware evoked associations with gaiety (rather than austerity), and a similar palette is found in contemporary Mexican ceramics that were also manufactured on a smaller scale in California, where Rhead had spent time as a studio potter prior to working for the Laughlin China Company.
Fiestaware retained some traditional elements such as the handles or feet for serving dishes and the concentric circles that suggest the technique of the potters wheel.
The service also introduced novel designs such as the cutaway pitcher, the handle of which is unified into its circular shape.
Frederick Hurten Rhead, Fiestaware earthenware, variable dimensions, Homer Laughlin China Company, West Virginia, 1936.
The Globus Collection.
Russel Wright, American Modern dinnerware, variable dimensions, designed 1937.
Steubenville Pottery, Ohio, manufacture beginning in 1939.
Collection of John C.
Waddell.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
Russel Wright (19041976) designed his American Modern dinnerware in 1937 for the Steubenville (Ohio) Pottery Company (fig.
10.31), but it was not manufactured until 1939.
With muted glazes in contrast with Fiestaware, it featured asymmetric, organic shapes for pitchers and dishes at a time when such ovoid forms were also being introduced for the manufacture of metals and plastics used in automobile manufacturing and in appliance housings.
The commercial success of American Modern came mostly after World War II, but Wright was active in the later 1930s promoting modern domestic products in connection with modest but comfortable, informal living.
With his wife, Mary, Wright published a Guide to Easier Living (1950).
Wright also was a pioneer in finding product applications for aluminum.
His pitcher of 1932 (fig.
10.32) uses the method of spun aluminum to create a smooth and swelling cylindrical form devoid of decoration.
Wrights product line of spun-aluminum serving ware, however, included a concession to consumers reticent attitudes toward Modernist aesthetics: the packages containing these wares included a piece of emery cloth and instructions for housewives to rub the surface with the abrasive to create the traditional look of handcrafted pewter.
Russel Wright, spherical pitcher, spun aluminum, 5 × 6 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (12.7 × 17.5 cm), 1932.
Private collection.

## Streamlining
A related area of American interwar industrial design concerns the broad topic of Streamlining in the transportation industry.
During the 1920s, wind-tunnel tests by engineers demonstrated that teardrop-shaped forms, rounded in front and tapering toward the rear, reduced wind resistance, enabling both faster speeds and improved fuel consumption for land-based and air travel.
By 1930, these results were adopted in the aviation industry, where bullet-shaped noses, farings placed over landing gear, and wings molded to the body of aircraft appeared in airplanes such as the Douglas DC1 in 1933 or the earlier German Junkers F-13.
The American railroad industry adopted streamlining for locomotive design in the 1930s.
Threatened with increasing competition from the automobile industry and commercial aviation, railway companies had seen a steady decline in passengers and profits since the 1920s.
Early examples of streamlined passenger trains were shown in the second year of the 1933 Century of Progress Worlds Fair in Chicago.
They employed lighter construction materials such as corrugated steel (rather than heavier steel of a uniform thickness) combined with diesel engines to improve fuel efficiency.
Broad curved front ends and reduced space between cars were features of the Budd Manufacturing Companys three-car commuter train for the Burlington Railway Company in 1934, appropriately named Zephyr.
Streamlining also appears in the bullet-shaped Union Pacific locomotive illustrated in figure 10.33 from 1934.
Adapting the benefits of wind-tunnel research to the automobile industry proved elusive, but several prototypes and limited production vehicles emerged in Europe as well as in the United States.
Hungarian designer Paul Jaray built a teardrop-shaped automobile as early as 1922, and in Britain A.
E.
Palmer designed a car in 1930 with a rear engine permitting lower ground clearance that also incorporated the new teardrop form.
Also, visitors to the Victoria and Albert Museums 2003 Art Deco 19101939 10.33 exhibition were treated to the streamlined Tatra car, manufactured in Czechoslovakia in 1937.
Inventor Richard Buckminster Fuller (18951983) designed a Streamlined three-wheel vehicle that achieved media notoriety at the Chicago Worlds Fair in 1933, but it was never put into production, while Streamlined prototypes for automobiles, boats, and aircraft were designed by Norman Bel Geddes and promoted in his journal Horizons beginning in 1932.
While the teardrop may have promised efficiency for production automobiles on the basis of research and testing, the American automobile industry was hesitant to invest in such a radical retooling of its factory equipment.
Bel Geddes did serve as a consultant to the Chrysler Corporation for the 1934 Airflow, which adapted a more unified approach to the construction of the grill, hood, and windshield to traditional front-engine production technology with flat sides.
The advertising campaign for the Chrysler Airflow, featuring photographs of the auto alongside a Union Pacific locomotive (fig.
10.33) generated excitement and numerous orders, but negative publicity stemming from flaws in the first units to reach the market doomed the car, and manufacturing ceased in 1937.
Airflow Imperial Coupe, manufactured by Chrysler Corporation, 1934, with Union Pacific Streamline Express, 1934.
While Streamlined automobiles in the United States remained experimental or limited to the custom market (in Europe the Volkswagen was an exception, though not manufactured widely until after World War II, see here), the tapered forms and lightweight materials adopted in aircraft design during the 1930s found popular expression in the Airstream trailer, first built in 1936 in Culver City, California, by Wally Byam (18961962).
Intended for leisure travel, the lightweight aluminum Airstream Clipper featured a distinctive tapered bullet shape to lessen wind resistance and increase fuel efficiency, along with its unified body and chassis (fig.
10.34).
Production halted when the United States entered World War II in December 1941 and aluminum was needed for military production, but the success of the Airstream during the Depression in the later 1930s illustrates the popular appeal of Streamlining.
The business of trailers as mobile homes for retirees and for vacation travel prompted a lengthy illustrated feature story in the monthly business magazine Fortune in March, 1937, citing trailer building as a growth industry for modern living, economical for owners, and making efficient use of limited space.
10.34 Airstream Clipper aluminum trailer, manufactured by Airstream Inc., California, 1936–1940.
Streamlinings appeal extended to a host of products unrelated to transportation.
Kem Webers electric table clock (see fig.
10.20) exhibits the smooth surfaces and swept-back contours of the style, while the Electrolux Model 30 vacuum cleaner designed by Lurelle Guild (18981985) dating to 1937 (fig.
10.35) used lightweight aluminum for the body that rested on chrome-plated steel skids that glided across the carpet.
Electrolux vacuum cleaners were manufactured in the United States in Dover, Delaware, though the companys origins were in Sweden before World War I.
Whether a clock, vacuum cleaner, or pencil sharpener, Streamlined housings communicated graceful, effortless movement, without tension or friction.
In a complex world with mounting social tensions and economic challenges in the later 1930s, Streamlining provided consumers with a combination of hope and escape, fueled by manufacturers and designers emerging attention to the varied motivations behind consumer behavior.
Criticized by the Museum of Modern Art as modernistic rather than Modernist, the idea of a Streamlined future fueled the imagination of consumers, offering freedom from resistance whether in an airplane, the sight of a shiny Airstream trailer, a table clock, or a radio.
Lurelle Guild, Electrolux Model 30 vacuum cleaner, chrome-plated steel, aluminum, vinyl, rubber, 8 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 23 × 7 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (21.6 × 58.4 × 19.7 cm), Electrolux Corporation, Dover, Delaware, 1937.
Brooklyn Museum, New York.

## The
New York World’s Fair The 1939 New York Worlds Fair centered upon the theme of Building the World of Tomorrow. Industrial designer Walter Dorwin Teague was on the planning board for the fair; Norman Bel Geddes designed the popular General Motors Corporations Futurama exhibit and ride, where viewers on moving chairs experienced a vision for an American city in the year 1960, with suburbs connected to the city by networks of multi-lane highways, and automobiles defining the Streamlined patterns of tomorrows modern living.
For both of these men, the Worlds Fair provided an opportunity to extend the range of their industrial design practice beyond consumer products and appliances and to realize, if only ephemerally and in miniature, a unified conception for a radically designed future that improved the conditions of everyday life.
This vision was embodied in the centralized design of the fair, where several multicolored avenues converged in a circular space that contained the symbolic Trylon and Perisphere.
Both the avenues to either side of the central circle were separated thematically for various activities such as transportation, international exhibits, and amusement and entertainment.
Democracity, a miniature world of tomorrow, was housed within the large globe-shaped Perisphere, viewed from two rotating balconies and connected by walkway to the other symbol, the tall pyramidal Trylon (fig.
10.36).
Designed by Henry Dreyfuss, Democracity was divided into zones separated by wide streets designed for vehicular traffic and tree-lined walkways for pedestrians that were elevated to avoid accidents.
Residential communities were located between the city center (Centerton) and farmland, and were named Pleasantvilles or Millvilles (the latter a factory town).
Democracitys accompanying brochure touted the elimination of the depressing sight of slums, pollution, and crime, whose design promised a manageable future based upon the common good achieved through cooperation and interdependence, a utopia recalling William Morriss News from Nowhere (see here) for the age of industry.
10.36 Aerial view of New York World’s Fair, 1939–1940.
Like Democracity, Bel Geddess Futurama exhibit, sponsored by General Motors, also managed traffic flow in the modern metropolis by multi-lane highways and banked exit ramps, pedestrian walkways that did not interfere with vehicular traffic, and by a radiocontrolled system that monitored speed and distance between vehicles on the highway (less individualized than features on todays cars to manage cruise-control).
The exhibit stressed the importance of highways, and paralleled the lobbying efforts of the automobile industry, tire manufacturers, and oil companies to expand government funding of the nations road system and further stimulated consumer desire for personal mobility.
Conspicuously absent were mass-transit systems (other than buses).
Like the utopian vision of Le Corbusiers Voisin plan from the mid-1920s, a single style prevailed in the Futurama, defining a controlled world that applied the efficiency and logic of large-scale modern technology and materials to erase differences, contradictions, conflicts, and irritants.
Many contemporary historians have noted the contrast between these managerial visions of tomorrow and the realities of unemployment, urban decay, and racism affecting industrial cities in the United States.
In turn, such overarching control of space and movement demanded compliance, the surrender of individual freedom and agency to patterns of movement akin to the predictable and efficient rhythms of industrial machinery.
Charlie Chaplin poked fun at such a mechanized future in his 1939 silent film Modern Times with a series of sequences in which the assembly-line worker (Chaplin) becomes a programmed victim rather than beneficiary of modern industrial technology.
In addition to the utopian Democracity or Futurama, other manufacturers displays commodified the future through the display and working demonstration of products and appliances, translating the clean, Streamlined vision of the future into a present rather than distant reality, often with an emphasis on the relationship of technology to leisure.
Exhibits documented the steady and sure progress of science, the attainment of frictionless speed in the transportation industry, for instance, and tested how machines reduced toil and increased free time.
In one exhibit for the Westinghouse Corporation, designed by Gilbert Rohde (see here), Mrs Drudge washed dishes by hand while her counterpart, Mrs Modern, loaded an automatic dishwashing machine.
Still in the wake of the Depression and hardship caused by high levels of unemployment and poverty, and fearful of mounting tension and conflict in Europe (already present in the exclusion of Nazi Germany from participation and the inability of a number of European nations to participate or having to modify their pavilions, such as Czechoslovakia, occupied by the Nazis beginning in 1938), the products and demonstrations of the fair exhibits provided some kind of tangible proof of progress through modern, efficient living.
Modern-day critics of the 1939 New York Worlds Fair have commented that its planners conditioned the experience of visitors, aiming through dramatic devices such as lighting and perspective to stage a sequence of particular responses leading to a climax that gave substance to the vision of tomorrows world today.
Such devices were the stock in trade of architects and interior designers such as Morris Lapidus (19022001), who was a successful storefront designer during the interwar period.
Lapidus employed techniques such as mirrors to create the effect of spaciousness and curving windows beckoning shoppers toward the entrance by removing sharp corners or barriers.
He installed bright signage and lighting to create contrast or what he called the moth principle.
Such devices may be seen in Lapiduss 1939 storefront for Hoffritz Cutlery in Manhattan (fig.
10.37).
The mingling of utopian ideology and consumer engineering was characteristic of the 1939 Worlds Fair, representing the strategies of advertising agencies and the balancing of competing, even contradictory priorities that characterized the profession of industrial design as it became part of the experience of modern living in the United States during the interwar period.
Morris Lapidus, storefront for Hoffritz Cutlery, New York, 1939.
Planners and promoters expressed optimism that the provocative exhibits of the World of Tomorrow would continue for five years, but even with publicity in newsreels and in print, the exhibits closed before the end of 1940.
Like much popular entertainment, the 1939 Worlds Fair caused great excitement initially but failed to sustain interest beyond the initial fleeting impact of glitter and a sense of escape from harsher realities.
Some of the organizers believed that the fair was educational in shaping public opinion and offering solutions and even proof of reduced hardship, alienation, and conflict, but its longevity depended upon ticket sales from a public who appeared to see the fair as a short-lived collection of novelties with little meaning beyond the immediacy and initial excitement.
As an experience based in part upon techniques derived from the advertising industry, it was, in a sense, a victim of the planned obsolescence that helped to shape it  without continued novelty and progressive change, the World of Tomorrow too quickly became yesterdays news.
Interestingly, the idea of a more limited but nonetheless progressive fair resurfaced during the 1950s with the traveling Motorama showcases sponsored by General Motors (see here) or the Monsanto House of Tomorrow, featured at Disneyland (see here).

## Photography
and Graphic Design In the mid-1930s, photography began to compete with and gradually to eclipse illustration for advertising.
Illustration persisted for magazine and book covers, along with illustrated fiction.
Although advertisements formed part of his extensive oeuvre, Norman Rockwell (18941978) enjoyed a long relationship with the popular weekly mass-circulation magazine Saturday Evening Post.
Rockwells color illustrations for the Post presented a variety of familiar themes drawn from common white middle-class experience, frequently involving seasonal activities and holidays.
Rockwell was familiar with the conventions of narrative art in the Western tradition, relying upon pyramidal composition to provide focus or climax as well as to guide the viewers eye through the carefully orchestrated compositions.
Frequently his covers and posters seem to suggest continuity with the sense of community and comfort provided by family and neighborhood, an antidote to the impersonal modernity of factory and office, and absent from the utopian visions of Democracity.
The use of reassuring shared experiences and techniques of naturalistic illustration to communicate those values were Rockwells hallmarks.
A Post cover from November, 1933 (fig.
10.38) illustrates a young mother spanking her child on a chair that is a simple design based upon a Neoclassical model, and less frequent in Rockwells illustrations than carved and more heavily upholstered furniture inspired by earlier eighteenth-century examples.
Notwithstanding the political incorrectness of implying any form of physical abuse or threat to children in our own day, the story is clearly and simply told.
The child has broken a piece of fine decorative china with a hammer, and the mother responds with a traditional form of punishment.
Her response, however, is not the result of an emotional outburst or of inherited child-rearing practice: while she raises her hand, she holds a psychology book that has guided her actions.
In fact, the read response is precisely the same as the spontaneous one, and modern psychology has recommended a solution with which the reader is already familiar.
The illustration makes the reader feel more confident with some of the discomforting information that makes us feel insecure in dealing with everyday existence.
Norman Rockwell, “Child Psychology” cover, Saturday Evening Post, November 25, 1933.
As Michele Bogart has suggested, Rockwell was ambivalent about his own success, despite the celebrity he attained; his attempts to experiment with more expressionistic approaches to painting were rejected by his editors at the Post.
It may also be helpful to view his success in the context of mass images that seek at once to reflect as well as to shape behavior in periods of great social and political change.
Rockwells poster illustrating a festive family meal is one of four from The Four Freedoms series, in this case Freedom from Want (fig.
10.39).
The composition suggests references to countless images of the Last Supper that lend formality, even solemnity, to the meal.
Rockwell executed the series in 1942, in the midst of World War II, amid government-imposed rationing and shortages in support of the war effort that raised more than thirty-two million dollars in war bond contributions.
Like advertising illustrations connecting products with the good life, Rockwells images steered away from troubling social or political problems, and his illustrations indulge in escapism as elements of mass culture.
Indeed, until the 1960s, minorities, for instance, find little place within Rockwells oeuvre, and popular appeal at the time seemed to preclude representing Black people or commenting on racism or social unrest.
10.39 Norman Rockwell, Freedom from Want, oil painting, 1943.
The Norman Rockwell Museum at Stockbridge, Massachusetts.
Other examples of contemporary public art seemed to include or at least reference more directly the hardship of many Americans during the Depression.
The murals painted for the federally sponsored Work Progress Administration (WPA) provided artists with an opportunity to work, most often in a traditionally accessible naturalistic style (Arshile Gorkys 1937 murals for Newark Airport, New Jersey, are an exception).
Thomas Hart Benton (18891975), for instance, was responsible for several murals in post offices and other public buildings and institutions during the 1930s.
Benton used swelling shapes and sweeping curvilinear lines to invest his figures with energy and movement, often lending a heroic character to the depiction of ordinary everyday activities of work and recreation during a time of high unemployment in the hope of building national unity and optimism (fig.
10.40).
Thomas Hart Benton, Arts of the West, tempera, 7 ft 10 in × 13 ft 5 in (239 × 409 cm).
The New Britain Museum of American Art, New Britain, Connecticut.
Beyond Rockwells appealing illustration and Bentons message of solidarity (and racial inclusion, as in his 1931 series of murals for the board room of the New School for Social Research in Manhattan) stood other artists whose realism moved in alternative directions.
The less narrative and more introspective realism of artists like Ben Shahn (18981969) and Edward Hopper (18821967) reveal an experience of alienation and isolation (physical or spiritual) in the modern world.
Only rarely, however, did their paintings reach the mass audience that read or subscribed to the Saturday Evening Post during the interwar period.
After the war, progressive art editors such as William Golden (19111959) and Cipe Pineles (19081991) invited Shahn and other contemporary American artists to contribute illustrations for stories in journals such as Seventeen and in print advertisements for CBS radio and television.
While illustration continued to find a place on the covers of weeklies such as the Saturday Evening Post, the launching of Life magazine in 1936 and Time (first published in 1923) provides evidence of a gradual shift toward photography (photojournalism) as the most compelling medium disseminating news, entertainment, and advertising.
Even earlier in the 1930s, a number of art directors turned to photographic reproduction for its sense of immediacy and visual impact.
Advertisers were attracted to the medium for the same reasons, as well as by the ability of commercial photographers to both simulate and manipulate narrative situations in order to make products appealing.
Instead of relying upon copy to sell products or report events, art directors and the advertising industry turned to photographs to reach an expanding readership.
In addition to product advertisements (which often accounted for 50 percent of their content), mass-circulation magazines carried regular features on contemporary fashion, literature, travel, and entertainment.
Photography played a key role in presenting such material, in particular studio portraits by Edward Steichen, Charles Sheeler (fig.
10.19), and other photographers.
10.41 M.
F.
Agha (art director), Edward Steichen (photographer), two-page layout from Vanity Fair, 1935.
With the hiring of European-trained artists to oversee art direction, monthly magazines began to acquire a more self-consciously modern, integrated presentation of photography, text, and display titling in the later 1920s.
At Vogue and Vanity Fair, art director Dr Mehemed Fehmy Agha (18961978) adapted some of the distinctive asymmetry of the New Typography to cover design and page layout.
Agha was born in Ukraine of Turkish parents and was working as art director for German Vogue when he was asked by Vogues publisher, Condé Nast (18731942), to be the magazines American art director in 1929.
Nast hoped that Agha would bring a new look to American Vogue, a feeling for modernity as present at the 1925 Paris Exposition but generally absent in American mass-circulation magazines.
Agha was concerned with the overall expressive arrangement of every element on the page, often across a two-page spread, utilizing contrasts and harmonies among shapes and tones to create striking rhythms and vivid effects.
The strong contrast and dramatic lighting employed by wellknown photographers such as Edward Steichen were integral features of Aghas art direction for Vogue and Vanity Fair, seen in a two-page spread from a 1935 issue of Vanity Fair, featuring Steichen photographs of the fashions for that spring season (fig.
10.41).
Vogues content throughout this period focused upon fashion and the leisure activities of international celebrities including royalty, film stars, writers, musicians, and artists.
Technically and creatively demanding as an art director, Agha brought to this lifestyle content the sensation of novelty, excitement, and the drama of the unexpected in its visual presentation.
His association with Condé Nast publications lasted until 1943.
In covers for Vanity Fair, Agha used simplified abstract forms together with text in subtle ways to convey meaning for content that included contemporary political and social concerns.
Vanity Fair introduced color photography and illustration in the early 1930s.
An example is a 1933 cover designed by Cipe Pineles (fig.
10.42), using the technique of collage to portray two figures against a dark background that includes a mass of red ink.
The figures, one bloated and smoking a cigar (1929), the other thin and rumpled (1933), are cut out of newsprint from the stock-market pages of the business section.
The tall hat and goatee of the thin figure identifies him as Uncle Sam, whose profile appeared frequently on the covers of Vanity Fair throughout this period.
Pineless focus upon compositional unity among the elements of page design led to both clarity and concision, initially compelling at a glance as well as sufficiently subtle to sustain visual interest and communicate symbolic meaning.
M.
F.
Agha (art director), Cipe Pineles (artist), cover for Vanity Fair, October 1933.
In the 1930s, Vogue competitor Harper’s Bazaar hired Russian émigré Alexey Brodovitch as art director.
Brodovitch had worked as a stage designer for the Ballets Russes in Paris prior to coming to the United States, and continued to oversee art direction at Harper’s Bazaar well into the 1950s.
The method of expressively orchestrating text and image as abstract elements on a magazine page or cover describes the activity of graphic design as practiced by Agha and Brodovitch and that was increasingly acknowledged in the commercial printing industry.
Using photography and adapting the experimental strategies of the European-inspired New Typography, interwar graphic designers set high technical and aesthetic standards for their publications.
Characteristics such as the reinforcement of diagonal movement across the page, contrast of images with white space, asymmetrical composition, unframed photographs that bleed to the edges of the page or blend completely with the white paper, and the juxtaposition of images helped to create visual interest in layouts and advertisements throughout the 1930s.
Art directors such as Agha and Brodovitch were not publishers, political propagandists, or social activists.
Their approach to visual communication involved a recognition that attracting modern readers attention demanded creativity and originality rather than cliché.
They applied their awareness of modern art, photomontage, and the principles of the New Typography to serve the commercial needs of the publishers who employed them, engaging the reader in a new awareness, appreciation, and identification with modern life that focused increasingly upon consumption as a vehicle for self-realization.
American artist Lester Beall (19031969) employed characteristics found in Russian Constructivism, the New Typography, and modern abstract art in a series of government-sponsored public-service posters promoting the use of electricity through the Rural Electrification Administration (REA) beginning in 1937.
Bealls approach appears in a poster illustrating a bright white, electric washing machine dominating a pictogram of a home with white arrows symbolizing electric current against a background of blue (sky) and yellow (earth) (fig.
10.43).
The sense of contrast is strong and reductive imagery is striking and operates without need for text or detailed illustration.
As art historian Michael Golec has noted, Bealls approach drew upon and complemented the brochures of Rudolf Modley, a disciple of Otto Neurath and trained in the use of Isotype (see here), who also worked for the REA.
Using pictograms to present statistical information to promote rural electrification, or the increase of electrification as a sign of improvement in the standard of living, is an example of information graphics, but information is rarely neutral: its presentation helps viewers to form opinions, often in line with the intentions of their sponsors.
The REA provided low-interest loans to electrical suppliers who in turn marketed labor-saving appliances to homeowners.
Lester Beall, “Wash Day,” poster, Rural Electrification Administration, 1937, poster, silkscreen, 40 × 30 in (101.6 × 76 cm), 1937.
Through illustration, photography, and graphic design, mass magazines and the advertising that underwrote production costs forged a modern visual culture in the United States.
Advertising was a necessary corollary to sustaining the growth of an industrially based capitalist economy.
The advertising profession gained recognition and respectability through its connection with elevating public taste through art and reinforcing shared beliefs and values, linking these public-minded interests to products.
Sales, whether of magazine subscriptions or of the products advertised on their pages, came to depend upon seductive images and asymmetrical layouts to attract attention and create distinction.
In this way, the New Typography gained ground in the competitive commercial context of interwar America, in which the new and the fashionable were interchangeable.
Techniques that first emerged in the service of radical utopian ideologies and political revolution were marshaled in the interests of businesses and governments.
As explained by Roland Marchand: Pictures surpassed copy not only in their ability to intensify emotion but also in their capacity to say several things at the same time.
Visual imagery effectively reached the less literate portions of the population.
It also conveyed dense messages.
By setting up harmonics of atmosphere and imagery that resonated at a variety of levels, visual images also obscured problems of internal contradictions or irrational association.
Such harmonics were exactly what gave style products their added value beyond pragmatic utility.
Evocative pictures upped the consumption ante by inducing the customer to obtain the fullest satisfaction by buying the ad along with the product.

## Industrial
Design and Austerity Alvar Aalto (see here onward) designed the Finnish Pavilion for the 1939 New York Worlds Fair, and in that same year the Museum of Modern Art sponsored an exhibition of Scandinavian design that featured a selection of Aaltos own modern furniture.
MoMA reacted in the 1930s against what they referred to as the modernistic commercial motivations that influenced American industrial design, and advocated responsible standards based upon suitability to purpose, material, and process of manufacture. Such standards, echoing the European tradition of design reform, were implied in the 1934 Machine Art exhibition (see here) and were embodied in the household products chosen for a series of traveling exhibits entitled Useful Objects under Ten Dollars.
In 1940, MoMA sponsored a competition entitled Organic Design in Home Furnishings. By organic curator Eliot F.
Noyes (19101977), an architect who later was responsible for formulating a unified design policy for the IBM corporation, meant molded forms that were manufactured using industrial processes and materials such as laminated woods.
Flexibility was also organic when understood as units or modules for furniture and storage pieces that might be easily constructed from prefabricated components, expanded, and configured to meet a variety of needs.
Department stores agreed to display the winning designs and were committed to finding manufacturers to produce and market them.
One of the winning designs was a molded plywood chair upholstered in foam rubber covered with fabric, entered by Eero Saarinen (19101961) and Charles Eames (19071978), both of whom trained as architects (fig.
10.44).
Saarinen was the son of the Finnish architect and president of the Cranbrook Academy of Art, Eliel Saarinen, and his wife, Loja (see here); Eames had remained at Cranbrook following a fellowship there as instructor and head of a new department in industrial design.
The originality of the Saarinen/Eames collaboration lay in the more contoured three-dimensional molding of the plywood, easily seen in comparison with the plywood seat and back of Aaltos armchair for the Paimio Tuberculosis Sanitarium from 1931 (see fig.
9.64).
In other respects, the industrial materials and processes as applied to furniture created an overall impression of lightness (the wooden legs were originally planned to be made from aluminum).
Eero Saarinen and Charles Eames, armchair, molded plywood and foam upholstery with fabric, produced for MoMA’s “Organic Design in Home Furnishings” exhibition, New York, 1940. Organic Design in Home Furnishings hoped to demonstrate the ability of an industrially based design to meet the practical needs of modern domestic living using technology and modern methods of manufacture and to replace the weary forms, materials, and methods of production in much traditional revival furniture.
After the bombing of Pearl Harbor by the Japanese, and the United States entry into World War II in December 1941, the emphasis upon usefulness appeared as a proper political and patriotic response to shortages, restrictions, rationing, and the retooling of private industry to meet the demand for goods and materials to outfit and support the war effort.
In this climate German émigré Hans Knoll (19141955) manufactured and marketed the furniture of Danish designer Jens Risom (19162016) for the company he had founded (Knoll Associates) in 1938.
Risom moved to New York in 1939; his 1941 stained birch and canvas chair (fig.
10.45) was originally manufactured using the synthetic material nylon purchased from US Army surplus and constructed from a small number of standardized and undecorated parts.
Jens Risom, chair, model 666W, stained birch and canvas, 31 × 17 <sup>1</sup>/ × 21 in (79 × 44 × 53 cm), Knoll Associates, USA, 1941.
In Europe, particularly in Britain, civilian austerity was a government-mandated response to the war with Germany; it provided conditions in which a utilitarian version of Modernism devoid of decoration communicated a sense of shared duty, sacrifice, and patriotic solidarity.
British designer Gordon Russell (18921980) created a range of utility furniture under the auspices of the British Board of Trade in the early 1940s (fig.
10.46).
Designs embodied restrictions to ensure economy in the use of government-controlled raw materials such as timber and took into account shortages in skilled labor.
Rather than experimenting with new materials such as plywood, the table and chairs in this dining-room ensemble used solid woods and traditional craft-based construction.
Such furniture aimed to meet the needs of newlyweds setting up households and victims of German bombing who had lost their possessions.
British utility dining room, 1945.
More experimental in terms of materials is the BA3 aluminum chair designed by Ernest Race (19131964) in 1945 (fig.
10.47).
The lightweight aluminum legs required little bracing and were efficiently produced by mold casting.
This chair was displayed at the Britain Can Make It exhibition held after the war in 1946 as evidence of innovation and economic recovery.
Other aluminum furniture of the period includes the Landi chair (fig.
10.48), designed by Hans Coray (19061991) for the Swiss National Exhibition held in 1939.
The perforated one-piece molded shell again takes advantage of the lightness and strength of the material, as well as permitting drainage for the chairs intended outdoor use.
Both examples draw upon Modernist attitudes toward economical industrial production and aesthetics, as well as functioning as propagandistic displays.
Ernest Race, BA3 chair, stove, enameled cast aluminum and cotton-velour upholstery, 28 $^ { 3 } / _ { 4 } \times 1 7 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 1 6$ <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in $( 7 3 \times 4 4 .
5 $ × 41.3 cm), manufactured by Race Furniture Ltd, England, 1945.
Hans Coray, Landi chair, molded, heat-treated, and stained aluminum, 30 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 21 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 22 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (77.5 × 54.5 × 56.2 cm), manufactured by Blattmann Metallwarenfabrik AG, Switzerland, 1945 (first manufactured in 1939).
Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh.

## Graphic
Design in Wartime While more conventionally representational posters using a naturalistic narrative style of illustration continued to be produced to support the war effort, a number of graphic designers began using the more direct and economical means of simplified text and visual image to serve a variety of public-service purposes during World War II.
French designer Jean Carlu (19001989) visited the United States in 1940 as an employee of the French Information Service and remained there during the Nazi occupation of France in May of that year.
He designed his Production poster for the Office of Emergency Management using a clever combination of typography and image for the letter o that serves also as a hex nut, turned by a wrench tightly gripped by a powerful, gloved hand (fig.
10.49).
Carlu connected industry with production and with patriotism in the use of red, white, and blue, emphasizing the workers strong hand but also the alliance of government and industry in wartime production.
The economy of means and symbolic use of letterforms signaled a shift away from illustration in the approach of the graphic design profession as it emerged after World War II.
Jean Carlu, America’s Answer!
Production, lithograph, 29 $^ 7 / _ { 8 } \times 3 9 ^ { 5 } / _ { 8 }$ in (76 × 100.6 cm), United States Government Printing Office, Washington, DC, 1941.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
Paul Rand (born Peretz Rosenbaum; 19141996) served as art director and designed covers for the cultural journal Direction between 1938 and 1945.
Figure 10.50 illustrates a cover chronicling Nazi Germanys occupation of a portion of Czechoslovakia in the autumn of 1938.
Rands map, placed against diagonal lines and a square, alludes to the table in a military strategy room; the red cross and square provide bold and dramatic contrast to the neutral map, as well as connoting blood and possibly the sacrifice of human life.
With an economy of means and absence of conventional narrative and representational techniques, Rands open-ended juxtapositions possess a lingering power that seems to reside in provocative associations that are immediate as well as thoughtful, provoking curiosity and inviting interpretation in the manner of solving a puzzle or riddle.
After World War II, Rand became an articulate spokesman for the emerging profession of graphic design, emphasizing the varied skills that characterize the designers role.
In a reflection from 1985, he wrote: Design is a way of life, a point of view.
It involves the whole complex of visual communication; talent, creative ability, manual skill and technical knowledge.
Aesthetics and economics, technology and psychology are intrinsically related to the process.
Paul Rand, cover for Direction, vol.
1, no.
9, December 1938.
Graphic designers during World War II not only created posters for recruitment, public service, and shaping public opinion, but also designed training manuals in which the efficient and strongly visual communication of information proved especially effective.
German-born Will Burtin (19081972) organized the presentation of visual and textual information in the design of instructions for the operation of aircraft gunnery.
His approach was neither entirely as artist nor propagandist, but rather as problemsolver and analyst, devising the clearest method for combining words and images for the purposes of facilitating instruction.
Burtin took into consideration eye movement as well as the hierarchy and flow of information across two-page spreads using a cut-and-paste approach to composition (fig.
10.51).
The design solution flowed from the requirements of the brief, and while not inevitable as the outcome of those requirements, the task of the designer suggested the methods of an engineer rather than the artist or advertiser.
According to graphic designer and historian Richard Hollis, Burtins training manual helped to halve the training time for gunners, from twelve to six weeks.
Whether for profit, persuasion, or information, graphic designers added a variety of new strategies and technologies to visual communication in the interwar period, shifting emphasis from illustration to collage, photography, and photomontage.
10.51 Will Burtin, training manual for A-26 Gunnery, United States Armed Forces, 1944.

## Conclusion
Design historians have generally divided the interwar period into two broad movements in design: Art Deco (or Art Moderne), and Modernism (in its early twenty-first-century survey exhibitions, the Victoria and Albert Museum made such a distinction with separate shows devoted to the interwar period).
While it may not be difficult to distinguish Ruhlmanns Grand Salon from Rodchenkos Soviet Workers Room at the 1925 exhibition of decorative and industrial art in Paris as opposing approaches to modern living, such obvious comparisons do not convey the complex relationship among visions of modernity over the course of these decades, nor the variations, internal shifts, and differences among particular Modernist ideologies and practices and the specific political contexts in which they took shape and developed.
In this treatment of Modernism, the intention is to demonstrate that despite the label International Style that emerged with the Museum of Modern Art exhibition of 1932, Modernist initiatives originated from specific local contexts that reveal the various meanings designers attached to the formal visual language they employed.
Many designers and movements rejected historicism yet also demonstrated continuity with the past: Art Deco with elements of progressive late nineteenth-century movements such as Art Nouveau, and Modernism with the German Werkbund and its search for more anonymous, practical forms for household goods and furnishings.
Certainly the aftermath of World War I lent urgency, a polemical tone, and utopian character to many Modernist projects, based upon an almost militant rejection of existing forms of authority, while the growth of advertising during this time sometimes made commercial exigencies overshadow radical ideologies and determined actual associations between design and industry.
Another concern of many Modernist designers and movements was working- class or universal needs rather than luxury living.
Still, the role of art in Modernist design varied among its practitioners, and makes any generalization difficult.
Nevertheless, socialized housing, minimum requirements for living, Le Corbusiers theory of mechanical selection, and theories of elemental geometric forms underlying the varieties of design practice, all discussed above, informed the activities of Modernist designers, and their often visionary ideas and projects gained broader currency in response to the worldwide economic depression of the 1930s and wartime austerity.
Even acknowledging the loose collection of ideas that comprises Modernism, it is important to recognize that the achievement of its utopian vision required more than the design and production of goods and furnishings in a competitive marketplace; behind the Modernist vision was the hope for a complete reorientation of living that required the education of the New Man and New Woman. Early expressions of this Modernist project often have an apocalyptic tone, forecasting the destruction of the old and the emergence of the entirely new.
The Russian Revolution and socialist governments in parts of Europe provided political support for several experiments in the design and construction of socialized housing along Modernist lines.
Yet at the same time designers such as Josef Frank in Austria and Alvar Aalto in Finland remained advocates of the frank use of industrial materials and modern techniques of production but took into consideration the individual and psychological needs of consumers.
Others, such as Mies van der Rohe, demanded high production standards and aesthetic purity that remained exclusive and less applicable to low-cost planning.
During the 1930s, Modernism was not a strict set of design principles, nor the result of revolutionary social and political ideology, but an increasingly flexible approach to the advantages and aesthetic possibilities of modern industrial materials and technology, eschewing traditional associations with luxury and ornament, and yet not entirely determined by the criteria of engineering.
Less revolutionary and utopian in vision, Art Deco designers reasserted the more traditional liberal belief in an alliance between art and manufacturing and the role of the decorative arts in elevating the taste and improving the quality of life through comfort, convenience, and expanded possibilities for leisure activity.
This movement gained momentum from post-World War I reconstruction, with the visual arts viewed as an expression of creative freedom, originality, and national identity and pride.
The style originated at the top, in the world of high fashion and hedonism, although designers responded to popular entertainment in the form of jazz as well as to modern dance that crossed class and racial lines, often by exposure to diverse cultural expressions in cosmopolitan centers such as Paris or New York.
Mass-circulation magazines, department stores, cinema, and advertising expanded its market and associations with an active and fun-loving lifestyle throughout the 1920s.
In the United States modern design flourished in the expanding consumer economy of the 1920s, stimulated by exhibitions stemming from the Paris exhibition of 1925 and the emigration of European designers working independently or under contract to manufacturers.
The extension of design to the utilitarian products of mechanized and standardized mass production, such as kitchen appliances or assembly-line automobiles, provided the basis for designers to work for large-scale industries in order to add consumer appeal to such products and stimulate sales, and in tandem with advertising agencies and departments.
The phenomenon of Streamlining offers an insight into the complex relationship among competing commercial, engineering-based, and aesthetic interests in the expanding role of design for industry in the 1930s.
In exhibitions and through competitions beginning in the early 1930s, the fledgling Museum of Modern Art in New York displayed and advocated for its own version of European Modernism, based at first upon architecture and then expanding to industrial design.
MoMA focused its attention upon a particular application of technology to manufactured products, emphasizing aesthetic purity as the result of mechanized production and eschewing original or historical revival decoration.
Further justifications for MoMAs design standards included hygiene and an avoidance of overt luxury during the depressed economic conditions of the 1930s.
And yet, in addition to models for low-cost housing drawn from the Weissenhof exhibition in Stuttgart in 1927, MoMA also included in its developing canon of Modernism one-off houses for the wealthy such as Le Corbusiers Villa Savoye (19281931) and Viennese émigré Richard Neutras Lovell House (19271929) in southern California, based upon a refined aesthetic sensibility responding to light, open transparent spaces, and smooth mirror-like surfaces whether expanses of glass or polished marble.
After World War II and amid economic recovery, MoMAs exhibitions continued to promote its approach to modern design under the name of Good Design, appealing initially to families purchasing homes during the post-war housing boom, to be treated in Part V.

## Global
Inspiration IV The Americas This fourth installment of Global Inspiration considers the broader Americas, a vast and exciting area encompassing North, South, and Central American nations, often marginalized as being somehow less central or significant to the history of modern design.
In the United States the Spanish-Colonial missions established in California from the later eighteenth century attest to the hybrid Spanish and Indigenous American element in the countrys history, not surprisingly in the American West.
The so-called Mission Style used the Indigenous building materials of stucco applied to brick that persisted well into the 1920s in southern California for houses, churches, and municipal buildings.
Travel, and perhaps year-round sunshine, drew tourists, artists, and designers to the southwestern United States and to the decorative arts traditions of Indigenous Americans and the monuments of Aztec and Mayan civilization in textiles, pottery, jewelry, and basket-weaving, in a sense not only keeping alive these skills but revitalizing them as well, albeit beholden to tourism and a collectors market.
Albert C.
Barnes and John D.
Rockefeller were among the twentieth-century buyers of Indigenous American artifacts, analyzed and published in catalogs, displayed in exhibitions, and preserved in their collections.
More elaborate decorative motifs resulting in original, if fanciful, combinations of Spanish colonial and Indigenous Latin American culture adorned the façades and interiors of theatres and hotels throughout the American West, at times treated abstractly as in the Phoenix Biltmore Hotel in Arizona (1929) or in the exuberant Hispano-Moresque molded decoration of the domed Bellagio Theatre in Los Angeles (1926).
GI4.1 Louis Ipsen and Victor F.
Houser, stacking storage dishes, earthenware, wood, steel, J.
A.
Bauer Pottery Company, Los Angeles, California, 1932.
Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
The compact, circular, and brightly colored stacking storage dishes from the early 1930s illustrated in figure GI4.1 were designed by Louis Ipsen and Victor F.
Houser for the J.
A.
Bauer Pottery Company near Los Angeles.
While they recall Mission pottery from the region in their tactile quality and matt finish, the ensemble was modernized by Ipsen and Houser with brighter glazes, introducing stacking to save counter or table space.
One has to wonder whether Frederick Hurten Rhead was aware of this living tradition of pottery design during his time in California as a studio potter and whether his tableware name Fiesta suggests a debt to Mexico (see fig.
10.30).
Colorful Mexican pottery also contributed to the concept of Mexicanidad that developed after the Mexican Revolution (191020), as seen in the objects, folk art, and colorful interiors of artists Frida Kahlo (19071954) and Diego Riveras (18861957) home (now a museum) in Mexico City and known as the Casa Azul. Kahlo enjoyed wearing clothing based upon traditional Mexican fashion including the square-necked huipil, and Mexican fashions were featured in the October 1937 issue of Vogue as well as in government-sponsored films promoting tourism to the region.
Despite the debt to Indigenous craft traditions, the commercial success of Mexican fashion was due to the introduction of the sewing machine for the efficient construction of skirt flounces with colorful geometric designs, and the use of machine embroidery, as seen in figure GI4.2.
GI4.2 Cotton huipil with machine-embroidered chain-stitched printed cotton skirt with embroidered holán ruffle, Museo Frida Kahlo, Mexico City.
In 1938 Argentinian architect-designers Antoni Bonet (19131989), Juan Kurchan (19131975), and Jorge Ferrari-Hardoy (19141977) traveled to Paris as assistants in the studio of Le Corbusier, who at the time was working on a plan for the redesign of the city of Buenos Aires (he also served as a consultant for the Ministry of Education and Health Building in Rio de Janeiro in 1937, part of an extensive urban reform project constructed under Brazilian dictator Getúlio Vargas).
Returning to Argentina, they formed the partnership Grupo Austral, producing a lightweight, collapsible wrought-iron-framed chair slung with folded fabric known as theBKF (fig.
GI4.3), named for the initials of their last names.
The chair consists of two bent and intersecting wrought-iron loops or hairpins that are welded to one another.
The quatrefoil-shaped leather seat and back fit round the upper bent corners of the two welded-iron loops.
Thin, lightweight, portable, assembled rather than elaborately crafted, the BKF exemplified Modernist concerns with industrial materials and inexpensive assembly.
It was manufactured by Artek, the same company that produced the designs of Finnish architect Alvar Aalto (see here) and was marketed and sold in the United States through a New York-based distributor.
Two BKF chairs were purchased by the Museum of Modern Art, and after World War II the chair was manufactured by the Knoll Corporation (see here).
When inexpensive knock-off versions of the chair appeared on the market, Knoll sued unsuccessfully to protect its exclusive rights to produce the chair, but the courts denied their claim on the grounds that the chair was simply a modified version of a late nineteenth-century wooden collapsible camp chair and was therefore not an original design.
In Buenos Aires, in addition to the Grupo Austral, Bauhauseducated graphic designer Grete Stern (19041999) and her husband, photographer Horacio Coppola (19062012), who had moved to the city in 1935, worked in the cosmopolitan city, producing photographs, photomontages, and advertisements that often celebrated modern urban life transformed by electricity at night and the bustling energy of the streets filled with shoppers and outdoor cafés.
