Grupo Austral (Antoni Bonet, Juan Kurchan, Jorge Ferrari-Hardoy), BKF folding chair, painted wrought iron, leather, (88.3 × 75 × 75 cm), Buenos Aires, Argentina, 1938.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
The scope of design produced in or inspired by the Indigenous and Hispanic Americas during the interwar period was broad and increasingly international.
Some designers were drawn to the social promise of European Modernist movements, while others sought to define a national identity based upon the revival of local craft traditions but updated through the introduction of modern industrial materials and production.
Both approaches reached broader audiences through marketing, travel, tourism, print, and entertainment.
Portuguese-speaking Brazil, and Rio de Janeiro in particular, appears in popular cinema as a free and fun-loving destination for European or North American tourists to escape more proper conventions of social behavior at home.
One can observe this stereotypical depiction in the 1933 RKO Pictures film Flying Down to Rio, starring the dancing-act team of Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire, who show off their skills at a nightclub to the rhythms of a lively tango band dressed in flounce-sleeved shirts and sombreros (fig.
GI4.4).
There is certainly a hint of Orientalism or cultural bias in the image of Latin America as it is represented in popular entertainment, alluring in its exotic, authentic traditions and pastimes, yet at the same time beholden, even subservient to Western technology and investment.
A carefree hedonism appears as well in colorful illustrated Brazilian magazines of the 1920s such as Para Todos or A Maça, often featuring scantily clad young women enjoying the citys night life but dressed in modern European fashion rather than in traditional folk costume.
A mixture of international and native elements also characterizes the landscape and garden design of Brazilian architect and landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx (19091994).
GI4.4 Film still, Flying Down to Rio, RKO Radio Pictures, Hollywood, California, 1933.
Humanism and Luxury: International Modernism and Mass Culture After World War II (1945–1960) he United States and the Soviet Union assumed leading and competitive adversarial roles internationally after World War II, in the period generally known as the Cold War.
Design demonstrated and promoted each of the two superpowers’ political and economic interests and ambitions both at home and abroad.
In Europe, as well as in Japan, severe hardship haunted the years immediately following the end of the war, with massive displacement of people, food shortages, material and housing insufficiencies, interruption of transportation and communication, high unemployment, and fears of working-class unrest.
While urgently needed supplies and aid came in the form of charity and relief from agencies that included the newly established United Nations (chartered in 1945 with headquarters in Manhattan), economic recovery required more substantial investment.
The role assumed by the United States in this effort was paramount.
Through the Marshall Plan (also known as the Economic Recovery Plan or ERP, 1948–52) the United States government provided funding to corporations abroad to promote industrial production, stimulate employment, and improve the standard of living.
The motivations behind such investment included expanding the market for the USA’s own goods and business-related services abroad, fostering free trade and economic cooperation among European nations (including Germany), as well as containing Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, Asia, and Latin America.
On both sides of the Cold War, design was a component of “soft power,” a form of political persuasion that included marketing the products of modern industrial design as evidence of technological, material, and social progress whether the result of capitalist free enterprise or of a communist command economy.
The prospect of international markets spurred the global ambitions of large multi-national corporations such as IBM and CBS in the United States, Braun in West Germany, and Olivetti in Italy, and their conscious development of prominent and unifying visual identity programs, as well as efforts to link their products and services with responsible business practice through exhibitions, sponsorships, and publications.
At the same time national identity persisted as a marker of sovereignty and independence from American hegemony in the forging of distinctive cultural values that might include a commitment to social responsibility parallel with welfare initiatives to improve living standards as well as to reduce social ills, income inequality, and avoid class conflict.
At times there was a didactic, mildly polemic tone accompanying the promotion of international modern design in the early post-war years, reminiscent of strains of nineteenth-century design reform.
In the United States, advocates such as the Museum of Modern Art, under the rubric “good design,” embraced familiar paternalistic themes of improving and educating the public to appreciate the aesthetic, social, and practical advantages of modern industrial design, including its broader contribution to fostering democratic values and a contemporary lifestyle that harmonized individualism and materialism with the self-imposed responsibility of citizens and businesses toward the wider community, in effect embodying a “new humanism.” At times the advocates of this approach leveled criticism against a narrow and monolithic view of commercialism, the advertising industry, and what designer Brooks Stevens termed “planned obsolescence,” which implied the absence of responsible standards and the exploitation of novelty, hedonism, and insatiable consumer desire.
Standards for post-war design featured technology in the form of new industrial materials such as plastic, fiberglass, and plywood with techniques such as molding to create furniture and furnishings that implied costefficient production, comfort, innovation, and an association with forms of modern abstract art.
This is seen most clearly in the relationship between furniture and abstract sculpture associated with the movements of Automatic Surrealism and Constructivism, and in the international recognition of artists such as Henry Moore and Alexander Calder (1898–1976), whose sculptures appeared not only in museums but also in large urban public places and parks.
Graphic designers in the United States such as Alvin Lustig and Paul Rand also adopted a sophisticated approach to advertising and magazine cover design that showed affinities with the symbolic associations of abstract art, while in Germany and Switzerland graphic designers often viewed their work in ethical terms, simplifying and clarifying complex information using the discipline of a two-dimensional grid system.
Addressing urgent material and housing shortages after World War II along with high rates of unemployment, Western European governments supported design as an element of economic recovery for both domestic and export markets, attempting to equal and then to surpass prewar trade and production levels.
Expanding beyond earlier design concerns with economy and efficiency in relation to minimum working-class needs, industrial designers and advocates in the postwar period often characterized their approach more broadly as “fitness to purpose.” This term embraced ergonomics and anthropometry, defined as the science of designing for the ease and comfort of human use.
Research-based design of this kind attempted to place the profession of industrial design within an empirical, “problem-solving” context and to enumerate criteria, beyond profits and sales, by which products might be judged successful and innovative.
Such views shifted the designer’s role from that of mere “product stylist” whose intentions were subverted or compromised by fashion and commercialism to one whose focus was upon meeting specific human needs.
Practitioners and advocates promoted the tenets or standards of modern international design as being in the public interest and distinct from the relativism implied by fashion and novelty.
Shared standards and limits to the expression of individual will, whether in product design, graphic design, or political or ethical attitudes, were viewed as bulwarks against manipulation by advertisers or demagogues, especially in an age of mass communication and amid lingering fears of totalitarianism and propaganda.
Indeed, mass media, whether as a vehicle for marketing products or for disseminating political views, permitted an unprecedented expansion of the ability of corporations and governments to influence public opinion.
The power of totalitarian propaganda prior to and during World War II suggested that ethically responsible standards provided designers with a political role, even a mission, in shaping and strengthening shared cultural values and democratic ideals.
As mentioned above, large and diverse corporations with interests in global markets and raw materials and resources (such as oil) were among the strongest advocates and clients for modern design: their headquarters, office interiors, products, organization, and promotional materials both expressed and shaped shared values of efficiency, rationalism, progress, dependability, responsibility, and public education.
A coherent design policy, or “house style,” not only informed the look of products, but also bred familiarity and trust through a more generalized brand identity.
It also reinforced loyalty and conformity among employees.
At the same time, fears of the concentration of power in the hands of too few emerged in United States President Dwight Eisenhower’s farewell address in 1961, where he noted the connection between industrial technology and the arms race, and possible conflicts with the national interest.
Post-war industrial design, promoted as “good design” or “Gute Form,” was effectively marketed through museum exhibitions seeking to raise awareness and increase the level of public discrimination, and through international events such as World’s Fairs and the Milan Triennale, the latter offering competitive awards.
In the USSR and its proxies, modern industrial design also flourished following the death in 1953 of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin as the basis for low-cost housing, domestic furniture, and household products.
Post-war modern design was also the subject of articles and illustrations in journals such as Domus, Industrial Design, and Design Quarterly, and was supported by organizations such as the Council of Industrial Design (COID) in Britain and its counterparts in Japan and Scandinavia.
Also important were schools such as the Hfg (Hochschule für Gestaltung) at Ulm in West Germany and graphic design schools in Zurich and Basel.
Yet for many consumers, the “good design” model was not understood as a universal set of standards that raised general cultural awareness or instilled responsible democratic values.
Rather its products were considered a matter of taste, simply offering one among many possibilities for individual fulfillment in an age of increasing affluence and expanding leisure, a matter of “both ... and” rathe than “either ... or.” Perhaps seeking to escape the shortages and governmentimposed restrictions on materials and manufacturing during the war years, the American middle class in particular responded enthusiastically to constant novelty, fantasy, and instant gratification, as manufacturers and advertisers of household goods recognized a seemingly insatiable appetite for products or gadgets that promised to reduce housework and provide outlets for spending leisure time, acknowledging and celebrating social and cultural difference, an exercise in freedom of choice rather than directed by museum professionals and public intellectuals.
Detroit-manufactured automobiles of the 1950s and their presence in Hollywood Technicolor films and on television most easily exemplify mass design after World War II, driving desire through the identification of materialism and consumer choice with freedom, leisure, luxury, power, and social mobility.
Another medium that stimulated mass taste was popular magazines, whose images and product advertisements promised a better life for the American family and vicarious thrills for a generation of youthful consumers.
Almost immediately such images were appropriated by the Pop Art movement in the United States, Britain, and elsewhere in Europe, whether as critique or celebration.
The allure of mass culture for artists ranged from a desire to challenge abstraction with the accessibility and immediacy of popular imagery, to the pure visual excitement of bold aesthetics, to a recognition of the seductive power of idealized mass-media images of beauty and fulfillment supplied by commercial artists, photographers, and illustrators, masking persistent racial inequality, discrimination, and other barriers to social advancement for minorities.
Post-war suburban housing communities were another part of the broader idealism embodied in mass design, a vision of life sometimes referred to as the American Dream.
Many Americans moved from inner-city neighborhoods to newly created suburbs, where the availability of land for affordable single-family housing and incentives for purchasing new automobiles helped to define post-war lifestyles.
Cheap gasoline prices, made possible by American-based corporate control of West Asian oilfields and refineries, made commuting both affordable and reasonably comfortable.
At the same time, mass-produced methods of construction for detached housing, initiated in communities such as Levittown, New York, offered alternatives to city apartment living and were equipped with conveniences such as automatic washers, dryers, and modern kitchen appliances.
For many Americans, individual home ownership brought with it the promise of leisure, green space, independence, security, and the freedom of personal mobility.
The exodus from city to suburb only exacerbated racial inequality and deteriorating inner-city living conditions, addressed with massive public-housing projects with limited success.
The emerging mass culture was criticized during and after World War II from a number of perspectives.
Some commentators complained about consumers’ lack of discrimination and questioned the morality of conspicuous consumption in encouraging submission to manufactured ideals of beauty and health, and in which superficial differences and consumer choice masked an underlying conservatism and conformity.
Others viewed mass culture as a form of social control reinforcing traditional family and gender roles of the white middle class.
Still others dismissed popular culture as “kitsch,” debased mass-produced imitations of authentic culture standing at the lowest common denominator of taste, that is, of pure physical sensation renewed and manipulated by a commercial culture industry.
In this view, culture is synonymous with leisure and entertainment rather than with more abiding values that contribute to well-being, enlightenment, self-realization, and active participation in a responsible democracy.
And as noted above, race was yet another area of concern: many suburban communities and subdivisions either prohibited or discriminated against Black people, leading to civil rights protests and finally through legislation addressing forms of racial segregation in education and voting rights.
Eventually the monolithic view of mass culture derided by social critics and educators crumbled, as it was too narrow to embrace a strain of vitality, popular expression, subversion, and irrationality found in comic books, film noir, tailfins, and rock ’n’ roll.
The dualism between “good” design and mass taste, between high design and popular culture, reflects a limited viewpoint demanding a broader and more nuanced cultural perspective.
The attitudes and artifacts of both approaches to design emerge as expressions of capitalist expansion, soft power as a means of persuasion in response to Cold War tensions that made consumer goods one of the battlegrounds of competing ideologies for material progress in a democratic society.
As in Part IV, generalizations about design approaches or movements are often belied by looking more carefully at examples in relation to their local contexts.
In sum, despite an acknowledged critical dichotomy between the new humanism and mass taste, both strains of post-war design coexisted, occasionally overlapped, and contributed to the identification between designed goods and an improvement of the social and material conditions of modern living.
Whether conditioned by a new and broader set of criteria for a discriminating international audience or giving playful, inventive form to popular images of power, dissent, freedom, and luxury for the American middle class, design thrived in the climate of economic recovery and growth in the United States and abroad during the postwar period amid the emergence of new technologies, unprecedented increases in production, and escalating levels of consumption.
In the Soviet Union a consumer culture emerged in the later 1950s as well, shifting from austerity and sacrifice in the pursuit of a collective work ethic to a focus upon material goods as barometers of an improved working-class standard of living, including kitchen appliances and entertainment in the form of radios, phonographs, and televisions.
A focus upon leisure was even more apparent in non-aligned countries such as Yugoslavia who brokered a greater degree of independence from Moscow, sometimes referred to as “Second World” communism.
Part V of the Global Inspiration takes a closer look at post-World War II Japan; following its defeat in the war and the suffering caused by the detonation of atomic bombs in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan launched a national program of economic recovery and identity building rooted in design and carefully constructed to appeal to international markets.

## Chapter
11 Modernism after World War II: The United States, Western Europe, and Scandinavia Although shortages, rationing, and austerity continued to affect design practice in Europe immediately following the end of World War II, economic recovery, optimism, and consumer confidence were stimulated by the example of the United States and by the staging of national and international exhibitions such as the Milan Triennale and the Festival of Britain (1951), the latter celebrating the centennial of the Crystal Palace.
In the United States, a number of modern industrial designers adapted new wartime materials and technologies to domestic goods: some products of this era continue to be manufactured today.
In 1947, Earl Tupper (19071983) began to market Tupperware (founded in 1945), a line of flexible, translucent plastic storage and serving containers with self-sealing airtight lids to prevent spilling and preserve freshness (fig.
11.1).
Tupperware utilized smooth, simple, often stackable forms in standardized sizes with interchangeable lids.
After being sold initially as conventional store-bought items, Tupperware was available after 1951 exclusively through catalogs supplied by neighborhood vendors who demonstrated the products in the home.
Such merchandising was essential to Tupperwares commercial success, identifying buyers with users rather than the less personal connection between buyer and salesperson, avoiding comparisons and competition with related shelf products.
Tuppers marketing strategy reduced consumer resistance to industrial materials being used in the home rather than traditional ceramic or glass storage containers.
His commercial success dated to the 1950s but was based upon his invention of a new pliable plastic called Poly-T in 1942, manufactured by DuPont and other chemical companies during World War II.
This interest in harnessing wartime technologies and high-volume industrial production to improve domestic living through new, inexpensive, and practical products played a large role in shaping positive attitudes toward industrial design in the decade following the end of World War II.
It also demonstrates synergy between chemical corporations and modern design, and encouraged further research and development of new materials and products that included synthetic fabrics that in turn demanded the services of designers.
Chemical and pharmaceutical companies also employed graphic designers who helped to explain and promote scientific concepts and their useful applications in visual terms to the public and to the business community through popular and professional magazines as well as trade fairs.
At the time there was little concern in the design community or among consumers about the health and environmental hazards associated with plastics; the same enthusiasm toward technology that today accompanies the development of plant-based alternatives to plastics and other synthetics accompanied the post-war products of the petrochemical industry.
Earl Tupper, cereal bowls and seals, polyolefin, 6 <sup>1</sup>/ in (16.5 cm) in diameter, manufactured by Tupper, c.
1949.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
In addition to Tupperware, designers developed a dazzling array of household domestic products after the war.
A series of Bubble hanging lamps was designed by George Nelson Associates beginning in 1952 and manufactured by the Michigan-based Howard Miller Clock Company.
The lamps were constructed from steel wire attached to rings (rather than welded) and sprayed with liquid plastic to create translucent shells in a variety of rounded shapes (fig.
11.2).
In articles for the trade journal Industrial Design, Nelson praised the vitality of the industrial design profession in comparison with traditional products and methods of production that were less relevant to modern living and could not compete in the dynamic arena of international business and markets.
The similarity between Nelsons plastic bubble lamps and the traditional use of rice paper for lantern shades and sliding (shoji) screens in Japan suggests an affinity between post-World War II industrial design and aesthetic elements of Japanese architecture and interior design that were promoted internationally at exhibitions (see Global Inspiration V, here and fig.
GI5.6).
George Nelson Associates, Bubble hanging lamps, steel wire and sprayed plastic shell, height of largest lamp 33 in (84 cm), manufactured by Howard Miller Clock Company, Zeeland, Michigan, from 1952.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.

## Problem-Solving,
Collaboration, and Marketing Industrial Design Consultant designer Henry Dreyfuss (see here) continued to emphasize, and to help define, research as a determinant in product housings for a variety of manufactured goods.
For his redesigned combined handset for Bell Telephone in 1946, Dreyfuss replaced the units metal housing with lightweight plastic and a receiver whose form could be cradled between ear and shoulder, the result of trial-and-error testing, freeing the hand and creating a more natural interface between product and user (see fig.
10.26 for the earlier model of 1937).
He was a staunch advocate for the study of measurement in the design process that would contribute to safety, and facilitate ease of use, efficient use of spaces, and the reduction of fatigue and injury whether at home or in the workplace (more recent examples of the danger of not considering such factors are lawsuits stemming from unstable IKEA dressers that were responsible for toddler deaths when they tipped over).
Dreyfuss published his The Measure of Man: Human Factors in Design in 1960 (fig.
11.3), a manual of detailed drawings in which measurement rather than aesthetics or guesswork informs design decisions.
Employing a series of average body sizes for men and for women that acknowledged different general types of users, The Measure of Man used observation, testing, and measurement to determine heights of tables, distances between operators and machines or appliances, and the form and placement of knobs and dials on devices and control panels for ease-of-operation, safety, and the reduction of error and injury.
While still involving choice, access to such information reduces the range of options available to designers in the interests of consumer safety, whether mandated by designers themselves, manufacturers, or government regulation.
Henry Dreyfuss, illustration from The Measure of Man: Human Factors in Design, height 13 in (33 cm), New York, 1960.
Another iconic example of the Dreyfuss offices post-war industrial design is the round, wall-mounted thermostat manufactured for the Honeywell Corporation (fig.
11.4).
Honeywell dominated the market for thermostats to regulate temperature in homes and offices, but the idea of a round control was attractive to the company from a marketing standpoint as it would differentiate the companys product visually from its competitors.
Although company records indicate some interest in a round model from the early 1940s, the new model did not appear until 1953.
Adapting the thermostat mechanisms to a round housing necessitated significant technical invention, credited to the company engineer Carl Kronmiller (18891968), who developed a spring coil to replace the conventional glass-enclosed mercury-filled thermometer that was difficult to manufacture in a curved form.
While the costs of development were considerable, the final manufactured product was less expensive than earlier models.
Dreyfuss liked the idea of the round control from the standpoint of mounting: that is, rectangular models almost always looked crooked when set on the wall.
A further refinement that Dreyfuss developed was a concentric metal plate that easily snapped around the clear plastic readout and control.
He was also responsible for suggesting that the concentric plate be manufactured in a variety of colors to match wall colors or blend in with wallpaper patterns.
Dreyfusss name appeared frequently in advertising campaigns, but the development process of this product was a collaboration and began long before he was hired.
Inexpensive, easy to operate, inconspicuous, and attractive in its compact concentric form, the Honeywell Round exemplified the advantages of post-war industrial design, and companies often promoted the integral and creative role of the industrial designer as a marketing tactic rather than a reflection of the complex nature of product development.
Henry Dreyfuss, Honeywell round thermostat, plastic and painted aluminum housing, 3 in (7.6 cm) in diameter, manufactured by Honeywell Corporation, 1953.
Advertisement in Life, November 9, 1953.
American designers were eager to demonstrate the advantages of modern materials and methods of production for furniture that contributed to a contemporary, efficient, and comfortable standard of living that accompanied the post-war boom in housing.
Clients included corporations and businesses whose offices projected an image of modern efficiency and increasingly sophisticated taste.
Original designs were manufactured and effectively promoted by the Herman Miller Company of Zeeland, Michigan (see fig.
10.29).
Following Gilbert Rohdes untimely death in 1944, company president D.
J.
DePree hired architect and writer George Nelson (19081986) as chief designer.
In turn, Nelson encouraged DePree to manufacture and market the furniture of contemporary designers, including Charles and Ray Eames.
Charles Eames (1907 1978) studied architecture at Washington University in St.
Louis and was hired as artistin-residence and instructor at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, where he taught from 1938 until 1941.
He met Ray (19121988) at Cranbrook, where she was a student in the weaving workshop, having first studied painting in New York.
Charles Eamess design for a molded plywood chair, a collaboration with Eero Saarinen (19101961), won first prize at the Museum of Modern Art-sponsored competition for Organic Design in Home Furnishings in 1940 (see fig.
10.44).
While working for the United States Navy during World War II, the Eameses experimented with plywood molding processes to develop lightweight, flexible splints to treat wounded soldiers.
After the war they adapted the technology to the molded forms for seating.
Unlike earlier plywood molding techniques used, for instance, by Alvar Aalto, the Eameses approach to molding was three-dimensional  what design historian Peter Dormer termed vessel and valley forms.
In 1946, the Eameses designed a molded plywood chair with separate seat and back supported by a thin, welded tubular-steel frame and mounted with rubber shocks, eventually manufactured by Herman Miller (fig.
11.5).
The couple continued to experiment with molded plywood and fiberglass in the later 1940s, and their unupholstered dining armchair of 1950, a single piece combining armrests, seat, and back, also mounted on a tubular-metal frame, won another international competition sponsored by the Museum of Modern Art for low-cost furniture, promoting economical solutions to meet the needs of returning veterans starting families with limited means.
In 1954, Miller introduced an armless, stacking version of the fiberglass chair; it was widely adopted for seating in schools and other institutions by virtue of its light weight and ability to be easily stored and moved.
Like Tuppers Poly-T plastic, fiberglass was used extensively as a lightweight and inexpensive material for aircraft during World War II, and was developed for use in the home and office afterward, connecting military industrial technology with modern living, with designers applying their creative and problem-solving skills to meet domestic needs on the civilian front.
Charles and Ray Eames, Eames Low Chair, molded walnut veneered plywood, chrome-plated steel rods, and rubber shock mounts, $2 7 ~ ^ { 3 } / _ { 8 } \times 2 2 ~ ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 } \times 2 5 ~ ^ { 3 } / _ { 8 }$ in $( 6 9 .
5 \times 5 6 .
