5$ cm), manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, 1946.
Vitra Design Museum, Germany.

## The
Aesthetics of Post-War Industrial Design Mechanized production and industrial technology were agents not only of improved efficiency and economy but also of an emerging aesthetic of biomorphic sculptural forms as well as geometric abstraction.
The Eameses, for instance, explored the organicism of molded plywood in their iconic 1956 lounge chair and footstool, designed for Herman Miller (fig.
11.6).
It was constructed of three separate pieces of molded plywood, upholstered in leather, and supported by a five-legged metal pedestal base.
The Eameses lounge chair emphasizes individual comfort, abstract sculptural form, and expense beyond their earlier low-cost furniture, with industrial technology extending beyond efficiency, often involving added material and labor costs.
Charles and Ray Eames, lounge chair and ottoman; chair: $3 3 \times 3 3 \% \times 3 2$ in (84 × 86 × 81 cm); ottoman: 24 ${ } ^ { 3 } / _ { 4 } \times 1 7 \times 2 1$ ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 }$ in $( 6 3 \times 4 3 \times 5 4$ cm), laminated rosewood, aluminum, and leather upholstery, manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, 1956.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Fueled by optimism stemming from faith in wartime technology, modern designers in the first post-war decade more expansively defined the relationship between their products and modern living standards, allowing for the self-expression of the designer and a projection of the owners taste.
In addition to a continuous supply of new designs with advantages to the consumer in terms of comfort, lightness, efficiency, or beauty, marketing strategies focused upon the individual designer, who lent uniqueness to serially manufactured goods.
Herman Miller, for instance, manufactured abstract sculptural designs by Japanese-American artist Isamu Noguchi (19041988), such as his glass table (fig.
11.7), supported by an ebonized wood base consisting of two irregular forms, suggestive of Automatic Surrealism.
Although elements of interwar Modernisms egalitarian social ideology remained after World War II, it was the transformation of that ideology that often best exemplifies post-war modern design in the 1950s.
This transformation produced a benevolent marriage of commerce and culture, in which an elevated taste merged with upper-middle-class economic prosperity.
The organic furniture of the period also accompanied the increasing appearance of monumental abstract sculpture in public buildings and spaces such as Alexander Calders mobiles or the bronze sculptures of Henry Moore (18981986), seen in Three Way Piece Number 1 in Philadelphia (fig.
11.8).
11.7 11.8 Isamu Noguchi, coffee table, glass and ebonized birch, 15 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 50 × 36 in (40 × 127 × 91 cm), manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, c.
1947.
Private collection.
Henry Moore, Three Way Piece Number 1, bronze, height 76 in (193 cm), Philadelphia, 1964–1965.
Another development of post-war modern design in furniture manufacturing was modularity, seen in storage and shelving, which had appeared earlier in Eliot Noyess vision of organic design for the Museum of Modern Art exhibition of 1940 to 1941 (see here).
Eero Saarinen and Charles Eames designed a series of modular units for domestic interiors for the Red Lion Company in Pennsylvania, constructed of plywood with dowel-like legs and sliding doors for cabinets.
The Eameses small shelving units, known as the ESU system, designed for Miller (fig.
11.9), used light steel bracing for strength and support, as well as rectangular molded plywood sliding doors with embossed circular designs to create colorful variations in color and texture.
Moreover, Miller designs and other modular shelving units approximated in three dimensions the asymmetrical balance of paintings by Mondrian.
Their transparency and thin structural components also echo the steel and glass architecture of the period, for instance, the Lever House office building on Park Avenue in Manhattan, designed by Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill, in 1951 to 1952 (fig.
11.10), across the street from Mies van der Rohes Seagram Building (1958).
11.9 Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill, Lever House, Manhattan, 1952.
Charles and Ray Eames, Eames Storage Unit (ESU), plastic-coated plywood, lacquered masonite, and chrome-plated steel, 58 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 47 × 16 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (148.6 × 119.4 × 42.5 cm), manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, 1950.

## 11.10 The refinement of the Eames lounge chair was also incorporated into furniture design
s manufactured by German émigré Hans Knoll, who established Knoll Associates in 1943.
Knolls wife and partner, Florence Schust Knoll (19172019), studied at the Cranbrook Academy in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, and did much to establish the companys association with modern design after the war.
Knoll manufactured the furniture prototypes of Modernist architect and former director of the Bauhaus, Mies van der Rohe (see here): for instance, his steel and upholstered leather Barcelona chair designed for the German Pavilion at the 1929 international exhibition held in Spain.
The company also manufactured designs by Cranbrook faculty and students such as the Italian-born sculptor Harry Bertoia (19151978).
Knoll produced Bertoias Diamond chair made of spot-welded steel (fig.
11.11) from 1952, which features the molded vessel and valley forms also seen in plywood and plastic designs for chairs by Saarinen and Eames (see here).
Bertoia had worked with Eames on molded plywood designs in California.
The chairs form approximates an abstract approach to the wingspan of a bird in flight, enhanced through the open and elastic weblike treatment of the welded steel wires.
Harry Bertoia, Diamond chair, steel wire and upholstery, 30 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 33 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 28 in (77.5 × 86 × 71 cm), manufactured by Knoll Associates, New York, 1952 The Eameses design activities included a trip to India in 1957, resulting in an India Report in 1958 at the invitation of the Indian government following independence from Great Britain in 1947.
In their report, the Eameses steered a flexible middle ground between the benefits of industrial technology in the post-World War II period and a respect for local craft traditions that demonstrated the broader humanizing aspects of their practice and may also be seen in the eclectic objects they collected and displayed in their Los Angeles home.
Rather than rejecting the past and embracing mechanized mass production, the Eameses report on India recognized value in preindustrial practices and the need to accommodate local identity within the framework of post-war Modernism.
Eero Saarinen designed a modern furniture group using pedestals as support for Knoll, manufactured in 1956 (fig.
11.12).
Like Bertoia, Saarinen explored the flexible, organic possibilities of modern industrial materials, in this case molded fiberglass, with chairs and tables supported by a painted aluminum base providing visual balance and harmony.
In the advertisement for the pedestal chair, designed by Swiss émigré Herbert Matter (who served as Knolls advertising director), the addressing model wears pants rather than a skirt or dress, communicating a casual informality and the appeal of a modern, active lifestyle (see also here).
While the intention of many post-World War II designers and manufacturers was to be inclusive (Charles Eames coined the dictum the best for the most for the least), the industrial design profession produced few designers of color, and like the nation, did little to address the discrimination that plagued economic, educational, and social progress for African Americans during the 1950s.
The growing taste for expressively treated modern industrial materials also helped to renew public appreciation for American architect Frank Lloyd Wright in the 1950s, thanks at least in part to articles written by George Nelson and published in Architectural Digest.
Wrights spiraling Guggenheim Museum on Fifth Avenue in New York (opened 1959) used reinforced concrete to create a series of sweeping interior ramps.
Other related architectural designs featuring the aesthetic possibilities of reinforced concrete included Eero Saarinens TWA Terminal at what is now John F.
Kennedy International Airport in Long Island, New York, built between 1958 and 1962.
The sculptural possibilities of new materials and production technologies for building are also found in Jørn Utzons dramatic Opera House in Sydney, Australia (begun 1958) and continue to provide the basis for originality in architecture, for instance, in Frank Gehrys Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain (1997), or his Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles (2003).
A more restrained sculptural aesthetic is seen in the interior design of passenger airplanes, in particular Walter Teagues design for the Boeing 707 aircraft of 1955 to 1956 (fig.
11.13).
Like Dreyfuss, Teague established his reputation as a consultant industrial designer in the interwar period and was committed to a consideration of human factors and an understanding of manufacturing processes (see fig.
10.23).
Teagues airline interior features recessed indirect lighting and curving molded plastic surfaces without projections or patterned decoration; such attributes met rigid industry safety standards and had a calming psychological effect, tested through the construction of a full-scale interior model to observe passenger reaction.
Teague remained a vigorous spokesperson for design research that included user experience, publishing books as well as articles in the journal Industrial Design.
Recessed surfaces, concave moldings around windows, and indirect interior lighting in commercial airliners remain legacies of Teagues approach.
More recently headphones and tilting touchscreen personal movie screens on the backs of seats on longer flights provide added means of more comfortably occupying travelers during longer flights and delays.
The same cannot be said of the industrys efforts to maximize profits by increasing the number of seats in coach (economy) class and of making flyers pay for added leg room.
When American Airlines began to advertise more leg room in coach class in 2000, the company based its claim on the measurement (known as pitch) between the bolts that secure each row of seats to tracks on the floor of the aircraft.
American had increased this measurement to 33 inches (83.8 cm) from the industry standard of 31 inches (78.7 cm).
In 2016, 31 inches remained standard for most carriers, while low-cost carriers reduced pitch to 29 inches.
By comparison, in his 1960 book The Measure of Man, Dreyfuss recommended the minimum pitch measurement for airline seating at between 34 and 35 inches (86 and 89 cm).
Today airlines direct much of their design efforts toward the higher end of the market, with millions of dollars spent on first-class seating that allow seats to convert into beds, making the benefits of design research a luxury rather than a reasonable standard expectation.
Walter Teague, full-scale model for interior, Boeing 707, published in Interior, 1955–1956.
Promoting Post-War Design: Museums, Art Direction, and the New Advertising In 1946, the Museum of Modern Art organized a solo exhibition of the Eameses furniture designs.
In 1949 the Detroit Institute of Arts also featured the Eameses work as well as that of other modern designers in an exhibition entitled For Modern Living. The furnishings for these exhibitions displayed characteristics of organicism and flexibility as well as new materials and technologies directed toward redefining the practical and aesthetic character of modern offices and domestic living spaces.
In addition to the Museum of Modern Arts exhibition of Good Design and Useful Objects, the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, installed an Idea House in 1947 outfitted with modern furniture and furnishings (fig.
11.14) and intended as a public service in the immediate post-war years to encourage new homeowners to adopt the style and the values of modern design rather than more commercially motivated alternatives.
The museum avoided endorsing particular manufacturers or products, but encouraged consumers paternalistically to recognize and appreciate the advantages of modern industrial design in terms of quality, comfort, convenience, and the aesthetics of modern fine art.
“Idea House,” reconstruction of 1947 exhibition (2000), Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, Minnesota.
Edgar Kaufmann, Jr.
(19101989), who directed the MoMAs industrial design department, was responsible for curating and promoting the museums good design program.
He was the author of a promotional booklet in 1950, and his advice recalls some of the prescriptions (and proscriptions) of design reform: modern design should fulfill the practical needs of modern life, express the spirit of our times, benefit by contemporary advances in the fine arts and pure sciences, take advantage of new materials and techniques and develop familiar ones, develop the forms, textures and colors that spring from the direct fulfillment of requirements in appropriate materials and techniques, express the purpose of an object, never making it seem to be what it is not, express the qualities and beauties of the materials used, never making the materials seem to be what they are not, express the methods used to make an object, not disguising mass production as handicraft or simulating a technique not used, blend the expression of utility, materials and process into a visually satisfactory whole, be simple, its structure evident in its appearance, avoiding extraneous enrichment, master the machine for the service of man, and serve as wide a public as possible, considering modest needs and limited costs no less challenging than the requirements of pomp and luxury.
Modern designs provided interior settings for Hollywood films such as The Man in the Grey Flannel Suit (1956), and were visible in manufacturer showrooms and in department store windows in major cities across the United States.
Post-war modern designs appeared in journals such as Art and Architecture, Industrial Design, and Architectural Digest, whose readers included the architects and interior designers who served as consultants for corporate, professional, and individual clients.
Articles featuring modern interiors also appeared in mass-circulation magazines in the early 1950s, such as Better Homes and Gardens (fig.
11.15).
Alternative voices in todays design community ask us to consider just who good design was good for, and remind us that the designers and manufacturers who promoted the approach represented a mostly privileged, Eurocentric, and white elite.
Modern interior, from Better Homes and Gardens, July, 1953, vol.
31, no.
7, here (“Houses can be built for less money”).
Advertisements for contemporary furniture and product designs were part of a marketing strategy known as the new advertising that favored photography over illustration and simple rather than narrative copy.
Graphic designer Herbert Matter focused on the element of surprise to advertise the inventive pedestal support of Eero Saarinens Tulip chair for the Knoll Corporation on two successive pages (see fig.
11.12; the first page shows the pedestal with seat and back covered with brown wrapping paper).
The advertisements ample white space and minimal copy were characteristic of the new advertising that emphasized bold and immediate visual impact with little or no copy, and the models direct confrontation with the viewer on the successive pages adds surprise and satisfies expectation.
The New York-based Art Directors Club featured examples of such advertising in its yearly publications (the Annual of Advertising and Editorial Art and Design) that illustrated award-winning ads and other forms of promotion in a variety of categories.
This professional focus emphasized creativity in the field with designers serving the needs of business, providing a stronger degree of independence and authority, touted in industry journals such as Printers Ink and Advertising Age.
The new advertising owed much of its power to an interdependence between copy and image that actively engaged the viewer.
Visual metaphors and puns informed the approach, as did inventive typography.
The more widespread use of photographic printing processes (rather than letterpress) stimulated experiment and the free use of techniques that combined to create layouts from which flat printing plates could be produced.
Newer agencies such as Doyle Dane Bernbach, founded in 1949, helped to introduce the more visually arresting approach to advertising, also seen in the work of Paul Rand, whose extensive work in advertising is sometimes overshadowed by his consultant work for corporations (see here).
Rand worked for the Weintraub Agency in New York, the same office where William Bernbach worked as a copy editor before forming his own firm.
Rands Thoughts on Design (1947) is a short but well-illustrated book on the new advertising, which discusses the enduring value of symbols, humor, and surprise to convey messages about products through a variety of pictorial means available to the designer.
Intuition and experiment play a major role in the designers toolbox, and freshness of vision is both creative for the artist and persuasive, even educational, for the viewer.
Rands quotations from philosopher and educator John Dewey (18591952), and his invocation of the integration of the beautiful and useful to describe advertising and other forms of visual communication, suggest a link to design reform, here directed against the outworn visual and narrative conventions of advertising illustration: Visual statements such as illustrations which do not involve esthetic judgment and which are merely literal descriptions can be neither intellectually stimulating nor visually distinctive....
The visual statement, on the other hand, which seeks to express the essence of an idea, and which is based on function, fantasy, and analytic judgment, is likely to be not only unique but meaningful and memorable as well.
Rands 1946 magazine advertisement for Coronet Brandy (fig.
11.16) features a collage of cocktail glasses being effortlessly juggled by a waiter whose head is shaped like a brandy snifter.
Rand explains that the dotted half-tone screen background suggests the effervescence of soda water used for mixed drinks.
As an added element of surprise, Rands flat cut-out shapes contrast with a photograph of a flower pinned to the waiters lapel.
Rands approach to visual communication stressed creative solutions to the presentation of products in which the artists originality and engagement of the viewers attention through surprise, symbol, and humor were compatible and satisfying to the Paul Rand, advertisement for Coronet Brandy, reproduced in Thoughts on Design, Wittenborn, New York, 1947.
The element of surprise, relationships with components familiar from an exposure to contemporary fine art, and expressive use of typography also characterize progressive post-war graphic design for book covers and record album covers.
Alvin Lustig (1915 1955) harnessed these vehicles in original designs using a wide variety of techniques for New Directions Publishing in New York.
Lustig employed a wide range of formal means, including photography, color, texture, and typography to convey a visual equivalent to content.
Whether using montage or abstraction, Lustigs book jackets, magazine covers, and album covers, like Rands advertisements, are suggestive rather than literal or illustrative in their integrated approach to the relationship of word and image.
A book cover for Rimbauds A Season in Hell from 1945 uses an asymmetrical arrangement of amorphous shapes reminiscent of Joan Mirós paintings against a fiery red background (fig.
11.17).
The theme of duality is suggested by the division of the shapes into equal areas of black and white.
While the red background may suggest an inferno, the lettering with its small circles as serifs resembles the star-filled heavens.
In an essay from 1954, Lustig characterized the artistic nature of the graphic designer: The role of the designer and his most important must is to remain free, as free as he possibly can, from the prejudices and the ruts which affect so many others in the field of design.
He must be constantly on guard, cleansing his mind of the tendency to relax into a routine format, ready to experiment, play, change, and alter forms.
If he lacks the inherent ability, the insight, the intuitive selection of what is right for his time, he will not go far and will eventually be forced to enter another field.
If he is equipped with these essential characteristics, he will lead the way to new and more effective approaches to design in all its forms.
Some of these characteristics are apparent in the art-directed magazines that circulated widely in American households after World War II.
Dr M.
F.
Agha (see here) remained as art director for Vogue, Vanity Fair, and other Condé Nast publications during most of the war years.
He was responsible for the modern, integrated approach to layout for feature articles on fashion, travel, health, and other activities characterizing modern living aimed at a discriminating readership.
Aghas approach to art direction stressed experiment and intuition in design decisions regarding typography, photography, illustration, margins, color, and composition.
Alvin Lustig, cover for Rimbaud’s A Season in Hell, New Directions Publishing, New York, 1945.
Such an approach demanded large staffs of copywriters and assistants, freelance photographers and illustrators, and also took advantage of the most up-to-date techniques for color reproduction and high-quality printing.
Fashion or style magazines were large in format (Vogue and its rival Harper’s Bazaar measured 9¾ × 12¼ inches; 25 × 32 cm) and replete with color.
Their covers used striking compositions of photography and inventive typography, while feature articles on fabrics or hair styling also used photography and color to advantage in conveying the vitality and excitement of contemporary life.
Such qualities are also found in new or revamped publications that appeared during and after the war, such as Seventeen, Glamour, and Charm.
Cipe Pineles (19081991) served as art director for Seventeen and Charm, after working under Aghas direction at Vogue in the 1930s.
Pineles, editor-in-chief Helen Valentine, and promotion editor Estelle Ellis were unique as a team of women in the male-dominated publishing industry, and Pineles became the first woman named as a member of the Art Directors Club in New York.
Seventeen acknowledged the particular tastes, interests, and buying power of young women in the United States as distinct from their adult parents, and was specifically geared, through the choice of models and the editorial pages, to both reflect and shape their experience.
Fiction articles were illustrated in full color by artists including Ben Shahn, who was often given wide latitude in interpretation for his images.
An often-repeated story involving creative freedom, related by Pineles, involves an illustration assignment for a short story: It [the story] concerned a 14-year-old boy, a keen tennis player, who is ashamed of his mother because she is very pregnant, and he is determined to keep this fact from his friends.
To do this he keeps them from using the family tennis court, which up to the time of the pregnancy had been the center of social activity.
I gave Ben a two-week deadline.
He could do anything he pleased, in any shape and under any number of colors.
There was only one restriction.
The hero and his friends must be clearly recognizable as youngsters in their teens.
Three days later the finished job came in and it was plenty clear.
There was no hero.
There were no friends to be seen.
Instead, stretching across two pages in a long, thin picture, was the most deserted, clearest, biggest tennis court in a brilliant color, marked with the sharpest, neatest, traditional white lines.
It was a breathtaking beautiful shock of a painting to go with that story.
Layout for Seventeen was generally asymmetrical but less varied than at Vogue or Vanity Fair under Agha.
Photographs rarely employed bleeding and were usually arranged with parallel vertical edges.
Typographically there was more experimentation, both in the sizes used for titles and in occasional integration of drawing for emphasis or visual puns.
An example of the latter is a feature that appeared in a 1951 issue of Seventeen on rainwear, where a sequence of models was juxtaposed with the black vertical lines of musical staves (rotated 90 degrees) that become a metaphor for rain (fig.
11.18).
The musical metaphor helps to connect rainwear with fashion, suggesting that inclement weather need not be an impediment to being active and having fun.
It anticipates the association between precipitation, fun, and romance in the 1952 MGM film musical Singin’ in the Rain.
Cipe Pineles (art director), feature layout for Seventeen, July 1949.
Other magazines rivaled the innovations and technical excellence achieved by Condé Nast publications.
Esquire, under the art direction of Henry Wolf (19252005) beginning in 1953, and McCalls, under Otto Storch (19131999), both provided examples of expressive possibilities for layout using the integration of photography, illustration, color, and typography.
The clever manipulation of type and use of photography helped to define the role of graphic design in communicating a mood or conveying an idea visually on a cover that was the subject of a feature article inside the journal.
An example is Wolfs Esquire cover from 1958 illustrating a wine glass filled with water into which a packet of powdered instant wine has been sprinkled (fig.
11.19).
The tagline below reads The Americanization of Paris in a bold sans serif mixing blue and red colors.
The classic wine glass (one may remember Beatrice Wardes essay The Crystal Goblet, see here) connotes a cultivated and time-honored French product, while the paper packet refers to the instant gratification that often characterized American culture at the time.
The clash and interrelationship between cultures are conveyed in the juxtaposition of symbols that are readily understood in connection with the text, whose colors stand for the flags of both nations.
The particular association of leisure with instant gratification as a form of American difference taps into a theme also found in American travel magazines such as Holiday (see also A.
M.
Cassandres 1932 poster for Dubonnet, fig.
8.11).
We might also be reminded of a strain of European ambivalence toward the long-term effects of American economic intervention through the Marshall Plan, including the fear of the threat the United States posed to French (and other countries) national identity and cultural traditions.
Photographer Irving Penn (1917 2009) featured images of occupations of the French working class for the February 1951 issue of Vogue that chronicled continuity with the past and celebrated French national pride.
THE AMERICANIZATION OF PARIS Henry Wolf (art director), cover for Esquire, “The Americanization of Paris,” July, 1958.
An expressive sequencing of images combined with text and titles emerged as well in Ballet (1945), a volume of black-and-white photographs by Alexey Brodovitch (fig.
11.20).
Brodovitch (see here) used the blurred and bled images of dancers, often caught off-guard and cut by the edge of the page in an effect reminiscent of the paintings of Edgar Degas.
The horizontal format, double-page spreads, and use of white space for the text convey the unique drama and excitement of the stage, taking full consideration of the range of graphic means at the designers disposal.
The striking aesthetic effect of Brodovitchs photojournalism continued in the work of many of his protégés and collaborators, such as Irving Penn at Vogue and Richard Avedon (19232004).
Avedon worked with Brodovitch at Harper’s Bazaar, where he served as art director until 1958.
Avedon photographed the New Look in fashion design, introduced by French couturier Christian Dior after World War II, using strong contrast to emphasize the contour of the model, the fullness of shapes and pinched waist.
Figure 11.21 appeared in an issue of Harper’s Bazaar in 1956.
11.20 Alexey Brodovitch (photographs) and Edward Denby (text), Ballet, 8 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 11 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (22.5 × 28.5 cm), New York, J.
J.
Augustin, 1945.
11.21 Suzy Parker, evening dress by Dior, Paris, August 1956, photographed by Richard Avedon for Harper’s Bazaar, October 1956 issue, here.
Utilizing an increasingly broad array of techniques derived from modern art, elements of the New Typography, creative latitude, and technical mastery, advertising designers and magazine art directors brought visual excitement and intellectual sophistication to the presentation of products and to feature stories focused upon the appeal of modern living as revealed in travel, fashion, entertainment, and cuisine.
Editorial features also addressed contemporary political and social issues and permitted considerable freedom of expression.
Beginning in the early 1960s, Doyle Dane Bernbach initiated a series of poster advertisements for the tiled station walls of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) in New York City in a campaign for Levys real Jewish rye bread with the tagline You dont have to be Jewish to love Levys real Jewish Rye. The posters included Black and Asian addressing figures, who were rarely represented in massmarket product ads (fig.
11.22).
Generally manufacturers and advertising firms were reluctant to include racial and ethnic minorities in ads despite the potential of expanding their markets.
The MTA poster campaign followed an earlier series of ads for the rye bread that featured working-class models eating rye bread sandwiches.
The sense of surprise in the series derives from the frontal poses of the smiling child and juxtaposition of the word Jewish with a careful selection of an easily recognizable non-Jewish addressing figure.
While this shift serves as another example of creative risktaking on the part of Doyle Dane Bernbach in rejecting the predictable whiteness that characterized mass advertising at the time, the campaign acknowledges industry recognition of an untapped market for products, one of the many economic and social benefits of inclusion.
The poster is also contemporary with emerging identity-based movements and racial tension in the 1960s and a reduction in the pressure or burden on the part of minorities to conform or assimilate to a single or dominant universal white American identity.
Nonetheless, the appearance of African Americans in advertising and as the subject of feature stories in mass-circulation magazines represented at least one form of progress, and was welcome: activist and photographer Laurence Henry captured the militant Black activist Malcolm X (19251965) smiling next to the Doyle Dane Bernbach poster in an issue of the magazine NOW! in 1964. # You don't have to be Jewish to love Levy's The combination of creative freedom with the effective visual communication of ideas provided an ethos that defined a progressive role for the graphic designer.
That role echoed themes familiar from design reform, namely raising the level of public awareness of design and harmonizing individual freedom and expression with responsibility in visual communication.
The glamorous world of Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, or Esquire may not always have corresponded to the social reality of the time for all Americans.
Yet the thrill of imagining oneself in the company of celebrities or dressed in haute couture fashion, or appreciating a clever visual pun, was pleasurable on many levels, and constituted a significant aspect of mid-century design  not necessarily the design of products, but the consumption of provocative images and the power of vicarious experience.
The enjoyment of that experience continues into our own time, where digital means of reproduction and manipulation (for example, virtual reality) provides todays designers with a wider range of options, allowing them to reach new levels of compelling, immersive visual engagement and expression.

## Graphic
Design and Technical Information During World War II, German-born graphic designer Will Burtin used the elements of graphic presentation to produce training manuals to teach airforce crewmen to understand and operate complex aerial guns (see here).
After the war, the clear visual presentation of technical information became a focus of Burtins long and distinguished career.
His assignments covered a wide range of activities, from art direction for Fortune magazine (19451949) to design consultant for the Upjohn pharmaceutical company where his work also included the design of three-dimensional exhibits.
Guiding Burtins varied projects was an abiding conviction that the increasingly complex and specialized scientific information upon which technological progress depended could be clearly and positively communicated to a broader public by graphic designers.
Translating information into effective graphic design was an act of creative problem-solving, a form of public education, and an effective means to associate technology and big business with progress and improvement.
Burtins success was testimony to his great powers of analysis and organization, as he searched for the underlying structure of complex processes.
As art director both for Upjohn and its house journal, Scope, as well as for the monthly business magazine Fortune, Burtin frequently juxtaposed images that included diverse media, drawing with photography, color with black-and-white, precise line drawing with spontaneous brushwork.
Cover designs were highly suggestive: juxtapositions between technical drawing, photography, and painting, with roots in Dada and Surrealist photomontage and collage in the interwar period, stimulated a creative, imaginative reading of medical research developments for an audience less familiar with particular technical knowledge of the field, while charts accompanying articles within the magazine clarified new research developments and their applications (fig.
11.23).
Burtins efforts for Upjohn were not limited to the printed page.
He expanded information design in three dimensions, designing a 24-foot (7.3-meter) wide working model of a human cell for Upjohn in 1958 (fig.
11.24) that was displayed at the annual convention of the American Medical Association, a tour-de-force that included lights and circuits to show movement and arouse interest in the beauty and wonders of science.
Will Burtin, cover design, Fortune magazine, June 1946.
Rochester Institute of Technology, Archives and Special Collections, New York.

## 11.24 Will Burtin, Upjohn cell exhibit, plastic model, 288 in (731.5 cm) in diameter, 1958
.
Upjohn Pharmaceutical Company.
Rochester Institute of Technology, Archives and Special Collections, New York.
In the realm of international relations, the Eameses designed a 12-minute multiscreen display for the American National Exhibition in Moscow in 1959 that featured images of technology and everyday life.
Informational exhibits and films were a growing part of the consultancys design activities, which included a series of exhibits for the IBM Corporation (see fig.
11.81).
Post-war designers such as Burtin and the Eameses saw themselves as contributing, through information design, to the shaping of shared beliefs and public confidence in broad cultural progress through technology within the framework of corporate capitalism and government investment, both nationally and internationally, as a component of soft power (see here).
Burtin occasionally used the services of the Czechoslovakian designer Ladislav Sutnar (18971976) for the presentation of charts and other quantitative information.
Sutnar had come to the United States to design and construct the Czech national pavilion for the 1939 New York Worlds Fair.
When the Nazis invaded Czechoslovakia in the fall of 1938, plans for the exhibit had to be modified and Sutnar remained in the United States, eventually bringing his family to join him.
Committed to the principles of the New Typography, Sutnar worked for Sweets Catalog Service, a company specializing in visual systems to communicate information for products primarily serving the architecture profession, building industry, and parts manufacturers.
In books such as Catalog Design Progress (fig.
11.25), published in 1950, Sutnar and his collaborator K.
Lönberg-Holm (18951972) created criteria for the graphic presentation of technical information based upon reduced use of text, visual clarity, and immediate impact.
The authors cited instances from the transportation industry, such as road signs on highways, as examples of the necessity and importance of clarity and recognition as guiding principles of information graphics.
They explained further in the introduction to their book that: To many people, standards mean only uniformity and restriction, something negative and static.
Opposed to this concept of the word is one which may be illustrated by a commonly used expression, like living standards.
This may suggest variation, as among the living standards of different parts of the world, or progress, as from the time of the earliest American settlers to the present.
In short, the word has potential for implying something dynamic, not static  something which is always changing, advancing.
Sutnar brought the same clarity and order to the creation of unified graphic standards for Carrs self-service department stores in New Jersey (19561957), and a system of easily recognized symbols for the Bell Telephone Company.
Both projects are examples of the adoption of visual systems for identifying products and communicating a sense of organization through visual order and consistency.
Such work made Sutnar a pioneer in the development of house styles for many large businesses in the post-war era.
Pages from K.
Lönberg-Holm and Ladislav Sutnar’s Catalog Design Progress, published by Sweet’s Catalog Service (Division of F.
W.
Dodge Corporation), New York, 1950.
Bauhaus student and instructor Herbert Bayer settled in the United States in 1938, and in 1953 produced one of the richest examples to date of information graphics, the World Geographic Atlas, published by the Container Corporation of America (CCA).
It featured technical and scientific information in a rich variety of subject areas related to geography, climate, and natural resources.
The Atlas also fit within a post-war humanistic framework: figure 11.26 from the World Geographic Atlas places a pictographic human figure at the center of a series of overlapping concentric circles to illustrate the interrelationship between ourselves, our natural resources, and the world we share and shape through research and experience.
The book also exemplifies the often close relationship between business and modern design after World War II: the compatibility of technology, commerce, and democratic cultural values.
During the 1960s, a number of graphic designers began to question the marriage of commerce and culture and sought alternative approaches to redefine the relationship between design and the business community whose interests they served; the document First Things First, which appeared in the British newspaper the Guardian in 1964 (see here), is one example.
Herbert Bayer, World Geographic Atlas, Chicago, for Container Corporation of America, 1953.
Whether through cover art, advertising, art direction, or information design, designers such as Burtin, Brodovitch, Agha, Rand, Sutnar, Bayer, and Lustig expanded the techniques and awareness of graphic design in a variety of contexts in the decade following the end of World War II.
These ranged from product advertisements to magazine covers and layouts, to logos and house styles, technical manuals, and information design for exhibits and displays.
Design projects used high-quality color reproduction of illustrations and photographs, and solutions proceeded with creative and technical freedom made possible through reduced reliance upon metal type.
Large corporations and publishers helped to provide designers with a wealth of varied opportunities to develop original solutions to the challenges not only of selling products, but also of building public support for the promise of research and technology to a post-war audience.

## Scandinavia
Nordic designers figured strongly in the expansion of post-war modern design through the manufacture of domestic and institutional furniture as well as glassware, metalwork, ceramics, and lighting.
Designers and companies consistently won prizes at post-war triennial exhibitions held in Milan, Italy, were represented in the Museum of Modern Art and other museum collections, and their work was manufactured by or influenced the production of furniture companies such as Herman Miller and Knoll.
The Nordic reputation for both new and traditional materials and efficient production technologies, and attention to comfort and fitness to purpose, included a respect for individual expression and national identity.
The continued influence of craft in the career of Alvar Aalto is seen in the persistence of materials such as brick or tile in the architects work, explored for their effects of color and texture on the exterior or even the interior of buildings such as the Baker House dormitory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, built between 1946 and 1949 (fig.
11.27).
The interiors feature exposed plumbing and maximized efficient storage, utilizing the space beneath beds as well as built-in closets and cabinets (all designed by Aalto and manufactured by Artek).
Such standardized elements are offset by rooms with varied and irregular shapes conforming to the undulating contour of the exterior rather than uniform cell-like proportions and repetition.
The combination of variety and standardization preserves a balance between individual and socially responsible design considerations.
It is not surprising that Aalto eulogized Henry van de Velde (see here) after his death in 1957, praising the individual artistic and human qualities of his oeuvre.
11.27 Alvar Aalto, student’s room, Baker House, campus of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1946–1949.
11.28 Poul Kjaerholm, chair, steel and wicker, height 28 in (71 cm), manufactured by E.
Kold Christensen Company, Copenhagen, Denmark, 1956.
Equally committed to industrial methods of production using lightweight materials and metals was Danish designer Poul Kjaerholm (19291980).
Kjaerholm was traditionally trained as a furniture-maker, and his chair designs continued to use natural materials such as leather, cane, and wicker combined with steel construction.
His steel and wicker chair (fig.
11.28) has a startlingly simple, open design based upon the balance of the opposing curves for the seat and one-piece footed legs, joined by clamps.
Manufactured in Copenhagen by E.
Kold Christensen in 1956, the chair combines an economical use of materials, industrial methods of production, as well as an emphasis upon comfort and fluid linear refinement.
Arne Jacobsen, Egg chair, fiberglass and chromed steel with leather-covered foam rubber upholstery, height 41 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (106.4 cm), Fritz Hansen, Allerød, Denmark, 1957.
The furniture of Danish designer Arne Jacobsen (19021971) illustrates the more individual and sculptural character of Nordic design in the post-World War II period.
Jacobsens Egg chair of 1957 (fig.
11.29) was constructed of molded fiberglass, upholstered in foam rubber, covered in leather (as well as in a variety of other fabrics), and supported by a stainless-steel pedestal base.
The Egg chair and accompanying ottoman were designed for the Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) hotel and terminal in Copenhagen.
Jacobsen also served as the architect for these buildings, and designed their full range of furnishings from carpeting to cutlery.
The organic forms of the Egg chair, with its deep cavities and winglike projections, go far beyond considerations of ergonomics and the psychology of comfort, recalling the abstract sculpture of Henry Moore or Jean Arp (see fig.
11.8).
Jacobsens designs are an intersection of technology and art rather than technology as a vehicle for economic production.
In addition to furniture, Scandinavian industrial design included other products with strong craft traditions in glassware, ceramics, textiles, and metal tableware.
In Nordic glassware and ceramics, a more practical, restrained expression in the postwar period continued with the work of Finnish designer Kaj Franck (19111989).
Franck served as artistic director for the Arabia Company in Helsinki, for whom he designed the Kilta earthenware table service beginning in 1952 (fig.
11.30).
This tableware exhibits a preference for slightly tapered cylindrical forms in a small range of colors (originally white, black, yellow, and green) with undecorated surfaces.
Handles and knobs are equally simple and unobtrusive, and the consistency of these elements surpasses in its purity and unity the equally utilitarian Fiestaware (see fig.
10.30), whose pieces retain molded and scalloped handles and bases.
Kaj Franck, Kilta table service, glazed earthenware, diameter of largest plate 9 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (23 cm), manufactured by Wärtsilä Arabia Company, Helsinki, Finland, 1952 In lighting, the hanging lamps of Poul Henningsen (18941967), manufactured by the Louis Poulsen Company in Copenhagen as early as 1926 (exhibited even earlier at the 1925 international exposition in Paris), combine simple curved geometric forms in concentric and inverted arrangements to evenly diffuse interior light (fig.
11.31).
After World War II, Henningsen expanded the vocabulary of elementary geometric components so characteristic of interwar Modernism into more intricate and sculptural designs, such as the Artichoke hanging lamp of 1958 (fig.
11.32).
The transformation is characteristic of an increasing artistic freedom in Nordic design, seen as part of an ideology stressing comfortable living as a refuge from a cold climate, long distances between major cities, and significant time spent indoors.
11.31 Poul Henningsen, hanging lamp, opal glass and brass, diameter $1 9 \%$ in (50 cm), Louis Poulsen Company, Copenhagen, 1926.
11.32 Poul Henningsen, Artichoke hanging lamp, copper, height 27 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (69 cm), diameter 33 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (84 cm), Louis Poulsen Company, Copenhagen, 1958.
Qualities of comfort combined with fitness to purpose may also be seen in Scandinavian industrial design, particularly in the Saab 92 automobile manufactured in 19501952 by Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget Company in Linköping, Sweden.
As a consultant to the airline company that produced the original model, Swedish industrial designer Sixton Sason (19121967) contributed to the Saab 92 (fig.
11.33).
With its swept-back hood and tapered body, the Saab is streamlined and strongly unified in appearance, and less geometric in form than the German Volkswagen.
Perhaps owing to the aviation orientation of the company that produced it, the gauges and controls on the Saab 92 and Saab 93 were placed to facilitate easy recognition and operation.
As a result of enabling drivers to operate controls intuitively and integrating an aerodynamic approach to the form of the body, these early models underwent few changes, remaining in production for almost 30 years.
The design of the dashboard and controls for the Saab 92 provides a model for later interest in user-centered design that incorporates a natural relationship between controls, the functions they perform, and the ease with which those functions and movements can be understood and effected by those who operate them.
These themes emerged in books by Donald Norman such as The Design of Everyday Things, published in 1988.
The Saab represented an alternative to the American automobile industry and its focus upon visual appeal, annual model changes, power, individual identity, and leisure.
11.33 Saab 92 automobile, Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget Company, Linköping, Sweden, 1950–1952.

## Post-War
Modern Design for Housing Flexibility remained a principle of Nordic design.
For instance, when designer and critic George Nelson praised the virtues of Scandinavian design in housing, he also cited the efficiency of design planning for open, multi-purpose apartments maximizing interior space with built-in storage and modular cabinets and seating arrangements, neither austere nor indulgent.
According to Nelson, such an approach extended to the provision of social services for childcare and emphasis upon how a sense of community reduced the need for individual families to own large homes or purchase products to satisfy every need.
As in other western European and Nordic nations after World War II, social democratic governments taxed citizens to provide funding for a social safety net to protect the unemployed, provide healthcare, guard against social unrest, and regulate the 11.34 Le Corbusier, interior, Unité d’Habitation, Marseilles, 1951. distribution of wealth, sometimes referred to as welfare capitalism. This approach may be seen in the apartment complex known as the Unité dHabitation built in Marseilles (France) and designed by Le Corbusier between 1947 and 1952.
The project was funded by the French Ministry of Reconstruction and Urbanism and aimed to provide housing for civil servants in the local region.
The complex is constructed with rough reinforced concrete and rests upon stubby concrete pilotis, with 17 stories and 337 apartments housing around 1,600 inhabitants.
Primary-color balcony panels in an asymmetrical pattern enliven the design of the exterior, and the design included several typical floor plans.
Individual apartments, while modest, consist of two floors, with an open staircase connecting them along with balconies (fig.
11.34).
Le Corbusier tried to incorporate the various elements of modern family living: privacy and common social spaces, a kitchen that opens onto the dining area, a loggia, and communal areas for exercise, play, shopping, a hotel, school; in sum, a vertical city. The built-in furniture in the illustration and the color scheme appear to require some conformity from residents, hardly allowing for heirlooms or shopping for knick-knacks aside from books and prints to hang on walls.
Something of the rejection of the past remains in the period after World War II in the Unité dHabitation, along with the urgency of meeting the challenges of housing and material shortages on a large scale, requiring standardization to achieve an egalitarian ideal for modern, modest responsible living.

## Britain
A gradual shift in modern industrial design from standardized and low-cost solutions toward more individual interpretations of Modernism may also be seen in Britain following World War II.
Between the wars, many British industrial designers followed a utilitarian and economical approach, seen, for instance, in the robot-like Anglepoise desk lamp designed by George Carwardine (18871948) in 1932 (fig.
11.35).
The exposure of the lamps mechanical parts suggests a relation to technical equipment rather than domestic furnishings.
Following the war, lingering austerity stemming from material shortages and rationing (not lifted until 1952) contributed to an economical approach to design at the expense of aesthetic considerations.
The liberal Labour Party government brought to power in 1945 instituted nationalized services, including healthcare and subsidized housing estates built to meet minimum working-class needs.
The legacy of Modernism was strong, favoring standardization, industrial materials and production, and modest modern living.
Government regulation required that furniture designs be approved before they could be manufactured on the basis of economy and a sense of aesthetic discrimination along restrained guidelines, as seen in photographs of a domestic interior from 1945 (see fig.
10.46).
Such guidelines formed the basis of the 1946 exhibition Britain Can Make It. Such narrow parameters for post-war design in Britain broadened through the later 1940s and began to incorporate the heritage of craft traditions and natural materials to give products a distinctively national identity in the hope of competing in the export market and appealing to popular taste.
At the same time, government-sponsored design initiatives such as the Design Research Group emphasized testing and research to encourage manufacturers to hire industrial designers, while department stores such as Heals offered modern furniture designs inspired by Scandinavian (chiefly Danish) models, focusing upon ease of assembly, lightness, industrial materials, and plain wooden components.
British examples of postwar modern design include Ernest Races (19131963) Antelope chair featuring the use of enameled metal wire (fig.
11.36).
The chair was exhibited at the 1951 Festival of Britain.
The timing of the Festival sounded a note of optimism, commemorating the 100th anniversary of the Great Exhibition of 1851 and Britains Victorian past (see here).
George Carwardine, Anglepoise lamp, lacquered metal and bakelite, height 35 $^ 7 / _ { 1 6 }$ in (90 cm), manufactured by Herbert Terry and Sons, Redditch, England, 1932.
National Museum of Science and Industry, Manchester.
Ernest Race, Antelope chair, enameled steel and painted plywood, height 31 <sup>1</sup>/ in (79 cm), manufactured by Race Furniture, England, 1951.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Modern British interiors after World War II generally had white rather than papered walls, while upholstery fabric emphasized textural variety with muted earth tones rather than bright colors.
For the Festival of Britain, designers developed a broad range of new surface patterns for curtains and ceramics, often featuring delicate line drawing in an abbreviated, playful style with a variety of abstract organic shapes as well as simplified representational motifs.
Examples include Viennese-born Marianne Mahlers (1911 1983) Bird and Bowl design from 1951, printed on the synthetic fabric rayon and manufactured by David Whitehead Ltd.
(fig.
11.37).
Another source of inspiration for abstract textile patterns was the microscopic world of molecular structures, revealed in the woven fabric entitled Surrey designed by Marianne Straub (19091994) for Warner & Sons Ltd. in 1951 (fig.
11.38).
In textile design, materials technology expanded the range of home furnishings; in marketing for the pharmaceutical industry, many initiatives in design internationally dealt with the humanization of science, whether through decorative patterns, information graphics, or new materials for domestic products (see here).
At the Festival of Britain and elsewhere, such efforts accompanied the search for common understanding in a complex, technological world of specialized scientific knowledge.
Industrial materials and methods of production also appeared in contemporary ceramics and interior furnishings from the early 1950s.
Sir Terence Conran (19312020) designed earthenware dinnerware in square and rectangular forms with rounded edges, decorated with a hand-drawn checkerboard background filled with colored swatches and irregular patterns of lines, dots, and dashes (fig.
11.39).
His work recalls other cheerful contemporary patterns in textile design (fig.
11.37).
11.37 Marianne Mahler, Bird and Bowl pattern, roller-printed rayon, 18 in (46 cm), manufactured by David Whitehead Ltd., 1951.

## 11.38 Marianne Straub, Surrey, wool and cotton tapestry, red, gold, and cream, manufacture
d by Warner & Sons Ltd. for the Festival Pattern Group Scheme and used for curtains in the Regatta Restaurant at the Royal Festival Hall, London, 1951.
Sir Terence Conran, Chequers range, molded earthenware with printed and sponged decoration, for W.
R.
Midwinter Ltd., Burslem, 1950s.
The 1950s also saw the introduction of new resins as an alternative to ceramics for table service.
A.
H.
Woodfull (19122011), together with John Vale and Roy Midwinter, designed a tea set in 1956 called Midwinter Modern.
Marketed as breakresistant, the white tea set was made of melamine, a form of hard industrial plastic.
Midwinter Modern featured round-edged rectangular plates and sloping edges for the creamer and sugar bowl, emphasizing smooth but irregular organic forms.
In the United States, Russel Wright also designed several comparable sets of dinnerware using plastics and intended for informal, festive home entertaining, with instructions for how to arrange plates and utensils for self-serving published by Wright and his wife Mary in their 1950 book Guide to Easier Living.
Chemists also developed industrial materials for textile manufacturing: for instance, fiberglass as a fabric for shower curtains and printed with designs resembling the playful abstract shapes of Joan Miró.
Lightweight aluminum appeared in a variety of lighting fixtures in Britain and elsewhere in Europe and the United States, from desk lamps to standing lamps resembling microphone stands.
Bulbs were enclosed in a variety of conical forms and the lamps were generally made of thin steel rods and painted aluminum, marketed for their adjustable height and direction (fig.
11.40).
Aesthetically their thin, wiry forms and lightness harmonized with built-in furniture, reduced upholstery, and more open interior spaces.
As design historian Jonathan Woodham has argued, it is difficult to assess popular reaction to post-war modern design in Britain, since our main sources of information come from groups such as the Council of Industrial Design (COID), which sponsored exhibitions and promoted shared standards and values.
To judge from British receptivity to American popular culture, legislating taste was no easier in 1951 than it was for design reformers a century earlier.
Anonymous, adjustable desk lamps, painted aluminum and brass, average height 20 in (51 cm), various manufacturers (Oswald Hollman Ltd., Beckenham, Troughton & Young Ltd.), London, c.
1955.
More or less official views of design promoted a clear understanding of the distinction between needs and wants and an acceptance of the realities and restrictions of urban population density.
Later in the decade, such values and the standards upon which they were based came under attack.
The result was a renewed emphasis on one hand upon the importance of research and ergonomics in product development and on the other hand skepticism toward practicality and utility as stable, self-evident determinants of design, especially in competitive economic conditions.
Yet despite growing fascination with American popular culture in Britain, the premises of economy and efficiency continued to inspire successful products, such as the 1959 Morris Mini automobile, designed for the British Motor Corporation by Alec Issigonis (fig.
11.41).
This efficient and space-saving vehicle was the British counterpart to the earlier Fiat 600 (fig.
11.44) in Italy for basic and inexpensive personal and family transportation.
Alec Issigonis, Morris Mini, Morris Motor Company, Birmingham, UK, 1959.
Also in Britain the legacy of craft and values associated with the dialogue between artisan and materials found expression in the oeuvre of Bernard Leach (18871979).
Leach was active at least from the end of World War I, when he returned from Japan after having studied pottery with well-known Japanese ceramic master Shoji Hamada.
Leach practiced the technique of raku ceramics, fired at lower temperatures and modeled rather than thrown on a wheel.
His designs, such as a stoneware bowl from 1957 (fig.
11.42), preserve and extend Japanese handicraft traditions that had became a part of the Aesthetic and related movements in the later nineteenth century.
Leach also designed teapots and other wares for serial production.
The persistence of craft and direct handling of materials remained a viable part of design in Britain, the United States, Italy, and elsewhere, and a marketable one as well.

## Italy
The conscious development of an international market and national image for modern Italian design was a phenomenon of the post-war era, and took place in a political climate of economic hardship and recovery, and social anxiety amid Cold War tensions in planning Italys future and defining democratic values.
Until 1948 communists were the political majority in Italy; the Christian Democratic Party gained control of Italys Parliament in elections that year, and sought to address pressing needs for housing, high levels of unemployment, and increasing industrial output.
One of the most potent symbols of progress allied with industrial design and production to emerge in the immediate post-war years was the Vespa motor scooter, designed in 1946 by Corradino DAscanio (18911981) for the Piaggio Corporation (fig.
11.43) located in the Tuscan town of Pontedero.
The Vespa contributed to overall growth in industrial output in Italy (averaging 6.3 percent per year beginning in 1945).
It was a practical, inexpensive mode of personal transportation, but streamlined housing, enclosed mechanical parts, and the cutaway profile of the seat added a graceful, expressive element to the design, communicating mobility, spontaneity, and personal freedom in relation to economic reconstruction.
Other standardized and affordable industrially manufactured products, for instance the compact Fiat 600 (1955) designed by Dante Giacosa, aligned with utilitarian and practical considerations in both economical production and reliability, providing four-wheel transportation and contributing to a tremendous domestic increase in automobile sales, estimated at 400 percent between 1950 and 1961 (fig.
11.44).
It is interesting to note that updated versions of both the Fiat 500 and the Morris Mini (re-introduced by BMW) appeared in the early 2000s as lower-end models for their respective manufacturers but hardly basic transportation, with options that increased cost and appeal generated by a combination of nostalgia mixed with personal identity as well as advantages in parking or fuel consumption that accrued from their compact size.
Corradino D’Ascanio, Vespa motor scooter, Piaggio Corporation, Pontedera (Pisa), Italy, 1946.
Dante Giacosa, Fiat 600, Fiat Motor Company, Turin, Italy, 1955.
Following the American industrial design model of the 1930s, and strongly supported by the Marshall Plan and a more centrist government after the 1948 elections, Italian companies adopting mechanized mass-production technology generally relied upon consultants to contribute new designs, often directed to the export market.
With a steady and inexpensive supply of labor, guaranteed by weak labor unions and government subsidies to industrial corporations, Italian manufacturers could justify the added cost of designers in order to compete in the international market for their products.
The value of those products was in turn enhanced by their association with architect-designers who left their individual mark upon manufactured goods.
