PRIMA FABBRICA ITALIANA MACCHINE PER SCRIVERE ING.C.OLIVETTIEC.IVREA Poster advertising Camillo Olivetti, MI typewriter, metal, height 14 1<sup>5</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (38 cm), Olivetti ING, Ivrea, Italy, c.
1911.
11.47 Giovanni Pintori, advertising poster for Olivetti, c.
1953.
The independence and contributions of the consultant designer is an acknowledged feature in Italian industrial manufacturing for corporations such as Olivetti after World War II.
Industrial designers were integral to a process that included marketing and engineering.
The dialogue among participants was often distinguished by a sense of drama and conflict rather than hierarchical directive.
As described by Sybil Kircherer in her study of Olivetti, the strategy resulted in creativity and a dynamic design identity.
Although he had been hired in the later 1930s by Adriano Olivetti, son of the companys founder, painter and architect Marcello Nizzoli (18871969) assumed a more significant role in product design after World War II.
An early example was the Lexikon 80 typewriter of 1948 (fig.
11.45), distinguished by its fluid, organic housing and integrated curved panel covering the mechanism, creating a sense of abstract sculptural form in comparison with earlier angular, black, standardized models (fig.
11.46).
Olivetti also employed graphic designer Giovanni Pintori (19121999) for advertising and corporate communication.
His colorful posters for the companys business machines use asymmetrical layouts and juxtapose product photography with a flat abstract design that suggests a machines dynamic action, whether a typewriter key or an ink ribbon (fig.
11.47).
Pintoris abstractions communicate the rhythms and excitement of mechanized movement, an aesthetic that extended to the companys showrooms as well, including hanging glass lamps designed and manufactured by Paolo Venini (Venini & Company, Murano) for the New York showroom in 1954 and designed by the architectural partners Ernesto Rogers, Lodovico Belgiojoso, and Enrico Peressutti (fig.
11.48).
The dramatic presentation placed the business machines outside of the context of office use value, adding aesthetic appeal and brand identity in an international market.
Ernesto Rogers, Lodovico Belgiojoso, and Enrico Peressutti, Olivetti showroom, New York, 1954.
Original product housing and promotion through posters and other forms of marketing provided an aesthetic dimension for any number of otherwise ordinary standardized utilitarian products, for instance, Gio Pontis (18911979) asymmetrically balanced commode and dramatically flared pedestal sink designed for Ideal Standard in 1953/4 (fig.
11.49), recognized at the 1957 Milan Triennale.
These exhibitions, organized as early as the 1920s and revived in 1948, increased the visibility of Italian design in an upscale international setting.
Italian products were featured alongside those of Scandinavian, German, American, and British designers, aimed at the sophisticated, high-end market and often exhibited in response to a theme, such as the Form of the Useful (1951).
The Triennale competition awarded prizes (the golden compass), sponsored by the Italian department store La Rinascente.
The journal Domus promoted Italian design in an international context, particularly under the editorship first of Ernesto Rogers (19091969) and then Gio Ponti (beginning in 1947), stressing the human, creative element in modern industrial design as well as its practical, economic, and social benefits.
Gio Ponti, sink and commode, porcelain, sink height 31 ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (80 cm), commode height 15 in (38 cm), manufactured by Ideal Standard, Milan, 1953/4.
Ponti brought a humanizing factor into Italian design, highlighting the persistence and continued transformation of traditional artisanal production.
A case in point is his Superleggera chair of 1957 (fig.
11.50).
This is a modern reinterpretation of a nineteenth-century wood and cane rush-seat design, emphasizing the light, tapered forms associated with tubular metal, but also implying a relationship between design and the Italian heritage of craft skills.
An earlier version of this chair, known as the Leggera, on view at the Good Design exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in 1951, used cellophane (a liquid-proof cellulose used primarily today for food packaging but explored for other applications since its invention in the early twentieth century) rather than cane for the seat.
11.50 Gio Ponti, Superleggera chair, tinted ash and cane, height 32 in (81.3 cm), manufactured by Figli di Amedeo Cassina, Milan, 1957.
The Turinese manufacturer Cassina adopted mass-production technology for furniture in the years immediately after World War II.
In the 1950s the firm emerged as an industrial leader, integrating the use of modern materials such as plywood and tubular steel with tapered, organic forms featured in other products, and allowing freedom for individual designers to explore aesthetic possibilities of new industrial technologies.
In many ways the experiments of Italian designers parallel those of designers such as Charles and Ray Eames in the United States or Robin Day in England in molded industrial materials.
Marco Zanuso (19162001) experimented with the use of solid-colored fabric over a foam-rubber core to replace conventional upholstery in his Lady chair, manufactured by the Arflex company in 1951 (a division of the Pirelli Corporation, otherwise known for rubber tire manufacturing, of which foam rubber was a byproduct).
The chair (fig.
11.51), composed of broad, regular curving forms supported by thin metal legs, received an award at the Milan Triennale of that year.
It also was featured on a cover for Domus photographed from above by Giorgio Casali (19131995) who worked regularly at the journal for more than 30 years.
The cover emphasizes both serial production and variety through differences in upholstery design and the crowded, haphazard arrangement of models.
Other Domus covers and photographs underlined modularity and clean, open interiors (with ample contrast and white space) that defined modern apartment living in Italian cities.
Marco Zanuso, Lady armchair, wood, metal, and elastic webbing, with fabric-covered foam-rubber upholstery, height 32 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (82 cm), manufactured by Arflex, Milan, 1951.
Italian lighting design in the decade following the end of World War II was equally inventive.
Simple and flexible, designs such as the 1949 Tubino by Achille (1918 2002) and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni (19131968) and manufactured by Arredoluce eschewed conventional fabric shades and pedestal bases in favor of plastics, light metal, and thin tubing to conceal electric wiring (fig.
11.52).
The simplicity of the Castiglionis designs derives from the brothers stated subordination of the fixture itself to the effects of light it produces. Yet the remaining form, however negligible, retains an undeniable abstract linear character, akin to a delicate line drawing or to automatic writing.
11.52 Achille and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni, Tubino desk lamp, enameled metal and aluminum, height 11 $^ 1 / _ { 1 6 }$ in (28 cm), manufactured by Arredoluce, 1949.
The flexible plastics used for a number of Italian lighting designs in the 1950s also appear in domestic kitchenware pioneered by the Milan-based Kartell Company, whose in-house designer, Gino Colombini (19152011), developed an array of containers and simple kitchen appliances with tapered forms that not only fulfilled functional requirements but also introduced a colorful, playful design element.
Bright colors and bold advertising combined to reduce the association of cooking and cleaning with demeaning labor or domestic science, making them instead part of a modern lifestyle linked to the pleasures of food and increased leisure.
As suggested above, a number of design historians have noted that the Italian furniture industry did not entirely abandon its craft roots, despite the shift to and marketing of industrial materials and other modern production technologies.
Small workshops, while at times consolidating and shifting from local to national and export markets, contributed to the design enterprise because they were capable of shorter, flexible production runs and were less reliant upon costly capital investment.
These factors led to a combination of innovation and variety together with standardization in products that included the Superleggera as well as the Margherita armchair designed by Franco Albini (19051977) and Franca Helg (19201989).
The latter (which won a golden compass award at the 1951 Milan Triennale) was manufactured by the Bonacina Company (founded in 1899 near Milan) in 1950 using traditional cane and a bentwood frame, in a design emphasizing abstract curved and oval shapes (fig.
11.53).
The craft element in Italian design surfaced as well in the growing reputation of leather goods, Murano glass, and fashion in the post-war period, allied with name designers to lend artistic identity to products and accessories.
While Fendi and Ferragamo are perhaps best associated internationally with this industry, these designers inherited and built upon a post-war tradition initiated by Gucci leather accessories (named for Guccio Gucci, 18811953).
Franco Albini and Franca Helg, Margherita armchair, rattan and upholstery, height 39 <sup>1</sup>/ in (99.4 cm), manufactured by Vittorio Bonacina, 1950.
Finally, while the Fiat models 500 and 600 dominated the domestic market for automobiles, accounting for 90 percent of sales in 1961, Italian car manufacturers also addressed the international high-end market with more streamlined, sculptural sports (rather than family) cars, where the legacy of custom coach-building expressed in graceful sculptural form continued.
A well-known example is the 1946 Cisitalia sports car designed by Battista Pinin Farina (18931966; fig.
11.54), while models for industrial production included the more restrained Alfa Romeo Spider from the mid-1950s.
11.54 Battista “Pinin” Farina, Cisitalia 202 GT Coupé sports car, Pinin Farina, Torino, Italy, 1946.
Contemporary with American and Nordic industrial designers, Italy helped to define the new humanism of the post-war era, embracing mechanized mass production and new materials technology while establishing a forceful role for the artist-designer within industry in the creation of useful, elegant products and an acknowledged aesthetic and individual creative element.
Through periodicals such as Domus, the Milan Triennale and other exhibitions, Italian design achieved visibility and national identity within an expanding international market for consumer goods, and as commerce in consumer goods and services became a benchmark for economic progress.
Italian designers explored the creative use of modern materials and technology, individual expression parallel to modern abstract organic sculpture, and modern reinterpretations of enduring craft traditions.
With the help of the Marshall Plan, design organizations, education, and the initiatives of companies such as Olivetti, post-war Italy exemplified designs role in expanding industrial production, rebuilding national economies, defining a modern, consumer-oriented lifestyle, and creating an aesthetically sophisticated and industrially progressive image of Italian design in the two decades following the end of World War II, widely perceived as the nations Second Renaissance. American travel magazine Holiday devoted its April 1955 issue to Italy, combining photographs of the iconic treasures of Ancient Rome and fifteenth-century Florence, the nations craft traditions and opportunities for shopping, and a vibrant modern film industry, recommending the joy of total relaxation, sunshine and balm, brilliant colors, constant, pleasantly distracting to and fro of Italys idlest hours, often focusing upon an active, youthful lifestyle.
This character is also captured in the posters, packaging, and window displays for the Milan-based La Rinascente department store designed by Max Huber (fig.
11.55).
Hubers poster creates a playful, visually active typographic composition out of the letters l and R. In addition to abrupt scale changes, overlapping, and inversions that recall the bold use of typography by the Italian Futurists (see here), Huber uses a combination of the sans serif R in Futura Bold with the more elegant (and Italian) Bodoni lower-case l. According to graphic design historian Richard Hollis, the juxtaposition of the two typefaces may symbolize Italys position between northern and Mediterranean cultural traditions.
This progressive image masked long-standing disparities in Italy that remained in the distribution of wealth and in cultural differences between the industrialized north (centered in Milan) and the more agricultural south that fueled a politically charged anti-design movement in the 1960s, critical of its exclusivity and the capitalist economic system.
Max Huber, advertisement for La Rinascente department store, Milan, c.
1954–1958.
M.A.X.
Museum, Switzerland.

## Germany
Design played a large role in the economic reconstruction of West Germany following World War II.
German industrially manufactured products demonstrate a kinship with the humanizing tendencies expressed through organic forms molded from modern materials for some hand-held products and compact kitchen appliances, but more typically German industrial design is associated with the systematic investigation of materials and processes, most often identified with the grid, modularity, and unobtrusiveness, blending in with the rectilinear forms of much post-war modern architecture.
Precision and functional simplicity were factors in the international success of electrical appliances manufactured by the Braun Corporation of Frankfurt, founded in 1921 and rebuilt in 1945.
The company collaborated with the newly founded Hochschule für Gestaltung (Design School) at Ulm (1953) through Fritz Eichler (19111991), a member of the schools board of directors.
Swiss-born Max Bill (19081994), the Hochschules first director, was a graduate of the Bauhaus and sought to revive an approach to industrial design that emphasized studio practice and social responsibility in the design of prototypes for simple, practical, and efficiently produced furniture and objects of everyday use to improve the general standard of living in an increasingly technological age, and that equated industrial technology with simplicity of appearance and function along interwar Modernist lines.
In many ways Bills approach to industrial design shared many elements not only with the Dessau Bauhaus but also with the stable, enduring product types debated at the German Werkbund in the early twentieth century.
This approach, under the label Gute Form, was the subject of exhibitions organized by Bill beginning in 1949 in Switzerland, which traveled in Germany and Austria during the 1950s.
Bills wall-mounted kitchen clock with timer (fig.
11.56) made of glass, ceramic, and plastic is an example of Gute Form: self-contained, free of decoration or sculpturally molded housing, and contributing to a wholesome but restrained modern lifestyle in the industrial age.
Corporations such as Braun and the Design School at Ulm tended to limit the role of individual expression and embraced a belief in research-based design solutions linked to performance and fitness to purpose. At the same time the establishment of a free-market-based international economy in Germany also played a role in promoting a national identity for German products, embracing pan-European cooperation as envisioned under the Marshall Plan.
All of these efforts were aided as well by the formation of a German Design Council in 1949 to stimulate industrial production, economic recovery, and the restoration of consumer confidence.
Between lingering animosities toward Germany among the allied countries and the nations division into zones occupied by the USSR, the USA, Britain, and France, the German economy was slow to develop, but the rebuilding of German industry was essential to overall European recovery, and levels of production rose quickly after 1949.
In that same year, the Russian zone was renamed the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG).
During the 1950s the West German economy led Europe in industrial production, mostly in the export of manufactured products.
While Italy might tout its own Second Renaissance, French political economist Jean Monnet (18881979) declared that Germany was the prize of Europe, a source of optimism in recovery and growth.
Max Bill (and Ernst Moecki), kitchen clock with timer, metal, glass, ceramic, and plastic, 10 ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 1 1 / { } ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 } \times 2 { } ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \mathrm { i n } ,$ manufactured by Gebrüder Junghans, Schramberg, Germany, 1956–1957.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Swiss-educated Hans Gugelot (19201965) and Dieter Rams (b.
1932), who worked as consultant designers for Braun, also served on the faculty at Ulm.
They created a unified product identity for the corporation, and for a wider variety of German products in general, in response particularly to miniaturization with the use of transistors in electronics equipment, a technology that had emerged in the early 1940s.
The SK4 radio-phonograph was designed by Max Braun, Rams, and Gugelot in 1956.
Nicknamed Snow Whites Coffin (fig.
11.57), the SK4 is a long rectangular box with hinged transparent plastic cover, housing controls, speaker grille, and other moving parts (tone-arm and turntable).
All visible parts are reduced to circular or rectangular forms placed against smooth and flat surfaces.
The arrangement of parts is controlled by a rectangular grid system.
The aesthetic purity and systematic approach to Braun design retain a relationship with the understated geometric abstraction of the period, seen for instance in Josef Albers series of paintings entitled Homage to the Square, or to Max Bills unexecuted project for a Monument for the Unknown Political Prisoner in Stuttgart in 1952, consisting of a connected series of boxlike structures set amid benches, far removed from traditional monumental heroic figural imagery.
Such examples declared a belief in art as a life-affirming activity in the wake of despair and destruction during World War II.
Just as these minimalist approaches to fine art seem to demand a sophisticated and educated audience, so Braun products and design policy were not directed toward a mass market but rather to a discriminating clientele with a more conscious awareness of abstract aesthetics and a belief in the connection between simple, undecorated forms and responsible, efficient modern living, rebuilding the German nation economically, socially, and spiritually.
In the 1970s Dieter Rams enumerated ten principles of good design that he followed in his practice for Braun: innovative, useful, aesthetic, understandable, unobtrusive, honest, long-lasting, thorough to the last detail, environmentally friendly, and as little design as possible. Max Braun, Dieter Rams, and Hans Gugelot, SK4 radio-phonograph, metal, wood, and Plexiglas, 9 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 22 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 11 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (24 × 58 × 29 cm), Braun AG Kronberg, West Germany, 1956.
Braun products emphasized enduring forms and determinants for design based upon considerations of production technology and fitness to purpose rather than upon rapid style change and obsolescence.
In addition, products such as the Kitchen Machine of 1957 (fig.
11.58) possessed a sense of restraint, precision, and laboratory-like efficiency expressed through smooth white surfaces, qualities mentioned above in relation to contemporary abstract fine art and seen as well in the cool impersonality of buildings such as the Lever House (see fig.
11.10) or Mies van der Rohes Seagram Building of 19541958.
This approach to architecture dominated large public and corporate building projects in the decades after World War II and was equally praised at the time for its beauty, efficiency, modularity, and industrial methods of construction.
A devotee of jazz music (oddly in a sense, since the improvisational nature of jazz seems at odds with the predictability of the grid), Dieter Rams designed housings for the majority of Brauns compact stereo equipment, including radios, televisions, speakers, and other components.
The more softly molded forms for kitchen appliances such as the Kitchen Machine were designed by Ramss associate at Braun, Gerd Alfred Müller (1932 1991).
The design of Braun products was not the inevitable outcome of a functional approach to industrial design, but rather the result of a combination of factors that included architectural and social theory, as well as a conscious and sophisticated aesthetic organization of geometrically abstract forms.
11.58 Gerd Alfred Müller, Kitchen Machine, polystyrol housing, 10 $^ 1 / _ { 4 } \times 1 5 \times 9 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in $( 2 6 \times 3 8 \times 2 4$ cm), manufactured by Braun AG Kronberg, West Germany, 1957.
Brauns design program also reveals an affinity with corporate identity and branding as a commercial strategy in international business: company house styles familiarized consumers with families of products and with logos and symbols that provided immediate recognition and differentiation among competitors in a capitalist free enterprise and increasingly international markets.
They also provided parameters and constraints for designers that managed change and emphasized design practice in the context of corporate communication and policy.
Designers not only gave form to products but also created an association between products and an image of efficient, technologically modern living.
Some designers criticized Gute Form for its failure to acknowledge diversity and playfulness within the German national heritage, but the approach helped to build an international reputation for German consumer goods and contributed to unprecedented economic growth after World War II.
501 limousine, manufactured by BMW, AG Bayerische Motorenwerke, Munich, 1951.
Shortly after the war, Germany put into mass production the inexpensive and standardized Volkswagen Beetle designed by Ferdinand Porsche in 1937 as a Peoples Car along Fordist lines during the Third Reich to meet basic personal and family transportation needs primarily for the national market (see fig.
9.35).
As in Italy, however, automobile manufacturing also extended to an international luxury market.
Companies such as Daimler-Benz, Porsche, and BMW combined fluid streamlined body housing with precision and a tradition of custom coach-building to produce highperformance vehicles in a higher price range, for instance the rear-engine streamlined 1952 Porsche 356 or the stately 1951 BMW 501 limousine model (fig.
11.59).
An equally restrained sculptural approach to product housing may also be seen in the stainless steel VE6 electric food-slicing machine dated to 1959 and manufactured by the Bizerba-Waagen-Verkaufsgesellschaft of Balingen (fig.
11.60).

## 11.60 VE6 electric food slicer, height 14 $^ 1 / _ { 8 }$ in (36 cm), Bizerba-Waagen-Verka
ufsgesellschaft, Balingen, 1959.

## The
Other Side of the Cold War This section concludes by looking toward the Soviet Union and other nations within the communist orbit that included Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Romania, and other eastern European nations, in particular Yugoslavia, which retained a stronger degree of autonomy from Moscow.
In Germany, the EastWest division was marked by the building of the Berlin wall in 1961, a visible reminder of EastWest tensions emerging after World War II and known as the Cold War.
Like their western European counterparts, eastern bloc countries were eager to address severe housing and material shortages along with unemployment after the war, at least in part with a focus upon urbanization and industrialization as means to stimulate the economy and improve working-class living standards along socialist lines, with state rather than private ownership of production and ambitious multi-year plans with goals for technological progress and growth along both domestic and military fronts.
Attitudes toward design were not monolithic; they varied in time and location within the Soviet bloc.
Until the death of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin in 1953 architects and designers adopted vernacular and traditional rather than Modernist industrial approaches to architecture and design, with party officials labeling international modern design as formalism, lacking in character and eschewing national traditions through its rejection of decoration and historicism, even employing terms such as primitive and degenerate at a conference held in east Berlin in 1953.
Grandiose urban redevelopment projects, such as the Stalinallee in Berlin (19531958), featured monumental government office buildings, department stores, a movie theater, bookstore, cafés, and spacious apartments in an updated and grand Neoclassical style, but rents and household furnishings during this time were beyond the means of laborers and out of touch with the scale of production required to meet urgent housing and material needs.
During its construction the project was the site of worker demonstrations for higher wages and better working conditions that prompted military and police intervention.
While criticized officially in the GDR (East Germany), however, interwar manufacturers of international modern furniture such as the Hellerau Workshops in Dresden found favor with the public, and under Stalins successor, Nikita Khrushchev (18941971), the official Soviet position on design showed more tolerance for standardized assembly, industrial materials such as steel and plywood, and a clean, pared-down aesthetic, succumbing to pressure to compete with the West in improving living standards as presented at international exhibitions and gaining ground in capitalist countries and colonial territories.
An example is a set of economical stacking plastic dishes offered in varied pastel colors, illustrated in figure 11.61, designed by Albert Krause in 1959.
Despite differences in the political and economic systems in which they were manufactured, goods on both sides of the Berlin wall and on both sides of the Iron Curtain might convey similar meanings in demonstrating broad access to modern, durable, industrially designed goods in a democratic society.
Social housing in the Soviet bloc during the 1950s resembled high-rise housing estates in West Germany, Britain, France, and elsewhere, built with rough concrete or using steel and glass construction, and open, flexible plans, adopting the efficiencies of labor and material costs through prefabrication, a greater or lesser degree of uniformity, and the elimination of decorative detail.
11.61 Albert Krause, set of dishes, plastic, long dishes 9 <sup>1</sup>/ × 5 <sup>3</sup>/ in (23.5 × 13.9 cm); square bowls 4 × 4 in (10.2 × 10.2 cm), manufactured by VEB Plast-Werke, Sonneberg, East Germany, 1959.
International Design Museum, Munich, Germany.
Consumer products were known in the Soviet government as kulttovary, roughly translated as cultural goods, affordable home products that enhanced everyday living in relation to household chores and leisure.
Musical instruments, sports equipment, radios, cameras, and phonographs are examples of kulttovary, and making them available provided an opportunity to bolster confidence in the Soviet economic system and communicate shared egalitarian cultural values.
An example is the standardized Moskvich radio (c.
19491957), made of Bakelite (resembling woodgrain) with rounded, streamlined edges reminiscent of American models of the 1940s (fig.
11.62), and whose manufacturing specifications were followed by several manufacturers throughout the Soviet Union.
Exposure through exhibitions and travel familiarized Soviets with Western design and by the later 1950s the Soviet government touted its own kitchen appliances to compete with American and western European products, an approach dubbed refrigerator socialism. While institutes were established to create prototypes for such goods, and while designers visited the West for inspiration and models of how design functioned in industry, it was difficult for Soviet bloc countries to compete with free-market capitalism in the area of consumer products without adopting many of its forms and strategies, including an increasing emphasis upon marketing and advertising.
And while Cold War competition existed in the realm of consumer products, political and media attention tended to focus more upon competition in the fields of space exploration, military strength, and athletic performance at the Olympic Games.
At the same time, party leaders continued to support collective rather than individual need and socialized rather than private services.
As an example of this position, speaking in response to an exhibition of American automobiles in France in 1960, Khrushchev proposed that the Soviet Union would develop a national system of rental cars to serve the needs of the Russian public rather than face the problems of too many cars caused by private ownership.
At the 1958 Worlds Fair in Brussels, the USSR pavilion proudly displayed its Sputnik satellite as a measure of technological superiority to the United States, raising fears in the West of military advantage should the Cold War become hot. Alexey Lavrov, “Moskvich” Three-Tube Radio, 1950.
Since around the second decade of the twenty-first century historians have revealed the diversity in architecture and design within the Soviet Union and especially its proxy states, including the independence exerted in Yugoslavia that extended to consumer products, fashion, and leisure.
Under Marshal Josip Broz Tito (18921980), Yugoslavia benefitted from a growing tourism industry, visits from celebrities, and an embrace of modern fashion.
Industrial furniture designer Niko Kralj (19202013) introduced tubular steel and molded plywood furniture for the 1956 stacking chair illustrated in figure 11.63, meant to attract residents who moved to the high-rise apartment blocks being built in Belgrade, Zagreb, and elsewhere during the decade.
Recent publications and exhibitions have shed a great deal of light on the role of industrial design behind the Iron Curtain and on the variety of approaches to modern living in the broader communist world: the home was a battleground during the Cold War and both rivals used design as a weapon to promote their political system and values, a form of persuasion sometimes labeled soft power. Niko Kralj, Lupina chair, 1956, steel, bent plywood and upholstery.
Private collection.
Rather than reject the comforts of time and labor-saving appliances and materialism, the USSR vowed to equal the American industrial output and wave good-bye as they surpassed the West.
Whether by state ownership and controlled distribution or private enterprise and competition, both political and economic systems judged progress by the dynamic of production and consumption and their relation to the everyday lives of their citizens.
This represented a paradox, as materialism seemed to conflict with collective values and sacrifice to a centralized state that accommodated their needs in exchange for compliance and conformity.
And in both systems, on both sides of the Cold War, attitudes toward consumption were a mixture of attraction and skepticism.
As seen in chapter 12 (see here onward), consumption and materialism might signal productivity, social progress and individual identity, the rewards of hard work and the cultivation of refined leisure or the saving of time and labor; at the same time, luxury goods might exacerbate class difference and inequality or manipulate rather than satisfy desire as a result of planned obsolescence and aggressive advertising.

## The
International Typographic Style (Die Neue Grafik) Also connected with Germany as well as Switzerland in the post-war period were standards for graphic design and typography often referred to as the International Typographic Style or Die Neue Grafik.
This approach to graphic communication for book design, posters, advertising, logos, and other business and organizational needs was promoted in such journals as Graphis and Die Neue Grafik, and formed the basis for educating graphic designers at the Hochschule für Gestaltung at Ulm and the Kunstgewerbeschule in Basel.
The combination of theoretical principles, the exploration of the visual components of graphic expression, and the use of those components for effective communication in an international context gave the movement a reputation for high professional practice standards and ethical responsibility in design.
The hegemony of the International Typographic Style as the voice of modern graphic design was promoted in the widespread adoption of corporate identity systems for business, museum exhibitions, and book design, and was contemporary with a similar faith in the modern aesthetic and practical advantages of the tectonic steel-and-glass architecture of the post-war International Style.
Max Bill (see here), who lived and worked in Switzerland during and after World War II before accepting the directorship at the Hochschule für Gestaltung at Ulm, contributed to the development of the International Typographic Style.
Along with several Swiss and other European artists and designers, Bill developed and worked within a framework of formal and ideological principles for graphic communication.
These designers consciously moved away from illustration, were committed to photomechanical reproduction, and adopted a carefully considered and judicious use of photography and color.
Their shared interest was to communicate ideas effectively with simple, reductive means.
At the foundation of their approach were an acknowledgment of the increasing complexity, fragmentation, and interdependence of knowledge, and a mistrust of the growing sophistication of the mechanical reproduction of images used to manipulate the public in mass advertising.
Bills posters show a mastery of Jan Tschicholds New Typography (see here), gained during the years he spent as a student at the Dessau Bauhaus from 1927 to 1929.
Allied with a commitment to modern, clear communication of ideas visually and simply, the abstract geometric relationships found in his exhibition posters and related print production also stem from an approach to abstract art known as lart concret that emphasized imagination and creativity.
Bills 1945 poster for an exhibition of architecture (USA baut) presents a coordinated approach to abstract composition including photographic and typographic elements (fig.
11.64).
The poster is composed of nineteen diamond shapes of five different sizes, each containing photographic views of contemporary American buildings, urban complexes, and highways.
The lower-case sans serif letterforms (Akzidenz Grotesk) and asymmetrical layout owe much to the principles of the New Typography, as does the careful attention to the relative weight and hierarchy of information.
Bill balances, for instance, the two larger diamonds right of center with the USA baut lettering to the left that gains visual strength from being isolated against a large area of white space.
Beyond Bills interest in eye movement as a basis for poster design, in this example the design is rich in other dimensions of visual communication: the blue and red tints applied to the photographs, along with the activation of white space, are, of course, the colors of the American flag, while the active arrangement of diamond shapes recalls the gridlike geometry of urban streets, intersections, and traffic as symbolized in Piet Mondrians late Boogie Woogie series of paintings, completed in the early 1940s while the artist lived in Manhattan.
Max Bill, USA Baut exhibition poster, offset lithograph, 50 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 35 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (127.8 × 90.2 cm), 1945.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
One of the main features of the International Typographic Style was the use of a grid system to govern layouts, subordinating all individual typographic elements to a system that maintained unity and governed relationships between those elements.
The grid utilized modular shapes as units of measurement to establish relationships for a hierarchy of information, and designers likened its standardized units to those of the prefabricated units and industrial standards of modern architecture.
Visual symbols also played an important role in the International Typographic movement.
Armin Hofmann (19202020) and Anton Stankowski (19061998) are but two among a group of artists who used simple shapes together with sans serif typography to convey complex or mundane information with striking clarity and elegance.
Swiss graphic designer and educator Hofmann was responsible for extensive series of posters for museums and other arts organizations in Switzerland, and used typography to convey the essence of a subject with utmost economy.
His work reveals how much may be accomplished with minimal means, seen in the Gute Form exhibition poster of 1954 (fig.
11.65): the closely spaced, white, monoweight sans serif letterforms appear against the black ground as interchangeable mechanical parts.
The viewer supplies each letters missing parts, becoming an active participant as if being rewarded for solving a puzzle, while the words become an image of a clean, economical functional aesthetic.
Armin Hofmann, Gute Form exhibition poster, offset lithograph, 35.4 × 11 in (90 × 28 cm), 1954.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
Cultural institutions were often the patrons of the Neue Grafik; dance, theater, film, and art contributed to the quality of life beyond the satisfaction of basic material needs, and fueled the shared optimism of both graphic and industrial designers.
Moreover, journals such as Neue Grafik and Graphis promoted the democratic social and political benefits of design and the arts rather than their association with commercial advertising or elite leisure.
In a remarkable series of posters, Anton Stankowski demonstrated how complex technological processes might be simply and effectively communicated.
This is seen in the diagram illustrating the chemical transfer of heat using a series of broken undulating lines that change color from cool blue to warm red as they cross a barrier indicated by a heavy red vertical line (fig.
11.66).
Stankowskis exploration of reductive abstract form in relation to the design of information recalls Isotype as well as the earlier and more intuitive research of Kandinsky to determine a systematic psychology of color while teaching in Russia in the early 1920s (see here).
Both the artist and the designer shared an interest in research and experiment as part of the creative process, as well as an inclination to see abstract form as being universal in nature, but whereas Kandinsky used abstraction to communicate and liberate emotion in his paintings and prints, the focus of Neue Grafik designers was the creation or shaping of a better-informed public.
Designers such as Stankowski and Otl Aicher (see here) used their skills to forge a trust between the public and the corporate or government clients who contracted for their services.
By the 1960s (and even before) in the debates that took place at Ulm and elsewhere, the bonds and trust between business, government, and design were beginning to fray (see here onward).
Anton Stankowski, diagram for the process of heat transfer, page from a calendar for Viessmann, 1957–1958.
The grid system and basic sans serif type families were well suited to the consistent presentation of information for corporations, disseminated in house-style manuals to ensure conformity to standards and identity.
An example is Stankowskis public graphics for the city of Berlin, all of which incorporated a thin horizontal line divided by a vertical line to symbolize the citys division into East and West in 1947 and the wall that was built in 1961 and remained in place until 1989.
The interest of large municipal organizations and multinational corporations in visual systems for products and publications during the post-war period created broad support for the International Typographic Style.
Clean and recognizable systems of information reduced the visual noise and confusion of urban landscapes and enabled designers to impart a sense of order and easy navigation in the manner of the London Underground maps two decades earlier (see fig.
9.54).
The International Typographic Style appeared in journals and was the subject of museum exhibitions in Europe and in the United States at the Museum of Modern Art.
The styles practitioners held teaching positions enabling them to publish guides and exercises intended to encourage students to develop the skills and adopt the values of the Swiss approach.
Armin Hofmann taught at the Applied Arts School in Basel and held faculty positions at the School of the Philadelphia Museum of Art (now the University of the Arts) and at Yale University.
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology created a graphic design program that utilized a unified visual system for the institute and its press that could be applied to a variety of academic and public relations materials.
In 1959, Swiss designer Karl Gerstner (19302017) published a trilingual history of modern graphic design entitled Die Neue Graphik – The New Graphic Art – Le Nouvel Art Graphique.
This book presented the history of graphic design as the linear development toward clarity and simplicity as principles for the presentation of information to suit the needs of advertising and technical information.
Gerstner illustrated canonical examples of chromolithographic posters from the later nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as beginnings, and the more systematic use of asymmetric layout and vertical typography from the interwar period as breakthroughs, all leading to the present, in which system and an economy of means prevail.
Gerstner illustrated numerous logos and reductive imagery, as well as product photography.
In one sequence of images he contrasted advertisements in which womens high-heeled shoes were photographed in profile and from a birds-eye view for Lord & Taylor (1949) with an advertisement for I.
Miller Shoe Company in which a womans leg is photographed wearing the shoe (1956) with the following caption, indicating the strong distinction that was drawn at times between the International Typographic Style and persuasive techniques of the advertising industry: One way of advertising shoes is to show a picture of them.
Another is to make the picture promise the fulfillment of a wish: If you buy my shoes you will have beautiful legs (the shoe itself seems to have become a minor consideration).
It is all rather like a fairy story and nobody troubles to check the truthfulness of such promises.
Gerstner and others presented graphic design as a creative and socially responsible professional activity, combining visual imagination and problem-solving skills, rather than as a branch of advertising whose role was primarily to stimulate consumer desire.
Comparisons to modern art and the near-universal application of the grid provided subjective and objective parameters of modern graphic design practice and the higher purpose of educating the public and cleansing public spaces of clutter with clear, concise, and unified information systems.
While it is quite common to equate the International Typographic Style with objectivity and emotional restraint, this definition mostly applies to advertising and concert or theatrical performance rather than to areas of public service and advocacy.
In 1952 to 1953 Zurich-based graphic designer Josef Müller-Brockmann (19141996) won a competition to design a series of traffic safety posters for the Automobile Club of Switzerland (ACS).
The competition brief asked designers to illustrate the tagline Schützt das Kind! (Mind or Protect the Child!; fig.
11.67), and was part of an ACS initiative that included a changing display of statistics and photographs reporting traffic accidents and deaths, shown on an Unfallbarometer (Accident Barometer, also designed by Müller-Brockmann) located in a prominent Zurich public square.
His approach rejected illustration in favor of black and white photography and employed a limited color palette, including a horizontal yellow band at the bottom of the poster that draws attention to that area; unprinted white space to the right of the motorcycle wheel that contrasts with and isolates the running child and emphasizes the disparity between him and the speeding wheel; and the crisp sans serif Akzidenz Grotesk font in the upper-left corner silhouetted against the cycles motor housing.
The tension created by the unequal formal arrangement of asymmetrical abstract shapes, dominated by the aggressive dark triangle of the wheel at the left and its lighter, smaller counterpart to the right; the repetition of parallel diagonal lines that includes the outer edge of the wheel and shock absorber and the left contour of the running child; and the overall simplicity of the composition produce a unified image with a striking and immediate impact upon the viewer.
And yet, when using the term objective, authors appear to conflate technical practice with emotional restraint, as if objectivity was the natural or inevitable result of applying the formal principles of the Swiss style and the use of photography.
Indeed, in his own A History of Visual Communication (1971), Müller-Brockmann stated that objectively informative designs are a socio-cultural task. And in commenting on the program at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Zurich, Müller-Brockmann tells his readers he developed an objectified course of training, that visual communication is a means of conveying objective facts (my italics), giving designers the ability to cope with highly complex problems of human society. The section of his survey devoted to graphic design after World War II bears the subtitle The Development of Objective Visual Communication after World War II. Yet there is nothing factual about Müller-Brockmanns use of photomontage in Schützt das Kind!: the dramatic contrast in scale between motorcycle and child creates a sense of impending, even frightening danger and elicits a strong emotional response. Schützt das Kind! makes a statement about the relationship between drivers and pedestrians, about the power and aggressiveness of the former and the vulnerability of the latter.
Indeed, compared, for instance, with pictograms (see here and fig.
9.13) Müller-Brockmanns poster is anything but neutral or factual, less a cautious reminder to slow down for school children or that children may be playing nearby with which todays drivers are more familiar than a frantic warning of an impending catastrophe.
It exemplifies the differences between the assumed neutrality of graphic design for advertising in Switzerland and graphic design for other purposes that sanctioned more persuasive rather than impersonal approaches to visual communication, in this case promoting the Automobile Club of Switzerlands concerns for traffic safety.
And so the moral responsibility of the graphic design profession, as envisioned by Müller-Brockmann, was not in all cases equated with facts: photography could be powerful and dramatic as well as emotionally neutral, demonstrating the relative, contextual meaning of terms such as subjective, fact, or objective. Josef Müller-Brockmann, Schützt das Kind! poster for the Automobile Club of Switzerland, 1953, offset printing, 50 × 35 <sup>2</sup>/<sub>5</sub> in (128 × 90 cm), 1960.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
Post-war designers in Switzerland and Germany favored sans serif typefaces for their simplicity and reduction of calligraphic embellishment.
Until the 1950s designers such as Max Bill were comfortable using the early twentieth-century typeface Akzidenz Grotesk (see here).
Then in 1957, Swiss designer Adrian Frutiger (19282015) produced the Univers typeface for the French foundry Deberny et Peignot (fig.
11.68).
In addition to numerous variations in weight and width that were made available when it was introduced, Univers letterforms have slight variations in stroke width as compared with interwar sans serif faces, for example, in the slight tapering of the bowls of the lower-case p and g as they near the vertical strokes, or in the narrowing of the o at the top and bottom.
Frutiger thought these changes made the face more versatile and better suited than monoweight sans serifs for reading as well as for display.
In response, the Berthold Foundry in Berlin began working on a revision to its Akzidenz Grotesk font with similar deviations from monoweight stroke widths, also released in 1957.
Originally named Neue Haas Grotesk, the name was changed to Helvetica, the Latin name for Switzerland (fig.
11.69).
The analysis of post-war sans serif typefaces reveals the painstaking process of developing letterforms in terms of small variations in stroke and space, in response to printing techniques, effects upon different kinds of paper, and an increase in the variety of printing that required extended font families.
Such design experimentation and research into the means of expression in typography brings to mind Josef Alberss Homage to the Square series of abstract geometric paintings, where laboratory-like testing of color combinations within restricted grid-based compositions reveal distinctions and variations in the perception of spatial relationships on a twodimensional surface.

Not all graphic designers in Europe subscribed to the exclusive use of sans serif typography as did the practitioners of the International Typographic Style.
Jan Tschichold became disillusioned with the dogmatism of his own New Typography, and his work after World War II for the Penguin publishing company in Britain shows a respect for tradition in both typography and traditional symmetrical layout in book printing (see here and fig.
9.58).
Such continuity with traditional fine printing is also seen in the new serif faces invented by graphic designer Hermann Zapf (19182015).
A self-taught calligrapher and art director for the Stempel type foundry in Frankfurt, Germany, Zapf was strongly influenced by the example of Rudolf Koch (see here).
Zapf developed several influential serif typefaces in the post-war period, including Palatino in 1948 (fig.
11.70); his wife Gudrun was also a prolific typeface designer, producing Nofret for the Berthold Foundry in Berlin in 1986.
In 1954 Hermann Zapf published the Manuale Typographicum, a compendium of typographic material revealing a great understanding of both tradition and new principles of design; the Hallmark Card Company of Kansas City, Missouri, was one of his clients.
Palatino was designed for letterpress printing and was intended to maintain its legibility for printing on inexpensive papers.
Its letterforms show a smooth and controlled transition from thick to thin strokes, a characteristic that is also found in Optima (fig.
11.71), which Zapf developed between 1952 and 1958.
Optima appears to lie somewhere between serif and sans serif typefaces.
It possesses the boldness and close spacing of the latter and yet preserves some transition between thick and thin strokes of Roman letterforms.
Some historians of typography praise Zapf for combining the best features of both traditions in the design of Optima.
