Swiss graphic designers sought common ground in visual communication, but the movements international pretensions were limited to industrially developed nations, multinational corporations, the Latin alphabet, and a theory of abstract reduction that may be less obviously universal than imagined.
With the rise of China as an economic power, increasing economic expansion and interdependence following the fall of the Soviet Union, and awareness of ethnic and racial difference more generally, the universal principles and assumptions of Swiss style appear more a matter of cultural debate than an accepted doctrine, and todays digital emojis may lay greater claim to universality (see here).

## Means
and Ends International Typographic Style advocates and practitioners saw their work as inherently creative and socially responsible.
Such work embodied a sense of restraint as well as reform, removed from the excesses of commercial art direction at one end and the indulgence and unrestrained freedom of individual expression for a more exclusive audience at the other.
In addition to the examples cited above, Ulm faculty member Otl Aicher (19221991) developed corporate identity and advertising for the German airline Lufthansa in the early 1960s, with specifications that included grid layout, typography, and symbols (see fig.
13.34).
On a more theoretical level, International Typographic Style relates to semiotics, defined as the study or science of signs.
Emerging first in the field of linguistics, semiotics holds that the meaning of language is the outcome of a process involving a signifier or means of communication (letters, words, images) and a signified, that is, the way in which those means of communication are understood.
Words, as well as images, do not have fixed meanings in relation to the objects or ideas they represent.
Rather, meaning is constructed or mediated socially in an active rather than passive process that involves both intention as well as reception.
In the absence of objective communication, graphic designers focused attention upon controlling the range of meanings in the signs they constructed and establishing clearly, even universally, understood information.
Word, symbol, image, composition, and hierarchy of information constituted the elements of a responsible approach to graphic communication within the framework of semiotics.
As we saw in Müller-Brockmanns Schützt das Kind! poster, designers could exercise considerable latitude dependent upon the nature of the commission and the expectations of the client.
The close relationship that developed between the International Typographic Style and corporate identity systems eventually complicated its claims of neutral or objective communication.
In 1955 Max Bill resigned as director of the Hochschule für Gestaltung (HfG), and Argentinian-born Tomás Maldonado (19222018) was appointed as his successor.
Maldonado shifted the curriculum of the school away from experimentation with materials and visual practice toward a stronger involvement with social theory, reducing emphasis upon studio work and concentrating upon redefining the role of design and the designer in a global context critical of materialism and capitalism.
As a practicing designer he served as a consultant to the Erbe medical equipment company in Tübingen, Germany, in the early 1960s, where his product housings employed hard-edged white geometric forms framed by black strips, simple manufacturing techniques, smooth surfaces to promote hygiene, and subordination to the impersonal architecture and sterility of the surgery (fig.
11.72).
11.72 Tomás Maldonado, medical equipment, Erbe Company, Tübingen, Germany, 1961.
Maldonado questioned the consumer orientation of post-war industrial design in the context of broader global considerations including hunger, disease, and pollution.
He also had reservations about the alliance between design and business, and argued for design education that emphasized social awareness and responsibility grounded in an understanding of the economic and political structures in which design practice functioned.
His views were echoed by Gui Bonsiepe (b.
1934), an Ulm student at the time who wrote in an essay from 1965: That the interests of business do not always coincide with the interests of society is a recognition nobody can avoid who works with the communication industry. Difficulty in gaining unilateral support among faculty for his vision of design and the education of designers led to tension at Ulm.
Following financial problems that forced consolidation with a nearby vocational school, the Hochshule für Gestaltung closed in 1968.
Maldonados interest in environmental design, however, was echoed by other contemporary theorists who were equally concerned with more radical possibilities of linking design with varied fringe efforts directed toward social change.
These views strayed farther from the more product-and-process-oriented mainstream of international modern industrial design into the realm of social and political activism.
In fine art as well, contemporary artists such as Joseph Beuys (18881958) were less concerned with making objects (objects-as-commodities) than with reaching audiences and provoking a response alternatively through performance and demonstration, suggesting the possibility for a relevant public role for the arts outside the gallery or museum.
Maldonado envisioned an expansion of the definition of design to include a wider range of activities that engaged users with technology, integrating information and other media to address pressing human and social needs.
The paradigm for the designer went beyond form-giving and products to services and human interaction with technology and mass media, promoting designs increasing role in modern life as a broadly defined tool of communication connecting people with the world around them.
These issues are further explored in Part VI in relation to the counterculture (see here onward) as well as to applications of digital technology to design (see here onward).
The primacy of global concerns also informed the theory and practice of other, more radical design practitioners and critics, including American architect and designer Buckminster Fuller (18951983) as well as Austrian-born architect Richard Neutra (18921970).
In the 1940s, Fuller, inspired by the development of lightweight building materials, devised a technique for constructing geodesic domes using triangular components.
Fullers ideas were often couched in utopian terms, and his embrace of prefabrication and uniformity implied a form of collectivism that did not resonate with manufacturers in an age of advertising and expanded materialism.
Fullers hopes for sponsorship of his building plans failed to materialize, perhaps as they were too far removed from the suburban ideal of individual home ownership and customization that was taking shape in Levittowns and other communities throughout the United States (see here).
Nevertheless, Fullers message of social responsibility and the conservation of natural resources helped to make him something of a cult figure in the later 1960s in a more volatile political and social climate.
Not surprisingly, he has made a comeback among those in the design community who think globally about the effects of design upon the environment.
Neutras response to post-war design was a book entitled Survival Through Design, published in 1954, an indictment of the commercial values inherent in post-war popular culture and a search for reform standards based upon basic human needs in a global setting.
In his writing Neutra championed the indivisibility of the man-made with the natural, and hoped that ecological thinking would inform the future of architecture.
He advocated stringent performance standards for industrially manufactured building materials, and the application of his ideas would have required a level of regulation and control of the building and manufacturing industries not possible in the expanding economic framework of developed capitalism involving new technologies, markets, and growth.

## Design
and Corporate Culture A conscious connection between corporations and the promotion of education and cultural awareness through information design may be seen in the advertising and broader marketing campaigns undertaken by the Columbia Broadcast System (CBS) under creative director William Golden (19111959) and the Container Corporation of America (CCA) under its president Walter Paepke (18961960).
These executives hired fine artists and designers to develop posters and advertisements for company products and services as well as for more general advertisements that link the corporation to creative activities perceived by many to be an expression of democratic values under capitalism.
Golden was responsible for a massive campaign to attract attention and sponsors to CBS with a series of creative advertisements to demonstrate the power of radio and the newer medium of television to reach diverse audiences.
In a trade periodical advertisement Golden chose an abstract drawing by artist Nathan Polsky that depicts small, white, ghostlike figures floating diagonally from left to right against a black background.
In the manner of the new advertising, brief copy appears to the lower right, while a heavier title reads The air is full of customers, referring to the medium of radio (fig.
11.73).
A designer in his own right, Golden also developed the eye trademark for CBS.
William Golden (art director), Nathan Polsky (artist), print advertisement for Columbia Broadcast System, thirtieth Art Directors’ Annual, New York, 1950.
Race has remained an obstacle to minority participation in the design professions.
One exception was the CBS networks hiring of Georg Olden (19201975) as graphic design director, one of the first (and very few) African American designers to hold an executive position with a major network.
Olden and other designers who worked under his direction embraced clever, reductive visual and textual strategies of the new advertising for titling, sequencing, and promotion.
Eero Saarinen designed the CBS Building in midtown Manhattan (known as the Black Rock) and some of its industrially manufactured office furniture, with interiors outfitted by Knoll International under the direction of Florence Schust Knoll.
Corporate design at CBS created a modern, sophisticated, clean image, free from historical associations and in alignment with news and entertainment programming that brings to mind elements of reform, that is, educating its expanding and diverse audience by exposing them to the fine arts and their association with freedom of expression, as well as current-events reporting acknowledged for its independence and trustworthiness.
Corporate identity at CBS also sought to combat charges of consumer manipulation by advertising and the dumbing down of content leveled by critics at the new medium, demonstrating that television was capable of presenting serious, challenging ideas.
Walter Paepke promoted designs educational value through his large Chicago-based company, the Container Corporation of America.
Paepke sponsored a series of advertisements by modern artists including French painter Fernand Léger, helped to support the creation of the New Bauhaus in Chicago under the direction of László Moholy-Nagy, and established the Design Conference in Aspen, Colorado (where he owned a vacation home), beginning in 1951, to advance progressive thinking in design.
Paepke saw the corporation as a participant in public education, identifying culture with high intellectual and creative pursuits, products of an enlightened democracy.
As an example, CCA published the World Geographic Atlas designed by Herbert Bayer (see fig.
11.26).
Bayer also designed a series of magazine advertisements for CCA titled Great Ideas of Man, beginning in 1950 and continuing into the 1970s.
Figure 11.74, dating from 1959, is one of this series: a photomontage of popular images on the dangers advertising poses to democracy.
The images reference glamor, gambling, alcohol (the dice are being thrown from a shot glass), and luxury; combined with the following warning from Theodore Roosevelt dating to 1917, the images communicate superficiality and materialism as seductive but false substitutes for more abiding values: The things that will destroy America are prosperity at any price, pace at any price, safety first, instead of duty first, and love of soft living, and the get-rich-quick theory of life. GREAT IDEAS OF WESTERN MAN . . . one of a series THEODORE ROOSEVELT on the preservation of America The things that will destroy America are prosperity at any price, peace at any price, safety first instead of duty first, and love of soft living and the get-rich-quick theory of life.
(Letter to S.
Stanwood Menken, January 10, 1917) From "The Letters of Theodore Roosevelt," Harvard University Press 11.74 Herbert Bayer, “Great Ideas of Man” series advertisement, 14 × 11.25 in (35.6 × 28.6 cm), Container Corporation of America, 1959.
As explained by author James Sloan Allen, Paepkes interests parallel the efforts of University of Chicago president Robert Hutchins to establish educational standards based upon a canon of great books that contribute to the education of the individual in a democratic society.
Like design reform in earlier periods, the view of culture promoted by CCA was paternalistic, promoting the interests and biases of an educated and powerful class, and removed from the complex social and economic realities of the post-war period that included minorities who were developing their own identities and subcultures.
Nevertheless, such endeavors and projects suggest the cultural climate of the post-war era, a time in which multinational corporations aligned their activities with education, standards, and the promotion of shared cultural values.
The Modernist formal language they employed served the purposes of unity and refinement, a mark of distinction distant from the negative associations of commercialism and profit.
As such, international modern industrial design, as well as the International Typographic Style, maintained something of their interwar polemical character, embracing decorative restraint as a visual metaphor for responsibility and a humanistic balance between individual and society.
By promoting a progressive and responsible image, multinational corporations also deflected congressional concerns about government regulation and the suggestion by some critics to impose taxes on business advertising.
Yet in the post-World War II world, the battle lines between production and consumption were not so easily drawn, and seemed to be less a matter of ethics or a hierarchy of values than a matter of taste, of choice, of both...and rather than either...or. American journalist Russell Lynes presented design as a matter of taste, horizontal rather than vertical, in his entertaining 1949 essay titled Highbrow, Middlebrow, Lowbrow, first published in Harper’s and later reproduced with an accompanying illustrated chart in Life magazine.
Lynes avoided references to reform or ethics, emphasizing lifestyle choices and fluidity among his three broad groups of consumers, discussed in greater detail in chapter 12 (see here).

## Corporate
Identity: Trademarks and Beyond In his 1947 book Thoughts on Design (see here), Paul Rand noted an almost magical power exerted by letterforms.
This aura surrounding letters found expression in the post-war period, especially in the proliferation of memorable logos for corporations and organizations operating on a multinational scale.
The role of letters as a leitmotif of midtwentieth-century industrial and business culture appears in the United States Pavilion for the Worlds Fair held in Brussels in 1958, designed by graphic artists Tom Geismar (b.
1931) and Ivan Chermayeff (19322017; fig.
11.75).
These hanging threedimensional letterforms echoed other exhibits at the fair that promoted an American way of life through fashion and modern kitchens (rather than the military technology that featured in the Soviet pavilion, including its Sputnik satellite that raised Cold War tensions in the United States).
The exhibit acknowledged the ubiquity of trademarks and logos in everyday life, and their associations with technology, organization, commerce, international relations, and global capitalist economic expansion.
Tom Geismar and Ivan Chermayeff, exhibition design for United States Pavilion, Brussels World’s Fair, Belgium, 1958.
Many large multinational corporations recognized the advantages of consistent policies toward design after World War II.
Recalling the precepts of the Werkbund (see here), standards of good design translated easily into industrial corporate culture, subordinating the individual to the group whose shared ethos was guided by dependability and consistent performance, building familiarity and trust.
Corporations such as Olivetti in Italy, Braun and Lufthansa in West Germany, and Sony in Japan all drew upon consultant or in-house designers to create identity programs, directed by top levels of management.
The increasingly international nature of business in many hi-tech industries such as pharmaceuticals, oil, transportation, and communications led naturally to a reliance upon letters or logos rather than lengthier company names for branding in a global market.
The economic climate of aggressive growth through takeovers and mergers with related businesses often created additional pressure to maintain a single image or company identity, and professional designers met the need, shaping marketing strategies and reinforcing organizational behavior.
Their contributions included logos, liveries, products, and packaging to establish corporate organizational standards and project a company ethos.
Product and logo design form only part of corporate identity.
Many corporations rely upon slogans, packaging, architecture, signage, advertising, and exhibition design to promote their image, particularly if their business is in similar products such as soft drinks, energy transmission, or oil and gasoline rather than in a line of consumer domestic wares such as coffee-makers, toasters, or cassette players.
Even in these areas, packaging and prominent logos often create as much differentiation as product housings, especially when miniaturization imposes a stronger degree of uniformity among similar goods, for instance, in electronic products, whether transistor radios or flat-screen televisions.
The broader context for the flourishing of corporate identity also includes legislation that permitted companies to protect their identities (and investment) through copyright.
More broadly, corporate identity dovetailed with soft power, mitigating the fear or threat of greater government control over private enterprise.
The corporate image of the Olivetti Corporation, as seen in showrooms throughout Italy in the later 1940s and in Manhattan from 1954 (see fig.
11.48), prompted IBM president Thomas Watson, Jr.
(19141993) to pursue a unified corporate identity program.
To direct this program Watson hired Eliot F.
Noyes (19101977), an architect who had served as curator of industrial design at the Museum of Modern Art.
IBM identity applied not only to the coherent design of products and promotional materials directed toward clients and investors, but also toward reinforcing community and exclusivity among employees, that is, a unified corporate culture.
Such a team-based approach had advantages in providing guidelines or standards for dress and behavior.
Some observers noted a downside to the new corporate culture.
In his book The Lonely Crowd (1950), sociologist David Riesman wrote that a corporate image could have an alienating effect upon individuals, who felt that they had to fit in with the group in order to be successful.
In Riesmans view, corporate behavior was part of a shift from inner-directed to other-directed values that he saw emerging as the dominant form of conformity particularly in the United States.
Being part of a corporation could be comforting as well as disquieting in discouraging the expression of difference.

## 11.76 Paul Rand, redesign of trademark for IBM Corporation, 1972 (first designed 1956). Pa
ul Rand (see here) redesigned IBMs logo in 1956 (fig.
11.76).
Like many global corporations, the IBM logo relies for its success upon simple recognition and the substitution of letters for longer, often complicated names.
Rand used a slab-serif display face known as City Medium, introduced in Germany in 1930.
Serif letters are less usual in corporate logos, but in this case contribute to strong figureground contrast through close spacing, creation of squared negative spaces between letters and in the counters for the upper-case B for added unity, and to the stability of the design.
Subsequently Rand retained the basic elements of his IBM logo, but expanded its treatment through repetition and color variation on packaging, introducing horizontal stripes that run through the heavy letterforms, and even playfully substituting an eye and a bee in place of the letters I and B. This last variation is indeed a testimony to the power of letters that Rand noted in Thoughts on Design.
A similar use of serif faces in the later 1940s and early 1950s is found in the logo by Swiss-born designer Herbert Matter for the New Haven Railway in 1954 and for the Knoll Corporation around 1950 (fig.
11.77); the letters of the Knoll logo consist of connecting thin lines of uniform thickness ending in rectangular shapes.
Herbert Matter, trademark “K” for Knoll Corporation, 1950.
Line drawing by John Langdon.
Paul Rand, trademark for the American Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), 1962.
11.79 Logos may be almost purely abstract, as is the case with IBM, or can relate to the nature of company products or services, as seen in Rands clever redesign of the Westinghouse W, where abstract circles and lines construct the letter and symbolize electrical circuitry (fig.
11.78) in the companys products.
More common in logo design, however, is sans serif typography, seen, for instance, in Rands design for the American Broadcasting Corporation in 1962 (fig.
11.79).
This trademark uses a variant of the Futura typeface with its bowl a rather than Roman lower-case a, and a single weight for all letter strokes, resulting in an identity among the shapes of the three sequential letters.
It is not surprising that graphic designers played so important a role in creating corporate identity.
It is not easy to differentiate between information and promotion: the image of unity brought about by logos reduced the distance between the public and the large private company, suggesting consistency and encouraging familiarity and trust.
The same clarity, consistency, production values, and clean page design apply to Rands annual investor reports for IBM (fig.
11.80).
Paul Rand, IBM annual report, with photograph of IBM electric typewriter designed by Eliot Noyes, 1958.
As well as directing its corporate identity program, Noyes was responsible for overseeing the product design of typewriters for IBM.
His success at IBM in building an identity system derived from a close working relationship with company president Watson.
Both men agreed that design, broadly understood, could be a tool for greater cooperation among the various IBM divisions as well as communicating a coherent and consistent public corporate image.
Noyess efforts were an extension of the belief in the ability of design to shape shared attitudes and values.
Standards in product design were based upon the adaptation of modern technology and restrained product housing, avoiding decoration and superficial detail.
Noyes worked as a young architect for former Bauhaus director Walter Gropius and faculty member Marcel Breuer after graduating from Harvard University and before his appointment as curator for industrial design at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
It is not surprising, given this familiarity with European-based interwar Modernism, that he extended to the multinational capitalist corporation the responsibility for creating and promoting consistent visual forms and organization that communicated efficiency, technical precision, and fitness to purpose in design.
For corporate identity, the practice of design merged the efforts of graphic and industrial designers and extended far beyond merely giving form to products, encompassing a broader and more complex discourse involving decisions that promoted the policies and objectives of large organizations and their constituencies both internally and publicly.
Design constituted product forms, offices, showrooms, annual reports to stockholders, advertising, and myriad other promotional and public relations activities.
In this context, design was a common denominator, its meaning linked increasingly to information and communicating with a variety of users or stakeholders.
While form was one aspect of information, other communications media played an increasingly prominent role in design, especially in relation to business practice and new technologies.
One outcome of this broader practice of design was Noyess hiring of Charles and Ray Eames as consultant designers of exhibits and films for the corporation.
The Eameses work for IBM focused upon communicating technological and economic progress through images, in exhibits for the IBM Pavilion at the 1964 New York Worlds Fair and in the three-dimensional timeline for the exhibit A Computer Perspective, held in the IBM corporate headquarters in New York in 1971 (fig.
11.81).
The Eameses exhibits, like those of Will Burtin for the Upjohn pharmaceutical company (see fig.
11.24), reinforced the post-war belief in the integration of business, government, and technology to improve living standards responsibly at home and abroad.
We might see this development as the continuation of a tradition of versatility in modern professional design practice, with designers viewing their varied and team-based efforts as means toward serving a broad range of human needs rather than directed solely toward creating products for a market.
Such a view implies a sense of trust and shared purpose between designers, their clients, and the public.
An undercurrent of mistrust in such common ground has perhaps always been present, but became more acute in the 1960s with debates about means and ends, and a stronger expression of radical alternatives directed toward addressing poverty, the environment, social and racial justice, and other grassroots initiatives treated below (see here onward).
The Eameses A Computer Perspective montage recalls El Lissitzkys powerful USSR pavilion for the 1928 Pressa exhibition in Cologne (see fig.
9.22) updated for the expanded technological age of information.
In addition to his special consultant relationship with IBM, Noyes also worked for Mobil, Westinghouse, and other large multinational corporations.
Charles and Ray Eames, panel from “A Computer Perspective” (History Wall or Timeline), one of six 94 <sup>1</sup>/ in (240 cm) panels, 1971.
Exhibit design, IBM Corporate Exhibit Center, New York.
Other examples of conscious policies toward design in a global market include the Philips Corporation of Eindhoven in the Netherlands.
Recognizing competition and global markets for a variety of products ranging from lightbulbs to stereos, televisions, and medical equipment in the post-war period, Philips developed a consistent design policy and integrated design into the corporate decision-making process.
This did not result in a recognizable look for products as with Braun, but rather in a process of training and communication across a number of product divisions and brand names that had grown autonomously.
While recognized as Philips for consumer electronics in Europe, in the United States Philips products were known by brand names such as Norelco, Sylvania, and Philco.
There was no effort to create uniformity among brands, but design was used to strategize considerations of product housing, ergonomics, fitness to purpose, as well as address target audiences for a wide range of consumer electronic goods for international markets.
Particularly in the United States, brand differentiation among products manufactured by a single company for the mass market was also an effective corporate strategy, expanding variety and choice under the control of tight policies governing the parameters of change and directing the scope of industrial design activity.
Such strategies involved coordinating design with recognizing and exploiting market segmentation, along with massive advertising investment (another instance of information), reducing competition from smaller companies, and is explored below in chapter 12 on mass culture.

## Chapter
12

## Design
and Mass Appeal: Taste in a Culture of Consumption After World War II, and concurrently with the movements described in chapter 11 under the general rubric of good design, middle-class and a growing segment of industrial working-class Americans reaping the benefits of increased production, higher wages, paid vacations, and low mortgage rates entered the expanding market for residential housing, personal products, and home goods, becoming consumers of an increasing array of manufactured products.
The attitudes and expectations of this broad and diverse market absorbed but also were not limited in their consumer preferences to the collections, exhibitions, and paternalism of museums, the consistency and dependability of corporate identity systems, and the new humanism that embraced social responsibility, aesthetic awareness, fitness to purpose, and comfort.
Indeed, postwar consumer experience was shaped not only by economic growth and post-war optimism but also by the unprecedented role assumed by mass media.
The term mass culture may be used to describe the United States market, especially after World War II.
This term includes the designed products that reached an expanding consumer base, but appreciating those products requires understanding the ways in which mass media shaped and reflected the experience of post-war Americans, as well as the perception of that experience abroad.
The apparent indifference of the mass market to good design may be seen in the success of a wide variety of post-war products ranging from automobiles to kitchen appliances and portable electronics.
In all of these examples there was tremendous receptivity (or susceptibility) on the part of consumers to planned obsolescence: that is, the calculated efforts of manufacturers to generate demand with a seemingly unending supply of new products, along the lines of seasonal fashion.
In fact, the term was coined by the Milwaukee-based industrial designer Brooks Stevens (19111995), acknowledging the connection between design, consumer desire, and continuous novelty: what advertising executives had referred to as consumer engineering from the later 1920s.
Obsolescence conditions the buying public to continual cycles of consumption, replacement, and seemingly unending desire.
In addition, while modern materials and methods of mechanized production prevailed in manufacturing, products made frequent references to the past and present, as well as to the future, replacing principles such as fitness to purpose and fine art or architecturally based aesthetic principles with greater freedom of choice, integrating expendability with a broader spectrum of tastes.
Indeed the phenomena of newness and an accelerated pace of change tended to erode in some degree the very notion of stable aesthetic, ethical, or performance standards and the authority they imply.
After all, standards suggest permanence and durability for products, while obsolescence and novelty imply a perpetual state of becoming, of desire, where consumption itself becomes a way of life, and the manipulation of consumer behavior a business strategy.
British design historian and critic Reyner Banham (19221988) termed this phenomenon a throwaway culture. Despite its commercial potential, implementing frequent product change entailed great economic risks: the retooling required for changes in the manufacturing process as well as the increased investment in the complex production process ran contrary to the tenets of Fordism, translating either into higher, less competitive prices or lower profit margins for companies and their investors.
Thus obsolescence required corporations to manage risks of higher investment costs, often by limiting the role of design to superficial elements of product housing rather than integrating design with engineering, ergonomics, or other research-based considerations (after all, it was called planned obsolescence).
Moreover, success also depended upon marketing products through a variety of media ranging from popular magazines and radio to the cinema and the emerging medium of television.
In many ways media outlets employed similar strategies for the mass production of entertainment.
An example is serial television programming, utilizing the same familiar characters facing new conflicts or crises each week, or stereotypical Hollywood film heroes following the same plotline in an array of different times and places.
In such cases originality was managed, limited to particular elements of the creative process in order to generate ever new products for consumers to watch or to buy while containing the costs of capital investment and time pressures.
Today, film studios greatest profits generate from sequels of their popular titles such as Spiderman, Rocky, or Star Wars.
Also, popular design and entertainment were even more interrelated, since advertising, whether on television or in print magazines and newspapers, was sold to corporate sponsors of products and services on the basis of delivering an audience for the purposes of marketing.
Most historians acknowledge that the success of product obsolescence for the mass market could not have taken place without advertising along with added incentives such as term and credit buying, allowing consumers to enjoy their purchases before they owned them outright.
Whether through illustration, photography, or television, advertisements linked products to individual identity, self-improvement, and social acceptance, the ability to look or feel like the person you imagine yourself to be.
On the basis of polls and other consumer studies, advertisers often targeted housewives and children, who played a large role in buying patterns for a majority of middle-class families.
Techniques extended Veblens theory of conspicuous consumption to the age of expanding industrial production and mass consumption.
Manufacturing and new strategies for design, marketing, and advertising combined to create forms and associations that appealed to a diverse audience linked by a belief that consumption and materialism were the means to individual fulfillment as well as contributing to national prosperity and stimulating the economy.
Such a seductive combination of forces was hard to resist.
Suburban strip malls, discount stores, supermarkets, seasonal sales, coupons, promotions, and expanded channels of distribution further reduced impediments to shopping for the products of mass culture.
The origin of national brands dates to the early twentieth century, but the post-war era accelerated the substitution of the national for the local and regional through franchised chain stores, hotels, motels, and restaurants  these include Korvettes, Holiday Inn, Sheraton Hotels, and Colonel Sanders Kentucky Fried Chicken or McDonalds.
The result was an emerging shared culture of shopping that defined American lifestyles.
Journalist Thomas Hine labeled the phenomenon Populuxe, a term that encompasses the dream of leisure, abundance and self-indulgence that exerted such widespread appeal especially during the 1950s.
The relationship between advertising and mass design reminds us that the interaction between products and users was mediated by images as seen in print and on television, with the latter assuming greater importance after the war, particularly in the United States.
Beyond the gallery, corporate office or showroom, or museum collection and exhibition, displays in retail outlets, catalogs, magazine and newspaper advertisements, on radio or on television, manufactured goods were entwined with the everyday lives of Americans and barometers of material progress that contributed to the achievement of the American Dream.

## Detroit:
Transportation as Symbol The post-war Detroit-manufactured automobile offers a paradigm for mass design and the attitudes of manufacturers and buyers that shaped its practice.
The manufacture of new automobiles for the civilian market had ceased in 1942 as automobile makers contributed to meeting the governments material needs in the war effort.
Although demand for new cars was strong when domestic manufacturing resumed after the war, there were signs of market saturation and a slowed rate of growth in automobile purchases in the early 1950s.
Post-war automobiles resembled their pre-war counterparts, and design was secondary to production efficiency and controlling capital investment costs.
Stimulating sales through annual styling changes was not a new idea in the automobile industry, and it re-emerged with renewed vitality in the early 1950s.
At General Motors, company president Alfred Sloan renewed his plan for greater brand differentiation and more noticeable annual styling changes, minimizing costs through standardized parts for the chassis and other mechanical elements that could be shared among the companys numerous brands and models.
It was Sloans dream to create a vehicle for every purse, defining a series of gradations from economy to luxury in terms of visible differences in styling and comfort.
Encompassing the ends as well as the broad middle of the market, General Motors effectively helped to equate car buying with social mobility as well as personal identity and to stimulate more frequent automobile purchases while remaining competitive with smaller manufacturers of both luxury and economy cars.

## 12.1 Advertisement for Cadillac Eldorado, from Life, September 9, 1957. Harley Earl (see h
ere), chief of General Motors Styling Department since its inception in 1927 as the Art and Color Section, benefitted from a close relationship with Sloan, and was able to carry out the presidents corporate vision with great imagination.
Earl preferred longer and lower bodies for GM cars with an integration of hoods, fenders, trunks, windshields, and roofs, accentuating these characteristics by adding chrome accents, wraparound bumpers, and introducing the tailfin.
Earlier prototypes, such as the 1937 two-door Buick Y-Job, prefigured Earls post-war approach, and Sloans embrace of planned obsolescence gave designers greater freedom and influence within the corporation, provided the results could be measured in increased sales and profits.
12.2 United States Air Force, P-38 fighter plane, 1941.
As explained by Stephen Bayley, designers working for Earl made prototypes in clay rather than wood or metal to achieve more unified and modeled sculptural forms; in production, longer lengths of steel, available as early as 1934, reduced the gap between prototype and realized assembly line product.
Earl introduced the tailfin first in the 1948 Cadillac, General Motors high-end luxury brand, and persisted with the feature despite its initial lukewarm reception by some company executives.
The fins were a form of overt product symbolism, the result of Earls fascination with the twin-body Lockheed P-38 fighter plane and its dual tailfins for increased stability (figs.
12.1 and 12.2).
In Earls estimation, the tailfin was a visible receipt for the consumers dollar.
Its widespread success in the 1953 Cadillac encouraged Earl to include variations upon the form in General Motors lower-end models, where it appeared in the 1955 Chevrolet, thus making available to average customers a form of product association previously available only to wealthier buyers.
General Motors encouraged this identification through advertising, for instance, linking the potential buyer of the 1954 Buick Roadmaster with success and status (fig.
12.3).
Interest in the tailfin and other features, for instance Buicks small bullet-shaped chrome portholes, wraparound bumpers, or curved windshields, were often derived from GMs futuristic dream cars. Dream cars were fantastic non-production models featured in traveling shows known as Motoramas or in dealer showrooms, related as well to a subculture of do-it-yourself car buffs throughout the period who crafted customized versions of standard production vehicles (fig.
12.4).
Placing cars on pedestals at the Motorama strengthened associations far beyond mere transportation, linking tailfins with the power of rocket engines and swelling forms and chrome protrusions with feminine sensuality. # You can make your someday come true now ROADMASTER BUICK 12.3 Advertisement for Buick Roadmaster, General Motors Corporation, Detroit, Michigan, 1954.
Better Homes and Gardens, August 1954.
The broad marketing strategy and financing of annual model changes across different brand names such as Oldsmobile, Pontiac, Buick, Chevrolet, and Cadillac favored large auto-makers and led to their increasing control of the market and production supply chains.
In addition to their focus upon brand differentiation through styling, the large automobile manufacturers possessed the resources for advertising investment and other forms of marketing, such as the Motorama.
Independent manufacturers like Hudson, Packard, Nash, Studebaker, and Kaiser either ceased production or became divisions of larger conglomerates, gradually losing their independence.
Despite the apparent variety and choice available to consumers in terms of brands, models, customized colors, and other options, American automobile manufacturing became more homogeneous, controlled by fewer large manufacturers with less room for competition in the mass market from smaller scale entrepreneurs.
These large companies were successful in strengthening differentiation between brands and particular groups of consumers.
Such a strategy also included the introduction of new brands or sub-brands, for instance, compact cars such as the Chevrolet Corvair, introduced in 1960 (see here).
Motorama, General Motors, Flint, Michigan, 1954.
The 1955 Chevrolet added not only the tailfin to the low end of its product line, but also the powerful, high-compression V-8 engine (introduced in the later 1930s).
For the average-income buyer, styling, horsepower, air-conditioning, and motorized convertible tops all added a feeling of power, individual expression, and instant gratification to the experience of personal mobility also found in the popular weekly television series Route 66 from the early 1960s (196064).
The continuing appeal of these associations was celebrated nostalgically in the 1973 film American Graf iti and the 1988 film Rainmaker, long after fuel prices, fears of gasoline shortages, pollution, foreign competition, and economic recession had taken their toll on the United Statess love affair with the automobile.
Advertisements for the American automobile of the later 1950s often combined references in the copy to practical advantages of roominess or advanced engineering with images that identified automobile ownership with luxury living.
These generally featured attractive, well-dressed (and exclusively white) couples returning home from an evening out or arriving in style at an upscale hotel (figs.
12.1 and 12.3).
Indeed, such product symbolism must be what Karl Gerstner had in mind when he endorsed straight product photography rather than emotional promises in advertising (see here).
Contemporary cinema captured the appeal of varied activities associated with personal mobility.
Examples include the family outing of Mr.
Hobbs Takes a Vacation (1962), the carefree spontaneity of Two for the Road (1967), or a reckless, self-destructive element in Rebel Without a Cause (1957).
Despite the absence of African Americans or other minorities in automobile advertising at the time, cars also formed part of the lyrics and pace of emerging rock n roll music, for instance, Black musician and songwriter Chuck Berrys No Particular Place to Go: Riding along in my automobile My baby beside me at the wheel I stole a kiss at the turn of a mile My curiosity running wild Cruisin and playin the radio With no particular place to go.
There is also a global component underlying the growth of the automobile industry in the United States during this period.
The development of the powerful V-8 engine for regular production vehicles took advantage of inexpensive gasoline prices in the United States, a result of favorable business agreements between American-based oil companies and refineries located in West Asia.
By the early 1970s, the oil-producing nations would assert their independence from Western oil companies, raise the price of fuel, and reshape automobile design as established by Detroit-based manufacturers in the period under discussion.
GM began to shed brands in 2004 with the elimination of Oldsmobile, followed by Pontiac in 2009 amid infusions of government investment and calls for restructuring of its business operations.
The rapport that GM had been able to establish with its customers eroded amid changing economic conditions, environmental awareness, and foreign competition.
When the once-mighty corporation declared bankruptcy and massive restructuring in May 2009, analysts cited a long list of miscalculations, perhaps none more significant than a failure to connect with consumers whose loyalty the company seemed to take for granted.
But for a time after World War II a large segment of the middle-class consuming public in the United States enjoyed the associations of styling, brand identity, low fuel prices, the anticipation of new annual models, and the comfort and emotional appeal of the open road.
12.5 Virgil Exner, Plymouth coupé, Chrysler Corporation, Auburn Hills, Michigan, 1957.
General Motors was perhaps the largest but certainly not the only manufacturer to adopt styling and planned obsolescence in industrial design.
The Ford Corporation introduced the Thunderbird sports car in 1954, a small two-seater appealing to the prospective buyers personal indulgence rather than practical considerations of family space or comfort.
The design, somewhat rectangular, seemed a restrained version of the more sculptural examples of Italian luxury coach-building (see here), but the Thunderbird was priced to appeal to a wider market of buyers who wished to indulge more overtly in the excitement of personal mobility.
In 1952 Chrysler Corporation promoted Virgil Exner (19091973), a former associate both of Harley Earl at General Motors and of Raymond Loewy, to vice-president in charge of styling.
Exners designs for Chrysler emphasized longer and lower profiles, but minimized the rounded panels and swollen forms of General Motors cars in favor of more angular, tapered forms.
In the industry this was known as the forward look, thought to be modeled upon the sabernosed body and swept-back wings of jet fighter planes that appeared in the early 1950s.
Decorative features such as overarching eyebrows above headlights contributed to the effect, with sweeping chrome strips reaching from front to rear and echoing the contour of the body, low and sloping rooflines, and tremendous tailfins with a pronounced upward sweep emphasizing length (fig.
12.5).
12.6 Brooks Stevens, Evinrude Lark outboard motors.
Models III, IV, V, and VI styled for 1959–1962.
Brooks Stevens Archive, Milwaukee Art Museum, Wisconsin.
Industrial manufacturers also employed consultant and in-house designers in areas outside of the automotive industry.
Brooks Stevens was a successful consultant designer for several companies both before and after World War II.
He anticipated the pent-up desire for eye-catching consumer goods following wartime shortages and rationing, and defended planned obsolescence on the basis of the joy and pride new designs provided their owners and the overall economic benefits of increased levels of employment and consumption.
Stevens designed engine housings for outboard recreational motor boats manufactured by Evinrude and Johnson that featured cutaway housings and two-tone colors reminiscent of Chryslers forward look in the later 1950s (fig.
12.6).
Other designers worked in-house for consumer electronics companies such as Motorola, or Zenith, both based near Chicago, Illinois.
These companies produced a wide range of portable and table transistor radios and phonographs.
In contrast to Braun (see fig.
11.57), their products were varied in form, color, and the design of operating controls (fig.
12.7), resembling automobile dashboards.
American industrial designers for the mass market rarely saw their role as educating consumers to appreciate restrained or sophisticated Modernist tastes; rather their designs acknowledged a wide range of consumer preferences and motivations, as well as perpetual technical innovation and novelty in which the only constant was desire, as Stevens stated in his definition of planned obsolescence: the desire to own something a little newer, a little better, a little sooner than is necessary. 12.7 Feature on portable radios and phonographs, Look, vol.
20, no.
21, October 16, 1956.

## Critics
of Styling By the later 1950s there was a tendency, even within the industrial design community, to criticize tailfins and other automobile styling features.
Raymond Loewy, for instance, who served as design consultant to the automobile manufacturer Studebaker, took aim at the American automobile industry in a speech of 1955, comparing that years new designs to gaudy merchandise and jukeboxes on wheels: even the author of Never Leave Well Enough Alone, who well understood the need to demonstrate the commercial advantages of design in industrial manufacturing, was offended by the degree to which design had departed from a more substantive relation to the automobiles mechanical basis, or from the ideal of beauty embodied in the characteristics of a unified streamlined Modernism.
Loewys own designs for Studebaker were original and aerodynamic, pioneering the sloping roofline later adopted by former associate Virgil Exner for the 1957 Plymouth (fig.
12.8).
But the Studebaker lacked the prominent symbolic jet-age tailfins of its General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler counterparts.
In the end it proved commercially unsuccessful; the company ceased automobile production in 1966.

## 12.8 Raymond Loewy, advertisement for Studebaker, Life, June 1954. Critics of the post-war
American automobile industry also viewed manufacturers as manipulators of consumer desire: the manufacturer is seen as active and the consumer as passive, the latter cast in the role of unwitting victim, conforming to social pressures and somehow programmed for shopping (see here).
And yet not all of the large automakers styling initiatives were successful: efforts to manipulate the public often resulted in disaster (as easily observed in the high number of short-lived network television series produced each autumn).
In other words, the phenomenon of mass design and consumer behavior was and remains an unpredictable enterprise, certainly more complex than many of its detractors imagined.
One of the most widely known mass-market miscalculations was the Ford Corporations 1958 Edsel, a project that failed to attract consumer interest despite a heavy investment in styling and promotion.
Historians have noted that family cars such as the Edsel were not attuned to consumer excitement at the time for luxury or sportier models aimed at youthful buyers.
As an exercise in design, the Edsel debacle reveals the complexity of predicting public reaction and figuring out whether a new product will prove profitable.
To summarize, two viewpoints toward mass culture emerged after World War II.
On one hand, mass design was seen as a form of exploitation manipulated from above and masking the desire for corporate profit and control under the banner of freedom of choice and the democratization of luxury and leisure, heavily dependent upon advertising and stimulated by product symbolism.
On the other hand, mass culture was also viewed as being empowering, responsive to the everyday experience and aspirations of ordinary folk, a popular and healthy assertion of individual expression that addresses common desires as well as fears for a diverse audience, increasingly geared to identifying, creating, and attracting segmented markets.
The rich strains of resistance, escape, self-expression, solidarity, and difference within popular culture emerge through fashion, products, and also through the medium of popular music, particularly rock n roll, with its roots in African American culture, its celebration of youthful energy, and its rebellious challenge to conventional behavior and authority.
The link between popular music and accessible grassroots expression appears in the career of rock musician legend and songwriter Bruce Springsteen (b.
1949).
When Springsteen accepted the Oscar for Original Score at the 1994 Academy Awards for the film Philadelphia (1993; the movie dealt with AIDS and discrimination against its victims), he accepted the award with the following remarks: You do your best and hope that it pulls out the best in your audience, and some piece of it spills over into the real world and peoples everyday lives and allows us to recognize each other through our veil of differences. Whether celebrating humanitys differences or recognizing our common emotions, however, the status of commodities, whether under capitalist free enterprise and the seductive images and slogans of advertising or Soviet economic efforts to demonstrate material progress, remains paramount, for even resistance often takes the form of consumption rather than threatening social or political action.
Moreover, whether owing to pent-up desire in response to rationing and shortages during World War II, or policies of Cold War containment that linked consumption to productivity and patriotism, designed consumer products acquired a wide range of meanings and associations, raising hopes as well as fears in popular and critical terms.
Author and journalist Thomas Hine noted that when United States Vice-President Richard Nixon met Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev in 1959 on the occasion of an exhibition of American goods in Moscow during a well-publicized meeting between leaders of the global superpowers during the Cold War, the Vice-President proudly showed the Soviet leader an American washing machine as evidence of the high standard of living enjoyed by a majority of Americas middle-class families.
Nixon identified, in effect, materialism with the achievement of democratic ideals under capitalist free enterprise.
While Americans might have feared competition with the Soviets in space and military technology in the wake of the two successful 1957 launches of Sputnik satellites, there was little doubt that in translating technological advancement into domestic products the United States occupied a position of strength and confidence.
Despite conflicting attitudes in the United States toward consumption and obsolescence, proponents of good design and the products of mass culture in the later 1950s could both promote design in terms that equated technology, leisure, and material prosperity with the achievement of democratic ideals under capitalism.
In a climate of free markets, investment in European industrial production, and international commerce, differences regarding consumption seem more a matter of taste than of ethics, as outlined by journalist Russell Lynes.
Lynes observed in his 1949 essay titled Highbrow, Middlebrow, Lowbrow that American society could be divided into the three broad social and cultural groupings of the articles title, each identified not primarily by wealth or family background, but by lifestyle and consumer behavior, that is, the goods and services they chose to purchase, the clothing they wore, the furniture with which they decorated their homes, the music they listened to, and the magazines they read.
Lyness categories have become part of our general twentieth-century cultural discourse, but the categories are not as rigid as they may first appear: according to Lynes, the three categories of taste in post-World War II America were neither monolithic nor entirely distinct: each could be divided into sub-groupings, and there were areas of overlap and fluidity among them.

## Resorts
and Luxury Together with the Detroit-manufactured automobile and the new suburban tract home (see here), popular design in post-war America was also defined by the resort hotel, first built in Miami Beach, Florida, and later in Las Vegas, Nevada.
Miami Beachs Fontainebleau, built in 1954 and named for the sixteenth-century French royal château outside of Paris, was one of several Florida beachfront hotels designed by Morris Lapidus (19022001).
Trained as an architect in New York, Lapidus had spent much of his career prior to the war as a successful designer of retail storefronts and interiors (see fig.
10.37).
Post-war affluence and paid vacations expanded the market for travel and leisure, marketed through television, film, and photograph-filled monthly travel magazines such as Holiday.
Investment in travel and tourism provided Lapidus with the opportunity to design on a larger and more lavish scale, and to indulge the popular middle-brow imagination for drama, escape, fantasy, and luxury gleaned from both the past and from a popular vision of a glamorous and indulgent future.
Lapiduss resort hotels often displayed sweeping curves and recurves, for instance in the opposition of entranceway and façade at the Fontainebleau (fig.
12.9).
Curving hallways rather than the repetitive axial rhythm of doorways and hall-lights created a sense of anticipation for the guest.
Mezzanines, grand staircases, suspended ceilings with circular holes for chandeliers, and support beams hidden beneath sheathings of wood and textured materials were closer in experience to movie sets than to reception areas.
In art historical terms, Lapiduss designs tended toward the openness and grandeur of the Italian Baroque, and seemed to reduce the barrier separating Hollywood from the experience of Eastern or Midwestern snowbirds escaping cold winters for a week of vacation at the beach.
Many of Lapiduss ideas derived from the expressive possibilities of shaping modern reinforced concrete.
He admired the experimental architecture of German architect Erich Mendelsohn (18871953) and the organic forms and recesses of Surrealist art.
Yet his hotels also featured imaginative if eclectic decoration drawn from eighteenth-century French furniture and Italian Renaissance architecture, as in the coffee shop at the Fontainebleau from 1954 and the Mona Lisa room at the Eden Roc, also in Miami Beach and built in 1956 (figs.
12.10 and 12.11).
It is no surprise that, paraphrasing Raymond Loewys Never Leave Well Enough Alone, Lapidus entitled his own 1996 autobiography Too Much is Never Enough.
The variety of Lapiduss conceptions, intended to satisfy his clients and appeal to the aspirations and fantasies of the hotels clientele, characterized a both ... and rather than either ... or attitude toward design that fueled desire and the promise of upward mobility.
It was this broad eclecticism that was often criticized at the time for its commercialism and lack of discrimination between architecture and amusement parks, but later in his long career Lapidus began to gain critical acceptance for his imagination and sense of playfulness and fun.
However indulgent or escapist, Lapiduss ideal of luxury gave to the many a glimpse of what they believed to have been the entitlement of the privileged, if only for a week or even a weekend.
And if not experienced directly, the version of luxury embodied in the Fontainebleau and elsewhere was experienced vicariously in film, on television, or by armchair travelers leafing through the features and advertisements in Holiday.
12.9 12.10 Morris Lapidus, coffee shop, Fontainebleau Hotel, Miami Beach, Florida, 1954.
Morris Lapidus, garden façade, Fontainebleau Hotel, Miami Beach, Florida, 1954.
It is hardly surprising that one of Lapiduss sources of inspiration for luxury interiors was France.
Following a trip to France in the mid-1950s, Lapidus commissioned dozens of copies of oil paintings after masterpieces in the Louvre, and even the name Eden Roc was inspired by a resort at Cap dAntibes on the French Riviera.
Indeed, the post-war period witnessed the resurgence of the association of France with the most cultivated tastes, particularly in regard to high fashion and especially with the success of French couture designers such as Christian Dior (19051957), Pierre Balmain (19141982), and Hubert de Givenchy (19272018; fig.
12.12), or designers working in France such as Spaniard Cristóbal Balenciaga (18951972).
These couturiers cultivated an international reputation for elegance and the highest levels of craft and individual creativity seen earlier in French fashion, furniture, and the decorative arts from the period before and after World War I.
Through commerce, travel, and support from a national organization that cultivated and protected an image of refined luxury (the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture), fashion contributed to Frances economic recovery after World War II.
Exclusive, haute-couture fashion and fashion designers came to the attention of a wider international audience through the medium of cinema, through more casual or ready-to-wear variations by American designers such as Mollie Parnis (18991992), as well as via photography published in art-directed magazines such as Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar (see fig.
11.21).
The mass media created a cult of celebrity around movie stars, whose images provided models of ideal beauty.
An example is film star Audrey Hepburn (19291993), known for her connection to fashion designer Hubert de Givenchy.
The haute-couture fashions of this period were varied and individuality was essential to the aura of the designer.
But in general, a fuller look for eveningwear and daywear represented the first reaction against the austerity and severity of the square-shouldered war years.
Called the New Look by the editor of Harper’s Bazaar in 1947, post-war high fashion called attention, through ample use of fabric and contrasts between slim waistlines and full skirts and bodices, to an ideal of sensuality in the female form.
Dior compared his creations to flowers, with stemlike waists and flowing, petal-like skirts.
The hourglass was another frequent metaphor for many post-war New Look fashions (see fig.
11.21).
Continuity with the past also figured through photography in travel magazines that featured masterpieces from the Louvre or views of French Gothic cathedrals, palaces, and châteaux.
Hubert de Givenchy with model, 1952, photograph reprinted in New Yorker, February 19, 1996.
The sensory excitement of Lapiduss Miami Beach resort hotels, heightened by neon lights and the added lure of gaming tables and slot machines in resort areas such as Las Vegas, was captured by Tom Wolfe (19312018) in articles published first in Esquire in the early 1960s and in book form as The Kandy-Kolored Tangerine-Flake Streamline Baby in 1963.
Wolfe likened the glitz and provocative sexuality of the Las Vegas strip to a garden of earthly delights for the senses above which humanity rarely rises.
Indeed, modern popular culture offered almost unlimited outlets for sensual pleasure, amplified through technology, available in fashion and vicariously through the cinema and magazines, or in reality through the vacation resort, and more accessible than in the past.
These included movies in Technicolor for the eyes, stereo sound for the ears, processed foods for the palette, just to name a few.
Like Russell Lyness observations on taste and even earlier than Tom Wolfe in the United States, British journalist and critic Reyner Banham (19221988) questioned the elitism and paternalistic overtones of good design in a series of articles written for newspapers and periodicals.
Banham recognized the appeal of mass cultures combination of fantasy, escapism, and healthy bottom-up expression of the popular will in an abundant consumer culture dominated by large multinational industrial corporations rather than individual producers.
Such attitudes also help to account for the emergence of Pop Art both in Britain and in the United States, in part as a reaction to personal sacrifice and the stoicism of British design and the elitism and esoteric tendencies of avant-garde art.
When Richard Hamilton (19222011) and Eduardo Paolozzi (19242005) created collages such as Hamiltons Just what is it that makes today’s homes so dif erent, so appealing?
(1956; fig.
12.13), appropriating photographs and illustrations directly from American mass-circulation magazines, the images were less an indictment of materialism and commercialism than a celebration of the pleasures (however ephemeral) of the senses, a time-honored theme of the fine arts in earlier eras when the arts were indeed more approachable in still lifes and scenes of taverns and banquets.
Hamiltons collage might be compared with Herbert Bayers 1959 advertisement for the Container Corporation of America (see fig.
11.74).
Richard Hamilton, Just what is it that makes today’s homes so different, so appealing?, collage, 10 <sup>1</sup>/ × 9 <sup>3</sup>/ in (27 × 25 cm), 1956.
Kunsthalle, Tübingen.

## Housing:
Suburbia, Domesticity, and Conformity Automobile styling under Earl and Exner in the United States was contemporary with the transformation of the housing construction industry and emerging patterns of life in large suburban developments.
New approaches to home building were a response to a severe housing shortage for returning veterans coupled with slow growth in housing starts during the Depression.
The elastic markets for housing and automobiles after the war were not unrelated.
Indeed the growth of new suburban communities, constructed on inexpensive tracts of land located further from commuter rail lines, increased dependence upon the automobile and the need for new multi-lane highways for commuting to the workplace.
They also account for the commercial success of new sprawling shopping centers and malls, designed to bring dozens of businesses together in an area built with abundant parking space.
In fact, both industries supported and even lobbied successfully for a government-funded interstate highway system.
Also contributing to the success of the suburban development was the ease of obtaining federally sponsored low-interest mortgage loans from government agencies such as the Veterans Administration (VA) and the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), encouraging young couples and families to purchase new homes rather than rent apartments in inner cities.
Builder William Levitt pioneered mass-production techniques in the housing industry after World War II in Levittown communities located in suburban New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania.
Using pre-assembled parts and teams of specialized workers, each repeating a particular task in a rationalized approach to the home building process, Levitt became the Henry Ford of the housing industry.
Houses were built in less than six weeks on inexpensively purchased land beyond the limits of urban centers, and in communities with as many as 17,000 new houses, suburbia began to come into focus.
Levitts houses were built on concrete slabs rather than on foundations with basements, and his construction process quickly became the industry standard due to the affordability of the units, which began as low as \$7,000.
In addition, buyers could purchase homes with as little as a one-dollar down payment and federally guaranteed mortgages at low interest that minimized the builders risk.
Post-war housing in the United States differed significantly from its European counterparts.
Whereas dense, efficient, and uniform apartments after World War II were the norm in communities within or outside of many large European cities, in the United States new building materials, inexpensive land, and mass-production techniques reinforced traditional associations between property ownership, independence, and security.
Individual home ownership implied stability and permanence, linked in the popular imagination with self-sufficiency and levels of comfort formerly available only to wealthier Americans.
In lowering the economic threshold for ownership, the singlefamily home became a realizable part of the American dream for the working and middle classes, and was a clear measure of technological, economic and social progress in comparison with the rental apartments and narrow row-houses in which many new homeowners had grown up.

Among the most common was the so-called Cape Cod style, rectangular in shape with a pitched roof sloping toward the front (fig.
12.14).
Buyers were attracted to the new suburban homes by modern practical features intended to make life more convenient and efficient.
Kitchens featured picture windows to allow parents to watch their children play in the yard, and attached garages kept automobiles off the street and allowed direct entry into the home.
The attraction of individual home ownership and the added convenience of appliances such as washing machines and even television sets, often included in the selling price, seemed to outweigh the conformity often noted by critics.
Author Lewis Mumford (18951990) was one such critic, who saw few advantages to the post-war suburb in comparison with its more idyllic, villagelike or garden city predecessors, predicting negative consequences should the trend continue: The ultimate outcome of the suburbs alienation from the city became visible only in the twentieth century, with the extension of the democratic ideal through the instrumentalities of manifolding and mass production.
In the mass movement into suburban areas a new kind of community was produced, which caricatured both the historic city and the archetypal suburban refuge: a multitude of uniform, unidentifiable houses, lined up inflexibly, at uniform distances, on uniform roads, in a treeless communal waste, inhabited by people of the same class, the same income, the same tasteless pre-fabricated foods, from the same freezers, conforming in every outward and inward respect to a common mold, manufactured in the central metropolis.
Thus the ultimate effect of the suburban escape in our time is ironically, a low-grade uniform environment from which escape is impossible.
What has happened to the suburban exodus in the United States now threatens, through the same mechanical instrumentalities, to take place, at an equally accelerating rate, everywhere else.
The identification of home ownership with the lifestyle of the average family was normalized in the emerging television industry.
Television families, such as the Nelsons of Ozzie and Harriet or the Cleavers of Leave It to Beaver, owned modern homes in suburban communities.
Notable exceptions were the childless Cramdens of The Honeymooners, who suffered renters frustrations of noise and lack of privacy found in urban apartment houses, or the family of nightclub entertainer Danny Thomas.
Thomass career required that his own precocious children live in a spacious Manhattan apartment dominated by adults rather than by other children.
While weekly entertainment shows such as the Sunday evening Ed Sullivan Show might feature Black entertainers, the casts and characters of weekly sitcoms were almost invariably white, with Black people generally cast in familiar stereotypes as cooks, servants, or dutiful companions.
While cracks in the color barrier were more prevalent in the fields of entertainment, music, and professional sports, racial discrimination continued to dominate the fields of business, including advertising and the design professions.
I recall a story in my grade-school reader from the later 1950s.
In this illustrated story the child of a young family who recently moved into a new subdivision is troubled by an inability to distinguish his own home from the others on his block.
The problem is solved when each family creates its own weathervane to add character and individual identity to otherwise bland and uniform surroundings as critiqued by Mumford and others.
The housing industry also offered solutions to the practical as well as social desire for differentiation in the market.
Attracting new buyers from the city to the suburb or encouraging suburbanites to trade up during the 1950s led to an expansion of the range of housing types, featuring much inventiveness in introducing variations and choices available for consumers to exercise taste and customize their purchase.
In addition to the standard Cape Cod home, builders began to include a wider variety of traditional types such as Colonial or Tudor, as well as modern Ranch models.
The last included large expanses of windows and low single-story designs, or a split level with half-stories to either side of a central entrance (fig.
12.15).
Informal family rooms and eat-in kitchens became ways to expand living space and move beyond basic housing needs toward comfort and entertaining guests.
12.15 Feature on prefabricated homes from Better Homes and Gardens, August 1954.
The reduction of standardization in interior design and decoration resulted from new industrial materials whose potential for variation was exploited by manufacturers.
Examples include Formica, a hard plastic available in a variety of patterns for use in kitchen surfaces to replace enameled metal or stainless steel, and Linoleum, a softer surface used for flooring in kitchens and recreation rooms.
The more colorful and textured effects of Formica and Linoleum, as well as Naugahyde upholstery, made the kitchen less of a laboratory or labor-saving workplace than a room for leisure and relaxation.
The reduction of toil was to a great degree supported by advertising, in which appliances such as dishwashers as well as household cleaning products were viewed as improvements bringing new quantities of freedom and leisure.
Fashionably dressed housewives were generally pictured along with the dishwasher or new dinette, marveling at the ease of loading the new appliance, admiring the sparkling cleanliness of the glassware, or enjoying time with family members (fig.
12.16).
Comfort found expression less in the plywood and pedestal-based Eames lounge chair than in the more massive and heavily upholstered reclining chair known as the La-Z-boy or variations such as the Barcalounger and Stratolounger (fig.
12.17).
The La-Z-boy derived from cushioned railway cars.
Advertisements focused upon the variety of available fabrics and upholstery styles from which the buyer could choose, as well as upon the relaxed (mostly male and, again, always white) occupant resting after a long day at the office.
The world of childrens leisure was filled with a never-ending array of ephemeral fads and toys available at the corner drug store and soda fountain in city neighborhoods or at the suburban mall, from spinning tops to butterfly yo-yos, hoola-hoops and frisbees, creating a market that is today augmented by an endless number of phone apps, puzzles, and videogames, all requiring the considerable contributions of a new generation of designers with a wide variety of increasingly computer-based skills that appeal to consumers and provide new opportunities for making use of leisure time.
Advertisement, refrigerator, manufactured by Frigidaire Corporation, Dayton, Ohio, Good Housekeeping, January, 1950.
12.17 Advertisement, Barcalounger lounge chair with Naugahyde vinyl upholstery, manufactured by U.S.
Naugahyde, Better Homes and Gardens, June, 1951.
Aluminum was another industrial material that appeared in domestic production and was successfully marketed in the 1950s in an effort to maintain wartime production levels.
The Alcoa Aluminum Company advertised creative uses of aluminum in masscirculation magazines as part of a forecasting program called imagineering. One of the more popular products to emerge was sets of anodized aluminum tumblers in rainbow colors manufactured as Heller Hostess ware (fig.
12.18).
Lightweight and certainly unbreakable, aluminum drinking cups were easily dented, especially around the lip, and their uniform weight created a high center of gravity that made them tip over easily when filled.
Despite such shortcomings, the festive colors, low cost, novelty, and associations with the informality of outdoor picnics and barbecues helped to make aluminum tumblers commercially successful.
Such products might be contrasted with the use of heavier and more sober or natural stainless steel in Scandinavian dinnerware of the same period, characterized by a plain metallic finish and used for serving rather than eating or drinking (fig.
12.19).
Another example of imagineering in the 1950s was the lightweight, portable and tubular folding aluminum chair (first developed for seating in the aircraft industry) with plastic webbing (fig.
12.20).
There was nothing durable or particularly ergonomic about this anonymous outdoor chair.
Unstable if placed on uneven ground and irreparable when the supporting skids bent or the plastic webbing was torn or detached from the rivets that held it to the frame, the chairs were and remain the kind of expendable, replaceable, and anonymous everyday product characteristic of mass culture, a paradigm of Banhams Throwaway Culture and a mainstay of our designed world.
The ephemeral nature of such designs and other fads contrasted with the tenets of good design, where research provided enduring solutions to problems or individual creativity contributed to an added, elevated aesthetic awareness.
While museums and international exhibitions seemed to favor the latter over the former, it was perhaps popular design that better illustrated the realities of design in the post-war economy on a mass scale.
Whether new products or variations of existing ones, design served to stimulate desire as part of an interdependent dialogue with advertising and branding strategies while sustaining ever-increasing levels of production.
