The increased availability and popularity of nationally branded packaged and processed foods was another component of post-war mass culture, a further instance of the equation between leisure with progress.
Instead of baking from scratch, cake mixes included pre-measured ingredients to enable housewives to perform instant miracles in the kitchen.
Endorsed by the matronly Betty Crocker, a creation of the women employed by the home services department at General Mills in 1921, the companys immensely popular Betty Crocker cookbook helped to preserve the comforting sense of pride in being a traditional homemaker (fig.
12.21).
As American studies scholar Karal Ann Marling relates, consultants to the General Mills Corporation (who manufactured and sold baking products) recommended that recipes call for using real eggs in cake mixes rather than powdered eggs to enable housewives to make a creative contribution to the process. This combination of new goods with reassuring values of home and family is a characteristic often found in the products of mass culture.
Processed foods such as cake mixes and TV dinners were modern in their accommodation to contemporary lifestyles, and also in their adaptation of the technology of dehydration and packaging used in the preparation and manufacture of meals for servicemen during World War II.
The conflicting desires for both increased convenience and ease along with the satisfaction of being a responsible homemaker are thus reconciled.
Packaged foods exemplify a shift from the commodity itself to the psychological motivation for its purchase, that is, from production to consumption.
Packaging, from toothpaste to dishwashing liquids, was often bright and festive, with lettering in different colors and in different alignments, a playful, even carefree accent to bathroom or kitchen.
Other products meant to reduce toil and encourage impulse buying included Jiffy popcorn, where the aluminum-foil fry pan itself could be disposed of after being used on top of the stove, and synthetic fabrics such as Dacron Permapress, which eliminated the need for ironing.
12.21 Advertisement for Betty Crocker products manufactured by General Mills Corporation, from Better Homes and Gardens, December, 1954.
While advertising outlined an array of products for improved living, and shopping occupied more newly found leisure time, some housewives found the conveniences of modern domestic life problematic.
Dissatisfaction with the suburban lifestyle and the ways in which it defined fulfillment found expression in Betty Friedans The Feminine Mystique (1963), an outgrowth of the authors experience as a mother and housewife in the 1950s.
Following the end of World War II, hundreds of thousands of women were displaced from jobs by returning soldiers and found little opportunity to resume or begin careers.
Mass media, in the form of womens magazines such as Ladies’ Home Journal, McCalls, and Redbook, as well as most network television housewives, encouraged women to focus their energies upon the home, defining their role primarily as consumers and caretakers while husbands went off to work.
Friedans experience demonstrated that the patterns of post-war suburban living and the ideals of beauty, comfort, luxury, and well-being advertised in magazines and on television did not always provide satisfaction for women outside a range of activities some found unrewarding.
It is no wonder that surveys conducted at the time indicated less satisfaction with suburban life among women in comparison with men.
In addition to the conformity described above, other issues involving design arose during the post-war suburban housing boom that conflicted with the idealized images and narratives presented through the mass media and advertising.
Particularly in the United States, Black Americans and other minorities were conspicuously absent from these new suburban neighborhoods and their television and advertising counterparts.
Historians of the period such as Kenneth Jackson have noted that in addition to the uniformity implied by mass production and standardization, suburban housing communities tended to produce racial as well as economic homogeneity.
This occurred particularly through zoning laws that inhibited industrial building and prevented housing construction for lower-income families, as well as overt policies by builders that prohibited access to Black buyers.
The process of redlining meant that banks deemed Black or racially diverse neighborhoods an unwise investment and would not issue mortgages for properties in those areas.
At the same time increasing numbers of Black families continued their migration from the rural South to the industrial North, seeking to escape Jim Crow laws, obtain a better education and higher-paying jobs, or start a new life following service in the armed forces during the war.
Equating American life with its image in advertising and through the mass media presents a limited, flawed picture that masks racial and gender inequality as well as revealing white privilege.
As in much of Western Europe, the seeds that blossomed into protest, activism, legislative reform, and ethically directed design in the 1960s were planted in the immediate post-war period.
Other critics have argued that the link between technology, consumer goods, and an improving standard of living not only masked racial or gender discrimination, but also brought into light the connection between technology and the Cold War arms race, arguing that the focus upon peacetime consumption and affluence diverted public attention from an unsettling alliance between big business and government in contracts for military hardware and information technology.
This alliance in turn concentrated power in both capital and in government, in effect an arms race that brought with it the potential for the outbreak of international conflict and fears of a cold war turning hot. Such tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union emerged in the capture of an American pilot in 1960 (the subject of the 2015 film Bridge of Spies that chronicled negotiations for his return in exchange for a captured Soviet spy), or the failed American invasion of communist Cuba in 1961.
The threat of hard rather than soft power raised ethical questions for some designers concerning their own relationship to industry, government, and the role of the designer in society.
These issues are treated in Part VI.
Throughout the first two decades of the post-war period, a number of writers and critics condemned virtually every manifestation of the emerging mass culture and mass media on political, ethical, and aesthetic grounds.
Most of this strain of criticism was based upon the views of an educated and sophisticated elite seeking to universalize a set of criteria that itself preserved and extended a reform-minded design discourse inherited from the very beginnings of industrialization and concerns about class conflict.
Much criticism adopted a polemical tone and dismissive treatment of its target.
In part this was a response to the exaggerated claims of early advertising as well as to the control of media and propaganda by fascist regimes during the 1930s and 1940s.
Common to both charges was the belief that the essentially passive masses could be easily manipulated with false narratives and promises.
Fears of the dangers of relativism (at the aesthetic or ethical level) may be sensed in the remarks of Robert Hutchins, president of the University of Chicago, in 1940: In order to believe in democracy we must believe that there is a difference between truth and falsity, good and bad, right and wrong, and that truth, goodness, and right are objective standards even though they cannot be experimentally verified....
Political organization must be tested by conformity to ideals.
Its basis is moral.
Its end is the good for man....
These are the principles which we must defend if we are to defend democracy.
Are we prepared to defend these principles?
Of course not.
For forty years and more our intellectual leaders have been telling us they are not true.
They have been telling us in fact that nothing is true which cannot be subject to experimental verification.
In the whole realm of social thought there can, therefore, be nothing but opinion.
Since there is nothing but opinion, everybody is entitled to his own opinion....
If everything is a matter of opinion, force becomes the only way of settling differences of opinion.
And, of course, if success is the test of rightness, right is on the side of the heavier battalions.
In 1957 consumer manipulation was the subject of a popular, sensationalist book by Vance Packard entitled The Hidden Persuaders.
The book brought to light sophisticated psychological techniques and motivational analysis by market researchers as well as advertising used to sell products to consumers.
Packards analysis emphasized the role of insecurity in the promotion of consumption, for instance in the need for men to feel masculine being met by cigarettes or aftershave lotions in a society where insecurity and conformity dictated the patterns and frustrations of everyday life.
Packard quoted extensively from advertising executives and marketing consultants, using the terms motivational research (abbreviated as MR in the book) and depth analysis as labels for the persuasive techniques of selling derived from psychological surveys of consumers.
Packard concluded that what motivates people to buy is not need but rather a desire to feel better about themselves.
He was alarmed that such techniques of persuasion were being used not only for consumer goods but also in the political arena, and feared the consequences.
Basic to Packards rhetoric is the manipulation of the publics irresistible unconscious urges by advertisers, what at times amounts to a big-business conspiracy.
The Hidden Persuaders saw advertising techniques as dehumanizing, suggesting that they were not benign, and might be used to program our actions and thoughts: What the probers are looking for, of course, are the whys of our behavior, so that they can more effectively manipulate our habits and choices in their favor.
This had led them to probe why we are afraid of banks; why we love those big fat cars; why housewives typically fall into a hypnoidal trance when they get into a supermarket; why men are drawn into auto showrooms by convertibles but end up buying sedans; why junior loves cereal that pops, snaps, and crackles.
We move from the genial world of James Thurber into the chilling world of George Orwell and his Big Brother, however, as we explore some of the extreme attempts at probing and manipulating now going on.
The criticism of mass culture was equally severe in Western European Marxist circles.
Here issues of taste were combined with bitter disappointment and disillusionment at the subversion of techniques of mass production and mass communication first by autocratic fascist regimes in the interwar period and then after the war by capitalist enterprise and the fetishization of commodities rather than for the attainment of more enlightened progressive egalitarian ends.
Part of the historical critique of capitalism in general focuses upon the need for large corporations to reap a return on their investment by guaranteeing a market for products of mechanized mass production through seductive advertising and marketing techniques.
The result is the combination of design change and mass advertising that magnifies the symbolism of the product in a process often referred to as commodification or reification.
While recognizing the much larger scale of mechanized mass production in the mid-twentieth century, the process nevertheless recalls the role of commodities as criticized by design reformers in Victorian England or social critics in turn-of-the-century America.
German critic Theodor Adorno (19031969), for instance, used the term culture industry to refer to the methods of mass media and the capitalist control of the means of production that underwrote the system of entertainment and related industries.
By equating culture with leisure there was a tendency to devalue and corrupt the entire enterprise of design under capitalism.
In this view consumption is the reward of compliance within a system so pervasive as to eradicate even awareness of its power to compromise and subvert individual freedom.
Such circumstances offer no escape aside from revolution or the pursuit of an alternative lifestyle akin perhaps to the Arts and Crafts communities of the late nineteenth century and their rejection of industrial society.
More recently the views of Adorno and other critics have been seen as being based upon a narrow understanding of mass culture, one which presupposes a monolithic cultural homogeneity and an elitist view of the ethics of taste.
Students of mass culture argue persuasively that even allowing for the manipulative, dehumanizing, and alienating associations decried by critics, the phenomenon of popular design produces a richness and complexity that earlier authors were too willing to dismiss.
As a result the facile dualism of many critics, so essential to the storied history of Modernist art and design, appears less tenable.
The appreciation of mass culture is based upon a number of considerations, including a better understanding of the complex and interconnected system of production, distribution, and consumption of cultural products, as well as recognition of the various ways in which an increasingly modern and diverse audience responds to those products.
Rather than the presumed passive role for the consumer, students of mass culture suggest that the audience participates, is active in its response to the products of design  thus the product not only is created for an audience, but is also in effect created and shaped by its audience, and expresses alternative preferences and values.
One example of the rich and varied reaction to American popular culture was demonstrated during the later 1960s when it was embraced by West German youth as a form of protest against government and corporate regulation of education and politics, or the popularity of Levi-brand blue jeans in the Soviet Union in the post-World War II era as a symbol of freedom of expression.
Other observers have described and championed the sociability of mass culture, that is, the way in which it appeals to a broad audience and communicates a variety of meanings.
The Marxist critique of popular culture has lost little of its ability to illuminate the underlying structures and mechanisms at work in our daily lives as citizens and consumers in a capitalist world, even if its political motivations and revolutionary aspirations have lost some of their credibility and if angry and revolutionary motivations tended to exaggerate their authors polemical tone.
In the end it is perhaps worthwhile to keep in mind the range of responses to popular culture and the dynamic relationship between the culture industry and an expanding, diverse new audience.
The middle class found an array of invitations to consume products, react to billboards and advertising images in weekly magazines, listen to commercial radio, attend cinema, and watch television at home.
As noted by author and literary critic Clive James (1939 2019), popular culture represented a step up for the working and middle classes, though perhaps not a step toward the enlightened culture envisioned by the advocates of good design who continued to lobby for educating the public in matters of consumer taste.
Curiously, while proponents of good design defended their activities on the basis of noble aims that included the education of the masses, the fine arts generally retreated from public engagement.
Instead, the emerging New York art world sought a more rarefied atmosphere in which creativity was unfettered either by commercialism, the mass market, or the international standards of good design and its ideology of shared cultural values and social responsibility.
Influential American art critic Clement Greenberg (19091994) neatly divided the post-World War II art world into three groups.
There was the avant-garde, advocates of high art who were the guardians of individualism and originality in the arts, seeking pure abstraction and autonomy as a field of interest.
A second group consisted of practitioners of middlebrow art, who interpreted aspects of high art in more useful goods but undermined and compromised their aesthetic purity and independence.
Finally there was low (mass) art, described simply as kitsch, catering to the uneducated masses with the appeal of the traditional and debased borrowings from more authentic forms of expression.
Such hierarchical distinctions are not to be found in Russell Lyness essay on taste, relinquishing their authority in the 1960s with the growing phenomenon of Pop Art and the development of more pluralistic approaches to the study of culture.

## Conclusion
The post-war period witnessed the expansion of industrial design involving the application of wartime technology to domestic products, fueled by the United States and its investment in the reconstruction of Western European and Japanese peacetime economies through support of manufacturing and corporate free enterprise.
There was a broadening of the industrial design profession that included ergonomics, psychology, and a wider range of problem-solving skills pertaining to product development and information design.
Industrial design continued to be associated with the names of individual designers, but their activities often involved a variety of skills requiring dialogue and cooperation.
The emergence of mass communication also served to affect the design of products for an ever-increasing audience through obsolescence and product symbolism.
In the context of Cold War tensions in the later 1950s, consumption, technology, and materialism, whether motivated by aspirations of social mobility or by social responsibility, became increasingly identified in the West with democracy and freedom under a system of capitalist free enterprise.
The result was a blurring of the distinction that critics had drawn between commercial styling and the more restrained approach understood as good design. Such critical awareness tended to provide justification for the appreciation of mass culture, while at the same time raised some doubts about the benevolent association between industrial design and social and economic progress.
An appreciation of the immediate post-war era includes thinking less in terms of a dichotomy between high and low art than in terms of a continuum in which commercial, aesthetic, reformist, scientific, and technological considerations operated in varied measure.
At the same time the activity of design began to overlap into related fields of communication and information, expanding and diffusing the practice and understanding of the term.
Whether through corporate identity, complex systems for transportation, consumer products, or advertising, design was seen increasingly as an interdependent rather than an isolated, individual activity within a larger enterprise that connected designers to users through technology, products, services, and the mechanisms of distribution and sales. # Global Inspiration V Japan Japan was an especially active participant in the vibrant network of international commerce in the period from 1945 to 1960, though the nation has had a long history of designing goods for foreign markets, and Western markets have shown a fascination as well as a certain degree of kinship with particular aspects of Japanese design.
Japan was central to the history of modern design in a variety of media during the interwar period, for instance in fashion accessories as well as in advertising and the success of department stores in Tokyo and Kyoto.
Frank Lloyd Wright visited Japan in 1905 and designed the massive Imperial Hotel and furnishings in Tokyo (1913 1923) that survived the great Kanto earthquake of 1923; and Jan Tschichold illustrated a page of advertisements from a Japanese newspaper as an example of modern asymmetrical layouts in his New Typography of 1928.
During the early post-World War II period the phrase made in Japan regularly connoted cheap toys and knock-off electronic products of often inferior quality, manufactured to the specifications of foreign agents and merchandisers interested in competing in the elastic market for inexpensive goods for the mass public that lacked the reputation or quality of the original items they imitated.
Design patent infringement plagued the reception of Japanese products, eventually leading to government efforts to create design organizations and policies that emphasized a Japanese identity or version of good design that might compete for foreign markets.
In the aftermath of Japans defeat in World War II, the American occupation (19451952) meant that the Japanese people had to work for an occupying military force.
Japanese industries provided necessary housing and furniture on an industrial scale for American armed forces and administrative personnel, requiring investment (spurred through the Marshall Plan) in mechanized mass production.
In addition to these lucrative contracts, Japanese companies such as Matsushita (later Panasonic) and Nippon Columbia turned their attention to the domestic market for standardized household appliances such as sewing machines and fans.
Sori Yanagis (19152011) radio-phonograph for Nippon Columbia in 1952 (fig.
GI5.1) is an example of a modern practical approach to product design in comparison with the more self-conscious aesthetic purity of Braun products (see fig.
11.57).
The compact radio-phonograph, with a grille-like metal panel and asymmetrical placement of control knobs, won a national competition for industrial design, and Yanagis approach may owe something to his association with French designer Charlotte Perriand (see here) who visited Tokyo in 1942 to consult with Japanese manufacturers.
Beginning in 1955 the Japanese economy was growing at a rate of 10 percent each year and evidence of economic progress was measured in the availability of affordable industrially designed products for the home, named the 3 $\mathrm { C s } { : } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$ color televisions, air conditioners, and cars.
The national market for consumer products also included ready-to-wear clothing, and industrial design celebrity Raymond Loewy was invited to Japan in 1951 to judge a fashion show.

M+, Hong Kong.
Akio Morita, founder of the Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation that later became Sony, pioneered portable electronic products in Japan, purchasing the technology for transistors from the American corporation Western Bell Laboratories in 1953.
Morita initiated Sonys production of inexpensive pocket radios for the domestic market, with round-edged plastic housing (fig.
GI5.2).
Signal and volume controls operated by turning crenellated disks that barely protruded to one side of the housing.
The station read-out was barely visible, the range of stations limited, the sound quality poor, and in general little attention was paid to usability that industrial designers were exploring at Braun, Philips, and elsewhere in the electronics industry.
Yet at the time there was little competition for affordable transistor radios whose portability satisfied a desire for entertainment while on the go, particularly among an underserved youth market who made up in numbers what they may have lacked in purchasing power.
Economist Clayton Christensen (b.
1952) cited the Sony transistor radio as an example of a disruptive technology, achieving success and recognition at the lower end of the market ignored by competing manufacturers who devoted more attention to aestheticor performance-based criteria.
However, improvements in these areas (such as a more legible read-out and better speakers) bolstered Sonys reputation for industrial design internationally.
This extended to the more expensive and highly coveted portable television sets, also initially manufactured and promoted for the domestic market.
Sonys portable electronics began to receive attention at international exhibitions including the Milan Triennale and the 1958 Worlds Fair in Brussels.
The Japanese reputation for affordable electronic products internationally continued with the Sony Walkman personal tape player in the 1970s.
What began as a disruptive technology at the low end of the market achieved increasing success internationally and critically as greater attention was paid to subtle design consideration and as its audience moved upmarket.

With government support, Japanese manufacturers began to make a conscious, pragmatic effort to enter the export market for the more sophisticated products of good design, focusing upon electronic communications, motor scooters and motorcycles, cameras, and eventually fashion design, ceramics, and furniture.
Through sponsored prizes for original products of industrial design, manufacturers were encouraged to hire designers and discouraged from pirating the original designs of other countries.
The role of government agencies in the success of Japanese industrial design emerges as a feature of the countrys post-war development, contemporary with similarly sponsored efforts in Britain, Italy, and Germany.
The Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), the Good Design Selection System, the Design Promotion Organization, and the Japan Design House are only the most well known of the agencies responsible for establishing standards for export products, for developing markets for Japanese goods, for promoting design through conferences and competitions, for integrating design as an element within corporate organization, and for helping to sustain a system for design education.
The results of this approach went beyond a particular style for Japanese products; rather, identity emerged through absorbing and building upon characteristics of practicality, individualism, human factors, and Indigenous craft traditions, as well as continual technological innovation in the design of modern appliances and electronic products with broad international market appeal.
Nikon SP camera, metal, $3 \% \times 5 \% \times 1$ <sup>5</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (8 × 14.3 × 4 cm), Nikon Inc., 1957.
Ernst Leitz, Leica M3 camera, injection-mold aluminum, brass, $5 ^ { 2 } / _ { 5 } \times 3 \times 1 ^ { 5 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in $( 1 3 .
8 \times 7 .
7 \times 3 .
4$ cm), Wetslar, Germany, 1954.
Japanese companies Nikon and Canon successfully competed internationally with high-end German counterparts such as Hasselblad and Leica in high-quality professional photographic equipment through refinements in design that appealed to the educated user.
Nikons 1957 compact SP single-lens reflex (SLR) camera (fig.
GI5.3) featured a wider horizontal viewing window than comparable models such as the Leica M3 of 1954 (fig.
GI5.4), demonstrating careful understanding of user requirements for the highly technical and specialized professional equipment.
Graphic designers also contributed to the branding of Nikon and Canon with clever identity systems that included distinctive logos and typographic sophistication consistent with the methods of the International Typographic School.
An example is Japanese designer Kenji Itohs 1954 poster for Canon Camera (fig.
GI5.5) that features the C corporate symbol that becomes a metaphor for a single-reflex camera lens and shutter as well as a human eye.
The reputation for Japanese 35mm photographic equipment later extended to the non-professional photographer via increased automation and mass-media marketing and advertising.
GI5.5 Kenji Itoh, poster for Canon Camera, silkscreen, 40 ½ × 28 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (102.9 × 72.6 cm), 1954.
Collection of Kenji Itoh.
The image of Japanese design for the home included points of contact with good design internationally, in particular open, flexible plans for interiors based upon modular units of space, large expanses of glass that permitted a closer relationship between interior and exterior, the use of tatami mats on floors, and a sparing use of simply constructed furniture.
These characteristics were presented as innately Japanese, drawing upon historical precedent.
Such is the case for the Japanese House that was sent from Japan to New Yorks Museum of Modern Art for display in the museums sculpture garden in 1954 and 1955 (fig.
GI5.6).
The house bears a close relationship to a seventeenth-century aristocratic residential complex in Shiga (Kojoin Kyakuden) but is less an attempt at historical accuracy than an effort to emphasize those particular elements of the architecture that bolster the view expressed by curator Arthur Drexler: A Japanese building was chosen ... because traditional Japanese design has a unique relationship to modern western architecture. GI5.6 Interior, Japanese House and Garden, 1954–1955.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
References to Japanese architecture can be seen in the Butterfly stool designed by Sori Yanagi for the Tendo Mokko company in 1956, constructed of two identical curved molded plywood pieces easily assembled by a metal rod (fig.
GI5.7).
The plywood technology was developed first in connection with industrial and wartime production for containers and aircraft requiring exact measurements, but later was used extensively in furniture primarily for public buildings as part of urban reconstruction after World War II.
Yanagis stool has been compared to the roofline of Japanese buildings, but the abstract contour also recalls the fluid brushstrokes of Japanese calligraphy as well as modern abstract sculpture.
GI5.7 Sori Yanagi, Butterfly stool, plywood and metal, 15 1 $^ 1 / _ { 1 6 } \times 1 6 ^ { 9 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 1 2 ^ { 3 } / _ { 1 6 }$ in (40 × 42 × 31 cm), manufactured by Tendo Mokko, Tendo, 1956.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
The beauty of natural materials, sensitive craftsmanship, original designs, and simple construction also characterizes the furniture of designer George Nakashima (1905 1990).
Nakashima was born in the United States but worked in Japan for an architectural firm after completing studies in architecture at MIT.
After World War II (during which he spent a year in an internment camp for Japanese Americans), Nakashima established a workshop for making his own furniture in the small town of New Hope, Pennsylvania (1946).
His Conoid Bench with back from 1961 (fig.
GI5.8) preserves the irregular beauty of natural forms often combined with slightly irregular and uneven dowel-like supports or rails for chair backs.
Nakashimas oeuvre relies upon a balance of modern and traditional approaches to furniture design.
Although a small number of early designs for chairs were manufactured by Knoll, Nakashima preferred workshop production and direct contact between craftsmen, materials, and processes.
The quiet beauty of his designs may also be appreciated in the bedroom furniture for the Japanese House built on the grounds of the Bloedel Nature Reserve on Bainbridge Island in Washington State in 1961.
Set in natural surroundings, the house and furnishings provide a refuge and sanctuary from the nearby city of Seattle.
Nakashimas approach to craft emphasized the workmans partnership with materials as related to Zen Buddhist philosophy and the connection between animate and inanimate nature.
George Nakashima, Conoid Bench, walnut, 32 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 84 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (82.6 × 214.6 cm), Nakashima Studios, New Hope, Pennsylvania, 1961.
The policies initiated through MITI and other design organizations in Japan revitalized the Japanese economy, raising the income level and standard of living at home, and establishing a reputation for quality, efficiency, affordability, technological improvement, and aesthetic refinement abroad.
At the same time the products of Japanese industrial design made personal electronic products a virtually ubiquitious accessory to a modern, mobile, active lifestyle, from transistor radios and portable television sets in the 1950s to pocket calculators and Sony Walkmen in the 1960s and 1970s, karaoke in the 1980s, and compact disk players (the Sony Discman) in the 1990s, all before the advent of streaming.
The 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games offered a showcase for Japanese design and featured a carefully constructed graphic identity including a series of pictograms as well as a logo that incorporated the Japanese flag with the five rings of the Olympic symbol that linked Japan to the international community.
And, as seen below, in transportation fuel-efficient and economical Japanese automobiles gained a foothold in the lower end of the American market in the 1970s amid rising gasoline prices (see here), making Honda, Mazda, and Nissan (then Datsun) household brands.
Whether at the high or more accessible end of the market, Japanese design triumphed after World War II domestically and internationally, accompanying economic recovery and growth.
As elsewhere in this survey of the period, the carefully cultivated image of Japanese design for the international market masked alternative approaches at home that included resentment of Japans close alignment with the continued US military presence, and an emerging counterculture movement that questioned the alliance between business and government and used design, primarily graphic design, to work outside of the aesthetic and political parameters of the mainstream professional design community.

## VI
Progress, Protest, Pluralism, and Responsibility (1961– 2020) ulfilling the promise of the partnership between technology and progress through design in the post-war period has proven to be a challenging, often elusive goal.
The ethical, racial, economic, and political tensions that erupted during the turbulent 1960s continued to be felt if not intensified in the third millennium.
Among the challenges facing designers today are our relationship to the environment and climate, not only affecting the development and choice of materials for manufactured goods, but also impacting international relations and the scale of concerns for global health and safety.
The specter of terrorism in the wake of the attacks of September 11, 2001, resulting wars, and displacement continue to threaten the safety, security, and freedom of movement we take for granted and often view as the bedrock of our confidence in shaping a progressive and inclusive global future.
Combating terrorism results in stronger degrees of vigilance and raises ethical and legal questions about the balance between surveillance and privacy.
Accompanying these third-millennium concerns has been the rise of nationalism, protectionism, and authoritarian regimes that replace pluralism and dialogue with xenophobia, polarization, and tense international relations.
While it is difficult to assess the effects of climate change, terrorism, and counterterrorism upon the design enterprise, a renewal of efforts by ethically motivated designers has been one recent development, along with continued innovation in digital devices, fashion, and related products.
Global health during the COVID-19 crisis engaged designers in meeting the needs of healthcare professionals with shortages of protective equipment and the monitoring of policies that assessed information and helped to ensure public safety, part of a coordinated, multi-disciplinary, and multinational effort to save lives.
Whether infected or not, citizens relied upon information designers’ timely interactive charts and graphs to track the virus and inform decisions by both governments and individuals regarding appropriate actions and behaviors to reduce cases and deaths while efforts to develop and distribute vaccines took shape.
While pharmaceutical companies and the medical community of front-line doctors and nurses took the lead in confronting the pandemic, in its broadest sense, that is, “changing existing conditions into preferred ones,” designers contributed but did not own change in fields as complex as healthcare, involving myriad stakeholders.
Amid the complexities and challenges involved in shaping our individual and collective futures, opportunities for designers have never been broader nor more urgent than at the present time.
Food processors, microwave ovens, compact disks, personal and handheld computers, MP3 players, interactive videogames, cellular phones, digital imaging, and global positioning systems and devices (GPS) are only the most obvious examples of technologies impacting contemporary lifestyles over the past 60 years, extending the range of our powers and redefining the relationship between the human and the artificial in the industrially developed nations of the world.
Personal computers and the Internet have not only stimulated the marketing and merchandising of these and countless other products, but also have expanded the sphere of design activity that encompasses all fields of information and communication.
The growth of the Internet is a clear indication of an emerging postindustrial age in which information, intellectual property, and a wide range of human services, including e-commerce and sophisticated target marketing, are increasingly the sources of economic power, while manufacturing often takes place in the less-developed nations of the world.
Since the 2010s “smart” technologies, centered around Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Human–Computer–Interface (HCI), inform the design enterprise and connect it with fields far beyond art and engineering.
The expansion of markets for commodities has been further stimulated by the deregulation and privatization of communications industries, by the growth and sophistication of credit buying and e-commerce, by computerized techniques of product development and 3-D printing, and by sophisticated online business practices that track and carefully monitor consumer behavior, providing such “big data” to advertisers.
The breakup of the Soviet Union in 1989 and the emerging independence of former Eastern bloc countries have extended the hegemony of market-based capitalist economies and their dependence upon innovation and expanding the production and consumption of commodities both domestically and internationally.
China is perhaps the most recent and explosive example of the effects of free enterprise, and the 2008 Summer Olympic Games in Beijing as well as the “Design China Now” exhibition (also in 2008) at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and other venues attest to the role of design in promoting tourism and a modern image for the country based upon rising incomes and consumer spending.
While design consultancies such as IDEO are often identified by the products for which they are responsible, products generally account for a relatively small percentage of the company’s design activity, which includes corporate identity and organizational systems to facilitate communication and commerce.
The visible form of products today is often the result of a lengthy process of observation and databased research, dialogue and compromise among viewpoints representing client interest, user experience, development and production costs, aesthetics, materials, and market research.
Design practice appears to be as much a model for nonhierarchical organizational behavior generally as a strategy directed toward producing physical objects; the term “stakeholders” is often used when describing contemporary design practice to indicate the dialogue among differing points of view.
For better, or worse, designers continue to contribute to the creation of new or “improved” consumer goods, an ever-increasing flood of products that raises questions as to whether we are the victims rather than the beneficiaries of both technology and the information age, defining us perhaps too narrowly as little more than machines for programmed consumption, reducing the exercise of freedom to the choice between endless varieties of products that complicate and fragment our lives.
Concerns with environmental as well as social responsibility on a broader global scale have become more urgent, undermining at least some of the confidence in the material future we are designing.
Sustainability has certainly shifted from the fringes to the mainstream, and is now the focus of corporate advertising strategies and interdisciplinary programs in universities, presenting tremendous challenges to designers that extend beyond innovation to rethinking basic assumptions about our relationship to the goods we produce and consume.
Green design triggers a broad-based consciousness that informs shared attitudes toward new products in relationship to the environment, but for some interest groups, to be effective that consciousness needs to extend to patterns of consumer behavior that are difficult to break or alter, especially when consumer spending remains a basic indicator of economic health, and when polarized politics pits short-term profits against ethics stemming from longer-term dangers.
Awareness of these contradictions and uncertainties, of the combination of hopes as well as fears for the future of design, forms the basis for the final part of this study.
In the final section of the Global Inspiration, we turn again to Asia and to the People’s Republic of China, whose rise as a world economic power since the opening of relations with the West in the 1970s in no small measure involves design, whether in terms of the domestic market, trade, technology, tourism, or the rapidly changing patterns of living that mirror social, political, and environmental conditions.

## Chapter
13 New Materials, New Products Material technology continued to stimulate original industrial product designs in the 1960s, reinforcing the ideology of good design as it had emerged in the first post-war decade.
A significant part of this growth revolved around research and development in synthetic plastics and production processes.
Like Charles and Ray Eames in the United States, Robin (19232000) and Lucienne (19172010) Day were Britains designing couple. Robin Day used a new flexible plastic known as polypropylene to compete with fiberglass in the design of seating.
Days 1963 Polyprop chair (fig.
13.1), manufactured by Hille, shares much in common with the Eameses and Saarinens earlier molded chairs (see fig.
11.5), but offered refinements in ease of assembly and a variety of thin steel supporting elements.
Designed by David Rowland (19242010), the 40/4 chair (fig.
13.2) is named for the economy of space it occupies when stacked: 40 of these chairs occupy but 4 feet of vertical space using a specially designed tilted trolley.
In 1963 the Chicago-based architectural firm Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill (SOM) needed 17,000 chairs to furnish new buildings for the University of Illinois at its Chicago campus.
Aware of Rowlands design, SOM selected the 40/4 and the designer licensed production to the General Fireproofing Company of Youngstown, Ohio, at a cost of \$16 per unit.
Developed independently by Rowland through many models and prototypes over a period of eight years (195563) amid rejections from Knoll Associates and other manufacturers, the stacking chair consists of a thin steel-wire frame with vinyl-coated molded steel plates for seat and back.
A horizontal steel rod at the front of the chairs frame adds stability and strength, while the flanges at the back of the frame connect one chair to another for seating in close rows.
Although aluminum and plastic were explored for the seat and back, the final design used molded steel plates and simulated wood veneer finishes in four basic colors.
Rowlands 40/4 may be seen both as an exercise in progressive problem-solving in the tradition of post-war good design for flexible, spacesaving, compact institutional seating (as well as persistence on the part of the designer), and for its relation to the more boxy and restrained aesthetic characteristic of much international modern industrial design in the 1960s.
The chair received a grand prize as best single object at the XIII Triennale in Milan in 1964, and was used to accommodate guests in St Pauls Cathedral in London for the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana in 1981.
Rowland once stated, steel wire fits a concept which I believe to be fundamental to good design: accomplish the most with the least.

## Plastics
and Their Progeny Also beginning in the 1960s, the process of injection-molding combined with stronger polymers further extended possibilities for furniture design using plastics initiated by the Eameses and by Eero Saarinen (see fig.
11.5).
Joe Colombos (19301971) 1965 side chair, manufactured by Italian company Kartell beginning in 1968, was designed as a single-piece molded seat and back into which plastic legs were inserted (fig.
13.3).
Less organic than most of its predecessors, Colombos plastic side chair was a unified design where legs, seat, and back were parallel or perpendicular to each other as well as to the walls, floors, and ceilings of the rooms they occupied.
We often think of plastics as cheap, even dispensable alternatives to other materials (plastic knives, forks, spoons, for instance), but, as argued by design historian Catharine Rossi, Italian manufacturers such as Kartell maintained high standards in prototyping and production that competed with, rather than undercut, wooden or metal furniture, and kept prices and exchange values high.
This applied as well to Ettore Sottsasss portable Valentine typewriter for Olivetti (see fig.
13.11), despite the designers ambition for a more affordable product.
Joe Colombo, stacking chairs, nylon and polypropylene (injection-mold plastic), height 28 in (71 cm), manufactured by Kartell, 1965.
Photograph: Kartell USA, Easley, South Carolina.
A single injection-molded form was used to manufacture Danish designer Verner Pantons (19261998) stacking chair, designed in 1960 and manufactured by Herman Miller beginning in 1967 (fig.
13.4).
Unlike Colombos side chair, Pantons unified design preserves the biomorphic forms of post-war furniture designers such as Isamu Noguchi, Eero Saarinen, or Arne Jacobsen, while the thin, concave base provides stability and permits interlocking.
Both designs eliminated the need for steel, wooden, or aluminum supporting structures, making the chairs light and easy to move, while bright colors provided variety.
Verner Panton, stacking chair, fiberglass-reinforced polyester, height 32 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (83.2 cm), manufactured by Herman Miller Company, 1960 (manufactured beginning 1967), Zeeland, Michigan.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Not every original design from the 1960s derived from newly developed materials or processes.
Aluminum emerged in the interwar period as a constructive material for lightweight industrial furniture in aircraft and outdoor use; after the war it was used in the fluid cone-shaped pedestals that support Saarinens Tulip furniture for Knoll (see fig.
11.12).
Knoll also replaced steel with aluminum in manufacturing Mies van der Rohes Barcelona chair, designed in 1929 and re-released after World War II.
In 1962, Charles and Ray Eames used aluminum for the Tandem Sling, manufactured by Herman Miller for seating that continues to be used in airport terminal gate areas (fig.
13.5).
The design responded to a variety of requirements.
Easily assembled in flexible units from a small number of parts, with seats made from nylon (like plastic, another synthetic polymer) contoured to lessen pressure on the back of the legs, this seating system also facilitated maintenance by airport custodial staff, who could operate vacuum cleaners more easily to reach underneath the seats.
As noted by designer and design historian Craig Vogel, armrests provided additional support for waiting passengers as they stood up, and prevented them from stretching out along the length of several units (airports and airlines felt this provoked negative associations of lengthy waiting times for departures or loitering).
Less playful and organic than a number of earlier Eames chairs for the home or molded designs for public spaces, this aluminum and nylon seating exemplified design as a creative problem-solving activity, integrating aesthetic, practical, and technical determinants for responsible industrial design.
Charles and Ray Eames, Tandem Sling multiple seating (five-seat unit), aluminum, black steel bars, padded vinyl, 33 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 117 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 28 in (86 × 298 × 71 cm), manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, 1962.
Modern furniture of the period, and in particular domestic (rather than institutional) seating at the higher end of the market, was often closely allied to tendencies in the fine arts.
While the biomorphic forms of the 1950s related to the improvisational forms of Automatic Surrealism, Colombos side chair and other designs shared suggested similarities with the hard-edged abstraction and precision of New York artists such as Frank Stella (b.
1936) or Ellsworth Kelly (19232015).
The audience for some of the most original examples appears to have been limited mostly to readers of international journals and visitors to exhibitions and museums rather than to the domestic or even contract markets favored by architects and interior design professionals.
Some industrially manufactured furniture of the 1960s seems more at home in a museum or art gallery than in a living room, better suited to reflection, comparisons with earlier examples, or as evidence of a designers creative imagination, as applied design for arts sake. An example is French designer Pierre Paulins (19272009) 1966 Ribbon chair manufactured by Artifort, made of upholstered rubber and wood on a metal base (fig.
13.6), or Chilean Surrealist painter Roberto Mattas (19221990) Malitte seating system for Gavina (1966), constructed of fabric-covered foam rubber units that fit together like a puzzle (fig.
13.8).
The work of both designers has much to do with originality and the appreciation of the restrained organicism of contemporary abstract painting and sculpture; Mattas seating system also emphasizes flexibility in possibilities for alternative arrangements of its components as well as building a novel room divider or screen.
Pierre Paulin, Ribbon chair, metal, rubber, and lacquered wood with fabric-covered foam upholstery, $2 7 \mathrm { ~ } ^ { \circ } / _ { 1 6 } \times 3 9 \mathrm { ~ } ^ { 3 } / _ { 8 } \times 2 9$ $^ { 1 } / _ { 8 } \mathrm { i n } ( 7 0 \times 1 0 0 \times 7 4$ cm), manufactured by Artifort, Maastricht, the Netherlands, 1966.
Roberto Matta, Malitte multi-function seating system (closed), fabric-covered polyurethane foam, height 63 in (160 cm) when stacked, manufactured by Gavina (Italy), 1966.
Hard-edged aesthetic qualities apply to the Eclisse (Eclipse) lamp designed by Vico Magistretti (19202006) and manufactured by Artemide in 1966 (fig.
13.7) in a variety of colors.
The lacquered aluminum lamp consists of two concentric semicircular shades attached to a semicircular base; the shades rotate, allowing users to adjust the amount and direction of illumination.
Again, the smooth shapes and compact design recall the purity of geometric abstraction, as well as its cool precision.
Both the name and the forms allude to the solar system.
In the 1960s, industrial designers played an important part in strengthening Italys international reputation for original and sophisticated products, supplying new designs and name recognition for furniture, machines, lighting, and household products manufactured by companies such as Venini (glass), Kartell (plastic), Pirelli (rubber), Flos, Arredoluce, and Artemide (lighting), and Gavina (furniture).
Vico Magistretti, Eclisse table lamp, lacquered aluminum, $7 \times 4 ~ { } ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (17.8 × 11.4 cm), manufactured by Artemide, Milan, Italy, 1966.

## Product
Housing Housings constitute a broad category of industrial design activity, but generally refer to the shells enclosing mechanical products ranging from domestic appliances to office and laboratory machines and audiovisual equipment.
During the 1960s, the bulbous and even streamlined forms of many appliances and office machines in metal housings were replaced by more compact, rectangular shapes in both metal and plastic, while transistor and other electronics technologies also tended to result in more compact, portable products.
Egidio Bonfante, poster advertisement for Olivetti Valentine typewriter, 1969.
A revealing comparison might be between Marcello Nizzolis 1948 Lexikon 80 typewriter for Olivetti (see fig.
11.45), and the tapered rectangular Praxis 48 electric typewriter (fig.
13.10) designed for Olivetti in 1964 by Ulm graduate Hans von Klier (19342000) and Ettore Sottsass, Jr.
(19172007).
Sottsass worked as a consultant to Olivetti to provide visual unity in the design of its Elea 9003 office computer system.
A further state of refinement and compact form may be observed in Olivettis sleek and rectangular manual portable typewriter known as the Valentine, also designed by Sottass beginning in 1969 and housed in a bright red smooth plastic sleeve (fig.
13.11).
Its color and product name also provided the machine with personality for added appeal directed toward an upscale and fashionable youth market, as seen in a poster advertisement by Egidio Bonfante (19222004; fig.
13.9).
Disappointed with the price point of the Valentine, Sottsass later questioned some of the negative social implications of modern industrial design, and his later practice explored new, independent directions.
The conflict that began to emerge between designers and corporate clients produced a number of alternatives to post-war international Modernism during the 1960s and is treated in greater detail below (see Chapter 14 onward).
Hans von Klier and Ettore Sottsass, Jr., Praxis 48 electric typewriter, plastic housing, 6 <sup>7</sup>/ × 17 <sup>5</sup>/ × 13 <sup>3</sup>/ in $( 1 6 .
5 \times 4 4 .
5 $ × 33.8 cm), manufactured by Olivetti ING, Ivrea, Italy, 1964.
13.11 Ettore Sottsass, Jr., and Perry King, Valentine portable typewriter and case, ABS plastic housing, 13 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 12 in (34 × 30 cm), manufactured by Olivetti ING, Ivrea, Italy, 1969.
Miniaturization continued to be a determining factor in the design of product housings such as televisions, tape recorders, and cameras.
Japanese company Sony pioneered the design of portable televisions using transistors as early as 1959, employing a thin metal casing around the irregular and slightly tapered picture tube, a carrying handle, and a steel track to support a visor that reduced glare.
A similar design, with plastic housing, was introduced in 1962 in Italy by Brionvega, designed by Richard Sapper (19322015) and Marco Zanuso (see here), also emphasizing lightness and portability.
These designs contrasted with conventional, wooden cabinetlike housings (often including hinged doors to hide the screen) in a variety of period furniture styles.
Perhaps the most widely accepted compromise between the appeal of traditional furniture and the advantages of portable television was the 1965 Sony Trinitron, rectangular in form, adaptable to built-in shelving or moving stands, with a wood-grained plastic laminate surface that harmonized more readily with furniture and paneling in the domestic interior (fig.
13.12).
Further miniaturization of the speakers and picture tube, and the use of remote-control operation, led to even more compact and minimal designs, characterized by ever-thinner rectangular integrated housings in flat-screen televisions that can be directly mounted on the wall.
Sonys approach to consumer electronics acknowledged that miniaturized technology dictated a degree of aesthetic conformity that was acceptable to consumers.
Instead of cockpit or dashboard-like features, Sony electronic products favored attention to user-friendly operation and frequent new models without significant changes in styling aside from color or lighter and more durable materials.
One example of this strategy was the replacement of reelto-reel tapes with cassettes in the 1970s.
Handheld mini-cassette recorders appeared in Japan in the mid-1960s, while Sonys portable cassette player, known as the Walkman, was introduced in 1978 (fig.
13.13).
In the early 1970s, Sony advertisements for its newest high-end reel-to-reel audio tape deck suggested that the product had reached a final, perfected form: This could be the tape deck youll leave to your great grand-son. The balance between novelty, innovation, continuity, and brand dependability reveals ongoing dialogue between competing perspectives that defined the expanding practice of industrial design for many electronics and information technology-based companies.
After all, Sonys first miniaturized electronics were inexpensive portable transistor radios (see here and fig.
GI5.2), but the companys line of higher-end electronic recording equipment (similar to Nikon cameras) entailed a marketing strategy that emphasized lasting value and high performance, reducing the negative connotations of a throwaway culture. Trinitron television, metal housing with wood-grained finish, manufactured by the Sony Corporation, Tokyo, from 1965.
Walkman portable cassette player, anodized aluminum housing, height 5 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (13.3 cm), manufactured by the Sony Corporation, Tokyo, 1978.
Gino Valle, Cifra 3, table clock, plastic case, 7 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>6</sub> × 3 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (18 × 9.5 cm), manufactured by Solari & C., Udine, Italy, 1966.
Ludwig Littmann, Visotronic DN 50 tabletop clock and alarm with electronic digital readout, plastic housing, $3 \times 5 ^ { 7 } / _ { 8 } \times 4$ <sup>3</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in $( \bar { 7 } .
5 \times 1 5 \times 1 1$ cm), manufactured by Braun AG, Kronberg, Germany, 1979.
The 1960s also saw the increased use of digital rather than analogue clocks, with numerical readouts that implied greater precision and accuracy (fig.
13.14).
Digital clocks reduced the digits of the Arabic numbers to a system using just seven dashes displayed electronically, as in the Visotronic tabletop clock manufactured by Braun in 1979 (fig.
13.15).
A similar mechanical read-out system that included the letters of the alphabet was employed for the Split Flap Board Information System in train stations, designed by Italian manufacturer Solari di Udine beginning in 1962.
Whether digital or mechanical (hence the name Flap), traditional clock hands contained in rounded forms were abandoned in favor of more compact housings.
In lighting, the development of high-intensity bulbs spawned a generation of minimal designs for table lamps, including Michael Laxs (19291999) metal Lytegem table lamp of 1965 for Lightolier, with a collapsible, antennalike arm, making the lamp into little more than a 6-inch (15-centimeter) tall paperweight when not in use (fig.
13.16).
Lightolier also developed systems featuring modular cylinder-shaped housings for lights, attached to ceiling tracks, integrated with architecture and permitting lateral and rotational flexibility and reducing the need for table or floor lamps.
Track lighting is compact, but still rather substantial in comparison with the more recent types of illumination using halogen lamps.
Halogen technology for lighting has further reduced the size while increasing the intensity (as well as the heat) of illumination, and has led to a variety of aesthetic possibilities as well.
The almost weightless appearance of halogen bulbs suspended from barely visible wires is seen, for instance, in Ingo Maurers (19322019) YaYaHo lighting system from the early 1980s (fig.
13.17).
This uses a vocabulary of standardized components to explore three-dimensional space, providing the experience of a work of installation art as well as interior illumination.
More recently, Maurers work has used LED (light-emitting diode) technology to illuminate interior spaces as well as to create exterior displays while saving energy and reducing heat.
Michael Lax, Lytegem table lamp, zinc, brass, and aluminum, height 15 in (38 cm) when extended, manufactured by Lightolier, 1965.
Ingo Maurer, YaYaHo lighting system, glass, ceramic, metal, and plastic, 19 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 118 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (49.5 × 300 cm), manufactured by Design M, Munich, Germany, 1981–1984.

## Laminated
Materials In addition to molded plastics, plywood and plastic laminates were also common materials for industrially designed furniture.
In 1964, Robert Propst (19212000) and George Nelson (see here) introduced the Action Office system for modular furniture, manufactured by Herman Miller (fig.
13.18).
Available in a combination of surfaces including hygienic white laminated plastic, the Action Office system was adaptable to large areas of open floor space, with the possibility of flexible configuration for group clusters or individual offices to manage workflow.
Dimensions were based upon the determination of average space needs and proximity between elements of individual components for the efficient and optimum performance of office-related tasks.
The plastic laminates of the Action Office system provided smooth and durable work surfaces that could be easily cleaned and maintained.
The appeal of this material also extended to table and cabinet surfaces for kitchens, manufactured and widely marketed by the Formica Company.
Originally developed as a form of plastic insulation and a coating for machine gears, the applications for Formica as a laminate for furniture grew after World War II.
Varied colors and pattern designs, like those for vinyl flooring, belong more to the history of mass design and are treated accordingly below (see here).
13.18 Robert Propst and George Nelson, Action Office system, manufactured by Herman Miller Company, Zeeland, Michigan, 1964.
Laminated plywood was also used for a variety of furniture designs in the 1960s.
A good example from Japan is Reiko Tanabes (b.
1934) teak plywood stool designed for Tendo Mokko in 1960 (fig.
13.19).
The self-contained form is designed for efficient construction with three identical molded components that are glued together.
Reiko (Murai) Tanabe, stool, teak, plywood, 14 <sup>3</sup>/ × 17 1<sup>1</sup>/ × 17 <sup>1</sup>/ in (36 × 45 × 43 cm), manufactured by Tendo Mokko, Tendo Company Ltd., 1960.

## Sports
Equipment and Progress While it is not possible to include all areas of new consumer products that emerged from new materials and technologies, sports equipment is one area that may demonstrate how product design and technology have developed during the last 60 years.
This is not simply because new materials may be linked to better performance, but also because small changes following the initial development of a product provide the basis for frequent replacement of existing models, blurring distinctions between progress and fashion.
A case study might be the tennis racquet industry, where metal racquets began to compete with traditionally crafted wood-framed racquets in the mid-1960s, with the T-2000 model aluminum racquet, first introduced by the Wilson Sporting Goods Company in the United States in 1967 (fig.
13.20).
The adoption of the new racquets, first among younger audiences, was stimulated through endorsements by younger tennis professionals such as Jimmy Connors (b.
1952), and increased exposure of professional tennis tournaments on television.
Wilson had used endorsements prior to the advent of television for its top-of-the-line Jack Kramer model  still a standard long after Jack Kramer retired from active tennis in the early 1950s, an almost unthinkable circumstance with todays marketing emphasis upon technology, change, and the current generation of star athletes.
A resulting tennis boom, beginning in the later 1960s, accompanied a series of equipment improvements, such as lighter racquets with larger heads, followed by the replacement of steel consecutively by aluminum, graphite, lightweight ceramic materials, even lighter titanium, and nanotubes combined with more traditional carbon fibers.
It becomes difficult to separate the development of new technologies from their relation to the tennis stars who market particular brands or whose personalities, both on and off the court, are linked to the product and by extension to the consumer who purchases it.
Once again, the complexity of the design enterprise during the 1960s makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish between technological progress, performance, and commercial competition, or more simply between improvement and novelty.
Manufacturers and consumers alike acknowledge a permanent state of impermanence that forms the basis of sustained economic growth and defines our relation to the world of designed products around us.
13.20 T-2000 tennis racquet, aluminum, nylon, and other materials, length 26 $^ 7 / _ { 8 }$ in (68 cm), manufactured by Wilson Sporting Goods Company, 1967.

## Retail
and Fair: Marketing Modern Design Robin Days designs for Hille were successfully marketed internationally, while British designer and entrepreneur Sir Terence Conran (19312020; see here) expanded his contract furniture and fabric design business by opening a number of retail outlets in London under the name Habitat, beginning in 1964.
Conrans Habitat stores expanded the marketing for international modern design beyond contract commissions from architects for institutions and sophisticated clientele who constituted much of its audience during the later 1950s.
Habitat obtained rights to manufacture and distribute contemporary designs from Italian and Nordic designers and manufacturers and offered practical mass-produced furniture recalling period styles, as well as imported craft items such as Japanese utensils.
Habitats advertising and merchandising, featuring displays filled with home furnishing products and accessories, also were beginning to blur the lines that had distinguished good design from mass-marketed commodities during the 1950s (fig.
13.21).
Increasingly the array of goods, changing merchandising displays, and variations 13.21 of new but similar products resembled marketing strategies such as obsolescence and relied upon rising levels of consumer spending aimed at design-conscious upwardly mobile consumers.
Habitat offered modern design as a refreshing lifestyle choice, a matter of taste rather than to the more broadly ethical, humanistic motivations of good design in the immediate post-war years.
A similar observation might also apply to the warehouse approach to modern design of IKEA discussed below (see here).
Counter display, Habitat store, London, c.
1965.
At the 1964 New York Worlds Fair, the USs major automobile manufacturers sponsored large pavilions as in 1939, but the earlier fairs vision of suburban living, personal mobility and interstate highways, labor-saving appliances, increased leisure, and individual home ownership, had for some (at least the white middle class and upwardly mobile blue-collar workers) largely been realized.
The future promised plentiful and peaceful atomic energy, exploring the exciting new frontier of outer space, and a dawning information age that would usher in a variety of benefits to an interconnected humankind.
These themes were symbolized by the Unisphere designed by Gilmore David Clarke (now the site of the National Tennis Center and United States Open Tennis Tournament), a tilted spherical stainless-steel (provided by the United States Steel Corporation) sculptural representation of the Earth, encircled by three rings evoking orbiting space satellites as well as electrons surrounding an atom.
Rather than displaying office products such as typewriters and calculators, IBM used multimedia displays and film to present their mainframe computers as powering highspeed information technology to solve complex problems in space travel, in short, to construct and manage the technological future.
Eero Saarinen and Charles and Ray Eames designed the IBM Pavilion, and the Eames office coordinated all aspects of the visitors experience.
Their goal was to humanize the computer, emphasizing the dizzying speed of its calculations, shifting attention away from Cold War fears of the destructive power of hi-tech missile systems and the specter of a nuclear Armageddon.
Presenting computers as sophisticated data-driven problem-solvers, the Eameses defined their expanded view of design as a series of informed decisions within an everyday context.
In their film Think (the IBM motto), the Eameses compared design to planning the seating arrangement of a dinner party (fig.
13.22).
The problem-solving metaphor of decisions that lead to a desired or preferred result constructed an understanding of design as a natural human capacity applicable to the widest possible range of activities.
By choosing a dinner party, the Eameses and IBM emphasized the relationship between design and everyday living and the ubiquity of innate human creativity; while the Eameses dinner party in figure 13.22 may look a bit formal to us today, comparing computing to dining, or including puppet shows in the companys pavilion, allowed visitors to relate to, accept, and feel comfortable with complex subjects such as the flight paths of jet planes or the management of highway and street traffic.
As explained by architectural historian John Harwood, the Eameses incorporated the playful aspects of problem-solving, creating a circuslike atmosphere with a variety of display strategies to suggest the magical as well as the logical and technical aspects of computers.
Charles and Ray Eames, still shot from the film Think showing the “design” of a dinner party, from the IBM Pavilion at the New York World’s Fair, 1964.
Before the advent of personal computers, tablets, and smart phones, the 1964 IBM Pavilion offered an encouraging response to information technology, not unlike presentday viewpoints about artificial intelligence or genetic design.
The idea of thinking machines was greeted with a combination of optimism and fear; whether through product housings, or promotional displays at Worlds Fairs, designers helped to define, and to promote an understanding of technology and how it related to human experience.
This included hiding their complex circuits in visually attractive and understated forms, and communicating with a broader public via films suggesting that artificial intelligence was both natural and full of excitement and promise.
Such efforts supported positive attitudes toward the close relationships between government and business, not only in manufacturing but also in the growing information and energy (service) sectors of the economy.
Through exhibitions and other forms of media, corporations engaged in public education and the promotion of pro-technology values: at the 1964 Worlds Fair, General Electrics space-age pavilion, for instance, featured moving theaters that presented the history and promise of a future of inexpensive electricity through the use of nuclear power.
The 1964 New York Worlds Fair was contemporary with the first manned space missions and with big-business support of cultural programming on television as a form of public service.
An early example of the latter was General Electric Theater, appearing first in 1954 and hosted by film actor and future US president Ronald Reagan (1911 2004).
Mobil Oil Corporations Masterpiece Theater premiered in 1971 through the Public Broadcasting System (PBS).
Such sponsorship increased with the growth of multinational corporations, which sought to minimize or offset possible areas of conflict between company self-interest and the greater public good.

## Nature
and Craft in an International Context In addition to new industrial materials and processes, preserving craft traditions also humanized design in the 1960s through the use of natural woods and fibers for furniture, curtains, rugs, and table-coverings.
The interest in craft may have owed something to the legacy of the Arts and Crafts movement (see Chapter 5), but there was also an element of revitalization that integrated rather than rejected industrial materials and changing methods of production.
In addition, and particularly in the field of textiles, it touched upon the renewal of national traditions and identity in a global economy.
Occasionally synthetic fibers such as polyester were introduced, for instance, with stretch upholstery, or to explore new textures or combinations of textures, as in Swiss textile designer Suzanne Huguenins (19162008) Nylon Homespun fabric manufactured by Knoll beginning in 1958 (fig.
13.23).
Sheila Hickss (b.
1934) Badagara fabric, dating to 1966 to 1967, is woven from cotton in horizontal bands of irregular diameter, one of several designs for the Kerala collection commissioned by a large manufacturing company in South India to stimulate interest in local craft production for an international market (fig.
13.24).
Many of Hickss works are monumental wall-hangings commissioned for display in public buildings throughout the world, employing handweavers to assist with production while maintaining a strong relationship between fine art and original studio craft.
Suzanne Huguenin, Nylon Homespun fabric, nylon, width 50 in (127 cm), manufactured by Knoll International, New York, 1958.
13.24 Sheila Hicks, Badagara fabric, cotton, width 120 in (305 cm), made by Commonwealth Trust, Calcutta, India, 1966–1967, and still made today.
Scandinavian designers remained at the forefront of modern textile manufacturing internationally, and served as an inspiration to designers in the United States, particularly at the Cranbrook Academy in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, where Finnishborn Loja Saarinen had established a strong craft program beginning in 1923 (see here).
In many cases woven and printed fabric designs were manufactured by Knoll and Herman Miller, as well as by Nordic companies such as Marimekko.
Finnish designer Maija Isolas (19272001) bold printed cotton Melooni fabric, manufactured in Finland by Printex (which also introduced the Marimekko name), dates to 1963 and is contemporary with the bold post-painterly abstract canvases of Ellsworth Kelly, Frank Stella, or Kenneth Noland (fig.
13.25).
Woven patterns in cotton and wool tended to respect the natural geometry of warp and weft, and were produced by Scandinavian manufacturers as well as by the American-based (but Scandinavian-named) Dansk Corporation beginning in the later 1950s.
Designers experimented with industrial materials including cellophane and synthetic silks, resulting in varied textures and degrees of transparency.
Their efforts appeared in museum and other international exhibitions and journals, and were promoted through the founding of the American Craft Museum in Manhattan in 1956 (the name was changed to the Museum of Arts and Design in 2003, along with its relocation from West 53rd Street to Columbus Circle).
13.25 Maija Isola, Melooni fabric, screenprinted, width 54 in (137 cm), manufactured by Printex, Helsinki, for Marimekko Oy, 1963.
13.26 Dorothy Liebes, fabric, Orlon and metallics, width 50 in (127 cm), manufactured by Dorothy Liebes Design.
Private collection.
Combinations of natural and synthetic materials in textile design appear in the work of many designers, including a number of remarkable women such as Dorothy Liebes (18991972), Sheila Hicks, and Anni Albers (18991994; wife of painter and Bauhaus teacher Josef Albers).
During the 1950s, Liebes designed window blinds using a combination of fabrics binding wooden slats.
In the 1960s she created fabrics for quantity production using a variety of media, including synthetics such as Orlon and metal foils (fig.
13.26).
Another American textile designer and manufacturer was Cranbrook-trained Jack Lenor Larsen (19272020), a promoter of traditional and contemporary craftsmanship, as seen in his Magnum Golden fabric (fig.
13.27).
Jack Lenor Larsen, Magnum Golden, wool, 54 <sup>1</sup>/ × 51 in (137.8 × 129.5cm), c.
1978.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
Original forms involving craft rather than industrial production characterize the work of Philadelphia area sculptor and furniture-maker Wharton Esherick (18871970), whose music stand accentuates the abstract tension of an arched curve (fig.
13.28).
Original craft-based furniture also characterizes the career of California-based Sam Maloof (19162009).
Wharton Esherick, music stand, cherry wood, 43 × 19 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 16 in (109 × 49.5 × 41 cm), 1962.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
Craft revival was an element of the 1960s counterculture.
Borrowings from Indigenous and non-Western traditions were part of a sympathetic response to preindustrial societies and communal lifestyles, with tie-dyed designs on cotton T-shirts and tops, at first done in ones own washbasin and later available off the rack (fig.
13.29).
Craft fairs often featured acoustic folk music and took place in the ambience of street festivals; self-sufficiency, organic foods and gardening, and the rejection of synthetic materials were choices that directed daily patterns of life toward a closer relationship to nature rather than an acceptance of and dependence upon technology and the modern conveniences provided by industrial design and production, regardless of efforts to humanize technical progress.
Whether as an underground movement in the 1960s or moving to the mainstream in response to climate change and related issues of social justice, resistance to the alliance between technology and progress along ethical lines continued to figure in design discourse, and to grow in the twenty-first century.
13.29 Joe Cocker wearing a tie-dyed T-shirt at Woodstock music festival, New York, 1969.
A dialogue with craft also persisted in Italy in the modern glass industry, whose revitalization for the higher-end export market after World War II depended upon collaboration with traditional workshops in Murano and the contributions of fine artists, industrial designers, and architects who introduced greater experimentation with forms and techniques.
An example is Ercole Baroviers (18891974) large glass vase dated c.
1961 (fig.
13.30), with its deep red triangular patterns played against the transparent glass walls of the vases bulbous form.
American designer Dale Chihuly (b.
1941), after studying architecture and design, pursued glass-blowing as a fine art, and today is celebrated both for his inventiveness and virtuosity.
The molded and free-blown-glass Deep Blue and Bronze Persian Set is but one example, dating to 1999.
Here a source for Chihuly was the suggestive organic forms of Persian glass, which also provided an inspiration for Louis Comfort Tiffany, featuring a variety of organic forms, textures, and patterns (fig.
13.31).
As a result of injuries he sustained in an automobile accident Chihuly began delegating fabrication of his designs to teams of trained assistants in his studio in the 1970s, including large commissions for museums and other public spaces.
Whether as an exploration of unmined sources for aesthetic effect, symbolism, or the enjoyment of physical contact with materials and processes, handicraft persisted as a strain of avant-garde applied art, industrial-scale design, and popular culture.
