13.30 Ercole Barovier, large glass vase, c.
1961.
Murano, Italy.
Dale Chihuly, Deep Blue and Bronze Persian Set, glass, with threading and twisted canes (filigree of various types), blown into an optic mold, free-blown, and handworked (overhead view), width 34 <sup>9</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (89 cm), 1999.
Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

## Visual
Identity, Information, and Art Direction Coordinated corporate identity programs, as described in the post-war era in Part V, gained prominence in the 1960s.
Paul Rand (see here), who was hired by Eliot Noyes to design the logo for IBM (1956), continued to develop a number of clear, bold logos for multinational corporations, including the Westinghouse Corporation (1960; see fig.
11.78), and the American Broadcasting Company (ABC, 1962; see fig.
11.79).
The New York-based firms of Chermayeff and Geismar (see here) as well as Saul Bass and Associates were responsible for consistent and recognizable corporate identity systems, including Mobil Oil Corporation (1964; fig.
13.32), American Telephone and Telegraph Corporation (AT&T, 1969; fig.
13.33) and the Chase Manhattan Bank, all employing easily recognized symbols and bold sans serif typography.
Along with Swissborn and educated graphic designer Steff Geissbuhler (b.
1942), Chermayoff and Geismar designed the far-reaching identity system for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1975.
In Europe, a group of faculty at the Hochschule für Gestaltung at Ulm, including Otl Aicher, developed the visual identity program for Lufthansa German National Airlines (1962), based upon a grid system and used for an inclusive range of labels, schedules, and advertising information (fig.
13.34).
Mobil 13.32 Tom Geismar of Chermayeff and Geismar Associates, trademark for Mobil oil, 1964–1965.
Line drawing by John Langdon.
13.34 Otl Aicher, in collaboration with Tomas Gonda, Fritz Querengasser, and Nick Roericht (Ulm Development Group), Lufthansa’s Boeing Fleet Department of Visual Communication, 1962.
13.33 Saul Bass and Associates, AT&T trademark, 1969.
Strategies for developing comprehensive visual systems for large organizations and corporations consider the characteristics of the audience to be served, for instance in terms of age and nationality.
Banks use common elements of color and layout for identity in series of brochures promoting their range of services.
The United States National Park Service, whose audience includes visitors of all ages and nationalities, uses a related approach involving careful analysis of multiple areas of content and their combination in unified ways for each of its parks and monuments.
The National Park Service identity system, developed from 1977 by a team of consultants including Massimo Vignelli (19312014), Vincent Gleason, and Dennis McLaughlin, consisted of a Unigrid design system for charts and brochures to provide consistent information for the nations federally maintained sites.
The system included bold white-on-black sans serif typography for bordered titles, color photography, maps, short text, charts, symbols identifying services for parking, camping, restrooms, and information, as well as diagrams (fig.
13.35).
Armed with foldout brochures, travelers can be assured of basic information in simplified and consistent visual form that reduces the anxiety of navigating the park and facilitates the selection and enjoyment of those areas one wants to visit.
Recognizing the international attraction of such sites as the Grand Canyon and the Liberty Bell, the printed guides were translated into Japanese, German, French, and Spanish with the text treated as an interchangeable part. Such systems produce signage and brochures, reducing complexity and providing a sense of order and familiarity to information to promote the use of a service.
13.35 Massimo Vignelli and staff, “Unigrid” system for National Park Service brochures, from 1977.
Massimo Vignellis career encompassed a wide range of activities including the design of furniture and products.
The firm Vignelli & Associates, with offices in New York and Milan, has also been responsible for visual systems that include brand recognition (American Airlines, 1967, Bloomingdales department store, 1972), information graphics (the New York Metropolitan Subway System, 1966), and creative freedom (Knoll International from 1966, where he succeeded Herbert Matter, see here).
The solution to each clients brief requires an understanding of the market, the flexibility of a basic visual system (adopting methods of International Typographic Style) in adapting to differing formats and future needs, and the careful manipulation and composition of a full range of technical graphic means including photography, drawings, diagrams, typography, and layout. # 五八 Yoshiro Yamashita, pictograms for the eighteenth Olympic Games held in Tokyo, 1964.
Graphic identity for the Olympic Games is another example of visual systems designed for easy recognition across linguistic barriers and attracting excitement for sponsoring nations who vie to be selected as hosts.
Yoshiro Yamashita designed a system of pictograms for the 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games (fig.
13.36).
Like logos, these pictograms use a simple series of related shapes to signify the parts of the human body and the field or equipment connected with a particular sport.
In an international context, such an approach became common on packaging to encourage careful handling and later for graphics developed for airports  for instance, the series of pictograms designed by Roger Cook (19302021) and Don Shanosky in 1975 for the United States Department of Transportation (fig.
13.37).
Similar reductionism in the transportation industry is seen in the cardboard tags used to identify luggage in airports, which are color-coded and display a code of three-letter abbreviations for the worlds airport terminals in a bold sans serif typeface that can easily be understood and separated by baggage handlers.
The code was developed for the International Air Transportation Authority (IATA).
Increasing globalization in a number of industries encourages the use of intuitively self-evident abstract symbols in information graphics, for instance, for the operation of tape decks, CD players, or a variety of digital media players without the need for written instructions for arrow-like commands such as forward or fast forward.

## 13.37 Roger Cook and Don Shanosky, signage symbol system for United States Department of T
ransportation, printed poster (detail), 29 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 21 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> in (76 × 55 cm), 1975.
Private collection.

## New
Directions in Graphic Design: Breaking the Rules, Bucking the System In addition to generating increasing demand for information graphics and corporate identity systems, post-World War II graphic designers also explored more open-ended, personal approaches to advertising and art direction.
The expressive use of typography is seen in the work of American Herb Lubalin (19181981).
Although Lubalin designed several eccentric typefaces combining elements from serif and sans serif families of type, his transformations of letters to convey the meaning of words visually demonstrates a fascination with the creative possibilities of type.
In figure 13.38, for instance, Lubalin creates the illusion of torn paper breaking apart the word cough to suggest irritation and roughness in an advertisement for a pharmaceutical company.
Whereas a biography of Eric Gill (see here) bears the title The Man Who Loved Letters, Lubalins future biographer might be tempted to entitle her work The Man Who Loved Words.
Taking liberties with letters without obscuring verbal recognition required intuition and experiment along with discipline and careful analysis.
Both sensibilities are complementary aspects of the graphic design profession.
PYRIBENZAMINE EXPECTORANT with Ephedrine ALSO AVAILABLE: PYRIBENZAMINE EXPECTORANT WITH CODEINE AND EPHEDRINE CEXEMPT NARCOTICS).
PYRIBENZAMINE CITRATE (TRIPELENNAMINE CITRATE CIBA) Herb Lubalin (of Sudler, Hennessey & Lubalin), advertisement for a pharmaceutical company.
Herb Lubalin Archive, Rochester Institute of Technology. # AVANI GARDE 13.39 Herb Lubalin, cover for Avant Garde, issue no.
3, height 11 in (28 cm), New York, 1968.
Private collection.
While successful in commercial advertising, Lubalin also worked independently to exercise greater freedom of expression.
He served as art director for several journals that challenged more conventional approaches to content, typography, photography, illustration, and layout, including Avant Garde, for which he also invented a sans serif typeface combining regular and forward-leaning italic forms for close spacing and a unified image (fig.
13.39).
Lubalin also worked for the short-lived quarterly periodical Eros beginning in 1962.
The magazine was both journalistically as well as graphically provocative, treating controversial political, racial, and sexual subjects; its publisher/editor, Ralph Ginzburg (19292006), was convicted on obscenity charges in a series of judicial proceedings that began in 1963.
In a spread from Eros (1962), a photograph of embracing interracial lovers accompanies Aristophanes play Lysistrata (also illustrated by Aubrey Beardsley in 1896), in which the women of late fifth-century BCE Athens withhold sex from their husbands to force an end to the long Peloponnesian war between Athens and Sparta (fig.
13.40).
The image asserts the plays contemporary relevance for its sexual, racial, and Cold War associations.
Lubalins creative efforts in graphic design aligned more generally with freedom of expression, even if that freedom conflicted with conservative attitudes politically and censorship in the publishing industry.
Journals such as Avant Garde and Eros were part of a broader movement in design and politics that placed individuals in conflict with the conservatism of both large businesses and government.
Lubalin also produced the journal U&lc beginning in 1970, devoted to typographical experimentation using filmsetting.
Filmsetting used photography rather than metal type to produce text in different sizes from drawn forms; negatives were exposed to thin metal plates for offset lithographic printing.
U&lc promoted the International Typeface Corporation (ITC), founded in the same year by Lubalin, Aaron Burns, and Edward Rondthaler, encouraging typographic invention.
The shift to filmsetting, and eventually to computer-generated typefaces, gave more control to designers in developing new fonts to meet a wider range of personal and broadly political expressive needs.
While the graphic design profession gained stature and respectability through its service to government and business, practitioners beginning in the 1960s sought alternatives that lay beyond mainstream channels of production and distribution for their activities, whether in underground publications, graphic novels, or other more active forms of protest, allied in some way with the counterculture movements of the period.
Herb Lubalin, spread from Eros, Lysistrata, vol.
1, no.
4, winter 1962, New York.
Photography by Ralph M.
Hattersley Jr.
Private collection.
Milton Glaser (19292020) also explored more intuitive approaches to graphic design during the 1960s and beyond, through perhaps less controversially than Lubalin.
His oeuvre owes much to testing the limits of traditional representational illustration through a variety of techniques and media as well as reductive and subjective approaches to drawing and typography.
Results emerge in a remarkable series of posters, book jackets, and logos, as well as in books of poetry and childrens book illustration.
A series of book covers for paperback editions of Shakespeare achieved unity through the use of ample white space, heavy black borders, and delicate wash drawings featuring a central character or grouping from each play.
Abbreviating both technique and narrative promoted the viewers active response, and distinguishes the series from other editions.
Suggestion and active response characterize Glasers childrens illustrations, as well as his poster for the Olivetti Valentine in 1969 (fig.
13.41), in which the small red portable typewriter is juxtaposed against a verdant landscape.
A seated dog presides over the typewriter while the sandaled feet of a reclining (or sleeping) figure imply an idyllic past.
The prominent canine may suggest the well-known His Masters Voice trademark for RCA Victor (the dogs name is Nipper), with the typewriter replacing the phonograph speaker and alluding to the written (typed) word rather than musical sounds.
Glaser relied upon a wealth of imaginative associations familiar enough to supply meaning to his designs.
His I NY logo, where the heart substitutes interchangeably for the word love, is among his best-known designs and has spawned countless variations.
Milton Glaser, poster for Olivetti Valentine typewriter, 1969.
Push Pin Studio, founded in 1954, included Glaser, along with graphic designers Seymour Chwast (b.
1931), Reynold Ruffins (19302021), and Edward Sorel (b.
1929).
Chwast treated familiar visual symbols and associations in new and often ironic ways using caricature and odd juxtapositions, not dissimilar from the collage techniques of Dada artists in the interwar period.
Chwasts work also could have a subversive edge  his designs protesting the United States involvement in Vietnam took shape during a competition for anti-war posters sponsored by the journal Avant Garde in 1968.
His entry (fig.
13.42) is reminiscent of early nineteenth-century wood-type posters with a centered layout and a variety of display lettering including sans and slab serif as well as shaded type in what appears to be a deliberately unsophisticated approach to design that borrows stock images for a seated soldier and matronly woman.
The text, emphasizing the words war, business, and invest, is a reference to the military-industrial complex that benefitted from armament contracts and that was criticized by anti-war protesters for an indifference to the growing number of casualties and motivations for the extended conflict.
Both in content and in form, Chwasts poster mocks the political and the graphic design establishment.
Seymour Chwast, Graphic Statement about War, 1967.
The work of Glaser, Chwast, and Lubalin, along with the journals they art-directed or contributed to such as Avant Garde and Eros, raises questions about visual communication in the 1960s, in particular whether the challenges such work presents to authority were directed toward the profession of graphic design or whether they also were politically motivated and activist in nature.
While references to racial inequality or to the anti-Vietnam war posters in Avant Garde were in sympathy with protest movements and grassroots resistance during the 1960s, their appearance on the pages of magazines with limited circulation rather than posted on the streets as propaganda or calls to action may suggest a limited impact outside of the professional design community.
Freedom of expression in graphic design does not always equate with or translate into active political dissent and the risks of direct confrontation with authority.
What emerges from the study of such work is that it operates outside of the professional parameters of the International Typographic Style and the New Advertising, whose practice is less able to accommodate fresh, and at times unsettling, approaches to visual communication.
The term underground is sometimes used to refer to this type of work, extending to comics, graffiti, and other work discussed below (see here onward) in the 1970s and beyond.

## Chapter
14 Dimensions of Mass Culture Planned obsolescence remained a guiding principle in industrial design for the mass market, but during the 1960s many products relinquished flamboyance and playful novelty in favor of greater standardization and conformity.
Appliances such as washing machines, refrigerators, electric toasters, and clothes dryers abandoned earlier bulbous or even streamlined housings for rectangular forms and sharp angles rather than rounded edges  an aesthetic change related at least in part to new developments in sheet metal fabrication.
Dashboard-like controls and instrument panels followed the lead of more restrained electronic products such as radios or televisions.
As a result, appliances could also more readily appear built-in, part of a unified and space-saving ensemble for the laundry or kitchen (fig.
14.1).
Color and accessories offered variety, but the range of choices was carefully managed among manufacturers and added little to production cost; at the same time greater overall uniformity reduced the form-giving role of the industrial designer in terms of styling and invention.

## 14.1 Advertisement for built-in kitchen appliances, Frigidaire company, Dayton, Ohio. Bett
er Homes and Gardens, March, 1962.
Equally noticeable during the 1960s was homogeneity in the Detroit automobile industry.
The differentiation provided by chrome detailing and flamelike tailfins in the 1950s was replaced by more rectangular body designs and less distinctive variation among models and brands.
Color options and interior accessories (such as jet-age bucket seats separated by instrument consoles) still allowed consumers to customize their purchases, but body styling was constrained by the risks of increased production costs and the fear of repeating failures such as the 1958 Ford Edsel (see here).
In place of variety in styling, the Big Three American automobile manufacturers  Chrysler, General Motors, and Ford  introduced a series of new compact cars such as the Ford Falcon, Plymouth Valiant, Chevrolet Corvair, and Chevy II, marketed primarily as second vehicles emphasizing economy and practicality (fig.
14.2).
A family-pleaser—with a price to match—It's THE NEW Chevy II Advertisement for Chevrolet Compact automobiles, General Motors Corporation.
Better Homes and Gardens, March, 1962.
More organic and tapered than many contemporary American automobiles of the 1960s, Raymond Loewys design for the upscale Studebaker Avanti (fig.
14.3) received much critical acclaim for its sculpted contour and innovative fiberglass body, but did not find a niche in a luxury market dominated by the barge-like General Motors Cadillac or Lincoln Continental of the early 1960s and their strong brand identity and loyalty.
Despite Loewys name value as a noted industrial design celebrity and the companys efforts to compete with lower-priced compact models with its Lark model, in 1964 the Studebaker Corporation finally went the way of Hudson, Kaiser, Packard, and other independent automobile manufacturers.
As a result, even fewer North American competitors remained to challenge the automobile giants.
14.3 Raymond Loewy, Avanti, Studebaker Motor Company, South Bend, Indiana, 1962–1963.

## Mass
Design and the Home: Progress and Criticism During the 1960s industrial designers applied new materials technologies to expand the range of new domestic products marketed to reduce housework and provide for individual aesthetic choice.
At the 1964 New York Worlds Fair, the Formica Company, owned from 1957 by the giant chemical corporation American Cyanamid, created a series of model kitchens for the companys Worlds Fair House.
Formica, a form of hard plastic laminate attached to plywood backing for tables and countertops, was manufactured in an ever-increasing array of colors, patterns, and textures to suit a wide variety of tastes, including simulated natural and traditional finishes such as wood, marble, and other types of stone.
Formicas success was contemporary with a similar expansion of varied textures and patterns for vinyl flooring suitable for game rooms, kitchens, and enclosed patios, and touted for the ease of cleaning and maintenance with household products such as Mr.
Clean and Spic and Span. Moreover, vinyl flooring, Formica, and plywood paneling appeared in popular magazine advertisements and continued to be featured in articles as prefabricated do-it-yourself products, manufactured in sizes to conform to the standardized dimensions of suburban housing tracts for ease of installation, maintenance, and remodeling projects (fig.
14.4).
More futuristic was the Monsanto House of the Future, built in 1957 in Disneyland and displayed at the 1964 New York Worlds Fair.
The Monsanto House was constructed almost entirely of molded plastics, with curved walls and large expanses of glass, raised above ground level to emphasize the materials lightness and suggest a connection to the space age.
The kitchen included plastic dishware and push-button kitchen controls to activate lighting, cabinet doors, and automated appliances.
Advertisement for masonite wall paneling, Masonite Corporation, Chicago, Illinois.
Better Homes and Gardens, January, 1962.
A backlash against synthetics in fabrics and products also emerged during the 1960s, part of a countercultural reaction to the environmental dangers of pesticides and the use of chemical weapons (such as Agent Orange, also manufactured by Monsanto) during the Vietnam War.
With at least some of the health and environmental risks of chemicals addressed and monitored through EPA standards and other regulatory agencies beginning in the mid-1970s, the link between chemistry, new materials, and design remained strong.
Today, synthetic products continue to fuel the mass homeimprovement and do-it-yourself markets, contributing to the nationwide success of large outlets such as Home Depot, Lowes, and more specialized suppliers.
Wall-coverings, paneling, cabinets, ceramic and lapidary tiles, and window blinds are only a sample of the myriad products used in home remodeling and decorating that offer variety and a steady stream of new variations that appeal to consumer tastes in home as well as other self-improvement industries.
Rising thresholds of comfort, convenience, and privacy, new materials and techniques of application that narrow the gap between professional and amateur, and the satisfaction of participating in the process of selection and installation combine to make home improvement an integral component of middle-class homeowning, and an example of the role design plays in our ordinary lives.
Former negative associations between synthetic products and kitsch tend not to apply so strictly to such products: increasingly industrially manufactured marble or leather can simulate their natural counterparts without obvious detectable difference, undermining both the aesthetic and social distinctions between real and fake, and rendering less obvious the meanings of authenticity and truth to materials. As seen in figure 14.4, the advertising for many of these products during the 1960s often featured women either marveling at their new products or dressed to play hostess, notwithstanding challenges to traditional gender stereotypes that emerged for instance in Betty Friedans 1963 book The Feminine Mystique and in the womens liberation movement.
During the 1960s, women debated and protested sexual discrimination and actively rebelled against gender stereotypes socialized through education and the mass media.
Certainly the marketing of home products at the time may be seen as a form of social control, tied to traditional associations with womens roles in the nuclear family and personal fulfillment within rather than outside of the home.
Toward the end of the decade the playful, inclusive, and creative element in mainstream consumer culture was also being recognized in books such as architects Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown, and Steven Izenours Learning from Las Vegas (based upon travels and teaching beginning in 1966, published in 1972).
These authors, in addition to coining the phrase less is a bore (appropriating and refashioning Mies van der Rohes Modernist encomium to reduction less is more), embraced the existing man-made, eclectic, artificial, and blatantly commercial billboards, neon signs, glitz, historical references, and sensory immediacy of the Las Vegas strip and its casinos.
Formica, vinyl flooring and tiles, avocado-colored electric frypans, and plywood paneling also provided a creative outlet and promised self-fulfillment for many middle-class homeowners, and represented a popular form of the expansion and democratization of leisure in post-war America.
Learning from Las Vegas questioned the aesthetic and ethical pretensions of international Modernism in the post-war period and argued for a more sociable understanding of design that probed hierarchical distinctions between good design and recognized the attraction of the products of popular culture.

## Capitalism
as Deception?
In addition to racial discrimination and class inequality that called into question the beneficial relationship between design, technology, and democracy, Marxist critics continued to argue that the increasing comfort associated with the domestic interior amounted to self-deception rather than liberation.
In their view privacy and comfort do little more than hide an often empty, insecure, and unsettling existence, reinforcing social control and conformity, all outgrowths of business practice in a capitalist system that exacerbates income (and racial) inequality and is increasingly closed off to avenues for self-realization other than consumption and materialism (see here).
Even the family is not immune from this critique, since the hegemony of the nuclear family is a twentieth-century (rather than universal) phenomenon that constructs a separation between work and leisure, private and public, which is itself artificial and normative only within advanced capitalism.
Marxist critics claimed that the advent of electronic media such as television and film only erodes the publics ability to discern the capitalist agenda at work amid increasingly seductive forms of communication and advertising, and as the alliance of big business and government consolidates rather than diffuses political and economic power.
For these reasons the apparent material and social progress of post-war Western democracies as promoted at Worlds Fairs and in advertising concealed inequities in the distribution of wealth and economic opportunity, not only within Western societies but globally as well.
Within their professional community, some designers questioned the partnership between art, business, government, and the promise of social as well as material progress that characterized more than a decade of expanded production, exhibition, and consumption following World War II.
In 1964, and with the signatures of several colleagues, graphic designer Ken Garland (19292021) published the manifesto First Things First that was reprinted in the journal Design and received notice in the British newspaper the Guardian.
Garlands text documents the self-examination and search for alternatives within the profession: We, the undersigned, are graphic designers, photographers and students who have been brought up in a world in which the techniques and apparatus of advertising have persistently been presented to us as the most lucrative, effective and desirable means of using our talents.
We have been bombarded with publications devoted to this belief, applauding the work of those who have flogged their skill and imagination to sell such things as: cat food, stomach powders, detergent, hair restorer, striped toothpaste, aftershave lotion, beforeshave lotion, slimming diets, fattening diets, deodorants, fizzy water, cigarettes, roll-ons, pull-ons, and slip-ons.
By far the greatest efforts of those working in the advertising industry are wasted on these trivial purposes, which contribute little or nothing to our national prosperity.
In common with an increasing number of the general public, we have reached a saturation point at which the high-pitched scream of consumer selling is no more than sheer noise.
We think that there are other things more worth using our skill and experience on.
There are signs for streets and buildings, books and periodicals, catalogs, instructional manuals, industrial photography, educational aids, films, television features, scientific and industrial publications and all the other media through which we promote our trade, our education, our culture and our greater awareness of the world.
We do not advocate the abolition of high-pressure consumer advertising: this is not feasible.
Nor do we want to take any of the fun out of life.
But we are proposing a reversal of priorities in favour of the more useful and more lasting forms of communication.
We hope that our society will tire of gimmick merchants, status salesmen and hidden persuaders, and that the prior call on our skills will be for worthwhile purposes.
With this in mind we propose to share our experience and opinions, and to make them available to colleagues, students and others who may be interested. signed: Edward Wright, Geoffrey White, William Slack, Caroline Rawlence, Ian McLaren, Sam Lambert, Ivor Kamlish, Gerald Jones, Bernard Higton, Brian Grimbly, John Garner, Ken Garland, Anthony Froshaug, Robin Fior, Germano Facetti, Ivan Dodd, Harriet Crowder, Anthony Clift, Gerry Cinamon, Robert Chapman, Ray Carpenter, Ken Briggs First Things First was tame, even gentle, in comparison with later condemnations of industrial design by Victor Papanek and others (see here).
Nevertheless it demonstrates a renewal of ethically motivated initiatives in design, suggesting that corporate communication and the responsible attitude toward advertising championed by International Typographic Style advocates no longer automatically qualified as worthwhile purposes, and that voices within the design community were rethinking the relationship between designers, technology, business, and progress.
But while a consumer culture certainly has its dangers and excesses, it has not precluded alternative approaches and strategies for design, including efforts aimed at social and environmental responsibility, and numerous forms of resistance and subversion.
Indeed, many recent discussions of mass culture focus upon an active and independent rather than passive role for both designer and consumer and a rethinking of the dynamics of production and consumption.
Responses to popular culture cannot always be programmed, as noted by Venturi, Scott Brown, and Izenour in Learning from Las Vegas: You can like billboards without approving of strip mining in Appalachia. Whether in the late nineteenth century or in the later twentieth century, and whether as a response to early or advanced industrialization, the appreciation for and creative use of materials and processes by designers, craftspeople, and ordinary renters or homeowners remains a tribute to the dynamism, diversity, and inclusiveness of consumer culture.
Without this complex, multi-layered character, such design forms could not exert their mass appeal nor provide avenues of resistance.
Some of these alternative readings and interpretations of the phenomenon of mass culture are considered below.

## Mass
Design: The Fringes Stimulated by the mass media of television, radio, and film, European countries, and in particular Britain, first absorbed and then contributed to and even dominated the expanding youth market for commodities and an insatiable appetite for the products of the music industry.
Economic recovery and growth during the later 1950s and 1960s in Europe challenged traditional class boundaries as well as social norms of behavior, finding expression in clothing, dance, film, and music, and emphasized freedom of expression predominantly through taste in fashion and popular music.
Occasionally reaction to the new youth culture resulted in condemnation and even censorship, but such initial threats to established social norms were often followed by tolerance and wider imitation, acceptance, and commercial exploitation.
Subgroups formed on the fringes of a generalized youth movement directed toward greater permissiveness and less inhibited self-expression.
As argued by British historian Arthur Marwick, an increasingly heterogeneous youth culture was joined by other marginal groups in the 1960s, including racial minorities, women, and the gay community, each with a strong desire for acknowledgment and recognition.
Rebellions against inhibitions and prohibitions during this period ranged from skirt lengths and marijuana use to support for abortion, freedom of speech, lowering the voting age, and opposition to the death penalty, racial discrimination, homophobia, and national foreign policy  for instance the United Statess involvement in the Vietnam War.
Media coverage of fringe or subculture activity in mass circulation magazines and television accompanied public demonstrations throughout the 1960s, increasing awareness.
Recognition of difference not only applied to popular culture, but could also be seen in the fine arts, where the splintering of the avant-garde and the emergence of galleries on the American West Coast contrasted with modern arts identification with abstract art and the dominance of the New York-based art world during most of the 1950s.
Mustang convertible, Ford Motor Company, Dearborn, Michigan, 1965.
New attitudes and behaviors were easily commercially exploited or commodified as fashion products and accessories, taming to a certain degree the threat of activism and confrontation with authority.
Even in the increasingly conservative and homogeneous United States automobile industry there were some popular successes stemming from a hedonistic youth culture, for instance the Ford Mustang (fig.
14.5), manufactured toward the end of 1964 and appealing to an expanding audience with features such as tapered concave cutaway door panels derived from earlier sports cars such as the Chevrolet Corvette.
The legendary appeal of the Pontiac GTO, introduced in 1964, was based more upon a powerful V-8 engine than its conventional rectangular body, and the exhilaration of pushing the speed limit was much celebrated in popular youth culture, embellished with customized flamelike pinstriping in the work of Kenny Howard (19291992; aka Von Dutch) or as the subject of the rock music hit Little GTO, recorded by Ronny and the Daytonas in 1964.
The song was a Top 40 hit in the United States, complete with simulated motor sounds: Little GTO, youre really lookin fine Three deuces and a four-speed and a 389 Listen to her tachin up now, listen to her why-ee-eye-ine Cmon and turn it on, wind it up, blow it out GTO.
Other examples of a non-conformist, youth-oriented popular culture in the period emerged early on in the world of fashion in England.
British designer and entrepreneur Mary Quant (b.
1934) designed and sold clothing aimed at young buyers, based upon simple, even traditional pinafore patterns but featuring higher hemlines, bold colors, and fashion accessories such as dark fishnet stockings and knee-length leather boots, creating a look associated with an active and rebellious lifestyle (fig.
14.7).
Quant has been credited with inventing the miniskirt and with helping to launch the careers of international models such as Twiggy in the mid-1960s who exemplified the new style, as well as with influencing the trend toward more youthful approaches to fashion among some Parisian haute-couture designers.
Such crossovers in taste occurred as well in fine art with the success of Pop Art and celebrity artists such as Andy Warhol (19281987).
Warhols oeuvre was quite varied, ranging from serial images of mass-produced Campbells soup cans or Brillo boxes that challenge notions of originality, to more politically charged work such as his series of stark, black-and-white silkscreen images taken from press photographs of suicide victims, fatal car accidents, and the electric chair chamber that provide a grim commentary on violence in the United States, where the grainy quality of the image and its repetition also demonstrate a combination of sensationalism with the often numbing fatigue of mass media exposure (fig.
14.6).
That such images retained a political edge in the early 1960s was demonstrated at the 1964 New York Worlds Fair when city officials whitewashed Warhols monumental mural of the 13 most-wanted criminals in America, commissioned for the façade of the New York State pavilion (the pavilion still stands).
Strategies employed by Pop artists used the familiar forms of commercial and news photography aswell as other techniques of massproduced imagery; like their counterparts in the rock music industry, Pop Art expanded the base of a new, vernacular art.
Integrating mass media imagery, cultivating celebrity and branding, the Pop Art phenomenon expanded beyond the rarefied space of the gallery and appears as the motivation behind happenings, performance art, earthworks, and other artistic efforts that promoted freedom of expression and mobilized creative engagement for a more broad-based audience.
14.6 Andy Warhol, Little Electric Chair, acrylic and silkscreen inks on canvas, 22 × 28 in (55.9 × 71.1 cm), 1965.
Private collection.
Mary Quant (center) and models presenting the “Viva Viva” line, Milan, 1967.
In music, the early recordings of Liverpool-based band the Beatles demonstrate a complete assimilation and mastery of 1950s forms of rock n roll music from the United States.
The bands performance skills and gifts for original songwriting achieved an unprecedented degree of international attention, in part through the marketing efforts of the groups manager, Brian Epstein (19341967).
The Beatles moplike hairstyles and modish clothing, live concerts, movies, and newsreel and television interviews were significant elements in disseminating not only their music but also a lifestyle that added to the allure and mystique of mass media celebrity.
By the mid-1960s, youth-oriented and American-inspired popular culture had not only become an international phenomenon, but had also expanded beyond its youthful audience, as popular weekly television variety programs such as the prime-time Sunday evening Ed Sullivan Show began to feature rock n roll bands as part of their regular entertainment, broadcast from New York and targeting mainstream audiences more than the daily lateafternoon, Philadelphia-based American Bandstand.
In addition to the wave of British rock n roll groups, Detroit-based (Motown) Black singing groups reached a national audience, including the Temptations, the Supremes, and the Four Tops.
The success of soul music for a broad national audience via the mass media stood in contrast to racial tension and increasing outbreaks of violence in American industrial cities and with the emergence of Black separatist movements, who reacted impatiently to the slow pace of economic and social progress for minorities, and who rejected the ideology of integration and assimilation in favor of a more independent and often more threatening African American identity.

## Pop,
Protest, and Counterculture The broad and varied role of rock music in the 1960s can hardly be overestimated.
From general sexual permissiveness and self-expression among youth and those older groups wishing to identify with a more modern, open lifestyle, to non-conformism and rebelliousness by some subculture groups finding an outlet in hairstyles and fashion or advocacy for drugs, to political and social activism, this most accessible medium of rock music involved an active, engaging role for the audience.
In short, the 1960s maxim do your own thing did not mean the same thing to everyone.
Amid growing racial tensions in large American cities such as Los Angeles and Detroit, reaction to the escalation of US involvement in the Vietnam War, worker strikes and student protests both in Europe and the United States, the politics of Pop Art and rock music appeared as part of a wider struggle of artists and designers to engage the mass media and public opinion in the interests of personal expression or wider political and social activism.

## Undercurrents:
Graphics and the Underground In addition to rock music concerts, festivals and happenings, protest movements and youth gatherings produced a number of distinctive cultural expressions in the field of graphic design outside of the parameters of mainstream professional practice.
The demonstrations and disruptive confrontations between police and students on college campuses over issues of free speech and the United Statess involvement in Vietnam were high-profile media events, performances, and provocations akin to art-world happenings and hard-rock concerts, a world where guitars were occasionally smashed and American flags burned, culminating in the 1969 gathering at Woodstock in upstate New York and in the currency of the term counterculture. Posters were a part of popular communication and protest in the later 1960s, accompanying the public sitins, demonstrations, and concerts in cities and on pedestrian-friendly university campuses throughout the United States and Europe.
Poster forms were also adopted for album covers for rock music groups.
Many poster designs eschewed precise, hard-edged letterforms and gridded layouts in favor of a more calligraphic and elastic typography inspired by Art Nouveau and blending lettering with illustration.
An example is Robert Wesley (Wes) Wilsons (19372020) poster for the Otis Rush/Grateful Dead/Canned Heat concert held at San Franciscos Fillmore Auditorium in 1967 (fig.
14.8; see also fig.
13.39).
Wilsons posters employed strong figureground reversals that reduced legibility and mirrored the experience of stroboscopic lightshows that often accompanied live concerts.
Psychedelic posters were often printed in small format and were equally found on the walls of dormitories or apartments as on the street.
Moreover the lettering, while inventive, also at times verged on the illegible, ignoring one of the functions of the poster medium for immediacy in identifying a product or service quickly and directly.
Whether in two or three dimensions, in still or moving images, such psychedelic effects were meant to intensify the underground drug experience popular among youth during the later 1960s and 1970s.
Techniques referencing 1960s drug culture appear on the cover of the Beatles 1967 album Sergeant Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, by Peter Blake and Janna Haworth (with photographer Michael Cooper), where a photomontage juxtaposes a collection of past and present movie stars and celebrities, reminiscent of the technique of Dada collage (rather than more simplified uses of the technique in the interwar period, see figs 9.49 and 9.50), and provides a visual analogue for insider references to psychedelic drugs contained in the lyrics for a number of the tracks on the album, for instance, the popular drug LSD in the track Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds (fig.
14.9).
14.8 Wes Wilson, concert poster, silkscreen print, 1967.
Peter Blake and Janna Haworth, Sergeant Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, album cover, 1967.
Underground graphics also include the illustrations by a number of artists including Robert Crumb (b.
1943).
Many images, such as Crumbs well-known Keep on Truckin’ (c.
1971) with its striding foreshortened foot, reached a popular audience via bumper stickers and decals.
Their origin, however, may be traced to the very private and often scurrilous world of underground comic books, from where they migrated to record jackets and a broader audience.
An example is Crumbs 1968 Cheap Thrills (fig.
14.10), an album cover featuring rock singer Janis Joplin performing with the band Big Brother and the Holding Company; originally the album was titled Sex, Dope, and Cheap Thrills, a title Columbia Records refused to allow.
Other subcultures of the era included the gay community and womens movements, directed toward inclusion and equal opportunity, 14.10 Robert Crumb, album cover for Cheap Thrills by Janis Joplin with Big Brother and the Holding Company, 1968.

## Posters
and Political Engagement in Poland In Soviet bloc countries on the other side of the Iron Curtain, posters constituted a significant popular art form, as in Poland after World War II during the decades of communist control (19451989), but more particularly after Stalins death in 1953.
Amid occasional censorship, a generation of artists who remained in Poland after World War II produced posters for state-sponsored theaters, film houses, and other forms of public entertainment.
Most of the designers were graduates of art schools rather than technical or industrial arts institutions, and they brought with them highly individual sensibilities to poster design.
The Polish poster phenomenon is yet another example of the varied nature of design under Soviet communism (see here).
For film posters, Polish designers eschewed many promotional Hollywood poster conventions that focused upon the identity and celebrity of film stars; neither were they forced to adopt the idealized and heroic illustrational approaches of socialist realism (see here).
Rather, artists exercised considerable personal freedom without specific commercial pressures or restrictive oversight.
An example is Jan Lenicas (19282000) 1964 poster for the international film The Visit (fig.
14.11), directed by Bernhard Wicki and starring Ingrid Bergman and Anthony Quinn, in which a female figure appears to morph into a menacing monarch butterfly, while a blurred face appears trapped in the figures right wing.
The treatment of the wings resembles the colors and design of European medieval stained glass, while the imagery and its varied associations serve as a metaphor for the films plot, in which a wealthy woman returns to a village to seek revenge on the man who fathered her child.
Compare, for instance, an American poster advertising the same film (fig.
14.12) Jan Lenica, The Visit, film poster, four-color offset print, 23 × 33 in (58.4 × 83.8 cm), 1964.
Private collection.
14.12 Anonymous, poster for The Visit, 1964.
Some artists left Poland for the West during the 1960s, but in the 1970s Polish posters began to acquire political overtones as growing labor movements questioned and eventually rebelled against repressive communist state control.
Jerzy Janiszewskis (b.
1952) logo for the Solidarity labor union (c.
1980; fig.
14.13) evokes in its sweeping and uneven strokes and drips the disruptive nature of public graffiti and suggests a banner-waving phalanx.
Not all Polish poster artists were sensitive to typography in their work, but Janiszewski, representing a second generation of poster artists, exploits the expressive and suggestive use of lettering as image.
In retrospect it seems ironic that such a vibrant and public form of popular resistance in graphic design thrived within a repressive political regime that came to an end with Polish independence in 1989.
14.13 Jerzy Janiszewski, Solidarity logo, c.
1980.

## Anti-Design
in Italy In 1968, student protestors and workers staged demonstrations in Milan, disrupting the Fourteenth Milan Triennale and forcing an early closing of this major international showcase for modern industrial design.
Protests, strikes, and sit-ins took place in many Italian cities during that year: on university campuses student demonstrators rebelled against authoritarian administrations and biased admissions policies, and in factories workers organized for higher wages in response to frustrated expectations for higher standards of living.
In solidarity with students and workers, a number of Italian industrial designers began to view their role in the creation of sophisticated and expensive domestic objects as part of a repressive collaboration between government and corporate interests that reinforced class distinction, fueled commodity consumption for the wealthy, and betrayed working-class hopes that the benefits of industrial design and increased production would accrue to the many rather than to the few.
In sympathy with unrest on campuses and in factories (at Fiat and Pirelli, for instance), designers looked to alternative strategies that might reshape their relation to society (on Ettore Sottsasss role in this movement, see here).
The theme of protest figured in the design exhibition Italy: The New Domestic Landscape held at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1972, curated by Argentinian architect and designer Emilio Ambasz (b.
1943).
It included both new and familiar examples of post-war modern Italian design in furniture, lighting, and product housings featuring molded plastics and abstract sculptural forms (see figs.
13.8, 13.14), as well as a section devoted to flexible modular designs for apartment seating and storage.
An additional category, however, was titled objects selected for their sociocultural implications, which Ambasz defined as follows: The second ... attitude is motivated by a profound concern for the designers role in a society that fosters consumption as one means of inducing individual happiness, thereby ensuring social stability.
Torn by the dilemma of having been trained as creators of objects, and yet being incapable of controlling either the significance or the ultimate uses of these objects, they find themselves unable to reconcile the conflicts between their social concerns and their professional practices.
They have thus developed a rhetorical mode to cope with these contradictions.
Convinced that there can be no renovation of design until structural changes have occurred in society, but not attempting to bring these about themselves, they do not invent substantially new forms; instead they engage in rhetorical operation of redesigning conventional objects with new, ironic, and sometimes self-deprecatory sociocultural and aesthetic references.
In addition to individual designers represented in this section, a number of design groups also were included, such as Archizoom and Superstudio, both founded in the later 1960s and devoted to experimental ideas in architecture and design, with collaboration replacing manufacturers marketing of individual star industrial designers.
Ambaszs essay and displays of experimental industrial design in the 1972 MoMA exhibition suggest that the meaning of designed products lies not only in their physical form but also in their relationship with users; in this context appropriating references to American consumer culture engaged the critical distinction between high and popular culture and might also be seen as an affront to the refined international Modernist sensibility.
Paolo Lomazzi, Donato DUrbino, and Jonathan De Pass Joe chair (1970/1), made of polyurethane foam covered in leather in the shape of a baseball mitt (fig.
14.14), eschewed the sophisticated abstraction of much contemporary Italian furniture and referenced images of banal consumer products associated with post-war American affluence and leisure.
According to Andrea Branzi (b.
1938), a founding member of Archizoom, one of the intentions of such objects was to appropriate and invert the message of popular culture, to create a design situation in which consumption coincides with opposition. Blatantly replacing the aesthetics of nonobjective abstraction with exaggerated decorative or representational elements drawn from luxurious Art Deco or American popular culture such as the model dream beds and interiors designed by Archizoom, these designers, whether individually or as members of a group, were operating outside of accepted parameters for industrial design as they developed in post-World War II Italy.
It is not difficult to see parallels for such subversive interpretations of banal objects in fine art of the same period.
For instance, Claes Oldenburg (b.
1929) also produced installations or environments of everyday objects and furniture, a strategy employed in the contemporary art world to move outside the white walls of conventional New York galleries and to more actively engage the spectator.
Such projects included his Bedroom Ensemble (1963; fig.
14.15), which featured diagonal rather than square beds and dressing tables, constructed of wood and covered in lively, clashing surface patterns of manufactured Formica, not unlike a walk-in Pop Art assemblage by Tom Wesselman (19312004; fig.
14.16).
Again, the acceptance of popular culture and open-mindedness to heterogeneity, playfulness, and multiple readings of cultural artifacts provide the basis for a new kind of artistic freedom involving greater participation on the part of the spectator.
Flaunting elements of kitsch through decoration and imitation materials, Oldenburgs Bedroom Ensemble transgressed the notions of good or highbrow taste and a linear modern design canon or trajectory.
14.14 Paolo Lomazzi, Donato D’Urbino, and Jonathan De Pas, Joe chair, polyurethane foam covered with leather, width 65 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (167 cm), manufactured by Poltronova (Pistoia, Italy), 1970/1.
14.15 Claes Oldenburg, Bedroom Ensemble, Replica 1, installation, 303 × 512 × 845 in (770 × 1,300 × 2,146 cm), 1969.
(Original installation 1963, Whitney Museum of American Art, New York.) Tom Wesselman, Still Life Number 30, oil, enamel, and synthetic polymer paint on composition board with collage of printed advertisements, plastic flowers, refrigerator door, plastic replicas of 7-Up bottles, glazed and framed color reproduction, and stamped metal, 48 <sup>1</sup>/ × 66 × 4 in (122 × 167.5 × 10 cm), 1963.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
Even where a dialogue or association with abstract sculpture might exist, such readings are subverted or opened to multiple interpretations.
An example is Gaetano Pesces (b.
1939) Donna chair, designed in 1969 and manufactured between 1970 and 1973 by Cassina and Busnelli (fig.
14.17).
The Donna chair, constructed of polyurethane foam covered with a nylon jersey fabric, brings to mind earlier post-war chairs with female names by Italian designers, most notably Marco Zanusos 1951 Lady chair (see fig.
11.51).
Its concave and convex forms are suggestive of the female form as evoked in Neolithic fertility figures as well as in the contemporary abstract sculpture of Henry Moore and allusions to universal human themes.
Yet the round ottoman attached to the chair with a cord alludes to a feminist reading.
As Pesce wrote: In this design I have expressed my idea of women.
A woman is always confined, a prisoner of herself against her will.
For this reason I wanted to give this chair the shape of a woman with a ball chained to her foot to use the traditional image of a prisoner.
One also recognizes that the works Ambasz characterized as sociocultural in intent were rhetorical rather than practical or commercial.
Most anti-design activities were not intended primarily for consumption: generally designers wished to liberate themselves from a repressive system in which they felt their efforts were circumscribed, and used exhibitions to provoke and undermine the practices of consumers and manufacturers alike.
Some, such as Enzo Mari (19322020), were more interested in language than in products, and viewed inactivity itself as a political stance; Mari produced a polemical essay rather than a physical environment for MoMAs 1972 exhibition.
While appropriating popular culture as subversion and advocating radical political change, the activities of this anti-design rarely extended beyond the boundaries of exhibition spaces, catalogs, and journals, with exceptions such as the amorphous and portable Sacco or beanbag chairs designed by the firm of Gatti, Paolini, Teodoro in 1968 to 1969.
The relation of most anti-design experiments to workers strikes, student protests, and other more direct forms of activism was often distant, rarely sharing the real-life dangers and confrontation on the front lines, although the boycott and demonstrations at the 1968 Triennale in Milan suggests that the militant spirit of the later 1960s in Italy did indeed have design practice as a target.

## Design
Activism: Safety, Technology, and the Environment The 1960s marked the resurgence of strategies to redirect the practice of the corporatebased industrial design community toward public and environmental responsibility, often calling attention in urgent terms to universal concerns with hunger, poverty, and safety on a global scale.
Calls for radical change ranged from consumer safety to a wider variety of technologies to improve living conditions in industrially less developed countries, to futuristic, utopian visions based upon an awareness and more efficient use of the worlds limited natural resources.
Criticism of design issued both from within and from outside the design community and often resonated with a public mobilized by articulate spokespeople and activists, advocating for the rights of consumers, better treatment of minorities, and a general skepticism if not outright hostility toward corporations and government.
The political impact of grassroots and other fringe movements remains part of our understanding of the 1960s, part of the perceived ability of ordinary citizens to effect change through strikes, sit-ins, rallies, boycotts, DIY efforts, and engaging the cameras and microphones of the mass media.
In general, radical design efforts stemmed from an ideological confrontation between the optimism and affluence of the post-war American Dream and European Economic Miracle and the realities of lingering inequities and unfulfilled promises.
One form of industrial design criticism targeted large corporations on behalf of the consumers whose interests the corporation pledged to support.
A pioneer in this effort was Ralph Nader (b.
1934), whose 1965 book Unsafe at Any Speed: The Designed-In Dangers of the American Automobile attacked the General Motors Corporation for neglecting significant consumer safety issues in the design of the companys aluminum rear-engine compact Corvair model, introduced by Chevrolet in 1960.
Ironically, the Corvair was Motor Trend magazines choice as Car of the Year. According to Nader, GM had ignored evidence that the Corvair had a tendency to spin out of control under certain road conditions, even though warnings of this and other design flaws during the models development were presented to management by company engineers.
Nader argued that GM spent significant sums on styling to boost sales, while ignoring safety, product reliability, and the public welfare.
Unsafe at Any Speed, and the subsequent Senate investigation of GM efforts to silence Nader by conducting surveillance in the hope of uncovering damaging information about his character and background, made this lawyer and author a champion for the rights and ability of individuals to question corporate power and practice, and to assert their power as private citizens through the mass media, boycotts, organized protest, and litigation.
Nader extended his investigations of corporate business practice to include chemical food preservatives in popular American products such as hot dogs; in this and other cases the evidence was convincing and the result undermined consumer and public confidence in corporate responsibility.
Such efforts also eroded confidence in governments that failed to adequately regulate business and protect its citizens.
Eventually such efforts resulted in legislation requiring truthful and informative product labeling as a measure of consumer education and protection, as well as other regulatory laws and agencies.
More recently, Nader played a role in the investigation of the Boeing Corporations 737 Max passenger airplanes after two horrific crashes in 2018 and 2019 killed all 346 passengers and crew and led to the temporary grounding of all 737 Max planes.
As with the Corvair, company management had ignored or downplayed engineers warnings for passenger safety during the aircrafts redesign.
Another reaction to corporate self-interest in the American automobile industry was a steady rise in the sales of imported cars less dependent upon the marketing strategies of annual model changes by large American manufacturers.
Rather than comply with planned obsolescence, buyers could exercise freedom of choice by opting not to buy an American car.
Perhaps the best-known alternative was the small rear-engine, air-cooled Volkswagen Beetle, designed in 1937 in Germany but not manufactured there continuously until after the end of World War II (see here).
Sales of the Beetle increased during the 1960s mostly through popularity with younger buyers, while individual owners sometimes customized its standardized form through hand-painted designs rather than factory options and accessories.
Volkswagen also benefited from a clever ad campaign by the New York agency Doyle Dane Bernbach (fig.
14.18), using the slogan Think small. The large amount of white space in the 1959 ad functions as a design element to reinforce the theme of economy, but the power of the ad also resides in the absence of drivers as well as the presumption of viewer familiarity with standard automobile advertisements (see figs.
