The appeal of smaller, standardized, and fuel-efficient vehicles received a boost after 1973 when the oil-producing nations of West Asia established a cartel (the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries; OPEC) that fixed oil prices and eliminated concessions to multinational oil companies that guaranteed inexpensive oil prices in the United States.
Within a year of the formation of OPEC, fuel prices in the United States rose from below 50 cents per gallon to over one dollar.
Both directly and through television, the sight of filling stations with gas lines and public fear of shortages and dwindling natural reserves for oil also spelled disaster for the big three United States auto manufacturers, locked into design strategies favoring large-engine vehicles, unconcerned with fuel efficiency and conservation, and unprepared to respond to changing economic circumstances or to resulting consumer attitudes.
As American auto-makers struggled to make fuel economy part of a new design strategy, foreign manufacturers became increasingly competitive.
Perhaps the biggest winner in the automobile market was Japanese manufacturer Honda, whose 1975 Civic met consumer expectations in a new era of fuel economy (fig.
14.19).
The rival Japanese Nissan Motor Company Ltd.
(under the brand name Datsun), as well as Toyota, also provided economical alternatives to gas-guzzling Detroit models, earning a foothold in the large North American market that has continued to expand with imports from South Korea.
These companies have weathered criticism by building production facilities in the United States in response to fears about the loss of jobs, added higher-end brands to compete in the luxury market, and maintained a reputation not only for efficiency but also for mechanical reliability.
The re-issue and updating of the Volkswagen Beetle, Morris Mini, and Fiat 500 in the late twentieth and early twenty-first century are but more examples of the persistence (and adaptability) of post-World War II concerns for economy and affordability in the automobile industry.
Honda Motor Company, Hamamatsu, Honda Civic automobile, 147 1<sup>3</sup>/ × 59 <sup>1</sup>/ × 52 <sup>1</sup>/ in (375 × 150.5 × 132 cm), American Honda Motor Company Inc., Torrance, California, 1975.
Urgency and anger directed at industrial design in the 1960s appears in the preface of a book published in 1971, Victor Papaneks Design for the Real World: There are professions more harmful than industrial design, but only a very few of them.
And possibly only one profession is phonier.
Advertising design, in persuading people to buy things they dont need, with money they dont have, in order to impress others who dont care, is probably the phoniest field in existence today.
Industrial design, by concocting the tawdry idiocies hawked by advertisers, comes a close second...
By designing criminally unsafe automobiles that kill or maim nearly one million people around the world each year, by creating whole new species of permanent garbage to clutter up the landscape, and by choosing materials and processes that pollute the air we breathe, designers have become a dangerous breed.
And the skills needed in these activities are taught carefully to young people.
Austrian-born and British-educated Papanek (19261998) was an outspoken critic of styling and obsolescence in industrial design, advocating instead an approach that took account of limited natural resources and addressed needs as opposed to wants.
His views were contemporary with those of economist Ernst Schumacher (19111977), author of the book Small is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered (1973) who lobbied for a fundamental change in the direction of scientific effort, away from production and toward conservation.
Less optimistic and utopian than R.
Buckminster Fuller, who supplied the preface to Design for the Real World, Papanek tended toward the apocalyptic: whether at the macro- or micro-level, both designers envisioned a world in which governments, individuals, and grassroots organizations directed design projects for housing and products in the broad public interest for safety and the efficient or appropriate use of technologies and resources, and warned of the global effects of unlimited production and consumption in terms of population, pollution, the distribution of wealth, and environmental hazards.
Fuller also lamented the lost opportunities for designers to play a more active role in meeting basic needs in developing countries.
The gravity, and the relevance, of Papaneks hopes and fears for design emerge again in this passage from Design for the Real World: Isnt it too bad that so little design, so few products are really relevant to the needs of mankind?
Watching the children of Biafra dying in living color while sipping a frostbeaded martini can be kicks for lots of people, but only until their town starts burning down.
To an engaged designer, this way of life, this lack of design, is not acceptable.
Papanek attempted to restore or to redirect a sense of purpose to design as an activity integral to the survival of the planet in environmental as well as in social terms.
Papaneks urgency reminds one of Le Corbusiers provocative and polemical question at the conclusion of Towards a New Architecture: Architecture or Revolution? Papanek also allows us to recognize that terms like progress are relative and invite alternative definitions and courses for future action.
Both designers believed in the ability of design to alter the conditions of life on a global scale.
Le Corbusier believed that the machine and mechanized manufacturing held the key to realize his utopian vision, whereas Papaneks efforts were directed more toward available or low-tech applications of technologies and a do-it-yourself approach that begins with individual commitment.
He provided numerous examples of socially and environmentally directed projects that explored the problem-solving context of his approach to design and took into account local conditions and circumstances, quite independently from aesthetic considerations.
He cited, for instance, an anonymously designed low-cost stove constructed of reused automobile license plates for families in underprivileged communities, as well as a design he developed with colleague James Hennessey (19452020) for a cooling unit to keep food products fresh without the need for electricity (fig.
14.20).
Papanek directed student projects at a number of universities.
Rather than being antitechnological, Papanek encouraged designers to consider local materials and energy sources, and available rather than hi-tech solutions to design problems  solutions that enable people to help themselves rather than reinforce dependence upon massive external technological investment and the environmental, economic, and negative political consequences of such investment.
His rhetoric, much like that of Modernists before him, was militant in tone, a battle cry directed as much against the current practices of professional industrial design as toward the grassroots alternatives he proposed.
Papaneks concerns also resonated with a countercultural group of younger designers who staged protests at the design conference in Aspen, Colorado, in 1970, critical of the industrial design professions lack of political, social, and environmental engagement.
Despite some successes and increased awareness, that critique continues today in the efforts of designers of color to lobby for inclusion and change in the design professions.
Victor Papanek and James Hennessey, drawing and prototype for cooling unit for perishable foods, using no electricity, from Design for the Real World, 1971.
Papaneks message resonates in the Whole Earth Catalog published by American-born activist Stewart Brand (b.
1938) and appearing regularly between 1968 and 1972 (fig.
14.21).
The Catalog featured stories, diagrams, instructions, and products for simple living with an emphasis upon conservation and self-sufficiency.
Sections included Shelter and Land Use, Industry and Craft, Community, Understanding Whole Systems, and Learning. One might use the term empowerment to characterize the Catalogs message: such efforts continue with organizations such as Design Without Borders and other service design organizations and initiatives throughout the world.
Their relevance in the twenty-first century is found in the grassroots exhibition By the People: Designing a Better America at the Cooper Hewitt National Design Museum in 2015 (see here) and in the appointment of a curator for socially responsible design.
Stewart Brand, ed., double-page spread from Whole Earth Catalog.
Access to Tools, Menlo Park, California, spring 1970. here.
Several less radical socially responsible design efforts also emerged in Scandinavia along humanistic rather than militant lines.
One of the best-known ethically responsible design organizations is Ergonomi Design Gruppen, established in Bomma, Sweden in 1979 (Veryay since 2012, now McKinsey).
Ergonomi designs solutions for specialneeds populations that also appeal commercially to broader markets, conducting studies, for instance, to determine the strength needed for holding and gripping objects and testing prototypes to see which forms are best suited to their purpose, primarily but not exclusively from the standpoint of disabled users.
Successful designs include the 1974 knife and cutting frame made of Propene plastic and stainless steel and manufactured in Sweden by Gustavsberg (fig.
14.22).
This design, based upon the principle of a carpenters miter box, not only accomplished the specific purpose for which it was intended by safely guiding the knife and protecting a user with special needs, but also attracted wider popularity.
The Oxo line of kitchen tools (see here and fig.
16.9) issued from similar concerns with the compatibility between designing for disability and an appeal to wider markets.
14.22 Maria Benktzon and Sven-Eric Juhlin, Ergonomi Design Gruppen, knife and cutting frame, Propene plastic and steel, width 13 <sup>3</sup>/ in (35 cm), manufactured by Gustavsberg AB, Gustavsberg, Sweden, 1974.
Statens Konstmuseer, Stockholm.

## The
Future of Housing R.
Buckminster Fullers career stretched over five decades, beginning with prototypes for a mass-produced Dymaxion house and the three-wheel streamlined Dymaxion automobile displayed at the 1933 Century of Progress Worlds Fair in Chicago (see here).
Fuller believed that conservation was an industrial design imperative in the twentieth century as well as an advantage in the Cold War, and that resource awareness could be implemented in a market-driven economy.
He hoped that his lightweight geodesic domes, used during World War II by the United States military for portable barracks and deployment facilities on or near the battlefield, could meet housing shortages after the war.
These structures were fabricated from standardized triangular components that could be made from a variety of materials; they functioned as a lightweight framework to support panels, windows, or even hang fabric to provide inexpensive and portable shelter.
Like many of Fullers projects, however, geodesic domes had limited commercial success (see here) despite his promotional efforts through magazine articles, interviews, campus lectures, and television appearances.
The apotheosis of the geodesic dome was the United States Pavilion at the 1967 World Fair in Montreal, Canada, labeled the Biosphere, a symbol of American technological innovation and its near spherical form, suggestive of the age of space exploration (fig.
14.23).
Unlike the Unisphere for the 1964 Worlds Fair in New York, the spherical form was not just a sculptural symbol but a space-age transparent architectural structure constructed of steel and acrylic cells with a light monorail system connecting it to other fair pavilions.
Fuller likened its surface to a skin that breathed through the use of light-controlled motorized shades.

## 14.23 R. Buckminster Fuller, geodesic dome for United States Pavilion, Montreal, Canada, 1
967.
The possibilities of lightweight inflatable buildings also inspired a group of French architectural students to create alternatives to permanent building materials.
They envisioned portable pneumatic architecture in projects with titles such as Pneumo City, which suggested a closer relationship between nature, with air as the primary element. Their efforts emerge in British filmmaker Graham Stevenss Atmosfields and Desert Clouds (1972) featuring amorphous billowing forms floating on water and moving rather than standing still.
Despite the collectivist implications of his vision, Fullers public appearances (lectures often lasting for hours on university campuses as well as television and news magazine interviews) appealed to many youth counterculture groups, who embraced self-sufficient communal living as an alternative to either the suburban single-family dwelling or urban apartments.
Fullers career intersects with the romanticism associated with youth counterculture movements of the later 1960s and the radical views of activists who wished to redirect technology away from materialism toward the elimination of human suffering.
Both movements were motivated by idealism, but in fact the social implications of Fullers utopia were not compatible with the unbridled sensory indulgence of the hippie counterculture of the 1970s.
Yet both were in their own ways anti-establishment, part of a broad spectrum of subcultures and countercultures with an alternative vision for a future society, rethinking the uses of technology, the relationship of individuals to nature, and the meaning of progress.
In addition to Fullers Biosphere, the 1967 Montreal Worlds Fair also featured Israeli-Canadian architect Moshe Safdies (b.
1938) Habitat 67, a large-scale residential housing community that combined modern prefabricated building materials and standardized construction units with flexibility and differentiation to preserve a sense of individuality along humanistic lines (see here on the Baker House and here on the Unité dHabitation).
The Habitat 67 complex was part of Canadas contribution to the fair, used reinforced concrete, and consisted of 354 modular units rising as high as twelve stories and combined horizontally or on two connecting stories to create more than 150 residences, each with a private terrace (fig.
14.24).
Safdies design was envisioned as a model for affordable high-density housing, but costs made the apartments more expensive than predicted, and the plan was not widely adopted in the housing industry.
14.24 Moshe Safdie, Habitat 67, Montreal, 1967.
While Fullers geodesic domes failed to attract attention in the building industry and Habitat 67 remained a one-off model for urban housing, there was a boom in the construction of low-cost, high-density social housing projects and neighborhood redevelopment initiatives in the later 1950s and 1960s in a number of American cities as well as in the Soviet Union.
In the United States inner-city housing projects were built with the aim of stemming the exodus of families to suburban communities and providing modern if modest residential housing that replaced decaying and mostly minority neighborhoods and improved the quality of life for their low-income residents.
There has been widespread agreement that these massive, well-intentioned governmentsubsidized building and redevelopment projects destroyed existing structures and deteriorated due to cost-cutting in the process of their construction, and that they also, and perhaps more importantly, failed to engage residents in their design or to build a sense of neighborhood community and shared responsibility among their inhabitants.
British historian David Harvey commented that the demolition of the 1955 Pruitt-Igoe housing development in St.
Louis in 1972 signified the demise of the belief that largescale high-rise social housing in line with Modernist principles could help advance the cause of social or racial justice.
As architectural critic and urban activist Jane Jacobs noted in her 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American Cities, housing standards based upon Modernist aesthetics or social determinism were not able to effectively address the challenges of creating safe and economically viable neighborhoods and communities.
In retrospect the design process must take into account a variety of factors that include the perspectives of the population being served, the psychological effects of the environment, and zoning considerations that affect the nurturing of community.
Despite the progressive and democratic intentions of slum-clearance and the war on poverty in the 1960s, Modernist design was judged harshly by many critics as a solution for working-class urban living, representing the viewpoint of architects and planners without sufficient input from the users whose lives were affected.
While some critics attribute the failure of high-rise social housing to the arrogance of elitist urban planners out of touch with those whose needs they are supposed to serve, more recent historians acknowledge the difficulties urban planners encountered and offer a degree of respect for the wellmeaning intentions that motivated such projects.
Today the revitalization of urban neighborhoods often entails maintaining existing local businesses and attracting new ones, preserving the character of residential housing, converting warehouses to lofts or other purposes, and creating appeal for young professionals and families.
But appeal creates demand which in turn raises housing prices, making such housing affordable only to wealthier and less diverse buyers, a process usually referred to as gentrification. Housing was a concern in the communist East as well as in Western Europe and the United States.
Modernist housing blocks were constructed in the Soviet Union, East Germany, Yugoslavia, and elsewhere in communist Eastern Europe.
In Belgrade, Ljubljana, and Zagreb (now the capitals of Serbia, Slovenia, and Croatia respectively), for instance, architecture played a key role in post-war reconstruction for housing, education, and recreation under socialism.
Apartment blocks constructed in the 1950s and 1960s combined modern materials and prefabrication to meet collective needs of working-class families but also avoided crowding and provided pleasant park-like spaces for circulation and socializing.
Examples are found in the apartment blocks in the New Belgrade section of the city designed by Mihajlo Mitrovič and other architects.
Cultural programming, education, and healthcare were free services provided to citizens by the countrys government to reinforce the benefits of a socialist system.

## Chapter
15

## The
Politics of Difference: Pluralism, Postmodernism, and Expanding the Parameters of Design Practice The 1960s did not spark the social or political revolutions forecast by campus riots in the United States, student protests in France and elsewhere in Western Europe, or the disruption of the 1968 Democratic Party National Convention in Chicago.
As argued, however, by British historian and author Arthur Marwick, the challenge to authority from under-represented and marginalized minority voices, whether women, Black people, LGBTQ+ people, or students, produced more open-minded attitudes toward difference and inclusion, leading to reform through progressive legislation establishing and protecting individual rights.
In the United States, federal enforcement of the 1964 Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act, and widely broadcast demonstrations such as Martin Luther Kings 1963 March on Washington, DC brought issues of racial inequality and opportunity to national attention.
Legislation created the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1970, while the passage of laws aimed at reducing highway deaths through seatbelt laws and mandatory manufacturer recalls on defective parts and systems eventually resulted from Ralph Naders spirited challenge to unquestioned faith in corporate power.
For almost 20 years, the oil crisis of the early 1970s and concerns for fuel efficiency and automobile safety produced lower speed limits (55 mph) on many of the nations highways.
Other legislation legalized abortion (Roe vs.
Wade, 1973; since overturned in 2022 by the Supreme Court), required the reading of rights to suspects placed under arrest (Miranda vs.
Arizona, 1966), and made divorces easier to obtain.
Universities abolished quota systems for admission, and the percentage of minority students able to attend college began to rise through need- and merit-based scholarships, loans, and affirmative action laws.
Universities and colleges developed new courses and programs for the critical and historical study of film, photography, jazz, race, womens studies, and forms of popular music.
The United States Cold War policy of communist containment and soft power (see here) continued, while broad-based pressure at home among youth and in the media helped to bring an end to the drawn-out war in Vietnam, a response to the questioning of policies regarding threats to American power and influence abroad.
The same questions attended US military intervention in Iraq and Afghanistan in the wake of the attacks of September 11, 2001.
The 1960s signaled recognition of ethnic, racial, gender, and generational subcultures with distinct identities in fashion and graphic design, the latter often in connection with protests and demonstrations seeking inclusion, recognition, or social justice.
The coexistence of alternative voices is often referred to as pluralism. This shift also produced a backlash against multiculturalism and globalism that simmered and began to gain ground in the twenty-first century in response to the attacks of 9/11 and with the backing of more authoritarian, nationalist governments and renewed political division and polarization.
The role of design in relation to renewed nationalism, climate change, social justice, and other global challenges is examined in Chapter 16.

## Pluralism
and Resistance: Punk In London and elsewhere in Britain, reactions to a decaying, post-industrial landscape of the 1970s and 1980s surfaced in the behaviors, dress, and personal accessories associated with the punk movement.
Contributing factors included globalism in the growth of interconnected supply chains for goods and the outsourcing of industrial labor from developed nations to Asia and elsewhere, and the substantial growth of a service economy increasingly employing immigrant workers for low-paying jobs.
Aggressive, belligerent, destructive, and uninhibited, punk culture in music, fashion, performance, poetry, and graphic design relished provocation, celebrating graffiti, personal tattooing, and body piercing, and making exaggerated, garish use of highly commercialized products such as cosmetics, hair gels for spiked hair styles, and hair dyes to achieve unconventional effects in personal appearance that consciously triggered resentment and outrage.
The origins of the punk phenomenon may be traced to a combination of alternative popular music and the attention it received in the media.
Punk bands were promoted through underground fanzines whose content focused primarily upon band members and their fans, and the commercial London clothing store Sex, owned by Malcolm McLaren (19462010), that included fashion designs by Vivienne Westwood (b.
1941).
Artist Jamie Reids (b.
1947) cover for the single God Save the Queen (1977) by the Sex Pistols featured the bust-length black-and-white image of Queen Elizabeth II, familiar from currency and postage stamps in the UK (the album appeared in the year celebrating the Queens Silver Jubilee), defaced with letters and words torn from newspapers in the manner of a ransom note.
The cover of the fanzine Anarchy from 1976 featured a photograph (by Ray Stevenson) of Sex Pistols fan Soo Catwoman wearing a chain-like necklace, heavy lipstick and eye make-up, single hanging earring, and closely cropped hair save for spiked ears to each side held in place by ample amounts of hair gel (fig.
15.1).
As with God Save the Queen, the ransom note lettering is pure Dada, and Catwomans frontal pose defies convention and screams confrontation.
McLarens Sex shop was originally named Let it Rock; clothing included T-shirts printed with sexually explicit imagery invoking taboo pornography and bondage with chains, tight-fitting elastic and shiny materials, and an unbridled freedom of expression flaunting difference and testing (if not outright breaking) the boundaries of propriety (fig.
15.2).
Exploiting sensationalism, punk subverted mass media to gain attention and campaign for aggressive, self-destructive behaviors and identity.
But was punk subculture a revolutionary social and political movement whose antics were meant to draw attention to deteriorating urban and social conditions in Britain?
Or did the movements provocateurs seek greater inclusiveness and an outlet for personal expression?
Perhaps part of the equivocal answer can be found in the career of McLaren himself, who once remarked, Punk was just a way to sell trousers. 15.1 Soo Catwoman, cover for Anarchy in the U.K., 1976.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
Sex, shop owned by Malcolm McLaren, London, 1976.
The graphic expression of punk culture is found in the work of many artists, among them British-born Barney Bubbles (born Colin Fulcher, 19421983) and Neville Brody (b.
1957).
Brody experimented with lettering and trademarks that parody the reductive style of corporate logos, as in his 1985 logo for a London hat company (fig.
15.3).
Brodys typeface Industria (1984) appeared in more sophisticated magazines (compared to fanzines) such as The Face, communicating aggressive moods and attitudes beyond the range of available commercial fonts (fig.
15.4).
In addition to typography and lettering, Brody designed record jackets and concert posters that evoke an emotional response in the viewer, accomplished through photographs, lower-resolution photocopies and video-generated images, and typography.
His album covers and posters relate to the content of the music, rather than following the mainstream music industrys tendency to promote the celebrity of rock stars through photography.
To this end he employed images suggested or even provided by the musicians themselves and cultivated an array of techniques that avoided a consistent style.
For a 1980 poster for the rock group Cabaret Voltaire (fig.
15.5), Brody juxtaposed the blurred, degraded image of a running man with a jet airplane against a blue background with black-andwhite textured strips as lateral borders and within the central image.
Photomontage, as well as the groups name (the Cabaret Voltaire, in Zurich, was a nightclub and meeting place for Dada artists and performers during World War I), recalls the juxtaposed and manipulated images of Dada graphics (see here), while the interlocking CV is reminiscent of a corporate trademark.
Neville Brody, “Kopf,” hand-drawn logo for a hat company, London, 1985. # 5+ 0 15.4 Neville Brody, Contents logo, The Face, no.
49, May, c.
1980.
Neville Brody, poster for Cabaret Voltaire, 1980.
Brodys comments about his work reveal the contradictory nature of punk graphic design.
There is a desire to deliberately subvert contemporary advertising strategies and the constraints upon freedom of expression they pose, and yet at the same time there is a recognition that living within that culture forces compromises and acknowledgement of the limited and ephemeral ways in which artistic freedom functions: On every cover I have done for Cabaret Voltaire, the dominant theme is decay through process, the loss of human identity that results from communication being transmitted through machines that condition, not serve, human interaction.
Decay through process is also about repetition, and the loss of quality that you suffer when information is abstracted from its human origin....
Punk was about individual expression, and more than anything, it was a reaction against authority.
It couldnt really describe itself as independent unless the authority was completely circumvented  which, for a very short time, it was.
But as soon as the whole phenomenon was categorized as the independent scene, this ensured that it would become exactly its opposite.
The punk phenomenon belongs within the framework of pluralism, complex in its relationship to popular culture, acknowledging rather than rejecting the multiple signs and messages inherent in our consumer culture.
An example of adapting the rebellious counterculture aspects of the punk movement to advertising for products otherwise characterized by brand standardization was the Philips Tracer electric shaver, sold in a variety of colors and targeting a youthful market (fig.
15.6).
And, in 1992, Vivienne Westwood was awarded the title Dame (the female equivalent of Knight) by Queen Elizabeth II at Buckingham Palace as a member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire.

ven, the Netherlands, c.
1983.

## Hi-Tech
The experiential context of punk culture was the urban, industrial environment  metallic, raw, and cluttered in comparison with the reductive aesthetic purity of interwar Modernism as seen, for instance, in MoMAs 1934 Machine Art exhibition (see here).
The reutilization of industrial products and materials for public and domestic spaces and the repurposing of abandoned warehouses and factories for studios and apartments emerged under the term hi-tech in the later 1970s.
The Castiglioni brothers Mezzadro stool, first designed in 1954 and manufactured by Zanotta beginning in 1957, prefigured this phenomenon, reinterpreting a metal tractor seat in a domestic setting with little transformation of its utilitarian associations.
Ron Arads Rover chair, made from tubular metal attached to a second-hand automobile seat, also exemplifies aspects of a hi-tech aesthetic.
Hi-tech interiors featured exposed ventilation ducts and riveted I-beams, pipe-railings, prefabricated industrial building materials, and perforated spiral staircases, seen, for example, in the waiting room of the Occupational Health Center in Columbus, Indiana, designed by Hardy Holzman Pfeiffer Associates between 1974 and 1977 (fig.
15.7).
Using color and emphasizing unfinished textures of concrete, unglazed brick, and metal, the interior exposes the new post-industrial aesthetic, acknowledging honestly rather than hiding the plumbing and HVAC systems that are an integral part of their design.
A more celebratory tone appears in the loud and busy exterior of Richard Rogers and Renzo Pianos Pompidou Center in Paris (completed 1977).
The exposure of industrial materials and fittings extended into a wide variety of household accessories, including plastic-coated wire shelving units manufactured by the Elfa company in Sweden, appearing first in the later 1970s (fig.
15.8).
Furniture was another focus for hi-tech design, seen in Japanese designer Shiro Kuramatas (19341991) How High the Moon chair (fig.
15.9), dating to 1986 and manufactured by Vitra.
Surprisingly, the metal mesh construction is both strong enough for support and flexible enough for comfortable sitting (the mesh conforms comfortably around ones body when seated).
Yet How High the Moon does not seem to have been designed with sitting as its main or sole intention, as the lightness and transparency of its material, together with the precision of its curves and joints, exert an especially strong aesthetic appeal that allows us to experience the material independent from or in addition to its function.

## Postmodernism
and Taste Capital investment in business on an increasing international scale following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989, the formation of the European Union in 1993 and trade negotiations between the United States and the Peoples Republic of China (beginning with President Richard Nixons visit to China in 1972), all demonstrated that economic expansion and free trade consistently dominated international relations despite political differences, with human rights serving as a bargaining chip to ensure the cooperation of governments on behalf of their broad-based constituencies.
Today, in general, the press and public it represents readily accept that US foreign policy is governed by balancing concerns for human rights and the protection of the nations intellectual property with the exploration of new markets for raw materials and goods, including designed products, technologies, and services.
Even the Peoples Republic of China, which celebrated the 70th anniversary of communist rule in 2019, is closely connected with global supply-chain networks for expanding international trade and competition.
Chinas economic growth and role in contemporary design is treated in Part VI of the Global Inspiration.
Within a framework marked by the hegemony of capitalism and the equation of economic and social progress with technology, innovation, and economic expansion in the later twentieth century, pluralism continued to dominate the modern production and consumption of design.
This generally healthy heterogeneity reduced the dichotomy between reform-based initiatives grounded in shared aesthetic and ethical values, and approaches to design governed by free enterprise and addressing a diverse market.
In the context of inclusiveness and relativism in taste, notions of reform, resistance, and subversion relinquished a measure of their power to define a vital current in the history of modern design, namely a desire to shape not just the experience of products and spaces but also the values of a future society that included ethical concerns and addressed the many strands of social justice.
More recent concerns regarding migration, displacement, racial and ethnic equality, and climate change in the twenty-first century have renewed a sense of urgency in directing the attention of the design community toward deteriorating environmental and social conditions at both the professional and grassroots levels.
These efforts are discussed in Chapter 16.
Toward the end of the 1970s, the popular and subcultural challenges to modern architecture and good design were becoming more widespread.
The catalog for the 1983 exhibition Design since 1945, held at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and curated by Kathryn Hiesinger and George Marcus, included essays advocating rational standards and abstract aesthetics in design by Dieter Rams, Max Bill, and George Nelson, but also contained an essay by University of Pennsylvania sociologist Herbert Gans, who argued that post-war international modern design was a treasure trove of upper middle class culture appealing to a particular class and reflecting particular (and exclusive) taste rather than universal democratic values.
At the same time, the more rhetorical Anti-Design initiatives in Italy and elsewhere in the later 1960s (see here) acquired an international high-end commercial cachet underwritten by manufacturers such as Alessi and Swid Powell.
In Milan, for instance, organizations espousing new directions in design were initiated in the later 1970s.
Alchymia (1976) and Memphis (1981) included the work of not only Italian but also Japanese and Latin American designers.
Memphis (see here) and other groups or individuals designing ambiguous appropriations of historical styles and popular culture were described as Postmodern, a term commonly used among critics and historians (although rejected by some designers) that filtered into more general usage.
Postmodern design encompasses projects and forms that signal a welcome end to the critical dichotomy between aesthetically or ethically directed design on the one hand and commercially motivated design on the other, an opposition that emerged in the early nineteenth century with the design reform movement and that dominated design theory through the two decades following World War II.
It may also be described even more broadly as an attitude through which various tendencies of Modernism in design are deprived of their reformist or revolutionary utopian pretensions.
For design, Postmodernism shares with mass entertainment and culture a user-oriented approach that emphasizes multiple interpretations and meanings, and embraces ephemeral criteria of evaluation for the design enterprise.

## 15.10 Paula Scher, Swatch advertising poster, offset print, 29 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>8</sub> ×
20 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (76 × 51 cm), 1984.
The term Postmodernism is often found in conjunction with other concepts such as post-industrialism and late capitalism, all referring to a culture that equates economic growth with progress and with individual freedom, strengthened in the early years of post-war affluence in the United States and spreading to Europe, Japan, and other industrialized nations.
Late capitalism signifies investment directed toward increasingly segmented audiences (rather than Fordist mechanized mass production), and the readiness of businesses to design, manufacture, and market products with increasing speed, responsiveness, flexibility, and sophistication in a highly competitive and constantly evolving commercial environment.
The design enterprise is also accelerated through the increased speed of batch rather than mass production, target marketing, and more recently communication and marketing through e-commerce (in 2021 IKEA ceased to publish its print catalog, see here).
Batch production focuses upon the assembly of limited quantities of varied products using similar components for flexible yet efficient manufacture.
One example is in the fashion industry, where a limited number of bodies are expanded through variations in trim to permit more individualized consumer choice.
As another example, British design historian Nigel Whitely cites the success of the Swatch wristwatches first in Britain and then internationally in the 1980s, the result of inexpensive plastic materials and production, and an especially fashion-oriented approach to wristwatches to complement clothing styles (fig.
15.10).
The ephemeral, virtually disposable Swatch (the name combines the words Swiss and watch, but also brings to mind the word switch), manufactured by Swiss company Eta beginning in 1983, targeted a young audience less likely to be influenced by the emotional attachments sometimes associated with personal objects and heirlooms (such as a grandfather clock).
Graphic designer Paula Schers (b.
1948) 1984 Swatch poster advertisement appropriates elements of Herbert Matters 1934 travel poster for the Swiss Tourism Bureau.
Schers photomontage technique and juxtapositions suggest a broad range of associations connecting wristwatches and Switzerland (snow-capped mountains, skiing, and the red Swiss flag emblem that forms part of the company logo), and timepieces, leisure, and with the history of Swiss graphic design.
The range of meanings here is open-ended, communicating at different levels to those with or without an insider knowledge of graphic design history.
As product advertising, Schers poster deviates from the emphasis upon the straightforward objectbased approach (without addressing figure) found in Swiss advertising design in the post-World War II era (see here and fig.
11.64).

## Postmodern
Products Postmodern design also emerged in organizations such as Memphis, composed of industrial designers liberated from their contracts with particular companies, enjoying the freedom to pursue directions beyond the parameters of good design. Postmodernism or pluralism was also the overriding theme of the exhibition Design Now: Industry or Art, held at the German Architecture Museum in Frankfurt in 1989.
15.11 Ettore Sottsass, Jr., Tartar table, reconstituted veneer, lacquer, and plastic laminate, 30 × 75 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> × 32 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (76 × 192 × 82 cm), manufactured by Memphis, 1981.
Alessandro Mendini, Proust armchair, painted wood with hand-painted upholstery, height 42 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>8</sub> in (107 cm), made by Studio Alchymia, Milan, 1978.
Ettore Sottsass, Jr., who worked under contract to Olivetti in the 1960s in the design of office machines, mainframe computer housings, and personal typewriters (see figs.
13.10 and 13.11), independently designed prototypes for furniture in the 1980s using commercial industrial materials such as plywood and plastic laminates in bright colors and decorative patterns.
These examples appropriated or exaggerated Hollywood-style historical set design, the sensory excitement of billboard advertising and rock music (Memphis is the home of rock icon Elvis Presley, immortalized in Andy Warhols silkscreen images and in the furnishings of the singers own Graceland mansion; it also figures in the title of Bob Dylans rambling 1966 song Stuck Inside of Mobile with the Memphis Blues Again).
One product is Sottsasss 1981 Tartar table (fig.
15.11), whose laminated surfaces and patterned decoration recall Oldenburgs 1963 Bedroom Ensemble or Wesselmans (19312004) Still Life Number 30 kitchen-table assemblage (see figs.
14.15 and 14.16).
Memphis organized group exhibitions in Milan, and the Formica Corporation invited members of the group to design furniture using its new ColorCore product, a solid variation of the material that could be molded and cut.
The conflicting, overlapping interpretations are typical of Postmodern forms and their eclectic appropriation of the past in a reflective and complex way.
Alessandro Mendinis (1931 2019) Proust armchair (1978; fig.
15.12), named for the introspective French writer Marcel Proust (18711922) and produced for Studio Alchymia, is another example: the Rococo Revival-upholstered armchair references mid-nineteenth-century comfort and artisanal craftsmanship, while the brightly colored upholstery cover is a clear appropriation of pointillism, a style of painting associated with Georges Seurat (1859 1891) and concerned with reproducing the harmony and luminosity of contrasting colors.
The materials and carving assert mass, while the flickering upholstery patterns deny it: the chair both affirms and dematerializes physical form at the same time, as if to illustrate the coexistence of multiple, even opposite perceptions.
Such interpretive dissonance was characteristic of many Postmodern design initiatives; in addition to welcoming the return of decoration and historicism in objects as a jab at the universal pretensions of international Modernism, such works also emphasize the shifting and complex relationship between objects and users in late twentieth-century design thinking and practice.
A similar explosion of complex pattern and saturated color appears in the printed cotton fabric designs of French artist Nathalie du Pasquier (b.
1957), also a member of Memphis.
Du Pasquiers Gabon textile dates to 1982 and was manufactured by the Milanese company Rainbow. Gabon combines tightly packed angular shapes, strong color contrasts, and irregular spatial dislocations in a bold, almost dizzying composition (fig.
15.13).
The pattern was one in a series Du Pasquier designed following her travels to Africa, and indicates the varied and eclectic appropriations of the Memphis group, alternately inspired by Hollywood glamour, history, and travel.
In the catalog for the Victoria and Albert Museum exhibition Postmodernism: Style and Subversion, 19701990 Jane Pavitt and Glenn Adamson likened the eclectic borrowing in Postmodern designers work to the theme of the road trip in literature or films such as Easy Rider (1969), whether thrill-seeking, soulsearching, or aimless wandering, an escape from the routines and responsibilities of ordinary working life.
Du Pasquiers travels to Africa, or Sottsasss fascination with India (seen in stupa-shaped ceramic vessels he designed in the later 1960s) incorporated oblique references to non-Western cultures, freely mediated by the designer, combined with other references to popular culture or history, and fabricated with modern industrial materials or experimental methods of production.
In some ways the global meanderings of Sottsass and Du Pasquier anticipate or accompany the accelerated flow of goods internationally, and increasingly broad awareness of the interconnected nature of design activity, whether to expand commerce, create interdependent supply networks, or address shared awareness of sustainability.
Part counterculture but also hardly a rejection of contemporary capitalist consumer culture, the products of Memphis reveal the complexity of the Postmodern Condition. Nathalie du Pasquier (designer), “Gabon” textile, screenprinted cotton, 107.3 × 150.7 cm, manufactured by Rainbow, Milan, 1982.
National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne.
Postmodernism of the early 1980s attracted high-end commercial interest, as in Robert Venturis (19252018) series of chairs manufactured by Knoll.
Venturis Chippendale chair of 1984 (fig.
15.14) appears to mock or rebel against foundational tenets of modern furniture design, first in appropriating an eighteenth-century style, second in using an industrial material to imitate an original design in a natural material (here made even more obvious through painting), and third by flaunting decorative pattern rather than eliminating it or treating it as subservient to function.
Indeed Venturi, who encouraged architects and designers to think of themselves as jesters, chose the chair as a focus, since it has been a paradigm of the very standards toward which contemporary designers direct their irony and through which they champion the complexity and contradiction of Postmodernism.
15.14 Robert Venturi, Chippendale chair, bent laminated yew and plastic laminate, $3 7 { ^ 3 / _ { 8 } } \times$ 25 ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } \times 2 3 { } ^ { 1 } / _ { 4 }$ in (95 × 65 × 59 cm), manufactured by Knoll International, New York, 1984.
Philadelphia Museum of Art.
French architect and celebrity designer Philippe Starck (b.
1949) emerged in the mid-1980s with an original and varied approach to furniture for sophisticated clients such as fashion designer Pierre Cardin and French President François Mitterrand.
He is in this regard an heir to the luxury French Art Deco tradition but using assembled industrial materials, employing often abstract geometric shapes with elegant solutions to construction and collapsibility, as in his tubular and sheet steel Tippy Jackson folding table manufactured in Italy by Driade in 1985 (fig.
15.15).
The tables name may allude to Michael Jacksons (19582009) 1982 album Thriller, and the MTV video featuring the performers gravity-defying moonwalk dance step.
There is also little that is straightforward or rational about Tippy Jackson: there is no obvious or logical explanation for the tables support system, with its bowed legs and struts of different lengths, and there are certainly more economical solutions to folding tables than the enigmatic solution Starck proposes.
Philippe Starck, Tippy Jackson table, painted tubular steel and sheet metal, height 28 in (71 cm), manufactured by Driade, Piacenza, Italy, 1985.
In domestic wares, Italian manufacturer Alessi has been active in promoting original design in silver.
In the early 1980s American architect Michael Graves (19342015) designed an Art Deco-inspired tea and coffee service that featured polished ribbed surfaces, ebony feet, ivory handles, and non-functional blue knobs (fig.
15.16).
The design appeared in a section of the 1989 Design Now exhibition entitled Microarchitecture, a reference to the resurgence of decoration and popular symbolism in architecture of the time, such as Philip Johnsons AT&T building in midtown Manhattan (1984) with its broken pediment or his Gothic Revival complex of glass and steel buildings for the Pittsburgh Plate Glass company (19811984).
Many of the furnishings in the exhibition were designed by major architects (starchitects), and their work invites playful associations on the part of the viewer/user, making the dinner or coffee table into a kind of game board on which users engage imaginatively with objects that come to life, generating desire for high-end Alessi products and associating the manufacturer with new directions in design and contemporary living.
Michael Graves, tea and coffee service (prototype), silver, lacquered aluminum, mock ivory, and Bakelite; tray 3 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> × 16 in (9 × 41 cm), manufactured by Alessi, New York and Italy, 1980–1983 Other contemporary designers reflected upon political and environmental awareness in their oeuvre, albeit in a rhetorical rather than activist or polemical way.
One direction includes the reuse of materials, seen, for instance, in Ron Arads (b.
1951) Rover chair of 1981, constructed from used automobile seats attached to a frame made of semicircular tubular-metal supports, incorporating the socially conscious initiative of recycling.
More complex in construction is Arads asymmetrical Big Easy Volume 2 sofa of 1988 (fig.
15.17).
This piece consists of sheets of industrial steel cut, shaped, and painstakingly welded to conform to the contours of a traditionally carved wooden seat and form of a heavily upholstered and well-worn sofa, bringing to the mind of an informed viewer the crushed metal sculpture of John Chamberlain (19272011), such as Glossalia Adagio, or French sculptor César Baldaccinis (19211998) The Yellow Buick (1961; fig.
15.18), made from the welded or compressed wreckage found in automobile graveyards.
These examples focus attention upon the aesthetic qualities and cultural associations acquired by discarded post-industrial materials in the setting of gallery or museum.
Clearly this kind of furniture is not intended for serial or mass production.
Often the results seem contrived and undermine any possible desire to reach beyond a sophisticated audience entirely prepared to view such objects # aesthetically or as a form of sociopolitical commentary in museums and galleries.
Ron Arad, Big Easy Volume 2 sofa, stainless steel and steel, height 34 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> in (87 cm), manufactured by One Off, London, 1988.
15.18 César Baldaccini, The Yellow Buick, compressed automobile, 1961.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
Despite museum exhibitions, commissions from companies such as Alessi or Formica to individual designers and groups such as Memphis, and the emergence of small galleries and boutiques that promoted the self-conscious complexities of contemporary experiments in furniture and other household commodities, the majority of furniture and other domestic products in the broad mass market initially owed little to the clever ironies of much Postmodern design.
Yet there was increasing evidence in the later 1990s that the forms of many Postmodern designers were reaching a wider market, such as Michael Gravess houseware designs for retail chain Target (see fig.
16.22).
Much of this activity demonstrated the belief that Postmodernisms eclectic sources encouraged a healthy receptivity to diversity, novelty, and difference in society, further eroding taste hierarchies in a tolerant, global society.
This view, however, was not without its critics.
Skepticism toward Postmodernisms inclusiveness was ongoing, and the issue of tolerance remained (and remains, especially in a climate of identity politics, nationalism, and polarized politics) a matter of debate: critic and author Robert Hughes, in Culture of Complaint: The Fraying of America (1993), found little cause for optimism, seeing instead a Balkanization of subcultures in the products of a fragmented culture obsessed with the delineation of difference rather than common ground or shared notions of quality.
Marxist critics lamented the absence of art and design that might nurture the seeds of resistance to capitalist hegemony.
In Postmodernism, or the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991), Fredric Jameson defined Postmodernism as a cultural dominant, the integration of a formerly autonomous aesthetic discourse with commodity production.
For Jameson the result of such an integration undermined true opposition in political terms and only demonstrated an aesthetic depthlessness, with mass media substituting for direct understanding, producing an experience rich in immediacy and association but essentially superficial and alienating.
Meanwhile, a gap in income levels and the standard of living between industrially developed and underdeveloped nations, or racial inequality in the United States, continued to signal, for some, the need for a more thorough commitment to social and ethical responsibility in design on a global scale, a need whose urgency has increased in the twenty-first century.
Cultural and technological disparity and inequality remain undercurrents in envisioning the future practice of design: lobbying efforts for Internet access throughout the schools and households of the United States are typical of the ideology of progress, yet ignore the fact that a majority of the population in many underdeveloped countries lacks the basic services many of us take for granted and call into question the meaning or reality of the Canadian educator and philosopher Marshall McLuhans (19111980) global village in the information age.

## Beyond
the Object: Expanding Design’s Reach Pressures both from within and outside the design professions led to new, expansive directions in practice, education, and promotion.
Global markets spurred businesses to adjust to increased competition and acknowledge more sophisticated, aware consumers who demanded products differentiated less by superficial styling than by a broad range of considerations focusing upon how well products communicated or interacted intuitively with users.
A human-centered design began to emerge, including new approaches to product design but also expanding to the design of services and other aspects of business practice, with hierarchical decision-making giving way to collaboration, and user experience as common denominator.
In mechanical products, historian Jeffrey Meikle suggested the 1988 Ford Taurus as an example of successful design in the American automobile industry from this period.
The Taurus (fig.
15.19) broke with industry practice by having designers, engineers, and marketing departments work together from the outset, ensuring that different points of view were considered strategically during development.
Such practice resulted in greater sophistication in styling, and generated excitement for consumers and profits from increased sales for Fords American division.
Such an integrated approach has also been cited as an explanation for the success of the Japanese automobile industry, where factory workers are included in discussions of quality and production efficiency.
Inclusion gives workers a stake in an expanded design process, encouraging loyalty, responsibility, initiative, and innovation, qualities generally subsumed under the term empowerment. The fact that many contemporary consultancies have group rather than individual names (Pentagram, Smart Design, IDEO, Frog, Droog) also suggests the effectiveness of the paradigm of creative collaboration in design.
Ford Taurus, sedan or station wagon, Ford Motor Corporation, Dearborn, Michigan, 1988.
Design consultancies that emerged in the 1970s, such as Pentagram, with offices first in London and expanding to locations in the United States and Europe, offered a wide range of integrated services to corporate clients that transcended boundaries of product design to include typography, graphic design, and office and retail interiors.
This involved regular meetings among partners to present and receive feedback on concepts, in close communication with the client.
Other international consultancies, such as Frog Design (founded 1969) offered a similar approach, describing themselves on their 2009 website as a global innovation firm.
Miniaturization in the electronics industry (see here) reduced obvious differentiation in terms of styling, leading to increasing homogeneity among similar competitive products.
Responding to these circumstances, designers shifted attention toward creating a closer relationship between products and users.
Mario Bellinis (b.
1935) design for the Divisumma 18 portable calculator for Olivetti in 1972 used a soft synthetic rubber housing and keypad, enclosing the miniaturized components in a tactile, skinlike shell with rounded edges and a warm color that connects emotionally with consumers (fig.
15.20).
This soft, anthropomorphic approach to product design has grown with newer materials and production technologies, and has been an essential component of the working methods of contemporary design consultancies.
The consultancy IDEO assembled examples of design from the collection of the Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum for a 2007 exhibition, and Bellinis Divisumma 18 was among the objects selected, demonstrating the consultancys focus upon intuition, inspiration, and empathy.
Theorists began to refer to contemporary approaches to design as being soft, implying several related concepts, including the designers manipulation of digital imaging in a more refined and flexible interactive process, or emphasizing the interface between users, products, and services. Soft design is linked as well to software and to the information age, that is, the virtual instructions that run our computer programs; and soft may refer to increasingly and pliable user-friendly materials, or to the complex layering and sensory richness that characterizes the work of a number of contemporary graphic designers.
15.20 Mario Bellini, Divisumma 18 handheld calculator, ABS plastic, melamine, and rubber, 1 <sup>7</sup>/ × 10 × 4 <sup>3</sup>/ in (4.8 × 25.4 × 12.1 cm), Olivetti ING, Ivrea, Italy, 1972.
User experience not only applied to user-friendly materials, but also to less visible means to foster a natural relationship between human beings and a broad range of mechanical and electronic devices.
Engineer and author Donald Norman (see here) considers user-centered design in a number of books such as The Design of Everyday Things, published in 1988.
Using a wide range of examples drawn from personal (yet common) experience, Norman describes the often frustrating relationships we have with objects whose increased functionality comes at the expense of transparent, intuitive controls and operation (such as programmable telephones with messaging and retrieval options or portable video cameras and players), and argues for the need to consider user error and physical interaction in designing products that are safer, easier, and more natural to operate.
While Bellinis Divisumma 18 remains within the familiar category of product housings and new industrial materials, computer technology introduced new ways of connecting products with users that reach beyond the object. Apple Corporations Macintosh personal computer, introduced in 1984 (fig.
15.21), offered an integrated monitor and hardware that saved space and reduced assembly time.
More importantly, the Macintosh design included the companys Graphical User Interface (GUI), which used a small hand-operated mouse that visualized the screen as a desktop and the mouses arrow-shaped cursor as a pointing device permitting access to documents, folders, and programs rather than having to type in a series of instructions, thus reducing learning time for users and removing a barrier to operation.
The Macintoshs distinguishing design feature was not just its portable compact form but the way in which the GUI created a direct link between personal computing and the familiar, reassuring physical act of organizing, manipulating, and accessing information visually and spatially, reducing the distance between machines and users and making personal computers, indeed, more personal: an extension and amplification of our human capacities.
Touch Screen Interface (TSI), in development since the 1960s but used extensively since the early 2000s for personal laptop computers, smartphones, gaming, and point-of-sale transactions, eliminates the need for pointing devices or cursors to access content or typing messages.
The role of design in TSI may best be described as facilitating navigation in the digital realm through touch rather than the intermediary of a mouse or touchpad.

The expanding framework for design in the information age is parallel and contemporary with the emerging field of artificial intelligence.
Herbert Simon (1916 2001), the Nobel-prize-winning economist and computer scientist, offered an inclusive definition of design in his 1969 book Science of the Artificial: Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones.
The intellectual activity that produces material artifacts is no different fundamentally from the one that prescribes remedies for a sick patient or the one that devises a new sales plan for a company or a social welfare policy for a state.
Design, so construed, is the core of all professional training: it is the principal mark that distinguishes the professions from the sciences.
Simons definition encompasses the act of form-giving in industrial design but acknowledges new territories for design activity that emphasize interaction between technology and human beings directed toward an imagined future, with information and users as the common denominators in such activity.
Simon also raises the possibility that the designed (or artificial) world becomes less and less distinguishable from nature itself as design draws humans and machines closer together.
We commonly refer to our handheld phones as being smart: they are extensions of ourselves, responding to our desire for information and expanding the range of our possibilities for future action, whether finding our way to the nearest gas station or letting a friend know we are running late.
Certainly the design of prosthetic limbs to enable mobility and independence exemplifies the sophistication and possibilities of smart design, along with wayfinding technology that leads to the promise of self-driving vehicles.
Simon expressed his vision in a spirit of optimism and confidence in innovation and progress with an expanded range of possibilities for areas of preferred results.
Others have voiced misgivings, raising doubts as to whether the promise of advanced information technology is benevolent and humanizing or dangerous and even dystopian, especially in relation to the use or misuse of surveillance technology and increased role of social media as a source for the dissemination of information.
Just as the industrial age unleashed a mixture of hope as well as fear, so has the information age produced its share of advocates for the benefits of AI as well as skeptics who reflect upon its limits and dangers  prefigured over four decades ago in the 1982 film Blade Runner, directed by Ridley Scott.
As designers engage with fields beyond products and services, their efforts become less specialized but also more diffused, less easy to define or clearly explain.
It is perhaps our job as historians to navigate the path from past to present, supplying the context that gives shape to the future and identifying how best to think meaningfully about the expanded role design plays in our lives.

## Chapter
16 # Contemporary Design in Context: Innovation, Responsibility, and Balance Somewhere between shared, increasingly urgent concerns for safety, health, social justice and sustainability, and a democratic embrace of more inclusive and creative innovation in combination with technology that stimulates the seemingly insatiable desire for individual fulfillment through commodity consumption in a competitive global economy, there lies a middle ground that provides hope for the future of design, a balance between the permanent and ephemeral, between nature and the artificial, between individual and society, between creative freedom and ethics, between what design has been and what it may be.
The shape of that future will depend upon the manner in which a number of competing and even conflicting viewpoints and approaches to the rapidly expanding field of design develop and also upon the degree to which such viewpoints and practices may be reconciled, regulated, and shaped.
Designs future includes the increasingly dynamic role of technology and production and the political and economic circumstances (local and global) in which they develop, consumption and commercialism, craft and aesthetics, as well as the ability of design to shape not only our products and services, but also our global societys individual, social, and environmental values.
Each of these considerations is increasingly interwoven and interdependent in a synthesis that is certainly challenging and yet may remain vital, enriching, and optimistic.
With the increasing reach of design activity and recognition of the ongoing economic, health, and environmental challenges we face, there is no better time, or perhaps no more urgent time, for designers to exercise their skills.
Twenty-First-Century Political, Environmental, and Social Motivations for Design Increased awareness of the effects of global warming, natural disasters, the migration or displacement of populations due to political instability, terrorism, natural disasters, dangers posed by air and water pollution, and the build-up of plastics and other synthetic waste materials, all pose threats as well as opportunities for the design community and the societies whose needs it serves.
What is remarkable is the wide variety of broadly defined design efforts that respond to environmental and social concerns, ranging from the futuristic and visionary to the mundane, from new technologies and materials to traditional craft and re-use to meet challenges and stimulate further effort.
Such dangers are hardly new, but climate and the environment have assumed renewed importance amid extreme weather conditions and catastrophes, and the reduction of government regulations to protect the environment from commercial exploitation whether in the rivers and streams of the United States or the rainforests of Brazil.
Conferences, symposia, the formation of organizations, and the media direct attention to sustainability, disability, safety, and the survival of displaced and Indigenous populations globally.
In 2005 the Cooper Hewitt National Design Museum in New York created the position of Curator of Socially Responsible Design to help develop the museums first international (as opposed to national) design triennial exhibition, titled Why Design Now? in 2010.
The international scope of Why Design Now? reinforced the importance of global attention to eight ethical themes: Energy, Mobility, Community, Materials, Prosperity, Health, Communication, and Simplicity.
While some well-known names in industrial and fashion design appeared (for example, Issey Miyake and Tord Boontje), many projects were community-based.
And while some projects were visionary (for instance, a futuristic plan for San Francisco  HydroNet  that included clusters of twisting plant-like, white-and-green, energy-collection structures popping up incongruously to protect the city from the rise in water levels and threat of flooding), the majority were realized objects or well-developed prototypes for production.
The definition of design offered at Why Design Now? was understandably inclusive, ranging from industrial design and crafts to graphic and information design, fashion, healthcare, and architecture.
Among the exhibitions themes, only one involved aesthetics (simplicity), and even here the projects encompassed compact space- and material-saving forms, flexible components, and easy production or assembly, implying ethical motivations and problem-solving as well as aesthetic purity.
There was an effort to include lo-tech and local projects rather than focus solely upon the most recent technological innovations in materials technology.
For instance, alongside a lightweight aluminum folding bicycle was the Samarth bicycle trailer, designed in the US for use in India by Radhika Bhalla (b.
1983), made from locally sourced bamboo, rattan, jute, and iron (fig.
16.1).
The message here was not only empowerment (that everyone can make a difference through design), but also that design innovation can be compatible with local practices and existing patterns of living.
In addition to state-of-the-art solar panels, other projects included food packaging (AgroResin) made from biodegradable plant fibers such as wheat, rice, and corn stalks.
The compatibility of ethical design and existing commercial practice related to the exhibitions themes of prosperity and communication.
Rather than the polemical, oppositional tone found in the writings of Victor Papanek (see here), Why Design Now? displayed Amazons Kindle tablet reader (fig.
16.2), noting the savings in paper (and recycling costs) along with the typeface, digital ink, and reflective illumination (like paper and unlike a typical computer screen) for a comforting interface that reduces eye fatigue.
16.1 Radhika Bhalla, Samarth bicycle trailer, locally sourced bamboo, rattan, iron, jute, coconut fiber, wheels, USA/India, 2008.
Amazon Kindle tablet Reader, plastic, acrylic, aluminum, E Ink®, 6.7 × 4.6 × 0.36 in (17 × 11.7 × 0.9 cm), 2009.
The Cooper Hewitts 2016 By the People: Designing a Better America exhibition was national in scope and focused upon community-based design efforts to address poverty, homelessness, responses to natural disasters that often affect the poor, urban redevelopment, voting rights, and even a redesign for a cheerful, welcoming waiting room for parolees, all accompanied by wall texts and an introductory documentary film chronicling the almost 50 million Americans living below the poverty line, the historical loss of manufacturing jobs, the elimination of government support for low-cost social housing (1973), and the devastating effects on low-income Americans caused by natural disasters such as Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
While projects were limited to the United States, By the People embraced and addressed with concrete examples the Millennium Development Goals of the United Nations from the year 2000, which included reducing child mortality, improving maternal health, ensuring environmental sustainability, and promoting gender equality.
Akin in its DIY approach to Stewart Brands Whole Earth Catalog (see here and fig.
14.21), but more community- rather than individually based, By the People brought socially responsible design from the margins of design history closer to a more inclusive mainstream understanding of design activity, extending beyond the counterculture into the subject of museum exhibition or media treatment of design.
That an holistic approach to sustainability includes public awareness and a participatory process is also demonstrated by efforts in South Korea, where 95 percent of food waste is recycled.
The program began at the grassroots level with neighborhood organizations working independently, and became nationwide with government investment and support.
The program includes mechanical waste bins for depositing food waste, which is separated and reprocessed to manufacture animal feed, compost, and biofuel.
Citizens separate their familys food waste into biodegradable bags (including used cooking oil) for deposit into the bins, which weigh the bags, and residents are charged a nominal monthly fee automatically.
The program has reduced the amount of food waste per family along with South Koreas carbon footprint.
The system is a paradigm for an integrated design effort that involves an awareness of the shared ethical values and responsibilities of citizens and governments, and the use of smart technology to manage and facilitate operation, resulting in economic and social benefit.
Other twenty-first-century catalysts for ethically responsible design have been global climate change and refugee crises.
In 2018 the theme and title of the Design History Societys annual conference (held in New York at the Parsons School of Design) was Design and Displacement, and in 2017 the Museum of Modern Art featured an exhibition entitled Insecurities: Tracing Displacement and Shelter, whose introductory text stated: For over 60 million persons in the world today, shelter is defined through constant movement or escape.
Insecurities: Tracing Displacement and Shelter explores the ways in which contemporary architecture and design have addressed notions of shelter in light of global refugee emergencies....
Refugee camps, once considered temporary settlements, have become sites through which to examine how human rights intersect with the making of cities.
Bringing together projects by architects, designers, and artists, working in a range of mediums and scales, that respond to the complex circumstances brought about by forced displacement, the exhibition focuses on conditions that disrupt conventional images of the built environment.
One example from the MoMA exhibition was an Emergency Temporary Shelter, the work of the Better Shelter design group.
A tent-like structure, the shelter is designed for families of up to five, using modular and portable lightweight materials (fig.
16.3).
Meant to last on average three years, thousands of these units have been built in Asia, Africa, and Europe.
The shelter recalls Buckminster Fullers proposed solution to housing shortages after World War II using his modular geodesic structures (see here), less novel perhaps but more flexible and easier to assemble.
Better Shelter was founded in Sweden, where team-based socially responsible design initiatives have had an uninterrupted history throughout the post-World War II period, only marginally affected by the politically motivated, anti-design and countercultural trends seen elsewhere in the industrialized world during the 1960s.
Emergency Temporary Shelter, steel frame, pololefin envelope, polypropylene, polyamide and ABS plastic components, photovoltaics 223 <sup>5</sup>/ × 130 1<sup>1</sup>/ × 111 <sup>7</sup>/ in (568 × 332.1 × 282.9 cm), Better Shelter, 2010.
Museum of Modern Art, New York.
In addition to urgent responses to violence or catastrophe, longer-range design thinking and initiatives address climate change by proposing a circular model, one in which recycling lies at the middle rather than at the margins of possible options.
Circular design seeks to redirect the linear trajectory for designed goods that proceeds from making and buying to disposal.
Instead, manufacturers are encouraged to design and produce goods that consider the sustainability of the materials they use, including waste materials, think in terms of products that might be repaired, components re-used in successive versions of personal electronics, or shared rather than owned.
The success of circular design also depends upon shifting consumer attitudes toward buying secondhand items, thinking beyond products and services toward wider economic systems that make sense economically as well as ethically.
Examples include Thomas Leechs Shoey Shoes, a line of childrens shoes using discarded leather and based upon the premise that children grow out of their shoes approximately every three months, resulting in a tremendous amounts of waste that ends up in landfill (fig.
16.4).
Interestingly, while circular design may be a novel term and designers have received funding support from foundations, many of the ideas it proposes have historical precedent.
Some, such as the ChargePoint Networked Charging Station, and on display at the Cooper Hewitts 2012 Why Design Now? triennial, were driven by environmental considerations, while others were motivated by economic rather than overtly ethical concerns: the parts of the Model T Ford could be easily replaced because the car remained relatively unchanged for well over a decade (see here); and at the height of the Cold War Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev proposed fleets of staterather than individually owned automobiles to meet the needs of Soviet citizens, and ride-sharing today offers an alternative to personal car ownership.
Despite what appears to be a combination of common and economic sense, changing corporate and consumer practices remains a challenge: since its debut in 2007 the Apple iPhone has gone through many iterations with considerable media fanfare, but without buyers being able to upgrade functions without purchasing the newest release.
16.4 Thomas Leech, “Shoey Shoes,” display of children’s shoes made from leather waste from the fashion industry, 2016.
While not specially directed toward climate change, the Cooper Hewitts triennial exhibition, titled Nature (20192020), included displays dealing with how we view our relationship with nature and the environment, using the study of nature to inspire and direct design activity.
One example is a collaboration between French aircraft manufacturer Airbus, architectural firm The Living, Autodesk software company (both based in the US), and German-based AP Works fabrication and 3-D printing company, to produce the partition that separates an aircraft cabin from its galley within very specific airline-industry safety requirements.
Applying algorithms based upon the study of the growth of slime mold that connects disparate locations of food, and the growth properties of mammal bones that maximize strength with minimum required mass, the collaboration produced a Bionic Partition (fig.
16.5), 45 per cent lighter than conventional partitions, resulting in reduced carbon emissions and savings in fuel.
While certainly novel in its harnessing of recent technologies, the Bionic Partition also connects at several points to design history; after all, designers have long been interested in the underlying structures of nature, seen, for instance, in the chair backs of furniture maker Charles Rohlfs in the early twentieth century (see fig.
5.15), or in the elimination of mass as a benefit of materials and construction technology in Modernist building and furniture design.
Airbuss Bionic Partition combines the study of the natural world with computing and 3-D printing in a complex interdisciplinary, collaborative, and global creative design effort.
Bionic Partition, Bastian Schaefer, Airbus, David Benjamin, The Living, Autodesk, AP Works, Metal Scalmalloy®, 82 × 66 × 2 in (208.3 × 167.6 × 5 cm), 2016– (ongoing).
Also on display at Nature, the Modern Meadow biotechnology company of New Jersey mimics the texture and performance of leather using genetically engineered yeast (fig.
16.6).
Animal-free leather may not replace the natural leather industry or the workers whose livelihood depends upon it (any more than plant-based hamburgers will supplant the cattle-based beef industry, but see fig.
16.4 for the re-use of leather waste), but in addition to being mindful of the animal world, it can be manufactured in a liquid state for spray applications or for use in molds, as well as combined as a backing or composite with other materials.

## 16.6 Zoa™ biofabricated leather, Modern Meadow, Zoa-biofabricated materials, 2019. The aut
omobile industry also has turned its attention to Green Design, developing hybrid and electric vehicles that address a combination of ethical and economic concerns.
