At present, hybrid and electric vehicles remain more expensive than their gasoline-powered counterparts in the same class, with the economic incentive being that the price difference will pay for itself over time in fuel savings.
The Toyota Prius, introduced in 1997, is the best-known and best-selling hybrid automobile.
Devoid of the human presence, the Prius advertisement illustrated in figure 16.7 combines the joy of leisure automobile touring with a verdant windswept landscape with billowing clouds connecting clean with green. Toyota Prius advertisement, photographer: Mark Holthusen; agency: Saatchi & Saatchi LA.
Designing for disability constitutes another area of socially responsible awareness in the expanding design community.
In the United States, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities, adding momentum to rising interest and legislative directive in providing access to buildings and services for that population as a civil right, whether motivated by a belief in social welfare and the collective value of a caring society or by a desire to enable people to function independently in the world.
Italian custom design company Snaidero designed a wheelchair-adaptive kitchen, with easy access to sinks and storage using indented rather than right-angled counter surfaces, with resulting circular areas used for swiveling storage (fig.
16.8).
Marketed successfully beyond people with disabilities are the soft, rubber-handled kitchen utensils created to require less effort to hold and grip and manufactured by the OXO corporation, founded in 1990 by houseware-industry entrepreneur Sam Farber (19242013), with the consultancy Smart Design (fig.
16.9).
Farber designed his Good Grips peeler for his wife, who suffered from arthritis that made it difficult for her to hold the traditional standardized stainless-steel kitchen peeler without pain.
OXO products embody criteria of Universal Design, embraced by a number of institutes and organizations and addressing the broad design needs of people with disabilities, the ageing, and children.
Supported by corporations and foundations, Universal Design groups develop solutions to problems ranging from transportation and park and playground access to housing and kitchens.
Universal Design is defined as the design of products and environments to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. Principles include equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use.
While they were initially designed to address the needs of specific populations, the wider public appeal of OXO utensils addresses how products communicate with different groups of users and satisfy needs beyond those originally targeted.
Not surprisingly, the redesign of a comfortable and appealing (forgive the pun) kitchen utensil, found in the displays of retail chain stores, exemplifies this approach and the added value Universal Design brings to our daily lives.
It is worth noting that added value also comes with added cost to the manufacturer that is passed along to the consumer; conventional stainless-steel peelers are priced well below OXOs model.
Smart Design, “Good Grips” peeler, rubber and stainless steel, length 6 in (15 cm), manufactured by OXO, England, 2000.
That environmentally and socially motivated design has become compatible with rather than opposed to a consumer-based economy (both-and rather than either-or) is also seen in products promoting healthy living and ethically conscious shopping.
Nigel Whitely notes, for instance, that the Body Shop stores equate the purchase of their cosmetics with promoting diversity in procuring ingredients for their products and adopting sustainable guidelines for packaging.
The Body Shop was one of the first companies to devote a link on their website to sustainability and trademarked the phrase Enrich not Exploit. Their promotional material asserts that The world is our source of beauty, but its facing devastation.
We actively help enrich the biodiversity where we grow our ingredients.
We act and campaign to enrich and support threatened areas of outstanding natural value to the planet. Ethical consuming promotes an awareness of the broader consequences of our buying habits, but many critics remain unsatisfied, arguing that the appropriate response to environmental concerns posed by the cosmetics industry lies in curbing consumption, not in making people feel better about the products they buy.
Global responsibility is also part of the mission of Starbucks Coffee chain, originating in Seattle, Washington, in 1971 and now operating more than 33,000 stores worldwide (in this books second edition, published in 2010, the number was 17,000).
Design communicates the companys mission to support a sustainable environment.
Although it claims its cups are recyclable, and aims to preserve elements of original architecture in many of its stores, using natural colors of green and burlap brown, is committed to ethical and responsible growing, and to fair trade in the interest of small-scale independent coffee growers, not all of these ideals are practical.
Attaching ethical values to a product through design also helps to offset the impersonal nature of big businesses in comparison and in competition with locally owned shops offering similar items or services.
Like circular design, other sustainable design efforts encourage designers to address the afterlife of manufactured products, whether using recycled materials in the production process or looking for plant and other substitutes for unsustainable materials.
Israeli-American designer Neri Oxman (b.
1976) has spent her career developing biodegradable alternatives to plastics, only roughly 10 percent of the more than 300 tons of which are recycled globally each year.
Her imaginative research hints at a (albeit more distant) future in which products might age and decay naturally without harming the environment.
Among her many ambitious projects as head of the Mediated Matter Group at the MIT Media Lab in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is Aguahoja (translating as Waterleaf), a material consisting of cellulose derived from plants along with the pectin found in many fruits, and a material called chitosan found in fungi and the wings of dragonflies.
Figure 16.10 illustrates an example of Aguahoja (II) that resembles woven fibers.
In the environment of a sponsored experimental laboratory, Oxman appears less concerned with immediate results or applications than with changing the way we think about how designers might work in relation to the processes of nature, focusing as much on how we dispose of things as on how we create them, designing products as if [they were] grown. Neri Oxman, Aguahoja (II), chitosan, cellulose, pectin, acetic acid, glycerin, water, 3-D printed, MIT Media Lab Mediated Matter Group, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 2017–2019.
The interconnected political and environmental crises of the twenty-first century have motivated many in the design community and the community at large to address social and ecological responsibility in a variety of ways.
Efforts are increasingly global: widespread migration, whether from Syria toward Eastern Europe, from North Africa toward Italy and elsewhere in Western Europe, or from Central America to the United States, is indeed an interconnected challenge, in which expansive, interdisciplinary design and global thinking play active roles.
Yet the challenge is complicated politically, producing resistance amid widespread fears of the loss of national identity and flamed by autocratic leadership and protectionist policies that undermine a pluralism that embraces difference, tolerance, and the hope of mutual understanding and benefit.

## Peering
into Possible Futures Neri Oxmans research was included in the 2019 to 2020 Designs for Different Futures exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where many displays seemed to belong more in a museum of science than in an art gallery.
The expansion of design into fields as diverse as food, shelter, biomimetic materials, personal cosmetics, robotics, and surveillance is as clear an indication as any of the growing territory design now shares with engineers, chemists, biologists, and computer and climate scientists.
As design becomes more collaborative and interdisciplinary, so the paradigm of the individual designer/creator, and with it the connection to fine art, fashion, or designer household products and furnishings, becomes but one way (rather than the primary method) of understanding how designers function in society. Designs for Different Futures focused less on consumer goods and services than upon experimental and rhetorical projects and displays, encouraging us to think rather than to buy, seeking to increase awareness that might influence behavior.
Catalog essays and wall texts suggested that looking far ahead rather than at the next seasons fashions yielded the realization that present global levels of production and population growth, resulting carbon emissions, and natural resource depletion are environmentally unsustainable, and that many of todays (and tomorrows) designers should address how best to prepare in the long term for the threat of extinction, looking to develop a closer relationship with nature as a guide to sustaining our planet and directing efforts to improve the human condition.
The curators noted that our unbridled faith in the success of the traditional paradigm of progress measured in relation to industrial technology, rising production, and consumption as presented at Worlds Fairs beginning in the mid-nineteenth century, has been shaken.
Not surprisingly, the authors reminded readers of Victor Papaneks (see here and fig.
14.20) call to arms to designers in light of global conditions, but the tone as well as some of the displays in Designs for Different Futures were less polemical and generally more tolerant of technology and of consumer culture, inclusive of but not confined to radical change.
As noted, displays included Neri Oxmans material explorations (see fig.
16.10), vases made from natural rather than synthetic polymers such as shellac, hi-tech wheelchairs that can climb or descend stairs, lifelike three-dimensional and virtual robots that explore the margins of intimacy, or mechanical robot arms to bottle-feed babies as prototypes for future living. Possibilities range from mutual-help groups to care communities, from smallscale distributed production to local food networks, and from community gardens to new forms of communal living. With the word different in the title and the plural rather than singular futures, the exhibitions organizers incorporated design for people with disabilities, signifying inclusion of populations marginalized from activities that enrich their, and our, lives.
While the Cooper Hewitts Nature exhibition was in its final days, and the Design for Different Futures was en route to Chicago from Philadelphia, the coronavirus pandemic (COVID-19) forced schools, restaurants, and museums worldwide to close, changing patterns of life for millions in a matter of days, prohibiting the freedom of travel and movement many of us take for granted.
Early responses to the virus involved containment, testing, and an urgent need for critical medical equipment, along with support for vaccine research.
In a polarized political climate in the United States and globally, media attention focused upon preparedness and balancing concerns for overall health with troubling economic fallout.
Neither politicians, nor health officials, nor journalists used the word design very often, and yet designers played an active role in addressing the crisis.
Perhaps most visibly, public awareness was critical in communicating in real time the spread of the virus and providing information to alert the public and suggest the importance of social distancing, hand washing, and protection provided by wearing masks in public.
Newspapers printed instructions for making your own masks at home, and those with time and a sewing machine used their skills to make masks for themselves, their families, neighbors, or local hospitals in a spirit of community-mindedness to combat fear and isolation.
Messaging depended in large degree upon graphs and color-coded maps that charted the viruss spread, hotspots, numbers of people affected, and mortality rates locally, nationally, and internationally.
Interactive information design, including myriad phone apps, was an essential communication tool, and graphic designers drew, consciously or not, upon decades of design history to create effective means to organize timelines and statistics clearly and hierarchically, promoting comprehension and guiding reader behavior, whether for testing or the need to stay at home or to take other protective measures.
In Britain, newspapers reported that James Dyson (see here) had designed a ventilator that could be quickly manufactured, addressing a shortage for critically ill patients in intensive-care units of hospitals.
Other manufacturers, including an Italian company that re-tooled its scuba mask as a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) device in lieu of ventilators that were in short supply, offered solutions demonstrating a sense of shared responsibility in the face of crisis.
However, such efforts also required tutorials to train medical staff to operate the equipment effectively, in short, proving the need for coordinating design at many levels, involving engineering and the interface between machines and their users.
Temporary shelter, mobile ICUs, sanitation, and air-filtration products constitute another area of health-related design whose importance grew in response to the pandemic.

## Contemporary
Design and Economic Growth As environmentally conscious design efforts have become more numerous, more varied, and more persistent in the twenty-first century, so economists have begun to question the paradigm of associating progress with growth in production and consumer spending (as measured, for instance, by gross domestic product, GDP), at least in more industrially developed nations where consumption not only exacerbates environmentally related problems, but also may result in greater income disparity and attending social ills (see here).
Nevertheless, new or redesigned products and furnishings, stimulating increased levels of production and advertising to spur consumption in the retail market, endure at, or close to, the center of our general public understanding of the design enterprise, with consumer spending and attending job growth, both national and international, remaining for business leaders and politicians a prime indicator of employment and economic health, with communication design and software related to e-commerce accelerating the flow of goods domestically and globally.
The gross domestic product of the United States comprises of business and government expenditure, exports, and personal consumption expenditures for goods and services.
Design operates in each of these categories, but personal consumption constitutes 70 percent of the US GDP.
Over the past 70 years, there has been a shift from expenditure on material goods to services such as healthcare and childcare, both of which include considerable investment in products and the design of interior spaces (see here on IDEO): in 1950 spending on services represented 40 percent of GDP, while in 2018 it was 70 percent, in part the result of higher levels of efficient manufacture in goods-producing industries that reduces labor investment, steering the design professions as well as consumer spending toward the expansion of services.
Minotti, Lawrence Seating System, Rodolfo Dordoni Design.
Products reach all sectors, but designer goods remain associated with the luxury market in fashion and furnishings whose boutiques line Madison Avenue in New York, Kings Road in London, rue Saint-Honoré in Paris, the branded pop-up stalls of highend department stores and upscale shopping malls worldwide, and reach a broader public in fashion magazines such as Elle, Vogue, or Cosmopolitan that promote the brands of new and well-known celebrity designers.
Individual designers continue to function effectively in the worlds of fashion and high-end furnishings identified with starchitects, occasionally trickling down to the mass market through contracts with larger retail outlets.
Frequent displays of luxury goods may be found in the Style issues of the Sunday New York Times Magazine, with ads for aesthetically sophisticated variations on Modernist tables (sometimes called Neomodernist), chairs and sofas set in highceilinged open interiors, as in this one for Minotti furniture (fig.
16.11), which suggests a connection with Le Corbusiers Pavillon de lEsprit Nouveau but perhaps without the architects societal intention of providing a practical machine for living.
Companies such as Vitra or Louis Vuitton preserve and cultivate a close relationship between luxury design, originality in applications for new industrial materials, innovation, and the fine arts in their products, collections, and publications.
Star designers, such as Danish Mathias Bengtsson (b.
1971), manufacture their own exclusive lines of inventive furniture often based upon the creative exploration of new materials or sophisticated computerized production techniques.
An example is Bengtssons sculptural 1999 aluminum Slice chair (fig.
16.12), constructed of thin, laminated, flat sheets of aluminum whose precisely laser-cut shapes are determined by computer calculations to produce the chairs wavy, swelling, and contracting contoured forms and subtly varied light reflections.
Bengtssons experimentation with inventive production techniques to create novel aesthetic experiences is part of a longer history that promotes equality among the visual arts achieved through freedom of expression, creative imagination, and production technology.
Mathias Bengtsson, Slice chair, laser-cut aluminum, 30 <sup>5</sup>/<sub>8</sub> × 36 ½ × 28 ¾ (77.6 × 92.7 × 73 cm),1999.
Other designers continue to experiment with new industrial materials, for instance using recycled plastics in the manufacture of furniture or lighter, stronger materials such as titanium or carbon fibers, whether for tennis racquets, chairs, or tables.
Italian designer Alberto Meda (b.
1945) designed a carbon-fiber chair he titled Light-Light in 1987 as a means of reducing both weight and mass (the chair weighs less than 1 kg or 2.2 pounds).
The seat is made from Nomex, a compound developed by DuPont that combines thinness with durability.
Despite the machine-like finish and precise construction, manufacture required handwork, and only 50 Light Light chairs were produced at a retail cost of around \$1,200 each.
Ron Arads Three Skin chair uses experiments with the lightness and strength of carbon fiber (fig.
16.13) but resulting in a more organic sculptural form.
16.13 Ron Arad, Three Skin chair, Nomex, carbon fiber-reinforced, 36 × 19 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>16</sub> × 23 <sup>9</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (91.4 × 49.6 × 60.2 cm), 2002.
16.14 Tord Boontje, Garland lights, laser-cut silver-plated brass wrapped around hanging halogen light, laser-cut sheet, 28 × 16 in (71.1 × 40.6 cm), manufactured by Artecnica, Los Angeles, California, 2002–2003.
The Postmodern rediscovery of ornament (see here) has renewed interest in pattern and decoration aided by newer technologies such as laser cutting and rapid prototyping, also known as 3-D printing.
Laser cutting allows designers new levels of precision and aesthetic exploration rivaling if not surpassing the consummate skill required in hand craftsmanship, seen, for instance, in the work of Dutch designer Tord Boontje (b.
1968).
Boontjes 2002 series of Garland Lights, manufactured by Artecnica (fig.
16.14), uses ordinary hanging lightbulbs to explore light filtered through intricately and asymmetrically cut paper-thin silver-plated brass (other examples are cut from the synthetic polyethylene fabric Tyvek, manufactured by DuPont).
Equally exciting is rapid prototyping equipment that produces three-dimensional designs directly from sketches.
On view at the experimental 2008 MoMA exhibition entitled Design and the Elastic Mind was a video demonstrating such technology for Sketch furniture by Swedish designers Sofia Lagerkvist (b.
1976), Charlotte von der Lancken (b.
1977), Anna Lindgren (b.
1976), and Katja Savström (b.
1976) (fig.
16.16).
Using video cameras and 3-D printing, the designers ideas, traced using a stylus in space like an orchestra conductors baton, are immediately translated into a unique piece of furniture made of polyamide resin.
Design and manufacture, whose separation has been an integral part of the history of modern design and rationalized through the division of labor and mechanized mass production, here become reunited and immediate.
The interface is seamless, and only time will demonstrate the impact for the future of professionalization and democratization within design.
One can imagine do-it-yourself facilities where consumers would buy time to fashion and customize their own furnishings or clothing.
16.16 Sofia Lagerkvist, Charlotte von der Lancken, and Katja Savström, Sketch Furniture, Acron Formservice AB, Sweden, 2005.
The fashion business remains heavily dependent upon provocative novelty and advertising in directing consumers to associate clothing with alternative lifestyles and personal expression, often exemplified by celebrity supermodels who serve as ideal paradigms for a particular look.
Fabien Baron (b.
1959) has, since the early 1990s, been a successful art director for several fashion magazines, including Harper’s Bazaar, the relaunch (2013) of Interview, and Italian Vogue.
He designed a lean, simple approach to page layout in these journals, incorporating large areas of white space and dramatic black-and-white photography as well as combining different sizes of a single typeface on the page.
In these practices he continues an inventive approach to art direction pioneered by Alexey Brodovitch and M.
F.
Agha (see here) both in Europe and in the United States beginning in the later 1920s, including the value of attracting readers with surprising, even shocking features and ads.
Baron is perhaps best known for using eroticism to sell clothing and such fashion accessories as perfumes, engaging the imagination of male and female spectators by appealing to sexual fantasies and homoeroticism, sometimes involving violence and sadomasochism.
This is seen, for instance, in ads for the Calvin Klein fragrance Secret Obsession (fig.
16.15), where attention is drawn to the suggestive shape of the bottle through the contrast of color with the black-and-white photograph.
The trend in such ads may have been triggered by earlier transgressions of accepted gender stereotypes pioneered in the punk era, but it appears in contemporary fragrance or clothing in a provocative but less threatening way.

## 16.15 Fabien Baron, advertisement for Calvin Klein’s Secret Obsession, photograph with fas
hion model Eva Mendes, 2008.
In 2016 the Cooper Hewitt Design Museum devoted its triennial exhibition to Beauty. The curators emphasized the elusive nature of beauty, naming several categories that influenced their decisions as to what to include: Extravagant, Intricate, Ethereal, Transformative, Transgressive, Elemental, and Emergent.
Fashion appeared in several categories, but most spectacular were a skirt and top designed by Italian-born Giambattista Valli (b.
1966) (fig.
16.17) in which cascading layers of impossibly varied tones of reddish pink created the delightful, captivating illusion of soft, billowing clouds rather than fabric.
Vallis pieces seemed to underline the curators view that beautys enduring value lies in its ability to stimulate our senses beyond the fleeting moment.
Alexander McQueen, ensemble, silk, cotton, metal, leather, wood, Spring/Summer 2003, Alexander McQueen “Savage Beauty” exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, 2011.
Giambattista Valli, skirt and top, tulle degradé, silk taffeta, from Fall/Winter 2014–2015 Haute Couture Collection, “Beauty” exhibition at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York, 2016.
While Vallis creation stood alone on a pedestal in the Cooper Hewitts first-floor gallery, the display of fashion is often embedded in performance via the runway or even in exhibition design, as with the Metropolitan Museums 2011 posthumous retrospective, titled Savage Beauty, of British fashion designer Alexander McQueen (19662010), which attracted more than 500,000 visitors. Savage Beauty celebrated McQueen for his romantic, sublime sensibility and technical ingenuity, touching upon emotional frailty expressed alternatively through metallic, armor-like materials, or through torn fabrics, as in the 2003 ensemble illustrated in figure 16.18.
Both Valli and McQueen explore the expressive possibilities of traditional and non-traditional materials and construction techniques in their oeuvres and benefit from technological innovations that complement and stimulate creative expression.
As in the Art Deco movement (see Chapter 8), the role of technology in relation to fashion is varied, either to reduce time and expense through labor-saving machines or to permit greater creative freedom for designers.
In addition to haute couture, fashion designers and fashion brands also address the broader retail market, attuned to youthful lifestyles and subcultures that might involve variations upon certain prototypes such as T-shirts or jeans that maintain currency.
Such items were the focus of MoMAs 2017 exhibition Is Fashion Modern? This aspect of the fashion industry involves manufacturing similar products while maintaining individual or group appeal.
The approach has become a successful strategy for a number of companies, for instance the GAP clothing brand or Levis denim, catering to a youth-oriented market attracted to an image of informal, fun-loving, and relaxed behavior easily recognized by fabrics such as chino, khaki, and cotton for pants and T-shirts.
Advertising merges standardized products with carefree, youthful behavior.
A pair of Levis chino Dockers was among the 111 items included in Is Fashion Modern? (fig.
16.19).
“Dockers,” men’s chinos, installation view of the exhibition “ITEMS: Is Fashion Modern?”.
Museum of Modern Art, New York, October 1, 2017–January 28, 2018.
A related, recycled approach to contemporary fashion and other fields of design emerged in the successful career of African American celebrity designer (and trained civil engineer and architect) Virgil Abloh (19802021), who was artistic director of menswear for French fashion house Louis Vuitton as well as head of his own line of streetwear called Off White. Abloh transformed gritty, urban streetwear such as T-shirts, hoodies, and Nike sneakers into collections for young, affluent professionals who disdain conventional office attire.
His clothing incorporates eclectic references to history (a collection of tie-dyed windbreakers suggests the counterculture of the 1960s), while a series for Off White features bold diagonal stripes of black and yellow resembling crosswalks or street signs.
Social media was among Ablohs sources of inspiration, providing images captured on iPhones and posted to Instagram, a rich and limitless sampling of experience and meaning, extending to interiors and furnishings.
Abloh partnered with IKEA, for instance, for one of its furniture lines that includes a rug printed as an IKEA receipt.
Drawn to fashion and to shopping as a teenager growing up in Rockford, Illinois, and as a student in Wisconsin and later in Chicago, Abloh admired the success of fashion designers Ralph Lauren and James Jebbia (founder of the skateboarding shop and clothing brand Supreme New York) as minds and spirits that show that clothing can be much more than just the tangible, physical garments for the human body. Race also enters into the meaning of some of Ablohs collections.
A profile for the New Yorker relates that the choice of the name Pyrex and the use of the number 23 for his earliest line of clothing were references to athletics (23 was the Chicago Bulls basketball superstar Michael Jordans jersey number) and drugs (the oven-safe glass cookware used to manufacture crack cocaine), the two economic paths available to a Black man who wanted to get out of Chicago: drug dealing and sports. Figure 16.20 illustrates a series of bright yellow hoodies printed with the number 23; also printed on some of the hoodies is a detail from Caravaggios painting The Entombment of Christ (16031604), now in the Vatican.
Virgil Abloh, Pyrex, 23 runway collection, 2012.
Although better publicized, Ablohs is but one of countless lesser-known stories of design history hidden beneath racism.
The abolition of slavery in the United States (1865) shifted rather than ended racial inequality, with discrimination, segregation, and incarceration preserving servitude and limited routes to opportunity and justice amid migration from South to North that began during World War I and lasted into the 1970s.
Another better-known example is the Super Soaker water gun of 1989, patented by Black mechanical and nuclear engineer Lonnie Johnson (b.
1949), who invented the Super Soaker while employed in NASAs Jet Propulsion Laboratory near Pasadena, California.
It is not simply ethics and justice that are at stake in telling the stories of Lonnie Johnson and others, but also the economic benefits of inclusion, the appreciation of Black contributions to technology and culture, whether the Harlem Renaissance, the blues, jazz, Motown, or hip hop, including lifestyles and their expression in design.
At the middle of the retail market for consumer goods stand electronic products such as smart phones and personal assistants as well as furnishings manufactured by large international companies such as IKEA and Japanese retailer Muji.
The IKEA Corporation of Sweden, originally founded in 1943, has successfully expanded and marketed a warehouse approach to Nordic modern design in many large European cities as well as (since 1985) in affluent North American suburbs and in Asia.
IKEA operates stores in more than 63 countries globally (the largest is in the Philippines).
Online catalogs of merchandise, off-the-shelf availability, flat, carry-home packaging, as well as do-it-yourself assembly instructions and tools for fastening standardized bolts and fittings within product lines all contribute to the appeal of IKEA and are integral to the companys design policy, together with the affordability of products ranging from furniture and lighting to fabrics, household, and kitchen wares, and storage systems.
IKEA offers a variety of molded plywood furniture and modular units for shelving using painted or wood-grained veneers attached to inexpensively manufactured pressed board; many products recall interwar and post-war furniture designed by Alvar Aalto or Kaare Klint (see here).
Other individual examples and ensembles include upholstered chairs and sofas, American Colonial designs, and craft-inspired furnishings in woven rattan or inexpensive cast metals with textured finishes.
Furniture designed especially for children is heavily marketed at IKEA, as are desks and storage for the apartments of young professionals and university-age students.
In the category of childrens furniture, IKEA has had to recall dressers and pay significant damages to parents whose toddlers have been injured or killed when dressers tipped over, raising concerns about safety in the design process.
The IKEA catalog and in-store showrooms feature coordinated interiors as well as off-the-shelf items, and prices appear in bold sans serif typography.
Despite the odd-sounding (at least to North American ears) names given to families of items, nowhere is the IKEA name linked to a specific country of origin.
The overriding character of the merchandise and the shopping experience is ease, that is, ease of packing, shipping, transporting, assembling (some might argue this point, but one is saving the cost of assembly by doing it oneself and not having to wait for delivery), affordability, and, perhaps most importantly, ease of replacing.
Planned obsolescence is taken for granted in an industry whose products usually take longer to make and are at least generally intended to last longer as well.
It also matches the transient lifestyles of students who would rather sell or leave their IKEA products than pay to move them from apartment to apartment or city to city.
Beginning in the 1990s, it was easy for families with small children to visit IKEA, as stores provided monitored playrooms that permitted parents to shop without distraction.
Thus design for IKEA includes the way products are packaged, assembled, displayed, marketed, and merchandised.
For the most part, IKEA interiors emphasize efficient storage, bright colors, and patterns for fabrics, all intended to maximize limited space and add comfort to smaller homes or apartments.
Figure 16.21, for instance, features a restrained modern dinette, more casual than a formal dining room, featuring molded Odger chairs and two hanging pendant lamps with spiral slats made of ABS plastic vaguely reminiscent of Poul Henningsens Artichoke lamp (see fig.
11.32).
The chairs are priced at \$95 each, but on the opposite page a prospective buyer can swap them for a less expensive side chair at \$69.99 (named Janinge).
Indeed, the merging of merchandising and packaging as components of design has given IKEA a distinctive identity in the marketplace with appeal that extends beyond students or children.
Even if individual items appear bland, IKEA makes decisions for living spaces a design activity in its own right, bringing to mind the Eameses analogy between design and planning the seating arrangement for a dinner party (see here and fig.
13.22).
In other words, the consumer is not only the recipient of design, but enters into the design process itself.
16.21 Interior spread from IKEA catalog, 2020.
Design has also become integral to the marketing strategy of the Target Corporation, with headquarters in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
Target is not a manufacturer but a retail distributor, and markets the term design, not as a style in the sense of a visual look, but as a brand communicating better living in the broadest sense of the term.
Their aim is to bring the benefits of design and design-consciousness to the discount-store shopper, with an array of designed and designer products, quite literally from A to Z; in fact, the Fall 2007 Style issue of the New York Times Magazine contained products for each letter of the alphabet in a multi-page spread.
Acknowledging design is certainly related in this case to progress, via an awareness of beauty, function, and other kinds of product associations (and the educational association of the advertisement itself with a childrens ABC book).
On one page the letter B displays a stovetop espresso maker by Italian company Bialetti first manufactured in the 1930s (fig.
16.22, left); under X appears the RX, a prescription labeling system designed by Deborah Adler (b.
1976) for multiple user groups, including pictograms for children, large type and color backgrounds for the elderly, and color-coding for different members of a family to more easily identify their prescriptions and prevent mis-use (fig.
16.22, right).
Target has launched an all-out embrace of design, incorporating Postmodern elements such as nostalgia with functional information graphics; the company leaves few stones unturned in the design/product/value-added equation.
The texts accompanying the products reveal the added value of their forms, and feel-good associations.
Shown here is the copy for the Michael Graves tea kettle illustrating the letter G (fig.
16.22, center): People love waking up with Michael Graves Design.
Starting with a hot cup of tea is one thing, having it announced by a cheery chirp and poured from a designed-to-feel-good-in-thehand kettle is another. In 1999, a Graves toaster for Target appeared in an advertisement with the phrase finding the fun in functional. In an ad campaign from August 2005, Target monopolized the pages of the New Yorker without including direct references to products.
Lifestyle along with various iterations of the Target logo were the themes: urban, youthful, provocative, even rebellious.
It is as if shopping, Target, design, and fashionable living were indistinguishable from one another, all merging into a cutting-edge brand.
16.22 Advertisement for Target stores products, New York Times “Style” Magazine, Fall 2007, letters “B” (Bialetti espresso maker), “G” (Michael Graves tea kettle), and “X” (Deborah Adler, Target Clear RX prescription system).
Target Corporation, Minneapolis, Minnesota.

## Redesign
versus Obsolescence Planned obsolescence remains a cornerstone of consumer-led design.
With the regular stream of new models of smart phones with added features and related tendencies in other electronic and digital products, planned obsolescence has been replaced by terms such as upgrade or redesign that imply improvement, progress, and creativity, suggesting that redesign is natural, normal, and inevitable.
In November 2016, the New York Times devoted its Sunday Magazine to design with an image of a square bicycle wheel and the tagline DO OVER: ON THE CURRENT OBSESSION FOR REDESIGNING EVERYTHING. Examples ranged from a mid-century modern-style sofa that can be easily shipped and assembled from modular components to a cell tower constructed of thin, hollow composite tubes whose form can be manipulated to transform it into a sculpture by pulling wires attached to the structure, to a bicycle lock designed by Rinat Aruh that attaches to the bar holding the seat and includes a GPS chip for tracking (fig.
16.23).
The accompanying articles author (Rob Walker) connects design with problemsolving, while the problem may be little more than a need in the marketplace, such as a lighter, less cumbersome, and more theft-proof bicycle lock.
The emphasis tends to focus on the individual designer and special nature of the creative process.
Yet from an historical perspective the cover image of the square bicycle wheel and word obsession in the tagline raise the issue of whether redesign is necessarily progress, or whether it is market rather than innovation driven.
In other words, does redesign result in improvement or is it just another word for consumer engineering most often aimed at the affluent shopper?
As noted above, circular design proposes different priorities for the design process (see here).
16.23 Rinat Aruh, bicycle lock, PVD titanium ion-plated steel with silicone rubber gasket, length 11 in (27.9 cm).

## Users
and Design Process The foregrounding of the individual in describing design process is in some ways a product of the marketing strategies of manufacturers who call attention to their products by associating them with well-known designers.
Another reason is the idea that the study of design history has grown out of art history, where individual artists (mostly male, European or North American, and white) play an outsized role.
Increasingly, however, observing and analyzing the needs and experiences of users has become an acknowledged part of the product and service design process.
One example is Dutch architect Rem Koolhaass Seattle Public Library (completed 2004; fig.
16.24).
This large steel and glass structure, constructed on an entire city block, lacks the unified profile of much modern architecture; moreover, the design of its interior was based upon suggestions from different groups of users to facilitate a variety of services rather than an over-riding scheme or single idea or system.
Relinquishing ownership can be difficult, but critics have applauded the buildings ability to cater to different types of users, and the library has generally been welcomed by Seattle residents, who feel they had a share in its design.
Koolhaas has seen a parallel for his approach to design not in traditional urban planning but in the haphazard growth of megacities with populations of upward of ten million such as Lagos (Nigeria) or Mumbai (India).
While such chaos conflicts with many of our associations between design and order, Koolhaas finds the fragmented aesthetic energizing and (somehow) navigable for many of those who live and work in such places (less so perhaps for tourists).
When the user-centered approach shifts from the realm of product and direct service design to virtual web-based applications or phone apps, the term user can take on other connotations.
Mining and analyzing data on user habits (with or without their knowledge) allows companies to chart and to introduce content that maximizes the continued attention of app visitors.
As reported by New Yorker staff writer Amy Weiner, the more time visitors spent on a site or an app, the more effective the companys efforts; users became addicts, drawn toward a subtle form of coercion to produce a desired result for marketers.
Rem Koolhaas, interior, Seattle Public Library, Seattle, Washington, 2004.
A related approach to contemporary design process is known as product semantics. Designer and critic Guy Julier has described the Dyson electric vacuum cleaner along these lines.
The Dyson vacuum cleaner (introduced 1993) uses clear plastic to demonstrate with visual immediacy the effectiveness of the dust collection as well as mudguards and fins to evoke efficiency, all to psychologically suggest the capturing of dirt and reduce resistance to a novel and more expensive design (fig.
16.25).
The underlying concept of product semantics is the analysis of consumer values and behaviors in order to break down barriers between ourselves and the products or services we use, and may consider purchasing.
Even James Dyson himself is part of the product semantics equation  he presents himself as part of the lore of invention itself, appealing to the tinkerer in each of us who has the capacity to question the status quo, think of something better through imagination, patent it, and profit from our insight.
In this light, it is not surprising that while we still may identify design with products, contemporary design consultancies such as IDEO report that only about 8 percent of their business involves product design, while the majority is in communications and expanded concepts of branding and service design.
Dyson, Dual Cyclone DC 24 vacuum cleaner, plastic housing, 43 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> × 11 × 13 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>10</sub> in (110 × 28 × 34.8 cm), c.
1998.
Diagrams of the contemporary design process tend to assign equivalent roles to designers, manufacturers, and users/consumers, often using a triangular model with arrows emphasizing communication or feedback loops that acknowledge multiple stakeholders and facilitate dialogue among them involving values and beliefs, marketing, distribution, manufacturing practice, and user research.

## Service
Design There is no single formula for success in the expanding design enterprise.
Consultancies such as Pentagram rely upon oversight from its various partners who attract customers, while others such as IDEO do not assign credit to individuals.
Both approaches engage a broader range of expertise to the user experience not only of products but also to navigate services toward creating preferred experiences.
An example of service design addresses wait time for travelers in the screening of luggage in large airports in response to the threat of terrorism in the wake of 9/11.
Screening luggage involves the use of cumbersome plastic bins into which travelers place their bags, coats, and personal accessories on a conveyor belt to be scanned by TSA (Transportation Security Administration) personnel before walking through screening metal detectors.
Long lines during peak travel times create delays, exacerbated by a shortage of available bins because airport staff have to move them from one end of the screening process to the other while also attending to their other responsibilities.
At Londons Heathrow airport, the MacDonald Humfrey Automation design consultancy developed a service system, Mach-Lane, that eliminated such delays: a double-tiered conveyor shuttles plastic bins automatically from the end of the line back to the beginning where travelers access them to fill with their belongings; and it works!

## Artificial
Intelligence, Smart, and Autonomous Products Digital technology paved the way for personal computers, including desktop, laptop, and handheld devices.
Pioneered by the Intel Company in 1971, the processing of digital information on microchips reduced the mechanical space requirements of earlier computers.
Beginning in the mid-1980s, personal computers eclipsed and eventually replaced typewriters, books, the Rolodex, and calculators for business, research, and home use.
With the growth of the Internet, computers have also vastly expanded the possibilities of information and data processing as well as banking and business transactions.
Like many contemporary electronic products, phones have become mobile resources of information tailored to our needs: appendages rather than accessories.
They are not only personalized through the apps we choose to download, but also quite literally become an extension of ourselves, a generally well-meaning but not terribly invasive shadow-self or even better self.
For instance, my phone tells me how many steps I take in a day, what my step goal is in relation to my age and weight, the number of calories I have burned; it congratulates me when I reach my goal, and gently chides me to get up and do something when I fall short.
As such, smart design means a level of interaction between machines (the artificial, human-made world) and the living, breathing world of nature.
In addition to phones and personal assistants like Amazons Echo or Alexis, designed artifacts provide us with information, save time, make us more efficient or productive, and move toward a seamless interface between human and machine worlds, mediated by buttons, by touch, or by voice.
Apples watch (2015) transferred functionality from the hand to the wrist, maintaining its association with the milestone iPhone but acknowledging that the further miniaturization of its hardware and the dexterity required to access its functionality might be limited to more tech-savvy users: Apple sold 2.4 million watches in the second quarter of 2015, while 75 million iPhones were sold in a single quarter of 2014.
The design of such products is complex, involving teams of individuals with diverse backgrounds in product design, engineering, biology, anthropology, ethnography, marketing, service design, and data management, with the boundaries among such fields increasingly fluid and interconnected.
With its expansion into software as well as hardware design, Apple operates in a horizontal way at all levels of production development, a voice in decisions from idea to final product.
In terms of hardware, Apples former senior vice-president of design (Sir) Jonathan Ive (b.
1967) seems a kindred spirit to German industrial designer Dieter Rams (see here), whose ten principles of design Ive appears to observe, along with an obsessive concern for detail that creates a unique and highly successful brand identity reaching to the mass market.
The design process includes packaging, creating out of each purchase the experience of opening a precious gift in a series of stages that offers an added surprise all of its own (fig.
16.26).
16.26 Packaging for the Apple iPod.
Industrial design for cellular phones and computers may be studied from a number of viewpoints.
Certainly miniaturization as a design strategy plays a role: designers develop the most efficient, lightweight, and compact plastic or aluminum product housings given the space requirements of the various integrated circuits, speakers, microphones, touch keys, and screens.
They use ergonomic studies and user-centered observations to determine the final form of a device and the location of various functions in relation to a hierarchy of information and ease of access, based upon how easy the device is to operate and how intuitively it communicates its function to the user.
For desktop computers, designers consider possible novelties in color, form, and even texture that might attract consumer attention in a competitive market through establishing a more individualized relationship with the user.
Even in housing for computers and cellular phones, the combination of miniaturized equipment with commercial considerations rarely results in stable type forms, although advocates for circular design place a premium on enduring forms that facilitate repair and replacement rather than disposal.
Stand-alone computer hard drives may be horizontal and located beneath the monitor, or vertical and more easily placed on the floor or held in place by metal straps, creating more work space on the surface of a table or desk.
Apple introduced its iMac desktop computer in 1998, after the return of CEO Steve Jobs (19552011) to the company after a 12-year absence.
The iMac launch took place before the advent of flat-screen monitors, and combined the cathode tube screen with the hard drive in a single unit.
Led by Ive, the design team developed a translucent housing in a rounded, contoured, sculptural form, with choices of vibrant colors with names such as tangerine, strawberry, and lime that seemed more suited to flavors of water ice than to existing desktops in the market at the time (fig.
16.27).

## Multiple
choice.
(Any answer is corect) iMac: \$999 inter 30 gam Advertisement for iMac desktop computer manufactured by Macintosh Corporation, Cupertino, California, 1998. software (interface) as well as hardware (product form, materials, placement of control mechanisms, buttons, and so on).
Software interface explains the success of the Apple iPod (2001; now discontinued).
Prior to the 2007 introduction of the companys first iPhone, this miniature MP3 outdistanced its competitor Sony, whose transistor radios, cassette players, and compact disk players formerly had been the acknowledged industry leader in handheld playing devices.
In a New Yorker article from 2006 profiling Sony Corporation CEO Howard Stringer, the subject of the interview turned to Apples lead in the MP3 market.
Stringer (and others) noted the appeal of Apple iPods sleek minimalist design, the companys marketing strategy emphasizing individual expression, and attractive features such as the responsive wheel (or later touch-activated) scrolling that made it fast and easy to see and select from a list of options, but the more significant consideration in its design was not the ease of operation, but the ease with which users could access or download content for the iPod.
Unlike the cumbersome security required to download music for Sonys MP3 player, which pre-dated Apples entry into the market, the iPod much more seamlessly connected the product to musical content, addressing a software rather than hardware issue.
In the words of the New Yorker writer, Sony approached proprietary digital-rights management as if it were guarding nuclear secrets; Apple built a security-lite system that could download music from the Internet to a computer to an iPod so simply that your grandmother could get the hang of it while brewing tea. It was the interface that explains the success of the product, not the interface with the wheel, but with the music.
Personal computers, smartphones, and Apple watches represent one path of interaction between technology and design, facilitating our interaction with information through software as well as hardware.
Another area connecting design with technology and artificial intelligence is robotics, referring not to products that assist us in performing tasks and actions but to autonomous devices that operate independently and replace the human presence.
A commercial example is the Roomba Scheduler Vacuuming Robot, manufactured beginning in 2002 by the iRobot Corporation in Burlington, Massachusetts (fig.
16.28).
This automated, intelligent device, despite its neutral appearance, not only reduces or eliminates a time-consuming household chore (theoretically at least), but also takes on the character of a family pet; owners can provide names and customize their Roombas with distinguishing stickers or painted decoration.
16.28 iRobot Roomba Scheduler Vacuuming Robot, plastic housing, AWARE™ Robot Intelligence System, 18 <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> × 14 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>10</sub> × 4 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>10</sub> in (46.5 × 37.3 × 11.9 cm), manufactured by iRobot Corporation, Burlington, Massachusetts, 2002.
Once the stuff of science fiction, the idea of self-driving cars is now becoming a reality, and similar to nineteenth-century reactions to mechanization, gives rise to fears as well as hopes.
For some designers as well as writers and theorists, the key to the design of robotic devices is reducing barriers to our interaction with them.
The term uncanny valley refers to robots whose resemblance to human beings is so seamless that we feel threatened and repelled rather than comfortable interacting with them, impeding rather than encouraging interaction.
For critics, artificial intelligence poses a threat to workers, for instance to the millions of people employed as truck drivers, cabbies, Uber and Lyft drivers who fear losing their livelihood with the advent of selfdriving vehicles that no longer require the service they provide, or operators who watch machines do the tasks they used to perform manually and from which they derived satisfaction.
Indeed, the history of design demonstrates that new technologies entail risks as well as advantages whose results may not in many cases be predicted; an improvement may benefit some but not others, and designers may embrace or attempt to reconcile the viewpoints of multiple constituencies or stakeholders.

## Materials
Technology and Softness New synthetic materials and new uses for older industrial materials also continue to blur boundaries between the natural and artificial worlds.
Soft materials replace traditionally hard ones, for instance in appliance design, as seen in Italian designer Marta Sansonis (b.
1963) Folpo soft plastic hand mixer (1998) manufactured by Alessi (fig.
16.29), whose blades resemble flexible tentacles rather than rigid metal beaters.
In the traditional hand mixer the action is mechanical and automatic, while in Sansonis version the metaphor is that of a biological organism, resulting in an interface that is personal rather than impersonal.
Marta Sansoni, “Folpo” hand mixer, plastic, height 9 <sup>9</sup>/<sub>16</sub> in (25 cm), manufactured by Alessi, New York and Italy, 2001.

## Politics,
Technology, and the Media There are voices critical of fundamental aspects of the information age, which seems for many to hold out such promise for humanizing technology, improving the quality of life, and making design more inclusive and expansive.
Part of this criticism is at the structural level; that is, the interactive digital technology that powers our iPhones, guides us with reasonable confidence by global positioning technology to unfamiliar places, and allows us to program and personalize our digital devices, may also be used for unauthorized surveillance, the dissemination of disinformation, or remote, destructive military strikes.
Such uses raise questions about the risks that technology poses to safety, and make us think about whether the progress we associate with information in cyberspace does in fact mask more dangerous relationships between political authority and those businesses that design and provide information technology.
It is hardly surprising that skepticism about the information age was stimulated by global terrorism and responses to the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the Pentagon and World Trade Center towers became powerful symbols and targets for destruction.
While advocates of Postmodernism optimistically connected pluralism with tolerance and an embrace of difference, 9/11 and the war on terror introduced a renewed and destructive ideological and political dualism that appears to have grown rather than subsided.
The media presentation of the World Trade Center attacks elicited strong patriotic feeling in the United States and a shared sense of sympathy for human suffering worldwide.
At the same time, subsequent global events, such as the Arab Spring (20102011) and refugee crises, stirred further, often hostile nationalist fervor and civil war.
The relationship of these political events to the history of modern design is at times direct, for instance in the development of devices to improve personal security or respond promptly to victims of violence and displacement.
Indirectly, politics affects international relations, for example, taking the form of protective trade policies that disrupt supply chains or impose tariffs and threaten free trade and the interdependence and sharing of information that maintains the design enterprise.

## Graphic
Design in the Digital Age Digital technology has made a major impact upon the practice of graphic design.
As the varied methods of graphic designers extend into the virtual space of the computer screen, user experience shifts from turning pages or unfolding pamphlets to triggering links by click or by touch to reveal multiple windows filled with content that is seen, read, and heard, often simultaneously.
The result is inherently more robust and interactive than traditional print media, riveting and distracting all at once.
While adapting to the new media seems almost natural for younger generations who grew up with personal computers, for older populations the interface can be challenging.
The rapidly evolving technologies that make such new explorations possible provide designers with flexibility and choices beyond those of photomechanical processes and allow them to produce typography and manipulate images with increased speed and an expanding range of possibilities.
Graphic processing and digital manipulation provide opportunities for designers to unite photography, filmmaking, and more traditional typography, illustration, and layout.
While the term digital media is sometimes used to refer to such activities, the degree of overlap with graphic design in undergraduate education and in practice makes discipline-based thinking appear narrow and out of touch with constantly evolving graphic design industry practice.
Such media convergence was at the root of the Media Lab developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology beginning in 1984, which continues to explore interrelationships and interactivity in the digital realm (on the Mediated Matters group at the Media Lab, see here).
At the same time, the technologies that equip the designer with new means for communicating information require an ability to balance versatility with specialized technical skills, resulting in challenges for traditional discipline-based university curricula and professional practice alike that yield discussion and an array of future educational models.
Using computers to generate digital type and manipulate digital images for graphic presentation began in 1984 with the operating system and user interface developed by the Apple Corporation for its Macintosh computers.
The translation of type and images into electronic code on a low-resolution computer screen was not entirely new.
However, creating and controlling those impulses with a computer mouse on a virtual desktop with pull-down windows rather than programming them with typed instructions on a keyboard was unique at that time to the Apple Corporation and catapulted the growth of personal computing.
This graphic interface used terms like cut and paste for functions familiar to graphic designers and amateurs alike (developed by computer scientist Larry Tesler, 19462020).
Amateurs used the new interface to democratize the printing and graphic design industries through desktop publishing.
Manipulating fonts and using a range of effects with the click of a mouse became commonplace, and office assistants could produce and edit reports and other communications with logos, borders, and images, generating a wide variety of materials formerly produced by professional printers and graphic designers.
In completing these tasks, amateur designers borrowed from among thousands of symbols and popular graphics (clip art) stored on five-inch compact disks or downloaded from the Web.
The Macintosh also appealed to a small group of enthusiastic professional graphic designers, not as a tool to replace existing camera-ready design or printed output, but as a distinct form of communication offering new possibilities for expressing a contemporary sensibility.
A pioneer in these explorations was the German-born and trained typesetter and graphic designer Wolfgang Weingart (19412021), who taught typography at the Basel School of Applied Art beginning in the early 1960s.
Looking beyond the more limited range of typefaces, grid layouts, and photomechanical techniques associated with Swiss Style (or International Typographic Style), Weingart expanded (and subverted) the techniques of letterpress and offset lithography through complex layering (overlapping) of photographic images and an ambiguous, suggestive use of symbols and letterforms, as seen in his poster announcing a 1984 exhibition of Swiss posters (fig.
16.30).
Los Angeles-based graphic designer April Greiman (b.
1948), who studied in Switzerland with both Armin Hofmann and Weingart in the 1970s, was receptive to this kind of complex layering and other experiments with type and image, while the graphical user interface of the Macintosh computer facilitated their introduction into her professional practice.
16.30 Wolfgang Weingart, Schweizer Plakat (The Swiss Poster), poster, offset lithography, 47 × 33 <sup>1</sup>/ in (119.4 × 84.3 cm), 1984.
Museum of Design, Zurich.
Poster collection.
Early computer-generated digital images and text appeared primitive in comparison with the refinement of letterpress or photomechanical typography.
A most recognizable aspect of early computer-generated fonts was the distinctive low-resolution effect of enlarged letters that revealed origins in coordinates based upon square pixels, resulting in jaggy transitions from vertical to horizontal elements of letterforms rather than smooth, curved ones.
Another early use of digital output was through patterns and textures, generated as tools by software programs such as MacDraw or by digitized photographs that produced simplified, abstracted images.
All three digital techniques are seen in a Greiman poster from 1986 (fig.
16.31).
At the same time, Dutch-born Rudy VanderLans (b.
1955) launched the first issue of the magazine Emigre in San Francisco in 1984.
In later issues of the journal, VanderLans worked with Czechoslovakian-born Zuzana Licko (b.
1961) and other contributors.
Emigre published work by international graphic designers in a variety of media, exploring new territories in graphic design including the Macintosh as well as other desktop technologies like xerography.
Licko, for instance, created modular typefaces on the Macintosh for Emigre, taking into account the jaggy letterforms, but with the freedom of an inexpensive alternative to costly equipment for typesetting.
These typefaces, such as Lickos Oakland (1985; fig.
16.32), employ modularity where possible to construct forms economically from a limited number of elements, similar to the strategy used by Herbert Bayer for his universal alphabet (see fig.
9.32).
New software and higher resolution eliminated the jaggy edges of earlier digital typefaces and led to new fonts that were published in Emigre in the 1990s, including Jeffery Keedys Keedy Sans (1991; fig.
16.33).
The label accompanying this font on the MoMA website notes how it frustrates viewers expectations of type with letterforms that are unfinished and imperfect. 16.31 April Greiman, poster for “Snow White + the Seven Pixels” presentation at the Maryland Institute College of Art, Baltimore, Maryland, 1986.

## Aa
Bb Cc Dd Ee Ff Gg Hh li Jj Kk LI Mm Nn Oo Pp Qq Rr Ss Tt Uu Vv Ww Xx Yy Zz 1234567890 # Aa Bb Cc Dd Ee Ff Gg Hh ii Jj Kk LI Mm Nn Oo Pp Qq Rr Ss Tt Uu Vv Ww Xx Yy Zz 1234567890 16.33 Jeffery Keedy, Keedy Sans typeface, 1991.
Lickos sentiments were democratic and alternative in nature, as revealed in the following remarks: For centuries the design of typefaces has existed as an exclusive discipline reserved for specialists; today the personal computer provides the opportunity to create customized alphabets with an increased potential for personalization and expression.
The design and manufacture of fonts can now be integrated into a single medium allowing for a more interactive design approach....
Digital technology has advanced the state of graphic art by a quantum leap into the future, thereby turning designers back to the most primitive of graphic ideas.
Integrating design and production, the computer has reintroduced craft as a source of inspiration.
Lickos analogy between computer and craft seems not to refer to the manual drawing of fonts or the cutting of punches, but to the digital designers independence and versatility.
The excitement of experiment recalls the explosion of wood display types in the early nineteenth century.
Just as the uses of typography expanded beyond the limited market for expensive printed books at that time, desktop publishing represented a late twentieth-century incarnation of this phenomenon, in which more individualized expression for projects such as invitations, catalogs, or even student term papers became desirable.
In addition to Emigre, new digital fonts now appear in a wider variety of publications such as U&lc.
Typography underwent tremendous expansion as a result of digitization, with the invention of new typefaces and experimentation producing a seemingly endless array of effects.
Among the most inventive and challenging experiments with the virtual workspace took place at the Cranbrook Academy of Art beginning in the 1970s under its graphic design director Katherine McCoy (b.
1945).
In this laboratory-like environment free from commercial pressure, students explored the possibilities of image and text manipulation, producing posters such as that illustrated in figure 16.34 (from 1990), promoting the academys graduate graphic design program with a suggestive but dizzying array of unevenly set words, overlapping images, and information to encourage multiple readings and individual interpretations.

## 16.34 Katherine McCoy, The New Discourse in Design, poster for Cranbrook Academy of Art, o
ffset lithography, 27 × 22 in (59.9 × 55.9 cm), 1990.
Developments in technology during the 1990s made desktop computers the industry and educational standard for the graphic design profession.
Students entering the field began to generate projects using software packages such as QuarkXpress and Adobe Photoshop, and universities replaced drafting tables and light tables (the latter used to cut and paste images and type for photographic reproduction) with computer workstations, scanners, and high-resolution printers.
Hand-drawn calligraphy gave way to computer-generated typography on the Macintosh operating system, many of whose features were incorporated into the Windows system, developed by the Microsoft Corporation for IBM and IBM-compatible personal computers.
Students began to carry packages of floppy disks (later Flash or keychain devices; now virtual cloud-based storage eliminates the risk of losing or forgetting even a portable device) in addition to (or rather than) toolboxes filled with X-Acto knives and felt-tipped markers, while administrators looked to the computer industry, foundations, and rising tuition fees to help underwrite the tremendous cost of software licensing and workstations.
Higher-resolution monitors, printers, and an expanding desktop toolbox allowed designers to achieve exacting standards on a par with the most technically advanced art-directed magazines, including a wide range of colors and subtle tonal effects, seamless manipulations of images, and complex layering.
Computer-generated images blur boundaries between animation and photography and create imagined worlds with a tremendous capacity to persuade and transport the viewer, especially in connection with advertising and more recently with gaming and virtual reality headsets.
The effect is seen in a 2001 advertisement for Sharp Electronics, which connects the high-quality resolution of a flat-screen television with the immediacy of being there (fig.
16.35).

## 16.35 Advertisement for flat-screen television, manufactured by Sharp Corporation, New Yor
ker, September 2001.
Computer-generated graphic design began as an underground movement by young artists experimenting outside mainstream professional channels with novel but unsophisticated, intentionally amateur production techniques invented by the first generation of Macintosh computer software developers.
Within a decade, the field expanded into the ultimate high-end technology of professional multimedia communication, with limitless possibilities both for the manipulation of images by designers (and interactive capabilities for users), the seduction of consumers, and endless tweaking by software developers and personal computer manufacturers to accelerate the range of the effects and encourage the purchase of upgrades and licenses.
Computer preparation of type and layout now dominates the printing industry, although much bulk printing continues to be done on offset presses from photographic plates rather than directly from the computer to the press.
Beginning in the early 1980s, daily newspapers such as USA Today began to rival weekly magazines with more color reproduction of photographs and advertisements, and daily rather than only Sunday editions use color for ads and features.
Magazine art directors use sophisticated approaches to layout for feature stories with integrated pictures, illustrations, titles, and text to interest the reader.
Moreover, journals such as the Sunday New York Times Magazine eschew a consistent branded identity, with each issue given a different typographic and layout format with fewer rules or restrictions, related to the theme of that issues content.
Matt Wileys art direction for the NYT Magazine for November 12, 2017, is an example (he was art director from 2014 to 2020, and is now a partner at Pentagram).
Aside from regular features such as the crossword puzzle, the content focused upon Tech and Design in the automobile industry, in particular self-driving (autonomous) vehicles.
The cover illustrated an abandoned, rusted steering wheel viewed from above in a scruffy patch of overgrown grass, dirt, and weeds, with a monarch butterfly perched at the right quadrant of the wheel (fig.
16.36); the table of contents used heavily pixelated lettering in yellow against a matt black background, colors associated with highways and their lane markings.
A double-page spread echoes the same approach to lettering, this time black on yellow and the words IN FORMATION, with rows of identical vehicles attached to trailers of various sizes moving in a controlled pattern, echoing similar icons used elsewhere in the issue (fig.
16.37).
16.36 New York Times Magazine cover, November 12, 2017, Matt Wiley (art director).
The use of simplified, reductive signs to communicate ideas or instructions quickly and clearly in place of words or more detailed illustrations has been a part of graphic design practice at least since Henry Becks London Underground map of 1933 (see fig.
9.61) or Cook and Shanoksys airport signage of the 1970s, the same era as the first version of Michael Hertzs (19322020) combined bus and subway map of Manhattan and surrounding boroughs, which commuters and tourists found more navigable than the more reductive abstract version designed by Massimo Vignelli in 1972.
A later iteration of Hertzs map is still in wide use today by the citys Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA).
In addition to maps and other areas of infographics, communication by texting on the go with smartphones also inspired the invention of abbreviated pictograms to express emotional responses in pictures rather than in words. Emojis, developed by the Japanese firm NTT DoCoMo beginning in 1999 with 176 emojis (picture+character in Japanese), were available to operating systems worldwide in 2010 and integrated with the Apple product line in 2011 (fig.
16.38).
Senders and receivers recognize emojis across language barriers (the same motivation for reducing the names of corporations to letters in a global business context), but as observed by design historian D.
J.
Huppatz, some critics noted a cultural bias, that emojis all seemed to heavily favor white faces, male professionals, and American foods. In 2018, emoji version 11.0 included female professionals, a wider variety of foods, and the ability of users to change facial color and skin tone, a nod to acknowledging difference and identity within its system of symbols.
16.38 Examples of emojis.

## Craft:
The Persistence of Process While electronic imagery and software extend the possibilities of image manipulation and projection, it has not been possible, nor even desirable, to eliminate skills in drawing, model-building, carving, turning, tooling, draping, tailoring, and a host of other traditional techniques common in most design professions.
Increasingly, computer interface also permits a great deal of experimentation, emphasizing the playfulness inherent in process rather than forming a shortcut to a predetermined result, as with 3- D printing and rapid prototyping and the flexibility they introduce into mechanical production.
Experimentation, tinkering, and intuition often exist in the very nature of the craft process, and even in front of the computer screen.
It was fear of the elimination of this aspect of process that aroused the indignation of John Ruskin and William Morris now well over a century ago.
Despite the sophistication of an expanded, collaborative design process as practiced in modern consultancies, it is interesting to note that when the forward-looking IDEO design consultancy selected objects from the permanent collection of the Cooper Hewitt National Design Museum for a small exhibition in 2007, the themes of the exhibition were intuition, empathy, and inspiration, rather than, for instance, research, analysis, testing, problem-solving, or even HumanComputer Interaction (HCI).
Sally Bowen Prange, Barnacle Teapot, stoneware, silicon carbide, $6 \times 1 1 \times 6 ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 }$ in (15 × 28 × 16 cm), 1991.
Despite an acknowledgment that its artifacts rarely occupy the same critical space as the contemporary fine art scene, craft remains a vehicle for aesthetic exploration and individual expression in a wide variety of materials, with a growing number of opportunities for exhibition in museums and galleries, and renewed interest in its history and cultural value.
With a market limited at times by high costs and criticism of the commercial exploitation of star names, craft continues to chart new territory for expression and materials exploration, often without the burden of theoretical and historical comparison and background found in the contemporary fine art critical discourse.
Craft also often includes the contributions of women, who are less represented in many areas of industrial design.
In ceramics, for instance, Sally Bowen Pranges (19272008) stoneware Barnacle Teapot of 1991 experiments with a variety of textures to simulate the effects of time and seawater upon human-made products, wearing them away while at the same time transforming them into new, almost animate, creations (fig.
16.39; see also Neri Oxman, here).
While Pranges teapot remains within a tradition of utilitarian products, weaver Olga de Amaral (b.
1932) focuses more on exploring aesthetic effects of new combinations of materials, as in her Alquimia XIII wallhanging of 1984, woven from cotton, linen, rice paper, gesso, paint, and gold leaf (fig.
16.40).
In this work, strands of thread hover in front of rectangles of linen painted tarnished silver at the bottom and gold as the eye moves upward.
The texture and color of the materials suggest a mysterious transformation or purification.
Modern weavings also provide continuity with local traditions throughout the world, preserving and extending the varied role of craft in non-Western and pre-industrial societies.
16.40 Olga de Amaral, Alquimia XIII, wall-hanging, cotton, linen, rice paper, gesso, paint, gold leaf, $7 1 \times 2 9 ~ \mathrm { ^ { 1 } / _ { 2 } }$ in (180 × 75 cm), 1984.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
Freedom of expression, the satisfaction that accompanies the process of working with materials, and the excitement of discovering the richness of effect, all combine to continually renew the inherent challenge and enjoyment of the craft process, and deserve to be included in any present or future understanding of design.
Craft exhibitions range from the local to the national and international scenes, and provide a venue for direct sales to the public or purchase prizes from major museums.
The range of media at most craft exhibitions is broad and includes self-taught, amateur, and professional makers.
Categories include, for instance, baskets and handmade fibers, as well as glass, furniture, leather, and ceramics.
Much work is highly individual rather than utilitarian.
Statements by makers occasionally refer to their commitment to keep alive self-sufficient, pre-industrial patterns of life, and using craft to humanize the impersonal character of contemporary existence dominated by standardization and technology.
While theoretical assessments note that craft does not easily approach the critical discourse of contemporary fine art practice (art historian Glenn Adamson calls it crafts inferiority complex), it enriches our appreciation of the meaning of materials, skill, and creativity, and encourages our reflection upon the human condition.
Design, History, and Common Ground Every day we encounter designs power and its effects upon our daily lives.
In 2018 I participated in a relatively small interdisciplinary conference in Philadelphia titled Common Ground. My paper was on a somewhat esoteric subject in the history of type, but throughout the days events and wrap-up I met older and younger scholars from near and far, listening, speaking, asking questions, and sharing knowledge.
Throughout my career I have enjoyed being part of such events, yet less than two years later such gatherings were being held remotely, if at all, in response to the spread of coronavirus.
