Zoom and related remote-conferencing technologies, and the design they entail that facilitates our ability to navigate their platforms and communicate with one another virtually, allowed many of us to function professionally and personally during the health crisis, even to virtually attend conferences, symposia, and webinars that would have otherwise been inaccessible due to travel costs or conflicts in scheduling.
As noted above, design also contributed to our understanding of the virus with published charts and graphs (interactive via the Web) that informed our responses through protection and social distancing.
And yet remote conferencing, like remote travel, hardly substitutes for direct experience, whether personal or cultural, reminding us of how much we take for granted in our daily lives and of the limits of technologies upon which we depend when things do not, or cannot, go as planned.
Crises also increase our awareness of disparities in income and opportunity that limit access and create hierarchies to the acquisition of knowledge.
Designs rich and evolving history, and strength, as well as its challenge, lie in its breadth, its interaction with so many sources of inspiration and expanded areas of practice, disciplinary interdependence, and the importance of the cultural context for its activities.
The difficulty, perhaps, is that with the promise of expansion comes diffusion and the fear of losing the common ground that connects one aspect of design practice to another, in turn making the expanded notion of design difficult to pin down and to instrumentalize toward desirable, and tangible results.
History may provide some understanding and appreciation for such common ground, or at least continuity.
Through technology, designers remain in constant contact with new materials and processes that stimulate ideas for original products or transformations in existing ones.
Through production, designers work with manufacturers, investors, taking into account markets, costs, and sales.
As artists, designers are able to integrate self-expression and experimentation that contribute to the value we place in goods and services.
With consumers in mind, designers increasingly work to incorporate human factors, user-friendly interfaces, and appealing forms for different tastes, along with a wide range of personal meanings and interpretations.
By observing actions as ordinary as peeling an apple or vacuuming a carpet, designers investigate new possibilities and alternatives to what exists.
And since the publication of this books second edition, the historical thread of ethically motivated solutions to shared concerns for safety, sustainability, response to crisis, accessibility, and inclusion, with a long track record of reform efforts motivated by concerns with social justice upon which to build, have been renewed and strengthened, even emboldened through events of the recent past, including climate change, migration, and movements such as #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter.
In todays world, design can be team-based, anonymous, individual, or heroic; ephemeral and self-indulgent, durable, or circular; negligent, hedonistic, or fueled by renewed interest in social and environmental consciousness and commitment.
Throughout this history, with its dynamic range of possibilities, designers remain actively engaged with the world of nature, with technology, and with the man-made environment in all their excitement, complexity, responsibility, and ambiguity.
While the increasing range and variety of the design enterprise can be overwhelming in its scope, its history helps us to provide some continuity with what design has been with what it is, and with what it might be, revealing relationships that offer a sense of assurance or reassurance and a context for ongoing change and shared discourse.
Moreover, design continues to be responsive to all of us who use its myriad and ever-expanding products and services, to all of us whose lives it transforms, hopefully, in the long run, for the better and common good.

## Global
Inspiration VI Revisiting China The history of China during the twentieth century included the end of the imperial Qing dynasty (16441911), the founding of the Republic of China (19121949), and a civil war ending with the establishment of the communist Peoples Republic of China (PRC) in 1949.
The PRC carried out massive state-controlled economic planning under the leadership of Chairman Mao Zedong (18931976) in two stages: the Great Leap Forward (19581962) and the Cultural Revolution (19661976).
Private property was abolished, industries nationalized, and a largely rural population organized collectively into communes under state control.
Improvements in infrastructure under centralized control were offset by massive mismanagement of resources and distribution leading to widespread famine between 1958 and 1961.
The Cultural Revolution saw continued improvements in transportation and infrastructure, the rejection of Western material products and fashion, and the molding of collective values through education, dress, communication, and devotion to Chairman Mao.
In design, the period under Maos leadership is most easily recognized in the standard uniforms worn by party officials and workers, and by heroic propaganda posters promoting individual sacrifice and collective solidarity through work and patriotism.
The poster illustrated in figure GI6.1 is a later (1977) example of this genre.
Its title, Willing to Contribute to the Development of Agriculture, references a Mao-era program that sent urban youth to the countryside to work and gain an appreciation of the rigors of rural life, forcing them to separate from their parents.
The program was officially called the Rustication Movement. Here, a postal worker unloads a small electric motor from the back of a parked motorcycle with the help of its recipient.
They smile as they hold the motor between them and seem to pose to face the viewer.
Millions of posters in this style, similar to Soviet socialist realism, were produced during the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution; while many are anonymous, this example was designed by the artist Zhang Jinghua.
The postal worker wears the standard green uniform while the figures in the countryside are dressed in practical clothing and have modest hairstyles.
Everyone is busy working, modeling clothing and behavior appropriate to an ideal image of satisfying rural living aided by communication with city- and government-sponsored service.
GI6.1 Zhang Jinghua, “Willing to Contribute to the Development of Agriculture,” poster for Zhujiajue Post and Telecommunications Office, Qingpu District, 30 ${ } ^ { 1 } / _ { 1 6 } \times 2 0$ ¾ in (76.5 × 52.5 cm), 1977.
Landsberger Collection, Amsterdam.
Beginning with United States President Richard Nixons official visit in 1972, China ended its isolation from the West and pursued an Open Door policy that permitted foreign investment in manufacturing, private enterprise, and trade.
The period from 1978 (two years after Maos death) to 2000 witnessed massive economic growth, the rise of a middle class, and the integration of China into an increasingly global economy.
Measured in GDP, the Chinese economy expanded seven-fold between 1989 and 2019 and thirty-six-fold between 1978 and 2019; in 2022, China was the second largest economy in the world.
But what does this mean in relation to design history?
Perhaps the most familiar link to design is the outsourcing of labor from other Western industrialized nations to China in the manufacture of consumer goods, creating jobs for Chinese workers and maintaining competitive prices for consumers.
However, there are also downsides: the manufacturing sector has hollowed out in other nations (including most notably the USA), and China and its workforce are now suffering environmental and health and safety consequences.
Furthermore, a lot of these cheap goods are made by the forced labor of Uyghurs and other ethnic minority groups, in a country often criticized for its human rights practices.
Cheap products can come at a very steep price.
A related phenomenon is the extraction of raw materials and manufacture of parts for a wide variety of products from electronic devices to clothing accessories that contribute to supply chains in an increasingly interdependent global economy.
While we might refer to an iPhone as a product of the United States-based Apple Corporation headquartered in Cupertino, California, the phone is made from hundreds of parts, with Chinese companies playing a large part in the complex process of production, although the Foxconn Corporation that performs much of the iPhones assembly is located in Taipei, on the island of Taiwan.
In addition to fashion and fast-food brands (the first McDonalds restaurant opened in mainland China in 1990), IKEA opened its first home goods store in China in 1998, increasing to nine stores by 2012, and 36 in 2021.
With rising per capita incomes and a population of more than 1.4 billion in 2022, Chinese citizens participated in an elastic consumer culture, while private enterprise inside the PRC led to Chinese companies competing domestically and internationally to market their products.
The open door policy was indeed a revolving door, permitting retail businesses to open stores in Chinese cities, and Chinese entrepreneurs to manufacture and sell their own products worldwide.
Fashion and product designers in China today are part of an international contemporary design scene for the luxury market, merging elements of traditional Chinese imagery with experimental materials, or traditional materials such as porcelain or lacquer with an abstract or Postmodern aesthetic.
An example is figure GI6.2, a highly polished stainless steel stool or coffee table designed by Shi Jianmin (b.
1962) whose organic form recalls the rock formations and rock sculptures found in Chinese gardens and public spaces, contrasting here the irregularity of natural materials with the smooth steel finish.
The artist/designer studied in two major cosmopolitan Chinese cities, Xian in Shaanxi province and further to the northeast in Beijing.
GI6.2 Shi Jianmin, stool or coffee table, stainless steel, 59.1 × 55.1 × 20.4 in (150 × 140 × 51.8 cm), 2005.
He Jingtang, Chinese Pavilion, Shanghai World Exhibition, 2010.
One might also consider design in modern China in relation to soft power, the term that describes how design functioned during the Cold War to promote individual and social values on both sides of the Iron Curtain.
Hosting the Summer Olympic Games in Beijing in 2008, the 2010 World Exhibition in Shanghai, and the Winter Olympic Games in 2022 provided the stage for presenting or constructing the image of modern China.
The events drew upon a long and active national tradition of spectacular display and pyrotechnics for visually exciting celebrations.
The summer Olympic Stadium, known popularly as the Birds Nest, was built by a team of Swiss architects, with little if any direct reference to Chinese identity.
The Chinese Pavilion at the 2010 World Exhibition, designed by Chinese architect He Jingtang (b.
1938; the pavilion is now a museum), is an inverted pyramid exemplifying sustainability through natural ventilation, thermal panels, and solar energy (fig.
GI6.3).
Its traditional Chinese deep red color and supporting interlocking bracket construction (known as Dougong) navigate elements of a national identity within a contemporary sustainable global context.
An anonymous exhibition poster from 2000 also exemplifies the results of Chinas opendoor policy: the poster advertises an exhibition of Danish modern design (The Danish Wave +) that toured three of Chinas largest cities (Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Beijing  the average population of the three cities is 20 million) and was sponsored by the Chinese Ministry of Culture, the Royal Danish Embassy in China, and other cultural institutions from both countries.
Chinese and English text appears on either side of the central photomontage image juxtaposing Arne Jacobsens 1951 biomorphic molded plywood three-legged Ant chair with a sixteenth-century Ming dynasty roundback armchair (fig.
GI6.4).
Anonymous, “The Danish Wave +,” poster, offset, 2000.
The material culture of modern China is both a product of and a contributor to the globalization that characterizes the later twentieth and our current twenty-first centuries and that frames the study of design in our time.
Communication and interdependence provide for the exchange of ideas, technologies, and materials that propel innovation and growth.
In some areas of design the results create a degree of homogeneity, for instance in smart phones or laptops, recognized designer clothing and accessory brands encountered in high-end shopping malls, fashion districts, and tourist destinations worldwide.
There are other aspects of the design enterprise that relate to China alone.
For instance, the governments use of artificial intelligence for facial recognition in order to identify and oversee citizens behavior, or the contrast between the use of environmentally responsible building practice for the 2010 China Pavilion in Shanghai and the air pollution and congestion that has choked the city of Beijing intermittently over the past ten years.
With stronger centralized political control and decision making in fewer hands, the future of design activity appears in flux, and it remains to be seen whether industrialization and increased production will stimulate ethical alternatives to the standard equation of progress with growth. # SELECT BIBLIOGRAPHY
